papers.abstract: In this paper, we propose an extremely efficient, training-free method to extract token-level reward signals directly from an existing deep reward model. Our core idea is to attribute the overall process reward to individual tokens by estimating each token's influence. This influence is defined as the change in the final macroscopic reward (e.g., the process reward) when a token is replaced with a semantically null token. Naively calculating this influence is computationally infeasible, requiring N forward passes through the PRM for an N-token sequence. We overcome this bottleneck by proposing a highly efficient gradient-based estimator. Specifically, we use a first-order Taylor approximation, which simplifies the influence calculation to the inner product of the difference between the token embedding and the null token embedding, and the gradient of the reward with respect to the token embedding. This requires only a single forward and backward pass. The resulting token-level rewards enable standard RL algorithms to perform precise credit assignment without requiring additional reward model training. Experiments on challenging reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that our method substantially improves policy optimization efficiency and enhances the generalization of LLM reasoning capabilities. Our P2T outperforms the outcome reward by +4.9% on MathVista for Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct, and +11.5% on AIME24 for Qwen2.5-Math-7B. The code will be released via https://github.com/stonewst/P2T.
authors: Sitong Wu, Haoru Tan, Bin Xia, Xichen Zhang, Jingyao Li, Shaofeng Zhang, Xiaojuan Qi, Bei Yu, Jiaya Jia
bullets: Addresses the inefficiency of assigning a sequence-level process reward to individual tokens, where exact influence estimation would require one model evaluation per token.
Defines each token’s influence by replacing it with a semantically null token and measuring the resulting reward change.
Uses a first-order Taylor approximation to estimate influence from the token–null-token embedding difference and the reward gradient.
The resulting token rewards can be used with standard reinforcement-learning algorithms for credit assignment.
Experiments report improved policy optimization and reasoning generalization, including gains over outcome rewards on MathVista and AIME24.

figures.caption: Figure 1 Overview of Process-to-Token (P2T) reward attribution. P2T converts the process-level rewards provided by a Process Reward Model (PRM) into fine-grained token-level rewards. Specifically, P2T first evaluates the specific influence (attribution score) of each token on the overall process reward, and then normalizes these scores to serve as weights for redistributing the original process reward among the tokens. Consequently, highly influential tokens in a correct step receive the most credit, while the “culprit” tokens responsible for an erroneous step incur the heaviest penalty. Finally, these fine-grained token-level rewards are directly incorporated into standard RL algorithms to enable precise credit assignment.

Figure 3 P2T raises the performance ceiling and improves the training efficiency of outcome-based GRPO. (a, b) Results of further training two models that have already been trained to convergence with outcome-based RL, (a) Vision-R1-7B [14] and (b) DeepScaleR-1.5B-Preview [12], using GRPO+P2T on their original training data (i.e., Vision-R1-10K and DeepScaleR-40K, respectively). (c) AIME25 Pass@1 of Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B during training with GRPO and GRPO+P2T. The dashed line marks the best accuracy reached by GRPO.

papers.title: Unlocking Token Rewards via Training-Free Reward Attribution
papers.tldr: P2T extracts token-level rewards from an existing process reward model in one forward–backward pass, enabling more precise credit assignment without reward-model retraining.

papers.abstract: Evaluating robot policies before deployment typically requires producing new trajectories through real-world execution, simulators, or learned world models. These rollout-based approaches impose infrastructure requirements; simulator and world-model evaluators additionally face prediction errors that can compound over the evaluation horizon. In this paper, we study off-policy evaluation as an alternative to rollout-based robot-policy evaluation methods. Specifically, we introduce RoboFQE, an evaluator that estimates the discounted expected return of a target policy from offline robot trajectories without estimating a behavior-policy density, combining fitted Q-evaluation with a pretrained vision foundation model and learned terminal success annotation to bridge the gap between standard OPE benchmarks and continuous-control visual manipulation. Controlled experiments across simulated and real-world manipulation tasks show that RoboFQE produces accurate discounted-return estimates and preserves policy rankings even on long-horizon manipulation tasks where video world-model evaluators are degraded by autoregressive prediction errors. Ablation experiments show that pretrained vision encoders substantially outperform from-scratch alternatives, particularly on long-horizon tasks, and that learned terminal success annotation enables evaluation without ground-truth reward labels with only slight reduction of accuracy.
authors: Yunfu Deng, Sangwoo Shin, Brahma S. Pavse, Josiah P. Hanna
bullets: Addresses the infrastructure and compounding prediction-error costs of real, simulated, and world-model rollouts.
Combines fitted Q-evaluation, a pretrained vision foundation model, and learned terminal-success annotation.
Works without estimating the behavior-policy density or requiring ground-truth reward labels.
Experiments in simulated and real-world manipulation show accurate discounted-return estimates and preserved policy rankings.
Pretrained vision encoders help most on long-horizon tasks; learned success annotation causes only a slight accuracy reduction.

papers.abstract: World models (WMs) and world-action models (WAMs) focus on future world prediction and executable action generation, respectively. Although these models learn shared physical dynamics and interaction semantics from embodied trajectories, they are typically trained in isolation, which restricts knowledge reuse between prediction and control. The central challenge is therefore to develop a unified learning framework that shares these dynamics while preserving the distinct modeling capabilities required by each paradigm. We propose UniW(A)M, a mixture-of-experts world-(action) model built upon diffusion Transformers that unifies action-conditioned world modeling and diverse WAM variants. Shared experts capture common dynamics, while atomic capability experts are reused across interfaces so that each interface keeps its own conditional pathway. At deployment, a plug-in adaptive interface router (PAIR) learns from a small subset of target-task chunk scenarios to select a suitable WAM interface for each execution chunk, balancing task success and execution efficiency while keeping the backbone frozen. We evaluate UniW(A)M on LIBERO, RoboTwin 2.0, and three real-world manipulation tasks, where it achieves 88.3% average real-world success versus 76.7% for the strongest baseline. On WorldArena, it leads action-conditioned world modeling on all three tasks. AC-WM co-training contributes to action generation on every action interface and PAIR raises OOD success from 63.3% to 76.7%.
authors: Jingbo Xu, Jianjie Fang, Zhuohang Li, Zihao Song, Zhaolu Wang, Xvyuan Liu, Xin Zhang, Haisheng Su, Yinzhou Tang, Chen Gao, Wei Wu, Yong Li
bullets: Addresses isolated training of world models and world-action models, which limits reuse of learned dynamics and interaction semantics.
Uses diffusion Transformers with shared experts for common dynamics and capability-specific experts that preserve each interface’s conditional behavior.
Introduces PAIR, a plug-in router that selects WAM interfaces from a small set of target-task scenarios while keeping the backbone frozen.
Achieves 88.3% average real-world success versus 76.7% for the strongest baseline across three manipulation tasks.
Co-training improves action generation across all tested interfaces, while PAIR increases OOD success from 63.3% to 76.7%.

papers.title: UniW(A)M: A Unified Mixture-of-Experts Framework for World and World-Action Models

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) struggle with metric and multi-view relationships that remain implicit in RGB observations. Geometry foundation models recover this structure from RGB, but existing methods either fuse the estimated features with visual tokens and learn to use them from question answering alone, or align VLM latents with geometry features. Capturing geometry, however, does not ensure its use: zeroing the aligned latents of a released feature-alignment model leaves its accuracy unchanged. We introduce GeoReader, a framework that learns geometric representations for the VLM that reads them. First, we train lightweight Geometric Readers to produce continuous input tokens, supervising them with geometry descriptions decoded by a frozen VLM, so that the Readers express geometry in a form the target model can already read. We then freeze the Readers to preserve this interface while fine-tuning the VLM on spatial QA, with geometry injection conditioned on the question. Geometry descriptions serve only as training targets: at inference, the VLM answers directly from the continuous geometric tokens without generating a geometry chain of thought. With geometry predicted from RGB images, our approach reaches 94.3 on MindCube-Tiny with Qwen3-VL-4B and, with a multi-source QA mixture, an average of 72.5 across six additional spatial benchmarks with Qwen3.5-9B. These results suggest that a useful geometric representation is one the receiving model can use, not merely one from which geometry can be reconstructed.
authors: Rong Li, Shijie Li, Jiangyong Huang, Lingdong Kong, Jiaming Zhou, Dongyue Lu, Zeying Gong, Baoxiong Jia, Junwei Liang, Siyuan Huang
bullets: Targets VLM difficulty with metric and multi-view relationships implicit in RGB observations.
Trains lightweight Geometric Readers to convert geometry into continuous tokens aligned with representations the frozen VLM can interpret.
Fine-tunes the VLM for question-conditioned geometry use while keeping the Readers fixed; no geometry chain-of-thought is needed at inference.
Achieves 94.3 on MindCube-Tiny and averages 72.5 across six additional spatial benchmarks in the reported Qwen-based settings.
Shows that reconstructible geometry features are insufficient unless the receiving VLM actually uses them.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces geometry-aware continuous tokens to improve spatial reasoning in VLMs, fitting spatial intelligence and geometry-aware multimodal modeling.
papers.title: GeoReader: Learning Latent Geometry for Spatial Reasoning in Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: GeoReader teaches vision-language models to directly use learned geometric tokens for stronger spatial reasoning from RGB images.

papers.abstract: Image-token compression must reduce computation without hurting the semantics. We introduce Varest, guided by semantic fungibility: tokens within a coherent semantic region can be summarized coarsely, while object boundaries and literal text require finer distinctions. Object and text localizers guide variable-resolution merging, preserving spatial coverage and finer detail at boundaries and text. Learned [REL] registers then prune visual tokens after early decoder processing. Training across budgets enables one checkpoint per backbone. Across three backbones and 13 benchmarks, Varest outperforms 15 baselines in mean performance retention at every evaluated budget, retaining 86.10-92.33% of full-token performance with only 5.56% of the original layer-averaged image-token count.
authors: Tianhao Fu, Austin Wang, Charles Chen, Roby Aldave-Garza, Victor Xie, Xiyue Jiao, Yucheng Chen, Martin Tin
bullets: Targets lower computation without sacrificing semantic understanding.
Uses semantic, variable-resolution token merging guided by object and text localization.
Preserves spatial coverage and finer distinctions at object boundaries and literal text.
Learned [REL] registers perform additional relevance pruning after early decoder processing.
Across 3 backbones and 13 benchmarks, retains 86.10–92.33% of full-token performance using 5.56% of the original layer-averaged image tokens, outperforming 15 baselines at every evaluated budget.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of Varest. Object boundaries and textness are passed through the Varest tokenizer with post-projector visual tokens, which are then partitioned into Km semantic regions and each region is merged into one image token. At layer L/2, 4 learned [REL] registers (the figure is not to scale) produce a score for each image token and keep the Kp image tokens that are most relevant to LLM reading. Optional adaptive halting removes all remaining image tokens once the information horizon has been detected.

Figure 5. Visualization of tokenization and [REL] pruning across budgets on LLaVA-1.5-7B. For each K, the left panel shows the tokenization (text tokens in orange) and the right panel shows the tokens kept by [REL]. Text remains identifiable at every budget, while semantic granularity becomes finer as K increases.

Figure 6. Benchmark-averaged performance retention versus layer-averaged image-token budget. 100% denotes uncompressedbackbone performance. Varest achieves the highest retention at every evaluated budget across all three backbones, preserving over 85% performance at r = 5.56% on all three VLMs.

Figure 8. Performance retention versus measured computation. Each point averages both axes independently over four budgets; higher and further left is better. Varest achieves higher retention with slightly less computation than HiDrop, the strongest baseline by mean retention. Adaptive halting (AH) further reduces computation with a small retention loss.

Figure 3. Visualized comparison of the baselines and Varest on LLaVA-1.5-7B. HiDrop and LearnPruner retain text but lose contextual information, while CORE’s coarse regions lose text. Varest keeps text cells at native resolution and separates the two people with object boundaries.

Figure 1. Per-benchmark performance of Varest across backbones and token budgets. General VQA benchmarks stay near or above full-token under compression, while text-dense benchmarks benefit most from larger budgets.

Figure 7. [REL] pruning behaviour under different prompts on LLaVA-1.5-7B. Varest keeps nearly the same tokens for two unrelated questions, yet answers both correctly, even when the named object is discarded.

papers.selection_reason: Image-token compression via semantic merging and relevance pruning directly targets token-level efficiency for vision-language models.
papers.title: Just Respect the Semantics: Image-Token Compression via Pre-LLM Semantic Variable-Resolution Tokenization and In-LLM Relevance Pruning
papers.tldr: Varest compresses image tokens by preserving fine detail for objects and text while coarsening redundant regions, then pruning less relevant tokens inside the LLM.

papers.abstract: Reliable robot autonomy requires reasoning about the world from partial and noisy observations. However, many perception systems model only visible scene regions, rely on fixed semantic categories, and assume reliable sensor measurements. These assumptions break under occlusion, novel object encounters, and sensor degradation. In this paper, I present a research vision for incompleteness-aware scene understanding. I organize this vision around three fundamental challenges: incomplete evidence, incomplete knowledge, and incomplete sensor reliability. I discuss my research contributions toward addressing these challenges through amodal perception, semantic occupancy forecasting, open-world scene understanding, label-efficient learning, and uncertainty-guided multi-modal fusion. Building on these contributions, I outline future research directions toward belief-centric 4D scene representations. These representations aim to jointly model geometry, semantics, motion, and uncertainty. I also discuss active sensing and safe adaptation strategies that allow robots to reduce uncertainty through interaction. The goal is to develop calibrated and actionable scene representations that support reliable autonomy in dynamic, open-world environments.
authors: Rohit Mohan
bullets: Identifies three challenges: incomplete observations, incomplete semantic knowledge, and uncertain sensor reliability.
Proposes addressing them with amodal perception, semantic occupancy forecasting, open-world understanding, label-efficient learning, and uncertainty-guided multimodal fusion.
Envisions belief-centric 4D scene representations combining geometry, semantics, motion, and uncertainty.
Highlights active sensing and safe adaptation as ways for robots to reduce uncertainty through interaction.
Focuses on calibrated, actionable representations rather than assuming complete visibility or fixed categories.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Illustrations of incompleteness-aware perception: (A) occlusion, (B) unknowns, and (C) sensor failure.

papers.selection_reason: Incompleteness-aware spatial scene understanding and belief-centric 4D representations for robot autonomy, relevant to embodied AI, spatial intelligence, world models, and 3D vision.
papers.title: Perception Beyond the Visible: Incompleteness-Aware Scene Understanding for Robot Autonomy
papers.tldr: A research vision for robot perception that explicitly models missing evidence, unknown objects, and unreliable sensors to enable safer autonomy in dynamic open-world environments.

papers.abstract: Language model systems repeatedly make test-time decisions by comparing similarity: they retrieve exemplars, rank candidates, and revise responses. Yet similarity is not unique: lexical, semantic, structural, and stylistic resemblance can point to different candidates, and the task-aligned notion can change across instances. We introduce BASIS (Bayesian Axis Selection via Interactive Signals), a training-free Bayesian method that uses weak test-time feedback to infer which criterion in a supplied, task-specific library governs the current decision. It maintains a joint posterior over candidate targets and criteria, updates it from scalar scores, pairwise preferences, or verifier outputs, and selects probes by expected information gain. In a finite noisy model, we characterize when the target-criterion pair is recoverable and show why fixed-criterion and fixed-mixture rules can fail under criterion shift. Across concept recovery, reasoning exemplar selection, and response refinement, BASIS improves six-probe concept-recovery Success@1 from 56.0% to 68.1%, reasoning accuracy from 72.3% to 73.1%, and refinement win rate from 61.4% to 63.8% over tuned static mixtures. It also exceeds compute-matched best-of-N selection on reasoning (72.1%) and refinement (61.2%). Gains are largest under criterion mismatch and with larger candidate pools, and matched controls indicate that adaptive criterion weighting explains much of the benefit, with joint target-criterion inference adding further value. BASIS selects only among supplied criteria and does not discover new ones.
authors: Weida Liang, Kenji Kawaguchi
bullets: Addresses criterion shift: lexical, semantic, structural, or stylistic similarity may be task-dependent.
Maintains a joint posterior over candidate targets and criteria using scalar scores, pairwise preferences, or verifier outputs.
Chooses informative probes via expected information gain without additional training.
Improves concept recovery, reasoning exemplar selection, and response refinement over static mixtures; gains are largest under criterion mismatch.
Scope: selects among supplied criteria and cannot discover new similarity dimensions.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies perform manipulation tasks using camera images and language instructions, but object slip or visual occlusion can disrupt execution. Recovery is typically learned during policy training or delegated to a monitor that triggers a scripted repair after detecting a failure. We introduce ForkCast, a predictive recovery framework that compares counterfactual futures to determine whether and how to intervene in a frozen VLA policy. At each decision point, ForkCast evaluates three candidates: executing the policy's nominal action chunk (Commit), adjusting the camera viewpoint (Reobserve), and replanning the arm trajectory (Replan). A candidate-conditioned world model forecasts the latent outcome of each candidate at a common future horizon, and a shared task-progress head scores the predicted outcomes. By evaluating the policy's own continuation alongside the repair candidates, a single comparison based on task progress determines both whether and how to intervene, without a failure detector, an intervention threshold, or updates to the VLA backbone. On five simulated RoboTwin 2.0 tasks with injected occlusion and object slip, ForkCast increases pooled success from 13.3% for the frozen $\pi_{0.5}$ policy to 30.0% and transfers to two additional VLA backbones without updating ForkCast. After adaptation on real-robot candidate rollouts, ForkCast also improves success over the base policy under both clean and visibility-limited conditions. Code will be released to benefit the research community.
authors: Chenru Wen, Huajian Zeng, Haokai Ding, Jian Kang, Anqing Duan, Dawei Zhou, Dezhen Song, Xingxing Zuo
bullets: Addresses manipulation failures caused by object slip and visual occlusion without retraining the VLA backbone.
Uses a candidate-conditioned world model to forecast common-horizon outcomes for Commit, Reobserve, and Replan.
A shared task-progress head selects whether to intervene and which recovery action to use, without a failure detector or intervention threshold.
On five simulated RoboTwin 2.0 tasks, pooled success increased from 13.3% to 30.0% for the frozen π₀.₅ policy.
Transferred to two additional VLA backbones and improved real-robot success under clean and visibility-limited conditions after candidate-rollout adaptation.

papers.selection_reason: Uses candidate-conditioned latent world models and counterfactual futures to recover VLA policies from failures.
papers.title: ForkCast: Predictive Recovery for Vision-Language-Action Policies via Counterfactual Futures

papers.abstract: The Key-Value (KV) cache constitutes a dominant source of memory consumption during large language model (LLM) inference, particularly in long-context and complex reasoning scenarios. Existing KV cache quantization methods have explored different compression granularities, including layer-wise precision adjustment and token-level information preservation. In practical deployment, however, the key challenge is not merely compression, but how to allocate limited quantization resources among heterogeneous precision preservation strategies under a fixed KV cache memory budget. We propose MultiAlloc, a profiling-guided precision allocation framework for KV cache quantization that adaptively distributes limited quantization resources between layer-wise precision enhancement and token-wise preservation. MultiAlloc employs lightweight offline profiling to characterize layer sensitivity and token importance, enabling adaptive precision allocation under a fixed memory constraint. Guided by the profiled memory--accuracy trade-off, it automatically derives an effective precision allocation strategy without online allocation search, and applies the resulting policy during inference. Extensive experiments on reasoning and long-context benchmarks demonstrate that MultiAlloc consistently improves over layer-wise, token-wise, and recent multi-granularity KV cache quantization methods under matched memory budgets across diverse models, including Mistral, Llama, DeepSeek-Qwen, and QwQ.
authors: Yangchengyu Zhou, Zhiping Wu, Runchang Jiang, Dongdong Ren, Youfang Han, Wei Zhao, Dongqi Cai, Wenbin Li
bullets: Targets KV-cache memory bottlenecks in long-context and reasoning-focused LLM inference.
Profiles layer sensitivity and token importance to guide adaptive precision allocation.
Balances layer-wise precision enhancement with token-wise preservation under a fixed budget.
Derives the allocation policy offline, avoiding online allocation search.
Shows consistent gains over existing single- and multi-granularity methods across diverse models and benchmarks at matched memory budgets.

Existing layer-wise and token-wise methods optimize individual preservation strategies, while MultiAlloc profiles these demands and allocates the shared memory budget across preservation strategies.

papers.title: MultiAlloc: Budget-Aware Precision Allocation for KV Cache Quantization
papers.tldr: MultiAlloc improves KV-cache quantization by allocating a fixed memory budget between layer- and token-level precision preservation using offline profiling.

papers.abstract: Combining pretrained models is a common strategy for building AI systems, whether by aligning a vision encoder with a language model or merging fine-tuned checkpoints. However, finding compatible pairs typically requires costly empirical search, as compatibility is known only after alignment or merging. We propose COMPASS (COMPatibility ASsessment Score), a theoretically motivated diagnostic that estimates whether a model pair will be compatible prior to alignment or merging. Building on the observation that representational convergence is most robust at the level of local neighborhoods, COMPASS decomposes model compatibility into two cheap-to-compute axes: a pair-specific ease, defined as the $k$-NN overlap between the two encoders, and a paradigm-level ceiling, capturing the maximum overlap their training paradigms allow. Together, these two axes provide a ranking of candidate model pairs and prescribe how to act on each pair: (i) prioritize pairs that already agree and whose paradigms are compatible, (ii) invest additional compute on pairs with compatible paradigms but low initial agreement, (iii) switch the pretraining paradigm when it cannot support sufficient agreement, or (iv) deprioritize pairs that score poorly on both axes. We apply COMPASS to $72$ cross-modal alignment experiments and $392$ task-arithmetic model merges and show that compatibility estimates by COMPASS strongly correlate with downstream success, achieving average Pearson correlation of $0.91$ on cross-modal alignment tasks and $0.70$ on model merging.
authors: Fabian Gr\"oger, Petar Damjanovi\'c, Maria Brbi\'c
bullets: Addresses the costly trial-and-error needed to identify compatible model pairs.
Measures compatibility using two axes: pair-specific k-NN overlap and a training-paradigm compatibility ceiling.
Ranks candidate pairs and recommends whether to proceed, spend more compute, change the paradigm, or deprioritize the pair.
Across 72 cross-modal alignment experiments and 392 model merges, COMPASS correlated strongly with downstream success.
Reported average Pearson correlations were 0.91 for alignment and 0.70 for merging.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Theorem 4.1 across four settings, each showing a start-condition score against the corresponding endpoint. Top: unimodal validation. Initial random k-NN overlap predicts final pretrained overlap across n = 21 vision family pairs (left; r = 0.69, p < 10−4) and n = 42 text family pairs (right; r = 0.91, p < 10−17). Bottom left: cross-modal alignment. Pretrained k-NN overlap predicts Flickr30k I2T R@1 after alignment (r = 0.84, p < 10−20) across n = 72 vision-language pairs. Bottom right: model merging via task arithmetic. k-NN overlap between fine-tuned checkpoints predicts merge quality (r = 0.67, p < 10−52) across n = 392 model merges. Color encodes the vision/text family throughout. In the top panels (unimodal) and bottom-left (cross-modal alignment), marker shape encodes the other family of the pair (text family in the cross-modal case). The bottom-right merging panel uses a single shape, since each point has a single base-model family. Initialization structure that underlies the unimodal panels is reported in Appendix H.1. The same qualitative pattern holds at k ∈ {20, 50, 100} (Appendix H.2).

Figure 1: Given a library of candidate encoders, the compatibility of a model pair is typically unknown before running the downstream transfer. Using COMPASS, we estimate the compatibility based on local neighborhood agreement: for each probe sample, we compare its local k-NN overlap across the two representation spaces. Aggregating this local overlap across different axes gives two scores computed before alignment or merging. Ease is a pair-specific score that measures how close the selected pair is at the start of the relevant dynamics: before encoder training in cross-modal alignment, and before weight merging in task arithmetic. Ceiling is a paradigm-level score that estimates how much agreement the corresponding training paradigms can support on average. Candidate pairs are ranked by combining ease and ceiling. Each axis is thresholded at its median value: green compatibility scores are above the corresponding median while the red ones are below it. The resulting high/low pattern assigns each pair to one of four regimes: act now (high ease, high ceiling), budget-limited (low ease, high ceiling), ceiling-limited (high ease, low ceiling), or incompatible (low ease, low ceiling).

papers.selection_reason: Proposes COMPASS, a diagnostic tool to assess model compatibility for alignment/merging based on representational convergence (k-NN overlap), a spatial/structural metric.
papers.title: To Align or Not To Align: Check Your COMPASS Before You Train
papers.tldr: COMPASS cheaply predicts whether pretrained model pairs will align or merge successfully before expensive training or merging.

papers.abstract: A robot's world model must remember objects that leave the camera's view. FloWM, a learned world model, keeps them in a spatial grid of features that it moves with five built-in velocities. A node memory instead keeps each object's position and velocity as numbers. We compare them in FloWM's own block world, with an oracle-fed Kalman tracker as the node memory. How the grid is read changes its score: a single-cell probe finds 66% of out-of-view blocks, while FloWM's own probe 89%. FloWM also scores 8 points higher in view although no frame is shown, which we attribute to its write-back of its own predictions. Out of view, the tracker reaches FloWM's range in 14KB against 5.6MB, with no probe. On diagonal motion, outside its five velocities, FloWM finds 11% of blocks even after fine-tuning, while the unchanged tracker keeps 93%. Faster blocks defeat both until one more allowed speed takes the tracker to 94%, where FloWM's built-in shifts would need 25 copies of its grid. A learned node memory must still replace the oracles and handle velocity under noise, long gaps, and the bounce.
authors: Justin McMillen, Yasin Yilmaz
bullets: FloWM stores object information in a spatial feature grid with five built-in velocities; the comparison uses an oracle-fed Kalman tracker as node memory.
Probe design strongly affects FloWM’s apparent recall: single-cell probing finds 66% of hidden blocks versus 89% with FloWM’s own probe.
Without camera frames, FloWM scores 8 points higher in view, attributed to writing back its predictions.
Out of view, the tracker matches FloWM’s range using 14KB versus 5.6MB and handles diagonal motion at 93% recall versus FloWM’s 11%.
Both struggle with faster motion; the tracker reaches 94% when given one additional allowed speed, while FloWM would require 25 grid copies.

papers.selection_reason: Studies object memory in learned robot world models under partial observability, directly relevant to embodied memory and world models.
papers.title: Grid or Nodes? Probing Object Memory in World Models Under Partial Observability
papers.tldr: In FloWM’s block-world tests, a compact oracle-fed node memory matches or exceeds grid-based object recall while using far less memory and handling unseen motion better, though it is not yet fully learned.

papers.abstract: The development of a digital twin brings together many stakeholders and technical components. We have previously investigated the reporting of the conceptual architecture for these digital twins as an artifact for discussion. However, we find that the activity of modeling the digital twin for visualization and consensus-building can be quite tedious and time-consuming. In this article, we explore the automation of model generation using large language models, targeting the model required for digital twin reporting. Our approach is designed to ingest digital twin documents and output both the conceptual architecture visualization and a reporting page for that digital twin. We first extract from the input the key details aligning with our twenty-one-characteristic Digital Twin Description Framework described in previous work. Then, we generate a description model in the Ontological Modeling Language, representing the digital twin as a constellation of models, data, enablers, and services. We utilize refinement loops with large language models acting as judges and ontological reasoning to increase artifact quality as measured by our metrics. We investigate how architectural and parameter choices affect artifact quality, such as how refinement loops enable local large language models to produce sufficiently high-quality results comparable to larger models. We also detail insights and lessons learned useful for practitioners, such that they can integrate our techniques to accelerate their digital twin reporting or for other model generation tasks. These insights include the use of medium-sized local models (around 20 billion parameters), the avoidance of large language models as judges and clustering for characteristic extraction, and the recommendation of at least two reasoner loops for Ontological Modeling Language refinement.
authors: K\'erian Fiter, Angelica Portocarrero, Bentley Oakes
bullets: Addresses the tedious, time-consuming manual modeling of digital twins for visualization and stakeholder consensus.
Extracts information from digital twin documents using a 21-characteristic Digital Twin Description Framework.
Generates an Ontological Modeling Language model representing models, data, enablers, and services, plus visualization and reporting outputs.
Uses LLM-based refinement loops and ontological reasoning to improve artifact quality.
Reports practical guidance: medium-sized local models can achieve sufficiently high quality, with at least two refinement loops recommended.

papers.abstract: Recent studies investigate the weight geometry through its spectral structure, which characterizes how the weights transform different input directions. Within this view, supervised fine-tuning (SFT) is shown to induce dense updates that perturb the spectral geometry of pre-SFT weights along their principal directions, potentially disrupting the model's prior knowledge. These observations motivate using the geometry of pre-SFT weights as a reference for refining learned SFT updates. We study this perspective as Geometric Calibration and develop SPACE Subspace Projection for Adapted Checkpoint Enhancement), a lightweight post-hoc method that selectively reverts SFT update components within the principal subspace of the pre-SFT weights while preserving those in its orthogonal complement. SPACE is a data-free, training-free method that requires only the pre- and post-SFT checkpoints. We evaluate SPACE on Qwen2.5, Qwen3, Qwen3.5, Llama-3.1, and Olmo-3 models ranging from 2B to 14B, across mathematical, coding, and medical SFT, as well as several SFT variants. Overall, SPACE mitigates out-of-domain (OOD) capability regression while further improving in-domain (ID) performance over the uncalibrated SFT checkpoints. For math SFT, SPACE yields average ID/OOD gains of 2.85/2.26 points on Qwen2.5-7B, and 2.41/1.52 points on Qwen3-14B-Base, respectively. These results highlight how the geometric relationship between SFT updates and pre-SFT weights shapes the adapted model's capabilities and, more broadly, motivate geometry-aware parameter updates for continual model improvement.
authors: Jianzhu Bao, Jia-Chen Gu, Qingyuan Liu, Haozhen Zhang, Kai-Wei Chang, Nanyun Peng, Wenya Wang
bullets: SFT can disrupt prior knowledge by perturbing the spectral geometry of pre-SFT weights along principal directions.
SPACE selectively reverts update components in the pre-SFT principal subspace while preserving updates in the orthogonal complement.
It is a lightweight, data-free, training-free post-hoc method requiring only pre- and post-SFT checkpoints.
Across Qwen, Llama, and Olmo models from 2B–14B and math, coding, and medical tasks, SPACE improves in-domain performance and mitigates out-of-domain degradation.
The approach is evaluated across multiple SFT variants; its scope is limited to checkpoint-based geometric calibration after SFT.

Blue and green denote preand post-SFT components, respectively, with color intensity reflecting the corresponding pre-SFT singular value. SPACE restores the pre-SFT transformation along the selected principal directions while retaining the post-SFT transformation along the remaining directions. (b) Results. After regular SFT on mathematical data, SPACE improves both in-domain (ID) and out-of-domain (OOD) performance over the uncalibrated SFT checkpoints.

papers.abstract: Relying on manipulable characteristics to target the allocation of resources is fraught with difficulties. Naively optimal rules lead to falsification and allocative inefficiency. Optimizing the rule for allocative efficiency while accounting for falsification typically induces falsification, at a heavy cost to the agents. Moreover, falsification generates negative externalities. We characterize optimal falsification-proof rules under a broad range of falsification technologies. We also provide an honesty condition under which they solve the unconstrained problem of a planner who maximizes a weighted sum of allocative surplus and agents' welfare.
authors: Eduardo Perez-Richet, Vasiliki Skreta
bullets: Naively targeting resources using manipulable characteristics can cause falsification and inefficient allocation.
Optimizing only for efficiency may still induce costly falsification and impose negative externalities.
The authors characterize optimal falsification-proof mechanisms across a broad class of falsification technologies.
An honesty condition ensures these mechanisms also solve the planner’s unconstrained weighted-surplus-and-welfare problem.

papers.abstract: An embodied agent must prioritise among competing bodily needs. In active inference, it can respond to an urgent need by increasing the precision of information about that need or by increasing its preference for outcomes that relieve it. We compare these two interventions, separately and together, in a foraging gridworld with three lethal needs, and ask how each changes survival, perception and the body model the agent learns. Precision sharpens interoceptive posteriors and improves survival. Preference reweighting keeps bodily states further from their lethal boundaries and changes the states from which the agent learns, so its learned model covers fewer need levels, with lower quality across all levels but slightly higher quality on the levels it visits. An experiment on 72 further layouts does not establish the predicted preference benefit on difficult layouts, but both interventions improve average survival there and their interaction is positive. Survival alone therefore gives an incomplete account of how a model prioritises needs and learns about its body.
authors: St John Grimbly, Nicolas Kuske, Evert A. Boonstra, Charel van Hoof, Rowan Hodson, Benjamin Rosman, Ryan Smith, Mark Solms, Jonathan P. Shock
bullets: Precision increases the reliability of interoceptive information, sharpening posteriors and improving survival.
Preference reweighting prioritises need-relieving outcomes, keeping bodily states farther from lethal boundaries.
Preference reweighting changes which bodily states are experienced and learned, narrowing model coverage while slightly improving accuracy in visited states.
Across 72 additional layouts, both interventions improved average survival and interacted positively, but the predicted preference benefit on difficult layouts was not established.
Survival alone does not fully reveal how an agent prioritises needs or learns its body model.

papers.selection_reason: Explores interoceptive prioritization in an embodied agent using active inference, comparing precision and preference reweighting to learn body models and survival strategies.
papers.title: Two Routes to Interoceptive Prioritisation: Dissociating Likelihood Precision and Preference Reweighting in Active Inference
papers.tldr: Precision and preference reweighting are distinct routes to prioritising bodily needs, producing different effects on survival, perception, and learned body models.

papers.abstract: Searching text-rich knowledge graphs requires following relations while examining textual evidence. Predefined graph interfaces constrain what evidence agents can access, even when they write code to combine tool calls or process retrieved subgraphs. We propose direct knowledge graph interaction (DKGI), a harness in which language model agents create graph access tools directly over complete node and edge files. The agent writes Python code to follow relations, combine node sets, and select textual evidence, interleaving execution with shell search and file inspection. This lets agents process large node sets in bulk while returning selected text for the model to assess. Execution feedback guides tool creation and revision, while the evolving tools determine what evidence the agent gathers next. On benchmark datasets spanning three domains, training-free DKGI exceeds the strongest published baseline by at least 6.7 Hit@1 points on every graph, even with a minimal harness. Controlled ablations show the benefits of multi-turn programming over shell-only access and predefined graph tools, while trajectories show agents revising code to extend searches or address errors. These findings highlight the value of allowing tool creation and tool use to co-evolve during graph search. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/leopoldwhite/DKGI.
authors: Yuyang Bai, Yu Wang, Yu Zhang
bullets: Predefined graph interfaces limit the evidence agents can access when searching relational, text-rich knowledge graphs.
DKGI gives agents direct access to complete node and edge files, enabling Python-based relation following, bulk processing, and selective evidence retrieval.
Agents interleave code execution, shell search, and file inspection; feedback drives tool revision and changes subsequent evidence gathering.
Across three-domain benchmarks, training-free DKGI improves Hit@1 by at least 6.7 points over the strongest published baseline on every graph.
Ablations support multi-turn programming over shell-only access and predefined graph tools; the approach is evaluated with a minimal harness.

papers.abstract: Visual agents must turn video observations into timely decisions to track progress and choose what to do next. Building on the emerging System One paradigm, we introduce VideoJev, a family of models that cast video understanding and interaction as structured decision tasks. We adapt pretrained multimodal large language models (MLLMs) by replacing autoregressive answer decoding with a shared head that scores temporal intervals and textual options against video evidence. These scores yield event spans or answer choices, unifying temporal grounding and multiple-choice video question answering. This combines the semantic flexibility of MLLMs with efficient decisions that agents can use directly. As an interaction unfolds, new goals and intermediate results prompt further queries about the same visual history. VideoJev therefore reuses visual computation through Cached inference for queries as they arrive and Joint inference for multiple queries in a single forward pass. Across three temporal grounding benchmarks, VideoJev-4B and VideoJev-35B-A3B improve mean mIoU over their backbones by 6.7 and 10.8 points, respectively, with measured inference speedups of $2.8$-$3.1\times$. On four video QA benchmarks, both achieve performance comparable to their backbones in Thinking mode, with measured inference speedups exceeding $100\times$. These results offer a unified, reusable decision interface for composing structured visual judgments into complex, open-ended workflows.
authors: Yuhan Zhu, Xiangyu Zeng, Qingyi Si, Chenxu Yang, Yifei Li, Luozheng Qin, Junhao Zhou, Dingyu Yao, Jun Zhang, Chuanyu Qin, Zhiqiu Zhang, Yuandong Yang, Yuqi Xu, Tianyu Zhang, Hongcheng Guo, Jiaqi Wang, Nan Duan, Limin Wang
bullets: Frames video understanding and interaction as structured decisions over temporal intervals or textual answer choices.
Adapts pretrained multimodal language models with a shared scoring head instead of autoregressive answer generation.
Supports cached inference for sequential queries and joint inference for multiple queries over the same video history.
Improves temporal-grounding mean mIoU over backbones by 6.7 and 10.8 points, with 2.8–3.1× inference speedups.
Matches backbone performance on four video-QA benchmarks in Thinking mode while exceeding 100× inference speedups.

papers.abstract: Self-distillation is an emerging approach that trains a model to imitate its own predictions when conditioned on privileged information, such as correct answers or environmental feedback. Recent methods have reported better sample efficiency and generalization than reinforcement learning (RL), but it remains unclear whether these gains extend beyond in-distribution evaluations and whether they stem from privileged distillation. In this paper, we revisit two representative methods, Self-Distillation Policy Optimization (SDPO) and On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD), across code, science, tool use, and math reasoning tasks. We find that their reported gains do not consistently generalize to unseen problems and are largely explained by overfitting or transferring existing reasoning behavior, rather than effectively using privileged information. Moreover, self-distillation gradients show weak alignment with policy gradients that directly optimize expected reward, questioning whether they provide an effective direction for policy improvement. Our experiments across Qwen3 models (1.7B-14B) and OLMo-3-7B suggest that effectively leveraging privileged information to improve reasoning remains an open challenge. Our code is available at https://github.com/sleepypandu/does-sd-improve-reasoning
authors: Jason Ken Adhinarta, Raina Wu, Ashutosh Sharma, Avinash Balakrishnan, Rameswar Panda, Polina Golland, Yoon Kim, Zhang-Wei Hong

Concludes that effectively using privileged information for reasoning remains unresolved.

papers.abstract: System One models such as Jev change how software makes decisions by mapping open-ended semantic contexts into structured judgments that directly drive program execution. However, this paradigm introduces a new security risk, which we term Jev Program Decision Hijacking (JPDH): attacker-controlled contexts can redirect program decisions through schema-valid Jev judgments. Existing evaluations focus primarily on model-level attacks or predefined injection channels, leaving attack reachability and downstream security consequences in real-world Jev applications underexplored. In this paper, we present JevProbe, the first automated framework to evaluate JPDH by tracing adversarial influence from reachable context surfaces through program-consumed decisions to downstream security consequences in real-world Jev applications. Our key insight is that application logic maps diverse Jev judgments to observable decisions, enabling systematic, program-grounded attack evaluation. Across 228 popular real-world Jev applications and 2,273 test cases, 81.5% exhibit decision flips, of which 98.6% lead to potential downstream security impacts. Compared with the strongest adapted baseline, JevProbe improves macro-average Decision Flip Rate (DFR) by 50.4 percentage points, while existing defenses offer limited protection. We further construct JevProbeBench to support systematic evaluation of JPDH in real-world Jev applications. We have responsibly disclosed our findings to Jev application maintainers, pending their responses. The source code of JevProbe and the JevProbeBench dataset are publicly available on GitHub (https://github.com/xiaoxiaohg8d/JevProbe-).
authors: Yang Luo, Tiantian Ji, Zifeng Kang, Yucheng Wang, Yong Liu, Zhiyi Yin, Xinran Liu

Outperforms the strongest adapted baseline by 50.4 percentage points in macro-average Decision Flip Rate; existing defenses provide limited protection.

papers.abstract: Dialogue and collaborative assistants repeatedly judge what a partner knows, believes, or intends. Typed decision models offer a potential alternative to generative large language models for bounded Theory of Mind (ToM) selection. We present Jev-ToM, comparing five typed decision models and seven generative baselines on 11,117 English text questions from nine ToM benchmarks across six capability groups. TypeSafe Jev reaches 73.2% source-balanced accuracy including native controls and ranks first or second across all six capabilities, leading beliefs, goals/desires/intentions, and emotions. Other typed models show distinct strengths across tasks. Separate resource comparisons suggest that Jev could reduce the cost and waiting time of repeated ToM selection. Confidence-based selection remains benchmark-dependent, and supplied reasons can repair errors or overturn correct answers depending on their attachment. Candidate expansion reveals distinct selection and output-validity problems. Related-question cues account for most of Jev's downstream gains, with task-dependent effects from predicted states. The findings motivate testing Jev as a ToM selection component in assistants, with task-specific confidence calibration, candidate design, and output validation as integration priorities.

papers.abstract: Large language models increasingly tackle tasks that require multi-step reasoning, where errors in intermediate claims can affect the final answer. Self-consistency (SC) improves reasoning by voting over sampled final answers, but its vote leaves intermediate disagreements unresolved. To address this problem, we introduce DDRG (Disagreement-Driven Verification Guided by Reasoning Graphs), a framework for selective correction from a frozen bank of reasoning traces. Our insight is that graph alignment can expose claim-level disagreements and provide correction evidence without expanding the sampled trace bank. DDRG builds source-grounded claim graphs and sends localized conflicts to an answer-blind verifier. A verifier-supported refutation that reaches the majority answer's supporting path triggers one focused repair; otherwise, DDRG returns the exact SC vote. Experimental results across five benchmarks show that native zero-shot DDRG improves macro-average accuracy over direct answering by 8.65 and 15.83 percentage points for Qwen2.5-7B and Llama3.1-8B. It also exceeds CoT, the evaluated GoT and GoV question-answering adaptations, and SC on this macro metric. DDRG links local verification to selective correction without enlarging the initial candidate bank.
authors: Haotian Liu, Yingjian Chen, Xiaohang Xu, Lang Huang, Yusuke Iwasawa, Yutaka Matsuo, Irene Li
bullets: Targets unresolved intermediate errors that final-answer voting in self-consistency cannot correct.
Builds source-grounded claim graphs and sends localized conflicts to an answer-blind verifier.
Applies one focused repair only when verifier-supported refutation connects to the majority answer’s supporting path; otherwise preserves the SC vote.
Across five benchmarks, zero-shot DDRG improves macro-average accuracy over direct answering by 8.65 points for Qwen2.5-7B and 15.83 points for Llama3.1-8B.
Outperforms the evaluated CoT, GoT, GoV, and self-consistency baselines without expanding the initial trace bank.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training improves robot foundation models (RFMs) beyond their demonstrations, but real-world deployment demands more: learning new tasks efficiently while retaining previously acquired behaviors. Existing continual RL methods on top of VLAs mitigate forgetting but rely on on-policy updates with limited forward transfer, whereas off-policy methods improve single-task sample efficiency without addressing learner persistence across tasks. We propose ACCRUE, a continual off-policy RL framework that carries lightweight actor and critic networks across tasks, allowing each stage to reuse behavioral and value knowledge acquired through prior RL. The inherited critic adapts only on current-task transitions and guides current-task actor learning, while prior behavior is preserved by distilling the actor toward cached targets on a small number of retained episodes. Fixed visual features keep the inherited learner and its replay compatible with base-policy updates. Across contact-rich assembly sequences in simulation and on real-robot hardware, ACCRUE accelerates subsequent-task learning with near-zero forgetting and significantly reduces real-robot training time by 31.0\% to 68.5\%.
authors: Changyeon Kim, Kimin Lee, Yashraj Narang, Yijie Guo
bullets: Addresses the need for task-efficient adaptation without catastrophic forgetting during real-world robot deployment.
Carries lightweight actor and critic networks across tasks to reuse behavioral and value knowledge.
Adapts the critic using current-task transitions and preserves prior behavior by distilling the actor on a small set of retained episodes.
Uses fixed visual features to maintain compatibility between inherited learners and replay data during base-policy updates.
Across simulated and real contact-rich assembly tasks, it achieves near-zero forgetting and reduces real-robot training time by 31.0%–68.5%.

papers.abstract: Multimodal Emotion Recognition (MER) aims to understand human emotions by integrating information from multiple modalities such as speech and text. Psychological studies suggest that emotions exhibit latent hierarchical structured relationships in their semantic representations. However, most MER approaches rely on Euclidean representations, which capture fine-grained cross-modal interactions but do not explicitly provide a geometric prior for organizing hierarchical emotional structures. To mitigate this gap, we propose GeoMER, a joint Euclidean-Hyperbolic modeling framework that introduces hyperbolic emotion-core routing to capture higher-level, abstract emotional representations for MER. The proposed framework jointly models token-level cross-modal semantic interactions and latent emotion representations in two complementary geometric spaces. Specifically, GeoMER consists of a Euclidean Multimodal Fusion Module (EuclFusion) for multimodal representation fusion and a Hyperbolic Geometric Core Routing (HypGeoRoute) module that performs geometry-aware core assignment and aggregation in a hyperbolic manifold to capture more abstract feature representations. The HypGeoRoute module complements the Euclidean token-level modeling. We experiment on the IEMOCAP multimodal MER benchmark and demonstrate that the proposed method achieves the best performance, with 83.54% weighted accuracy and 83.35% unweighted accuracy, outperforming Euclidean baselines, including MemoCMT.
authors: Ting Zhu, Huizhi Liang, Boguslaw Obara, Shufei Duan, Varun Ojha
bullets: Targets the lack of explicit geometric structure in predominantly Euclidean multimodal emotion recognition methods.
Uses EuclFusion for token-level cross-modal semantic fusion and HypGeoRoute for geometry-aware emotion representation routing in hyperbolic space.
Evaluated on the IEMOCAP benchmark, achieving 83.54% weighted accuracy and 83.35% unweighted accuracy.
Reports the best performance among evaluated methods, outperforming Euclidean baselines including MemoCMT.

The resulting hyperbolic representations are mapped back to Euclidean space and concatenated with Euclidean features for the final emotion classification.

papers.abstract: Sampling-based test-time scaling enhances LLM reasoning by aggregating multiple reasoning paths for the same query. Existing methods use answer frequencies or path confidence to compute candidate scores, which do not explicitly characterize comparisons between competing answers. Inspired by the Condorcet principle in social choice theory, we introduce pairwise confidence comparisons between paths supporting different answers to capture answer-level comparative advantage. We combine this comparative evidence with voting support through a KL-regularized objective. Theoretically, we show that this comparative-advantage is equivalent to the adjustment to the traditional voting logits. In this way, our proposed Pairwise-Guided Logit Adjustment (PGLA) framework allows comparative evidence to compensate for weaker voting support and correct voting-based ranking errors. Experiments on 10 challenging benchmarks including mathematical reasoning, knowledge reasoning, and code generation with 7 models ranging from 1.7B to 32B parameters speak to the effectiveness of this plug-and-play term. Additional evaluations with external reward scores and online sampling further demonstrate its applicability.
authors: Cong Hua, Qianqian Xu, Zitai Wang, Zhiyong Yang, Shilong Bao, Linchao Zhang, Qingming Huang
bullets: Existing methods rank candidate answers mainly by frequency or path confidence, missing direct comparisons between alternatives.
PGLA adds pairwise confidence evidence for paths supporting different answers, inspired by the Condorcet principle.
A KL-regularized objective combines comparative evidence with voting support and yields an equivalent logit adjustment.
The framework is evaluated across 10 reasoning and code-generation benchmarks with 7 models, plus external-reward and online-sampling settings.
The method is presented as a plug-and-play way to compensate for weaker vote counts and correct ranking errors.

papers.abstract: Automated post-training transforms pre-trained large language models (LLMs) into models capable of handling diverse domains by automatically constructing and optimizing a recipe of coupled decisions over data sources, data processing, cross-domain composition, and training configuration under a limited experimental budget. Existing automation either searches predefined recipe spaces that enable systematic optimization but remain fixed rather than adapting their available choices to the target tasks, or uses open-ended agents that discover task-specific choices but leave them implicit in trial-level edits, limiting their systematic reuse and recombination across trials. To fill this gap, we introduce optimization over a task-adapted recipe space, a novel paradigm that can adapt the recipe space itself to the target tasks while representing its choices explicitly for systematic reuse, recombination, and joint optimization. We instantiate this paradigm with Structured Recipe Optimization (SRO), comprising an LLM-based Recipe-Space Designer that constructs the task-adapted recipe space and a Multi-Domain Recipe Optimizer that uses structured trial evidence to guide LLM candidate construction and multi-objective Bayesian trial selection. Extensive experiments show that SRO achieves the highest average score in all evaluated target-model and agent-LLM combinations. In joint post-training across three capability domains and six benchmarks, SRO reaches 41.1 versus 15.4 for the strongest baseline on Qwen3-1.7B with GPT-5.4, and 53.8 versus 40.8 on Qwen3-4B with DeepSeek-V4-Flash. Our code is available at https://github.com/RuohLiuq/SRO.
authors: Ruohong Liu, Bohan Tang, Lekang Jiang, Jack Umenberger, Yiwen Guo
bullets: Addresses the rigidity of predefined recipe spaces and the implicit, hard-to-reuse edits of open-ended agents.
Introduces task-adapted recipe-space optimization, with explicit choices that support reuse, recombination, and joint optimization.
Uses an LLM-based Recipe-Space Designer and a Multi-Domain Recipe Optimizer guided by structured trial evidence and multi-objective Bayesian selection.
Reports the highest average score across all evaluated target-model and agent-LLM combinations.
In joint post-training across three domains and six benchmarks, scores 41.1 vs. 15.4 and 53.8 vs. 40.8 for the strongest baselines in two evaluated settings.

papers.title: LLM Agents for Automated Post-Training via Structured Recipe Optimization
papers.tldr: Structured Recipe Optimization (SRO) lets LLM agents adapt and systematically optimize post-training recipes for target tasks, achieving the best reported average scores across evaluated settings.

papers.abstract: Different MRI modalities reveal different parts of a brain tumor. Segmentation models combine information from these modalities to outline tumor regions. Many models use a separate encoder for each modality. However, exchanging features among these encoders at several stages can increase model complexity. We introduce the Block-Wise Shared Adapter (BWSA), which combines compressed features from the modality encoders in a shared path and returns adapted features to each stream. In its fixed-blending form, BWSA adds the adapted features to the original features. Its trainable-gated variant (TG-BWSA) instead learns separate weights for the original and adapted features at each modality and encoder stage. We evaluate both variants on BraTS 2020 and BraTS 2023 with four segmentation backbones. On the official BraTS 2023 online validation set, BWSA increases average region-wise Dice by 1.3--7.6 percentage points relative to the corresponding unmodified backbones. TG-BWSA increases it by 2.8--7.7 points. Both variants add approximately 0.85--3.73% parameters and reduce average HD95 relative to the unmodified backbones.
authors: Milad Rostamian, Mohammadreza Mohammadi, Ender Konukoglu, Mohsen Soryani
bullets: Separate modality encoders can become complex when exchanging features across multiple stages.
BWSA compresses and combines encoder features in a shared path, then returns adapted features to each modality stream.
TG-BWSA learns stage- and modality-specific gates to balance original and adapted features.
Across four backbones on BraTS 2020/2023, both variants improve segmentation; TG-BWSA yields larger reported Dice gains on the BraTS 2023 validation set.
The adapters add approximately 0.85–3.73% parameters and reduce average HD95 versus unmodified backbones.

papers.abstract: Latent planners often rank candidate action sequences by terminal Euclidean distance to a goal latent. Exact agreement with transition distance would make this score ideal, but is stronger than planning requires: along a transition-shortest rollout, the essential requirement is that latent distance does not reverse true transition progress. We show that this pathwise no-reversal requirement is precisely the classical self-approaching condition. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to identify self-approachingness as a planner-facing compatibility condition for terminal Euclidean latent planning and to connect its violation to an exact finite-horizon candidate-order reversal. Because visual world models predict discrete latent sequences, we analyze their polygonal interpolation. We prove that an acute bend creates a nonempty region in which terminal Euclidean distance ranks a transition-worse candidate ahead of one that makes genuine progress, even under exact rollouts. We further interpret latent dimension as angular capacity through a classical spherical-code bound. A controlled six-branch experiment, including a zero-padded three-dimensional baseline, validates the predicted ordering failure and separates angular arrangement from ambient dimensionality.
authors: Junlin Wu, Wen Fan, Dandan Zhang
bullets: Frames pathwise no-reversal of latent distance as the classical self-approaching condition.
Proves that acute bends can cause terminal Euclidean scoring to prefer a worse candidate over a genuinely progressing one, even with exact rollouts.
Analyzes discrete world-model predictions through polygonal interpolation.
Relates latent dimensionality to angular capacity via a spherical-code bound.
A controlled six-branch experiment, including a zero-padded 3D baseline, validates ordering failures and distinguishes angular arrangement from ambient dimension.

(c) A three-dimensional cross-polytope embedding with directions {±e1,±e2,±e3}, in which all branch pairs are non-acute. The comparison separates angular arrangement from ambient dimension alone.

papers.selection_reason: Theoretical and empirical analysis of latent geometry for planning in world models, introducing self-approachingness as a planner compatibility condition.
papers.title: Order-Consistent Latent Geometry for Reliable Short-Horizon Planning in World Models
papers.tldr: The paper shows that reliable short-horizon latent planning requires distances to preserve progress along shortest transition paths, and identifies self-approaching geometry as the key condition.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies excel at generalist robotic manipulation but generate actions without explicitly modeling their environmental consequences. World action models (WAMs) incorporate future prediction, yet most rely on costly video generation, while latent alternatives either use predicted futures only as auxiliary targets or infer latent actions from suboptimal visual transitions through costly large-scale video pretraining. We introduce WAVE-0 (World-model-Augmented VLA Execution), a framework that bridges VLAs and WAMs through a lightweight latent world model. By connecting the semantic understanding of pretrained VLAs with explicit future prediction, WAVE-0 allows anticipated action consequences to directly guide action generation. Built on a pretrained VLA, its 257M world model translates VLM-generated latent action plans into predicted future representations that condition the action expert, unifying latent planning, future prediction, and action generation. The world model is trained directly on ground-truth robot actions with a counterfactual ranking objective, requiring neither pixel reconstruction nor large-scale video pretraining. WAVE-0 achieves success rates of 91.47% on RoboTwin 2.0 and 98.7% on LIBERO, along with 88.0%, 61.4%, and 75.0% on LIBERO-Plus, LIBERO-Pro, and LIBERO-Para, respectively. On real-world tasks, it improves the success rate of $\pi_{0.5}$ from 38.3% to 73.3%. These results demonstrate strong manipulation performance and generalization across diverse distribution shifts.
authors: Haomin Wang, Anqiong Ji, Ke Wang, Zhongshan Liu, Ru Ying, Ran Zheng, Zhipeng Zhang
bullets: Addresses the lack of explicit environmental consequence modeling in VLA policies without relying on costly video generation or large-scale video pretraining.
Uses a 257M-parameter world model to translate VLM-generated latent action plans into predicted future representations that condition action generation.
Trains the world model directly from ground-truth robot actions with a counterfactual ranking objective, avoiding pixel reconstruction.
Reports strong simulation performance across RoboTwin 2.0, LIBERO, and its distribution-shift variants.
Improves real-world success for π0.5 from 38.3% to 73.3%, demonstrating better generalization across distribution shifts.

The frozen world model predicts the visual consequences of these plans, and a resampler compresses them into future tokens that condition the action expert alongside the original VLM context.

papers.abstract: Video understanding benchmarks are the primary yardstick for measuring progress in video-language modeling, and a growing body of work relies on them to claim improvements. The reported benchmark scores in these works, however, are almost always produced by frameworks (e.g., lmms eval) used as black boxes: certain evaluation choices like frame sampling, preprocessing, and input formatting are inherited from preset defaults and seldom inspected carefully. We show these unexamined choices are a major source of variance. Even for the same model checkpoint, evaluation configuration alone can shift accuracy by up to 19.5pp. Hence, it is unclear whether reported gains reflect genuine improvements in capability or differences in evaluation setup. Moreover, many benchmark samples offer little evidence of visual capability, since they can be answered without the video, and the full suites are expensive to evaluate. We address these issues in two parts. First, we curate existing suites for discriminability and efficiency, producing Meta-Video, a balanced 1,000-question benchmark over 791 videos spanning diverse tasks and durations, which largely preserves model rankings, at 5 times inference speedup for a full-frame count sweep experiment (4-128 frames). Second, we establish a standardized evaluation protocol by sweeping the configuration space to isolate choices that measurably affect results, distill them into best practices and reporting standards, and release reproducible reference scores across five models and seven benchmarks. We hope that the proposed evaluation framework and the Meta-Video benchmark will support video understanding research by providing a reproducible and efficient foundation to measure progress in a reliable way.
authors: Soumya Shamarao Jahagirdar, Anna Kukleva, Vishaal Udandarao, Samuel Thomas, Brian Kingsbury, Rogerio Feris, James R. Glass. Ameya Prabhu, Hilde Kuehne
bullets: Evaluation settings such as frame sampling, preprocessing, and input formatting can change accuracy by up to 19.5 percentage points for the same model.
The authors curate Meta-Video, a balanced 1,000-question benchmark covering 791 videos, diverse tasks, and varied durations.
Meta-Video largely preserves model rankings while enabling a 5× speedup for a full-frame-count sweep experiment.
The work proposes best practices and reporting standards based on a systematic evaluation-configuration sweep.
Reproducible reference scores are released for five models across seven benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive language models produce, at every prediction step, a vocabulary-sized logit vector whose structure determines the conditional next-token distribution. We empirically identify that the ordered vocabulary-head logits follow a remarkably consistent log-linear relation \[ z_{(r)} \approx \mu - \alpha \log r. \] across prediction contexts, architectures, and scales, emerging progressively during pretraining. To our knowledge, this is the first systematic analysis of the logit geometry underlying the distributional assumptions used in the prior decoding work. While controlled order-statistic baselines spanning bounded, light-tailed, and heavier-tailed distributions can largely explain the observed log-linear geometry, they do not explain the systematic shift in the slope $\alpha$: trained language models exhibit $\alpha \approx 1.4$--$1.7$, sitting well above the initialization baseline ($\alpha \approx 0.2$) . Moreover, $\alpha$ correlates with predictive performance, suggesting that it captures learned structure beyond generic extreme-value effects.
authors: Swathi Shree Narashiman, Aravind Ramana Venkatramanan, Nambi Seshadri
bullets: Ordered logits approximately satisfy $z_{(r)} \approx \mu - \alpha \log r$ across contexts, architectures, and scales.
This geometry emerges progressively during pretraining.
Order-statistic baselines explain much of the pattern but not the learned slope shift.
Trained models show substantially larger slopes than initialization, with $\alpha$ linked to predictive performance.

papers.selection_reason: Provides a systematic analysis of the log-linear geometry of LLM logits, contributing to the understanding of LLM architectures and decoding mechanisms.
papers.title: The Geometry of Language Model Logits: Generic Structure and Learned Departures
papers.tldr: Language-model logits generally follow a log-linear rank pattern, but training shifts the slope in a way associated with predictive performance beyond generic statistical effects.

papers.abstract: Post-training pruning enables efficient deployment, but conventional methods do not explicitly preserve internal-gradient alignment between sparse and dense models. We study novel connections between downstream performance of compressed models and the ability to retain gradient information via influence-function preservation. Central to this connection is a curvature-aware objective that accounts for both layer activations and backpropagated gradients. Despite its promise, this objective remains underexplored in pruning due to a lack of efficient solvers. We introduce $\texttt{CACTUS}$, a novel ADMM-based optimizer supporting both pruning and sparse-plus-low-rank decompositions of pre-trained weights. Compared to LLM-Surgeon which targets the same objective, $\texttt{CACTUS}$ can achieve over an order-of-magnitude speedup. At $50\%$ pruning of Qwen3-4B, $\texttt{CACTUS}$ reduces the C4 perplexity gap to the dense model by $45\%$, improves compressed-to-dense per-sample gradient cosine similarity on WikiText-2 from $0.670$ to $0.755$, and runs over $28\times$ faster than LLM-Surgeon on substantially weaker hardware. By preserving influence functions, $\texttt{CACTUS}$ supports effective data selection. On Llama-3.2-3B, fine-tuning a fresh dense model on the $5\%$ of data selected by $\texttt{CACTUS}$ achieves $49.44\%$ accuracy on BIG-Bench Hard, compared with $47.22\%$ using ALPS and $49.54\%$ using dense-model selection. Finally, integrating $\texttt{CACTUS}$ with LoGRA, a recent gradient-projection strategy, on Qwen3-4B with MLP layers pruned to 2:4 sparsity and a rank-64 correction retains a $0.711$ cosine alignment with dense LoGRA-projected C4 gradients.
authors: Mehdi Makni, Natalia Ponomareva, Rahul Mazumder
bullets: Targets the gap between efficient pruning and preservation of internal-gradient alignment with dense models.
Optimizes layer activations and backpropagated gradients through a curvature-aware objective.
Supports both pruning and sparse-plus-low-rank weight decompositions via ADMM.
At 50% Qwen3-4B pruning, it narrows the C4 perplexity gap by 45%, raises WikiText-2 gradient cosine similarity from 0.670 to 0.755, and runs over 28× faster than LLM-Surgeon on weaker hardware.
Preserved influence functions enable effective data selection; 5% CACTUS-selected data reaches 49.44% BIG-Bench Hard accuracy, close to dense-model selection at 49.54%.

papers.abstract: The safety of LLM-based agents currently rests on alignment training and safety classifiers, neither of which can rule out that a sophisticated indirect prompt injection (IPI) goes through and causes significant harm. Recent work therefore builds agents with information-flow guarantees that rely on structured tool interfaces to interact with the environment. Computer Use Agents (CUAs) act visually on the computer screen, which does not provide a boundary between trusted first-party interfaces and untrusted, potentially attacker-authored content. Actions are equally ambiguous: a click may land on an application toolbar or a button controlled by an attacker. Treating the user as the source of trust and confirming each sensitive decision produces confirmation fatigue, with the risk of missing harmful actions. We introduce SA-CUA, a dual-LLM framework that generates a reliable trust boundary for CUAs by deriving conservative deterministic rules from the accessibility tree for unmasking trusted regions from the privileged LLM's screenshot, keeping trusted and untrusted content separated. Human interaction is only required for proper task specification in the beginning. During the task a robust endorsement channel allows values to pass from the untrusted to the trusted domain by verifying information via trusted channels. This allows the agent to autonomously handle tasks involving untrusted information. SA-CUA maintains much higher utility than CaMeL-CUA while keeping the attack success rate at zero.
authors: Dominik Seip, Bartol Markovinovi\'c, Matthias Hein
bullets: Computer-use agents lack clear trust boundaries because screenshots mix trusted UI with attacker-controlled content and actions are ambiguous.
SA-CUA uses a dual-LLM design and conservative deterministic rules from the accessibility tree to identify trusted regions.
A robust endorsement channel verifies values from untrusted content through trusted channels.
Human input is limited to initial task specification rather than repeated confirmations.
The abstract reports zero attack success while retaining substantially higher utility than CaMeL-CUA.

papers.selection_reason: Addresses safety for LLM agents acting on computers, proposing a dual-LLM framework to establish a trust boundary and prevent prompt injection.

papers.abstract: Recently, Morris et al. introduced TinyLoRA, a strategy for LLM fine-tuning which introduces arbitrarily few parameters, and demonstrated accuracy improvements using less than $10$ parameters rather than the ${\gtrsim 10,000}$ typically demanded by LoRA-based methods. However, that study continued to use gradient-based local search methods of the kind deployed for training multi-billion parameter LLMs in the first place. This article is predicated on the observation that, in the low dimensional setting, global optimization methods become tractable, unlocking Large language Model Bayesian Optimization (LlMBO). LlMBO is sample-efficient, gradient-free, memory-light, parallelizes across devices without synchronization, and, unlike policy-gradient methods, can optimize greedy-decoding accuracy directly. We describe numerical experiments comparing LlMBO against GRPO on fine-tuning tasks for a variety of models on a math benchmark suite which show that LlMBO can be a suitable alternative in this regime, matching or exceeding GRPO's fine tuning gains, while using a fraction of the compute and memory.
authors: Aditya Kulkarni, Davide Sartor, Carlos Soto, Nathan Wycoff
bullets: Targets the low-dimensional regime enabled by TinyLoRA, where only a handful of parameters are tuned.
Replaces gradient-based local search with global, gradient-free Bayesian optimization.
Is sample-efficient, memory-light, parallelizable without synchronization, and directly optimizes greedy-decoding accuracy.
Experiments across models and math benchmarks find LlMBO competitive with or better than GRPO while using a fraction of the compute and memory.
