papers.abstract: The world encompasses both physical environments and human actors. Predicting its evolution requires understanding both physical laws and how emotions shape human actions. However, existing world model benchmarks primarily assess physical plausibility and perceptual quality, leaving emotion-driven world evolution largely untested.We introduce AffectWorld, a benchmark that evaluates the chain Emotion-Action-World State through three tasks: World-State Consistency, Emotion-Action Consistency, and Causal Consistency. It comprises 1,498 everyday video samples annotated with plausible emotions, action tendencies, and atomic world-state constraints. A counterfactual subset of 233 samples tests whether changing an agent's emotion under fixed scene and event conditions yields corresponding changes in actions and consequences. We define eight metrics across the three tasks and an additional counterfactual metric, combining automatic visual assessment with human-calibrated VLM/LLM judgments. Evaluations of five SoTA world models (e.g., Cosmos3) required world-state change scores of 0.100-0.280 and counterfactual emotion sensitivity scores of 0.027-0.070 on a [0, 1] scale. These results reveal substantial gaps in generating the consequences of emotion-driven actions and adapting future predictions to emotional interventions. AffectWorld provides a testbed for advancing world models that capture how emotions shape future physical and social states.

papers.abstract: Guardrail approaches that rely on reasoning-based large language models (LLM) improve safety decisions, but come with substantial inference overhead due to the explicit reasoning. We introduce LR-Guard (Latent Reasoning Guardrail), an efficient and explainable guardrail that jointly learns structured latent reasoning and on-demand reasoning reconstruction. Our method distills a frozen teacher's analysis of safe and unsafe prompt interpretations and their comparison into compact latent representations. Joint training optimizes these representations for both safety prediction and reconstruction of the teacher's explicit reasoning traces, enabling human-readable explanations without requiring intermediate text generation for every decision. Experiments show that LR-Guard outperforms its explicit-reasoning teacher in most in-domain and out-of-domain settings on safety classification and explanation extraction, while achieving a 19.4x inference speedup at batch size one. Further, reconstructed reasoning traces from the latent information exhibit high semantic similarity to the teacher's explicit reasoning.
authors: Md Asiful Islam, Fahmida Alam, Mihai Surdeanu
bullets: Addresses the inference overhead of reasoning-based LLM guardrails.
Distills a frozen teacher’s safe/unsafe interpretations and comparisons into compact latent representations.
Jointly trains latent representations for safety prediction and on-demand reconstruction of human-readable reasoning traces.

Achieves a 19.4× inference speedup at batch size one, with reconstructed traces showing high semantic similarity to the teacher’s reasoning.

papers.abstract: What binds large language models on auditable, hypothesis-driven decision tasks, where every candidate can be checked against the evidence? On the public TCMEval-SDT benchmark for Traditional Chinese Medicine syndrome differentiation (200 cases), the binding constraint is output discipline and reasoning structure, not model capability alone: two years of model scaling move zero-shot scores by only -0.03 to +0.08, while output-discipline failures (non-terminating reasoning, format non-compliance, large run-to-run spread) persist even in frontier models. We test this with a model-agnostic agent framework formalizing decision making as a five-stage closed loop, enforced by a candidate x evidence matrix falsification protocol: every candidate is judged against every evidence item, at least half of the candidates must be falsified before a conclusion is licensed, and survivors are emitted in a machine-verifiable single-line format. Across five base models, the effect is sign-conditional on zero-shot output discipline: it rescues models whose discipline fails (DeepSeek-V4-Flash: +0.267/+0.271, entirely termination rescue), reduces a high-variance model's run-to-run standard deviation from 0.218 to 0.007 (Kimi K3), and significantly costs already-disciplined models (-0.087 to -0.120 on budget-matched Qwen3-4B/32B). Ablations attribute the cost to the candidate-bounded format layer and show the effect is independent of injected knowledge content (protocol-knowledge decoupling). The protocol also transfers to misinformation-robust mathematical reasoning, detecting injected false premises at 89.8% recall with a 6.8% false-positive rate (MCC 0.54; a flag-everything baseline scores 0) and restoring accuracy to the no-misinformation ceiling. Where zero-shot output discipline is weak, the reasoning protocol sets the floor; base-model capability always sets the ceiling.
authors: Jing Liu, Yongxing Qi, Ping Yao, Ting Wu
bullets: On the 200-case TCMEval-SDT benchmark, scaling alone changed zero-shot scores by only −0.03 to +0.08, while termination, format, and variance failures persisted.

It improved DeepSeek-V4-Flash by about 0.27 through termination rescue and reduced Kimi K3’s run-to-run standard deviation from 0.218 to 0.007.
It lowered scores for already-disciplined Qwen3-4B/32B models by 0.087–0.120; ablations linked the cost to the candidate-bounded format layer, not injected knowledge.
On misinformation-robust mathematical reasoning, it detected false premises with 89.8% recall and 6.8% false-positive rate, restoring accuracy to the no-misinformation ceiling.

papers.title: Output Discipline Sets the Floor: A Falsification-Guided, Model-Agnostic Agent Protocol for Auditable Hypothesis-Driven Decision Making

papers.abstract: Autoregressive video diffusion models have emerged as a foundation for long-horizon world rollout. However, when extended far beyond their training windows, these models suffer from progressive drift: visual quality deteriorates, motion becomes inconsistent, and object identity gradually collapses as generated frames are recursively reused as context. We study a supervision-horizon gap: short-horizon distillation leaves later rollout states without direct supervision. We show that matching short-window marginals need not determine long-horizon behavior, while longer on-policy trajectories expose delayed failures to training. This motivates temporal manifold matching at scale for long-horizon world models. Building on this insight, we introduce LongForcing, a distillation approach that scales teacher supervision to long student self-rollouts. LongForcing preserves the short-horizon teacher-forcing and causal ODE-distillation stages, while replacing the realscore teacher in the final distribution-matching stage with an extended-horizon bidirectional teacher. The long-horizon teacher supervises extended student self-rollouts using the standard distribution-matching formulation, without modifying the student architecture or increasing inference cost. We evaluate LongForcing on text-to-video generation and interactive action-conditioned world models, achieving a VBench Quality score of 85.52 and improving WorldRoamBench 60s action score by 23.9 points in first-person ablations. Qualitative stress tests further sample interactive rollouts up to 24 hours, far beyond the training horizon. These results suggest that scaling supervision along the temporal axis is a practical step toward long-horizon world models. The project website and code are at https://github.com/Fantasy-AMAP/LongForcing.
authors: Ziyu Zhu, Zhaoxu Sun, Fan Jiang, Mengchao Wang, Junfeng Ni, Ting-Bing Xu, Zhicheng Liu, Mu Xu
bullets: Targets progressive visual degradation, motion inconsistency, and object-identity collapse beyond the training horizon.
Identifies a supervision-horizon gap: short-window distillation does not constrain delayed rollout failures.
Extends temporal manifold matching by replacing the final-stage realscore teacher with an extended-horizon bidirectional teacher.
Preserves the student architecture and inference cost while supervising long self-rollouts.
Reports a VBench Quality score of 85.52, a 23.9-point improvement on the WorldRoamBench 60s action score in first-person ablations, and qualitative rollouts up to 24 hours.

papers.abstract: Benchmarks are essential for evaluating and improving large language models (LLMs). Yet many widely used benchmarks are redundant, making evaluation unnecessarily expensive. Benchmark compression lowers this cost by estimating full-benchmark scores and rankings from a partial evaluation. Research in this area has grown rapidly since 2024, but to our knowledge no survey has systematically organized its methods and findings. We review 119 papers to explain how methods choose what to evaluate, recover full-benchmark results, and verify their reliability. From this analysis, we develop a taxonomy covering compression within individual benchmarks, across benchmark suites, and during adaptive evaluation, together with work on redundancy and reliability. We compare their information needs, total costs, reliability checks, and limitations. Methods reduce evaluation costs by selecting representative subsets, using cheaper or reusable information, and testing adaptively, but risk poor coverage, inaccurate estimates, and sequential delays. The resulting taxonomy and practical guide help researchers choose, validate, and deploy methods for more efficient and reliable LLM evaluation.
authors: Guoming Ling, Yupei Lin, Zhongzhan Huang, Junxin Li, Junjie Liu, Shanshan Zhong, Hefeng Wu, Liang Lin
bullets: Identifies redundancy in widely used LLM benchmarks as a major source of unnecessary evaluation expense.
Taxonomizes methods for compression within benchmarks, across benchmark suites, and through adaptive evaluation.
Analyzes how methods select evaluations, reconstruct full-benchmark scores and rankings, and verify reliability.
Finds that representative subsets, cheaper or reusable information, and adaptive testing can reduce costs.
Highlights risks including poor coverage, inaccurate estimates, and delays from sequential evaluation, and offers practical guidance for method selection and validation.

papers.abstract: Multi-agent debate (MAD) aims to improve large language model reasoning by exposing agents to alternative solutions and enabling iterative revision. However, standard broadcast-style MAD makes peer answers visible without requiring agents to engage with a particular peer claim. As a result, reliable reasoning may be suppressed by conflicting or majority responses, limiting achievable performance, while erroneous reasoning may persist and degrade final predictions without actionable feedback. We propose TrueMAD, a backbone-agnostic test-time plug-in that introduces one-to-one, free-form peer advice between answer broadcasting and self-revision. Each source agent responds to a target's current reasoning through support, rebuttal, refinement, or further questions, while the target retains control over how to revise. The same mechanism can augment standard MAD and its improved variants without parameter updates. Across AIME, GPQA-Diamond, and TruthfulQA with Qwen3-30B-A3B, TrueMAD improves agent-level and strict-majority accuracy over MAD by 3.62 and 3.52 percentage points on average, while TrueDMAD improves DMAD by 4.72 and 4.06 points, respectively. Analyses at the utterance, agent-transition, and group levels further show more peer-specific deliberation, more correction-oriented revisions, and more favorable consensus dynamics.
authors: Dezheng Bao, Sihang Du, Renhong Huang, Zhizhang Yuan, Yifei Sun, Yang Yang
bullets: Standard broadcast debate can leave agents disengaged from peer claims, allowing errors or majority influence to persist.
TrueMAD adds one-to-one, free-form peer advice—including support, rebuttal, refinement, or questions—between answer sharing and self-revision.
It is a backbone-agnostic, parameter-free test-time plug-in that can augment standard MAD and improved variants.
On AIME, GPQA-Diamond, and TruthfulQA using Qwen3-30B-A3B, TrueMAD improves agent-level and strict-majority accuracy over MAD by 3.62 and 3.52 percentage points on average.
The method produces more peer-specific deliberation, correction-oriented revisions, and favorable consensus dynamics.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) have been widely adopted for document parsing and optical character recognition (OCR), as they can accurately extract page-level elements. However, downstream applications such as retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) also require coherent document-level structure. Although these models indicate heading levels using different numbers of preceding ``\#'' symbols, page-by-page prediction often lacks document-level consistency. In practice, input-resolution and context-length constraints make it infeasible for a VLM to jointly process all page images in documents containing tens or hundreds of pages. To address this limitation, we propose a VLM-based framework that incrementally reconstructs heading hierarchies with a \emph{level-wise multimodal memory}. The memory retains a compact subset of all previously processed pages, selected by anchors. Our framework supports flexible anchor selection, and in this work we select the most recent node at each level, allowing the VLM to observe the visual, textual, and layout patterns of headings at every level. For comprehensive evaluation, we also introduce the Complex and Long Document Heading Hierarchy Reconstruction Benchmark (CLDoc-HHRBench), comprising 250 documents and 11,212 pages with expert-verified annotations. Experiments on CLDoc-HHRBench and three existing benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of our method.
authors: Qian Chen, Xianyin Zhang, Lifan Guo, Chi Zhang
bullets: Addresses inconsistent heading-level predictions caused by page-by-page processing and VLM context or resolution limits.
Maintains visual, textual, and layout information from selected anchor pages at each heading level.
Uses the most recent node at every level as anchors, while supporting flexible anchor-selection strategies.
Introduces CLDoc-HHRBench, a benchmark of 250 documents and 11,212 pages with expert-verified annotations.
Shows effectiveness on CLDoc-HHRBench and three existing benchmarks; specific quantitative results are not reported in the abstract.

papers.abstract: System One models answer typed questions in a single forward pass and promise the same answer for the same input. For choice questions, this promise fails: the answer depends on the order of the options, increasingly so as they grow in number, and averaging over their cyclic shifts reduces this dependence without removing it. Scoring each option alone, which the order cannot affect, shows that the order changes the answer mostly when the model is unsure among its top few options, even though the listwise answer looks confident. We therefore propose $\textbf{Runoff}$, which considers, then chooses: it scores each option alone to keep a few candidates, then compares them in listings where each candidate takes every position. It needs no training and can run in two forward passes, and its answer does not depend on the option order by construction. On two open models and five datasets, it changes no answer under shuffling, against 9.3% for cyclic averaging, and with 20 options it is about as accurate and three to four times faster. Wrapped around eight System One models, it removes the order dependence of the five benchmarks, while cyclic averaging changes up to 15.4%.
authors: Jianguo Huang, Yao Long Teng, Yanchen Deng, Bo An
bullets: Option order can change answers substantially, especially when models are uncertain among their top few choices despite appearing confident listwise.
Runoff requires no training and can operate in two forward passes.
It is order-invariant by construction and produced no answer changes under shuffling in the reported evaluations.
Across two open models and five datasets, Runoff was about as accurate as cyclic averaging with 20 options and ran 3–4× faster.
Applied to eight System One models, it removed order dependence on all five benchmarks, whereas cyclic averaging changed up to 15.4% of answers.

papers.abstract: LLM agents can adapt to task feedback by revising the textual context that guides their behavior, without changing their model parameters. However, turning execution rewards into reusable context updates is challenging: individual trajectories offer limited comparative evidence about what to change, while task-specific fixes may overgeneralize when incorporated into a shared context. We introduce TextualRL, a gradient-free reinforcement learning framework that treats a group of rollouts from the same task under the same context, rather than an isolated trajectory, as the unit of policy critique. Groupwise Policy Critique contrasts successful and failed rollouts within a task; when outcomes are uniform, it draws on cross-task evidence to identify behaviors worth preserving or formulate repair hypotheses. Cross-Group Policy Update reviews the resulting proposals against evidence pooled across groups, including observations that yield no proposed edit, to refine their content and applicability. Reviewed proposals form a bounded textual patch, with adoption of the candidate context determined by held-out validation rewards. Together, these components establish a reward-driven policy optimization loop in which multiple attempts jointly inform reusable context updates. We evaluate TextualRL with five target agents on six benchmarks. Averaged over the six benchmarks, TextualRL improves test accuracy over the base model by 24.4 and 15.3 percentage points for GPT-5.5 and Qwen3.8-27B, respectively.
authors: Tianyu Huai, Jie Zhou, Bo Mao, Qin Chen, Liang He, Xipeng Qiu
bullets: Addresses the challenge of converting execution rewards into generalizable context edits from limited, task-specific evidence.
Uses Groupwise Policy Critique to compare successful and failed rollouts within the same task and context.
Uses Cross-Group Policy Update to refine proposed edits against evidence pooled across tasks, including cases with no proposed edit.
Builds bounded textual patches and adopts candidate contexts based on held-out validation rewards.
Across six benchmarks, improves test accuracy over the base model by 24.4 points for GPT-5.5 and 15.3 points for Qwen3.8-27B.

papers.abstract: Cross-domain few-shot action recognition (CD-FSAR) aims to recognise unseen action classes in a target domain from a handful of labelled videos. Despite advances in representation learning, CD-FSAR inference still relies on prototypes estimated from extremely limited support examples. To assess this bottleneck, we perform an oracle analysis with the representation fixed. Constructing oracle prototypes and decision boundaries from ground-truth query labels improves 5-way 1-shot accuracy by 7--20 percentage points across five target datasets. This reveals a substantial estimation gap: the representation contains useful discriminative information, but prototypes and boundaries estimated from scarce supports fail to capture each episode's true class structure. Motivated by this, we propose TRACE, a training-free transductive inference framework that improves episode-level estimation without modifying the backbone. TRACE comprises two complementary stages. Confidence-Thresholded Transductive Prototype Refinement (CTPR) refines support-based prototypes using confidently predicted queries. The refined prototypes initialise a lightweight per-episode classifier, which Transductive Classifier Refinement (TCR) further adapts by encouraging confident, class-balanced predictions over all queries. Together, the two stages improve prototype and boundary estimation, enabling better use of information in the unlabelled queries. Across five target datasets (HMDB51, UCF101, SSv2, Diving48, and RareAct) in both 1-shot and 5-shot settings, TRACE consistently improves a strong CD-FSAR baseline, including gains of more than six percentage points on HMDB51 1-shot, while recovering much of the oracle-estimated gap. These results suggest that improving test-time estimation is a powerful, broadly applicable complement to representation learning for CD-FSAR under extreme support scarcity.
authors: Changyi Li, Zeyu Yang, Yu Xiao
bullets: An oracle analysis shows that scarce-support prototype and decision-boundary estimation is a major bottleneck, despite useful learned representations.
TRACE uses two training-free transductive stages: confidence-based prototype refinement (CTPR) and class-balanced classifier refinement (TCR).
The method leverages confidently predicted unlabelled queries to better estimate each episode’s class structure.
Across five target datasets and both 1-shot and 5-shot settings, TRACE consistently improves a strong baseline, with gains exceeding six percentage points on HMDB51 1-shot.
The approach recovers much of the oracle-estimated gap, but its scope is limited to test-time transductive settings with available unlabelled queries.

papers.abstract: Parallel generation is widely regarded as an inherent advantage of diffusion large language models. Yet our fixed-quota evaluation of four representative models reveals severe degradation across mathematics and code, with all scores below 15% at 16 tokens per step. Token-level probes identify local predictive potential near the observed prefix, especially in mathematical text. We propose RePara, which reinforces short consecutive token blocks through group-relative policy optimization and reduces rollout and log-probability recomputation costs. On LLaDA and SDAR, \ours improves GSM8K and MATH-500 accuracy over JustGRPO under reduced denoising budgets, with a 1.96x training-step speedup in our LLaDA/MATH setup.
authors: Jiahao Kuang, Yangfan Gao, Tao Gui, Yuanbin Wu, Qi Zhang, Xuanjing Huang, Tao Ji
bullets: Fixed-quota evaluation finds severe degradation on math and code, with all tested models scoring below 15% at 16 tokens per step.
Token-level probes show useful local predictive potential near the observed prefix, particularly in mathematical text.
RePara applies group-relative policy optimization to reinforce short consecutive token blocks.
On LLaDA and SDAR, RePara improves GSM8K and MATH-500 accuracy over JustGRPO under reduced denoising budgets.
The method achieves a reported 1.96× training-step speedup in the LLaDA/MATH setup.

papers.abstract: Robotic manipulation systems commonly learn object affordances from human-annotated datasets, which reflect interaction possibilities for a human hand rather than the physical constraints of a specific robot. For example, a surface region of an object identified as graspable by a human annotator may be geometrically unreachable or mechanically infeasible for a robot, yet this mismatch is rarely addressed explicitly. To tackle this challenge, we proposed a framework that translates human affordance annotations into robot-executable affordance predictions conditioned on the physical properties of the robot. The network predicts which surface regions of an object are physically executable by the robot, given a 3D point cloud of an object and a descriptor encoding the robot's geometry and constraints. The model was trained using human-annotated affordances together with robotic execution outcomes from multiple sampled approach trials in simulation, where execution outcomes determined which regions are executable for the robot. The evaluation was performed on a household objects dataset using two parallel-jaw gripper configurations on a UR5e robot arm. The framework outperformed a model that does not receive information about the robot. The experimental results demonstrated that affordance prediction must be conditioned on the robot and that human annotations alone are insufficient for learning robot-executable affordance representations.
authors: Sawera Yaseen, Serge Thill, Rekha Raja
bullets: Human grasp affordances may be unreachable or mechanically infeasible for a robot.
The model combines object 3D point clouds with a descriptor of the robot’s geometry and constraints.

Evaluation uses household objects with two parallel-jaw grippers on a UR5e arm.

papers.abstract: Modern text-to-video (T2V) models generate visually compelling videos, yet meaning-preserving changes in prompt wording can substantially alter semantic realization and overall quality. Existing prompt rewriting modifies the inference input, whereas conventional post-training constructs supervision from one prompt formulation at a time; neither explicitly optimizes reliability across equivalent forms. We introduce VARI (Verified Alignment over Representations of Intent), a group-structured framework that treats automatically verified formulations of the same visual intent as a shared supervision unit. VARI builds matched form-seed rollout pools, cross-scores each video against all forms, and applies a wording-independent structured intent audit to identify valid realizations and hard semantic failures. Group-Consistent Distillation (GCD) aligns every verified form with interchangeable valid realizations, while Form-Contrastive Flow-DPO (FC-DPO) learns group-level preferences from audited positive-negative pairs, prioritizing same-seed, different-form contrasts. On HunyuanVideo-1.5, VARI attains the highest T2V-CompBench, VBench, and StoryEval scores among the evaluated methods. On prompt-form extensions of T2V-CompBench and VBench, it improves weakest-form alignment over the strongest prompt-level baselines by 2.45 and 3.55 points and reduces cross-form drop by 30.5% and 32.2%, respectively, while preserving visual quality. Human evaluation, natural-caption controls, prompt-enhancement experiments, diversity analyses, and transfer to LTX-2.3 further support the robustness and transferability of these gains, while VARI requires no additional inference-time module.
authors: Mingxuan Zhu, Hohei Chan, Shiyuan Liu, Yuanxing Zhang, Lu Chen
bullets: Addresses inconsistent semantic realization and quality when equivalent prompt wording changes.
Builds verified groups of formulations for the same intent, using matched form-seed rollouts and cross-form scoring.
Group-Consistent Distillation aligns valid realizations, while Form-Contrastive Flow-DPO learns preferences from audited positive-negative pairs.
On HunyuanVideo-1.5, VARI achieves the best reported T2V-CompBench, VBench, and StoryEval scores among evaluated methods.
On prompt-form extensions, it improves weakest-form alignment and reduces cross-form performance drops; results also transfer to LTX-2.3.

papers.abstract: Learning robot policies from demonstrations is often limited by the cost of collecting diverse, high-quality expert data. While an appealing alternative is to expand a single successful demonstration into a diverse set of successful trajectories, existing augmentation methods typically rely on manually designed transformation rules or complex trajectory planning, requiring substantial task-specific engineering and human effort. We introduce OneDemo, a reinforcement learning framework that learns to edit a single successful demonstration for new task configurations. We formulate demonstration editing as a structured reinforcement learning problem, in which an editor learns, from sparse task-success rewards, both when to transition between object-centric trajectory segments and how to geometrically adapt each segment. The learned editor serves both as a task policy and as a reusable demonstration generator. Across 15 Meta-World tasks, OneDemo reaches a 92.7% success rate within 53.7k environment interactions on average. Across 9 DexMimicGen tasks, it generates successful demonstrations with a 98.4% average success rate, and BC-RNN policies trained on the generated data achieve 99.6% average success at matched dataset scale. These results show that learning to edit a single successful demonstration provides a structured and effective basis for both policy learning and scalable demonstration generation.
authors: Ying Qian, Jianshu Hu, Han Fang, Shuguang Li, Yutong Ban
bullets: Addresses the cost and task-specific engineering required to collect or manually augment diverse expert demonstrations.

papers.abstract: Proactive human-robot collaboration requires autonomous systems to infer not only immediate actions but also the underlying hierarchical intentions governing human behavior. Current deep learning approaches predominantly focus on flat action classification, failing to capture the structural dependencies connecting kinematic motion to high-level goals. A Neuro-Symbolic Graph Transformer (NSGT) is proposed within this multimodal framework, a Human Reasoning Graph (HR-G) is integrated into the self-attention mechanism via learnable topological biases. Furthermore, the architecture is augmented with a differentiable First-Order Logic (FOL) loss, acting as a structural regularizer by which ontological consistency is enforced across four levels: atomic actions, composite activities, Low-Level Intentions, and High-Level Intentions. Evaluation is performed on the synthesized NTU-Hierarchy dataset, a four-level ontological extension of NTU RGB+D 120, wherein existing sequences were mapped into 119,383 complex hierarchical episodes (85 actions, 16 activities, 8 LLIs, 4 HLIs). To prevent circular supervision, strict isolation between label generation and FOL constraints was maintained. In the base configuration, 91.65% top-1 action accuracy is achieved by the NSGT. When the FOL loss is incorporated into the baseline, logic consistency is improved by 3.26 percentage points to 96.67%. Through the HR-G biases, a tunable trade-off between accuracy and structural coherence is established. In the primary consistency-maximizing configuration ($\lambda$ = 0.5), a logic consistency of 94.59% is reached and ontological contradictions are reduced by 33%, while a robust 89.90% top-1 action accuracy is retained. Finally, interpretable reasoning evidence is provided by the learned HR-G weights, wherein transition edges are strongly exploited ($\beta$ trans $\approx$ +2.6) without explicit supervision.
authors: Farnaz Soleimani (LISSI), Abdelghani Chibani (LISSI), Yacine Amirat (LISSI), Ghazaleh Khodabandelou (LISSI)
bullets: Addresses the limitations of flat action classification for inferring hierarchical human intentions in proactive human–robot collaboration.
Integrates Human Reasoning Graph topology into self-attention and uses a differentiable First-Order Logic loss to enforce consistency from atomic actions to high-level intentions.
Evaluated on the synthesized four-level NTU-Hierarchy dataset containing 119,383 hierarchical episodes.
The base model achieves 91.65% top-1 action accuracy; a consistency-focused configuration reaches 94.59% logic consistency, reduces contradictions by 33%, and retains 89.90% action accuracy.
Learned graph weights provide interpretable evidence, with transition edges strongly used despite no explicit supervision.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Overview of the NSGT framework. Four sensor streams (skeleton Xs, RGB Xr, infrared Xir, depth Xd) are encoded by frozen pretrained encoders and concatenated into a single fused representation. The NSGT reasoning module augments standard self-attention with a learnable HR-G structural bias (Section 3.3). Four prediction heads produce joint estimates of atomic actions, composite activities, Low-Level Intentions (LLI), and High-Level Intentions (HLI). The total loss combines cross-entropy with a differentiable FOL regulariser λFOL×LFOL that penalises ontological inconsistency across prediction levels.

Fig. 2: The four-level Human Reasoning Graph (HR-G) over the NTU-Hierarchy evaluation universe: 58 atomic actions, 39 composite activities, 28 Low-Level Intentions (LLI), and 8 High-Level Intentions (HLI). Layer 1 (grey): atomic actions. Layer 2 (blue): composite activities. Layer 3 (teal): LLIs. Layer 4 (orange): HLIs. A representative subgraph is shown; every drawn edge is taken from the ontological parent tree, and every drawn node belongs to the evaluation taxonomy of Table 1. The dashed orange path traces how eat meal is propagated through EatFood and LightBreakfast to MorningRoutine. Several mappings are deliberately non-injective: the activity EatFood is shared by two LLIs that resolve to different HLIs (MorningRoutine vs. MealConsumption), and the intention PhoneCheck is reachable under four distinct HLIs. The non-injective mappings motivate the lookup baseline evaluated in Section 6.2 and require an explicit rule for resolving multiple valid parents.

Fig. 3: Training dynamics of NSGT+FOL (λ = 0.5), averaged over five seeds. (a) Training and validation loss across epochs, with the best checkpoint marked at the epoch selected by validation LLI macro-F1. The training loss decreases steadily while the validation loss flattens and then rises gradually, a calibration effect on the softmax heads that does not degrade decision-level performance, as the validation macro-F1 in panel (b) remains stable across the same range. (b) Validation LLI macro-F1 across epochs, shown with a one-standard-deviation band over seeds. LLI macro-F1 is the checkpoint-selection metric.

Fig. 4: Per-level macro-F1 and hierarchy consistency on the held-out test split. Bars report the mean over five seeds and error bars denote one standard deviation. The first four groups report macro-F1 at the action, activity, low-level intention, and high-level intention levels, computed over all classes of the taxonomy (Table 1). The fifth group reports the hierarchy consistency rate, which measures the proportion of predictions satisfying the parent-child constraints of the ontology and is therefore not a macroF1 score. Hatched bars denote conditions trained with the first-order logic objective. Improvements attributable to the logic objective are concentrated in hierarchy consistency rather than in per-level macro-F1. The vertical axis starts at 40% to resolve differences among the stronger conditions.

Fig. 8: Audit trail of held-out test episode ep 0004228 (seed-42 checkpoint, NSGT with λ = 0.5). Thirty of the 31 nonzero entries of the bias matrix carry the sameintention relation, weighted by the largest of the three learned scalars (βtrans = 0.09, βact = 0.05, βlli = 0.60). The resulting parent-intention resolution is shown in Figure 9.

Fig. 5: High-level intention confusion matrices under two supervision configurations in which the high-level head is actively supervised, evaluated on the held-out test split at seed 42 and normalised by true-class row. Cells report the percentage of episodes of each true class predicted as each candidate class. The left panel is supervised at the two intention levels only, the right panel under the full hierarchical objective. Chance recall is 12.5 percent. Under intention-only supervision the mean diagonal recall is 69.2 percent, and under the full objective it reaches 78.7 percent, with residual confusions concentrated among ontologically adjacent classes. The improvement shows that the lower-level heads contribute non-redundant information to the highest level under joint training.

Fig. 9: Parent-intention resolution for the held-out episode of Figure 8. Candidate parent intentions of each predicted low-level intention. Three transitional intentions leave OfficeWorkSession and ReturnHome plausible; DigitalTasks, whose only parent is OfficeWorkSession, resolves the ambiguity. The chain check passes at both parent conditions and the prediction is a joint exact match.

Fig. 6: Evolution of the three HR-G bias scalars during training, averaged over five seeds, with shaded bands denoting one standard deviation. Panel (a): trained without the logic objective; panel (b): trained with the logic objective at λ = 0.5. In both settings βlli, initialised at the smallest value of the three, overtakes the other two scalars within the first epochs and continues to grow throughout training, reaching approximately 0.61 at the final epoch, while βtrans and βact remain near their initialisation. The two panels are nearly indistinguishable, indicating that the logic objective does not change which edge type the attention exploits.

papers.abstract: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) have emerged as a promising alternative to autoregressive LLMs, yet remain susceptible to hallucination. Activation steering offers a promising mitigation approach by guiding parallel token predictions through internal representations. However, existing steering methods largely overlook two characteristics of dLLMs: dynamic denoising states and temporal hallucination risks, which challenge predefined steering vectors and uniform intervention strengths. We propose TRACESTEER, a trace-driven activation steering framework that uses preceding denoising predictions as feedback to jointly adapt steering direction and strength. Specifically, Denoising Feedback Steering (DF-Steering) constructs step-specific steering vectors from preceding predictions and current hidden states. Trajectory-Guided Steering Gate (TS-Gate) regulates their strength using prediction uncertainty and the denoising timestep. With the backbone frozen, factual supervision and magnitude regularization jointly guide the learning of adaptive steering interventions, promoting factual reliability and stability throughout denoising. Experiments on two dLLMs show improved factual reliability on TruthfulQA and generalization across five downstream benchmarks.
authors: Xin Zhang, Yili Wang, Yue Tan, Xin He, Rui Miao, Yixin Liu, Yi Chang, Xin Wang
bullets: Targets dLLM-specific challenges: changing denoising states and time-varying hallucination risk.
Uses Denoising Feedback Steering to derive step-specific steering vectors from prior predictions and current hidden states.
Uses a Trajectory-Guided Steering Gate to adjust intervention strength based on uncertainty and denoising timestep.
Learns adaptive interventions with the backbone frozen, combining factual supervision and magnitude regularization.
Improves factual reliability on TruthfulQA and generalizes across five downstream benchmarks in experiments on two dLLMs.

papers.abstract: Accurate prediction of object trajectories is fundamental to mechanical understanding and robotic control. However, autoregressive models inherently suffer from cumulative errors, leading to severe drift in long-horizon rollouts. Observing that in many physical systems with dissipative or convergence-to-rest behavior, the final states are often more predictable than transient dynamics (e.g., a sliding object resting under friction or a pendulum stabilizing at equilibrium), we propose ReStep, a cascaded approach that reverses the conventional forward-prediction paradigm. ReStep first employs a stochastic model to directly predict the final state, then leverages Anchored Diffusion to generate goal-conditioned intermediate trajectories. By conditioning on both ''boundary states'', it effectively constrains dynamics and reduces uncertainty, producing physically plausible and temporally coherent transitions. We further integrate ReStep dynamics as the physical engine within a 3D Gaussian Splatting pipeline, enabling a unified physical-visual framework for intuitive inference from images. Extensive experiments on diverse rigid and non-rigid collision datasets show that ReStep achieves superior long-term accuracy, substantially mitigating error accumulation via reverse-consequence modeling.
authors: Leyan Zhang, Nantian He, Jiajun Ma, Yanpeng Zhao, Yunbo Wang
bullets: Addresses cumulative errors in autoregressive trajectory prediction, especially for dissipative systems that converge to rest or equilibrium.
Uses a stochastic model to predict the final state, followed by Anchored Diffusion conditioned on both initial and final states.
Produces physically plausible, temporally coherent trajectories by constraining intermediate dynamics with boundary states.
Integrates the dynamics model into a 3D Gaussian Splatting pipeline for image-based physical-visual inference.
Experiments on rigid and non-rigid collision datasets report improved long-term accuracy and reduced error accumulation.

papers.abstract: End-to-end autonomous driving has achieved remarkable progress by planning trajectories directly from raw sensor data. Yet the step from planning to control still relies on hand-tuned tracking controllers that block the gradient path from vehicle motion back to the network. This gap stems from non-differentiable vehicle dynamics, aliased supervision from coarsely sampled expert labels, rate mismatch between high-rate control and low-rate re-planning, and vehicle model discrepancies between training and deployment. This paper proposes DIVA (Differentiable Identified Vehicle dynamics for end-to-end Autonomous driving) to close this gap. An identified actuator-level vehicle model is embedded in the training loop of the end-to-end driving network, forming a differentiable chain from perception to vehicle states. A learning-based control decoder replaces the external controller and is supervised on the rolled-out vehicle states, bypassing the aliased control-input labels. A rate-consistent control-input parameterization reconciles the heterogeneous sampling rates and enables asynchronous execution with a 3.8 ms control-only cycle. On-policy re-identification and an online disturbance observer address training-time distribution shift and deployment-time model mismatch respectively. On the closed-loop Bench2Drive benchmark, DIVA achieves a driving score of 86.7, surpassing the widely adopted state-of-the-art approach by 3.3 points while nearly halving mean jerk and reducing brake switching by 64%, and maintains superior path tracking accuracy under significant vehicle model mismatch at deployment.
authors: Zhidong Wang, Zirui Li, Zitong Shan, Zhiqi Mao, Qihang Huang, Zhan Chen, Jingsong Liang, Han Yu, Chen Lv
bullets: Addresses the gradient gap between trajectory planning and hand-tuned vehicle control, along with coarse labels, mismatched control rates, and model discrepancies.
Embeds an identified actuator-level vehicle model in training to create a differentiable perception-to-vehicle-state pipeline.
Uses a learned control decoder supervised on rolled-out vehicle states and a rate-consistent parameterization for asynchronous control.
Adds on-policy re-identification and an online disturbance observer to handle distribution shift and deployment-time mismatch.
On Bench2Drive, achieves an 86.7 driving score, reduces mean jerk nearly by half and brake switching by 64%, with stronger path tracking under model mismatch.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Overview of DIVA: the control decoder cross-attends to memory tokens that combine the scene and planning features, the explicit route and target-speed reference, the state feedback and the disturbance estimate, and its control-input knots pass through a first-order hold into the identified differentiable vehicle dynamics, whose longitudinal and lateral actuator channels drive a single-track model integrated at 20 Hz. Under imitation learning in state space, the state loss propagates along the gradient path back through the vehicle dynamics into the control and planning decoders, and at deployment the control decoder runs on a fast path over cached perception, executing receding-horizon control inputs conditioned on the disturbance estimate of the online observer.

Fig. 2. On-policy re-identification: (a) coverage of the identification excitations (gray) and of the base controller (red, 50% and 85% contours); (b) map at throttle 0.7; (c) 141 on-policy upshifts; (d) 49 on-policy launches; (e) speed bias of both models under the controller’s commands; (f) position error on held-out drives; kinematic bicycle: the constant-parameter model of [31] shipped with TF++.

papers.abstract: Robot manipulation policies trained through imitation learning commonly rely on costly demonstrations recorded in one task direction and at one temporal resolution. We propose Reversal and Stride-based Trajectory Augmentation (RESTA), which exploits time-scaling data augmentation to improve data efficiency through trajectory reversal and temporal resampling. Trajectory-reversal augmentation reverses and relabels demonstrations between paired tasks with opposite objectives, reusing recorded rollouts without additional environment interaction. Because contact-rich manipulation is not exactly reversible, we treat reversal as an approximate paired-task prior rather than a physical symmetry. Temporal-stride augmentation varies observation and action sampling strides and conditions the policy on the resulting offsets, enabling fixed or randomized temporal schedules. Experiments across 16 paired bimanual manipulation tasks show that trajectory reversal is particularly effective in the low-data regime and that temporal-stride augmentation improves success under randomized temporal schedules. With 25 and 50 independently collected demonstrations per task, RESTA achieves 78.4% and 85.2% average success, respectively, matching or exceeding baselines trained with twice as many demonstrations (77.3% and 85.4%). These results show that RESTA can improve data efficiency in robot imitation learning.

Across 16 paired bimanual tasks, reversal helps especially in low-data settings and stride augmentation improves robustness to randomized schedules.

papers.abstract: On-policy self-distillation improves a model using guidance from the model itself, but it still requires a teacher that provides more useful predictions than the student. Existing approaches obtain such guidance by giving the teacher additional context or instructions. We ask whether it can instead come from changing how the same model uses its own layers. To address this, we introduce LoOPSD, which searches over a model's layer execution order to construct a stronger teacher and distills its advantage into the student. Specifically, we keep the model weights unchanged while searching for layers to repeat, and use the resulting teacher's predictions on student-generated prefixes to guide learning. We then alternate search and distillation, rebuilding the teacher from the updated student in each round so that the student progressively absorbs the gains from alternative layer execution. Experiments on mathematical and logical reasoning tasks show improvements across models. On GSM8K with a 400-token thinking budget, LoOPSD raises Qwen3-1.7B accuracy from 42.30% to 79.61%; subsequent distillation rounds yield further gains beyond the first round. Together, these findings show that by searching layer execution to construct teachers, we can turn a model's additional computation into improved student capabilities, opening a new avenue for self-distillation to derive supervision from the model's own computation.
authors: Wei Fan, Qingyue Yang, Chao-Hong Tan, Qian Chen, Wen Wang, Xiangang Li, Kejiang Chen, Weiming Zhang, Nenghai Yu

papers.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have demonstrated strong zero-shot reasoning across diverse domains, but their potential for Human-Object Interaction (HOI) remains unexplored. Unlike traditional HOI approaches that rely on extensive labeled datasets and fixed interaction taxonomies, MLLMs offer flexible reasoning, making them well-suited for dynamic, real-world scenarios. In this work, we present the first systematic study of MLLMs for HOI recognition and detection within a pipeline that combines an external object detector for entity localization with zero-shot multimodal reasoning for interaction understanding. We introduce a benchmark framework for principled zero-shot evaluation, consisting of (i) a unified taxonomy of zero-shot prompting strategies, and (ii) a methodology that transforms token-level logits into interaction scores, enabling fair comparison with specialized HOI models under standard metrics. To support prompt-based evaluation, we additionally construct new question-answer annotations for standard HOI datasets, transforming them into a format suitable for MLLMs. Building on this, we propose two visual prompting strategies, namely Objects as Context and Black Other Objects, that guide MLLMs to target objects while preserving scene context. Experiments on HICO, HICO-DET, and V-COCO demonstrate state-of-the-art zero-shot performance, achieving 53.50 mAP on HICO and 23.69 mAP on HICO-DET. Overall, our work provides a principled benchmarking framework for MLLMs in HOI, opening the door to new models and datasets and enabling flexible open-world interaction understanding.
authors: Oriol Rabasseda, Zenjie Li, Kamal Nasrollahi, Sergio Escalera

papers.abstract: Robotic harvesting of cherry tomatoes in greenhouses remains challenging due to dense fruit clusters, delicate skin, and the need for gentle yet effective detachment. This study presents a force-data-driven framework for autonomous cherry tomato harvesting that integrates six-axis force/torque sensing, a bio-inspired compliant gripper, and deployment on a mobile robotic platform. A wearable ATI six-axis force/torque sensor mounted on the index finger captured kinetic signatures of three elemental picking patterns (gripping, twisting, and lateral pulling) across 150 manual trials (50 per pattern) in laboratory and greenhouse settings. Gripping required a peak normal force of 3.92 and 0.45 N, twisting produced a dominant torque of 19.20 2.10 Nmm about the pedicel axis with minimal truss disturbance, and pure lateral pulling alone was insufficient for reliable detachment. These measurements informed a novel fingertip-localised Finray gripper, with compliant TPU 95A Finray geometry restricted to the fruit-contact region and a rigid PLA body, emulating the dual-stiffness human fingertip. A Dynamixel XM430-W350 servomotor under current-based torque control applies the measured gripping force and a 45{\deg} wrist twist. Finite element analysis showed a maximum von Mises stress of 0.24 MPa under the 3.92 N load, below the bruising threshold of cherry tomato skin. Integrated on a UR5 arm and Clearpath Husky A200 base, the system was validated in NVIDIA Isaac Sim and in 50 autonomous trials at the SILAL commercial greenhouse, Abu Dhabi, UAE. The hybrid grip-twist-pull strategy achieved an 86.0% picking success rate, 2.3% fruit damage, and an 8.4 s cycle time per fruit, outperforming vacuum (66.3%), rotating (70.1%), clamping (76.0%), and suction-cutting (52.4%) end-effectors. These results demonstrate preliminary feasibility under the tested facility and cultivar conditions
authors: Rajmeet Singh, Manveen Kaur, Yusuf Adamu, Irfan Hussain
bullets: The study addresses reliable detachment of delicate cherry tomatoes in dense greenhouse clusters.

The integrated system achieved 86.0% picking success, 2.3% fruit damage, and an 8.4-second cycle time in 50 autonomous trials.
Performance was evaluated under the tested facility and cultivar conditions, so broader generalization remains preliminary.

papers.abstract: We present a real-time framework for expressive legged locomotion that enables independent control over velocity and style. Unlike existing data-driven controllers, which typically require explicit style labels for training, our method efficiently leverages large-scale unstructured motion data and generalizes to unseen styles. We disentangle style from functional locomotion through a tailored sampling strategy used to train a style encoder whose output conditions an autoregressive diffusion model. During inference, the user provides a style reference clip and a joystick velocity command. The diffusion model then generates a kinematic reference tracked by a reinforcement learning controller. To improve user controllability and stylization strength, we propose an attention biasing mechanism and a velocity command correction strategy. We demonstrate our method on a physics-based humanoid character in simulation and on a physical robot, showcasing robust real-time control and continuous style modulation. The results can be best seen in our supplemental video (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=roFnS6N7nJ4).
authors: Joshua Aurand, Agon Serifi, Sammy Christen, Ruben Grandia, Espen Knoop, Marco Hutter, Moritz B\"acher
bullets: Separates locomotion function from style using a tailored sampling strategy and a learned style encoder.
Conditions an autoregressive diffusion model on style to generate kinematic motion references.
Uses reinforcement learning to track generated references on a physics-based character.
Adds attention biasing and velocity correction for stronger stylization and user control.
Demonstrated real-time control and continuous style modulation in humanoid simulation and on a physical robot.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview. We train an autoregressive diffusion model on unstructured motion datasets. We explicitly encode style in the style encoder, enabling generalization to unseen style references of varying length at inference. During inference, users can control the robot’s velocity through joystick commands, while selecting a desired style clip. The motion diffusion model’s output is autoregressively rolled out and passed to an RL-based tracking controller.
Figure 4: G1 Robot Deployment. Left: Continuous joystick control with dynamic style modulation. Right: Demonstration of the framework generating five distinct motion styles.

Figure 3: Style Encoding. Generated motions conditioned on interpolated style latents of styles from the 100STYLE dataset (top and middle row) and latents computed from unseen motions extracted from videos (bottom row).
Figure A.3: Baseline Comparison. We show two motion sequences generated by the same commands with CAMDM [6] and our model.

Figure A.2: Interactive Control. Example of interactive control where a physics-based humanoid follows velocity commands in various styles. The green dots indicate the trajectory generated from the given velocity commands.
Figure A.5: Attention Bias Quality. We compare unmodified inference with CFG and attention biasing for improved stylization.
Figure A.8: Velocity Correction. Qualitative analysis of applying velocity correction over a number of different trajectories.

Figure A.4: Sampling Scheme. We show the first frame of 5 consecutively predicted motion windows of models trained with and without our proposed sampling scheme. Without our sampling approach (“same window training”), the model collapses and keeps repeating the reference motion. With our sampling approach (“different window training”), the model learns to extract the style characteristic from the reference motion.

Figure A.1: Smoothing Scheme. To achieve smooth transitions between consecutive diffusion calls, we predict the next F states Mnxt fut at the current timestep t, then blend the first K states in Mnxt fut with the last K states of the previous prediction Mprv fut , then copy the next F − 2K states from Mnxt fut before incrementing the timestep t := t + (F −K) and repeating the process. More formally, we weight state mnxt i by w = i/(K+1) and state mprv (F−K)+i by 1 − w to form the blended states mt+i for i = 1, . . . ,K. The visualization shows the F = 6,K = 2 case.

Figure A.6: Attention Bias Sensitivity. We show how varying bias parameters affect performance by varying one weight at a time while keeping the other fixed at 0. Increasing either weight to large magnitudes worsens command adherence while increasing generation artifacts. Large positive wpst weights specifically result in frozen poses, which is why foot sliding is at zero.
Figure A.7: Unseen Style. Generation of motion with unseen styles from 100STYLE, shown as the green snapshots.

papers.abstract: Prefix reuse improves LLM inference by sharing the KV cache of common prompt prefixes. This helps only if the scheduler can execute a matched branch in the current worker round. Schedulers assume that a matched prefix is ready, which holds for full attention but fails for hybrid LLMs. There, a branch (the consumer) may need recurrent state that another branch (the producer) is still computing in the same round. The native scheduler stops its waiting-queue scan at this blocked consumer, and the resulting head-of-line blocking creates \emph{execution bubbles}: idle batch slots that independent work could fill. We introduce RadixFlow, which decouples prefix matching from state readiness. Its state-ready traversal turns a global scan barrier into a local wait: only the consumer is blocked until the next round, while feasible independent branches keep filling the batch under the native state check. On five hybrid models, RadixFlow lowers mean latency by 3\% to 24\% and worker rounds by 11\% to 44\% at almost unchanged reuse. On the larger Qwen3.5 models, ablations show that most of the gain comes from traversal, which adds little on a full-attention control. Heavier rounds limit how much of this saving reaches latency.
authors: Huihao Jing, Wenbin Hu, Shaojin Chen, Haochen Shi, Haoyu Huang, Sirui Zhang, Yuxuan Liu, Zhongwei Xie, Haoran Li
bullets: Prefix matching can fail when a hybrid-LLM consumer depends on state still being computed by a producer in the same round.
The native scheduler stops scanning at the blocked consumer, causing head-of-line blocking and idle batch slots.
RadixFlow decouples prefix matching from state readiness through state-ready traversal, turning a global scan barrier into a local wait.
Across five hybrid models, it reduces mean latency by 3%–24% and worker rounds by 11%–44% with nearly unchanged prefix reuse.
Traversal provides most gains on larger Qwen3.5 models; heavier rounds limit latency improvements, while full-attention workloads see little added benefit.

papers.abstract: Prompt optimization and generator post-training are two complementary ways to improve text-to-video (T2V) generation, and recent systems increasingly train both modules jointly. However, optimizing a prompt policy and a video generator from the same terminal reward creates two ambiguities: prompt quality is confounded with stochastic generation, and the two modules may realize overlapping local improvements. We introduce FlowCred, a two-level framework for joint T2V post-training. First, hierarchical credit assignment uses matched prompt-seed rollout grids to separate prompt-level credit from prompt-conditioned generator residuals under shared randomness. Second, functional coordination probes alternative current-policy prompts at states from actual generation trajectories, providing generator-aware evidence for prompt optimization while selectively attenuating generator updates already supported by conditioning changes. Across multiple T2V benchmarks, FlowCred consistently improves matched joint-training baselines. On LTX-2.5, FlowCred improves a strictly matched joint-training control from 61.47 to 64.46 on T2V-CompBench and from 55.58 to 58.08 on StoryEval, without increasing decoded-video or reward-model-call budgets. Factorial and realized-update analyses show complementary contributions from prompt shaping and generator routing, while human evaluation and transfer across backbones and updater families provide further supporting evidence.
authors: Mingxuan Zhu, Yanwei Huang, Shiyuan Liu, Xinzhi Zhang, Shujie Li, Yuanxing Zhang, Lu Chen
bullets: Addresses two ambiguities in shared terminal-reward training: prompt quality versus stochastic generation, and overlapping improvements between modules.
Uses matched prompt–seed rollout grids to assign prompt-level credit and prompt-conditioned generator residual credit under shared randomness.
Probes alternative prompts along actual generation trajectories to make prompt optimization generator-aware and selectively reduce redundant generator updates.
Improves matched baselines on multiple T2V benchmarks; on LTX-2.5, scores rise from 61.47 to 64.46 on T2V-CompBench and from 55.58 to 58.08 on StoryEval.
Analyses and human evaluation support complementary prompt shaping and generator routing, with evidence across backbones and updater families.

Once both modules are trained from a common terminal reward, two distinct issues arise: statistical credit ambiguity between prompt choice and prompt-fixed stochastic variation, and functional overlap between conditioning-side and generator-side local effects. FLOWCRED addresses them with hierarchical credit assignment (Q− V versus R−Q) and functional coordination based on same-state response geometry.

papers.abstract: Omnimodal large language models (OLLMs) are susceptible to cross-modal hallucinations under audio-visual interference. We find that, for a substantial fraction of incorrect joint predictions, the question-relevant unimodal branch can still recover the correct answer, suggesting that task-relevant evidence can remain recoverable from the relevant modality even when it is not reflected in the joint prediction. We refer to this recoverable failure pattern as \emph{modality misrouting}. We propose CaRe (Conflict-aware Residual Intervention), a training-free inference-time method for identifying and correcting modality misrouting. CaRe uses a text-only modality probe to identify a candidate modality-specific counterfactual branch, and flags potential misrouting when its prediction conflicts with the original joint prediction. For such cases, CaRe computes a residual direction from the discrepancy between the counterfactual and fused representations and uses it to steer the original multimodal state toward the relevant modality evidence, while retaining both modalities in the original audio-visual inference path. The intervention strength is adapted based on the confidence of the counterfactual branch. Experiments on CMM and AVHBench across two OLLMs show that CaRe consistently outperforms the evaluated inference-time hallucination-mitigation baselines.
authors: Yu Mi, Licheng Pan, Jiayi Zhu, Qirui Liu, Yitong Qiao, Changtong Xu, Tao Wei, Fei Sun, Zhixuan Chu, Kui Ren
bullets: Audio-visual interference can cause incorrect joint predictions even when the question-relevant unimodal branch predicts correctly.
CaRe is a training-free, inference-time method that uses a text-only modality probe to find conflicting modality-specific predictions.
It derives a residual direction between counterfactual and fused representations to correct the multimodal state while preserving both modalities.
Intervention strength is adapted according to the counterfactual branch’s confidence.
Across CMM and AVHBench on two OLLMs, CaRe consistently outperforms the evaluated inference-time mitigation baselines.

papers.title: Mitigating Cross-Modal Hallucinations by Correcting Modality Misrouting in Omnimodal LLMs

papers.abstract: Running large language models (LLMs) on consumer hardware is bottlenecked by the key-value (KV) cache, which grows with every decoded token and quickly exhausts the memory and bandwidth of a single consumer GPU. We present SparPR (Sparse Partial Recomputation), a runtime KV-cache recovery mechanism that does not modify model weights and requires no offline training. SparPR couples three online decisions: Query-Aware key-block selection scores historical blocks against the current query; dynamic budget control estimates per-block copy and recompute costs to decide how many blocks to retain; and on-demand local recomputation with cost-aware fallback merges retained blocks into continuous spans and switches between sparse recomputation and full recovery according to a runtime cost comparison. Implemented on FlexGen/FlexLLMGen, SparPR is evaluated on a single consumer laptop (RTX 3070 Ti 8GB, Ryzen 9 6900HX, 16GB RAM). It cuts end-to-end latency by 31%, 52%, and 63% at 1k, 2k, and 4k prompt tokens respectively, with 1.4x-2.7x higher throughput, and completes an 8k-token workload in 44 minutes where the FlexGen baseline times out. Under a fixed cache budget, SparPR retains a Needle Accuracy that stays well above StreamingLLM and H2O at every keep ratio, and ablation studies confirm that the three mechanisms act jointly.
authors: Jieyun Deng, Keming Hu, Yanghe Liu, Li Feng
bullets: Targets KV-cache growth that can exhaust single consumer GPUs during long-context decoding.
Combines query-aware key-block selection, dynamic retention budgets, and cost-aware local or full recomputation.
Requires no model-weight changes or offline training and integrates with FlexGen/FlexLLMGen.
On an RTX 3070 Ti laptop, it reduces latency by 31%–63% across 1k–4k prompts and achieves 1.4×–2.7× higher throughput.
Completes an 8k-token workload in 44 minutes, while the FlexGen baseline times out; cache retention remains strong across keep ratios.

papers.abstract: World-model-based visual navigation enables action planning by predicting future states under candidate trajectories. However, long-horizon rollout remains challenging: models are often trained with ground-truth visual histories but deployed in closed-loop prediction, and evaluating many candidates with step-by-step rollout is computationally expensive. We propose SkipWorld, a latent skip planning framework for efficient visual navigation. SkipWorld introduces three components: (i) Latent AutoRoll, which trains a world model to recursively roll out future states in latent space, reducing the mismatch between training and closed-loop inference; (ii) SkipDistill, which distills the latent autoregressive model into a skip world model that directly predicts long-stride future latent states; and (iii) Skip-then-Refine Planning, a dual-model coarse-to-fine planner that first filters candidate trajectories with the skip model and then reranks selected candidates with the stronger autoregressive model. This design preserves accurate trajectory evaluation while reducing redundant rollout computation. Experiments on RECON, HuRoN, SCAND, and TartanDrive show that, compared with NWM, SkipWorld reduces the average ATE by 4.2% and RPE by 2.7%, while decreasing planning time by 62.4% with a 2.7-fold speedup.
authors: Yifei Yang, Zehua Fan, Zike Yan, Zhongyu Li, Yan Wang
bullets: Addresses closed-loop rollout mismatch and the high cost of evaluating many candidate trajectories.
Latent AutoRoll trains recursive latent-space prediction to better match deployment conditions.
SkipDistill creates a skip world model that directly predicts long-stride future latent states.
Skip-then-Refine Planning combines fast coarse filtering with accurate autoregressive reranking.
On four benchmarks, it reduces ATE by 4.2%, RPE by 2.7%, and planning time by 62.4%, achieving a 2.7× speedup versus NWM.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of SkipWorld. First, Latent AutoRoll trains an autoregressive world model that rolls out directly in latent space. Second, SkipDistill trains a skip student to predict longer-horizon latent transitions through teacher endpoint distillation, where the latent alignment error (Section A.5) visualizes the spatial discrepancy between the student skip endpoint and the autoregressive teacher endpoint. Third, Skip-then-Refine Planning uses the skip student to cheaply filter candidate trajectories and then uses the autoregressive teacher to accurately rerank only the selected candidates.

Figure 1: Overview and performance of SkipWorld. Top: SkipWorld performs coarse-to-fine planning by first using a skip student to filter N candidate trajectories into a compact Top-P subset, followed by latent autoregressive teacher refinement. Bottom-left: Example trajectory prediction on RECON, where SkipWorld more closely follows the ground-truth trajectory than NWM. Bottomright: Compared with NWM, SkipWorld reduces average ATE by 4.2% and RPE by 2.7%, while achieving a 2.7× planning speedup.
Figure 3: Predicted trajectories on the four evaluation datasets. SkipWorld produces trajectories that better follow the ground-truth path across diverse indoor, outdoor, and driving scenes.
Figure 4: Additional scene-aware qualitative results on RECON.
Figure 5: Additional scene-aware qualitative results on SCAND.
Figure 6: Additional scene-aware qualitative results on HuRoN.
Figure 7: Additional scene-aware qualitative results on TartanDrive.

Table 1: Main comparison on four visual navigation benchmarks. Lower is better. The best result is shown in bold and the second best is underlined. NWM (original) is from its original paper. NWM (pretrained) denotes our four-dataset retrained baseline. Due to privacy restrictions, only a low-resolution HuRoN subset is available. For fair comparison, We thus fine-tune it from the 100K-step checkpoint for another 50K steps with identical settings.
Table 7: Horizon-wise error analysis averaged over four datasets. Lower is better. The best result is shown in bold and the second best is underlined.

Table 8: Loss ablation of SkipDistill under the same Skip-then-Refine planning setting. Time is average planning time per query. Lower is better. The best result is shown in bold and the second best is underlined.
Table 4: Ablation on coarse candidate budget with skip stride fixed to s = 8. Time is seconds per query. Lower is better. The best result is shown in bold and the second best is underlined.
Table 3: Ablation on skip stride with candidate budget fixed to P = 20. Time is seconds per query. Lower is better. The best result is shown in bold and the second best is underlined.
Table 2: Component ablation averaged over four datasets. Time is seconds per query. Lower is better. The best result is shown in bold and the second best is underlined.
