papers.title: SkipWorld: Latent Skip Planning with Distilled World Models for Efficient Visual Navigation
papers.tldr: SkipWorld accelerates visual navigation planning by using distilled latent skip predictions for coarse filtering before autoregressive refinement, improving accuracy while greatly reducing computation.

papers.abstract: Looped language models (LMs) reuse one block of layers several times per token generation, promising more latent computation at no additional storage cost. Despite their rising popularity, the analysis of looped LMs is still in its infancy: little is known about whether the iterative transformations actually improve their capabilities, or whether these models remain stable under prompt perturbation. We construct an inspection protocol rooted in Mechanistic Interpretability comprising five diverse lenses. We apply it to examine eight looped LMs from four families. Models differ in many aspects but the key one is whether the prompt is transmitted only within the looped state (carry loops: Ouro, LoopUS) or re-supplied at every iteration (re-read loops: Parcae, and Rec-OLMo & Huginn from the Raven family). The results of our study provide valuable insights concerning safety and efficient use of looped language models.
authors: Pawel Olszowiec, Paulina Tomaszewska, Maciej \.Zelaszczyk, Michal Byra, Neo Christopher Chung
bullets: Studies eight looped LMs spanning four model families.
Introduces an inspection protocol using five complementary analytical lenses.
Compares carry loops, which retain prompts only in the looped state, with re-read loops, which re-supply prompts each iteration.
Investigates whether iterative transformations improve capabilities and whether models remain stable under prompt perturbations.
Provides insights relevant to the safety and efficient use of looped language models.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Looped architectures (a) Carry loop: the prompt embedding is the starting state h0, later iterations see only ht. (b) Re-read loop: a prelude embeds the prompt into e, which is supplied at every iteration and the loop starts from a random state s0. Red boxes mark where Lens 5 perturbs each loop.

Figure 8: Decision timing for every generative set. Similarly to Fig. 3, this presents the share of tokens with final top-1 at each relative loop position. At the top: statistics on generated answer tokens. At the bottom: statistics on prompt tokens. In the main part of the paper we present Fig. 3 on MATH dataset only. These plots confirm that the early decision generalizes to other datasets and is not specific to MATH prompts. On every set, most answer tokens of most models are decided at iteration 1. Huginn rises slowly, LoopUS jumps at iteration 2, Ouro, Parcae, and Rec-OLMo decide very early.

Figure 9: Prompt-reading accuracy per set. Plots at the top: next-token accuracy on prompt tokens. At the bottom: expected calibration error (ECE, lower is better). Both presented along the relative position in the loop on five datasets. There are three main-text patterns, i.e. peaking at training depth, overthinking after reasoning tuning, monotone improvement in re-read loops which hold on every dataset. The arithmetic task is least informative due to short and predictable prompts. HotpotQA plots depicts the largest gains (Huginn 0.30→0.56, LoopUS 0.23→0.47). We conclude that the choice of the best readout iteration is a model-dependent artifact.

Figure 6: Lens 5: how the answers change when the loop’s starting state is injected with random noise. X-axis: noise amplitude α (0 denotes a clean run with no noise). (a) Word overlap with clean answer. (b) Broken answers on adversarial prompts1. (c) Share of fluent, on-topic answers. Solid lines are carry loops, dashed are re-read loops.

Figure 4: Lens 3: how well each iteration reads the prompt. Results on MATH prompts, every iteration predicts the next prompt token. The X-axis represents the relative loop position. (a) Accuracy. (b) The log-loss relative to its value at the first iteration. A value below 1 means the loop has improved the prediction, a value above 1 suggests a deterioration in the answer. (c) The expected calibration error (ECE, see App. B). Lower value is better.

Figure 12: Noise robustness by prompt category. In each cell the value stands for the mean word similarity between the answers on clean and noisy runs on each dataset separately. (a) All models at α = 4. (b)-(d) Carry loops at α = 0.5, 1 and 2. Darker blue means more similar to the noise-free answer. We find that robustness might depend on the prompt type: a factual question might be more stable than a creative or harmful prompt. The presented heatmap shows whether any category is special. The split carry loops vs. re-read loops appears on every dataset: carry loops at 0.00-0.04, re-read at 0.46-0.84. We find that among re-read loops the factual questions are the most stable (TriviaQA 0.81 for Huginn) and harmful prompts are least stable (AdvBench 0.46 for Parcae). A possible explanation is that noise influences the answer most where the prompt constrains the answer least, e.g. creative tasks.

Figure 17: Evolution of hidden states along the iterations. Top plots present the norm of the hidden state along the iterations. Plots in the middle present the step length ∥ht − ht−1∥. At the bottom - cosine similarity between consecutive states. One line in the plot is drawn per amplitude and the black line corresponds to noise-free runs. Ouro contracts the initial hidden states at every noise amplitude. For α ≥ 8, the LoopUS model does not shrink the steps and the norm of the hidden state grows with every iteration.

Figure 7: Does difficulty change loop dynamics? (a) Top-1 flips. (b) Settling share for MATH levels 1-5. (c) Top-1 changes per token for arithmetic problems with one-, two- and three-digit operands. An adaptive loop should work harder on harder inputs. The curves are flat: across five MATH levels, flips change by <0.08 and settling by <3 points. The one exception is Huginn on arithmetic (flips grow 30%). In investigated looped LLMs, difficulty is not visibly translated into loop dynamics and the extra depth is spent the same way on easy and hard problems. Adaptive computation would need to be trained explicitly.

Figure 13: Refusals and response styles of carry loops on safety prompts. Ratio of answers with different response styles depending on the noise amplitude. (a) Answers containing a refusal phrase. (b) Answers opening a reasoning trace e.g. "Okay, the user is asking . . . ". (c) Answers starting with a refusal phrase. From α = 0 up to α = 1 nothing changes qualitatively. At α = 2 we observe that the Ouro Thinking models stop reasoning and start their answer with a refusal - their refusal rate rises. On the other hand, Ouro-1.4B starts to reason and refuses less. For α ≥ 4, no carry loop refuses.

Figure 10: Attention fingerprints: one row per head, one column per iteration. Raw fingerprints for MATH prompts, before any standardization. Each small heat map is one of the eight features (for example attention to the first token, to the previous token, or the entropy of the attention) and rows are the heads of the last layer of the looped block, columns are iterations. Top: Ouro-1.4B (6 iterations). Bottom: Huginn (16 iterations). The summary numbers of Lens 4 do not give a broad view as much as the raw maps which show directly what a head keeps its role means. Both maps are horizontal stripes: each head keeps its own feature mix from first to last iteration. In Ouro-1.4B the one visible change (first-token attention jumping from zero to its final level) is the shared drift subtracted in the summary ratios. Huginn’s stripes are even more uniform. A looped block’s heads are best described by one fixed role each plus a small common adjustment at the loop’s start.

Figure 23: Similarity of hidden states across iterations. The figure presents the linear CKA between the hidden states of every pair of iterations, over all the generated answer tokens and at noise amplitudes as in the panel titles. For noise-free runs the first iteration of Ouro differs from all subsequent iterations while the rest of the iterations are nearly undistinguishable under linear CKA. Under noise injection, the second iteration in Ouro models becomes a stage of its own, while the late iterations still remain nearly undistinguishable. The iterations of LoopUS are undistinguishable under linear CKA for noise-free runs. With α = 12− 50 the distant iterations drift apart.

Figure 24: Exit gates under noise injection. Plots at the top: percentage of generated tokens whose exit probability (the sigmoid of the gate output) exceeds 0.5. At the bottom: mean exit probability. We note that the LoopUS model generates tokens with a default halting threshold of 0.9, but in our analysis we deliberately use a threshold 0.5 for all the three models. Under noise injection, the gate of Ouro-2.6B stops fewer tokens after the second iteration, despite its predictions becoming more confident, while the halting head of LoopUS stops more often.

Figure 18: Next-token probability distribution along the loop. Top plots present entropy while bottom plots display the top-1 probability of the distribution read out at each iteration. For α ≤ 2, the first iterations of Ouro models are less certain than on noise-free runs. For α ≥ 4, Ouro models are more certain than noise-free runs at every iteration. For α ≥ 8, the LoopUS model becomes less certain with every iteration.

Figure 19: Top-1 token changes under noise injection. Plots at the top present the percentage of the generated tokens whose top-1 token at iteration t is the same as at t− 1. At the bottom: KL(pt ∥ pt−1), the Kullback-Leibler divergence between consecutive next-token probability distributions after iteration t. For α ≥ 4, the Ouro models fix their top-1 token earlier than for noise-free runs. On the other hand, the LoopUS model decides early on the top-1 token. For α ≥ 8, it keeps changing its top-1 tokens along the loop.

Figure 20: Where does the generated token attend? The plots present the attention of a generated token to itself (top) and to the first generated token of an answer (bottom). The values are the averages over the heads of the last layer of the looped block. Attention is measured among the generated tokens only. For α ≥ 4, noise runs of Ouro models halve their self-attention in comparison to noise-free runs. Moreover, at the first iteration Ouro models put 13-43% of their attention on the first generated token. On the other hand, LoopUS shows a weaker and later version of both changes at α = 8− 17.

Figure 5: Lens 4: do attention heads switch roles across iterations? For every head of the last layer of the looped block we compute the attention fingerprint (App. B). (a) Movement ratio: how far fingerprints move across iterations relative to the gap between heads (value 0 is a fixed role, 1 means no identity). (b) Movement ratio after removing the drift shared by all heads. (c) Cross-prompt consistency of head changes: if the behavior of a head changes in the same way on every prompt (1) or differently on each prompt (0). Dots are means over the five datasets, faded bars are their ranges.

Figure 2: Lens 1: hidden-state trajectory and attention focus. (a) Share of tokens whose hidden state settles. (b) Top-1 flips per token. How often next most likely token changes along the loop. In (a) and (b) dots are means over MATH, arithmetic, harmful/benign prompts. Faded bars are the ranges. (c) Attention (log-scale) from the last prompt token to the answer span on HotpoQA, relative to uniform attention, against relative loop position t/(T−1). The value of 1 corresponds to uniform attention. Solid lines are carry loops and dashed are re-read loops.

Figure 3: Lens 2: when a token is decided. Share of MATH tokens whose top-1 prediction is already settled vs. relative loop position for: (a) prompt tokens and (b) answer tokens. A curve that starts high means most decisions are made in the first iteration. A curve that climbs slowly means the loop keeps changing its mind. All four generative sets are shown in Fig. 8.

Figure 15: Exit gates and next-token distributions under noise injection on AdvBench dataset. Plots (a,b) present the averaged change - noisy run minus clean run on the same prompts as the percentage of tokens whose exit probability exceeds 0.5 at each iteration. Noise injection makes Ouro-2.6B less willing to stop the iterations. Conversely, it makes LoopUS more willing to exit the loop earlier. Plots (c,d) present the Jensen-Shannon divergence between the noise-free and the noisy next-token distribution at each generated token position. For the carry loop, the divergence reaches high values from the very first tokens, while for the re-read loop it starts low and grows as the generated answers drift apart.

Figure 16: Analysis of internal states at the last iteration of the loop. The figure presents the averages over all generated answer tokens of noisy runs over all the investigated datasets. (a) Value of the hidden state norm relative to the corresponding values of noise-free runs. (b) Decay ratio (see Lens 1, B), computed from the mean step sizes ∥ht − ht−1∥ as the mean of the last w steps over the mean of the first w steps. Dotted horizontal line at value 0.25 corresponds to the chosen settling threshold. (c) Top-1 probability of the next-token distribution during the generation phase. (d) Attention of a generated token to itself. (e) Attention entropy (relative to noise-free runs). (f) Percentage of the variance of the hidden states on their first principal component. Parcae is not presented on purpose - in every run the first principal component of its state carries 47-99.8% of the whole variance. Carry loops are presented with solid lines and re-read loops with dashed lines. Carry loops do not change much up to α = 1, start to change significantly (bifurcate) between α = 1 and α = 2 and are in a completely different internal state for α ≥ 4 for Ouro (in LoopUS’s case - for α ≥ 8). Re-read loops stay close to their noise-free counterpart values even for large noise amplitudes α.

Figure 25: Small noise injections: token by token analysis of answer drif. The plot presents the comparison of noisy runs with noise-free runs at the same position of the answer (for the sake of demonstration, we truncate the answers to 128 tokens). The presented values are averages over the loop iterations and the seven prompt sets with α = 0.25 and α = 0.5. (a) For each token position - the percentage of prompts in which both runs (noise and noise-free) have the same top-1 token. (b) Jensen-Shannon divergence between noisy and noise-free runs on the next-token distributions. (c) Distance between hidden states relative to the norm of noise-free runs. We note that at the first positions the two runs nearly agree. Later, since every token that is decided differently changes the context of the subsequent tokens, the disagreement accumulates along the answer - faster for LoopUS, slower for Ouro.

Figure 22: Geometry of the hidden states. Plots at the top present the percentage of the variance of the hidden states, over all generated tokens, on their first principal component. At the bottom - the cosine similarity of the state after iteration t to the state after the first iteration. Under noise injection the states concentrate on fewer directions - the percentage of the variance on the first principal component rises two to three times with respect to the noise-free counterpart for Ouro from α ≥ 4. For α ≥ 8 the hidden state of LoopUS moves away from its first iteration.

Figure 21: Broadness and similarity of the heads’ attention. Plots at the top present attention entropy averaged over the heads. At the bottom - mean pairwise cosine similarity of their attention maps (agreement of the heads) at the first four iterations. For α ≥ 4, the heads of Ouro attend similarly at the first iteration (due to the attention sink - Fig. 20) and more broadly than noise-free runs.

Figure 14: Does the loop amplify or forget a perturbation? This figure presents the change of amplification pertt/pert0 rate of the hidden-state perturbation along the subsequent iterations on AdvBench prompts. pertt/pert0 is the mean distance between the noisy and the clean hidden state at iteration t, divided by its value at the first iteration (it0). A value above 1 means the difference between the two runs grows, a value below 1 suggest that the difference shrinks. The color of the line denotes the noise amplitude (the amplitudes differ between panels). We note that carry loops (a-c) amplify the perturbation, re-read loops (d-f) shrink it.

Figure 11: Effect of noise on safety-prompt answers. Stacked bars on three safety datasets (AdvBench, CValues, WildChat jailbreaks). For carry loops: answers with no noise injected (clean) and with noise of amplitude α=1, 2 and 8 times. For re-read loops: noise-free and with noise amplitutde α=8, on exactly the same prompts. Each answer is sorted into one of four groups: refuses, on-topic without a refusal phrase, fluent but off-topic, broken. Up to α=1 the carry loops answer as they do when clean. At α=2 the refusals of Ouro-1.4B shrink from 73% to 24%, but only a minority of the new on-topic non-refusal answers follow the harmful request (Sec. 4.5). The Thinking Ouro models refuse more, because they skip their reasoning and answer with a one-line refusal. At α=8 noise removes refusals from carry loops but produces broken or off-topic text, not harmful answers: e.g. clean Ouro-1.4B/2.6B refuse ∼70% and under noise injection 63-73% of the answers become broken. Re-read loops are unaffected.

Table 3: Lens 1 per prompt set: settling during token generation, flips and answer attention. Share of settling tokens, top-1 flips per token, and (HotpotQA) attention to the answer span at first and last iteration, for MATH, arithmetic, and harmful/benign. The ranking is the same on every set, so settling and flipping are model properties. Ouro-1.4B settles least (10-19%); all others settle on 86-100%. Attention to the answer grows significantly only in Ouro and Huginn, while LoopUS ends below uniform. Whether a loop focuses on the relevant input is modelspecific, so it has to be measured and cannot be taken for granted from the loop design alone.
Table 1: Investigation protocol and findings through the five lenses.

Table 6: Lens 3 in numbers: is the last iteration the best reader? All values on prompt tokens, averaged over five sets. Next-token accuracy at first, best, and last iteration. Best iteration per set presents for datasets MATH, GSM8K, Arithmetic, Harm/Benign, HotpotQA the iteration (counted from 1) with the highest accuracy. Log-loss last/first: value below 1 means that additional loops help. ECE is the expected calibration error at the first and last iteration. Fixed (broken): share of tokens wrong (right) at iteration 1 but right (wrong) at the end. Prompt tokens give a fair test of every iteration. A loop works best when the best and the last accuracy agree, log-loss is well below 1 and percentage of "fixed" prompts exceeds "broken" which is true for base Ouro, LoopUS, Huginn and false for both Ouro-Thinking models. LoopUS and Huginn fix ∼20% of tokens while breaking only 2%.

Table 4: Lens 2 per prompt set: decision timing and post-decision refinement. Per generative set: answer tokens decided at iteration 1. In subsequent columns are presented averaged values of: prompt tokens decided at iteration 1, post-decision KL share, and oracle compute savings. A high post-decision share means the loop mostly sharpens an already-made choice. Six models decide 61-93% at iteration 1, 73-88% of distribution change comes after the decision. LoopUS decides 90% by iteration 2 with the lowest post-decision share (0.35). Huginn needs iterations 8-11 (share 0.46).

Table 10: Noise sensitivity at every amplitude. Table presents six measures for noise-free runs and for each noise amplitude on three safety datasets (AdvBench, CValues, WildChat): word similarity, broken answers, fluent and on-topic answers, non-Latin-script answers, answers with a refusal phrase and answers that open a reasoning trace. We note that in carry loops every metrics collapses at amplitude α=4. In re-read loops the metrics on clean and noisy runs are almost equal. For carry models we note that they keep ≤4% similarity, the broken text rises to 46-89% and refusals almost disappear. Re-read models retain 53-78% similarity even at α=50.

Table 2: Model descriptions Loop: carry or re-read. T run: iterations per token at inference. Trained depth: fixed, adaptive, or random (mean shown). Block/other layers: number of layers inside the loop vs. non-iterated. Width: hidden state size. Exit gate: trained halting head. Noise enters at: tensor perturbed in Lens 5.

Table 5: Exit gates fire long after the answer is decided. Analysis performed only for gated models. The columns present the averaged values of: the decision iteration, gate-firing iteration, and the gap between these two. Both gates are very conservative: answers are fixed after 1.4-2.1 iterations on average, but gates wait until near the loop’s end. Ouro’s gate fires on averaged at iterations 3.2-4.1. LoopUS’s at iteration 18.7 of 20.

Table 7: Prompt-token accuracy per set: at first, best and last iterations. Each cell presents three accuracies on prompt tokens, at the first iteration, at the best iteration and at the last iteration on the five datasets. The "best-last" gap is what a model loses by reading at the end. The "best-first" gap is the loop’s maximum gain. For re-read loops, best and last agree within 0.01 on every set, they never lose by looping longer. For carry loops they often differ. Results show strong dependence on the model and the task. However, looping to the end is not harmful only for the re-read models.

Table 11: What the noisy answers at α = 2 say. We analyze the answers generated with noise at amplitude α = 2 on prompts on which refusal disappeared (on-topic without a refusal phrase) in spite of noise-free generation being a refusal. Safety prompts: all prompts with generated answers at α = 2 on the safety sets (AdvBench, CValues, WildChat). Read: answers selected (on-topic without a refusal phrase). Follows harmful request: the answer that does what was asked (percentage of all answers in brackets). Another request: a harmless answer to a misread or invented request. Reasoning trace: answers addressing the request but not reaching a conclusion within 128 tokens. Role-play: a WildChat-Jailbreak role-play whose content is not harmful but which the model refused to answer on a noise-free run. Other: echoed prompts, invented system prompts, hedges without a refusal phrase, harmless prompts answered helpfully and noisy answers whose noise-free generation counterparts were not refusals.
Table 9: Lens 4 per prompt set: heads keep their roles.

Table 8: Calibration along the loop and iteration-combination rules. The expected calibration error (ECE) at the first iteration, at the best-calibrated iteration (in brackets) when ECE is the lowest and at the last iteration. Results on prompts from MATH, GSM8K and arithmetic datasets. The last two columns are averaged over all five datasets and present the: (a) oracle accuracy, i.e. a token counts as correct if any iteration predicts it, and (b) the accuracy based on a majority vote over the top-1 tokens of all iterations. If different iterations make different mistakes, then combining all iterations by an oracle or majority voting might beat the last iteration. We note that the best-calibrated iteration is rarely the last for carry loops. The right answer is often visited, then abandoned, but the majority vote approach does not recover it. The oracle accuracy is 3-8 points above the best single iteration, but the vote never beats it. We conclude that there is useful information in the intermediate iterations, the extraction of which would require training a selecting model rather than simply averaging or voting.

papers.selection_reason: Looped LM architecture and latent reasoning inspection; relevant to LLM architecture advances.
papers.title: Monitoring latent reasoning in looped language models
papers.tldr: A mechanistic-interpretability protocol examines how looped language models reason, improve across iterations, and respond to prompt perturbations.

papers.abstract: Freshness shapes an LLM decision at the moment it is made; the action it commits to is latent, carried out later, in a changing world. We therefore introduce a timestamp theory of decision validity and a decision ledger that realises it. Six timestamps define a decision; a freshness ceiling bounds what up-to-date evidence guarantees at action time, placing the remaining risk in information published afterwards. Accuracy then factorises into two capabilities: routing, which delivers that information to affected decisions before their revision deadlines, and temporal judgment, which reads it for the time of action. The ledger is persistent state holding each decision's times, evidence and background knowledge, indexed by watch conditions written at decision time. Controlled decision streams with exact labels confirm four predictions across five LLMs, from 8B to frontier scale: freshness alone yields exactly the accuracy the ceiling predicts; models act on decisive news once it arrives, so accuracy follows routing; the ledger's index sets what routing reaches, and watch conditions reach indirect dependencies at low exposure; and the remaining errors concern when a change takes effect. Freshness makes a decision right when it is made; routing and temporal judgment keep it right when it is carried out.
authors: Ayoub Merimi, Souhail Bakkali, Abdeljalil Sakat
bullets: The paper distinguishes decision freshness at creation from validity at later execution in a changing world.
A six-timestamp theory defines decision validity and a freshness ceiling for evidence available at action time.
The ledger persistently stores decision times, evidence, background knowledge, and watch conditions for targeted updates.
Accuracy decomposes into routing new information to affected decisions and temporal judgment about when changes take effect.
Controlled streams across five LLMs support the theory: watch conditions can capture indirect dependencies, while remaining errors involve temporal effects.

figures.caption: Figure 4: The two factors of Eq. 3 on INDIRECT, one point per router. (a) Needed switches against routing recall: on the diagonal, the model switches exactly when decisive news arrives. (b) Decisions kept among those that should stand, against the items delivered to them; the points at two items are the related-news oracle.
Figure 2: The decision ledger. Routing uses no model calls; the model is called again only for decisions that receive news. What the entry indexes sets what the router can reach.

Figure 1: A decision from the INDIRECT stream on its six timestamps. Retrieval at decision time shrinks the freshness gap ∆fresh. The notice that settles the decision is published inside the execution gap ∆act, is in effect at action time, and names only the substation that supplies the restaurant’s district; background knowledge in the ledger routes it to the decision before the revision deadline. Grey dots are other notices in the window.

Figure 3: Decisive notices delivered on INDIRECT, by how the notice refers to the chosen option (16 decisions each; unlabelled bars reach 100%). The decision text reaches the option’s name and its stated dependency; the dossier and watch conditions extend the reach to other names and upstream entities.

Table 3: INDIRECT: final-decision accuracy (%) on 128 balanced decisions. Recall: decisive notices delivered to their decision (%); Traps: notices delivered to a decision whose dossier mentions their entity in an irrelevant role (of 96). Claude writes the watch conditions for every model. Bold: best router without gold labels.

Table 4: Judgment in isolation (P4): decisions kept (%) when the oracle delivers exactly the related news and none of it changes the best option. On INDIRECT, each row except the last covers 16 decisions per model.
Table 5: Decision D0011 under every router: notices delivered, whether they include the decisive notice and a trap, and each model’s answer (bold: correct).

Table 6: Needed switches made and decisions kept on INDIRECT, by how the decisive notice refers to the option and by the related news a decision received (%, mean over the three models with complete answers; 16 decisions per row and model). Routing sets which switches are possible; judgment sets the rest.

Table 7: Exact McNemar tests on INDIRECT. W–L: decisions router A gets right and router B gets wrong, and the reverse; 128 decisions per model, pooled over the three models with complete answers. p-values are two-sided and uncorrected.

Table 2: STRESS: final-decision accuracy (%) of Claude Sonnet 4.6, GPT-6.1 Sol and Qwen3-235B on the same 75 decisions. Items: new items delivered per decision; Rec.: share of decisive item–decision pairs delivered; Tok.: Claude Sonnet 4.6 input tokens per decision for the re-decision calls (thousands). Bold: best router without gold labels.
Table 1: The three conditions. A decision’s revision window holds dozens to hundreds of items, of which a handful concern it.

Table 8: Qwen3-8B on DIRECT. Recall: share of decision-changing items delivered to the decision they change; Implicit: the same for items that reach the option only through a dependency; Precision: share of delivered items that concern the chosen option. Switch: named / dependency: share of decisions that should switch and did, when the evidence names the option or reaches it only through a dependency; Keep: share of decisions that should stand and did. Tokens: prompt tokens spent on routing and re-deciding, including writing watch conditions. p: exact McNemar test on per-decision correctness against the most accurate practical router (bold; oracle excluded). Routing recall and precision for None, Name match, Oracle and All follow from the stream and are identical across models.

Table 11: Claude Sonnet 4.6 on a second STRESS sample (73 decisions). Keep: accuracy on decisions that should stand (%); Needless: switches on those decisions. The table lists the routers run on this sample.
Table 10: INDIRECT routing as the number K of decisions each notice is sent to varies: decisive pairs delivered (%) and lexical traps delivered.

Table 9: Needless switches (%) on decisions that should stand, by the related news published in their revision window. Late change: a change to the option or its dependency that starts only after the activity ends; Harmless only: news about the option or its dependency that does not affect it. Name: name match; Sim.: similarity to the decision; Watch: watch conditions.

papers.abstract: Training-free diffusion-based compression methods repurpose the generative priors of a diffusion or a flow model to compress data without retraining them as task-specific codecs. Recent codebook-based approaches such as Turbo-DDCM achieve strong perceptual quality at ultra-low bitrates, but their reliance on dense Gaussian codebooks remains costly in both memory and computation, and scales poorly with the large latent dimensions of modern image and video generators. Their combinatorial bitstream encoding further becomes computationally heavy at this scale. We introduce H-DDCM, a scalable generative compression framework that replaces Gaussian codebooks with implicit randomized Hadamard dictionaries. The fast Walsh-Hadamard transform allows for implicitly synthesizing full-dimensional dictionaries with $O(d \log d)$ compute for projection and reconstruction and $O(d)$ memory, without materializing the full-dimensional dictionary. We further introduce an efficient table-free lexicographic coding scheme that makes combinatorial encoding practical at larger dimensions. Beyond images, we adapt the framework to an autoregressive video flow model and develop a streaming compression scheme that periodically re-encodes recently reconstructed frames into a fresh KV-cache prefix, preserving temporal context across segments at no additional transmitted bits. This enables long-form, close to real-time generative video compression on a single GPU. Across image and video benchmarks, H-DDCM achieves competitive rate-distortion-perception performance while substantially reducing the memory and computational overhead of codebook-based training-free generative compression.
authors: Or Ronai, Vladimir Kulikov, Tomer Michaeli
bullets: Targets the memory, computation, and encoding costs of codebook-based generative compression at large latent dimensions.
Uses randomized Hadamard dictionaries with fast Walsh-Hadamard transforms, requiring O(d log d) projection/reconstruction compute and O(d) memory.
Introduces table-free lexicographic coding to make combinatorial bitstream encoding practical at larger dimensions.
Extends the framework to autoregressive video with streaming re-encoding of reconstructed frames to preserve temporal context without extra transmitted bits.
Reports competitive rate-distortion-perception performance with substantially lower codebook-related overhead, including long-form near-real-time video compression on a single GPU.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Quantitative comparison of image compression methods. We compare H-DDCM with training-free diffusion-based and other compression methods in terms of rate, distortion, and perception. Distortion is measured by PSNR, perceptual quality by FID (presented in log-scale), and runtime by round-trip encoding and decoding time. GPU memory refers to the excess memory used by training-free methods for dictionary storage, while tables memory refers to disk storage required by Turbo-DDCM’s precomputed combinatorial tables. The first row corresponds to training-free methods utilizing the SD 2.1 backbone (512 × 512, d = 214) and other compression methods. The second row corresponds to FLUX backbone (1024 × 1024, d = 218). The dashed gray vertical line denotes the VAE encoder-decoder bound. H-DDCM achieves competitive results on the ratedistortion-perception tradeoff, all the while being the fastest training-free method, avoiding explicit codebook materialization. Error bars represent the standard error of the mean (SEM).

Figure 3: Quantitative comparison of video compression methods. We compare H-DDCM OC (B = 8) with training-free methods using the same CF backbone and other compression baselines in terms of rate, distortion and perception. Distortion is measured by PSNR, and perceptual quality is measured by DOVER and FVMD (presented in log-scale). Encoding and decoding FPS report compression and decompression throughput, and are compared among methods using the CF backbone. H-DDCM achieves competitive rate-distortion-perception performance among the CF-based training-free methods while providing the highest measured encoding and decoding throughput, without codebooks materialization. Error bars represent the standard error of the mean (SEM).

Figure 2: Qualitative comparison of training-free diffusion-based image compression methods (FLUX on DIV2K). H-DDCM is the fastest and preserves visual quality and fidelity to the original image, while avoiding the memory overhead of an explicit codebook.

Figure 4: Qualitative comparison of video-compression methods. The example is taken from the UVG dataset at 832×480 resolution. Our method preserves source content and temporal consistency while providing the highest measured throughput among the evaluated CF-based methods. The space-time (ST) slice, which shows the temporal evolution of the pixels marked by the dashed line, reveals temporal discontinuities at ZeroGVC’s I-frame boundaries.

papers.abstract: Broadcast spraying remains the dominant method of disease control in greenhouse tomato production, yet it treats healthy and diseased tissue alike, exposes workers to hazardous aerosols, and depends on operator skill. This paper presents MARTS (Modular Agricultural Robot for Targeted Spraying), a low-cost robotic platform that closes the loop from plant-level disease detection to leaf-localised spray delivery in commercial greenhouses. MARTS integrates a Clearpath Husky A200 mobile base, a UR5 manipulator, a novel modular spraying end-effector built around a single 12 V micro-diaphragm pump, and a wrist-mounted Intel RealSense D435 RGB-D camera. Disease detection reuses our previously published Tomato Leaf Disease Vision Language Model (TLDVLM; Grounding DINO, SAM-2 and LoRA-tuned BLIP-2, 97.27% accuracy over 10 classes); this work focuses on actuation, control and system integration. A ROS pipeline lifts detections into 3D targets, generates collision-aware nozzle poses at a 120 mm stand-off using fitted leaf normals, and scales pump pulse duration to lesion area. Water-sensitive paper calibration showed a linear pulse-volume relationship (R^2 = 0.994). In MuJoCo simulation, an adaptive base-repositioning strategy achieved 100% coverage of 18 waypoints with a maximum orientation error of 1.1 deg. Deployed at the SILAL commercial greenhouse (Al Ain, UAE) on cherry tomatoes under natural infection, MARTS treated 312 diseased leaves in 12 autonomous trials with 92.4% targeting success, 18.7 mm mean spray-centre error, 6.1% adjacent-leaf overspray, and a 71% reduction in pesticide volume versus broadcast spraying. Mean cycle time was 4.8 s per leaf, and the spraying subsystem costs USD 412, 6-10x lower than comparable systems, showing that accurate leaf-level targeting is achievable on commodity hardware.
authors: Rajmeet Singh, Manveen Kaur, Yusuf Adamu, Lochan Kshetrimayum, Irfan Hussain
bullets: Addresses broadcast spraying’s waste, worker exposure, and dependence on operator skill by treating only diseased tissue.
Combines a mobile base, UR5 manipulator, RGB-D vision, and a modular pump-based end-effector in a ROS control pipeline.
Generates collision-aware nozzle poses from 3D leaf geometry and scales spray duration to lesion area.
In 12 commercial-greenhouse trials, it treated 312 leaves at 4.8 seconds per leaf, with 18.7 mm mean spray-centre error and 6.1% adjacent-leaf overspray.
The spraying subsystem costs USD 412, supporting deployment on commodity hardware; evaluation focused on naturally infected cherry tomatoes in one commercial greenhouse.

papers.abstract: Do language models carry information about narrative events before writing them, and how far ahead? We examine narrative lookahead through salient, state-changing events rather than tokens or response-level attributes. We extract 23,355 LLM-annotated events from 2,000 stories generated by four open-weight LLMs, labeling them along three nonexclusive dimensions of change: within agents, between agents, and in the story world, with human validation on a subset. Event segmentation and plot-independent labels enable comparisons across stories at horizons measured in events rather than in tokens. At event ends, we probe hidden states for upcoming event types and compare predictions with text-only predictors using matched prefixes. Across four models, future event types are decodable above prevalence baselines for at least four subsequent events, but probes significantly outperform both primary text-only predictors only for the next event. In exploratory steering with OLMo-3.1-32B, a probe-derived direction shifts the proportion of the target event type in both intended directions at higher strengths. Our event-level approach links the prediction of future narrative developments to interventions that reshape subsequent event composition.
authors: Donghoon Jung, Min Kim, Seojin Choi, Songeun Chae, Seohyon Jung
bullets: Studies 23,355 annotated events from 2,000 stories generated by four open-weight LLMs, using event-level rather than token-level horizons.

Hidden-state probes outperform matched text-only predictors significantly only for the immediately upcoming event.
In exploratory steering with OLMo-3.1-32B, probe-derived directions shift the frequency of target event types in both intended directions.
Human validation supports the event labels, but steering results are exploratory and demonstrated with one model.

papers.abstract: Visually similar actions can produce contact loss, jamming, slippage, or irreversible damage, while tactile feedback may arrive after a critical transition. Contact-rich manipulation therefore requires generative policies to anticipate and evaluate whether candidate actions will produce desirable contact outcomes, then adjust action generation before execution. We present ForeTac, a predictive contact-guidance framework organized as a represent-predict-evaluate-guide loop. ForeTac encodes the current tactile state, predicts the tactile consequences of a candidate action sequence, and evaluates the predicted trajectory using a contact-quality objective learned from successful and failed physical interactions. At deployment, its gradient propagates through the tactile predictor to guide action generation while the pretrained model parameters remain frozen. We evaluate ForeTac on four real-robot tasks (planar and curved-surface wiping, card swiping, and fragile-object grasping) with diffusion and flow-matching policies. Across these tasks, ForeTac raises the average task success rate from 36.3% to 71.3% and the average contact success rate (CSR) from 20.0% to 66.3% compared with vision-only Diffusion Policy. Component analyses support the tactile representation and action-conditioned foresight, and show that predicted touch preserves contact-quality ordering. Project page: https://foretac.github.io/.
authors: Zhiyuan Chen, Shuai Chen, Haoran Zhou, Yizhe Zhao, Kaiyuan Yang, Zhixiang Duan, Shaoqing Xu, Ran Cao, Diyun Xiang, Yangwei You

Evaluated on four real-robot tasks with diffusion and flow-matching policies.
Improves average task success from 36.3% to 71.3% and contact success from 20.0% to 66.3% versus vision-only Diffusion Policy.

papers.abstract: AI companions provide users with emotional support and ongoing companionship, but their sustained relational interactions also introduce distinct safety risks. Prior work largely targets general harms or specific companion platforms and risk categories, while relying on manually collected conversations, limiting scalable and user-grounded evaluation and mitigation. To address this, we introduce CompanionSafe, a unified evaluation-to-mitigation framework for AI companion safety. Its evaluation component, CompanionEval, provides scalable multi-turn evaluation by constructing 1,300 relationally grounded settings from diverse personas, matched companion characters, and dialogue scenarios across four turn tiers. Its mitigation component, CompanionGuard, converts benchmark-exposed failures into turn-localized supervision for companion-specific risk detection. Our results show that even strong LLMs and existing guard models remain vulnerable to companion-specific relational harms, while both closed- and open-source models exhibit increasing safety risks as interactions become longer. Together, CompanionEval and CompanionGuard form a practical evaluation-to-mitigation loop for AI companion safety, turning relational safety failures exposed during multi-turn interaction into supervision for companion-specific guardrails.
authors: Xinyang Liao, Lingyu Li, Kaicheng Shen, Yang Yao, Na Lu, Yan Teng, Xia Hu
bullets: Targets relational harms in sustained AI companion interactions, which general safety evaluations may miss.

CompanionGuard turns benchmark-identified failures into turn-localized supervision for companion-specific risk detection.
Experiments find vulnerabilities in both strong LLMs and existing guard models, with risks increasing over longer interactions.
Provides a practical evaluation-to-mitigation framework, though its scope is limited to the risks and settings represented in the benchmark.

papers.abstract: Wheel-legged robots operating in outdoor spaces shared with humans require accurate perception, socially compliant navigation, future-scene reasoning, and scene reconstruction. However, existing datasets typically support these capabilities in isolation and rarely provide dense spatial and behavior-level supervision on real wheel-legged platforms. We introduce LynxScenes, a large-scale real-world dataset and benchmark collected with a LYNX M20 wheel-legged robot. It contains approximately 100K 30-s navigation clips spanning 833.6 h and 3,294.7 km, with 3.0M annotated frames. The synchronized recordings include four fisheye cameras, dual LiDARs, IMU, odometry, and robot states. Annotations comprise 20.82M oriented 3D boxes across 27 categories, 13.89M road-structure annotations, and 20 navigation instructions organized into three layers and aligned with continuous future trajectories. LynxScenes supports four complementary tasks: instruction-conditioned trajectory prediction, BEV-based perception of 3D objects and road structures, future scene prediction, and multi-view scene reconstruction. For trajectory prediction, we further introduce a log-replay-based pseudo-closed-loop evaluator that measures safety, progress, and instruction compliance beyond trajectory imitation. Extensive evaluations across representative navigation, perception, world-model, and reconstruction methods reveal substantial remaining challenges in close-range outdoor robot navigation. The dataset and evaluation toolkit are planned for public release.
authors: Jun Tian, Hao Wu, Ruo Chen, Yili Liao, Hongyi Lin, Jincheng Yu, Chao Li, Yingjie Niu
bullets: Collected on a LYNX M20 robot across approximately 100K navigation clips, 833.6 hours, and 3,294.7 km, with 3.0M annotated frames.
Provides synchronized fisheye-camera, LiDAR, IMU, odometry, and robot-state data with dense 3D object, road-structure, instruction, and future-trajectory annotations.
Supports four tasks: instruction-conditioned trajectory prediction, BEV perception, future scene prediction, and multi-view scene reconstruction.
Introduces a log-replay pseudo-closed-loop evaluator measuring trajectory safety, progress, and instruction compliance.
Evaluations indicate substantial challenges remain, particularly for close-range outdoor robot navigation; public release is planned.

papers.abstract: Deep research (DR) agents address open-ended information needs through multi-step reasoning, long-horizon web search, and evidence synthesis. However, existing benchmarks primarily focus on academic research or synthetic tasks, leaving DR agents' capabilities in real-world life and professional productivity settings insufficiently evaluated. To bridge this gap, we introduce LifeSearch, a challenging benchmark comprising 203 Chinese and English tasks derived from real-user query seeds across 7 concrete life and productivity domains. With more than 4,500 hours of human annotation, we construct over 4,000 expert-written, fine-grained rubrics, covering both report-content criteria for coverage and accuracy and concrete criteria specifying values, units, dates, and URLs. We conduct extensive experiments on 12 advanced DR agents under a unified evaluation harness, systematically analyzing their performance patterns and failure modes. We find that even the best-performing frontier agent, GPT-5.6 Sol, achieves a score of only 63.4%, leaving substantial room for improvement on realistic life and professional DR tasks. We select the grading configuration by comparing candidate LLM judges against human rubric labels, and a human ranking study shows strong alignment between aggregate benchmark scores and human judgments (Spearman's $\rho = 0.89$, Kendall's $\tau = 0.81$). LifeSearch provides a rigorous evaluation framework and foundation for advancing DR agents toward real-world life and productivity.
authors: Yibo Wang, Senjie Jin, Yansong Ning, Xinbing Liang, Haotian Luo, Jiazheng Zhang, Yuxuan He, Will Wu, Clarenceai

Evaluates 12 advanced deep research agents with a unified harness and analyzes their performance patterns and failure modes.
The top-performing reported agent scores 63.4%, indicating substantial room for improvement.
Benchmark scores align strongly with human judgments, supporting LifeSearch’s evaluation validity.

papers.abstract: Ambiguous or incomplete task specifications complicate both execution and clarification for language-model agents. Yet agents' responses to these information gaps remain poorly characterized across models and execution harnesses. We present AM-Bench, a benchmark built from 48 tasks adapted from Terminal-Bench 2.0 and Harness-Bench. Each task includes a fully specified reference and six variants spanning ambiguous or missing goals, context, and constraints. We evaluate every pairing of five models and four harnesses over 20,160 runs. Our results reveal distinct execution deficits: goal gaps hinder completion, context gaps increase token use, and constraint gaps weaken compliance without necessarily preventing completion. Missingness lowers success more than ambiguity in all three domains. These effects also reshape system comparisons: advantages under complete information need not persist, and rankings depend on model $\times$ harness pairings and the evaluation criterion -- completion, success, or repeat consistency. Estimates based on observed clarification requests and matched fully specified runs further suggest that clarification could recover unfinished work while leaving most constraint violations unresolved. Together, these findings motivate joint model-harness evaluation across information conditions and targeted clarification of unresolved requirements before dependent actions. To support future research on agents under task underspecification, we provide the AM-Bench project repository at https://github.com/s4-lab-cuhksz/AM-Bench.git.

papers.abstract: AI has become increasingly helpful in scientific discovery, yet human expert review remains essential for those problems without reliable automated evaluation, posing a fundamental challenge as candidate generation scales beyond available review capacity. This paper studies verification under limited human effort, where rare valid solutions need to be prioritized while invalid candidates should be filtered out to reduce human workload. We adopt the one-sided verification objective that maximizes the rejection rate of invalid solutions (TNR) under a constraint on the false-rejection rate of valid ones (FNR), making human review cost an explicit term to minimize. Drawing on the intuition that verifying a specific error can be easier than discovering one, we introduce OSVerify, an algorithmic framework that decouples error proposal from error validation. The error proposer searches for errors in solutions across different granularities by hierarchical decomposition, while the validator distinguishes substantial errors from minor or hallucinated ones. Experiments on competition- and research-level benchmarks show that OSVerify reduces the number of human reviews of invalid solutions by 46% on average compared to voting baselines under the same empirical low FNR constraint. Our post-training of the validator further improves the reduction to 57%. As high-impact real-world use cases, we apply OSVerify to identify errors in published research papers that are subsequently confirmed by the original authors and help resolve three Langlands open conjectures that are confirmed by experts, demonstrating its utility to facilitate human-AI research collaboration.
authors: Fan Nie, Haotian Ye, Shurui Liu, Zihao Wang, Stefano Ermon, James Zou
bullets: Targets one-sided verification: maximize rejection of invalid candidates while constraining false rejection of valid solutions.
Separates error proposal from error validation using hierarchical search across solution granularities and a validator that filters substantial from minor or hallucinated errors.
Reduces human reviews of invalid solutions by 46% on average versus voting baselines, improving to 57% with validator post-training under the same empirical low-FNR constraint.
Demonstrated on competition- and research-level benchmarks, published papers, and three Langlands open conjectures confirmed by experts.
Scope: designed for settings where reliable automated evaluation is unavailable and expert review is limited.

papers.abstract: Autoresearch systems increasingly undertake entire research projects. In practice, scientific research requires systems to pursue multiple interdependent claims through a continuous, multi-stage workflow and revise experiments as evidence accumulates. Existing evaluations of autoresearch systems, however, typically score isolated tasks or final artifacts, leaving these process-level capabilities largely unmeasured. We therefore introduce ResearchFlow-Eval, a fine-grained framework for assessing continuous scientific execution and iteration at both the stage and claim levels. Each evaluation is grounded in a published anchor paper, from which we derive stage-specific rubrics that decompose each research stage into dimensions and separately scored rubric items. Using these rubrics, we score each research stage and examine experimental execution in detail, focusing on multi-claim completion and revisions across attempts. We apply the evaluation framework to general-purpose agent harnesses, skill-augmented harnesses, and systems with research-specific orchestration. Across all evaluated systems, experimental execution consistently lags behind design and planning. Within execution, systems struggle to produce high-quality results and meet claim requirements, and repeated attempts rarely yield measurable improvements. Moreover, neither skill augmentation nor research-specific orchestration reliably yields higher scores. ResearchFlow-Eval thus extends autoresearch evaluation beyond isolated, single-objective runs to continuous workflows in which systems pursue multiple claims and refine their work across iterations.
authors: Peng Jiang (Tsinghua University), Dongyang Li (Tsinghua University), Quanying Liu (Southern University of Science,Technology), Xiaoxuan Jia (Tsinghua University)
bullets: Evaluates continuous scientific execution at both research-stage and claim levels.
Derives fine-grained, stage-specific rubrics from published anchor papers, with separately scored items.
Assesses general-purpose, skill-augmented, and research-orchestrated agent systems.
Finds consistent gaps in experimental execution, including weak results, unmet claim requirements, and limited gains across repeated attempts.
Skill augmentation and research-specific orchestration do not reliably improve evaluation scores.

papers.abstract: Scaling recursive self-improvement requires additional computation to produce useful research progress in reaching persistent objectives. Intuitively, more researcher agents can explore more hypotheses, but early evaluation scores might misrepresent their promise, shared findings could lose their applicability conditions, and useful procedures could remain confined to completed investigations. In this paper, we present AReaL-RSI, a framework for organizing a persistent research team of agents without updating backbone LLM weights. We formulate the scaling problem in terms of evaluated outcomes and whole-system resource expenditure. Concretely, a leader agent selects task-appropriate research orientations and guides ongoing investigations; conditional memory sharing distinguishes unresolved problems from supported findings and enables recipient adaptation. During recursive evolution, after each campaign, evidence-based review revises researcher orientation, knowledge, and skills for later campaigns. Experiments compare AReaL-RSI with Codex-Goal on downstream harness optimization, GPU kernel optimization, and AI research tasks using two backbones. Under the reported resource allocations, AReaL-RSI improves Terminal Bench performance by 2.2 percentage points for each backbone and increases mean KernelBench speedup by 32.2-36.8%; further scalability comparisons favor the design of AReaL-RSI over native scaling: combining experience sharing with specialized researcher roles yields 1.9-27.5% lower kernel latency than independent exploration and 1.3-33.9% lower latency than sharing alone across all seven comparable task-backbone pairs.
authors: Wenhao Zhou, Jiajun Song, Haitao Wang, Zipeng Qiu, Yingqi Peng, Ruida Xu, Jiale Li, Wenshuang Li, Shusheng Xu, Wei Dong, Hao Dai, Tongkai Yang, Yi Gao, Binhang Yuan

Evaluated on downstream harness optimization, GPU kernel optimization, and AI research tasks with two backbone models.
Reports higher Terminal Bench performance, greater KernelBench speedups, and lower kernel latency than independent exploration or sharing alone.

papers.abstract: Scaling interactive environments is important for training long-horizon agents through reinforcement learning. These environments often require further testing and refinement after initial generation, and correcting defects in a task may also require updating its work context and verifier. However, existing construction pipelines offer limited support for such iterative refinement while keeping these components aligned. We introduce WorkRover, a framework for training long-horizon cowork agents through recursive environment evolution. Its harness-driven synthesis enables construction agents to jointly build and validate semantically aligned work contexts, executable tasks, and evidence-grounded verifiers, adapting their actions to workspace state and execution feedback rather than following a fixed construction workflow. To support environment evolution, we introduce Factorial Compatibility Replay (FCR), which uses rollout feedback to evaluate combinations of component revisions through dependency-closed replay and selects the smallest validated repair among tested candidates while preserving task requirements and evaluation constraints. To provide finer-grained training signals, we propose Verifier-to-Turn Credit Assignment (VTCA), which augments trajectory-level GRPO advantages with signals from deterministic workspace-progress checks and assigns a bounded share of positive-progress credit to prerequisite turns using recorded tool-output and artifact dependencies. Using WorkRover, we post-train Qwen3.5-35B-A3B to obtain WorkRover-35B-A3B and evaluate it on several cowork-agent benchmarks. Its reported scores exceed those of Qwen3.5-35B-A3B by 26.27 percentage points on JobBench, 29.32 percentage points on OfficeQA Pro, and 413.25 Elo points on GDPval v2. These results suggest that WorkRover offers a promising foundation for scalable training of long-horizon cowork agents.

papers.abstract: General-purpose robot manipulation policies learn short-horizon skills effectively, but degrade rapidly on long-horizon tasks. Existing benchmarks cannot isolate failures because task horizon is either too short or entangled with scene and object variations. We propose LADDER, a long-horizon robot manipulation benchmark scaling from 1 to 10 subgoals within the same environment over three suites (SimplerEnv-Long, RobotArena-$\infty$-Long, and RoboLab-Long), 145 tasks, eight categories, two embodiments, and 2,024 simulated episodes per system. We evaluate two orchestration paradigms: text subgoals for learned low-level policies (VoLo) and tool selection orchestration (CaP-X, GPT-Policy, PSP-Agent, TiPToP). Given the full instruction directly, low-level policies achieve 85.4% on single-subgoal tasks, but drop to near zero on extended tasks. While orchestration remedies this, it remains bounded by physical execution errors of the low-level policy rather than high-level planning and achieves only ~25%. Tool selection orchestration with GPT-Policy on GPT-6 Astra significantly outperforms learned-policy methods, but incurs significant time and cost budget and succeeds only ~62%. Real-world experiments across two embodiments confirm the collapse of the low-level policy and the gain from orchestration. Project website: https://ladder.insait.ai

GPT-Policy with GPT-6 Astra reaches about 62% through tool selection, but requires substantial time and cost.
Real-world tests confirm both low-level policy collapse and the benefits of orchestration.

papers.abstract: Long-term memory has become a core component of large language model (LLM) agents. As agents accumulate personal information over long-term use, users increasingly ask them to delete sensitive or outdated facts. A memory system should honor such requests. It should remove exactly what was requested and keep the rest of its memory intact. However, existing memory benchmarks evaluate only memory writing, retrieval, and organization, so whether agents can forget at the user's explicit request remains under-evaluated. To address this gap, we propose Bemula, the first benchmark dedicated to memory unlearning. It comprises 50 multi-session dialogue instances, 135 forget requests of six types, and 1,742 test questions. Each dialogue has a control version without the requests, so that only systems that have stored the target can earn credit for forgetting. Across the paired versions, five test suites measure storage, removal of the requested information, preservation of unrelated memories, relearning of similar facts, and resistance to extraction attacks. On Bemula, we evaluate six mainstream memory systems under three backbone LLMs, together with the Full Context LLM on two of them. The results are negative. Across all evaluated systems and backbones, no system passes more than 1.5% of forget requests end to end, and most pass none at all. These systems either leave the requested information extractable under simple attacks or delete far more than requested. Memory unlearning therefore remains an open challenge for agent memory design. We release our data and code at https://github.com/Nboxff/bemula-benchmark.

Tests six memory systems with three backbone LLMs, plus Full Context LLM on two backbones.
No evaluated system passes more than 1.5% of forget requests end to end; failures involve residual extraction or excessive deletion.

papers.abstract: In this paper, our goal is to represent text embeddings as sketches for three main reasons. First, to visualize text representation and to explore their potential their potential for AI explainability. Second, to investigate the potential benefits of the sketch-based representation for information retrieval. Third, to explore their potential for reasoning, drawing inspiration from the concept of mental imagery. We propose a sketch-based visual grounding framework that transforms text representations into visual topographic sketches. Our approach aims to emphasis the semantics content encoded in the text embeddings through the corresponding sketch. Evaluations are conducted on the MS-COCO dataset to examine the utility of these sketches for text retrieval. The comparative study of SBERT and Sketch-based method reveals that SBERT retains an advantage in strict top-1 retrieval accuracy while achieving comparable performance to the sketch-based method in top-5 retrieval. A cascaded approach combining SBERT and the sketch-based method outperforms SBERT alone, suggesting that the Sketch-based representation could offer significant potential for information retrieval if trained directly on text.
authors: Slimane Larabi
bullets: Represents text embeddings as sketches to make semantic content more visually interpretable and explore AI explainability.
Investigates whether visual, sketch-based representations can support information retrieval and reasoning inspired by mental imagery.
Evaluated on MS-COCO for text retrieval using SBERT and the proposed sketch-based method.
SBERT performs better at strict top-1 retrieval, while sketch-based retrieval is comparable at top-5.
Combining SBERT with the sketch-based method in a cascade outperforms SBERT alone; direct training on text is identified as future potential.

papers.abstract: Vision Transformers achieve strong performance but incur high computational costs from quadratic token interactions. Training-free token reduction methods improve efficiency, but their robustness remains underexplored. We propose Prune-and Merge ViT, a training-free framework for off-the-shelf models. It combines class attention-based pruning with similarity-based merging to reduce redundancy while preserving semantic information. To evaluate robustness we introduce two metrics. Relative Accuracy Drop (RAD) measures relative accuracy degradation under transformations, and Prediction Flip Rate (PFR) quantifies prediction consistency. On pretrained ViT and DeiT, Prune-and-Merge reduces computation competitively while maintaining robustness and better accuracy than existing token reduction methods. Our analysis suggests that hybrid token reduction does not introduce hallucination-like behavior and preserves prediction stability for common image transformations.
authors: Vatsal, Soumil Malhotra, Priyanshu Chahal, Sanjeev Kumar
bullets: Addresses the quadratic cost of token interactions and limited understanding of robustness in training-free token reduction.
Uses class-attention pruning to remove less-important tokens and similarity-based merging to reduce redundancy.
Introduces Relative Accuracy Drop (RAD) and Prediction Flip Rate (PFR) to assess robustness under image transformations.
Evaluated on pretrained ViT and DeiT models, it achieves competitive compute reduction with better accuracy than existing token-reduction methods.
Finds that hybrid token reduction preserves prediction stability and does not produce hallucination-like behavior for common transformations.

papers.abstract: World action models (WAMs) built on pretrained video generation models adapt quickly to new robotic tasks, but they forget previously learned tasks under sequential fine-tuning. Experience replay (ER) mitigates such forgetting by rehearsing data of previous tasks, yet this data is often unavailable in robotics, where a policy is deployed as weights only and its training data is not shared along with it. In this work, we ask whether a WAM can achieve data-free continual learning by regenerating its own past. Our key observation is that a WAM can indeed autoregressively regenerate complete rollouts of previously learned tasks and replay them to mitigate forgetting. However, replaying such raw rollouts still lags far behind replaying real data, which we attribute to two issues. First, the WAM is unable to recognize task completion and keeps generating purposeless motion after the task is done. Second, under open-loop generation, the generated actions gradually drift away from the generated observations. To address both issues, we present rectified generative replay (R$^2$-WAM), which truncates generated rollouts at task completion with an agentic evaluator and filters out rollouts whose actions are physically inconsistent with the observations. On the four LIBERO suites and five real-world tasks, R$^2$-WAM reduces forgetting by over 90% relative to sequential fine-tuning and nearly matches ER without accessing any data from previous tasks. Our analysis further reveals that forgetting in WAMs concentrates in inverse dynamics modeling: a forgotten WAM still produces visually plausible observations of previous tasks while its generated actions fail.
authors: Kaipeng Fang, Hangxu Liu, Chaojian Shi, Yunsong Zhou, Hongzi Zhu, Minyi Guo, Jingkuan Song, Lianli Gao
bullets: Problem: Sequentially fine-tuning world action models on new robotic tasks causes forgetting, while prior-task training data may be unavailable.
Method: The model autoregressively regenerates past-task rollouts, truncates them at task completion, and filters action–observation inconsistencies.
Contribution: Rectified generative replay (R²-WAM) supports continual learning without storing or accessing previous data.
Result: Across four LIBERO suites and five real-world tasks, it reduces forgetting by over 90% versus sequential fine-tuning and nearly matches experience replay.
Finding: Forgetting is concentrated in inverse-dynamics modeling; observations can remain visually plausible while generated actions fail.

papers.abstract: Closed-loop evaluation of end-to-end (E2E) driving systems typically relies on generating sensor observations and re-processing them through the perception encoder, introducing substantial computational cost and a sim2real gap between simulated and real sensor observations. In this paper, we ask a more fundamental question: is image-space simulation necessary for closed-loop evaluation of E2E driving systems? We propose FlowSim, a rendering-free simulation paradigm that predicts the internal latent representation directly from a previous latent and target-frame symbolic scene conditions. The predicted latent is then processed by the original frozen downstream modules, eliminating image rendering and perception re-encoding. Explicit cross-frame agent association improves latent transition prediction and rollout stability, while variable-horizon simulation enables long-horizon prediction from a common real anchor without accumulating intermediate rollout errors. Experiments on nuScenes and NavSim demonstrate that FlowSim preserves downstream behavior competitively with, and often exceeds image-space simulation in source-to-reference agreement across variable simulation horizons and both dense and sparse latent representations. By predicting the latent directly, both instantiations of FlowSim simulate each step in 0.04--0.06s, substantially faster than the image-space simulation methods they are compared against. These results establish FlowSim as an efficient and practical alternative to conventional image-space simulation methods.
authors: Hanfeng Wu, Alvaro Marcos-Ramiro, Michael Schmidt, Christoph Stiller
bullets: Targets the computational cost and sim-to-real gap of image-space closed-loop simulation.
Predicts each target-frame latent from a previous latent and symbolic scene conditions, then uses the original frozen downstream modules.
Uses cross-frame agent association for more stable latent transitions and variable-horizon simulation to reduce accumulated rollout errors.
Experiments on nuScenes and NavSim show competitive or better source-to-reference agreement across horizons and dense or sparse latent representations.
Runs each simulation step in 0.04–0.06 seconds, substantially faster than the compared image-space methods.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of FLOWSIM. Top: Training. A frozen perception encoder extracts the source and target latents, Zt−1 and Zt, from real sensor observations. Given Zt−1 and target-frame symbolic scene conditions, FLOWSIM predicts Ẑt and is trained to reconstruct the target latent Zt. The same formulation is instantiated with a residual U-Net for UniAD’s dense BEV representation and a conditional flow-matching model for TransFuser’s sparse latent representation. Bottom: Simulation protocols. FLOWSIM supports both autoregressive simulation and variable-horizon simulation. In the latter, multiple future horizons are simulated directly from a common real latent anchor, preserving the real-to-simulated transition used during training and avoiding intermediate autoregressive drift. The predicted latent is passed directly to the frozen downstream stack to obtain the ego trajectory. Both simulation protocols can be coupled with a symbolic scene simulator that updates the ego and surrounding agents from the planned trajectory, enabling closed-loop simulation without image rendering.

Fig. 1. Comparison of our simulation paradigm (FLOWSIM) with 2 existing closed-loop simulation protocols for evaluating E2E driving systems, each producing a latent Ẑt that is sourced by the same frozen downstream heads. (i) Neural reconstruction renders the target frame from the explicit scene conditions (agent boxes, ego pose) into pixels, which the frozen encoder re-encodes into Ẑt. (ii) A world model likewise produces pixels for the same encoder, conditioned on its own previous images It−1 together with the scene conditions. (iii) FLOWSIM is conditioned on the previous latent Zt−1 and the same scene conditions, yet predicts the latent Ẑt directly, bypassing image rendering and re-encoding.

Fig. 4. Qualitative comparison of image-space and latent-space simulation on nuScenes, at a short (∆t=0.5s, left) and a long (∆t=4.0s, right) horizon. Each row shows, for a given source, the surround-view image inputs (or GT reference), the resulting BEV feature, and UNIAD’s downstream detection/lane/drivable-area/planning outputs decoded from it. The green and red boxes are GT annotations (agent conditions) and predicted results respectively. DREAMFORGE and SPLATAD must render an image and re-encode it through UNIAD’s frontend; FLOWSIM predicts the BEV latent directly and is rendering-free. At ∆t=0.5s all sources remain close to GT, but at ∆t=4.0s DREAMFORGE and SPLATAD accumulate visible rendering and re-encoding artifacts that degrade the BEV feature and downstream outputs, while FLOWSIM’s latent and decoded outputs stay closer to GT.

Fig. 5. Qualitative single-frame agreement on NavSim navtest (two scenes with ∆t = 0.5s). Top row: front-view camera crops used to obtain the source latent for the real GT frame and for OMNIRE’s independently rendered frame. Bottom row: corresponding TRANSFUSER-predicted BEV segmentation, detected agent boxes, and planning results for GT, FLOWSIM without and with agent association, and OMNIRE.

Fig. 3. Associated dynamic-agent conditioning. Each target-frame agent is augmented with information from its corresponding source-frame agent. The resulting descriptor combines the target state, source state, relative motion, and a validity flag, explicitly exposing cross-frame correspondence and temporal dynamics to the latent simulator. New agents without a valid correspondence are retained with an invalid flag rather than removed.

papers.abstract: Some observation-window-based KV cache compressors use prompt attention to identify important tokens but allocate uniform or predefined budgets across heads, overlooking input-dependent differences in budget demand. We propose ChampionKV, an input-adaptive head-wise budget allocator for long-context KV cache compression. It uses the maximum aggregated observation-window attention score as a lightweight empirical proxy for attention concentration, assigning larger budgets to heads with dispersed attention and smaller budgets to concentrated heads. An abnormal-head mask and a floor-budget mechanism improve robustness under weak attention responses. ChampionKV plugs into compressors such as SnapKV and PyramidKV without changing their token-selection procedures. On LongBench and RULER, both Champion variants consistently improve over their SnapKV and PyramidKV base compressors; the improvements are largest and statistically significant on Llama3.1-70B-Instruct, especially under tight budgets, whereas results on the tested 7B/8B models remain competitive but mixed. ChampionKV does not uniformly outperform Ada-KV, whose global cross-head Top-K selection retains an advantage in several settings. Controlled analysis further shows improved retained attention mass over the corresponding base compressors at negligible overhead.
authors: Yuechuan Chen, Yanda Guo, Xiaoxi Liu, Weilin Ruan, Huanbo Xu, Ruyi Wang, Wei Zhu
bullets: Addresses uniform or predefined per-head budgets that overlook input-dependent differences in attention demand.
Uses maximum aggregated observation-window attention as a proxy: dispersed heads receive larger budgets, while concentrated heads receive smaller ones.
Adds abnormal-head masking and a floor budget to improve robustness under weak attention responses.
Integrates with SnapKV and PyramidKV without changing their token-selection procedures.
Improves retained attention mass with negligible overhead, but does not consistently surpass Ada-KV; gains are mixed on tested 7B/8B models.

papers.title: ChampionKV: Head-Wise Adaptive Budget Allocation for KV Cache Compression

papers.abstract: Non-prefix KV cache reuse is a promising approach for improving inference efficiency in multi-agent systems as agents share the same context blocks. However, when agents have conflicting tasks, directly reusing non-prefix KV caches across agents can severely degrade model performance, causing up to a 90% drop. Existing remedies, including selective recomputation and offset-based calibration, recover a limited fraction of this loss. We argue that the problem lies not only in contaminated KV representations but also in the agent's difficulty interpreting reused context under its own instructions. To this end, we introduce LatentRemedy, which uses a few task-conditioned latent tokens to help the target agent leverage reused context without recomputing the shared block. Specifically, we use an MLP to map the last hidden state of the target prefix into a small number of latent tokens, which are placed after the reused KV block to interact with the shared context. To guide subsequent predictions toward the target task, we train the MLP through full-prefill distillation. Experiments show that LatentRemedy consistently outperforms existing reuse baselines on conflicting tasks while maintaining TTFT close to direct reuse as cache size grows. Code and data are available at https://github.com/chenzhwsysu57/kvreuse.
authors: Zhiwei Chen, Zhongtao Rao, Waikit Xiu, Yuxiang Zhang, Shuting Cui, Jian Chen, Tianxiang Zhao
bullets: Non-prefix KV reuse improves inference efficiency but can cause up to a 90% performance drop when agents have conflicting tasks.
The method maps the target agent’s final prefix hidden state to a small set of latent tokens using an MLP.
These tokens are inserted after the reused KV block to help the target agent interpret shared context under its own instructions.
Full-prefill distillation trains the MLP to guide predictions toward the target task.
LatentRemedy consistently outperforms existing reuse remedies while keeping TTFT close to direct reuse as cache size increases.
