papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student on its own rollouts under a frozen teacher, mitigating the distribution mismatch of off-policy supervision. While prior work has primarily trained on problems a student can largely solve, we ask whether OPD can improve a student when training is restricted to problems it currently fails. We evaluate five representative OPD mechanisms with Qwen-3 and Phi-4 models under a unified competition-mathematics protocol. We find that OPD does not improve accuracy on this hard subset, with most mechanisms instead degrading performance despite continued decreases in training KL divergence. All eight configurations show a decline, and the two-sided sign test gives p=0.0078. In contrast, the same pipeline improves accuracy by 4.6 percentage points when training is not concentrated on failures, showing that the failure is conditional on the training regime rather than systematic. These findings suggest that OPD is effective when supervision is dominated by correct student prefixes, but can reinforce existing errors when training is concentrated on problems the student currently fails.
authors: Shuo Yang, Zheyu Zhang, Mahito Sugiyama, Gjergji Kasneci
bullets: Evaluated five OPD mechanisms with Qwen-3 and Phi-4 under a unified competition-mathematics protocol.
Failure-focused OPD reduced accuracy in all eight configurations despite continued decreases in training KL divergence.
A two-sided sign test found the degradation statistically significant (p=0.0078).
When training was not concentrated on failures, the same pipeline improved accuracy by 4.6 percentage points.
The results suggest OPD benefits from correct student prefixes but can amplify errors in failure-heavy regimes.

papers.abstract: Surface reconstruction from range scans is challenging in the presence of noise and outliers, as fidelity to observations must be balanced against sensitivity to measurement errors. Yet, most neural approaches discard the sensor positions and corresponding visibility information, compensating for this loss with geometric priors or regularization terms. We instead formulate surface reconstruction as robust regression of the predicted first surface intersection along each acquisition ray against its measured depth, which penalizes predicted surface intersections within the segment between the sensor and the observed point. We represent the surface as the zero set of a 1-Lipschitz multi-layer perceptron, allowing the use of linearly convergent sphere tracing to compute the first hit, and use a robust Huber loss for regression. Our formulation requires neither oriented normals, sampled off-surface points, nor an eikonal loss. Comparisons with the state of the art on synthetic and real data with varying levels of noise and outlier contamination demonstrate competitive performance on clean data and much improved fidelity and robustness under even moderate corruption. Our analysis further confirms a trade-off between fidelity and robustness: greater fitting capacity improves data fidelity in the clean case but increases sensitivity to the measurement errors inherent in real acquisitions, with a sweet spot typically emerging at intermediate capacity.
authors: Gabriel Lenain, Edmond Boyer, Jean Ponce
bullets: Addresses noise and outliers while preserving sensor positions and ray visibility information.
Models the surface as the zero set of a 1-Lipschitz MLP and computes first intersections with sphere tracing.
Uses robust Huber regression on predicted versus measured ray depths, penalizing premature surface intersections.
Requires no oriented normals, off-surface samples, or eikonal loss.
Shows competitive clean-data performance and improved robustness under moderate corruption; intermediate model capacity often balances fidelity and robustness.

papers.abstract: Diffusion language models (DLMs) enable flexible parallel generation by resolving tokens according to the model's evolving predictability rather than a fixed left-to-right order. This flexibility, however, introduces training choices absent from standard autoregressive teacher forcing: which reference tokens are visible when a target is supervised and how much generation space is allocated. Standard supervised fine-tuning (SFT) typically makes these choices through random masking, independently of inference. Our analysis shows how this training-inference mismatch can misdirect supervision. Random masking can conceal prediction errors or penalize uncertainty that decoding would otherwise resolve, while the attention-visible input length can change which response formulations the model favors, even when the underlying solution is unchanged. Motivated by these findings, we propose Predictability-Aware Canvas Selection and Supervision (PACS), an SFT method. PACS uses the model's own predictability to select each example's attention-visible input length and supervises reference tokens immediately before their confidence-guided revelation. Across reasoning and code-generation benchmarks, PACS consistently achieves the highest mean accuracy among the compared SFT methods, with gains of up to 12.84 percentage points over vanilla SFT on individual benchmarks. Code will be released upon publication.
authors: Miao Li, Hanyang Jiang, Hengyu Fu, Baihe Huang, Yating Liu, Yuhang Cai, Changkun Guan, Zhongzhu Chen, Jiecheng Lu, Michael A. Boateng, Pascal Van Hentenryck
bullets: DLMs generate tokens in flexible, predictability-driven orders, making visibility and generation-space choices important during training.
Random masking can mismatch inference by hiding errors or penalizing uncertainty that decoding would resolve.
PACS selects the attention-visible input length using the model’s predictability and supervises tokens just before their confidence-guided revelation.

Across reasoning and code-generation benchmarks, PACS achieved the highest mean accuracy among compared SFT methods, with gains of up to 12.84 percentage points over vanilla SFT on individual benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Humanoid behavior foundation models (BFMs) enable diverse whole-body control, but adapting a pretrained controller to a new embodiment remains challenging because of kinematic and dynamic mismatch. We present TRACE, a framework for efficient cross-embodiment adaptation that preserves pretrained motion representations while specializing feedback control to the target robot.TRACE first injects kinematic priors into input and output projection layers and aligns nominal joint dynamics to reduce embodiment mismatch and support stable fine-tuning. It then combines encoder distillation with low-rank reinforcement learning on a compact, quality-screened motion set, using a two-phase curriculum to establish stable tracking before refining difficult motions. We apply TRACE to transfer SONIC from Unitree G1 to Unitree H2 using 10 million motion frames and approximately eight hours of training on a single RTX PRO 6000 GPU, at less than 0.1% of the GPU-hour cost of training SONIC from scratch. The adapted controller achieves 96.08\% success on 67,953 evaluation motions under a height-scaled tracking criterion. Real-robot demonstrations span dynamic motion tracking and whole-body teleoperation, with collected demonstrations supporting downstream vision-language-action policy post-training. These results demonstrate practical reuse of a pretrained humanoid controller across robots with different body scales and dynamics.
authors: Qingyu Lan, Zhihao Tian, Zifan Wang, Junwei Liang
bullets: Addresses kinematic and dynamic mismatch when transferring controllers across humanoid robots.
Injects kinematic priors, aligns nominal joint dynamics, and uses encoder distillation with low-rank reinforcement learning.
Trains with a compact quality-screened motion set and a two-phase curriculum for stable tracking and difficult motions.
Transfers SONIC from Unitree G1 to H2 using 10 million motion frames and about eight hours on one RTX PRO 6000 GPU.
Achieves 96.08% success on 67,953 evaluation motions and supports real-robot dynamic tracking, teleoperation, and downstream policy post-training.

papers.abstract: Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) are promising for energy-efficient neuromorphic computing, but they still suffer from catastrophic forgetting when learning tasks sequentially. This work investigates the integration of Experience Packing and Replay (EPR) as a memory-efficient continual learning strategy for deep SNNs under low-latency constraints. The proposed framework combines Batch Normalization Through Time stabilized VGG9 SNNs with Spike Activation Maps (SAM), which provide forward-only explanations based on spike activity. These explanations are temporally aggregated into spatial attention maps and used to select the most informative image patches for replay, instead of storing full images. Experiments on Split CIFAR10 and Split CIFAR100 show that SAM-guided EPR improves the accuracy-memory trade-off under tight memory budgets, and remains competitive while requiring substantially less storage.
authors: Francesco Panetta, Federico Di Valerio, Michela Proietti
bullets: Targets continual learning in energy-efficient deep spiking neural networks under low-latency and tight-memory constraints.
Combines Batch Normalization Through Time-stabilized VGG9 SNNs with forward-only Spike Activation Maps.
Aggregates spike-based explanations into spatial attention maps to identify patches for replay.
Experiments on Split CIFAR10 and Split CIFAR100 report improved accuracy–memory trade-offs and competitive performance with substantially lower storage.
Scope is limited to the evaluated datasets, architecture, and memory-constrained replay setting.

papers.abstract: A medical vision-language model may analyze a given CT scan and correctly detect both kidneys in view. Continuing this conversation, if a user provides a prescription with an opposite direction, medical VLMs often sycophantically choose to realign their diagnosis. In this work, we study regressive sycophancy under fabricated evidence, where a model abandons a correct answer when pushback comes with a fake document. We test four open VLMs on 400 VQA-RAD yes/no questions in 19,200 multi-turn conversations, with and without a fabricated prescription. Without a disclosure that documents are synthetic, the models abandon 80.1% of 6,488 correct answers. Notably, under one script each, the same prescription raises the flip rate of Qwen2.5-VL-7B from 45.9% to 89.6% and lowers that of Qwen3-VL-8B from 77.7% to 50.9%. A model rejected the prescription while still preserving the correct answer in 915 of 3,232 conversations with the prescription (28.3%), and 40% of these flipped in later turns. System-prompt sentences that disclose the documents as synthetic lower one model's flip rate from 77.8% to 47.3%. Thus, we conclude that awareness about a forgery does not prevent a model from adopting its answer.
authors: Sadif Ahmed, Soumya Swagata Biswas, Rifat Shahriyar, Chowdhury Mohammad Rakin Haider
bullets: Evaluates four open VLMs on 400 VQA-RAD yes/no questions across 19,200 multi-turn conversations with or without fabricated prescriptions.

papers.selection_reason: Studies failure modes of multimodal LLMs under fabricated evidence, relevant to multimodal foundation model behavior and reliability.
papers.title: Seeing Through the Forgery Is Not Enough: Regressive Sycophancy under Fabricated Evidence in Medical Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: Medical VLMs frequently abandon correct CT interpretations when confronted with fabricated prescriptions, and simply recognizing the forgery does not reliably prevent this regressive sycophancy.

papers.abstract: Recent Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models, such as $\pi_{0.5}$, have demonstrated impressive generalization capabilities by scaling behavior cloning across massive datasets. However, these models frequently suffer from distributional convergence, a phenomenon where the policy regresses to "safe" but suboptimal mean behaviors due to mode averaging in the training data. This often results in generic grasp strategies, Convergent Defaults, that fail in constrained or long-tail scenarios. In this work, we propose a novel framework to identify and correct these behaviors without parameter updates. We introduce a three-stage methodology: (1) Probing for Defaults, identifying task-specific mode collapse; (2) Diagnostic Root Cause Analysis, utilizing the VLA's latent reasoning capabilities to verbalize the logic behind suboptimal actions; and (3) Structured Guidance Injection, where concrete, distinct alternatives are encoded into reusable "Lens Prompts" that shift the sampling distribution. We validate this approach using $\pi_{0.5}$ in ManiSkill3 simulation environments. We hypothesize that our method outperforms vanilla $\pi_{0.5}$ and standard Chain-of-Thought prompting by effectively breaking convergent defaults in complex manipulation tasks.
authors: Mohammed Daba (University of Electronic Science and Technology of China, Chengdu, China), Waleed Abdulrahman Saleh AlAkwa (University of Sana'a, Sana'a, Yemen)
bullets: Targets distributional convergence in behavior-cloned VLA models, where mode averaging produces safe but suboptimal “Convergent Defaults.”
Probes task behavior to identify task-specific mode collapse.
Uses diagnostic reasoning to uncover why the model selects suboptimal actions.
Injects concrete alternatives through reusable “Lens Prompts” to shift action sampling without parameter updates.
Evaluated with π₀.₅ in ManiSkill3 simulations; the abstract states a hypothesis of improvement over vanilla π₀.₅ and standard Chain-of-Thought prompting, not confirmed results.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. The Diagnostic Lens Framework. We treat the VLA as a reasoning engine to diagnose its own action priors. By extracting the root cause of a default behavior, we construct a textual ”Lens” that reshapes the flow matching distribution during inference.

Fig. 3. Illustrative Example: Constrained Mug Grasping. This figure demonstrates the practical application of the methodology. The ”Convergent Default” (top-down grasp) is identified, diagnosed as a statistical bias, and corrected via a specific Lens Prompt containing concrete alternatives.

Fig. 1. Breaking the Convergent Default. VLA models often regress to the mean of their training data, causing failures in constrained environments. Our method identifies these modes and injects structured guidance (Lens) to shift the action distribution toward expert behaviors.

papers.tldr: A prompt-based, parameter-free framework diagnoses and redirects robotic VLA models away from generic manipulation behaviors that fail in constrained or long-tail situations.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon robotic manipulation requires robust execution over sequences of interdependent actions. Existing methods typically handle execution deviations by replanning the remaining action chunk or correcting actions step by step as new observations arrive. However, a local deviation may affect only a few actions under distribution shift, yet replanning regenerates the entire chunk from an unfamiliar state, potentially introducing errors into otherwise valid actions. Step-wise correction may react too late, as it does not explicitly anticipate how the deviation affects subsequent actions. We propose ReEnvision, a future-guided selective action repair framework that updates a joint future-action belief using execution feedback. It then learns how the resulting belief revision affects each unexecuted action. The resulting belief revision enables selective repair of only the affected actions within a cached action chunk, preserving valid actions and reserving full replanning for severe deviations. On CALVIN, L-CALVIN, and RLBench, ReEnvision achieves 86.6% 5-step success, improves 10-step success from 56% to 63%, and reaches an average success rate of 88.8%, respectively. On five real-world manipulation tasks, it achieves an average success rate of 82.8%. Controlled repair experiments further demonstrate the benefits of localizing affected actions and preserving valid ones during execution.
authors: Xiyin Zeng, Xuewei Huang, Yi Lu, Weihao Yuan, Hao Wang
bullets: Addresses the risk that full replanning introduces errors into otherwise valid action sequences, while step-wise correction may react too late.
Updates a joint belief over future actions using execution feedback and estimates which unexecuted actions are affected.
Repairs only affected actions in a cached action chunk, reserving full replanning for severe deviations.
Reports 86.6% 5-step success, improves 10-step success from 56% to 63%, and achieves 88.8% average success across simulation benchmarks.
Achieves 82.8% average success on five real-world manipulation tasks; controlled experiments support localized repair and preservation of valid actions.

papers.abstract: Do vision-language models use depth information to judge which object is closer, or rely on image-plane cues? We investigate this question through controlled depth--cue conflicts, representation analysis, and interventions. Among the many image-plane cues relevant to depth perception, we focus on apparent size and vertical position. We compare depth judgments under cue-consistent and cue-conflict conditions in both rendered scenes and real-world photographs. Across model families and scales, depth judgments systematically shift toward misleading cues. Yet the correct depth order remains decodable from the queried objects' visual representations, including when the model answers incorrectly. Image and category controls support interpreting this signal as image-dependent depth information beyond the two target cues. Strengthening the model's own depth readout through object-level write-back can correct conflict decisions without updating model parameters or using ground-truth depth annotations. Interventions show that the effect of this correction depends on the direction and target tokens of the written signal, while its strength varies across architectures and domains. Together, these findings reveal a mismatch between a model's ability to represent depth and use this information when deciding the answer. VLMs can retain useful depth information while allowing competing image-plane cues to exert greater influence on their answers.
authors: Zhengtao Zou, Pekka Marttinen

papers.abstract: Long-running agents retain KV caches across turns and sessions for hours or days. Compressing these persistent caches requires reducing storage while controlling reconstruction error. We present AlignPred, a codec that combines local alignment with predictive coding under a configurable KV reconstruction-error budget. Local orthogonal transforms align related heads or layers into a common coordinate frame, allowing AlignPred to combine token-wise prediction with same-token prediction across heads or layers. Residuals are quantized on an error-bounded lattice and entropy-coded, without learned predictors, encoder-side mode search, or large joint transforms. Across three attention mechanisms, AlignPred requires less storage than the evaluated baselines at comparable measured reconstruction error. Against the evaluated CPU codec implementations, it decodes at least 1.6 times faster while matching or improving encode time. AlignPred achieves near-native task scores at substantially compressed operating points on LongBench-Pro at 128K context. AlignPred's SGLang HiCache integration reduces persistent target-KV storage by 42-72% relative to native HiCache, with comparable latency.

papers.abstract: Modern Transformers rely on many scale-control mechanisms, including normalization, residual scaling, attention temperatures, loss weighting, and adaptive updates. To explain how these mechanisms maintain scale consistency, we introduce Neural Dimensional Analysis (NDA), a unified framework based on dimensional consistency. We define neural units that specify how tensors rescale and which quantities can be added, just as physical units do in physics. Our rules match residual units, nondimensionalize attention and gate inputs, combine losses across units, and convert gradient units into parameter units. We implement NDA through dimensionless Unit Violation Indices (UVI) for diagnosing scale mismatches within Transformers, a unit-consistent multi-loss objective, and the Gauge-Canonical Transformer (GCT) with normalized coordinates and orthogonalized residual additions. In language-model experiments spanning 51M to 1B parameters, GCT remains stable during training across a broad sixteenfold learning-rate range, outperforming Pre-LN, LLaMA-style, and QK-Norm in 124M validation loss at tuned learning rates. GCT's normalized residual stream also shows improved robustness to quantization. At 1B parameters, calibrated per-tensor int8 quantization increases GCT's validation loss by only 0.009 nats, compared with up to 5.51 nats for the baselines. Vision and physics-informed neural network experiments further confirm NDA's benefits beyond language modeling. These results establish dimensional consistency as a neural network design principle.
authors: Bum Jun Kim, Makoto Kawano, Yusuke Iwasawa, Yutaka Matsuo
bullets: Motivated by the many scale-control mechanisms required in modern Transformers, including normalization, residual scaling, attention temperatures, and loss weighting.
Defines neural units and dimensional-consistency rules for tensor rescaling, valid additions, attention and gate inputs, multi-loss objectives, and gradient-to-parameter conversion.
Introduces Unit Violation Indices for diagnosing scale mismatches and the Gauge-Canonical Transformer with normalized coordinates and orthogonalized residual additions.
Across language, vision, and physics-informed experiments, the approach supports stable training over a broad learning-rate range and improved quantization robustness.
In the reported 1B-parameter experiment, calibrated per-tensor int8 quantization increased validation loss by 0.009 nats for GCT versus up to 5.51 nats for baselines.

Figure 1: NDA at a glance. (Left) Scale-control mechanisms in deep learning, including normalization, residual scaling, attention temperature, loss weighting, and adaptive updates, manage scale at different interfaces of a Transformer. Unit Violation Indices (UVI) flag deviations from the intended scale regime, locating the interface where a scale mismatch arises. (Middle) NDA expresses these mechanisms through unit-consistent operations and a factorization into scales and canonical coordinates. (Right) The Gauge-Canonical Transformer (GCT) builds the whole network on this factorization. Every block computes on dimensionless coordinates (blue), ensuring matching units at every interface, including attention and multilayer perceptron (MLP) branches. The scale (gold) is reattached only when an output needs units.

(a) QK-Norm repairs attention variance and entropy, while (b) QK-Norm’s residual RMS still reaches values between 1.6× 102 and 3.3× 102. GCT keeps both readouts controlled. The annotations report final-step statistics: the layer median of v, the mean attention entropy as a fraction of the maximum attention entropy, and the across-layer range of the stream RMS. Figure 5: Validation loss under internal rescaling h → ch at the embedding output and mid-depth, with fp32 block error. The intervention changes the hidden state’s magnitude while preserving the state’s direction. GCT and nGPT preserve validation loss, with block invariance errors near the numerical floor, showing insensitivity to the imposed magnitude change. UCT loses invariance at c = 10−2 because the hidden state shrinks while the small constants in UCT’s normalization denominators and the stored evaluation-time scale estimates remain fixed. papers.abstract: Long-context inference makes the key-value (KV) cache a major memory bottleneck for large language models. We propose BELT, a low-rank KV cache compression framework. Its key-side objective targets attention distributions rather than raw keys or pre-softmax logits, yielding a quadratic surrogate with a closed-form low-rank solution. A learned global rank allocator uses differentiable soft selection during training and hard selection at deployment to meet a user-specified component budget. Experiments demonstrate improved model quality under aggressive compression and increased decoding throughput at comparable accuracy. Evaluated across three LLMs and multiple benchmarks, BELT achieves up to 70% low-rank KV cache compression while outperforming the strongest baseline by up to 23.3 points on LongBench, and up to 17.8x overall KV cache reduction when combined with quantization. With Triton-based GPU kernels and a quantized cache, BELT delivers up to 2.7x speedup for the attention module and 3.3x end-to-end decoding throughput.
authors: Yaoyang Liu, Shuwei Shen, Jincheng Tang, Jinguang Liu, Jinbao Xue, Hailong Yang, Ke Zhang, Yinjun Wu
bullets: Targets attention distributions rather than raw keys or logits, producing a quadratic objective with a closed-form low-rank solution.
Learns global top-k rank allocation using differentiable soft selection during training and hard selection at deployment.
Across three LLMs and multiple benchmarks, achieves up to 70% low-rank KV-cache compression and up to 17.8× reduction with quantization.
Reports up to 23.3-point LongBench gains over the strongest baseline and up to 3.3× end-to-end decoding throughput.
Uses Triton GPU kernels and quantized caches to reach up to 2.7× attention-module speedup.

papers.abstract: The design of attention mechanisms in long-context large language models faces an ``impossible triangle'' among KV cache size, training and prefill FLOPs, and model quality. GQA achieves strong quality but incurs high KV cache overhead; alternative approaches such as MLA and MFA can compress the cache, but MLA suffers from quality loss while MFA substantially increases training and prefill compute. We propose Virtual Head Attention (VHA), which simultaneously improves all three vertices through two lightweight linear operations: Q Premix applies a near-identity transformation to queries within each KV group to recover virtual head diversity from halved physical query heads, and Linear Postmix fuses inter-head features via a low-rank $I + AB^\top$ residual structure. Since VHA introduces no nonlinear operations, Premix can be folded into the query projection and Postmix into the output projection at inference time, reducing the model to a standard GQA-2 architecture that directly reuses all existing GQA inference optimizations. With only two KV heads, the group size in large models readily reaches 64, fully exploiting Tensor Core parallelism during decoding. Across four scales with 4K-context 50B-token pretraining, VHA consistently surpasses the standard GQA baseline at every scale ($+$0.05\% to $+$0.81\%), while reducing KV cache by $4\times$ vs.\ GQA-8 at dense scales and $2\times$ vs.\ GQA-4 at the MoE scale, and lowering training and prefill FLOPs by 7.9\% (1.7B, $S{=}4096$). On an industrial 30B-A3B MoE model trained on 500B tokens at 8K context, VHA outperforms both MLA and GQA-4 by $+$0.70\,/\,$+$2.60\,\% on a 12-benchmark base-model evaluation suite; in a separate matched 10B-A1B MoE comparison after long-context mid-training, VHA attains an average RULER score of 84.4 over 8K--128K versus 73.0 for GQA, while using two rather than four KV heads in the full-attention layers.
authors: Xibo Ding, Guoxia Wang, Jinle Zeng, Jiabin Yang, Sirui Tao, Chao Yang, Dianhai Yu
bullets: Targets the trade-off among KV-cache size, training/prefill compute, and model quality in long-context LLMs.
Uses two lightweight linear operations: Q Premix restores virtual query-head diversity, while Linear Postmix fuses inter-head features with a low-rank residual structure.
The operations can be folded into existing projections at inference, yielding a standard GQA-2 model compatible with GQA optimizations and Tensor Core decoding.
Across four model scales, VHA improves over GQA while reducing KV cache by 2–4× and training/prefill FLOPs by 7.9% in one reported setting.
On industrial MoE evaluations, VHA outperforms MLA and GQA and achieves higher long-context RULER scores than GQA while using fewer KV heads.

papers.abstract: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) have attracted increasing research attention due to their bidirectional attention and arbitrary order decoding. However, there are two issues in dLLMs inference: the decoding difficulty is dominated by the tokens on the right side of the block, and the block-wise decoding inherently suffers from boundary contextual discontinuity. To tackle these limitations, we propose HaloBlock, a difficulty-aware adaptive halo mechanism for dLLM inference. We first leverage bidirectional cumulative entropy to characterize block decoding difficulty. Then, based on the bidirectional decoding difficulty, we adaptively allocate bidirectional halo regions on both sides of each block to mitigate boundary contextual discontinuity. The difficulty-aware design of HaloBlock smooths cross-block context propagation and lowers decoding difficulty for hard tokens, yielding better generation quality and faster convergence. Evaluated on LLaDA-8B-Instruct, Dream-7B-Instruct and LLaDA-1.5 across mathematical reasoning and code generation benchmarks, HaloBlock demonstrates consistent accuracy improvements and higher inference efficiency. Source codes are publicly available at https://github.com/PolyU-VCLab/HaloBlock.
authors: Zhaohui Zheng, Chenhang He, Jinrui Zhang, Ming-Ming Cheng, Lei Zhang
bullets: dLLM block-wise decoding is challenged by difficult right-side tokens and discontinuous context across block boundaries.
It estimates block difficulty using bidirectional cumulative entropy.
It adaptively allocates halo regions on both sides of each block to improve cross-block context propagation.
Experiments on LLaDA-8B-Instruct, Dream-7B-Instruct, and LLaDA-1.5 show consistent accuracy gains and higher inference efficiency on math and code-generation benchmarks.
Source code is publicly available.

papers.abstract: Traditional time-series classification methods often operate as black boxes, providing a class prediction without indicating which time point or time interval within the series led to that prediction. To improve temporal interpretability, MILLET (Multiple Instance Learning with Temporal Explanation), which combines an InceptionTime encoder with Conjunctive Pooling, provides both classification and temporal explanations. However, MILLET contains approximately 424 K parameters, making it unsuitable for deployment on resource-constrained micro-controllers, and it achieves an overall time-series accuracy of 0.888 and an explanation score of 0.681 NDCG@n. We therefore propose SEA-Net, a lightweight architecture using small multi-scale depthwise-separable convolutional TSC encoders and improved Multiple Instance Learning (MIL) pooling heads. Our SEA-Net bottleneck encoder with Top-k pooling achieves 0.931 accuracy and 0.765 NDCG@n with only 41 K parameters. Another variant, using a gated encoder with Top-k pooling, achieves 0.955 accuracy and 0.750 NDCG@n with 62 K parameters. These results demonstrate that lightweight architectures can maintain strong classification performance and temporal explanations while substantially reducing model size. The proposed variants address specific limitations of the pooling strategy used by MILLET, providing a practical direction for interpretable time-series classification on resource-constrained edge devices.
authors: Ubaid Ur Rehman, Tanmoy Mondal
bullets: Addresses black-box time-series classifiers that do not identify influential time points or intervals.
Uses small multi-scale depthwise-separable convolutional encoders with improved multiple-instance-learning pooling heads.
The bottleneck encoder with Top-k pooling achieves 0.931 accuracy and 0.765 NDCG@n using 41K parameters.
The gated encoder with Top-k pooling achieves 0.955 accuracy and 0.750 NDCG@n using 62K parameters.
Targets practical deployment on microcontrollers and edge devices while preserving temporal interpretability.

papers.abstract: Table reasoning with language models typically assumes access to clean textual tables. In practice, tables are often serialized into text, which can corrupt cell contents, distort structural relationships, and discard visual cues, leaving the model to reason over incomplete evidence. In contrast, table images retain this information, but using it requires both accurate perception and reasoning grounded in the relevant cells. To address this, we propose MERIT (Multimodal Evidence Reasoning over Image Tables), a three-stage framework for learning to reason over table images, with serialized tables serving as optional auxiliary inputs (if provided). Our analysis identifies visual evidence acquisition as a bottleneck, motivating table-specific encoder adaptation through reconstruction, localization, and color-conditioned supervision. Building on the adapted representations, supervised fine-tuning teaches explicit evidence selection and reasoning using verified trajectories. Finally, reinforcement learning refines the policy with separate rewards for evidence correctness, calculation, final answers, and output format. By providing feedback on intermediate steps, the framework targets retrieval and computational errors that final-answer supervision alone does not distinguish. We evaluate the approach on table question answering and fact verification, analyze the contributions of visual inputs and training components, and assess generalization to additional datasets with different table structures and visual presentations.
authors: Haoyang Jiang, Zhuotong Fan, Mingyang Yi, Ju Fan, Lanqing Hu, Xiao Zan
bullets: Addresses information loss and structural corruption caused by serializing tables into text.
Adapts a table-specific visual encoder using reconstruction, localization, and color-conditioned supervision.
Uses supervised fine-tuning with verified evidence-and-reasoning trajectories.
Applies reinforcement learning with separate rewards for evidence, calculations, answers, and formatting.
Evaluates visual inputs, training components, and generalization across varied table structures and presentations.

papers.abstract: Dynamic 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) provides an efficient framework for dynamic scene reconstruction. Most existing approaches model scene dynamics with deterministic deformation fields, assuming each Gaussian follows a distinct geometric trajectory over time. This assumption breaks down underwater, where light scattering, refraction, marine snow and low visibility create substantial physical ambiguity in captured images. We present PUGS, a physics-guided uncertainty model for underwater dynamic 3DGS. PUGS learns inherent uncertainty induced by underwater image formation and leverages it as a physical signal for dynamic scene modeling. Rather than estimating a single deterministic displacement, it parameterizes each Gaussian's motion as a probability distribution with expected deformation and physical uncertainty. We adopt stochastic deformation optimization to sample Gaussian trajectories via local reparameterization, exploring multiple physically plausible solutions during training. We further propose uncertainty stochastic annealing and a dual-path self-consistency distillation objective, converting stochastic exploration to deterministic reconstruction while preserving temporal coherence. Extensive experiments on underwater dynamic datasets and physics-aware benchmarks demonstrate superior rendering quality, temporal consistency and reconstruction robustness. Our method achieves 1.16 dB PSNR gain over the strongest baseline on UVEB and 3.99 dB on DRUVA.
authors: Tingjun Li, Yuxi Wang, Guoqiang Zhong, Zhaoxiang Zhang
bullets: Targets ambiguity in underwater imagery caused by scattering, refraction, marine snow, and low visibility.
Represents each Gaussian’s motion with expected deformation plus physical uncertainty.
Uses stochastic deformation optimization to explore multiple plausible trajectories during training.
Applies uncertainty stochastic annealing and dual-path self-consistency distillation for deterministic, temporally coherent reconstruction.
Reports PSNR gains of 1.16 dB on UVEB and 3.99 dB on DRUVA over the strongest baseline, with improved rendering quality and robustness.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of the PUGS Pipeline for Underwater Dynamic Scene Reconstruction. Given a monocular video, SfM initializes a set of canonical Gaussians. To address the observational ambiguities caused by underwater physical disturbances, our deformation field predicts not only the displacement mean ∆µ but also the positional uncertainty ∆σ, yielding a complete characterization of the motion distribution. A deterministic rendering path (clean path) and an uncertainty-aware rendering path (uncertainty path) are then constructed in parallel and jointly optimized via a self-consistency distillation constraint. Meanwhile, Gaussians with high uncertainty are adaptively split to enhance local representation capacity, thereby improving the robustness of underwater reconstruction. In this way, underwater dynamics modeling addresses the failure of deterministic deformation fields under ambiguous observations, while uncertainty-guided optimization leverages the learned uncertainty to allocate representation capacity and stabilize training.

Fig. 1. We present PUGS, a method that explicitly models physical uncertainty in dynamic 3D Gaussian splatting. On the challenging underwater sequence, a deterministic deformation-based method (Row 1) entangles structural motion with optical interference, producing floaters, blur, distortion, and ghosting artifacts. In contrast, PUGS (Row 2) learns a per-pixel physical uncertainty signal ∆σ (visualized as heatmaps) that captures where and when the optical medium degrades observation reliability. This uncertainty is annealed over time β(t) : 1 → 0, enabling the model to progressively resolve physical ambiguity and produce clean, artifact-free renderings that closely match the ground-truth reference.

papers.abstract: Unknown payloads alter robot dynamics and make precise contact execution difficult when foothold margins are small. We present LOAD, a perceptive locomotion framework that combines explicit inertial estimates with implicit dynamics features for narrow-beam traversal. Separate recurrent modules infer torso inertial changes and task-relevant history from proprioception, while a height-map teacher is distilled into a depth-based student. We extensively evaluate LOAD and its variants in simulation and on hardware across beam widths and payload configurations. The results show that implicit dynamics features accelerate training, while explicit inertial estimation further improves traversal success; combining both enables LOAD to approach the performance of a privileged policy supplied with ground-truth inertial parameters. Hardware experiments demonstrate traversal with unilateral payloads of 6 kg on a 10 cm beam and 9 kg on a 15 cm beam, and an evenly distributed 11 kg payload on a 15 cm beam. These results support combining physical estimates and history features for precision locomotion under unknown loads.
authors: Kunzhao Ren, Zhishuo Zhu, Xiaobin Xiong
bullets: Targets precision footholds when payload changes make robot dynamics uncertain.
Uses recurrent proprioceptive modules for explicit inertial estimation and implicit task-history features.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in vision-language models (VLMs) have substantially improved the capabilities of GUI agents, while memory augmentation has emerged as a promising approach for reusing knowledge from past interactions. However, existing memory augmented GUI agents typically adopt a fixed representation strategy, providing retrieved experience as a static modality. It remains unclear whether a single memory modality is consistently optimal, or how modality preference changes across interaction steps. In this work, we conduct a systematic study of memory modality in VLM based GUI agents. Across GUI benchmarks, we find that the preferred memory representation is strongly step dependent. Motivated by the finding, we introduce \textbf{SwitchMem}, a routing framework that dynamically selects between textual and visual memory representations at each step. Across three GUI benchmarks, SwitchMem outperforms memory augmented baselines that rely on static memory representations. Our findings validate our claim that memory modality is a step dependent decision rather than a fixed design choice. Code and project resources are available at https://txxnrd.github.io/switchmem
authors: Taeyun Roh, Suhyeong Park, Gijin Kim, Wonjune Jang, Jaewoo Kang
bullets: Existing memory-augmented GUI agents typically use one fixed memory representation.
A study across GUI benchmarks finds that the best memory modality varies substantially by interaction step.
SwitchMem routes each step to either textual or visual memory.
Across three GUI benchmarks, it outperforms baselines using static memory representations.
The results support treating memory modality as a dynamic, step-dependent choice.

figures.caption: Figure 5: Overview of SwitchMem. papers.abstract: Autonomous navigation in real-world environments often requires long-horizon operation under partial observability and evolving goals. Existing mapless navigation approaches predominantly assume fixed goals throughout an episode, limiting applicability to practical scenarios where goals change online during execution. We study online chained-goal navigation, where goals evolve through existing-goal redirection or new-goal emergence without explicit transition signals. Under this setting, we find navigation may require either continued exploration or strategic revisitation, creating conflicting memory requirements. We propose Global-Local Spatio-Temporal Belief Learning (GLST), a memory-decomposition framework that separates latent beliefs into global-local spatial and long-short temporal representations for long-horizon reasoning. We further introduce goal-conditioned rewards to balance exploration and exploitation under evolving goals. Extensive experiments in simulation across diverse terrains demonstrate improved chained-goal navigation performance over baselines. Real-robot experiments using the Spot quadruped further validate our memory decomposition framework.
authors: Yousef Liang, Ryan Ardalan, Yarden Goraly, Chenhao Zhu, Yue Yin, Jonas Frey, Claire Tomlin, Marco Pavone, Shankar Sastry
bullets: Targets chained-goal navigation under partial observability, where goals may be redirected or newly introduced without explicit transition signals.
Separates latent beliefs into global/local spatial and long/short temporal representations to support exploration and strategic revisitation.
Uses goal-conditioned rewards to balance exploration and exploitation as goals evolve.
Experiments in simulated diverse terrains and on a Spot quadruped show improved chained-goal navigation over baselines.
The approach is evaluated in simulation and real-robot settings; broader scope beyond these settings is not established in the abstract.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overall framework and training pipeline of the proposed GLST method. (a) GLST framework showing the global-local spatial and temporal belief branches and actor-critic policy. Real-robot depth images or simulated height scans serve as shared inputs to both spatial branches. (b) Training pipeline including locomotion policy training, global spatial supervised pretraining, environment generation with chained-goal sampling, and navigation policy training.

Figure 6: Detailed architecture of the proposed GLST framework. Observations are decomposed into global-local spatial and temporal belief representations. Global beliefs are recursively accumulated and refined through goal-conditioned attention, while fused belief representations are processed by a shared actor-critic policy. Auxiliary prediction heads supervise spatial belief learning through height, mask, and confidence reconstruction.

Figure 3: Visualization of learned spatial beliefs in two simulation environments: (1) maze and (2) pillars. (a) Global spatial beliefs reconstructed from predicted height, mask, and confidence maps, with robot trajectories overlaid. (b) Local observations obtained by fusing depth images from five cameras (front-left, front-right, left, right, and rear) into local height maps. (c) Simulation environments with the quadruped robot and executed trajectories overlaid.

Figure 4: Real-robot navigation experiments on the Spot quadruped across diverse indoor and outdoor environments. (1) Indoor experiments. (2) Outdoor forest experiments. (a) Experimental scenes with ghost robot overlays illustrating executed trajectories. (b) Inferred global spatial beliefs reconstructed from latent representations. (3) Long-horizon online chained-goal experiments with dead ends and dynamic obstacles. Additional chained-goal indoor and outdoor experimental results are provided in Appendix G.

The lower figures show the compounded success rate from 100% to the final success rate under the assumption of independent goal completion. The upper figures show the single-goal success rates reported in prior work, which are used to construct the chained-goal success rates. Data are adapted from (a) [2], (b) [40], (c) [41], (d) [42], and (e) [9].

Figure 7: Additional real-robot experiments: (a) single-goal navigation on stairs, (b) indoor navigation with three chained goals, and (c) forest navigation with three chained goals. Images are contrast-enhanced for visualization.

(b) Single-goal SR and failure decomposition into timeout, collision, and excessive roll. (c) Navigation efficiency measured by SPL and optimal path length distributions. papers.abstract: Autoregressive video generation relies on memory retrieval to model long-range dependencies. This capability becomes particularly critical for multi-shot generation, where models must reconcile substantial visual changes across shot transitions with persistent semantic continuity. Existing methods tend to perform memory retrieval at the frame level and share the same historical context across all query tokens, overlooking the heterogeneous information needs and leading to redundant retrieval and inefficient use of historical memory. To bridge this gap, we introduce CineMem, an attention-aligned fine-grained memory retrieval framework that combines online memory organization with query-adaptive retrieval for autoregressive multi-shot video generation. Specifically, guided by intrinsic memory-access patterns revealed through attention analysis, we propose an online-clustered KV cache as a memory organization strategy over all historical tokens, enabling semantic-aware memory grouping and more precise retrieval. In addition, we introduce a query-level retrieval mechanism that provides broader access to historical information under a fixed retrieval budget, thereby improving long-term memory utilization. Together, these designs enable the multi-shot video generator to preserve long-range consistency across shot transitions, particularly in revisitation scenarios, while approximating full-memory access under a constrained memory budget. To facilitate evaluation, we further introduce a suite of task-specific, VLM-assisted metrics for faithful inter-shot consistency assessment. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework.
authors: Xiaoxue Wu, Xinyu Gao, Fang Yu, Yu Qiao, Xinyuan Chen
bullets: Targets redundant, frame-level memory retrieval that gives all query tokens the same historical context.
Organizes historical KV-cache tokens into online semantic clusters guided by attention patterns.
Uses query-adaptive, fine-grained retrieval to broaden historical access under a fixed memory budget.
Improves long-range and inter-shot consistency, especially when earlier content is revisited, while approximating full-memory access.
Introduces VLM-assisted metrics for evaluating faithful consistency across shots; experiments support the framework’s effectiveness.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of CineMem. Existing autoregressive video generation methods tend to perform memory retrieval at the frame level, which may result in redundant retrieval, inefficient memory utilization, and overlooked heterogeneous information needs across query tokens. CineMem combines an online-clustered KV cache with query-adaptive retrieval to enable a finer-grained memory retrieval strategy. As illustrated by the attention receptive fields, CineMem provides broader (2/3 vs. 12/12) access to historical information under the same retrieval budget.

Figure 3: Our memory retrieval framework. Through multi-stage initial adaptation, we convert a bidirectional model into an autoregressive multi-shot model with memory retrieval. During inference, queries access memory from the first chunk, adjacent chunk, and retrieved candidates via token-wise and head-wise retrieval. Previous adjacent chunks are progressively integrated into retrieval candidates through online KV-cache clustering with cluster balancing. During training, resampling ground truth frames provides memory inputs to alleviate error accumulation.

Figure 5: Qualitative Results. We compare CineMem with representative causal and bidirectional baselines on 15s multi-shot video generation. Representative examples illustrate the qualitative improvements of our method.
Figure 6: Implementation of PTCS. PTCS assigns low scores when either unchanged semantic elements are not preserved or intended changes are not correctly realized.

Figure 4: Intrinsic memory-selection patterns under the full-memory setting. Memory tokens exhibit semantically meaningful clustering structures, while different query-head pairs show distinct preferences over memory tokens. Although each query-head pair selects a subset of the most relevant tokens, their union covers nearly the entire memory. See Appendix A for more details.

Figure 10: Visualization of token clustering before and after RoPE. Compared with Pre-RoPE representations, Post-RoPE similarities exhibit stronger positional dependency and weaker semantic clustering structures.

Figure 9: Comparison of memory-token coverage and selection overlap under three selection granularities: query-head-wise, query-wise with head averaging, and head-wise with query averaging. The horizontal axis denotes the fraction of memory tokens selected by each selection unit. The left panel reports the percentage of distinct memory-token positions covered by the union of all selections, while the right panel shows the percentage of selected positions with multiplicity at least two.

Figure 11: Precision (left) and recall (right) of different retrieval strategies under varying fullmemory attention thresholds. For each query-head pair, full-memory attention serves as the oracle, and retrieved tokens are considered matched if they fall within the top-x% oracle-ranked memory tokens. Online-clustered KV cache retrieves tokens from query-specific selected clusters, while Latent-group, Frame-group, and Sliding Window perform frame-level or fixed-context retrieval. All curves are averaged over attention blocks. Online-clustered KV cache achieves a better precision-recall trade-off, providing a selective approximation to full-memory access.

Figure 7: Visualization of query-wise memory selection diversity. For the selected memory frames, different queries exhibit distinct spatial preferences within the same frame, revealing heterogeneous memory selection behaviors. Each query corresponds to the first latent of the current chunk, and each memory unit is formed by grouping neighboring 3× 3 spatial tokens.

Figure 8: Visualization of head-wise memory selection diversity. For the selected memory frames, different attention heads exhibit distinct memory preferences. We visualize multiple query regions for generality. The variations among highlighted regions across rows in each heatmap illustrate the diversity of head-wise memory selection.
Figure 15: A case of qualitative result of ablation study.
Figure 16: Distribution of evaluation prompts across different content categories, shot counts, and revisit distances.

Figure 12: Practical efficiency comparison during autoregressive rollout. The left figure shows the per-chunk denoising time, and the right figure shows the peak allocated GPU memory during 42-chunk generation.
Figure 17: Cases of longer video generated by CineMem.

Figure 13: Qualitative comparison between PTCS and similarity-based inter-shot consistency metrics. The examples illustrate cases where PTCS better reflects transition correctness by jointly considering semantic preservation and prompt-specified changes.

Figure 14: Comparison between query-wise retrieval and the query-group retrieval variant. Querywise retrieval performs independent memory retrieval for each query token, while the query-group variant recursively partitions query tokens based on intra-group content diversity. Queries with similar content preferences are assigned to the same group and share the retrieved memory.

Figure 18: A failure case in complex multi-entity scenarios. Although the generated video preserves revisitation consistency across shots, inconsistencies such as character disappearance and detail changes occur during the transition from Shot 1 to Shot 2. This example highlights the difficulty of handling multi-entity reasoning and spatial relationship preservation in autoregressive video generation.

Table 3: Ablation study. The best and runner-up are in bold and underlined. C: clustered KV cache; F: frame grouping; Q-wise: query- and head-wise retrieval; Shared: shared across queries.

papers.tldr: CineMem enables efficient long-video generation by retrieving semantically relevant historical information separately for each query token, preserving consistency across multi-shot transitions.

papers.abstract: Decisions that weigh several reward signals against each other require the joint distribution of the return vector. Categorical critics scale exponentially in the reward dimension, and quantiles have no canonical multivariate analogue. Multivariate distributional critics therefore represent each return distribution by M equal-weight particles trained with a discrepancy loss. Beyond their atoms, the particles provide no sampler and cannot resolve events rarer than 1/M. We propose Stein variational distributional RL (SVDRL). Its critic outputs Stein particles, which Stein variational gradient descent transports along a learned score field of the distributional Bellman target. We learn this field by bootstrapped denoising score matching across noise levels and tie it across the Bellman recursion by a consistency loss, which we prove is a non-expansive temporal-difference scheme in score space. The same field certifies the particles. Its reverse-diffusion sampler satisfies a supremal Wasserstein policy-evaluation bound that holds for bounded, possibly multimodal returns. The Stein particles inherit this bound up to a gap that we measure without ground truth, and the sampler answers tail-risk queries below the particle resolution at any sample size. Empirically, SVDRL is more accurate on rare events than particle critics with the same number of particles, and on par on MuJoCo continuous control.
authors: Manuel Hau{\ss}mann, Melih Kandemir
bullets: Multivariate distributional RL needs joint return distributions, but categorical critics scale exponentially and quantiles lack a canonical multivariate form.
The critic represents returns with Stein particles transported by Stein variational gradient descent along a learned score field.
Bootstrapped denoising score matching and a Bellman consistency loss learn and stabilize the score field across recursion.
A reverse-diffusion sampler supports tail-risk queries below the resolution of the particle set, with Wasserstein evaluation guarantees for bounded, possibly multimodal returns.
SVDRL is more accurate on rare events than equal-particle critics and performs comparably on MuJoCo continuous control.

papers.abstract: Action-conditioned world models can reduce costly real-robot interaction in reinforcement learning for Vision-Language-Action models (VLA-RL), but hallucinations can mislead policy optimization. Extending them to richer VLA interfaces and long-horizon tasks raises challenges in spatiotemporal and cross-modal consistency, exploration-reliability balance in RL, and compounding rollout errors. We present WoVR+, extending WoVR's hallucination-aware WM-RL framework by redesigning the learned environment and imagined interaction protocol: A VLA-interface-aligned world model provides multi-view prediction and proprioceptive updates while mitigating hallucinations. Chunk-wise noise preserves flow-based policy exploration while limiting prediction-degrading action jitter. For long-horizon tasks, stage-local imagined training combines stage-entry resets, stage-specific rewards, local horizons, and controllable sampling to shorten generated prefixes and balance training across stages. WoVR+ improves success over SFT by 21.09% and 16.7% on RoboTwin and 6 real-robot tasks. Long-horizon phone-packaging success rises from 30% to 75%. Videos are available at https://youmo445.github.io/WoVR_Plus.github.io/.

Reports higher success than SFT on RoboTwin and six real-robot tasks; phone-packaging success increases from 30% to 75%.

papers.abstract: As generative language models become more capable and widely used, inference demand grows, making efficient serving increasingly important. Discrete diffusion language models (dLLMs) offer a promising path to more efficient inference through parallel token generation. Prior dLLM decoding methods, however, focus on improving inference efficiency for individual sequences. We formulate fixed-budget dLLM batch decoding and introduce Batch-Paced, a training-free method that jointly optimizes the allocation of decoding compute across requests to improve overall batch quality. Across two dLLM backbones, five benchmarks and their representative mixtures, Batch-Paced improves batch performance under matched budgets; gains generally grow with batch size and largely persist across decoding configurations. Analysis of requests' decoding trajectories suggests that these gains arise largely by raising the committed-token confidence of lower-confidence requests. We further show that Batch-Paced's batch decode time remains competitive and that adding a decoding-depth allowance during Batch-Paced decoding can shorten it further at a modest performance cost.
authors: Shuai Zhang, Zhanchao Zhou, Huachuan Qiu, Anqi Li, Zhenzhong Lan
bullets: Targets inefficient batch serving when inference compute is limited.
Introduces a training-free scheduler that jointly allocates decoding effort across requests.
Improves batch performance across two dLLM backbones, five benchmarks, and representative mixtures under matched budgets.
Benefits generally increase with batch size and persist across decoding configurations.
Maintains competitive batch decode time; limiting decoding depth can reduce latency with modest performance cost.

papers.abstract: Post-hoc linearization is an attractive way to accelerate pretrained Video Diffusion Transformers (Video DiTs), yet existing methods largely treat the quality loss induced by attention replacement as a recovery problem. We show that a more fundamental bottleneck lies upstream: \emph{initialization}. Random initialization discards pretrained knowledge, whereas manual weight reuse transfers it through rigid and incomplete source--target correspondences. We introduce \textbf{LinMorph}, which recasts Video DiT linearization as a learnable softmax-to-linear weight transformation problem. Instead of copying predefined counterparts, LinMorph learns a cross-parameter morphism that lets each target Gated DeltaNet (GDN) parameter draw jointly from pretrained query, key, value, and output projections, including for parameters with no direct softmax counterpart. A single morphism is shared across layers and learned through local teacher alignment, while producing layer-specific initializations from their respective pretrained weights. The resulting weights are then materialized as independent GDN modules for progressive distillation and joint recovery.Since the morphism operates in weight space rather than token space, it can be learned on short, low-resolution clips and directly reused at larger video scales. Across pretrained Video DiTs, LinMorph enables markedly faster recovery and better final generation quality than random initialization and heuristic weight reuse. Results show that efficient linearization depends not only on how a converted model is recovered, but critically on how pretrained knowledge is transferred before recovery. papers.abstract: Continual learning (CL) adapts pretrained models to a sequence of tasks while retaining knowledge acquired from earlier tasks. When task data are sensitive, differential privacy (DP) provides record-level protection, but maintaining both adaptation and retention under privacy constraints remains challenging. We study this problem in continual low-rank adaptation (LoRA) and observe that: 1) private training increases forgetting primarily during subsequent adaptation rather than initial task acquisition; 2) jointly perturbing both LoRA factors introduces a non-negligible bilinear noise interaction; and 3) DP aggravates the stability-plasticity dilemma, hindering both knowledge retention and adaptation to new tasks. Based on these observations, we propose DP-SPA, which constructs a stable subspace from previously privatized updates and a plastic subspace from pretrained weights within its orthogonal complement. The method fixes these bases and privately optimizes only the LoRA factor, eliminating the bilinear noise interaction within each step. Before merging each task update, it rescales stable-direction coefficients using historical and current update energies. We establish a privacy guarantee and show that recalibration does not increase historical overlap and tightens a conditional upper bound on old-task loss increase. Experiments across five datasets, eight settings, and multiple privacy budgets show that DP-SPA improves average accuracy and reduces forgetting compared with the evaluated baselines.
authors: Jin Liu, Ning Xi, Yinbin Miao, Junkang Liu, Ke Cheng, Jianfeng Ma
bullets: Problem: Differential privacy makes it difficult to retain earlier task knowledge while adapting LoRA to new tasks.

The design avoids bilinear noise interactions from jointly perturbing both LoRA factors.
Before merging updates, stable-direction coefficients are rescaled using historical and current update energies.
Across five datasets, eight settings, and multiple privacy budgets, DP-SPA improves average accuracy and reduces forgetting versus evaluated baselines.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) and world models have demonstrated strong capabilities in semantic understanding and future scene evolution for autonomous driving. However, effectively integrating both capabilities for trajectory generation remains challenging. In this work, we propose DriveWLA, a unified World-Language-Action model based on Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) that jointly models semantic understanding, future scene dynamics, and trajectory generation. DriveWLA consists of three experts: a World Expert for future prediction, a Language Expert for semantic understanding, and an Action Expert for trajectory generation. We further introduce Cross-Expert Attention, which enables controlled information flow across experts while aligning semantic and dynamic representations. To improve trajectory generation beyond imitation learning, we apply Flow-GRPO reinforcement learning post-training to refine the Action Expert. Extensive experiments show that DriveWLA achieves superior performance in both open-loop and closed-loop evaluation. DriveWLA achieves 92.3 PDMS on NAVSIM v1 and 90.1 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2, demonstrating strong performance among VLM-based and world-model-based planners. Without specific fine-tuning, DriveWLA further demonstrates strong zero-shot generalization to HUGSIM, nuScenes, and Bench2Drive. These results validate the effectiveness of our unified World-Language-Action modeling, establishing DriveWLA as a generalizable framework for autonomous driving.
authors: Shuzheng Wang, Haoxuan Li, Shengzhen Li, Chenxi Wu, Yajing Sun, Lu Hou, Wenyu Liu, Xinggang Wang

Reports 92.3 PDMS on NAVSIM v1 and 90.1 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2, with strong open- and closed-loop performance.
Shows zero-shot generalization to HUGSIM, nuScenes, and Bench2Drive without specific fine-tuning.

papers.abstract: Visual question answering models often produce plausible responses even when the available visual evidence is insufficient to support a valid answer. Although prior work has introduced benchmarks and abstention mechanisms for unanswerable visual questions, it remains unclear which signals derived from a frozen vision-language model reliably indicate answerability on unseen image-question pairs. We systematically evaluate answerability signals on a stratified 10K subset of UNK-VQA using frozen InstructBLIP, covering predictive uncertainty, cross-modal alignment, visual grounding, visual dependence, internal representations, and learned probes. Answerability discrimination remains weak, with test AUROC largely confined to 0.50-0.54. CLIP alignment yields the highest point estimate but does not significantly outperform generation confidence under paired bootstrap analysis. Targeted removal of question-relevant visual evidence causes substantially larger changes in answer confidence than same-size random masking, yet intervention sensitivity provides essentially no answerability discrimination. Increasing probe capacity, combining multiple signals, and adding reason-aware supervision do not provide robust improvements, while post-freeze cross-validation yields similarly weak discrimination. Selective-answering analysis shows limited usable coverage under low-risk operating criteria. Failure-mode analysis shows that the relative utility of individual signals varies across perturbation mechanisms. Taken together, these results show that, on our UNK-VQA subset with frozen InstructBLIP, visual dependence, uncertainty, semantic alignment, and static representations are not robust standalone proxies for answerability. Our findings emphasize the need to distinguish a model's reliance on visual evidence from whether that evidence is sufficient to support an answer.
authors: Minjun Kim, Hyunmin Song, Changwon Lim
bullets: Evaluates answerability signals across uncertainty, cross-modal alignment, grounding, visual dependence, representations, and learned probes.

Removing question-relevant visual evidence changes confidence more than random masking, yet intervention sensitivity remains uninformative for answerability.
More powerful probes, signal combinations, reason-aware supervision, and post-freeze cross-validation yield no robust gains; useful selective-answering coverage is limited.

papers.abstract: Long-context training of large language and multimodal models couples structured attention masks (document, prefix-LM, share-question, sliding-window, block-sparse) with multi-node context parallelism, making the mask a dominant bottleneck. FlashMask's column-wise sparse mask compresses them from $O(n^2)$ to $O(n)$ via four query-axis boundary vectors, covering broad structured patterns. Implemented for Ampere GPUs, it neither exploits FlashAttention-3's TMA/WGMMA warp-specialized pipeline on Hopper nor supports distribution. The column-wise sparse mask is indexed by key positions but stores query-axis interval boundaries. Under any multi-chunk context-parallel assignment, it reduces per-rank mask localization to a provably zero-communication \emph{clip--shift--max} on the boundary vectors, compatible with the single-GPU kernel. FlashMask-3 introduces a mask-aware Hopper kernel with three-role warp specialization atop FlashAttention-3's TMA/WGMMA pipeline, plus a mask-aware distributed extension: zero-communication mask localization, a sparsity-aware load balancer (HCC-IPO), and a mask-aware compute-communication overlap with mask-driven communication pruning, whose forward all-gather uses topology-aware hierarchical routing. On a single H100 across 12 masks at 4K--128K context, it improves achieved TFLOPs over FlashMask, FlexAttention, and MagiAttention by 45--141%, 34--71%, and 2--44%. At context-parallel degrees 4--32 with 8K sequence per device, it attains 31--75% compute-communication overlap efficiency and improves throughput over Megatron-Core CP ring, Megatron-Core CP all-gather, and MagiAttention by $1.80\times$--$3.71\times$, $1.71\times$--$2.92\times$, and $1.09\times$--$1.46\times$. In end-to-end training of a 118B-A14B MoE at 128K on 128 H100 GPUs, it raises throughput by 7.3--11.0% over a Dual Chunk all-gather baseline, with attention forward+backward 24.5--44.9% faster.
authors: Guoxia Wang, Qianyue He, Siming Wu, Haoyang Xie, Qiwen Bao, Jinle Zeng, Jiabin Yang, Tian Wu, Dianhai Yu

On a single H100, improves achieved TFLOPs by 2–141% over prior mask-aware attention systems across 12 masks and 4K–128K contexts.
Across 4–32 context-parallel degrees, improves throughput by up to 3.71×; in 128K end-to-end MoE training, raises throughput by 7.3–11.0%.

papers.abstract: Extended chain-of-thought reasoning improves problem-solving performance but increases inference cost and latency, motivating more accurate answers with shorter reasoning. We introduce PaceReasoner, a label-free test-time reinforcement learning framework that uses a model's LONG responses to improve its SHORT-mode accuracy. Both modes share a trainable policy, creating a need for reliable supervision, sufficient SHORT training samples, and continued LONG responses to guide learning. PaceReasoner combines all-response and LONG-only answer consensus through progressive, confidence-weighted supervision. A behavior reward gradually shifts from encouraging SHORT exploration to rewarding agreement with LONG answers, while a ratio controller regulates the balance between modes. Across three model backbones and four benchmarks, PaceReasoner improves average SHORT accuracy over the baselines by 7.4--13.5 percentage points, with fewer than 25 reasoning tokens per response on average. Ablations support the key components, and cross-dataset results demonstrate transfer beyond the adaptation set.

Uses a shared policy with label-free test-time reinforcement learning to train SHORT responses from LONG responses.
Combines all-response and LONG-only consensus with progressive, confidence-weighted supervision.
Gradually shifts rewards from encouraging SHORT exploration to matching LONG-answer guidance, while regulating the mode balance.
Across three backbones and four benchmarks, improves average SHORT accuracy by 7.4–13.5 percentage points; results transfer beyond the adaptation set.

papers.abstract: Effective collaboration among large language model (LLM) agents in multi-agent systems requires sharing relevant evidence, requesting missing information, and incorporating teammates' contributions into decisions. Training these behaviors is challenging because final task outcomes provide limited feedback on the value of individual messages. We introduce CoSIR (Collaboration via Surprisal-based Information Rewards), a post-training approach that uses a simple, verifiable environment to teach collaboration behaviors that generalize to more complex, unseen tasks. We propose a Bayesian evaluator that scores shared information by its reduction in team surprisal, defined as the sum of the negative log probabilities assigned to the correct option given each agent's available evidence. Requests are scored by the potential reduction in the same quantity if the requested information were truthfully provided. Separate rewards encourage agents to use the received information in their private choices and calculations. We post-train Qwen3-4B, Qwen3-8B, and Gemma-3-4B-it through self-play and evaluate transfer to seven unseen natural-language collaboration tasks. CoSIR achieves the highest aggregate score, while its performance in general tasks remains competitive. Behavioral analyses show increased disclosure of private evidence and fewer judged failures to use teammates' input.
authors: Keru Chen, Sen Lin, Yingbin Liang, Nathaniel D. Bastian, Shaofeng Zou
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of crediting individual messages when only final task outcomes are available.
Uses Bayesian surprisal reduction to score shared information and the potential value of requests.
Adds rewards for incorporating received information into agents’ choices and calculations.
Post-trains several LLMs via self-play and evaluates transfer across seven unseen collaboration tasks.
Achieves the highest aggregate score, with more evidence disclosure and fewer failures to use teammates’ input.

Self-play updates a policy shared by all agents, which is then evaluated on seven unseen collaboration tasks. The table and briefings illustrate one training instance.

papers.abstract: Microscopic simulations resolve spatial patterns but are feasible only over small domains and short timescales, whereas bulk descriptions erase those patterns through spatial averaging. Mesoscopic fields preserve this spatial organisation, but their effective equations are known only for selected microscopic systems and scaling limits. We introduce Deep Mesoscopic Dynamics (DeepMesoD), which uses neural networks to learn an effective mesoscopic field equation from microscopic trajectories at a prescribed coarse-graining scale. For the nonconserved dissipative dynamics studied here, DeepMesoD learns the free-energy functional with a spatial interaction kernel and a state-dependent dissipation operator constrained by the fluctuation-dissipation relation. We first validate the construction in the Ising-Kac model, where the learned mesoscopic equation recovers the known hydrodynamic limit and rollouts remain stable far beyond the training horizon. We then treat two systems without closed-form mesoscopic descriptions. For a two-dimensional Heisenberg ferromagnet governed by atomistic spin dynamics, DeepMesoD learns a mesoscopic model whose predictions match atomistic references up to 1 ns, and a rollout with an unseen initial condition remains bounded up to 25 ns. For layered CrBr$_3$, the learned kernel captures the suppression and sign reversal of interlayer coupling at a stacking fault whose location and strength are not supplied as inputs. Controlled changes to the learned interaction show how fault number and placement shape multistep magnetic responses, complementing our magneto-photoluminescence measurements. Across the two atomistic systems, DeepMesoD achieves a three-to-four-order-of-magnitude reduction in wall-clock time compared with atomistic spin dynamics.
authors: Yue Zhao, Shiqi Wu, Yihang Ouyang, Sergey Grebenchuk, Magdalena Grzeszczyk, Xiaoxu Zhao, Kostya S. Novoselov, Maciej Koperski, Qianxiao Li
bullets: Addresses the gap between detailed but costly microscopic simulations and overly averaged bulk models.
Learns a free-energy functional, spatial interaction kernel, and state-dependent dissipation operator constrained by fluctuation–dissipation relations.
Recovers the known hydrodynamic limit for the Ising–Kac model and remains stable well beyond its training horizon.
Models two systems without closed-form mesoscopic equations: a Heisenberg ferromagnet and layered CrBr₃ with stacking faults.
Reduces wall-clock time by three to four orders of magnitude versus atomistic spin dynamics in the studied atomistic systems.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Long-term stability and thermodynamic-structure recovery in atomistic spin dynamics. A. Long-term rollout from a triangular-domain initial condition on the same lattice. The DeepMesoD prediction is noise-free with the Itô thermal drift retained. Training uses random-initial-state trajectories. The triangular-domain initial condition is used for geometricinitial-condition extrapolation, not for fitting these stages. The dashed boundary at 1 ns separates the interval with an atomistic reference (“Observed”) from the interval without a reference (“Extrapolation”), ending at 25 ns. Time labels are in ps. The atomistic reference permits accuracy comparisons over 0–1 ns, but extending it to 25 ns is computationally costly. The 1–25 ns learnedmodel rollout assesses numerical stability and qualitative relaxation. B. Predicted magnetisation fields at the indicated times in ps. The triangular minority domain contracts towards a uniform magnetised state. C. Recovered Kernel. Left: spatial decay of the learned dissipation operator, quantified by the Frobenius norm of the block Ki,i+d with distance d relative to the on-site block. Middle: dissipation coupling constants K⊥ and K∥ as functions of centre spin mz, exhibiting an even (symmetric) profile that peaks near the disordered state and reflecting the expected axial anisotropy between the two coupling modes. Right: learned interaction kernel, revealing a dominant nearest-neighbour structure consistent with short-range exchange coupling. D. Recovered free energy. Left: free-energy landscape F (mz, Jmz) exhibiting a double-well profile with minima at mz = ±1, consistent with the underlying uniaxial anisotropy. Middle: thermodynamic force ∂F/∂(Jmz) recovered by DeepMesoD, which is a general nonlinear function of both mz and Jmz and exhibits non-trivial contour structure. Right: the hydrodynamic limit ∂F/∂(Jmz), which assumes an additive dependence on mz alone, yields a purely striped pattern independent of Jmz, demonstrating that the additive assumption fails to capture the full free-energy structure of this system.
