Each curve is shifted independently so that its minimum is zero. G. Conditional dissipation-operator response E{[K[ϕ]1](x) | ϕ(x) = m}, compared with the reference in (4) computed from the corresponding microscopic trajectories. H. Off-centre interaction weights, averaged over offsets with the same radial distance and compared with the Gaussian Ising–Kac kernel. For DeepMesoD and the CNN baseline, lines show the mean across three training seeds, and shaded bands indicate one standard deviation.

Figure 4. A learned stacking-fault interaction connects internal geometry to multistep magnetic response in CrBr3. A. Structural and magnetic schematic of layered CrBr3. Left: crystal structure of CrBr3 (Cr atoms in purple, Br atoms in gold). Middle: top and side views of representative M-stacking and AB-stacking configurations, where M denotes monoclinic stacking and AB denotes rhombohedral stacking and the two adjacent layers are coloured purple and green. Right: schematic AFM (antiparallel) and FM (parallel) interlayer spin alignments across a stacking fault, shown alongside the simulated three-dimensional magnetisation field mz at the final time step. The light-blue plane marks the stacking-fault interface between coarse slabs 13 and 14 (zero-based indices), and the pink (AFM) and green (FM) dashed circles highlight representative anti-correlated and correlated magnetic subdomains on either side of the fault. B. Effective interaction kernels learned by DeepMesoD without supplying the fault location as a model input. Left: learned interlayer kernel Jz as a function of layer indices a and b, showing a predominantly tridiagonal structure. The coupling across the stacking-fault interface between coarse slabs 13 and 14 (zero-based indices) has the opposite sign to the bulk interlayer coupling. Right: learned in-plane kernel Jxy as a function of in-plane displacement (∆x,∆y), showing an isotropic, short-range profile. C. Learned free-energy landscape for configurations with spatially uniform magnetisation within each of the two blocks. The coordinates are the mean magnetisation m = (mtop + mbottom)/2 and block contrast ∆m = (mtop −mbottom)/2. The four minima represent correlated states at (m,∆m) = (±m0, 0) and anti-correlated states at (m,∆m) = (0,±m0). The red curves indicate minimum-energy paths connecting these basins. D. Magneto-photoluminescence signature of magnetic transitions on a roughly 50 nm CrBr3 flake. The normalised PL intensity is shown as a function of out-of-plane magnetic field for sweeps from −2 T to 2 T and from 2 T to −2 T, with a step-like PL response to the applied magnetic field. The purple and orange curves show smoothed traces, while the faint traces in the background show the corresponding unsmoothed experimental data. Arrows indicate the magnetic-field sweep directions. The inset shows a schematic of exciton–magnetisation coupling in CrBr3. X denotes a CrBr3 exciton, represented here by an electron–hole pair with both carrier spins oriented upward. The σ+ label denotes the circular polarisation associated with this representative optically active exciton configuration. The local magnetisation vector M is chosen to point downward. E. Calculated equilibrium mean interfacial sign correlation ξsim versus external field for the 51.4 nm film containing one, three, five, or seven approximately uniformly spaced stacking faults. This observable averages the product of longitudinal magnetisation signs across each fault

papers.title: Deep Mesoscopic Dynamics

papers.abstract: Can an AI agent turn high-level user intent into a functioning robot and teach it how to behave? We study this question from two complementary aspects: embodiment and behavior creation. For embodiment creation, we investigate how well current multimodal models capture mechanical requirements, and introduce computational metrics for evaluating generated designs before fabrication. For behavior creation, we present Roboforge, an agentic framework that turns task specifications into executable policies through motion generation, policy learning, and execution-grounded revision. Given a robot embodiment and task, the agent generates a reference motion, configures the learning objective, and trains a policy. Crucially, motion remains in the loop: rollout feedback can revise the reference motion, reward, or both. We evaluate a generated embodiment across multiple MLLMs and behavior creation across four diverse robots against reward-refinement and one-shot motion baselines. Our computational metrics expose recurring mechanical failures in generated designs, while behavior experiments show that execution-grounded refinement improves task-level behavior and execution quality. Finally, we fabricate an agent-generated Gorilla and directly deploy learned behaviors on the physical robot.

papers.abstract: Multi-agent Large Language Model (LLM) systems typically commit to a deliberation protocol before inference. A fixed protocol cannot allocate computation differently to resolved and unresolved instances, and it may mistake repeated support for independent confirmation. We study this failure as semantic false consensus: a confident group answer supported by narrow, duplicated, or correlated rationales. We introduce ECMR, an evidence-aware controller over frozen role-conditioned LLMs. At each step, ECMR summarizes answer concentration, support diversity and independence, contradictions, role behavior, verification history, and remaining budget, then selects whether to propose, challenge, verify, arbitrate, diversify, correct a role, or stop. We formulate this decision as finite-horizon budgeted control and derive sufficient conditions under which state conditioning, risk-triggered verification, and role correction improve cost-adjusted utility. Across a declared held-out evaluation of 9,000 records from MedQA, CaseHOLD, and FinQA, ECMR-Full increases pooled accuracy from 62.1% to 84.9%, reduces false-consensus rate from 40.7% to 17.0%, and raises evidence-support rate from 58.0% to 88.7%. State shuffling loses 11.7 accuracy points with only 0.7 fewer rounds, while harder traces shift from early stopping toward arbitration. ECMR-Full uses the largest token budget, yielding the strongest absolute reliability rather than uniformly superior token efficiency.
authors: Yuan Liu, Haoyue Peng, Fanliang Hu, Lei Huang, Wenli Cai
bullets: Targets fixed deliberation protocols that waste computation and can mistake duplicated or correlated support for independent confirmation.
Controls frozen, role-conditioned agents by choosing among proposing, challenging, verifying, arbitrating, diversifying, correcting roles, or stopping.
Tracks answer concentration, evidence diversity and independence, contradictions, role behavior, verification history, and remaining budget.
On 9,000 held-out records across MedQA, CaseHOLD, and FinQA, pooled accuracy rose from 62.1% to 84.9%, while false-consensus rate fell from 40.7% to 17.0%.
The full controller uses the largest token budget, achieving stronger absolute reliability but not uniformly better token efficiency.

papers.abstract: Diffusion language models apply bidirectional attention over the whole context at every denoising step, so a longer context makes each step substantially more expensive. Sparsifying only at inference leaves the pretrained weights unchanged, so the model is never trained under the sparse pattern it runs with. We propose Prefilling-dLLM v2, which continues training a diffusion language model so that it routes with its native mask token. One mask is appended at the end of each chunk, and a learned role offset marks it as a routing slot. On every fourth layer, a query keeps a bidirectional local window and the top-K chunks scored from that mask; the other layers use a bidirectional sliding window. Starting from Dream-v0-Base-7B extended to 16K with YaRN, we compare Prefilling-dLLM v2 with bidirectional NSA, DSA, and SWA under the same layout, key budget, and dense initialization, using the same Fast-dLLM decoder. With the YaRN factor scaled to the evaluation length, Prefilling-dLLM v2 leads the other sparse methods on all three RULER tasks from 16K to 128K. Its mean accuracy at 128K is 7.4 points above NSA, the next sparse model, while DSA and SWA remain near zero. At the same length, decoding is 172x faster than with full dense attention.
authors: Qi Han, Jing Xiong, Ziyuan Zhang, Ngai Wong
bullets: Addresses the high per-step cost of bidirectional full-context attention in diffusion language models.
Adds one learned routing mask per chunk; every fourth layer selects the top-K chunks while other layers use local sliding-window attention.
Continued training aligns the model with the sparse attention pattern used at inference.
Outperforms bidirectional NSA, DSA, and SWA across three RULER tasks from 16K to 128K; at 128K, it is 7.4 accuracy points above NSA.
Achieves 172× faster decoding than dense attention at 128K, within the evaluated setup and context range.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Mean accuracy of the four sparse methods on the three RULER tasks. The YaRN factor scales with the evaluation length.

Figure 2: What query q can see. Each chunk is three cells, and q sits in the middle so the local window extends both ways. Teal cells are the local window and orange cells are selected. The bar above each NSA chunk is its summary. DSA reads scattered tokens, and Prefilling-dLLM v2 marks the last cell of every chunk as a mask.

Figure 3: Computation on a route layer. A chunk is S − 1 content tokens followed by one routing mask. The role offset r is added to that mask at the input. Its query pools the content keys with an intra-chunk softmax, and the weighted sum is the summary key sc. A content query adds a lowrank residual and scores these summaries. Inside a GQA group (Ainslie et al., 2023) the scores are reduced by a maximum, and the top K chunks are shared by every head in the group. Attention mass puts the selected chunk scores and the local-window log-sum-exp in one partition, then a second softmax distributes each chunk’s mass over its content tokens.

papers.abstract: Agent Skills improve LLM agents by making task knowledge reusable across sessions. Learning transferable Skills requires evidence about a procedure and its conditions of use, which a successful task attempt can leave untested. We introduce Socratic Skill Learning (SSL), which interleaves expert teaching with Student practice. An Educator guides investigation while the Student remains the sole environment operator and Skill author, able to question, test, and adapt advice. To test reuse beyond the learning task, we construct SkillTransferBench, with 35 task families and 408 executable cases, pairing public variation specifications with held-out evaluation in fresh solver sessions. On the main 22-family, 155-case cohort, Fixed-Window SSL reaches 0.801 utility, versus 0.723 without a Skill, 0.761 for adapted Trace2Skill (trajectory distillation), and 0.751 for adapted SKILL-KD (contrastive distillation). Across three model pairs on shared families, interleaved guidance outperforms expert authoring and post-hoc teaching. Process analysis links guidance to Student writing and package revision; a case study shows the Student testing and refining a proposed procedure for later reuse. As demand for new lessons falls, the cost of fixed-window review grows. Issue-Guided SSL tracks unresolved questions across Skill revisions to select and focus review, reaching 0.805 utility with 61.7% fewer Educator tokens and 16.9% fewer total acquisition tokens than Fixed-Window SSL on the main cohort.
authors: Letian Zhu, Han Li, Yifan Yao, Xinping Lei, Xinyu Che, Jiahao Wang, Dianyi Wang, Yucheng Fu, Jiakai Wang, Zhiqi Bai, Wenbo Su, Jiaheng Liu
bullets: Agent Skills need evidence about both procedures and when they apply, which successful task completion alone may not provide.
SSL keeps the Student as the sole environment operator and Skill author, while an Educator guides investigation through questions and advice.
On SkillTransferBench, Fixed-Window SSL achieved 0.801 utility, outperforming no Skill and adapted trajectory/contrastive distillation baselines.
Issue-Guided SSL reached 0.805 utility while using 61.7% fewer Educator tokens and 16.9% fewer total acquisition tokens than Fixed-Window SSL.
The study covers 35 task families and 408 executable cases; results focus on transfer to fresh solver sessions and three model pairs.

papers.abstract: Time-series analysis is increasingly studied in multimodal settings, yet most benchmarks pair temporal signals with text or with visualizations derived from the same signal. This leaves open whether multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can integrate time series with real-world visual evidence. We introduce MMTA (multimodal temporal analysis), a benchmark of tri-modal tasks with diverse cross-modal complementarity patterns among time series, text, and vision. MMTA spans nine domains -- robotics, autonomous driving, human action, manufacturing, AR assistance, healthcare, recommendation, finance, and climate -- under video+TS and image+TS layouts, with a 3,524-sample test split covering classification and forecasting. The benchmark standardizes heterogeneous real-world sources into a shared schema with domain-specific prompts, provenance documentation, and success-weighted metrics that penalize both wrong answers and failed generations. Evaluating eight open-source and proprietary MLLMs reveals a shared bottleneck: representing time series as text creates very long token sequences and weakens fine-grained alignment with visual evidence, especially in long-video settings. We then introduce TimeOmni-v, a multimodal LLM extension with a dedicated time-series encoder, temporal positional alignment, modality-aware token layout, and a forecasting head. TimeOmni-v improves long-video classification and time-series inference efficiency, showing that MMTA not only exposes representation and grounding failures but also motivates targeted model design.
authors: Ziyang Zhang, Shenyi Li, Yilin Wang, Ziyun Cui, Bowen Zhou, Wen Wu, Chao Zhang
bullets: Introduces tri-modal classification and forecasting tasks across nine domains using video+time-series and image+time-series layouts.
Standardizes heterogeneous sources with shared schemas, domain-specific prompts, provenance documentation, and success-weighted metrics.
Evaluates eight open-source and proprietary MLLMs, finding that text-based time-series representations produce long token sequences and weak visual alignment, especially for long videos.
Proposes TimeOmni-v with a dedicated time-series encoder, temporal positional alignment, modality-aware token layout, and forecasting head.
TimeOmni-v improves long-video classification and time-series inference efficiency, though the abstract does not report quantitative results.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces a tri-modal benchmark and a multimodal LLM extension integrating time series, text, and vision, directly fitting multimodal foundation models.

papers.abstract: Proactive dynamic grasping requires robots to predict the future state at which physical contact will occur, rather than reacting to the currently observed object pose. But what future must the robot predict, and at what level of abstraction? We argue that contact-relevant rigid-body state in SE(3) is a compact task-sufficient abstraction for this problem: it directly determines where and when the robot should establish contact, without requiring visually complete future scenes. This insight leads to a lightweight object-centric forecast-then-select framework that predicts future rigid-body trajectories from short pose histories and uses a reachability-aware interception selector to choose feasible contact states under kinematic and timing constraints. Trained with randomized physics simulation over primitive shapes, the forecaster transfers to real objects once their metric geometry and SE(3) state histories are recovered. Experiments across simulation and real-world dynamic grasping tasks show that our framework improves the average success rate from \(24.5\%\) to \(62.0\%\) in simulation, and from \(15.3\%\) to \(67.3\%\) in real-world catching, conveyor, and turntable interception. The SE(3) forecaster runs in \(15\,\mathrm{ms}\), orders of magnitude faster than dense visual future prediction, enabling real-time contact decision making. Our results suggest that effective proactive grasping does not require imagining the entire future scene. Instead, predicting the compact physical future that determines contact provides an effective and practical abstraction for real-time dynamic grasping.
authors: Yirui Zhou, Hongli Xu, Ying Zheng, Yi Wang, Lap-Pui Chau
bullets: Frames contact-relevant rigid-body state in SE(3) as a task-sufficient abstraction for predicting when and where contact should occur.
Forecasts future object trajectories from short pose histories, then selects reachable interception states under kinematic and timing constraints.
Trained in randomized physics simulation on primitive shapes and transferred to real objects using metric geometry and SE(3) histories.
Improves average success from 24.5% to 62.0% in simulation and from 15.3% to 67.3% in real-world catching, conveyor, and turntable tasks.
Runs in 15 ms, supporting real-time contact decisions while avoiding dense visual future prediction.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of PAF-Grasp. The Neural SE(3) forecaster is trained on Genesis-generated primitive-object trajectories to learn reusable rigid-body dynamics. At deployment, an anchor RGBD observation is used offline to recover object-specific geometry and an approximate inertia prior, while the online RGB-D stream continuously updates the object’s SE(3) history for closed-loop forecasting and interception. The forecaster encodes recent motion history, estimates initial velocities, and integrates a Newton–Euler-structured neural ODE to predict future rigid-body trajectories. The forecast-guided interception selector then propagates task-specific contact frames along the predicted trajectory and selects a reachable end-effector target under timing and kinematic constraints.

papers.abstract: Multi-agent deliberation can improve recognition by criticizing and revising candidate answers, but fixed controls cannot respond to changes in disagreement or reasoning quality. We present an adaptive multi-agent controller (ADMA) that learns continuous policies for proposal, challenge, arbitration, and coordination while keeping the task model frozen. Shared trace features describe quality, agreement, and progress, while role-specific features support decentralized control during inference. One controller trained on legal and financial reasoning is transferred without policy updates to four textual and multimodal benchmarks and two successive task-model versions. With Qwen3.5 held fixed, ADMA-Full improves accuracy by 6.2-14.2 percentage points over Direct and by 2.8-3.0 points over ADMA-Fixed. Paired bootstrap ranges for the Full-Fixed comparison are positive on three tasks. Outcome decompositions show that recoveries exceed introduced errors, while process assessment records fewer false-consensus events and more supported correct outcomes. Transfer to Qwen3.6 remains task dependent, which bounds the generality of the learned policy. Median token and latency ratios are 14.3-18.7 and 7.8-16.5 relative to Direct. These results show that adaptive deliberation can improve fixed-model recognition when its task-dependent gains justify the additional computation.
authors: Yuan Liu, Haoyue Peng, Fanliang Hu, Lei Huang, Wenli Cai
bullets: Fixed deliberation controls may fail when disagreement or reasoning quality changes.
ADMA learns continuous proposal, challenge, arbitration, and coordination policies from shared and role-specific trace features.
A controller trained on legal and financial reasoning transfers without policy updates across four textual/multimodal benchmarks and two model versions.
With Qwen3.5, ADMA-Full improves accuracy by 6.2–14.2 points over Direct and 2.8–3.0 points over ADMA-Fixed; recoveries exceed introduced errors.
Transfer to Qwen3.6 is task dependent, while token and latency costs are substantially higher than Direct.

papers.abstract: Multimodal Diffusion Transformers (MM-DiTs) have recently emerged as a powerful framework for unified text-vision synthesis, surpassing traditional U-Net architectures in generative tasks. One key innovation lies in its Multimodal Self-Attention (MM-SA) interaction, where image and text tokens are concatenated and processed via self-attention. However, this mechanism poses significant challenges for editing, rendering conventional U-Net-based attention manipulation methods ineffective. To address this limitation, we propose QK-Edit, a training-free framework that exploits the unique attention dynamics of MM-DiTs for precise text-guided image and video editing. By introducing a novel query-key manipulation strategy, our method isolates and adjusts critical attention components to achieve an optimal balance between prompt fidelity and structural consistency. This enables seamless edits across various tasks, including object addition, object removal, object replacement, changing background, changing material, changing color, and style transformation. Notably, it can be easily implemented with feature replacement in inference. QK-Edit demonstrates superior editing performance on state-of-the-art models, such as FLUX and HunyuanVideo, effectively bridging the gap between generative power and editable flexibility in MM-DiTs, and paving the way for scalable multimodal content creation.
authors: Tiancheng Shen, Zilong Huang, Xiangtai Li, Zhijie Lin, Jiyang Liu, Yitong Wang, Jiashi Feng, Ming-Hsuan Yang, Jun Hao Liew
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of applying conventional U-Net attention-editing methods to MM-DiTs with concatenated image-text tokens.
Manipulates query-key interactions to balance prompt fidelity with preservation of the original structure.
Supports object addition, removal, replacement, background and material changes, color edits, and style transformations.
Implemented through feature replacement during inference, without additional training.
Demonstrates effective editing on MM-DiT models including FLUX and HunyuanVideo.

papers.abstract: Existing approaches to training and evaluating search agents focus heavily on final-answer quality, largely neglecting how generated answers map back to retrieved evidence. Recent methods track citations to enforce grounding, but citation support alone does not establish source independence or whether an answer appropriately handles conflicting evidence. We argue that credibility in open-web retrieval depends on principled cross-source evidence grounding that accounts for source independence and systematically attributes and adjudicates conflicting evidence, while hierarchical judgments of these grounding decisions provide a unified signal for training and evaluation. To this end, we propose an evaluation framework, Cross-Source Evidence Grounding (CSEG), that employs a fine-grained, six-layer decision tree over the complete search trajectory. We introduce CSEG-Bench and trainable reward models to provide targeted supervision following this framework. Our approach helps eliminating the severe data skew of natural trajectories by providing targeted coverage over complex, deep-layer decision paths, such as cross-source conflict resolution and nuanced attribution, that standard rollouts fail to capture. Specifically, (1) we define the hierarchy at label, node, and path levels; (2) we construct 1,160 verified trajectories over nine canonical paths by rewriting answers on real retrieved document pools, with independent frontier judges reproducing the entire gold path and human experts deciding inclusion; (3) we train CSEG-RM, which reaches 83.9% exact accuracy on our benchmark while lying on the performance-token efficiency Pareto frontier. Experiments that use this reward alone to supervise a frozen-retrieval answer policy raise the independently judged mean label from 2.83 to 4.19, and show that learning the hierarchy generalizes across layers at a fraction of frontier-judge cost.
authors: Haochen Zhao, Minsheng Hao, Zheng Li, Yifan Li, Zikang Liu, Bowen Qin, Yuhao Cheng, Chuang Fan, Haosheng Zou, Jeff Chen, Sujian Li

papers.abstract: Edge-cloud collaboration combines the lower inference overhead and greater data locality of edge-side execution with the stronger capabilities of cloud-hosted models. However, as LLM agents increasingly operate in long-horizon scenarios, cloud participation becomes interleaved throughout execution rather than a one-shot decision for each query. Such interleaved participation introduces trajectory-level effects that remain insufficiently understood. To address this gap, we introduce EC2-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating edge-cloud collaboration in long-horizon agent execution. It provides executable digital-workspace agent tasks and a unified evaluation framework covering task performance, resource usage, and privacy exposure. Using this benchmark, we empirically study diverse forms of edge-cloud collaboration. Our study reveals three findings. First, collaboration achieves a favorable balance among task performance, resource usage, and privacy exposure compared with edge-only and cloud-only execution. Second, as edge models become stronger, collaborative execution approaches cloud-only performance, and performance differences across strategies shrink, while privacy exposure remains strongly strategy-dependent. Third, stronger edge capability shifts preferred collaboration from externally controlled cloud participation and direct cloud execution toward more edge-controlled collaboration. Further analyses identify cloud-invocation decision-making and instruction following as important edge-side abilities for effective collaboration. These findings provide a systematic understanding of edge-cloud collaboration in long-horizon agent execution and insights for designing future edge agents that effectively collaborate with cloud models. Code and resources are available at https://github.com/OpenBMB/EC2-Bench.

papers.abstract: Collision rate remains a dominant metric for evaluating autonomous driving trajectory safety, but its binary nature obscures substantial safety differences among collision-free trajectories. Existing surrogate-safety metrics provide finer-grained assessments, yet often trade off physical interpretability against adaptivity to interaction context. We introduce FutureRisk, a continuous metric that quantifies the latent future risk of a trajectory by how closely and persistently its realized interactions approach unsafe states. At its core, our Context-Adaptive Risk Model (CARM) combines a context-dependent safety-time distribution with an independently supervised critical-event-time distribution. Its safety criterion is bounded around a closed-form physical prior, while a bounded residual provides additional adaptation without abandoning this physical anchor. Experiments on DeepAccident and Bench2Drive show that FutureRisk achieves stronger agreement with native collision labels than existing surrogate-safety measures, discriminates risk among collision-free trajectories, and transfers zero-shot across datasets. Comparisons across four planners further show that FutureRisk reveals safety differences hidden by binary collision outcomes. Together, these results establish FutureRisk as a fine-grained, interpretable, and context-adaptive metric for trajectory safety evaluation. Code is available at https://github.com/Xuewen2025/safety-evaluation.

papers.abstract: Robot manipulation has traditionally relied on end-effector-centric interactions. In contrast, humans routinely exploit whole-arm contacts to improve efficiency, robustness, and adaptability, especially when the hands are occupied or when precise grasping is unnecessary. Enabling similar capabilities in robots remains challenging: the robot must select where on its arm to make contact, generate effective non-prehensile interactions, and satisfy task-specific pose or safety constraints on the end-effector. We propose Whole-Arm Contact Learning (WACL), a hierarchical framework that describes each whole-arm contact task with three robot-agnostic representations and hands them to a quasi-static surface-contact optimizer: semantic keypoints that summarize the scene, a reference contact trajectory that specifies where and how the arm presses on the object, and safety-aware path constraints that a vision-language model generates from the task description to protect the end-effector's task. The robot's kinematic chain enters only in this optimizer, which grounds these representations onto the arm by jointly searching over which link makes contact, where on that link, and the joint configuration that realizes it. This decomposition lets WACL learn the contact trajectory from 10 bare-hand human demonstrations per task collected without teleoperation, while new end-effector constraints change only the optimizer's input rather than any trained component. Real-world experiments on a 7-DoF arm across four whole-arm tasks show that WACL sustains contact under end-effector constraints where a strong link-pose baseline fails (78% vs. 33% success) and generalizes to new constraints without retraining. Website: https://wacl-robot.github.io
authors: Bo-Ruei Huang, Daniel Seita, Erdem B{\i}y{\i}k
bullets: Addresses the challenge of choosing arm-contact locations while preserving task-specific end-effector pose and safety constraints.
Uses three robot-agnostic representations: semantic scene keypoints, a reference contact trajectory, and vision-language-model-generated safety-aware path constraints.
A quasi-static surface-contact optimizer grounds these representations onto a robot by jointly selecting the contacting link, contact location, and joint configuration.
On a 7-DoF arm across four tasks, WACL achieved 78% success under end-effector constraints versus 33% for a link-pose baseline.
Demonstrations use bare hands rather than teleoperation; the method’s scope is whole-arm, non-prehensile contact tasks.

Safetyaware path constraint generation. A VLM grounds a fixed vocabulary of primitives into path constraints that preserve the primary end-effector task. Surface-contact trajectory optimization. The optimizer searches each link’s reachable anchors with surface-contact inverse kinematics and beam search under the constraints.

papers.abstract: Online reinforcement learning (RL) enables driving policies to adapt to changing deployment conditions, but requires safe exploration throughout training. Safety filtering alone does not ensure stable policy improvement or reduced dependence on corrections. We propose Safe Online Adaptive Refinement (SOAR-Flow), a framework for safe and stable online fine-tuning of offline-initialized Flow-based driving policies. A control barrier function (CBF)--model predictive control (MPC) filter corrects potentially unsafe actions before execution. To support stable policy updates, we introduce Gaussian-return-aware value calibration based on calibrated Q-learning (Cal-QL), using recorded behavior returns and predicted return variability to smooth conservative critic updates and mitigate policy degradation. Paired corrective learning teaches feasible action adjustments, while an intervention-to-go predictor encourages decisions requiring fewer future corrections. Its predictions also regulate guidance strength, allowing recovery supervision to weaken as predicted dependence decreases. Together with gradually reduced calibration regularization, this supports continued task improvement while preserving hard execution constraints. We analyze conditions for safe execution at control steps and diminishing auxiliary learning influences. We evaluate SOAR-Flow in simulation and on an uncrewed ground vehicle (UGV). The results demonstrate improved driving performance and reduced reliance on safety corrections during protected online fine-tuning. The demonstration video and project overview are available at https://lzqw.github.io/SOAR-Flow/.
authors: Zeqiao Li, Yijing Wang, Haoyu Wang, Zheng Li, Zhiqiang Zuo
bullets: Addresses unstable policy improvement and persistent safety-correction dependence during online RL for autonomous driving.
Combines a CBF–MPC safety filter with Gaussian-return-aware value calibration to enforce safe actions and mitigate policy degradation.
Uses paired corrective learning and an intervention-to-go predictor to guide feasible actions and adaptively reduce recovery supervision.
Evaluated in simulation and on an uncrewed ground vehicle, showing improved driving performance and fewer safety corrections during protected fine-tuning.

papers.abstract: Understanding facial behaviour in video requires answering three fundamental questions: when a key facial expression occurs, where the model attends on the face at that moment, and why that evidence is necessary rather than merely correlated. Today's multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can label and describe video, but they rarely provide faithful explanations, especially for small facial movements that change over time. We present VideoFace-X-LLM, a framework for explainable facial video understanding comprising two key components. First, we introduce ExplainFace, a weakly supervised video-text corpus for facial behaviour understanding, automatically constructed from CelebV-HQ videos and validated through human evaluation and a two-model audit (at most 2.3% contradictions), demonstrating consistent gains across two backbone architectures. Second, H-TCC (Hierarchical Temporal Spatial Causal Concepts), which finds the key temporal moments (When), the facial regions (Where), and verifies its causal necessity (Why) through targeted occlusion. Fine-tuning on ExplainFace raises appearance Macro F1 from 19.48% to 32.87% (+13.39), with gains of +4.38 on actions, +6.77 on temporal emotion, and +11.84 F1 on deepfake detection. We also measure the explanations pointing lift, face/edge lift, stability, an Adebayo sanity check, and a necessity test rather than only showing examples. Our models, code, and corpus are available on request for research use.
authors: Anubhav Kataria, Shreya Ghosh, Jingwen Ye, Abhinav Dhall

Uses H-TCC to identify key moments, relevant facial regions, and causal necessity through targeted occlusion.
Fine-tuning improves appearance Macro F1 from 19.48% to 32.87%, with additional gains for actions, temporal emotion, and deepfake detection.

papers.abstract: A long-horizon manipulation task consists of primitive skills and the transitions connecting them. Learning skills that can be executed in sequence requires supervision for both, which is costly to collect on a robot. Human videos offer a scalable source of demonstrations, but transferring them to robots requires extracting robot-compatible observations and actions together with their skill structure. We present DexStitch, a framework that cuts long-horizon human videos into skills and transitions, converts them into aligned robot observation-action-skill data, and stitches the learned skills into a requested sequence. A skill classifier first segments the videos into manipulation skills and transitions. DexStitch then converts the human demonstrations into robot observations and actions while retaining their corresponding skill labels. During conversion, per-finger human-object contacts guide dexterous hand retargeting and robotic inpainting, preserving contact geometry and finger-object occlusion ordering. To stitch the learned skills into a sequence, a shared skill-conditioned policy is pretrained on the resulting synthetic data and finetuned on a mixture of synthetic data and a small set of single-skill teleoperation episodes. Conditioning on the current and next skills guides each transition toward the following skill, while predicted skill progression enables closed-loop switching. On a held-out session, the classifier agrees with manual annotations on 92.4% of frames. Across four household skills, DexStitch achieves 80.0% single-skill success and 77.5% sequence success.

Reports 92.4% frame-level agreement with manual skill annotations, 80.0% single-skill success, and 77.5% sequence success across four household skills.

Together, the retargeted robot and the inpainted scene produce a robot-domain visual sequence.

(b) A shared skill-conditioned policy predicts robot actions and skill progression from the current observation and the current–next skill pair. (c) At inference time, the policy executes the given skill sequence in closed loop, advancing to the next entry according to its predicted skill progression.

papers.abstract: We introduce Diffuplex, a full-duplex spoken language model based on discrete diffusion that achieves an unprecedented balance between linguistic intelligence and response efficiency. With thinking mode, Diffuplex delivers 13.0 tokens per forward pass, reaching an average of 1872 tokens per second and substantially surpassing the frontier autoregressive (AR) models in decoding speed. Without thinking, Diffuplex matches the first-audio latency of existing full-duplex models while achieving markedly stronger linguistic intelligence. This capability is enabled by separating when to say from what to say at the training level, rather than compressing both into a single autoregressive timeline. During inference, Diffuplex continuously tracks the user speech through an AR interaction policy, while independently generating and refining response content through parallel diffusion. Consequently, semantic computation is no longer bounded by the perception audio frame rate, allowing intelligence and responsiveness to improve simultaneously. Taken together, these results establish a new paradigm for spoken agents that can sustain real-time dialogue while devoting parallel computation to intelligent response generation. Training code and checkpoints will be avaliable soon.
authors: Chen Chen, Pin-Jui Ku, Ankita Pasad, Ante Juki\'c, Zhehuai Chen, Boris Ginsburg

papers.abstract: Theory of mind (ToM), the ability to reason about others' mental states, underlies effective communication and coordination. Its higher-order form enables reasoning over nested perspectives in strategic interactions. However, existing evaluations often equate belief-nesting depth with reasoning order, allowing nominally higher-order questions to admit lower-order shortcuts. We formalize effective order through the distinct events supporting successive belief prefixes, revealing widespread order inflation across existing benchmarks. We introduce HopToM, with certified full-order questions and controls for lower-order alternatives. Under direct prompting, mean accuracy across four frontier LLMs falls from 73.5% at first order to 20.0% at fourth order, and human participants also struggle. Causal interventions link a recurring class of errors to evidence for shallower belief prefixes. We introduce HopTrace, a plug-and-play inference-time method that encodes each interaction once into perspective records and resolves nested queries deterministically. On certified narrative questions, it improves fourth- and fifth-order accuracy by 22.0 and 38.5 percentage points over strong prompting baselines, while using 20-39 times fewer tokens than multi-call methods. These results sharpen how higher-order ToM is evaluated and offer a practical way to improve perspective reasoning in interactive agents.
authors: Shanshan You, Zhengqi Wang, Hao Liu, Yuqin Liu, Ya He, Xin Hao, Liyuan Wang
bullets: Existing benchmarks can mistake belief-nesting depth for genuine reasoning order because lower-order shortcuts remain possible.
HopToM certifies full-order questions and controls for lower-order alternatives, exposing widespread order inflation.
Across four frontier LLMs, mean accuracy drops from 73.5% at first order to 20.0% at fourth order; humans also struggle.
HopTrace improves fourth- and fifth-order accuracy by 22.0 and 38.5 percentage points over strong prompting baselines while using 20–39× fewer tokens than multi-call methods.
Error analyses link recurring failures to reliance on shallower belief prefixes.

papers.abstract: Large reasoning models (LRMs) achieve strong performance by externalizing explicit reasoning traces before producing the answer, yet suffer from overthinking challenge that allocates uniformly heavy computation to queries of varying difficulty. While proprietary models mitigate this via opaque routing, open-source LRMs still lack an efficient mechanism to internalize adaptive reasoning due to both expensive training cost and limited disclosure of training recipes. In response, we introduce RPO (Root-token Policy Optimization), a framework that enables LRMs to self-determine when to reason by training only the initial root token (e.g., whether to invoke the tag) via group relative reward and group-wise advantages. By focusing on this pivotal branching point, RPO drastically reduces training overhead and VRAM usage. Across multiple model families and scales, RPO learns difficulty-aware adaptive thinking at just ~2% of the training compute of prior adaptive-reasoning methods.

papers.abstract: Long-term memory supports agents across sessions. Repeated retrieval and write-back can let one historical claim occupy multiple retrieval positions and influence current answers without independent evidence. Existing work examines retrieval, updating, and question answering, leaving same-source record accumulation and post-correction persistence underexplored. Motivated by research in social cognition and memory psychology on repeated exposure, retrieval, and revision, we define \emph{Memory Echo} as the excess retrieval exposure gained by historical information from the same source without additional independent evidence, and introduce MEchoBench to evaluate its emergence, correction resistance, persistence, and effect on answers. To address this phenomenon, we introduce the Family--Provenance--Authority framework (FPA). Specifically, FPA selects one representative per source family, conditions the eligibility of old records for the answer context on verified corrections, and constrains final answers with authoritative evidence. In paired replay on 190 fixed questions across four memory frameworks, FPA raises accuracy from 0.825 to 0.920 with DeepSeek V4 Flash and from 0.782 to 0.916 with Kimi K2.6; mean Decision Contamination Effect falls from 0.106 to 0.030 and from 0.109 to 0.038, respectively. These results show that agent memory can preserve traceable history without allowing repeated historical information to govern current decisions. The code is available at https://github.com/OrcasSam/memory-echo-benchmark.

papers.abstract: Robotic assistance for human mobility could benefit care recipients and reduce caregiver burden during physically demanding tasks such as Sit-to-Stand (STS) and Lift-and-Transfer (L&T). Learning robot policies for these whole-body assistive tasks is challenging: real-world data collection for human-robot interaction is costly and safety-critical, making simulation an attractive alternative. Prior work, however, typically treats the human as static or minimally responsive and thus fails to capture the cooperative nature of mobility assistance. We present a simulation-based framework for learning whole-body assistive robot policies. At its core is a human policy trained with an adversarial motion prior that produces realistic care-recipient motion in response to the robot's actions. A human-adaptive scripted controller interacts with this policy to collect diverse robot demonstrations at scale. From these demonstrations, we train 3D diffusion policies that map segmented human point clouds and robot joint positions to whole-body actions for a mobile manipulator, without relying on privileged human state at deployment. The resulting robot policies successfully perform both STS and L&T assistance in simulation. Preliminary experiments further demonstrate sim-to-real transfer for STS after fine-tuning on a small amount of real-world data. Videos are available on our project page: https://rchi-lab.github.io/human-gen-mobility-assistance/
authors: Shikun Ban, Shohei Nagai, Qingyang Song, Hanxi Wan, Eric Zhao, Thomas Wang, Zackory Erickson

Trains 3D diffusion policies from segmented human point clouds and robot joint positions, without privileged human state at deployment.
Policies perform both tasks in simulation, with preliminary Sit-to-Stand sim-to-real transfer after limited real-world fine-tuning.

papers.abstract: Policies trained offline from teleoperated demonstrations can degrade outside their training distribution. This gap is particularly acute in long-horizon whole-body mobile manipulation, where long horizons amplify compounding errors and coordinated arm, torso, and base motion makes exhaustive demonstration coverage impractical. We introduce I3L, an integrated hardware and learning system that combines whole-body correction with iterative policy refinement to address this last-mile reliability gap. Its low-cost, open-source JoyLo+ interface uses policy-tracking leader arms and touch-triggered takeover to enable coordinated corrections across the body parts, while iterative deployment and retraining allow operators to target failures of the updated policy. We evaluate I3L across three robot embodiments and eight simulated and real-world tasks, including four long-horizon whole-body mobile manipulation tasks. Controlled simulation experiments show that four-round HG-DAgger achieves the highest final success on both tasks. Under this protocol, I3L improves autonomous success over the base policies by an average of 68.3 percentage points and achieves at least 90% success on every task, outperforming demonstration-only training by 35.6 percentage points on average with the same number of training trajectories. Averaged across tasks, takeover duration per episode decreases by 72% over four rounds. Together, these results show that I3L helps close the last-mile gap between offline training and reliable deployment and provides practical insights into collecting and using corrections for long-horizon whole-body mobile manipulation. Videos, visualizations, and appendix are at https://i-3l.github.io/.

Evaluated on three robot embodiments and eight simulated and real-world tasks, including four long-horizon tasks.

papers.abstract: A robot may know how to perform a task yet fail when a human asks for it naturally. We study this human--VLA communication gap by separating an \emph{information gap}, where task semantics, grounding, or event structure remain unresolved, from a residual \emph{execution gap}, where even a fully specified task depends on how it is organized and invoked. To do this, we characterize how people naturally express demonstrated objectives and evaluate controlled variants of the same physical tasks, with detailed analysis on $\pi_{0.5}$ and consistent trends on $\pi_0$-FAST and Cosmos3-Edge. Our study reveals that humans increasingly compress instructions as tasks grow, relying more on contextual grounding and implicit execution structure. Current policies are misaligned with this behavior: they tolerate grounding dependence relatively well, but struggle when task semantics or event structure must be reconstructed. Even after the information gap is resolved, execution remains sensitive to command granularity and invocation state. These findings identify concrete targets for human-centered policy learning and interfaces that better bridge natural human objectives to robot behavior. Project website: https://commgap.github.io/.
authors: Yiqing Xu, Jiajun Wu
bullets: Separates the communication gap into an information gap—unresolved semantics, grounding, or event structure—and an execution gap involving task organization and invocation.
Analyzes how humans describe demonstrated objectives and evaluates controlled variants of the same physical tasks across several policies.
Finds that people compress instructions more as tasks become complex, relying increasingly on context and implicit execution structure.
Policies handle grounding dependence relatively well but struggle to reconstruct task semantics and event structure.
Even fully specified tasks remain sensitive to command granularity and invocation state, motivating human-centered policy learning and interfaces.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Human–VLA communication gap. For the same physical task, human specifications vary in task content, reference, and composition, producing substantially different VLA performance (top). We separate this mismatch into an information gap, where task semantics, grounding, or event structure remain unresolved, and a residual execution gap, where the fully resolved task remains sensitive to command organization and invocation state (bottom), distinguishing recovering the intended task from reliably executing it through the policy’s learned interface.

Fig. 6: From human specifications to measurable information gaps. The same physical objective can be expressed through substantially different human specifications. Our taxonomy classifies each instruction by its task content, reference form, and composition, and maps these choices to the executable information made available to the policy: which actions, objects, and destinations are directly specified, require grounding, or are omitted. This yields quantitative measures of semantic coverage, groundedness, and decomposition ratio. Rather than studying instructions only as lexical variants, we can therefore relate VLA performance to the information they carry and identify which missing structure the policy can recover and which it cannot.

Fig. 2: Humans increasingly compress execution structure as tasks grow. Instruction length increases with the number of events (left), but the executable structure made explicit decreases (right): coverage declines moderately, while groundedness and decomposition fall sharply.

papers.abstract: Exploration bounds learning efficiency in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). Current methods explore mostly through independent sampling, without fully using the information gathered along the way, such as known wrong answers and environment feedback. We propose LEAF, which injects a dynamic, problem-specific memory into the context before every rollout. The memory contains the most recent response, its reward, and other environment feedback. It is updated after every verifier call. We decouple policy updates from rollouts and update the policy through self-distillation. On four benchmarks and two open models, LEAF accelerates exploration by about 4x compared with a random sampling baseline. On unseen test sets, it improves accuracy over the strongest baseline by 1.59 and 1.83 percentage points on the two models, while using less compute than any RL baseline. These results highlight the potential of LEAF in improving both exploration and learning efficiency. Code is available at: https://github.com/on1262/LEAF
authors: Yutong Chen, Zhichao Xu, Rui Liu, Kunpeng Liu
bullets: Targets inefficient independent sampling in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards.
Stores recent responses, rewards, and verifier feedback in an evolving per-problem context memory.
Separates rollouts from policy updates and uses self-distillation for learning.
Across four benchmarks and two open models, it accelerates exploration by about 4× versus random sampling.
Improves unseen-test accuracy by 1.59 and 1.83 percentage points while using less compute than RL baselines.

papers.abstract: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) often underperforms full fine-tuning. We investigate this performance gap through a tangent-space lens: factorized updates are confined to the tangent space of the current low-rank factors, leaving gradient components outside this space unexploited. An analysis of ten representative LoRA variants reveals that these residual components account for most of the gradient energy and exhibit strong spectral concentration. Motivated by this finding, we propose Dynamic Tangent LoRA (DT-LoRA), which partitions a fixed rank budget into a stable branch and a dynamic branch to capture the principal residual gradient directions. We show that these directions define the optimal update of a local quadratic model under orthogonal-complement and rank constraints. Matrix-free randomized SVD recovers them without materializing the residual gradient, while controlled write-back preserves accumulated updates and stabilizes training within the allocated rank. DT-LoRA adds no trainable parameters or inference cost over LoRA. Experiments across computer vision and natural language processing tasks demonstrate consistent improvements over LoRA and its variants. Moreover, despite being a general-purpose adaptation method, DT-LoRA outperforms task-specific approaches to open-vocabulary domain generalization for semantic segmentation, achieving state-of-the-art results. Code is available at https://github.com/Snipine/DT-LoRA.
authors: Yangming Zhang, Ling Yi, Datong Li, Jinliang Ding, Xiaojie Wang, Tiecheng Song, Zhaolong Ning
bullets: LoRA misses substantial, spectrally concentrated gradient components outside the tangent space of its low-rank factors.
DT-LoRA divides a fixed rank budget into stable and dynamic branches to capture principal residual-gradient directions.
It uses matrix-free randomized SVD and controlled write-back to identify useful directions while preserving accumulated updates and stabilizing training.
Experiments across vision and NLP show consistent gains over LoRA variants; it also achieves state-of-the-art results for open-vocabulary domain generalization in semantic segmentation.
The method is evaluated within a fixed rank budget and is designed to add no inference overhead over LoRA.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of DT-LoRA. A fixed rank budget is split into a Stable branch and a Dynamic branch. Every τ steps, Matrix-Free Randomized SVD extracts the principal directions of the tangent-space residual gradient from the cached activations X and output gradients R, yielding a candidate update H . Controlled Write-back then merges H into the Dynamic branch, keeping the branch at rank q. After training, both branches are merged into the pre-trained weights, so inference costs the same as LoRA.

Figure 1. Analysis of the tangent-space residual gradient. (a) Tangent-space residual gradient energy ratio ρ of ten LoRA variants. (b) Cumulative spectral energy Ek of the tangent-space residual gradient. (c) Gradient coverage 1 − ρ of four LoRA variants and DTLoRA during training. For various LoRA variants, the tangent-space residual gradient accounts for a large proportion of the gradient energy and exhibits spectral concentration. Our DT-LoRA explicitly accounts for this property, and its gradient coverage keeps increasing during training, indicating that the principal directions of the tangent-space residual gradient are effectively exploited.

papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents excel at complex, multi-step tasks but suffer from catastrophic forgetting during continual learning--acquiring new skills often degrades previously mastered capabilities. Existing post-training paradigms face a fundamental trade-off: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) is sample-efficient but prone to severe forgetting, while Reinforcement Learning (RL) preserves prior capabilities but converges slowly without expert guidance. To bridge this gap, we introduce Trigger-based Supervised Reinforcement Learning (TSRL), a framework that integrates the strengths of both paradigms through an adaptive, state-dependent expert supervision mechanism. TSRL employs RL as the optimization backbone, activating SFT selectively on "hard states" where the policy fails. Theoretically, we show that restricting supervision to failure states derives an upper bound on the cumulative parameter updates, thereby reducing forgetting compared to full SFT. Empirically, TSRL achieves consistent gains across three agent benchmarks (ALFWorld, WebShop, and Deep Search) at both 7B and 32B scales. In continual learning scenarios, our method retains up to 9.6 points more capability on prior tasks than SFT->RL baselines, while matching or exceeding target-task performance.
authors: Yuqian Fu, Kaiwen Jiang, Zijun Song, Jiawei Wang, Yuanheng Zhu, Dongbin Zhao
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between sample-efficient but forgetful SFT and slower, capability-preserving RL.
Uses RL as the main optimizer and selectively activates SFT on state-dependent “hard states” where the policy fails.
Provides a theoretical bound showing that failure-state supervision limits cumulative parameter updates.
Improves performance across ALFWorld, WebShop, and Deep Search at 7B and 32B scales.
In continual learning, retains up to 9.6 more capability on prior tasks than SFT→RL baselines while matching or exceeding target-task performance.

papers.abstract: Agents build knowledge graphs as memory, and building them has become easy. Maintaining them has not. When a source is retracted, overruled, or erased, everything built on top of it (entity merges, entailed edges, community summaries) must be re-examined, and the maintainer must choose between deleting too much and too little. Deployed pipelines delete only the directly extracted facts: on our corpus that reduces contaminated queries from 32.2% to 28.0% under a real retraction and changes nothing under predicate revocation. Rebuilding is no repair for a constructor that samples: two builds of the same 300-document corpus differ in 29,475 artifacts, five times the 6,248 that removing the 61 retracted documents changes. PolyGraph instead asks the constructor for receipts: for every artifact, alternative bundles of source evidence, each claimed sufficient on its own, emitted in the call that creates it. Cleanup is then set arithmetic over the receipts, with no model calls. Because receipts are the model's own self-report, a re-derivation audit checks them by deleting the cited evidence and testing whether the constructor still produces the artifact. The audit finds that a receipt is trustworthy when it is shaped like the claim it backs. Merge receipts, each backing one narrow claim, agree with re-derivation 68% and 85% of the time. Summary receipts, elicited per sentence but stored as one flat list for the whole text, are wrong about two thirds of the time, almost always by keeping dead content. One receipt per sentence instead is 100% and 88% faithful and lets cleanup keep 33 of 35 touched summaries. The result holds under a second oracle model, a claim-blind prompt, ten further deletions, a second domain and a second constructor. Distrusting the summary layer cuts contaminated queries to 0.4% and 0.8% at 99.8 to 100% of the recall a perfect maintainer would return.
authors: Vishisht Choudhary
bullets: Retractions or predicate revocations can invalidate merges, inferred edges, and summaries, while deleting only directly extracted facts leaves substantial contamination.
PolyGraph captures alternative sufficient evidence bundles when each artifact is created, enabling cleanup through set arithmetic without additional model calls.
A re-derivation audit tests whether receipts actually support their artifacts; narrow merge receipts were faithful 68%–85% of the time.
Per-sentence summary receipts were substantially more reliable than one flat receipt list, achieving 100% and 88% faithfulness across reported settings.
Distrusting unreliable summary evidence reduced contaminated queries to 0.4%–0.8% while retaining 99.8%–100% of perfect-maintainer recall across robustness tests.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Two real chains from the corpus. Deployed deletion removes only the extracted claims (dashed). The entity merge keeps one evidence source from a paper that still stands, so it is correctly retained (green); five of five re-derivations agree. The entailed edge and the summary rest only on retracted evidence, mention no retracted paper, and keep reaching the retriever (red). Support labels delete the edge with one disjointness test. The summary’s label wrongly claims it still stands, the failure Section 6 measures; the layered policy of Section 6.4 removes it.

papers.abstract: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) has been widely used, yet the adapted model suffers catastrophic forgetting of pre-trained knowledge. While most existing work hardens the adapter by constraining where the weight update may lie, we note that constraining this weight channel does not constrain the activation channel. In this paper, we propose Concept-Guided Retention (CGR), a plug-and-play regularizer that constrains both for any PEFT base. CGR reads a frozen sparse autoencoder (SAE) and treats two disjoint concept sets differently. It softly confines the update to the task-concept subspace (via weight channel), and anchors a selected set of general-purpose concepts to the frozen model (via activation channel). We also provide anchor value bounds based on weight updates to understand how they interact, and show that both terms are necessary. On a CLIP vision panel, CGR significantly improves retention at comparable accuracy for every base, and the same pattern holds for world-knowledge retention under Llama-3.1-8B instruction tuning. Because the protected directions are named SAE concepts, CGR remains inspectable and controllable.
authors: Ibna Kowsar, Ivan Medri, Fanyu Meng, Xin Liu
bullets: Addresses the gap between constraining PEFT weight updates and preserving activation-level knowledge.
Uses a frozen sparse autoencoder to identify task and general-purpose concepts.
Applies two complementary regularization terms: task-concept subspace confinement and general-concept activation anchoring.
Improves retention at comparable accuracy across a CLIP vision panel and in Llama-3.1-8B instruction tuning.
Named SAE concepts make the retention constraints inspectable and controllable.

figures.caption: Figure 5: The weight update concentrates on the task-driven concepts (FGVC). Left: per-concept residual-write projection ∥Wdec[:, j] ⊤∆W∥ under a plain LoRA adapter (horizontal) against the same quantity under CGR (vertical), on a linear scale. Blue marks the task set Stsk, red the retention set Sret, and light gray all remaining concepts. Both sets are computed on the frozen backbone, independently of either adapter, so the same partition applies to both axes. The diagonal marks equal write under both methods. A concept above it receives more update under CGR than under LoRA, a concept below it less. LoRA alone does not separate the two sets (both horizontal-axis means are 0.20). CGR lifts the task concepts above the diagonal (from 0.20 under LoRA to 0.26 under CGR) and drops the retention concepts below it (from 0.20 to 0.11), so the update is reallocated, not enlarged. Right: the four task concepts CGR concentrates its update on, named by their top-activating FGVC images. Bars are blue throughout because all four belong to the task set, hollow under LoRA and solid under CGR.

Figure 7: Drift over training: full CGR pins the activation channel and confines the weight write on all three datasets. Columns: FGVC-Aircraft, CUB-200, DTD (3 bases × weight-only dashed / +CGR solid, mean±std over 3 seeds, rows share y-limits). Top row: every weight-only method’s retention-concept activation drift climbs (to ∼0.06–0.09) while all +CGR arms stay pinned at ∼0.01. Bottom row: the confine term also bounds the adapter write magnitude on every base (e.g. LoRA-Null on FGVC 37→22), so the drift gap is not explained by larger weight moves.

Figure 1: CGR confines the weight update to task concepts and anchors retained concepts to the frozen model, both read from one frozen SAE. Left: one pass of task data through the frozen backbone and SAE selects the task set Stsk by causal attribution and a disjoint retention set Sret by firing presence. Right: two CGR regularizers attach to any PEFT base. Confine penalizes the part of ∆W outside the task subspace and anchor holds the retention-concept read-out at its frozen-model values.

Figure 2: CGR pushes the attainable-retention frontier toward the ceiling (CLIP vision panel). One point per (task, base) of Table 2 where gray is for the base and red for +CGR. The shaded band shows the retention CGR adds.

Figure 4: CGR pins the concepts that drift most under plain LoRA (FGVC). Each concept is named by its top-firing Caltech-101 exemplars. Bars show the activation drift under LoRA (gray) and under +CGR (red).
Figure 3: The quantity the anchor reads predicts realized retention (FGVC). MeasuredSret drift vs. zero-shot retention (CIFAR-10/100 mean) over all runs.

Figure 9: Selected concepts are causally load-bearing. In each trained model we zero the |Sret| = 128 selected retention concepts at layer 8, subtracting their SAE contribution from the residual stream with no retraining, and re-measure zeroshot retention. The control applies the same surgery to 128 random alive concepts. Bars show retention drop per natural probe (mean±std over 24 FGVC runs, with the intervention instrumenting three of the four retention probes and SUN397 excluded). The random set is inert. Removing Sret destroys natural-image retention.

Figure 11: Steering the selected concepts controls retention (FGVC). On the frozen backbone we scale the selected Sret concepts’ layer-8 contribution by α (red). Retention peaks at the unmodified model (α=1) and falls on both sides, toward removal at α=0 and under amplification at α=1.5. A sizematched random control is flat (gray). Retention is averaged over the CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 probes.

Figure 6: Weight-space control and activation-space drift across task and retention concepts. Each point corresponds to one SAE concept, grouped into the task set Stsk and the retention set Sret. The left column reports the weight change magnitude, ∥Wdec[:, j] ⊤∆W∥. The right column reports the corresponding activation drift, Ex|fj(hft(x)) − fj(h0(x))|. Horizontal lines denote per-set means, and the boxes report task accuracy and CIFAR-100 zero-shot retention. Confine concentrates the weight update on the task concepts and suppresses its projection onto the retention concepts, but does not by itself prevent retentionconcept activation drift. Anchor directly suppresses activation drift, including when applied only to the selected retention set. Combining the two terms in full CGR separates their roles: task concepts remain free to support adaptation, while the retention concepts constrain the resulting representation change. papers.abstract: Imitation learning typically treats every demonstration state as equally important, optimizing a behavior-cloning objective uniformly across the dataset. Yet not all states are created equal: in a small number of critical states, even a slight deviation from the expert action can lead to a failure, while in many other states such errors are recoverable and inconsequential. We formalize state criticality in imitation learning as the worst-case degradation in downstream value induced by a bounded perturbation of the expert action at a given state. We then propose SCRIM, a practical State CRIticality Measure that estimates this quantity by training an adversarial disturbance policy and a value critic around a fixed imitation policy. SCRIM assigns each demonstration state a score reflecting how vulnerable the task outcome is to small, policy-relevant action errors. We show that these scores can be used to reweight behavior-cloning losses, improving imitation at consequential states and increasing overall task performance. We further show that SCRIM enables data curation by selecting compact, high-value subsets of demonstrations that preserve performance while substantially reducing the amount of training data. We evaluate SCRIM across various simulated and real-world robotic manipulation tasks, and demonstrate that SCRIM improves policy training, enables efficient data selection, and provides interpretable insights into which moments in a demonstration are most critical for task success. Project website: https://sia-lab-git.github.io/SCRIM/
authors: Yusuf Umut Ciftci, Joonwon Kang, Ajay Suresha Sathya, Somil Bansal
bullets: Uniform behavior cloning overlooks that some states are critical while others are recoverable.
State criticality is defined by the worst-case downstream-value loss from bounded perturbations of the expert action.
SCRIM estimates criticality using an adversarial disturbance policy and a value critic around a fixed imitation policy.
Criticality scores reweight training losses and select compact, high-value demonstration subsets.
Evaluations on simulated and real-world robotic manipulation tasks show improved training, efficient data use, and interpretable critical-state analysis.

papers.abstract: Large vision-language models often exhibit object hallucination, generating claims that are not supported by the input image. To mitigate this issue, we propose Evidence-Guided Visual Claim Admission (EGVCA), a training-free framework that admits a semantic claim only when it receives sufficient image-dependent support. EGVCA measures this support by comparing the claim likelihood under the observed image and a visual-null input. For captioning, it controls semantic expansion without altering token generation. For binary visual question answering, it combines atomic visual support with the image-induced change in the model's native Yes--No margin. Experiments on CHAIR, POPE, and MME across three LVLM backbones show that EGVCA substantially reduces object hallucination while preserving caption quality. It achieves the highest POPE F1 in eight of nine backbone--sampling settings and improves the native MME total score on all three backbones. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of claim-level admission as a simple alternative to token-level distribution correction.
authors: Hyeonggeun Han, Taehyun Cho, Sangwoo Hong
bullets: Targets object hallucination: models generate claims unsupported by the input image.
Compares claim likelihood with the observed image against a visual-null input to measure image-dependent support.

Across CHAIR, POPE, and MME on three backbones, it reduces hallucination while preserving caption quality.
Achieves the highest POPE F1 in eight of nine backbone–sampling settings and improves native MME total scores on all backbones.

papers.abstract: 3D scene graph prediction is commonly supervised with local object and predicate classification losses. Although effective for slot-wise label prediction, this formulation does not provide a graph-level semantic distance between a predicted scene graph and its ground truth: semantically mild label errors and structurally disruptive relational errors can be treated similarly, and subject-predicate-object facts are not compared as scene-level units. We propose Contextual Hellinger Triplet Geometry, a graph-level supervision objective that measures the semantic and structural discrepancy between 3D scene graphs. Our key idea is to reinterpret the conventional classifier outputs of a 3D scene graph predictor as an aligned probabilistic scene graph field, where object and predicate predictions jointly define contextual subject-predicate-object facts. This formulation yields a differentiable metric-based training objective with an efficient factorized implementation and can be applied to existing 3D scene graph prediction architectures without modifying their network design. Experiments on 3DSSG demonstrate that our supervision improves downstream graph-conditioned 3D scene generation, while ablation studies confirm the complementary roles of the proposed graph-level terms and user studies show better graph descriptiveness, relation plausibility, and structural preservation.
authors: U-Chae Jun, Yoonhyuk Choi, Jiwoo Kang
bullets: Addresses the limitation of local object and predicate classification losses, which do not compare complete scene-level relations.
Recasts classifier outputs as an aligned probabilistic scene graph field over contextual subject–predicate–object facts.
Introduces a differentiable, factorized graph-level metric that can be integrated into existing 3D scene graph architectures without redesigning them.
Experiments on 3DSSG show improved downstream scene generation, with ablations supporting complementary graph-level terms.
User studies report better graph descriptiveness, relation plausibility, and structural preservation.

Figure 5: Qualitative graph prediction examples from generator-limited scene domains. Because the 3D-FRONT-based graph-conditioned generators support a restricted set of room types and object categories, laundry- and bathroom-like scenes are difficult to include in the generation-based FID/KID evaluation. We therefore compare the predicted graphs directly, before graph-to-generator conversion. OCRL often produces locally plausible but domain-inconsistent graphs, such as replacing laundry appliances with generic furniture or replacing shower-related components with unrelated objects. In contrast, our method better preserves domain-compatible object semantics and the relational scaffold of the scene.

(b)–(e) For each backbone, we compare the original predictor on the left with the corresponding “+ Ours” variant on the right, followed by the scenes generated from each reconstructed graph by CommonScenes and EchoScene. Red annotations in the reconstructed graphs highlight predicted object or relation labels that differ from the reference graph, and blue titles indicate variants trained with our graph-level supervision. Our supervision yields more coherent graph reconstructions, leading to generated scenes that better preserve the reference object composition and spatial layout across both downstream generators.

Figure 6: Failure case of the proposed graph-level supervision. The input point cloud depicts a kitchen-like scene, and the reference 3D scene graph contains a contextually atypical object label, commode, together with fine-grained directional predicates such as front and right. Our method preserves the overall relational scaffold of the scene, including standing on, build in, attached to, and higher than, but predicts the atypical commode as a contextually plausible kitchen cabinet and relaxes some directional predicates into the broader proximity relation close by. This case illustrates that the contextual semantic prior improves global graph coherence in general, but can occasionally favor common scene-compatible labels over rare or fine-grained annotations.

papers.abstract: We introduce HelpMeOut, an embodied AI benchmark for error-aware monitoring of household task execution. Existing embodied household benchmarks typically assume that humans execute tasks correctly, but this assumption does not hold for cognitively impaired persons or older adults whose everyday activities produce structured execution errors. To address this gap, HelpMeOut operationalizes research on everyday action errors into 20000 paired activity episodes, covering nine neuropsychologically motivated error categories. In each episode, agents observe a streaming human activity trajectory and must monitor whether the execution is unfolding correctly, diagnosing any structured errors as early as possible. We evaluate learned-monitor, symbolic, change-point, and frontier LLM prompting baselines. Results show that these methods perform poorly as error monitors, often missing when execution goes wrong. These results suggest a gap left by standard goal-inference and task-completion benchmarks, making HelpMeOut a testbed for error-aware assistive agents.
authors: Haoran Wang, Jingwei Huang, Anqing Duan, Ho Seok Ahn, Bruce Macdonald
bullets: Targets error-aware monitoring for activities performed by cognitively impaired people and older adults.
Provides 20,000 paired activity episodes spanning nine neuropsychologically motivated error categories.
Agents monitor streaming human trajectories and must identify execution errors as early as possible.
Evaluates learned, symbolic, change-point, and frontier-LLM-prompting baselines.
All tested approaches often miss errors, exposing a gap in standard goal-inference and task-completion benchmarks.

papers.abstract: 3D scene graph prediction is commonly optimized with object-node and relation-edge classification losses. These objectives encourage exact object and relation label recovery, but they do not directly optimize semantic proximity to the ground-truth scene graph: two wrong graphs can receive comparable penalties even when one is much closer in object roles and relation contexts. A direct graph-distance loss is difficult in general, since graph matching and graph edit distance require correspondence search and edit-cost design. Our key observation is that prior supervised 3D scene graph prediction protocols are conducted on fixed object-node indices and supervised edge slots. This can turn a scene graph comparison into a well-defined aligned graph-distance problem. To this end, we propose SWORD, a Scene-Grounded Wasserstein Object-Relation Distance that builds block-normalized object and relation ground distance metrics from training scene graph annotations through a deterministic base-to-context order, without external semantic priors. SWORD lifts these metrics to Wasserstein distances over aligned node and null-augmented edge marginals, providing semantic graph-distance supervision beyond exact-label penalties while preserving the ground-truth graph as the unique zero-distance solution in aligned marginal probability space. We prove that SWORD is a strict metric on aligned marginal probabilistic scene graphs, preserves scene-graph-grounded substitution ordering, controls additive graph-grounded semantic observables, and yields a surrogate upper-bounding decoded semantic error.

bullets: Problem: Exact-label losses do not distinguish between wrong graphs that are semantically closer or farther from the ground truth.
Method: Exploit fixed object indices and supervised edge slots to define aligned graph comparisons without correspondence search.

Method: Learn block-normalized object and relation ground metrics from training annotations using a deterministic base-to-context ordering, then lift them to Wasserstein distances over nodes and null-augmented edges.
Contribution: SWORD is proven to be a strict metric on aligned probabilistic scene graphs, preserve substitution ordering, control semantic observables, and upper-bound decoded semantic error.
Scope: The approach relies on aligned node and edge supervision protocols.
