papers.abstract: Occupancy world models provide a structured, metric representation of future driving scenes, making them a promising basis for end-to-end autonomous driving. However, existing occupancy-aware planners typically couple occupancy prediction and action generation through either hierarchical coupling or parallel multi-task learning. Hierarchical methods use occupancy either as a fully predicted future preceding action generation or as an action-conditioned rollout for trajectory evaluation, whereas parallel multi-task methods predict occupancy alongside planning through a separate branch or auxiliary objective. These interfaces retain either an explicit generation order or a role asymmetry, limiting reciprocal interaction between world prediction and action generation during trajectory formation. We propose OccWAM, an occupancy-native world-action model that jointly generates dense future occupancy and continuous ego trajectories via flow matching conditioned on scene representations. Building on this joint formulation, we introduce scene-to-ego world-action flow matching, a two-stage formulation. The first stage predicts scene-centric occupancy together with an absolute ego trajectory, providing a stable representation of future scene evolution. The same predicted world is then re-indexed into the future ego frames induced by the initial trajectory, where ego motion is represented through adjacent pose increments and a second joint flow refines ego-centric occupancy and motion for action-aligned planning. Unlike video-based world-action models, OccWAM preserves explicit semantic geometry for direct planning reasoning without pixel synthesis. Extensive experiments on Bench2Drive and nuScenes demonstrate state-of-the-art performance in closed-loop driving, open-loop planning, and future occupancy prediction.
authors: Qihang Huang, Wenhui Huang, Collister Chua, Shiyu Fang, Zhan Chen, Songyan Zhang, Zhidong Wang, Daiying Tian, Chen Lv
bullets: Addresses limited reciprocal interaction in hierarchical and parallel occupancy-aware planning methods.
Generates dense scene occupancy and continuous ego trajectories jointly from scene representations.
First predicts scene-centric occupancy and an absolute ego trajectory, then refines ego-centric occupancy and motion in future ego frames.
Uses explicit semantic geometry rather than pixel synthesis for direct planning reasoning.
Reports state-of-the-art results in closed-loop driving, open-loop planning, and future occupancy prediction on Bench2Drive and nuScenes.

papers.abstract: Longer contexts allow large language models (LLMs) to condition their predictions on more information, but inference costs grow prohibitively with context length. An emerging alternative uses test-time updates to encode context as temporary changes to model weights. However, encoding this information into weights that already represent general knowledge obscures its role as context, so the LLM may fail to use it properly to condition subsequent inference. To restore this contextual role, we first associate each context with an identifier during encoding, thereby distinguishing the newly encoded information from pre-existing knowledge. Invoking the identifier at inference then enables the LLM to recite the encoded context. Nevertheless, successful recitation does not ensure that the LLM will use the recalled information as context. We therefore further introduce a prompting framework that explicitly guides the LLM to use this information as context. Across diverse controlled tasks and practical benchmarks, our method outperformed the baseline using only off-the-shelf LLMs, showing its advances in context encoding.
authors: Yue Wang, Qizhou Wang, Feng Liu, Gang Niu, Masashi Sugiyama, Bo Han
bullets: Long-context inference is costly, motivating test-time encoding of context into model weights.
Weight-encoded information can be confused with the model’s pre-existing knowledge and ignored as context.
The method associates each encoded context with an identifier, enabling the LLM to recite it later.
A prompting framework further guides the model to use the recalled information for subsequent inference.
It outperformed a baseline across controlled tasks and practical benchmarks using off-the-shelf LLMs.

papers.abstract: High-fidelity surgical video generation is increasingly important for surgical education, simulation, and downstream AI training, as conventional simulation pipelines are limited by cost, realism, and scenario diversity. Adapting generic text-to-video diffusion models to surgical procedures remains difficult, however, due to complex anatomical structures, intricate tool-tissue interactions, the inherently hierarchical nature of surgical workflows, and the scarcity of curated training data outside a few well-studied procedures. We propose a surgical video generation framework that combines hierarchical procedural annotation with curriculum transfer learning. Surgical procedures are decomposed into three levels (phase, task, and action) and a pretrained text-to-video diffusion model is progressively adapted from coarse to fine-grained surgical context, supported by a dynamic sampling strategy that handles variable-resolution and variable-length surgical clips. We instantiate the framework on Bilateral Axillo-Breast Approach robotic thyroidectomy, a procedure for which no curated benchmark currently exists. Relative to the preceding task-level model, the final action-level model reduces FVD by 20.1% and FID by 15.7%, and a matched-budget ablation indicates that these gains arise from the curriculum design rather than from additional training. A user study with six clinicians rates visual realism highly while highlighting remaining gaps in anatomical accuracy and clinical reliability. The proposed framework offers a step toward AI-driven surgical simulation in procedures where curated data are scarce.
authors: Youngbin Kong, Seungho Lee, Jae Kyung Shin, Jong-hyuk Ahn, Hyoun-Joong Kong, Kyu Eun Lee
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of generating surgical videos with complex anatomy, tool–tissue interactions, hierarchical workflows, and scarce curated data.
Decomposes procedures into phase, task, and action levels, then progressively transfers these contexts into a pretrained text-to-video diffusion model.
Uses dynamic sampling to accommodate surgical clips with varying resolutions and lengths.

On Bilateral Axillo-Breast Approach robotic thyroidectomy data, the action-level model improves FVD and FID over the task-level model; matched-budget ablation attributes gains to the curriculum design.
Six clinicians rated visual realism highly but identified remaining limitations in anatomical accuracy and clinical reliability.

papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) improves reasoning but incurs substantial autoregressive rationale cost. Continuous CoT moves intermediate computation into recurrent hidden states, yet typically uses a fixed number of updates even though the best budget varies across questions and accuracy need not improve monotonically with $K$. We introduce Dynamic K-Head, a question-conditioned, pre-rollout budget selector. It is jointly trained with the reasoner under selected budgets, using difficulty supervision based on scores assigned from the question alone. We also show that latent-update count can misrepresent end-to-end cost because a short latent rollout can shift computation into a longer explicit continuation. We therefore count latent updates, implementation-specific special tokens, and all decoded text. Instantiated with CoDI on Llama 3.2 1B and GSM8K, Dynamic K-Head reaches 54.44% exact-match accuracy at 12.03 average reasoning/output tokens, compared with 52.31% at 15.21 tokens for fixed-$K=6$ CoDI---a 2.12-point gain with 20.9% lower token cost. Across three out-of-distribution arithmetic datasets, it reduces cost by 19.3--25.7% while improving accuracy by 0.30--2.22 points. These results demonstrate that difficulty-supervised budget selection can improve both accuracy and efficiency, while stable budget selection remains a central challenge.
authors: Ying Li, Yuqi Chen, Sixuan Li, Yunfeng Cai
bullets: Fixed latent-update budgets are inefficient because question difficulty varies and accuracy may not increase monotonically with computation.
The method jointly trains a question-conditioned budget selector and reasoner using difficulty supervision derived from the question alone.
It measures end-to-end cost using latent updates, special tokens, and decoded text, rather than latent updates alone.
On GSM8K with CoDI and Llama 3.2 1B, it achieves 54.44% exact match at 12.03 average tokens versus 52.31% at 15.21 tokens for fixed K=6.
Across three out-of-distribution arithmetic datasets, it lowers cost by 19.3–25.7% while improving accuracy by 0.30–2.22 points; stable budget selection remains challenging.

papers.abstract: Diffusion models and Flow Matching can represent flexible distributions over robot actions, but many reinforcement learning algorithms also require the probability of each action. We introduce PrT-Flow (Probability-Tractable Flow Matching), which computes probability density while retaining multimodal, multi-step action generation. Its Jacobian-Tractable Transformer (JTT) makes each sampling step invertible and enables efficient computation of its Jacobian determinant. We train these finite steps with Conditional Euler-step Training (CET), which supervises their displacement over one step during sampling rather than their instantaneous velocity. We prove that, under certain assumptions, CET has the same minimizers as fitting the Euler-solver updates of Flow Matching. PrT-Flow achieves 96% success on Robomimic Lift after 300 epochs of imitation learning, matching the diffusion policy reference, and 96% success on OGBench Cube-Triple after 600k online steps. These results demonstrate that invertible networks with tractable probability densities can learn effective robot policies and support SAC-style actor-critic training. Our code is available at https://github.com/Sunlight-zero/PrT-Flow .
authors: Congzhong Sun, Ning Tan
bullets: Addresses the need for action likelihoods in RL while preserving the flexibility of diffusion and Flow Matching policies.
Uses Jacobian-Tractable Transformers to make each sampling step invertible and efficiently compute its density.
Trains finite sampling steps with Conditional Euler-step Training, which theoretically aligns with fitting Flow Matching Euler updates under stated assumptions.
Reaches 96% success on Robomimic Lift and OGBench Cube-Triple, and supports SAC-style actor-critic training.
Scope: the theoretical equivalence relies on specific assumptions, and reported evaluation is limited to the stated robotic tasks.

figures.caption: Figure 2: The architecture of Jacobian-Tractable Transformer (JTT). (A) A complete update applies M map heads in sequence and returns the next noisy sample xk+1 and the absolute Jacobian determinant D. (B) A causal Transformer with L decoder blocks uses shifted scalar tokens to predict monotone spline parameters. Cross-attention provides time and observation information. The projected outputs are converted to bounded parameter rates and multiplied by h to obtain offsets from the identity settings. These offsets determine the spline parameters. Between the two orthogonal rotations, the splines transform the unshifted scalar values. (C) For a fixed coordinate prefix, time, and observation, yi determines where its spline is evaluated, but not the spline’s shape. The positive analytic derivatives form the diagonal of the lower-triangular spline Jacobian, and their product gives the head determinant without evaluating off-diagonal entries. The orthogonal rotations preserve its magnitude. At step k, summing the head log-determinants at their respective inputs gives ℓk = logD.

Figure 1: The overview of PrT-Flow. (a) Conditioned on an observation, the Jacobian-Tractable Transformer (JTT) transforms standard Gaussian noise through K invertible steps of size h = 1/K. Each step returns both the updated sample and the Jacobian determinant D, without constructing a dense Jacobian matrix. (b) The deformed grid illustrates how the probability density of a sample evolves under these steps. At each step, JTT computes the absolute Jacobian determinant D. The local volume is scaled by D and the corresponding density is divided by D, allowing us to track the probability density of a sample. (c) A final tanh transformation maps the generated sample to a bounded action chunk a with its probability density p(a). SAC-style actor–critic training then uses sampled actions, their log-densities, and learned Q-values to update the FM policy.

Figure 3: Learning curves on Cube-Triple for PrT-Flow and Flow-G (σ = 0.01 and 0.05). Panels A and B show success rate and mean return on the shared set of 50 development episodes. Lines connect evaluations without smoothing. At 600k online steps, success rates are 94% for PrT-Flow, 88% for Flow-G (σ = 0.01), and 56% for Flow-G (σ = 0.05). papers.abstract: Can vision-language models turn 2D observations into 3D understanding that supports precise action? This requires inferring object geometry, anticipating the effects of rotation, and refining actions through visual feedback. We introduce RoTA-Bench to evaluate these abilities through interactive 3D-to-2D projection alignment. Given a target silhouette, a model observes a rotated object and chooses successive rotations to recover the target projection within a limited action budget. Our automated pipeline constructs silhouette-preserving 3D objects from 2D icons and uses reversible initialization to guarantee solvability, yielding 674 tasks and a stratified 100-task test set. Empirically, we find that (i) a substantial human-model gap persists: GPT-5.6-Sol succeeds on only 17% of tasks, whereas 20 undergraduate participants collectively complete the test set four times with a 100% success rate; (ii) image-space and pose-space progress can diverge: at matched states, the model more often improves silhouette overlap while worsening pose alignment than humans (19.4% vs. 10.9%); and (iii) fine-grained control is sensitive to interaction history: removing it leaves 96.8% of the model's actions at a coarse 30-degree step size and sharply reduces observed task success. These findings highlight the challenge of converting visual evidence into precise 3D control, beyond recognizing or matching individual images.
authors: Qingchuan Ma, Yuexiao Ma, Xiang Meng, Yixuan Zou, Tianyu Xie, Wang Chen, Yuhui Zeng, Yuhang Wu, Xiawu Zheng, Rongrong Ji
bullets: Models iteratively rotate a 3D object to match a target 2D silhouette under a limited action budget.
The benchmark contains 674 solvable tasks, including a stratified 100-task test set built from 2D icons and reversible initialization.
GPT-5.6-Sol succeeded on 17% of tasks, while undergraduate participants achieved 100% success across repeated test-set completion.
Models sometimes improve silhouette overlap while worsening pose alignment more often than humans (19.4% vs. 10.9%).
Removing interaction history led 96.8% of model actions to use coarse 30° rotations and sharply reduced task success.

papers.abstract: Although chain-of-thought prompting has improved multimodal reasoning, it is still difficult to produce correct final answers, as the reasoning can drift away from the image. Besides, the trace is already fixed when the answer is generated, leaving no room for self-correction. Considering the image is still available at the final-answer step, we think it is reasonable to fix the answer there without rewriting the reasoning. As such, the problem becomes to correct the final answer using the image under fixed reasoning. Unlike methods that improve trace generation through training, resampling, or decoding-time grounding, we repair the final-answer readout while keeping the reasoning trace fixed. The motivation is based on our finding that a wrong option can become prematurely committed in the reasoning while the correct option still has stronger image support in middle-to-deep layers. Thus, we propose Text-to-Visual Evidence Reallocation (TVER), a training-free method for final-answer repair. Specifically, TVER selects answer-related text and question-matched image patches, and moves bounded attention from text to patches. Furthermore, the patches are chosen in a middle-to-deep layer window based on question relevance. Our method improves answers across benchmarks and backbones, with gains in both multiple-choice and open-answer evaluations.
authors: Yulan Pan, Xiaoyu Xu, Zhihong Shen
bullets: Addresses answer errors caused when reasoning drifts from the image or prematurely commits to a wrong option.
Uses a training-free final-answer repair step rather than retraining, resampling, or modifying the reasoning trace.
Selects answer-related text and question-relevant image patches, then reallocates bounded attention from text to patches.
Chooses patches from a middle-to-deep layer window based on question relevance.
Improves performance across benchmarks and backbones in both multiple-choice and open-answer settings.

papers.abstract: Reliable video reasoning requires models to produce correct answers and expose supporting visual evidence. Open-o3-Video enables verifiable reasoning by embedding timestamps and object-level bounding boxes into reasoning traces, but is restricted to frames from an initial sparse sampler. We introduce Open-o3-Video-v2, which formulates video reasoning as a unified agentic evidencegrounded process. The model identifies missing information, acquires additional observations, grounds the moments and objects supporting its reasoning, and writes this evidence into the trajectory before continuing or answering. To support this behavior, we construct STGR-v2-CoT135K, including 52K multi-turn agentic grounded reasoning trajectories, and STGR-v2-RL-13K for reinforcement learning. We further propose Clue-Seek GRPO (CS-GRPO), which tracks how tool calls change accumulated evidence, rewards clue coverage and step-wise gains, and penalizes excessive, repetitive, or uninformative retrieval. On V-STaR, Open-o3-Video-v2-4B achieves 40.4% mAM and 56.3% mLGM, outperforming its Qwen3-VL-4B backbone by 8.5% and 12.6%, respectively. It also delivers consistent gains across general video understanding, long-video reasoning, and temporal grounding benchmarks. These results show that active evidence acquisition and verifiable object-level grounding are complementary for reliable video reasoning. The code and models are released at https://msalab-pku.github.io/projects/Open-o3-Video-v2.
authors: Jiahao Meng, Zhongyuan Bao, Yue Tan, Haiquan Wen, Renrui Zhang, Anna Wang, Jason Li, Yanwei Fu, Yunhai Tong, Ming-Hsuan Yang
bullets: Frames video reasoning as an agentic process: identify gaps, retrieve additional observations, ground relevant moments and objects, then answer.
Introduces STGR-v2-CoT135K and STGR-v2-RL-13K datasets for multi-turn grounded reasoning and reinforcement learning.
Proposes Clue-Seek GRPO, rewarding evidence coverage and useful retrieval while penalizing repetitive or uninformative tool calls.
The 4B model achieves 40.4% mAM and 56.3% mLGM on V-STaR, with gains over its Qwen3-VL-4B backbone and across multiple video benchmarks.
Code and models are publicly released.

figures.caption: Figure 2 Overview of the data construction pipelines and STGR-v2 data statistics. (a) Open-o3-Video constructs single-turn spatio-temporal grounded reasoning data through initial annotation, bounding-box filtering, and selfconsistency checking. (b) Open-o3-Video-v2 extends this pipeline to agentic multi-turn reasoning through strict data filtering, spatio-temporal evidence annotation, CoT (chain-of-thought) rewriting with tool observations, and quality checking. (c) STGR-v2-CoT-135K contains 135K SFT samples across seven task groups, including 59K spatio-temporal grounded reasoning samples, while STGR-v2-RL-13K contains 13K RL samples selected through strict filtering.

Figure 3 Overview of the reinforcement learning designs in Open-o3-Video and Open-o3-Video-v2. (a) Open-o3-Video produces a single-turn spatio-temporal grounded reasoning trace and optimizes it with format, answer-accuracy, and grounded thinking rewards; the thinking reward jointly evaluates temporal proximity and spatial overlap with the target evidence. (b) Open-o3-Video-v2 extends this formulation to multi-turn agentic reasoning with CS-GRPO. The model iteratively calls crop_video to acquire denser observations, while CS-GRPO tracks how the accumulated evidence evolves across calls and assigns credit according to whether each interaction contributes useful new evidence.

Figure 1 From single-pass spatio-temporal grounded reasoning to agentic evidence seeking and grounded reasoning. In contrast, Video-o3 searches an incorrect temporal interval and produces an incorrect count. Bottom: For counting the people in the car, both methods inspect the relevant 10–12 s interval, but Open-o3-Video-v2 further grounds the car and its occupants, allowing it to distinguish three individuals rather than two. In both cases, explicit instance-level grounding complements temporal evidence acquisition by resolving the individual visual entities required for accurate counting.

Figure 4 Qualitative comparison with Video-o3. Open-o3-Video-v2 inspects the correct 468–470 s interval, grounds the three girls at 469 s, and identifies their group handshake. In both cases, the acquired observation is converted into explicit spatio-temporal evidence and used directly in the subsequent reasoning process.

Figure 8 Representative failure cases of Open-o3-Video-v2. Top: Insufficient identity knowledge leads to an incorrect answer even after a relevant face is retrieved. Middle: During a camera pan, inaccurate instance discrimination and association across changing views lead to an incorrect count of the women appearing offstage. Bottom: The model anchors its reasoning to the wrong scoring event and misidentifies the player who ends the game. In both cases, targeted temporal observation together with explicit object-level grounding exposes the decisive visual evidence and yields a human-verifiable spatio-temporal reasoning trace.

papers.abstract: Recent coding large language models (LLMs) can synthesize dynamic 4D worlds from natural language, but the resulting content remains a visual artifact. It lacks physical semantics such as the collision geometry, mass, friction, inertia, and joint structure, required to enable it to simulate the physical world, and its dynamics are scripted to look plausible rather than designed to execute. What is needed is an executable world: one that a physics engine can load and step, resolving contact physically. We present Code2Worlds-2, an extension of Code2Worlds that turns 4D world generation into an embodied world simulation. We keep the original dual-stream generation pipeline intact and append two modules. First, a SimReady Scene Compiler that turns a generated visual scene into a simulator-compatible representation: it assigns collision meshes via convex decomposition, estimates physical attributes with a vision-language model, infers a lightweight support graph, instantiates the engine's contact, friction, and dynamics constraints, and applies a gravity settling pass, before exporting the scene as MuJoCo MJCF. Second, a Simulator-in-the-Loop 4D Refiner that implements an automated agent harness-a compile, simulate, critique and refine loop-that converts visual dynamics into executable rigid and articulated dynamics and evolves the physical settings rather than only the code, replacing the purely visual motion critic with a simulator critic that inspects penetration depth, collision pairs, stability, contact forces, joint limits, and robot reachability. We further propose SimCode4D, a state-based benchmark with five task templates for evaluating embodied simulation. Experiments on SimCode4D and across natural, indoor, industrial, urban, and service scenes show that Code2Worlds-2 produces physically plausible, simulator-compatible, and robot-interactable scenes.
authors: Haoyu Zhang, Siming Li, Zeyu Zhang, Yi Zhang, Tat-Seng Chua, Hao Tang
bullets: Addresses the gap between visually plausible generated worlds and scenes with physical semantics needed for simulation.
Adds a SimReady Scene Compiler that infers collision geometry, physical properties, support relations, and dynamics constraints, then exports MuJoCo MJCF.
Introduces a Simulator-in-the-Loop 4D Refiner that iteratively compiles, simulates, critiques, and adjusts physical settings.
Uses simulator feedback on contacts, penetration, stability, forces, joint limits, and robot reachability instead of only visual motion critique.
Proposes SimCode4D, a five-template state-based benchmark, and evaluates scenes across natural, indoor, industrial, urban, and service settings.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of Code2Worlds-2. Two modules are appended to the original Code2Worlds pipeline to produce a simulator-compatible, interactable 4D world, and the illustrated scenes span five domains.

Fig. A.3. Natural outdoor. Rows: the Unitree Go2 disturbing the source-bound rock on the generated canyon terrain, the Clearpath Jackal driving the authored route across the hills, and the amphibious rover moving from the water field onto dry land. The non-convex height field is sliced into per-cell convex prisms so that contact follows the local surface. The canyon, hill, and shore terrains are generated scene-code assets; the rock, the route obstacles, and the water field are frozen benchmark entities carrying their own physics-seed perturbations, and all three rollouts are rendered at 1080p from the same compiled worlds that the evaluator scores. The canyon wall, the route markers, and the shore bank are compiled colliders, so the robots’ contacts with them are resolved by the same collision pipeline as in the indoor and urban suites. The rows correspond to Natural outdoor-1 (rock kick), -2 (hills turn stop), and -3 (water land) of the frozen index; the rock’s terminal rest, the Jackal’s stop inside the goal region, and the rover’s arrival on dry land are the terminal predicates checked by the case validators. Frames are sampled uniformly across each rollout (early, middle, late).

Fig. 1. The feedback loops of the two systems. (a) Code2Worlds [1] corrects a scene by rewriting its code from rendered images—a visual loop, which cannot guarantee physical validity. (b) Code2Worlds-2 instead closes the loop through the simulator: Module 1 compiles a SimReady scene, Module 2 critiques the rollout, and simulator feedback guides the revisions to the physical settings and dynamics.
Fig. 7. Representative task rollouts from the five evaluation domains. Rows show one case per domain, and columns show six temporally ordered keyframes.

papers.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) frameworks place teacher and student on the same GPUs, so per-GPU memory limits the teachers that fit. DisaggKD separates them across nodes: teacher replicas stream hidden states to the student, a KD loss over row windows and vocabulary shards equals the full-vocabulary loss in exact arithmetic without forming the full-vocabulary logits, and a prefetch ring paces producer and trainer. Closed-form memory and traffic models locate the memory limits of each layout. On the Qwen3.5-35B-A3B to 9B pair, the disaggregated layout matches the LM loss of the colocated run with the same loss and is faster than that run; our fused loss also lets a colocated run train on as few nodes at faster speed, while the split is memory efficient when the student spans several nodes. On the larger pairs, colocated runs with a fused loss still run OOM where the split trains, because teacher weights and student states fill the budget.
authors: Ruixuan Tu, Yuyang Dong
bullets: Teacher replicas stream hidden states to student nodes, avoiding colocated teacher-memory limits.
A row-window and vocabulary-shard KD loss matches the full-vocabulary loss in exact arithmetic without materializing full logits.
A prefetch ring coordinates teacher production and student training, while memory and traffic models identify layout limits.
On Qwen3.5-35B-A3B to 9B, the split matches colocated LM loss and runs faster; larger pairs fit in split layouts when colocated runs OOM.
The fused loss also reduces node requirements and increases speed for colocated training.

papers.title: DisaggKD: Efficient Knowledge Distillation through Teacher-Student Disaggregation and a Fused Loss
papers.tldr: DisaggKD separates teacher and student across nodes and uses a fused, memory-efficient distillation loss to enable larger KD workloads without changing the loss.

papers.abstract: Spatial understanding is essential for embodied agents navigating and interacting with the physical world. As observations arrive incrementally, agents must reason in a streaming manner. Yet streaming understanding must also be closed-loop: task-relevant evidence may require both recalling past observations and actively acquiring new views. Existing streaming approaches largely emphasize processing incoming observations, leaving task-driven active exploration underexplored. We introduce MemAct, a framework for streaming spatial understanding with memory and action. A shared vision--language model incrementally writes structured historical memory, retrieves records and past frames on demand, and acquires additional evidence through movement and turning. Retrieved evidence and action observations inform subsequent decisions, enabling the agent to continue exploring or answer within a unified reasoning loop. We develop the MemAct suite, a data generation pipeline and collection across real and simulated environments, with approximately 1M training examples for spatial reasoning, memory writing, retrieval, and exploration. Its MemAct-bench comprises 20,000 main QA pairs evaluating current-observation understanding, historical evidence use, and active exploration, plus 2,000 separate Timing questions. MemAct combines supervised fine-tuning for memory and interaction with counterfactual action optimization using cumulative evidence gains, action costs, and terminal answer quality to improve exploration and stopping decisions. Experiments show that MemAct outperforms existing spatial understanding and streaming baselines and approaches frontier multimodal models on MemAct-bench while retaining streaming inference efficiency.
authors: Yuxi Wei, Wei Huang, Qirui Chen, Lu Hou, Xiaojuan Qi
bullets: Addresses the gap between passive streaming observation and task-driven exploration that acquires missing evidence.
Uses a shared vision-language model to write structured memories, retrieve past frames, and guide movement or turning.
Introduces MemAct data and benchmarks spanning current observations, historical evidence, active exploration, and timing.
Trains memory and interaction with supervised fine-tuning plus counterfactual action optimization for evidence gain, action cost, and answer quality.
Outperforms existing spatial and streaming baselines, approaches frontier multimodal models, and maintains streaming inference efficiency.

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) use generative visual representations to condition robot actions, yet how these representations organize action-relevant information remains poorly understood. We identify persistent high-norm spatial outliers in WAM representations and find that their action relevance persists even after normalization and K/V projection attenuate their extreme magnitude. Motivated by this observation, we introduce RegisterWAM, which adds learnable non-spatial registers to the world model and uses them directly for action conditioning. Registers alone do not fully eliminate spatial outliers; pairing them with observation flow-matching (FM) loss supervision suppresses spatial outliers while concentrating high-norm responses in registers. Beyond this reorganization, observation FM loss supervision also improves action learning without registers, motivating an additional noised-observation FM objective that learns current-scene recovery from corrupted inputs. The resulting model achieves 81.64\% success on LIBERO-Plus without additional embodied pretraining data or foundation models, reaches 93.0\% average success on RoboTwin 2.0, and improves real-world manipulation performance.
authors: Yiwei Zhang, Yantai Yang, Jin Gao, Jin Lou, Andong Chen, Yufei Liu, Boyang Xing, Yuchen Zhu, Weiming Hu, Zhipeng Zhang
bullets: WAMs contain persistent high-norm spatial outliers that remain action-relevant even after normalization and K/V projection.
RegisterWAM adds non-spatial learnable registers for action conditioning, while observation flow-matching supervision suppresses spatial outliers and concentrates responses in registers.
Flow-matching supervision improves action learning even without registers, motivating a noised-observation objective for recovering current scenes from corrupted inputs.
The resulting model reports 81.64% success on LIBERO-Plus and 93.0% average success on RoboTwin 2.0, with improved real-world manipulation performance.

papers.abstract: Since scaling laws were introduced for modern LLMs (Kaplan et al., 2020), several works have extended them to account for quantization, tracking the emerging low-precision data types supported on AI accelerators. We develop a more accurate scaling law for quantized pretraining with mixed precision across the forward and backward passes, grounded in optimization theory and validated empirically. Our formulation separates the effects of quantization on model capacity and on optimization efficiency, and explicitly models the persistent optimization error from forward and backward quantization identified through convergence analysis. To select the regimes for fitting and evaluating our law, we first decompose existing 4-bit training recipes into their forward and backward components, isolating those that most affect loss. Our Qwen3 experiments under selected 4-bit regimes, together with published Llama-style experiments, show that our law predicts loss with up to $11\times$ lower MSE than existing laws as model size and token count scale. Finally, we extend our law to layer-wise mixed precision and identify the optimal quantized-pretraining recipe, i.e., model size, training tokens, and per-layer forward/backward precision, under a hardware-aware compute budget. Unlike prior precision scaling laws, our law predicts that the optimal precision increases with the compute budget.
authors: Jinuk Kim, Rajarshi Saha, Muhammed Fatih Balin, Youngsuk Park
bullets: Separates quantization effects on model capacity from optimization efficiency.

papers.abstract: In outdoor environments, varying terrain and contact conditions can cause identical action commands to produce different motion outcomes for quadruped robots. Predicting these outcomes is essential for reliable navigation and informed path selection. Existing video world models can generate visually plausible futures, yet often struggle to capture robot dynamics and terrain interactions, leading to overly optimistic predictions of action outcomes. We present DR-WM, a physically consistent world model that incorporates robot-terrain contact dynamics to predict the consequences of quadruped actions. Starting from an initial RGB image, our method reconstructs scene geometry and integrates dense, dimensionless priors over terrain contact properties, calibrated using real-world action-response data. The resulting terrain model supports the simulation of physics with spatially varying contact properties such as friction. Given the initial state of the robot and candidate action sequences, we simulate its future motion and use the resulting camera trajectories and rendered geometry to guide the training of a video world model. The generated future observations are then used to update the terrain reconstruction, enabling iterative model rollouts without additional real-world images. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DR-WM substantially outperforms geometry-only baselines and baselines with uniform physical parameters on key physical metrics characterizing action outcomes, while achieving the best performance among the evaluated baselines. These physically grounded predictions support more informed action selection: across 90 challenging scenarios, an 8B vision-language model augmented with DR-WM outperforms an unassisted 32B vision-language model on five of six evaluation metrics.
authors: Ruo Chen, Jiahua Pang, Yingjie Niu, Hongyi Lin, Jun Tian, Yang Zhu, Chao Li
bullets: Addresses unreliable action-outcome prediction when identical commands encounter different terrain and contact conditions.

Simulates candidate robot actions, uses camera trajectories and rendered geometry to train a video world model, and iteratively updates terrain estimates without new real-world images.
Outperforms geometry-only and uniform-physics baselines on physical action-outcome metrics.
Improves action selection: a 8B vision-language model using DR-WM surpasses an unassisted 32B model on five of six metrics across 90 challenging scenarios.

papers.abstract: For video generation in dynamic world modeling, observed static and dynamic content should be efficiently reused to provide conditions for repeated generation at different times and viewpoints. We introduce 4LC, a 4D latent cache with composite visual representations and a flexible spatiotemporal access interface. As a latent cache, 4LC directly reuses visual representations of static and dynamic content to provide generation conditions, avoiding per-request RGB rendering and re-encoding. As a composite cache, 4LC binds visual representations from multiple visual encoders (e.g., VAE, DINO, V-JEPA, VGGT) to shared geometry and motion, allowing the composite representations to describe the dynamic world with rich information. Besides, we design a flexible spatiotemporal interface, which directly reads the cache at independently specified times and viewpoints and combines readouts across observations, providing a common conditioning format for diverse downstream tasks. Building on 4LC, we develop 4LC-Video to address multiple video generation tasks through different configurations of source observations, spatiotemporal requests, and historical reuse, including camera control, temporal control, novel-view synthesis, scene revisits, and long-term generation. Our experiments show more efficient condition acquisition, effective spatiotemporal controllability, and scene consistency across tasks using a single 4LC-Video model without task-specific fine-tuning.
authors: Jianhui Zhang, Zuyao Lin, Pengxin Xu, Jingdong Wang, Xingyu Chen

Combines representations from multiple visual encoders with shared geometry and motion for richer world conditioning.
Provides flexible spatiotemporal access at independently specified times and viewpoints, with readout combinations across observations.
4LC-Video supports camera and temporal control, novel-view synthesis, scene revisits, and long-term generation.
Experiments report efficient condition acquisition, strong spatiotemporal controllability, and scene consistency across tasks.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon coding requires agents to maintain an evolving view of the project they are changing: what problem is currently being solved, what has already been learned or modified, which other artifacts may be affected, and what work remains unresolved. When this information is scattered across a growing interaction history, local edits can become disconnected from their later consequences and progress can be difficult to carry forward. We introduce StateHarness, a runtime framework that maintains evolving project state without updating model parameters. The working agent records its current problem and hypothesis, important findings and decisions, discovered repository relationships, and unfinished work. Runtime support prompts record updates, searches for callers, tests, and documentation that may be affected by a change, and maintains a compact working brief for subsequent decisions. When behavioral signals accumulate, a separate diagnostic session revisits the recorded history and surfaces overlooked evidence. Across three repository-level evaluations, StateHarness improves task completion and several measures of change consistency. On RefactorBench, full-chain completion increases from 29.4% to 35.3% and cleanup-check accuracy from 87.0% to 95.4%. On five LHTB software-engineering tasks, mean reward improves from 0.427 to 0.576, exceeding LongHorizon-Harness at substantially lower recorded execution cost. On ChainSWE, bug-fix rate increases from 35.1% to 39.5% and residual debt decreases from 60 to 43 items, although pass-to-pass regressions increase. These results show that maintaining project state can improve long-horizon coding while introducing measurable execution and regression trade-offs.
authors: Chuan Zou, Yujun Zhou, Xiaonan Luo, Xiangliang Zhang
bullets: Addresses project knowledge scattered across long interaction histories and disconnected local edits.
Maintains hypotheses, findings, decisions, repository relationships, and unresolved work without changing model parameters.
Uses runtime prompts for updates, impact searches, tests, documentation checks, and a compact working brief; diagnostic sessions revisit history for overlooked evidence.
Across three repository-level evaluations, it improves completion, change consistency, and bug-fix outcomes, while reducing residual debt in one evaluation.
Scope limitation: pass-to-pass regressions increase, showing a trade-off between stronger state maintenance and execution consistency.

papers.abstract: Recently, the integration of generative priors has revolutionized Monocular Depth Estimation (MDE), achieving state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance with remarkably high data efficiency. However, although methods based on Text-to-Image (T2I) models excel in general scenes, their efficacy degrades sharply when confronted with open-world environmental perturbations, such as illumination variations and adverse weather. Since T2I priors are optimized for semantic synthesis rather than preserving pixel-level structure, they struggle to decouple geometry from appearance under severe visual shifts, easily triggering structural hallucinations. Therefore, our core insight is to model open-world depth estimation as consistent geometric inference across multi-style images, fully leveraging the powerful structure-preserving editing priors of Image-to-Image (I2I) models. Based on this, we propose OpenDepth, a robust open-world MDE framework that introduces "Intra-Domain Awareness" -- the capability to map diverse stylistic inputs sharing identical geometry into a unified latent space. To achieve this, we first align shallow features within the Diffusion Transformer (DiT) to anchor degraded observations to unified geometric representations. Additionally, we introduce a joint RGB latent reconstruction task, requiring the model to recover clean RGB information from degraded inputs. This multi-stage strategy effectively decouples environmental style interference, compelling the model to focus strictly on underlying geometric recovery. Extensive evaluations show that OpenDepth sets new SOTA records for robust zero-shot depth estimation across standard and extreme weather benchmarks, demonstrating exceptional structural integrity and adaptability.
authors: Mengke Zhang, Tianyi Yang, Xinzhuo Li, Anlong Ming
bullets: T2I-based depth methods can hallucinate structure when environmental appearance shifts severely.
OpenDepth treats depth estimation as geometry-consistent inference across differently styled versions of the same scene.
It aligns shallow DiT features to unify degraded observations with shared geometric representations.
A joint RGB latent reconstruction task helps separate environmental style from underlying geometry.
Experiments report state-of-the-art robust zero-shot performance on standard and extreme-weather benchmarks, with strong structural integrity and adaptability.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of the OpenDepth framework. This dual-constraint strategy projects diverse degraded inputs into a unified latent domain, strictly decoupling environmental styles from geometric structures.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models are increasingly used to identify and describe places, yet their recognition and knowledge of specific cultures remain poorly understood, particularly in underrepresented regions such as the Philippines. This study introduces the Tanawpamana Dataset, a repository of Philippine heritage site images with metadata based on the Talapamana registry of the National Commission for Culture and the Arts of the Philippines. We also introduce the Tanawpamana Benchmark, comprising 4,046 tasks designed to evaluate models' recognition and knowledge of heritage sites. Evaluating seven vision-language models, we find that they struggle more with fine-grained visual discrimination among similar heritage sites than with coarse recognition, and that their geographic knowledge is weaker when inferred from image inputs than from text.
authors: Ivan Yuri De Leon, Hiroki Ouchi, Sakriani Sakti
bullets: Introduces a dataset of Philippine heritage-site images with metadata from the NCCA’s Talapamana registry.
Provides 4,046 benchmark tasks assessing heritage-site recognition and knowledge.
Evaluates seven vision-language models on visual and geographic understanding.
Models perform worse on distinguishing visually similar sites than on coarse recognition.
Geographic knowledge is weaker from images than from text inputs.

papers.abstract: Language provides a natural interface for humans to specify and reason about goals, but training language-conditioned robotic policies and reasoning typically requires expensive manual annotations. We propose Action Self-Distillation (ASD), a method for learning language-conditioned reasoning for robotic navigation without human-annotated language or reasoning labels. ASD uses an open-source VLM, which contains broad world knowledge and reasoning capabilities, as both a teacher network and a student policy. During training, the self-teacher receives privileged trajectory feedback and infers the underlying navigation goal together with goal-oriented reasoning. The student is then trained to condition on the inferred navigation goal, predict future ego-frame trajectory, and provide a description of the scene semantics, plan, and reasoning, from onboard observations alone. Across 13 challenging indoor and outdoor real-world navigation tasks, our method improves success rate over the strongest baseline by $30\%$ in indoor settings, $30\%$ on multi-stage tasks, and achieves $95\%$ success rate on outdoor tasks, validating that privileged trajectory feedback can enable self-distillation for scalable generalist navigation policies without human annotations.
authors: Bowen Feng, Keqin Wang, Yulong Yang, Amogh Joshi, Christine Allen-Blanchette, Dhruv Shah, Felix Heide
bullets: Addresses the cost of manually annotating language-conditioned robotic navigation and reasoning.
Uses an open-source VLM as both a self-teacher and student policy; the teacher infers navigation goals and reasoning from privileged trajectory feedback.
The student uses onboard observations to predict future ego-frame trajectories and describe scene semantics, plans, and reasoning.
Evaluated on 13 challenging indoor and outdoor real-world navigation tasks.
Reports 30% higher success than the strongest baseline indoors and on multi-stage tasks, plus 95% success on outdoor tasks.

papers.abstract: Estimating simulation-ready material parameters from visual observations is crucial for deformable-object manipulation but challenging because material properties are only indirectly revealed through physical responses. We introduce physical-field-bridged material inference, a single-pass framework that uses dense physical responses to connect multi-view RGB deformation videos with constitutive-type classification and continuous parameter regression. Unlike inverse-physics methods requiring per-scene reconstruction, online tuning, or simulation-in-the-loop optimization, our model predicts force/contact masks, projected motion-flow fields, and projected stress-response maps, then conditions material inference on these fields to reduce reliance on appearance or category shortcuts. We construct DeformFieldBench, a 3DGS MPM learning environment comprising 5,000 simulations across 100 object shapes and five mechanically informative loading modes, with dense pixel-aligned physical supervision. Our method achieves the best median errors on all four continuous parameters, improves stress-hotspot recall from 0.0762 to 0.5121, and attains 0.8676 SSIM/36.82 dB PSNR in same-simulator replay on unseen objects. Under a protocol-matched GSO evaluation, inference and future-state prediction take approximately 30 seconds, compared with 15-120 minutes for per-scene optimization. The method also yields measurable replay agreement on five real-world sequences. These results support dense physical fields as an effective bridge for fast material inference, while cross-simulator and real-world tests reveal remaining domain and identifiability gaps.
authors: Linrui Shou, Jie Li, Yu Liu, Tao Huang
bullets: Addresses the challenge of recovering simulation-ready material properties from visual deformation, where properties are only indirectly observable.
Predicts force/contact masks, motion-flow fields, and stress-response maps, then uses them to guide material classification and parameter regression.
Introduces DeformFieldBench: 5,000 simulations spanning 100 shapes and five loading modes with dense pixel-aligned supervision.
Reports best median errors across four continuous parameters, improved stress-hotspot recall, and strong same-simulator replay quality on unseen objects.
Inference and future-state prediction take about 30 seconds versus 15–120 minutes for per-scene optimization; cross-simulator and real-world tests expose remaining gaps.

papers.abstract: Diffusion language models (DLMs) have attracted wide attention for their fast, parallel decoding, but they are believed to be far less efficient to train than autoregressive language models (ARMs): a widely cited study reports that a DLM needs roughly 16x the training compute of an ARM to match its likelihood, a figure that has made pretraining DLMs from scratch look prohibitive at scale. We find that the methodology behind this figure has fallen out of step with current DLM practice: it scores the model with its evidence lower bound (ELBO) and trains a full-sequence, decoder-only model. We therefore revisit the scaling laws of DLMs, adopting the exact likelihood under the model's own decoding order, block diffusion training, an encoder-decoder architecture, and a sweep over the block sizes used in practice. Under this new protocol, we study across ten model variants, about 1,700 models in total, and find that pretraining DLMs is far cheaper than previously thought. Concretely, scoring with the exact likelihood reduces the compute multiple to 12.8x; block diffusion training and an encoder-decoder architecture further reduce it to 7.8x at block size 32, and smaller block sizes narrow it to 4.6x at block size 8 and 3.0x at block size 4. We complement these scaling analyses with an empirical rule for the optimal decoder depth of encoder-decoder block diffusion, a held-out compute budget beyond the fitting range at which the gap between variants persists, and downstream benchmark results where likelihood improvements carry over to accuracy. Overall, the 16x figure substantially overstates the pretraining cost gap between DLMs and ARMs, and pretraining DLMs from scratch is far more viable than previously assumed.
authors: Guanghan Wang, Bing He, Zhan Shi, Benoit Dumoulin, Hanqing Lu, Volodymyr Kuleshov
bullets: The prior estimate used ELBO scoring and full-sequence decoder-only training, which do not reflect current DLM practice.
Using exact likelihood, block diffusion training, encoder-decoder models, and practical block sizes reduces the compute gap from 16× to 3.0×–12.8×.
The study evaluates about 1,700 models across ten variants and tests scaling behavior beyond the fitting range.
Likelihood gains also transfer to downstream accuracy, supporting the practical relevance of the revised scaling results.
Overall, training DLMs from scratch appears substantially more viable than previously assumed.

papers.abstract: Operational mobile networks are rich in observations but poor in interventions: they continuously generate large volumes of passive telemetry, while controlled action--response trajectories remain comparatively scarce and costly to collect. This observation--intervention asymmetry is a central obstacle to building practical world models for RAN control. We address this problem with RAN-JEPA, an action-conditioned world model that separates representation learning from intervention learning. The model first learns a predictive latent representation from observation-only network data, adapts that representation to the target deployment domain, and then learns action-conditioned latent dynamics from controlled sleep/wake trajectories while keeping the encoder fixed. We evaluate RAN-JEPA using public operator performance data for pretraining and a real-equipment four-cell 5G testbed for domain adaptation, post-training, and control. Across four future 15-minute intervals, RAN-JEPA achieves lower action-conditioned prediction error than a GPT-2 world-model baseline and a mechanistic rule, while remaining close to a strong persistence reference. What-if evaluation further shows that the model produces distinct and coherent future trajectories under matched SLEEP and KEEP plans. In closed-loop control, RAN-JEPA consistently supports higher sleep ratios than the two baselines at comparable congestion cost. These results show that observation-first, action-conditioned learning can turn abundant passive telemetry and limited intervention data into a practical predictive model for energy-aware RAN control.
authors: Binghan Wu, Kai Zeng, Kai Yang, Ya-Qin Zhang, Joseph Sifakis, Ye Ouyang
bullets: Addresses the scarcity and cost of controlled action–response data in mobile networks.
Pretrains predictive representations on observation-only data, adapts them to a target domain, then learns sleep/wake-conditioned dynamics with the encoder fixed.
Evaluated with public operator data and a real-equipment four-cell 5G testbed.
Achieves lower action-conditioned prediction error than a GPT-2 world model and mechanistic rule, while remaining near a persistence baseline.
Supports higher sleep ratios at comparable congestion cost and generates distinct futures for SLEEP versus KEEP plans.

papers.abstract: Tracking object motion within a gripper provides essential feedback for robotic manipulation. However, limited contact coverage and uneven deformation make tactile estimation challenging. In this study, we present TacSpin, a method that tracks in-gripper object rotation on SO(3) using only two vision-based tactile sensors. The key idea is to estimate the axis and magnitude of the rotation response separately, rather than fitting a rigid-body model by least squares. Each finger's response is further refined with contact-boundary cues. The two fingers are then fused according to their agreement. On standard objects, TacSpin achieves lower mean checkpoint errors. Qualitative demonstrations on real-world objects, using calibration transferred from a standard sphere, illustrate tracking under different contact geometries.

papers.abstract: Self-supervised pretraining has expanded the pool of 3D medical foundation models, but published evaluations use different datasets, endpoints and fine-tuning protocols. Models also differ in architecture, pretraining objective and data, while downstream targets range from voxel-level masks to patient-level diagnoses and outcomes. As a result, published findings provide little directly comparable evidence for choosing a model for a new task. Direct comparison of adaptation performance requires fine-tuning candidates on labelled target data, at substantial computational cost. We benchmark 23 candidates across the same 14 segmentation, classification and regression tasks spanning multiple anatomies and modalities. No candidate ranked among the top three across all segmentation tasks or across all classification and regression tasks; a convolutional encoder could outperform a transformer trained with the same objective on one task but underperform it on another. We benchmark transferability estimators against the fine-tuned rankings and find that their agreement varies across dense segmentation, classification and regression. InsightRank uses task-appropriate frozen-feature statistics and architecture-aware pairwise comparisons to rank candidates before fine-tuning. Across the 23-model pool, mean Kendall tau-b was 0.431 for segmentation and 0.352 for classification and regression. The segmentation Top 3 contained a task winner on four of nine tasks; the image-level Top 3 contained none on the five tasks, despite better full-ranking agreement than the matched conventional estimators. A three-model shortlist reduced recorded extraction-plus-training job time by 85.8% across seven segmentation tasks. Together, the benchmark provides a common reference for model selection and InsightRank offers a lower-cost way to prioritize fine-tuning, with shortlist performance that differs by target type.

No model ranked among the top three across all tasks; architecture advantages varied by task.
Transferability estimators agreed with fine-tuned rankings differently for segmentation versus image-level prediction tasks.
InsightRank uses task-specific frozen-feature statistics and architecture-aware comparisons to rank models before fine-tuning.
A three-model shortlist reduced recorded extraction-plus-training job time by 85.8% across seven segmentation tasks, but shortlist effectiveness varied by target type.

papers.abstract: While expert demonstrations on real robots are difficult to collect, human ego-centric videos are easy to collect and abundant on the internet. However, learning dexterous manipulation policies from human videos remains challenging---one of the most important challenges being the difficulty of reconstructing physically grounded robot trajectories due to the large embodiment gap. In this paper, we propose EgoCPT, a novel paradigm for learning high-quality retargeted dexterous hand trajectories directly from an ego-centric video, which can then be deployed directly on real robots. The only inputs to our method are an ego-centric RGB video and a reference hand pose trajectory, which can be easily obtained through off-the-shelf software or specialized cameras during recording. Our method is particularly robust to noisy hand poses attributed to our novel contact-aware optimization framework, which iteratively optimizes the contact points between the robot hands and objects. Across five manipulation tasks, our method achieves overall success rates of 67.3% on noisy EgoDex hand-pose reconstructions and 92.0% on high-quality TACO reconstructions collected using motion-capture hardware, outperforming multiple baselines on both benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Multi-robot exploration under communication and mobility constraints requires balancing information gain with reachability. We present a distributed semantic exploration framework that combines Dirichlet mapping, budget-constrained trajectory selection, and Resource-Aware distributed Greedy (RAG) coordination. Each robot clusters frontiers, computes terrain- and heading-aware least-cost paths with a single budget-limited Dijkstra search, and selects feasible paths by marginal information gain, represented by the expected reduction in Dirichlet entropy. Each robot's per-round selection is exact, the team's joint per-round information gain is at least half the centralized optimum, and the bound degrades gracefully under limited communication. Ten-run gridworld ablations show improved coverage, semantic mIoU, and map certainty with lower entropy and traversal cost per unit distance than shortest-distance frontier selection. Budget-sensitivity experiments show that an intermediate budget best balances path reach and receding-horizon execution. In photorealistic full-system simulation against five coordination rules run in their native published forms, the proposed method attains the highest mean coverage and semantic accuracy while being the only one that respects the per-trajectory mobility budget.

papers.abstract: Complex and long-horizon agent tasks often rely on frontier models deployed in the cloud to achieve strong performance. However, using these models for every step of a long-horizon trajectory incurs substantial inference cost, even though not all steps may require the same level of model capability. In this paper, we find that allocating the LLM to only a small subset of key steps can achieve performance comparable to full LLM execution while significantly reducing inference cost. Motivated by this observation, we propose EdgeWise, an edge-cloud collaboration framework that deploys an SLM on the local device as the primary solver and selectively delegates critical steps to a cloud LLM when stronger model capacity is needed. To enable autonomous delegation without additional models at inference time, we introduce a step-level RL method that jointly optimizes task solving and delegation, with fine-grained credit assignment for individual delegation decisions. We also introduce an external judge-based delegation strategy and use it to systematically investigate key design choices in edge-cloud collaboration, including when to delegate, how delegation decisions should be made, what context should be shared, and how frequently the cloud LLM should be invoked. Experiments show that EdgeWise matches or outperforms pure-LLM execution while reducing inference cost up to 62% on SWE-Rebench and 34% on Terminal-Bench 2.1. We further deploy EdgeWise on a local workstation, demonstrating comparable cost savings in a practical edge-cloud setting.

Also evaluates an external-judge delegation strategy and design choices around timing, context, and invocation frequency.

papers.abstract: We propose ATOM (Abstract Transition and Option Modeling), a hierarchical navigation framework that combines higher-level graph planning with reusable lower-level option policies for efficient repeated navigation in large-scale 3D environments represented by hierarchical structures such as 3D scene graphs (3DSGs). ATOM operates on a hierarchical graph representation, implemented using, for instance, the Rooms and Places layers of a 3DSG, where each directed abstract transition is associated with a navigation option. For each transition, ATOM computes and stores a reusable option policy along with its state-dependent cost-to-go. Across repeated navigation tasks, ATOM maintains a smoothed empirical distribution over option initiation states and uses it to progressively refine the corresponding abstract transition cost. Ablation studies show that ATOM reduces cumulative repeated-planning time by 97.5% relative to a monolithic MDP baseline while maintaining trajectories within approximately 7% of a Global Places A* shortest-path reference. Experience-informed refinement further reduces abstract transition-cost estimation error by 10.3%. Physical experiments validate ATOM on an F1Tenth vehicle, successfully completing all five navigation queries with 43% of inter-region option executions reusing previously generated solutions.

papers.abstract: Recent video super-resolution (VSR) models achieve efficient one-step generation through diffusion distillation. However, high-resolution inference remains costly, and distilled models are difficult to align with human preferences. These challenges call for improvements in both model architecture and training strategy. We present \textbf{FlashVSR+} to address both limitations. On the architecture side, we introduce hybrid attention based on the strong locality observed in pretrained VSR models, while retaining sparse global interaction for long-range consistency. It achieves up to $2\times$ DiT speedup and 45\% lower peak memory, enabling spatially untiled 4K VSR on a single 24GB RTX 4090. On the training side, we propose Reward-Yield Distribution Matching Distillation (Ry-DMD) for preference-aligned one-step generation. Ry-DMD uses reward-weighted teacher rollouts to incorporate black-box rewards into distribution matching, without backpropagating through the reward model. We further show that Ry-DMD generalizes beyond VSR to T2I generation. Together, FlashVSR+ delivers stronger restoration quality and substantially improves high-resolution efficiency, with consistent gains in user preference. We release our code, models, and training data at \href{https://www.flashvsr.tech}{\textcolor{FlashBlue}{\textbf{www.flashvsr.tech}}}.
authors: Ruchang Yao, Shi Guo, Junhao Zhuang, Mingde Yao, Xin Cai, Jiahao Zhan, Bin Fu, Xinyuan Chen, Yu Qiao, Tianfan Xue

Reports up to 2× DiT speedup and 45% lower peak memory, enabling untiled 4K VSR on a single 24GB RTX 4090.
Achieves stronger restoration quality and consistent user-preference gains; Ry-DMD also generalizes to text-to-image generation.

papers.abstract: Thought templates, skill libraries, agent memories and caches turn many reasoning steps into one. We call this reasoning contraction. A contracted memory saves reasoning steps and errors until its facts change, then quietly answers wrong. Most systems trust memories by counting successes and failures. We prove that such counters are badly tuned change detectors: a symmetric counter notices a partial change only after a power of its false-alarm horizon, and an unclipped one may never notice it. On five LLMs answering multi-hop questions over edited facts, ExpeL- and ACE-style counters serve 7.0-13.5x more stale answers than certified memories given the same information, and on code tasks with an exact verifier 35-73x more. Safety also has a price. When facts change and each memory is judged only by its own verified outcomes, one number, the certification load, sets how much reasoning any safe memory can skip, and under Zipf demand it yields a scaling law. Our recipe weighs each memory's failures by its own likelihood ratio, certifies its utility against live reasoning, and restarts the certificate when facts change, with the likelihood-ratio detector as the safety net for unannounced changes; for large edits it also invalidates the memory.
authors: Jianghong Zhou, Hao Rong, Chen Lin, Daoan Zhang
bullets: Reasoning contraction compresses many reasoning steps into reusable templates, skills, memories, or caches, but becomes unsafe when underlying facts change.
The paper shows symmetric and unclipped counters can detect partial changes extremely slowly or not at all.
Across five LLMs, ExpeL- and ACE-style counters produced 7.0–13.5× more stale answers than certified memories; on verified code tasks, the gap was 35–73×.
The proposed approach weights failures by likelihood ratios, certifies memory utility against live reasoning, restarts certification after changes, and invalidates memories after large edits.
Certification load determines how much reasoning a safe memory can skip; under Zipf demand, the paper derives a corresponding scaling law.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Trusting a contracted memory is a sequential test. (a) Top: the lifecycle of a contracted memory (a macro). In shadow mode a betting certificate scores the macro’s verified answers and folds it (one-step answers) once its wealth reaches 1/δ; a likelihood-ratio CUSUM (LR-CUSUM) alarm or an edit notice retires it, and the next candidate restarts the test. Middle: both tests on one real macro (Qwen3-8B, KQA-STREAM; per candidate, no notices). Its log-wealth reaches ln 20 (δ = 0.05) after 33 labels; an edit then drops its reliability from 1.00 to 0.37, below break-even (r⋆ = 0.49), and the LR-CUSUM crosses h = 7 on the fourth label. papers.selection_reason: Addresses safe memory reuse, certification, and change detection for LLM agents, fitting LLM memory.
papers.title: Many Steps into One: Reasoning Contraction and the Limits of Safe Memory Reuse for LLM Agents
papers.tldr: Safe reuse of compressed reasoning memories requires principled change detection and certification, because common success/failure counters can silently preserve stale answers after facts change.

papers.abstract: Textual reasoning before acting has improved vision-language-action (VLA) models, but at the cost of latency: every action conditioned on the reasoning text must wait for autoregressive decoding. We show that actions do not need to wait for or condition on the generated reasoning to benefit from it, because the reasoning supervision already improves the backbone representation. We introduce TacitVLA, a reasoning VLA whose action expert never attends to the reasoning it generates for the current call. On long-horizon tasks where the reasoning text also serves as episodic memory, it can generate each entry during action execution rather than before acting. We evaluate it in a controlled study on four benchmarks spanning manipulation and autonomous driving, memory and non-memory tasks: RoboMME, RMBench, LIBERO, and PhysicalAI-AV. On all four, TacitVLA matches the performance of its explicit-reasoning counterpart at up to 3.4x lower latency, and matches the latency of the same architecture trained without reasoning at up to +17.1% success. In absolute terms, it surpasses the best previously published results on the RoboMME Counting suite (82.7% vs. 66.8%) and RMBench (77.5% vs. 56.5%), and reaches 72.9% on LIBERO-Plus and a 52.5% scene score on the public split of the PhysicalAI-AV closed-loop driving challenge. Project page: https://tacitvla.github.io.
authors: Jack Lu, Yurong You, Boyi Li, Yulong Cao, Thomas Tian, Chaowei Xiao, Xiangyu Chen, Wenjie Luo, Boris Ivanovic, Marco Pavone, Yan Wang
bullets: Reasoning text improves the VLA backbone, even when the action expert does not attend to the reasoning generated during the current call.
For long-horizon tasks, reasoning can be generated during execution and used as episodic memory rather than delaying action.
Across four manipulation and driving benchmarks, TacitVLA matches explicit-reasoning performance with up to 3.4× lower latency.
It matches the latency of non-reasoning training while achieving up to 17.1% higher success.
It reports strong results on RoboMME Counting, RMBench, LIBERO-Plus, and PhysicalAI-AV.

figures.caption: Figure 1: TacitVLA retains the benefit of reasoning supervision without conditioning its actions on the generated text. Left: how the policies act in one call. Given the context 𝑐𝑡, on memory tasks including the ledger 𝑀𝑡 of past subtasks, the backbone generates the reasoning 𝑟𝑡 and conditions the action expert that outputs the action chunk 𝑎𝑡. In Explicit Reasoning, the action expert attends to 𝑟𝑡, so every action chunk waits for it. TacitVLA trains on the same sequence with 𝑟𝑡 masked from the action expert, bypassing the need to generate 𝑟𝑡 on non-memory tasks. On memory tasks, 𝑟𝑡 still becomes the next ledger entry (dashed loop), but is generated asynchronously during execution instead of making the action expert wait. No Reasoning is the same architecture trained without reasoning supervision. Right: TacitVLA matches Explicit Reasoning’s success at 1.7× and 3.4× lower latency, andmatches No Reasoning’s latency at +3.5% and+5.3% success (Tables 3, 5, 15).

Figure 3: TacitVLA matches the latency of No Reasoning on every benchmark, and Explicit Reasoning’s latency is 1.4× to 3.4× higher. Each bar is one policy’s latency per call: 𝑇action for No Reasoning and TacitVLA, and 𝑇action + 𝑇reason for Explicit Reasoning, whose actions wait for text generation. The ratio above each group is Explicit Reasoning’s latency over TacitVLA’s. On the memory tasks, TacitVLA generates the ledger entry during execution, taking at most 23% of the execution window, so the next call never waits for generation. All values are means over model calls on one H100, with the per-stage breakdown in Table 15 (Appendix C).

Figure 2: Training and deployment of Explicit Reasoning and TacitVLA. The two policies share the training sequence and differ in one attention-mask cell, which decouples TacitVLA’s actions from text generation at deployment. (a) The backbone predicts the reasoning 𝑟𝑡 and the tokenized actions ?̃?𝑡 (an auxiliary target) under cross-entropy, and the action expert denoises the action chunk 𝑎𝑡 under flow matching. (b) Rows attend to columns. The backbone is causal. The action expert attends to 𝑐𝑡 and its own action chunk, to 𝑟𝑡 only in Explicit Reasoning, and never to ?̃?𝑡. The crossed cell is that difference. (c) On non-memory tasks, Explicit Reasoning needs to generate 𝑟𝑡 before denoising and executing the action chunk, while TacitVLA does not. Onmemory tasks, both generate the ledger entry 𝑟𝑡: Explicit Reasoning before action execution, TacitVLA during it concurrently.

The RoboMME policies use the 𝜋0.5 architecture with RoboMME’s frame-sampling memory. The RMBench, LIBERO, and driving backbones share the Qwen3-VL-2B architecture and differ in vocabulary.

The 𝜋0.5 and MolmoAct2 rows are LIT’s baselines (Lin et al., 2026b), trained this way from the vision-language backbones. Table 15: Stage times and the latency per call (ms). The left columns give the execution window 𝑇exec and each policy’s action path 𝑇action and reasoning cost 𝑇reason (Section 3.3), and the right columns give the latency per call: 𝑇action for No Reasoning and TacitVLA, and 𝑇action + 𝑇reason for Explicit Reasoning, whose action waits for the generation. TacitVLA generates during 𝑇exec on the memory tasks and not at all on the non-memory tasks. All values are means of per-call stage timers on one H100. RMBench’s window is the motion planner’s mean time to execute a plan.
Table 9: Training settings. Learning rates are for the vision tower, the language model, and the action expert, respectively, and RoboMME uses one rate for all three.

On RoboMME, the total also includes the 0.315B frame-sampling memory, whose history frames pass through the same frozen SigLIP as the current image. A policy that generates no text (No Reasoning, and TacitVLA on the non-memory tasks) uses only the keys and values of the last language layer and not the rest of that layer or the final norm.

Table 12: LIBERO-Plus by perturbation axis. Success (%) on each of the seven perturbation axes and on the full 10,030-case suite, mean ± standard deviation over three evaluation seeds.

papers.abstract: While it is known that quantization of large language models (LLMs) reduces memory usage via lower-bit weights, studies quantifying the resulting impact on energy usage and carbon intensity are scarce. We present the first unified evaluation of weight-only quantization strategies for LLM inference across varying input/output lengths and GPUs, highlighting differences in energy efficiency in addition to accuracy degradation and runtime. We study quantized inference on Llama 2 7B, Phi 3.5 Mini Instruct, OLMo 1B, Qwen 2.5 7B, and Qwen 2.5 14B across GLUE MNLI, MMLU, HumanEval, and GSM8K datasets, evaluating 10 post-training quantization (PTQ) strategies on NVIDIA H100, A6000, A100, and L4 GPUs. We identify a novel trend showing that quantization techniques tend to exhibit peak energy efficiency relative to full-precision baselines when inputs are sufficiently long and outputs are short. Furthermore, we show that quantization strategies become marginally more energy-efficient relative to full-precision models as batch sizes increase, though gains are modest. Notably, fused-kernel implementations such as EETQ int8 and Bitsandbytes int8 offer the highest energy savings, up to 4x compared to FP32 on short text generation, with negligible accuracy loss. Finally, we observe that energy usage closely tracks runtime on our evaluated benchmarks, indicating that, in practice, latency optimization can serve as a reliable proxy for reducing the environmental footprint of LLM services. We conclude with suggested directions for strategically selecting low-carbon quantization strategies based on specific inference requirements.
authors: Petar Basta
bullets: Quantization is assessed for energy use, carbon intensity, runtime, and accuracy across five LLMs, four GPUs, four benchmarks, and 10 PTQ strategies.
Energy efficiency relative to full precision is strongest when inputs are long and outputs are short; batch-size increases provide modest additional gains.
Fused-kernel methods, particularly EETQ int8 and Bitsandbytes int8, achieve up to 4× energy savings versus FP32 on short-text generation with negligible accuracy loss.
Energy consumption closely follows runtime, making latency optimization a practical proxy for reducing inference environmental impact.
The findings support selecting quantization methods according to workload and low-carbon inference requirements.
