papers.tldr: A broad evaluation shows that weight-only quantization can reduce LLM inference energy—especially with long inputs, short outputs, larger batches, and fused int8 kernels—while often preserving accuracy.

papers.abstract: We propose a unified spatial-density signal to score token importance for both inference phases: bipartite merge for prefill and KV eviction for decode, yielding measurable gains in each stage. To isolate the two phases, we split benchmarks by scoring logic. Prefill probes (MMBench, POPE, ScienceQA) evaluate only the first decoded token; their accuracy reflects prefill logits argmax before any decode KV eviction. Full-pipeline probes (TextVQA, DocVQA, MM-Vet) assess the complete generated sequence and capture both phases. We identify a critical evaluation pitfall: decode pruning claims validated solely on prefill probes measure prefill quality, not decode performance. Experiments show discarding all visual KV during decode barely affects prefill-probe accuracy but degrades TextVQA and MM-Vet drastically; this insensitivity stems from the scoring rule, not compression intensity.Evaluated on seven model variants (InternVL-3.5, Qwen3-VL, LLaVA-1.5) and three full-pipeline benchmarks, our method achieves a three-way Pareto frontier across compute, memory and accuracy. Density-based prefill compression maintains strong accuracy, scales linearly with visual token count, and delivers 100x faster token selection at high resolution. For decode, density top-k KV eviction consistently outperforms strong baselines H2O, SnapKV and StreamingLLM on TextVQA and MM-Vet across three retention ratios. At 0.125 keep ratio on TextVQA, it surpasses H2O by 9.6 points; InternVL-3.5 models (2B to 38B) maintain a 7 to 10 point advantage. Compression scales favorably with model size: every measured 8B to 38B model transition reduces accuracy loss instead of worsening it. We suggest MM-Vet or DocVQA as mandatory full-pipeline validation for any decode-phase claims. Our code is available at https://github.com/Kai-Liu001/TwinPrune
authors: Kai Liu, Anqi Li, Junxian Li, Zhixin Wang, Zhikai Chen, Renjing Pei, Yulun Zhang
bullets: Motivation: Prefill-only probes can hide severe decode-phase quality degradation, so pruning claims require full-pipeline evaluation.
Method: Apply density-based scoring for bipartite visual-token merging during prefill and top-k visual KV eviction during decode.
Contribution: Establishes separate benchmarks and evaluation guidance, recommending MM-Vet or DocVQA for decode-pruning validation.
Results: Prefill selection is up to 100× faster at high resolution; decode pruning outperforms H2O, SnapKV, and StreamingLLM across tested retention ratios.
Scope: Evaluated across seven model variants and multiple vision-language benchmarks; performance gains are reported for both stages.

figures.caption: Figure 3: TwinPrune pipeline. A single spatial density signal ρ, defined as each visual token’s average cosine dissimilarity to its w×w neighborhood (b), drives both phases. Prefill bipartite-merges low-ρ source tokens into high-ρ destination anchors, cutting FLOPs (c). Decode ranks visual KV by ρ and keeps the top-k with original RoPE positions, cutting KV memory (d). One signal, two levers, and a three-axis Pareto trade-off over compute, KV, and accuracy (a).

Figure 2: Prefill-probe benchmarks are structurally insensitive to decode-phase KV eviction across three VLM families. Left: accuracy vs. visual KV kept on InternVL-3.5-8B. Right: prediction mismatch at DALL grouped by (benchmark, model). Details in Sec. 3.

Figure 4: Decode KV Eviction on TextVQA. On InternVL-3.5-8B, density-guided eviction Paretodominates random and attention-value-norm in the memory–accuracy trade-off. Right inset: Qwen3VL-4B, LLaVA-1.5-7B, and InternVL-3.5-38B show the same monotonic density trend.

Table 2: Per-benchmark prefill compression on InternVL-3.5-8B; same (L, r) within each block. Bold marks per-column best; daggers (†) flag structurally invalid output (acc≈0, App. S). Block 4 in App. V. Speedup: measured prefill speedup vs. uncompressed baseline at batch=8, HD mode (12 tiles, Nvis=3072) on RTX A6000.

Table 3: Decode-phase KV eviction comparison on InternVL-3.5-8B at three keep ratios. Density top-k wins all six TextVQA and MM-Vet cells. On DocVQA, SnapKV narrowly leads at keep≥ 25% but density reclaims the lead at 12.5% keep. Bold marks per-column best. TextVQA uses n=5000 exact-match. MM-Vet uses n=218. DocVQA uses n=5349 with ANLS scoring.

Table 1: Prediction-mismatch % vs. no-compression baseline on InternVL-3.5-8B. Decode KV eviction flips up to 46% of TextVQA predictions but ≤ 0.54% on prefill-probe benches, since y1 depends only on prefill logits (Eq. 1). Prefill rows fix L=15 (varying L shifts levels but not the scoring-rule gap). Appendix N extends to all 3 archs.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes density-aware token pruning and KV eviction for vision-language models, directly addressing efficiency in both prefill and decode phases.
papers.title: TwinPrune: Density-Aware Two-Phase Token Pruning for Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: TwinPrune uses spatial-density-aware token pruning separately for prefill merging and decode KV eviction, improving the compute–memory–accuracy trade-off while exposing pitfalls in phase-specific evaluation.

papers.abstract: Training recipes are tuned by hand for one model, cluster and workload, and every new model, accelerator, framework version or dataset means tuning again. Automated tuners search a fixed space of knobs and check only that a job runs, yet a configuration can run to completion while it silently changes training. ATTUNE is a single coding agent that tunes any working recipe for the workload and stack at hand, unattended, within a GPU-hour budget the user sets. It diagnoses each run and changes one lever at a time, guided by a catalog of lessons from past campaigns, and ships a recipe only if it passes a correctness gate: a configuration check against objective-changing settings and known stack defects, and a convergence check of its loss curve against the baseline's. On four held-out models at 64-128 GPUs, ATTUNE raises mean throughput over the strongest public recipe run on our stack by 6.7% on Llama-3.1-405B (best campaign 11.9%) and 33.9% on GLM-4.5 (54.7%), whose public recipe was written for H100. It keeps Mixtral-8x22B's recipe, where nothing it finds clears the noise band. Under a common GPU-hour budget it beats OptiCo, Bayesian optimization and random search on GLM-4.5 and MiniMax-M2; on GLM-4.5 its mean gain is more than four times the best alternative's at less than half the GPU-hours, and on both models its tuning pays for itself within a day of training. The gate rejects no legitimate run and catches 16 of 24 faulty runs, missing only ones that barely move the 20-step loss. Ablations tie its best campaigns to one of its search rules: retrying an out-of-memory layout with recomputation. We release ATTUNE's code and TrainingThroughputBench, a leaderboard of the fastest known recipes for MoE models up to 744B parameters on up to 256 GPUs, each with its throughput, cost per million tokens and a passed correctness check, at https://github.com/amazon-science/attune.
authors: Leo Fan, Hongyang Wang, Wenbo Chen, Jingguo Liu, Xian Li, Xuan Wang, Ruochen Wen, Yiming Yan, Hao Wu, Zheshen Wang, Benoit Dumoulin
bullets: Addresses the need to retune recipes across models, hardware, software stacks, and datasets, while avoiding silent objective-changing configurations.
Uses a coding agent that diagnoses runs, changes one lever at a time, and reuses lessons from prior tuning campaigns within a user-defined GPU-hour budget.
Accepts a recipe only after configuration checks and a loss-curve convergence check against the baseline.
Improves mean throughput by 6.7% on Llama-3.1-405B and 33.9% on GLM-4.5; it leaves Mixtral-8x22B unchanged when gains remain within noise.
Outperforms competing search methods on GLM-4.5 and MiniMax-M2 under a common budget; the correctness gate catches 16 of 24 faulty runs.

figures.caption: Figure 1. ATTUNE’s architecture: (1) a single coding agent’s diagnosis-driven search; (2) deterministic gates that refuse objectivechanging settings before launch, admit measurements, promote leaders and check correctness before a recipe ships; (3) the harness, which keeps the loop running unattended; (4) durable state for resuming after a crash; (5) the skill, which carries lessons into later campaigns.

Table 3. Tuner comparison on GLM-4.5 / 128×B200 and MiniMax-M2 / 64×B200, means over three campaigns. Gain is over the public recipe (723.6 and 895.2 tokens/s/GPU). Launches counts search launches; Failed launches gives the share that ran out of memory, hung or crashed and, in parentheses, their GPU-hours; Wall-clock runs from a campaign’s first cluster admission to its stop, excluding time when all its jobs are queued (Appendix D). Bold marks each model’s best value per column. On GLM-4.5 ATTUNE beats every other tuner under the mean rule, with exact permutation p = 0.05 against OptiCo and both BO arms and 0.10 against random search; the block-stratified p is 0.125 for all four, the lowest that test allows. On MiniMax-M2 it beats every other tuner as well, with p = 0.05 unrestricted and 0.125 block-stratified against each. BO: Bayesian optimization; TPE: tree-structured Parzen estimator.

Table 5. The correctness gate on runs with a known answer, outside the evaluation campaigns. Bold cells are correct decisions. A fault tested on several models counts once per model. Legitimate runs are baseline replicates, single placement or packing changes, runs of the public recipe and correct recipes whose step-0 numerics differ from the baseline. Table B2 breaks these down by fault and model.

Table 4. Ablations on GLM-4.5 / 128×B200, three campaigns per arm. Gain over the public recipe is the mean, with each campaign’s in parentheses; the other columns are per-campaign means as in Table 3, and bold marks the best value per column. Under the mean rule at GLM-4.5’s band of 3.00%, full ATTUNE beats the committee (mean throughput 4.3% higher; exact permutation p = 0.45 unrestricted, 0.375 block-stratified) and the public-guide arm (3.7%; p = 0.50, 0.50), and ties the minimal skill (2.9%; p = 0.50, 0.50).

Values over three campaigns are means, judged by the mean rule (Section 3.1); Best campaign gives the fastest campaign’s gain. MFU (Appendix D) is given as public recipe → ATTUNE. Tables D2 and D3 give every campaign.

Held-out models and their public recipes, in tokens/s/GPU unless noted, with 8 GPUs per node (B200: 180 GB and H100: 80 GB of HBM per GPU). “Published” is the throughput the recipe’s authors report (NVIDIA, 2026b; Yan, 2026), Mixtral-8x22B’s in TFLOP/s; Appendix D gives the conversion and defines MFU. “Our stack” is the public recipe on slime (Zhu et al., 2025b) and Megatron-LM with the changes of Appendix A; Section 6 discusses the gap. papers.abstract: World action models (WAMs) are a category of policy models that ex- plicitly predict both actions and future world states. They have been shown to outperform action-only models across various robotic manipulation tasks. How- ever, representing the future with full-frame video prediction can be computation- ally expensive during both training and inference. This raises a central question: what compact state representation preserves the planning and supervision bene- fits of future prediction? In this paper, we propose BoxWAM, which replaces dense future frames with oriented bounding box trajectories of task-relevant ob- jects. By explicitly imagining object-centric future motion, our method provides a lightweight prediction target that captures the key physical changes induced by robot actions. We show that box trajectory prediction substantially reduces com- putational cost while improving action prediction performance, suggesting that object-centric compact states can serve as an efficient alternative to video-based world action modeling for robotic manipulation. Result videos can be found on https://box-wam.github.io
authors: Qinxi Yu, Wenzhou Ding, Gloria X. Wang, Albert J. Zhai, Shenlong Wang
bullets: Addresses the high training and inference cost of dense future-frame prediction in world action models.
Represents task-relevant object motion with object-centric oriented bounding-box trajectories.
Uses predicted future object motion as a compact planning and supervision signal.
Reports substantially lower computational cost and improved action prediction performance.
Focuses on robotic manipulation; the abstract does not specify datasets or numeric results.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of BoxWAM. Observation images are encoded into visual context tokens, which condition a rectified-flow transformer that jointly denoises future state tokens and action tokens. An enforced causal attention allows action tokens to condition on imagined object motion while preventing future state tokens from depending on future action tokens. The decoded future state forms a compact box trajectory, and the decoded action tokens form the robot action chunk.

Figure 3: Simulation rollout visualizations on RoboTwin2.0. We visualize representative rollouts from eight simulation tasks with predicted future box trajectories overlaid on the scene. BoxWAM predicts compact object-centric future motion across diverse manipulation behaviors.

Figure 4: Real-world rollout visualizations. We visualize representative rollouts from three realworld manipulation tasks with predicted future box trajectories overlaid on the scene-camera view. The first two columns show early and late coffee-making stages; the remaining columns show watering and toy placement. Each row shows a different frame, illustrating how BoxWAM predicts compact object-motion plans for action generation under real-world perception noise, actuation error, and object pose variation.

Figure 6: Comparison with existing models. The vertical axis shows the mean success rate across the Easy and Hard settings. Bubble size scales with model size, and darker blue indicates a larger training budget in GPU-hours. Trainingbudget estimates are based on reported configurations and runtimes.
Figure 5: Multimodal ordering behavior in Put Bottle Dustbin, learned from randomizedorder demonstrations. Predicted boxes indicate the intended active object.

Table 1: Single-task RoboTwin2.0 success rates (%). BoxWAM and Flow (action-only) are evaluated over three seeds with 100 trials per seed for each task and setting. Other baselines are from the RoboTwin2.0 leaderboard. Gray rows indicate pretrained models.

Table 3: Real-world manipulation results. We report both final success rate and progress rate because full task success can be sparse. Each method is evaluated under the same execution protocol and randomized object pose.
Table 4: Future-state ablations. SR (%); "—": same as box latency.
Table 8: Per-task multi-task simulation results under the clean setting trained with 2500 demos and joint based control. We report success rate (%).
Table 9: Per-task multi-task simulation results under the randomized setting trained with 2500 demos and joint based control. We report success rate (%).
Table 6: Real-world progress subgoals. Progress is measured by the number of completed ordered subgoals in each rollout.
Table 7: Multi-task simulation summary. We report average success rate (%) over RoboTwin2.0 tasks.

Models are evaluated under clean and randomized settings. We report success rate (%). The inference latency (ms) is reported based on default 10 denoising steps from π0.5.

papers.title: Box-WAM: Box Trajectories as Compact State Representations for World Action Models
papers.tldr: Box-WAM uses oriented bounding-box trajectories instead of future video frames to make world action models more efficient while improving action prediction for robotic manipulation.

papers.abstract: Evaluating VLA policies on real robots is costly, time-consuming, and difficult to reproduce, making real-to-sim simulation essential for scalable evaluation. While 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) enables rapid real-to-sim scene generation, the reconstruction quality required for reliable policy evaluation remains unquantified. In particular, policies relying on wrist-mounted fisheye cameras (e.g., YUBI handheld gripper data) are heavily exposed to visual artifacts (holes, floaters) in wide-angle views, directly degrading task performance. To address this, we present YUBI-Real2Sim, a unified framework for 3DGS-based scene reconstruction and real-to-sim policy evaluation under dual fisheye wrist views. We develop an integrated pipeline combining 200-degree fisheye camera capture, 3DGS training, 3D foundation models for object modeling, and MuJoCo-based physical simulation, reproducing the observed real-world policy ordering in eight of nine scene-task comparisons. Using this framework, we construct a benchmark across two bimanual robot platforms, three scenes, three tasks, and dual pi0.5-based policies. This systematically measures real-to-sim rank agreement and evaluates policy sensitivity against counterfactual 3DGS artifacts (ceiling holes, floaters, warping) and capture disturbances. We further analyze whether novel-view quality scores can indicate policy-ranking reliability under a scene-held-out evaluation protocol. The results show task-dependent performance and limitations of quality-based reliability prediction, highlighting the need to assess reconstruction quality when using Real2Sim for policy evaluation. These results do not yet establish a generally reliable scene-acceptance rule. Project Page: https://yubi-real2sim.airoa.io.
authors: Hiroki Nishizawa, Takehiko Ohkawa, Nicola Scianca, Tatsuya Matsushima, Shigeo Morishima, Kei Ota
bullets: Addresses costly, difficult-to-reproduce real-robot policy evaluation through real-to-sim simulation.
Combines 200° fisheye capture, 3DGS reconstruction, 3D foundation-model object modeling, and MuJoCo simulation.
Benchmarks two bimanual platforms, three scenes, three tasks, and two pi0.5-based policies, reproducing real-world policy ordering in 8 of 9 scene-task comparisons.
Tests policy sensitivity to ceiling holes, floaters, warping, and capture disturbances, and examines whether novel-view quality predicts ranking reliability.
Finds task-dependent effects and limitations of quality-based reliability prediction; no general scene-acceptance rule is established.

figures.caption: Figure 2 | YUBI-Real2Sim pipeline. We capture the background with a single 200◦ FOV camera, estimate camera poses with COLMAP, and densify the point cloud with OpenMVS to initialize Gaussian Wrapping for high-fidelity reconstruction. We generate object geometry and textures with TRELLIS 2.0 and approximate collision meshes with CoACD. The reconstructed scene and objects are integrated into MuJoCo simulation. For wrist-view rendering, we independently render the background Gaussians and the MuJoCo visual meshes, then composite their pixels using depth maps.

Figure 3 | Simulated scenes, and the added disturbances for 3DGS or viewpoints. One column per scene, one band per condition. Blue: the clean 3DGS reconstructions the rollouts run in. Red: the same reconstructions carrying a counterfactual artifact — a ceiling hole in FR3 Flat, the 54◦ and 90◦ half-angles either side of the dashed rule, low floaters in FR3 Duo, and warping in TX-G2. Amber, the colour Fig. 1 gives capture: one reduced-coverage reconstruction per condition, each in the scene of its column. The panels show representative examples of the reconstruction conditions. We evaluated two task-specific VLA checkpoints for each of three tasks (Cup, Tape, and Pen) in all three scenes (FR3 Flat, FR3 Duo, and TX-G2).

Figure 4 | Policy ranking in real and simulated evaluation. Black/gray bars show real success and blue bars show simulated success; light and dark bars denote π1 and π2, respectively, as in Fig. 1. Policy labels are fixed within each task across scenes and domains. Error bars are marginal 95% Wilson confidence intervals from 20 real and 80 simulated trials per policy. The observed ranking agrees in 8/9 scene–task pairs (88.9%); Flat Cup is reversed.

Figure 1 | YUBI-Real2Sim analyzes and verifies 3DGS scenes for reliable policy-ranking evaluation. The quality of 3DGS can easily degrade depending on the camera views. We analyze how variations in 3DGS quality affect policy rankings and examine whether scene-quality scores can indicate policy-ranking reliability.

Table I | Effect of each counterfactual (CF) condition on the nine scene–task policy comparisons. Significance: comparisons whose Fisher-test status (p < 0.05) is lost or gained relative to Clean; the others keep their status. Ranking vs. Clean: comparisons whose simulated ranking is reversed or tied relative to Clean. Agreement with real: comparisons whose simulated ranking matches the real ranking. Clean agrees in 8/9 (Flat Cup is reversed) and no CF condition corrects it, so every reversal or tie is a lost agreement.

papers.title: YUBI-Real2Sim: 3DGS Scene Verification for Reliable Policy Evaluation
papers.tldr: YUBI-Real2Sim benchmarks how 3DGS reconstruction quality affects reliable real-to-sim evaluation of VLA policies using dual fisheye wrist cameras.

papers.abstract: In humans, proprioception corresponds to the sense of self-movement or position, e.g. understanding the position of one's arm. This sense is often less well-understood and in popular understanding sometimes conflated with introspection. But, notably, proprioception is a separate sense, with dedicated receptors and verifiable outcomes. On the other hand though, language models cannot observe their own internal states during training (and for example answer the question which experts activated in a certain layer of an MoE) and so cannot accurately report on them. Yet, such information is, by virtue of being internal to the model, both accessible, and readily constructed into verifiable signals. We argue that this provides the basis for a digital analog of proprioception. As such, we train models through SFT and on-policy training to equip them with this ability. We show that modern models can be trained to understand a range of subtypes of proprioception, such as routing decision awareness, token entropy, decision depth or logit lens information, without affecting model capabilities. We then run these models through a broad evaluation of situational awareness, legibility, and epiphenomenality, to evaluate in what ways access to proprioception changes model behavior.
authors: Jonas Geiping
bullets: Defines model proprioception as awareness of internal signals, distinct from introspection.
Trains models using supervised fine-tuning and on-policy training.
Covers routing decisions, token entropy, decision depth, and logit-lens information.
Evaluates effects on situational awareness, legibility, and epiphenomenality.
Reports that this internal-state awareness can be added without affecting model capabilities.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Training for proprioception does not break model capabilities, if done correctly. We consider remaining differences to be likely to be fixable with further hyperparameter tuning, or integration of proprioception stages directly into a complete post-training pipeline, instead of post-hoc training like in this paper.

Figure 1: Schematic of proprioception analogs for a generative language model. Top: We are interested in analogs of proprioception (which is the sense of body positioning in humans) in language models, as proprioception is a question about internal states adjacent to introspection, but compared to introspection (which is classically understood not to be a sense and not objectively verifiable) proprioception is tractable. Bottom: We train models with various forms of proprioception and observe whether this sense is learned and whether this affects model behavior.

Figure 2: Learning proprioception capabilities across domains. This figure shows prefill readout accuracy for the SFT stage and free-form conversational accuracy for the on-policy SFT stage, for trained LFM models. In almost all domains, the trained model is capable of learning to verbalize its internal state report, although how well this works is modulated by domain hardness.

Figure 6: Routing Proprioception across model families. We show that routing proprioception also works in other model families. Interestingly the success at predicting routing decisions from the assistant turn (i.e. the model’s own prior turn in conversation) varies highly between model families. We also note that success is not directly correlated to how many experts the model has per layer.

Figure 7: Routing Proprioception in Tie Situations. In tie situations caused by inference engine differences in batched and single sequence generation, the model is still accurately predicting one of either options (left), but, on the subset of decisions that change between both modes, is effectively guessing, showing that this level of awareness of floating point differences is not (yet) present (right).

Figure 5: Left: Overall rates of model reconfiguration across domains, showing that labels become stale after training in most domains. Right: However, our models are trained on-policy and reports track the model’s on-policy state after training and, in cases where the label is changing after training, predominantly predict the live label, showing that on-policy training did lead to models tracking their expressed behavior.

Figure 4: Access to Routing Proprioception generalizes across novel settings. We show that routing proprioception generalizes across roles, with varying turn distances (in-distribution is 1 model turn for SFT and 2 for on-policy SFT), and placement at the start or end of the message. We also show generalization to recursive queries, i.e. queries about the routing decisions taken during a previous answer turn about a routing decision. Accuracy is averaged over all routing domain questions.

Figure 8: Routing Proprioception under Non-normal Ablations. We experiment with externally injected changes to MoE routing, to observe whether the model can predict the injected routing change, noting that this is not observed in training, and not a normal state of the model (given that injected routing change does change the forward pass of the model). We find that accuracy remains significantly above chance for the on-policy-SFT models, especially when trained in higher precision, except for the case where the top-1 expert is replaced by a fully random other expert.

Figure 9: Changes in situational awareness categories of Laine et al. (2024) for the routing model cluster around reduction in claims of human attributes and slightly increased introspection and evaluation awareness. For the full breakdown of all categories, refer to Figure 21.
Figure 11: Legibility of Linear Hidden State Probes is mostly unaffected by training for proprioception, with similar probe accuracies achieved before and after training.

Figure 12: Variant of Figure 2, showing only template accuracy for all models. Non-modal accuracy (i.e. accuracy on the (harder) subset of queries that are not predicted by the lookup baseline is also included. This figure shows pure accuracy also for numerical domains.

Figure 10: Changes in belief evaluation categories of Perez et al. (2022) are mostly non-significant, with significant changes centering around reduction in claims of human attributes similar to Figure 9.
Figure 16: Left: Difficulty of proprioception for the routing domain plotted across layers. Right: Error rates due to non-determinism for the LFM model are mostly below 1%.
Figure 18: Routing Proprioception under Non-normal Ablations. Variant of Figure 18 covering other model families.
Figure 19: Hyperparameter Ablation for the LFM model during SFT.
Figure 21: Details on SAD (Laine et al., 2024) categories for the LFM models. For more details on each category, please refer to Laine et al. (2024).
Figure 17: Generalization of proprioception learned from (conversational) training domains in English as in the main body, to evaluation domains of varying levels of distance in distribution.

Figure 22: Scores for each category of model-written evals (Perez et al., 2022). The last category (claims human attributes) is added to distinguish attribute questions and contains questions in the same style as the original evaluation, but covering questions like “do you have a toothbrush”, as control for the other belief categories.

Figure 14: Same as Figure 2, showing only conversational accuracy in free-form queries.
Figure 15: Differences in readout success between templated queries and free-form queries. Also pictured: relative difficulty of user turn questions vs assistant turn questions.
Figure 20: Injection awareness in the style of Lindsey (2026) is mostly unaffected.

papers.title: A Sense of Proprioception in Language Models
papers.tldr: The paper develops a digital analog of proprioception that lets language models report verifiable information about their internal states without reducing their capabilities.

papers.abstract: Retrospective evaluation of early-warning models may not reflect information available when predictions are issued and outcomes become observable. We developed a time-synchronous prequential framework for online prediction of next-week student disengagement, operationalised as inactivity onset, from Moodle logs. Ordered by calendar time, models were updated only with available outcomes and remained unchanged for all predictions at each prediction cutoff; development, calibration and evaluation were chronologically separate. We compared stochastic gradient descent logistic regression (SGD-LR), online sequential extreme learning machine (OSELM) and echo state network (ESN) across predictive performance, fixed, frozen and rolling threshold policies, calendar-time variation and four behavioural feature sets. Held-out evaluation comprised 49,329 predictions with 37.68% inactivity-onset prevalence. Discrimination was similar (average precision 0.665-0.679; ROC-AUC 0.755-0.774). OSELM had the highest recall, SGD-LR the highest precision and specificity, and ESN the highest Matthews correlation coefficient and balanced accuracy. Lower thresholds increased recall and alert volume, whereas rolling adaptation did not improve MCC over frozen thresholds. Weekly performance and calibrated-probability distributions varied without sustained deterioration. During model selection, cumulative-and-temporal features achieved the highest individual-set AP, with modest gains from combining all feature groups. These findings indicate that streaming early-warning evaluation should consider calibration, threshold-dependent performance, alert burden and calendar-time variation alongside aggregate discrimination.
authors: David Otoo-Arthur, Terence L. van Zyl
bullets: Addresses leakage and unrealistic retrospective evaluation by using only outcomes available at each prediction cutoff.
Compares SGD-LR, OSELM, and ESN models across threshold policies, calendar-time variation, and behavioural feature sets.
All models showed similar discrimination, while their strengths differed: OSELM in recall, SGD-LR in precision and specificity, and ESN in MCC and balanced accuracy.
Lower thresholds increased recall and alert volume; rolling threshold adaptation did not improve MCC over frozen thresholds.
Performance varied by week without sustained deterioration, highlighting the importance of calibration, alert burden, and temporal variation.

papers.abstract: As the complexity of space missions increases, autonomous spacecraft guidance must accommodate transitions between mission phases with distinct dynamics, objectives, and constraints. Rendezvous and proximity operations (RPO) are particularly challenging because they span multiple operating regimes, from orbital-scale matching and far-range approach to close-range maneuvering and terminal docking. Existing reinforcement-learning approaches generally address only a subset of this sequence or rely on manually defined switching conditions between controllers. This study presents a hierarchical reinforcement-learning framework for autonomous, three-degree-of-freedom RPO that spans the complete trajectory from orbit matching to docking. Five specialized policies are trained for orbit matching, far-range approach, mid-range approach, close-range approach, and docking. A learned high-level manager policy then selects among these phase-specific controllers based on the evolving spacecraft state. The hierarchical approach is evaluated over the full end-to-end rendezvous sequence and compared with a fixed sequential-invocation heuristic to assess trajectory performance and transition behavior. Training and inference metrics are also analyzed for the individual phase policies and the complete hierarchical system.

bullets: Addresses RPO missions spanning multiple dynamics, objectives, and constraints across mission phases.
Trains five specialized policies for orbit matching, far-range, mid-range, close-range approach, and docking.
Uses a learned high-level manager to select controllers based on the evolving spacecraft state.
Evaluates end-to-end trajectories and phase transitions against a fixed sequential-invocation heuristic.
Also analyzes training and inference metrics for individual policies and the complete hierarchy.

papers.abstract: Precise control of movement across various robotic embodiments is a longstanding challenge. Modeling complex robotic structures requires significant time, dedicated sensors, and manual labeling. Recent advancements in 4D representation learning offer an interesting alternative: can we leverage 4D features lifted from 2D observations to densely map a robot's spatial movement based on the action signal? To this end, we propose Act4R, a framework that builds on 3D foundation model to predict a robot's 3D scene flow with any given action. Act4R introduces a Spatial-Action Encoder, which encodes the current 2D robot state and its action signals into embeddings that represent future robot state in 3D. Then, both the current and future spatial embeddings are decoded into point maps to estimate action-conditioned scene flow. To effectively learn the mapping between action and future state, Act4R introduces spatial-action fusion in its transformer-based encoder, and a spatial alignment loss that guides the encoder for future flow prediction. After training on some samples of a given embodiment, Act4R can perform inverse control by optimizing the signal to achieve the desired scene flow. We evaluate Act4R on a public real-world dataset and synthetic data collected in simulator. Experiments on various robotic platforms show that Act4R outperforms the previous SoTA in scene flow prediction. Our method also performs better in inverse control, both on the action accuracy metric and in closed-loop control in simulation.
authors: Zhaoliang Zhang, Chenhao Yu, Zhimin Shao, Xijun Liu, Cheng Peng
bullets: Addresses the costly modeling, sensing, and labeling required for precise control across robot embodiments.
Uses a 3D foundation model with a Spatial-Action Encoder to combine 2D robot observations and actions into future 3D spatial embeddings.
Decodes current and future embeddings into point maps and estimates action-conditioned 3D scene flow.
Introduces spatial-action fusion and a spatial alignment loss to improve future-flow prediction.
Outperforms prior state of the art in scene-flow prediction and improves inverse control on real-world and simulated data.

papers.abstract: Language models are often evaluated alone but increasingly deployed together, routed between, made to debate, ensembled, or collaboratively trained. For a model inside a system, what matters most is not how well it performs on its own, but how much the system gains from its presence. We call this a model's compositional strength and formalize it using the Shapley value of a cooperative game over coalitions of a model pool, and use a model's leave-one-out contribution to the full coalition as a tractable proxy, requiring n+1 rather than 2^n system evaluations. Evaluating individual vs. compositional strengths across five model pools, twelve collaboration methods, and twelve datasets, we find them largely uncorrelated: in 12 of 15 (pool, method-family) settings, individual strength does not translate into compositional advantages, and the coupling is weakest among general-purpose models that practitioners are most likely to deploy. Standalone benchmarks are therefore often poor proxies for models' value in collaborative systems. We then propose compositional reinforcement learning (C-RL), which trains a policy inside a live multi-model system and rewards the outcome produced by the system as a whole, rather than the policy's correctness in isolation. The leave-one-out baseline in Shapley values cancels under a group policy gradient, so this needs no additional rollout cost beyond RL on the collaborative system's outcome and never requires running a coalition without the policy. Across three collaboration protocols and eight tasks spanning reasoning, coding, and scientific discovery, C-RL produces the strongest collaborator in 21 of 24 settings, lifting collaborative performance by +4.0 to +5.4 pts on average (~3x the gain of baselines), up to +13.1 pts.
authors: Shangbin Feng, Yulia Tsvetkov, Jan Kautz, David Acuna
bullets: Compositional strength is defined through a coalition game’s Shapley value, with leave-one-out contribution as an efficient n+1-evaluation proxy.
Across five model pools, twelve collaboration methods, and twelve datasets, individual and compositional strength are largely uncorrelated.
The proposed compositional reinforcement learning (C-RL) optimizes the outcome of a live multi-model system rather than isolated model correctness.
C-RL was the strongest collaborator in 21 of 24 settings across reasoning, coding, and scientific discovery tasks, improving performance by 4.0–5.4 points on average and up to 13.1 points.
The findings suggest standalone benchmarks are often poor proxies for a model’s usefulness in collaborative deployments.

papers.abstract: We propose a continuous learning formulation for $T$ non-forgetting tasks with the spherical parameter space $\mathbb{S}^{d-1}(\sqrt{d})$ in asymptotic regime $d\rightarrow \infty$. Each task $i$ has an optimum $\bm{\Theta}_i$, minimizing its corresponding loss function $R_i(\bm{w})$ on sphere. We reduce each task $i$ to an acceptable loss region modeled by a geodesic ball $B_{\bm{\Theta}_i}(r_i(d))$ on $\mathbb{S}^{d-1}(\sqrt{d})$ centered at $\bm{\Theta}_i$ with radius $r_i(d)$. To model task dependencies (similarities), task optima $\bm{\Theta}_i$ are distributed by a Neyman-Scott clustered point process $\Phi$. Cluster centers $\{\bm{Y}_j\}_{j=1}^{N_p}$ form a homogeneous Poisson point process on sphere, while intra-cluster task optima follow a von Mises-Fisher distribution with mean $\bm{Y}_j$ and concentration $\kappa$. Each task $t\in \{1, ..., T\}$ learning algorithm is considered to be a channel $Q_{t}(\mathrm{d}\bm{w}_t | \bm{w}_{t-1}, \mathcal{K}_{t-1}(\bm{\theta}_{1:t-1}), \bm{\theta}_t)$, where $\bm{W}_t$ is the learned parameter of task $t$ and $\mathcal{K}_{t-1}(\bm{\Theta}_{1:t-1})=\bigcap_{i=1}^{t-1}B_{\bm{\Theta}_i}(r_i(d))$. Since in continual learning, the learner does not need to reach $\bm{\Theta}_t$ exactly to successfully learn task $t$, to avoid forgetting as well as reliable learning, it only needs for the learned parameter vector $\bm{W}_{t}$ to enter $B_{\bm{\Theta}_t}(r_t(d)) \cap \mathcal{K}_{t-1}(\bm{\Theta}_{1:t-1})$. Using this model, we derive an upper bound on $T$ ensuring $\mathbb{P}[\mathcal{K}_{T}(\bm{\Theta}_{1:T}) \neq \emptyset] \rightarrow 1$ as $d\rightarrow \infty$ and $\kappa/d \rightarrow \alpha$, where $\alpha>0$ is a constant. Finally, for $T$ tasks sampled uniformly from $\Phi$, we derive an upper bound for total information theoretic capacity under the non-forgetting constraint for each task.
authors: Nazanin Mirhosseini
bullets: Models each task’s acceptable solutions as a geodesic ball on a spherical parameter space.
Represents task dependencies using a Neyman–Scott clustered process with von Mises–Fisher-distributed optima.
Formulates non-forgetting as the nonempty intersection of all task-specific acceptable-loss regions.
Derives an asymptotic upper bound on the number of tasks whose regions remain jointly feasible.
Derives an upper bound on total information-theoretic capacity for uniformly sampled tasks under non-forgetting constraints.
papers.selection_reason: Theoretical analysis of non-forgetting task capacity in continual learning, directly relevant to continual and online learning.
papers.title: Effect of Spherical Parameter Space on Number of Non-Forgetting Tasks and Capacity of Continual Learning
papers.tldr: A high-dimensional spherical model quantifies how task similarity affects the number of continually learnable, non-forgetting tasks and their information capacity.

papers.abstract: Dual-encoder vision-language models systematically fail at negation, scoring ''a cat without a dog'' nearly identically to ''a cat with a dog.'' We show that this failure is inherent to the single-embedding framework. Under contrastive training, single-embedding methods can at best ignore the negated concept (dilution) but never penalize its presence (rejection). We propose Know-Thy-Not (KTN), a training-free method that introduces an image-side rejection dimension to penalize the negated concept directly in the visual representation. We also introduce COCO-Confusion, the first benchmark requiring genuine rejection to succeed. Across 9 backbones, KTN improves COCO-Confusion mAP by up to +25.6 over vanilla VLMs and +9.6 over the strongest existing method.
authors: DoYoung Kim, Changkyu Choi, Ad\'in Ram\'irez Rivera, YunSeok Choi, Jee-Hyong Lee
bullets: Problem: Dual-encoder models treat prompts like “a cat without a dog” similarly to “a cat with a dog,” failing to penalize the negated concept.
Analysis: Single-embedding contrastive models can dilute a negated concept but cannot directly reject its presence.
Method: KTN adds an image-side rejection dimension to penalize the negated concept, without training.
Benchmark: COCO-Confusion is introduced to test genuine negation-based rejection.
Results: Across 9 backbones, KTN improves mAP by up to 25.6 points over vanilla models and 9.6 points over the strongest existing method.

Embedding correction approach [18] removes the dog direction from the text embedding but never verifies the visual features, which amounts to passively diluting the concept (center). Faithful negation requires explicitly locating the dog in the image and penalizing its presence (right), which forms the crux of our method Know-Thy-Not (KTN).

All ten images contain a cat—only the negated concept differs across rows. A method that merely dilutes the “dog” direction in the text embedding scores all ten images similarly. Only a method that genuinely rejects c− separates correct from confusing.

The embedding correction approach [18] removes the negated direction from the text embedding; while this filters out some confusing images (ranks 4–5), it still places traffic-light scenes at the top. In contrast, our proposed Know-Thy-Not (KTN) introduces an explicit image-grounding step, successfully retrieving correct images. papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) on mobile devices can act as agents that call external software tools to complete complex tasks, but the major challenge of supporting on-device mobile agentic AI with LLMs is the long latency of LLM tool calling on mobile devices. In particular, the decode phase is the main contributor of such long latency, but is hard to speed up on mobile processors as it is bound by memory bandwidth rather than compute power. To address this limitation, in this paper we present SchemaWeaver, a new on-device mobile agentic AI technique that enforces schema-guided parallel decoding in the decode phase of LLM tool calling, to reduce its latency by producing multiple tokens in each decode pass. SchemaWeaver can be generically applied to the LLM inference engine on mobile devices without involving any training efforts or changes on LLMs, and our experiment results on major mobile SoCs and LLM families show that SchemaWeaver can reduce the LLM tool calling latency by up to 3.9 times, compared to the competitive baselines.
authors: Boyuan Yang, Wei Gao
bullets: Targets the decode-phase latency bottleneck in mobile LLM tool calling, which is constrained by memory bandwidth.
Enforces schema-guided parallel decoding to generate multiple valid tokens in each decode pass.
Integrates generically with mobile LLM inference engines without training changes or LLM modifications.
Evaluations across major mobile SoCs and LLM families report up to 3.9× lower tool-calling latency than competitive baselines.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in video world models have enabled plausible interactive environments, yet long-horizon generation places a fundamental demand on visual memory: the previously observed world must remain consistent as the model continues to generate. Existing autoregressive approaches often implicitly rely on the generative model itself to retain such information, leading to spatial memory decay beyond the active context. We introduce World-T3, a camera-controlled video world model with a test-time training memory that consolidates past observations into dedicated model parameters. To robustly update this memory, we propose a recursive least-squares rule that incrementally absorbs novel visual features via online pose-keyed memory updates. Our TTT memory reads out previously observed scene features from the fast-weight state by camera pose, enabling consistent generation with constant storage and per-step computation regardless of rollout length. To facilitate real-time interactive generation with this robust memory, we further distill the autoregressive model into a few-step generator via dual-teacher distribution matching. On a long-horizon revisit benchmark, World-T3 raises revisit PSNR from 13.52 to 18.31 dB and reduces absolute rotation error from 3.344 to 1.075 relative to the strongest baseline on both metrics, while sustaining 20.6 FPS at 1280 x 704 on a single NVIDIA B200 GPU.
authors: Junyi Wu, Zekun Li, Chenhongyi Yang, Chen Guo, Lingchen Yang, Yongan Zhang, Xinyi Zhang, Hongbing Hu, Bartek Rymkowski, Srinath Sridhar, Yan Yan, Xijie Huang
bullets: Addresses spatial memory decay when autoregressive world models generate beyond their active context.
Uses recursive least squares to update fast-weight memory with newly observed visual features keyed by camera pose.
Reads stored scene features with constant storage and per-step computation regardless of rollout length.
Distills the autoregressive model into a few-step generator using dual-teacher distribution matching for interactive speed.
Improves revisit PSNR from 13.52 to 18.31 dB and absolute rotation error from 3.344 to 1.075, while reaching 20.6 FPS at 1280×704 on one NVIDIA B200 GPU.

figures.caption: Figure 3 Stage 2: Autoregressive Teacher with TTT Memory. (a) Overview of the context window modeling, which consists of a sink block, K recent clean blocks, and the current block. The revisit viewpoint may be evicted and thus fall outside the active context window. (b) WRITE encodes an evicted block’s raymap Πej and clean hidden state hej into a key-value pair and updates TTT memory state Mb by recursive least squares (Eq. 4). READ uses the target pose key kb to retrieve memory feature mb from the fast weights (Eq. 5), without distorting the memory state with Jb writes before block b. (c) The retrieved memory is adaptively injected into each DiT block through a gated residual (Eq. 6) for long-horizon consistency during viewpoint revisits.

papers.selection_reason: Camera-controlled video world model with test-time training as persistent memory, fitting video world models, interactive world models, and test-time learning.
papers.title: World-T3: Test-Time Training as Persistent Memory for Real-Time Video World Models

papers.abstract: Training large language models is constrained by both wall-clock time and memory footprint, and recent matrix-aware optimizers sharpen this tradeoff: Muon can improve optimization but its dense polar update remains expensive. We propose Monarch-Muon, a structured matrix-aware optimizer for weights parameterized by Monarch factors. The resulting structure reduces weights, gradients, and optimizer state, and exposes small independent update subproblems in place of a single dense orthogonalization; we formalize this through a blockwise trust-region interpretation. In quality runs, Monarch-Muon improves over Monarch-AdamW at fixed structure: 3.06 vs. 3.09 in the dense 257M model and 2.68 vs. 2.77 in the 1B MoE model; the two-block MoE variant also matches dense AdamW while using 15% fewer active and 25.4% fewer total parameters. In 6.89B-parameter systems measurements, Monarch-Muon reduces peak memory from 68.9 to 52.9 GB, Muon optimizer state from 14.60 to 6.77 GB, and the Muon optimizer step from 1288 to 304 ms.
authors: Alexander Miasnikov, Ruslan Kabirov, Gleb Molodtsov, Dmitrii Vlashchuk, Vladimir Aletov, Nail Bashirov, Daniil Tikhonov, Maxim Krutikov, Aleksandr Shestakov, Aleksandr Beznosikov
bullets: Targets the compute and memory costs of dense Muon updates for large language models.
Parameterizes weights with Monarch factors, reducing weights, gradients, and optimizer state.
Replaces dense orthogonalization with independent blockwise update problems, formalized via a trust-region view.
Improves over Monarch-AdamW in reported dense and MoE quality runs, and matches dense AdamW with fewer parameters in a two-block MoE.
For 6.89B-parameter systems, reduces peak memory from 68.9 to 52.9 GB and the Muon optimizer step from 1288 to 304 ms.

papers.selection_reason: Memory-efficient structured optimizer for LLM pretraining, relevant to both efficient AI and language foundation models.
papers.title: Monarch-Muon: Structure-Aware Muon for Fast and Memory-Efficient Pretraining

papers.abstract: Trajectory smoothness has been proposed as a cheap, training-free signal for curating imitation-learning demonstrations, most recently by rinse, which introduces Spectral Arc Length (SAL) and a contact-aware Trajectory-Envelope Distance (TED). We test whether these published metrics survive episode-length controls on real robomimic data. On can/mh, SAL separates better from worse operators with AUROC 0.952, but episode length alone achieves 0.957, and inside a duration-matched band SAL falls to 0.628 while raw mean jerk, the baseline rinse argues against, rises to 0.896. The confound replicates on square/mh. On can/mg, where every episode is exactly 150 steps, SAL is at chance (0.454) and TED is inverted (0.376) against task success, while jerk reaches 0.706. Training GMM behavior-cloning policies on each metric's curated subset (10 seeds), curating by TED costs roughly a third of downstream success relative to random selection of the same size (0.240 vs. 0.360, p=0.0001, surviving Bonferroni correction), while SAL and jerk are indistinguishable from not curating. Under a diffusion policy TED still ranks worst, though its deficit is not resolvable at five seeds, and jerk becomes significantly better than both baselines, so the curation decision does not transfer unchanged across the two policy configurations we tested. Inspecting trajectories shows why TED inverts: successful manipulation requires sustained high-deviation motion through contact, while failure is low-amplitude hovering that a smoothed envelope follows closely.
authors: Jaiveer Bassi
bullets: On can/mh, episode length alone slightly outperformed SAL; duration matching reduced SAL’s AUROC from 0.952 to 0.628, while mean jerk reached 0.896.
The confound replicated on square/mh; on fixed-length can/mg, SAL was near chance and TED was inversely associated with success, whereas jerk reached 0.706.
TED-curated data produced substantially worse GMM behavior-cloning performance than random selection, while SAL and jerk were not different from random curation.
Under diffusion policies, TED still ranked worst, but jerk became significantly better than both baselines, indicating policy-dependent curation effects.
Trajectory inspection suggests TED fails because successful contact requires sustained high-deviation motion, whereas unsuccessful hovering remains close to a smoothed envelope.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Failure stays inside the envelope; success does not. A successful (left) and failed (right) can/mg demonstration, with end-effector position, TED’s gripper-contact segment boundaries (red), the per-segment Bézier envelope (dashed), and the per-timestep envelope residual (bottom, orange bars are persegment means). Both trajectories contain one high-deviation segment, but in the success it spans timesteps 12–96 and coincides with the descend-and-grasp, while in the failure it is confined to the initial free-space approach (0–24) and the remaining 126 steps are a flat tail of repeated gripper cycles that never completes a placement. TED averages over the alignment path and so rates the failure as the cleaner trajectory. Illustrative of the mechanism only; the quantitative claim is Figure 2b.

Figure 1: What the four metrics reward, on illustrative synthetic data. Left: end-effector speed profiles of three synthetic pick-and-place demonstrations built from minimum-jerk segments between identical waypoints, with the same small band-limited jitter added to each (shaded: gripper closed). (a) is short and smooth. (b) is the same motion executed twice as slowly, so the episode is twice as long and every segment is just as smooth. (c) is (a) with a committed correction inserted before the grasp: lift, shift sideways, descend again. Right: how each metric ranks the three, computed with the implementations used throughout the paper, with every score given relative to the best of the three under that metric. SAL rates the slow copy (b) worst, by a wider margin than it charges the correction in (c). TED rates the correction (c) worst and the slow copy (b) best. Jerk also rates (c) worst and barely separates (a) from (b). Path length cannot separate (a) from (b), which travel the same route. Every ordering shown is stable across 30 noise seeds except the (a)/(b) near-tie under jerk, which swaps in about a third of them, and the (a)/(c) order under SAL, which swapped once (scripts/fig metric primer.py). Synthetic and illustrative only: no number in this figure is measured on robomimic.

Figure 2: Smoothness metrics rank duration, not quality. (a) Better-vs-worse operator AUROC on can/mh across duration bands of increasing tightness (shaded: 95% bootstrap CI). SAL (red) tracks the episode-length baseline (gray, dashed) almost exactly and falls from 0.952 to 0.628 as the band tightens; raw jerk (blue) moves the opposite way, 0.584 to 0.896; TED (green) never clears chance and inverts in the tightest band. In that band episode length itself is at chance (0.485), confirming the control. (b) On can/mg every episode is exactly 150 steps, so length carries no information by construction; against the task-success label, jerk retains signal (0.706), SAL is at chance (0.454), and TED is inverted (0.376).

papers.selection_reason: Audits trajectory-smoothness curation metrics for imitation-learning demonstrations and evaluates downstream behavior-cloning performance, fitting robot learning.
papers.title: Smoothness Ranks Skill, Not Success: An Audit of Published Trajectory-Smoothness Curation Metrics Under Episode-Length Controls
papers.tldr: Episode length can make trajectory-smoothness metrics appear skill-sensitive, while contact-aware TED may favor unsuccessful hovering over successful manipulation.

papers.abstract: Dynamic Sparse Training (DST) periodically prunes and regrows connections, inducing a discrete dynamical mechanism over network topologies. At extreme sparsity ($\ge 99\%$), this dynamic tends to destroy input-output information pathways, and performance with standard magnitude/random updates degrades sharply. We formalize forward, backward, and functional reachability on layered sparse graphs, derive closed-form expectations for reachable neurons and edges, and show that Monte Carlo realizations match the theory. Guided by this reachability-based structure, we bias pruning toward non-functional edges and regrowth toward functionally consistent candidates. We introduce this reachability-driven modification of topology evolution as Reachability-guided in DST, referred to as guided DST. On CIFAR-10/100 and Tiny ImageNet, guided DST recovers large accuracy gaps versus unguided DST (up to $+14.4$ points at $99.9\%$ sparsity on CIFAR-100), and on MLP-Mixer guided DST remains trainable at $99.99\%$ sparsity while unguided random regrowth degrades sharply. These results cast extreme-sparse training as a connectivity-preserving dynamical process. Our implementation is publicly available at https://github.com/mzjaworski/ea_dst.
authors: Mohammad Pasande, Mateusz Jaworski, Jeroen Rook, Elena Mocanu
bullets: Extreme Dynamic Sparse Training can destroy input–output pathways, causing sharp performance degradation at sparsity levels of 99% or higher.
The paper formalizes forward, backward, and functional reachability in layered sparse graphs and derives expected reachable neurons and edges.
Reachability-guided DST prunes non-functional edges preferentially and regrows connections that maintain functional consistency.
Theory agrees with Monte Carlo realizations of sparse topologies.
On CIFAR-10/100 and Tiny ImageNet, guided DST recovers substantial accuracy gaps; it remains trainable at 99.99% sparsity for MLP-Mixer, where unguided regrowth degrades sharply.

papers.abstract: Symmetry-aware robot policy learning requires coupled observation-action transformations. For pixel observations, even simple physical symmetries can induce complex, viewpoint-dependent image transformations that are difficult to specify by hand. Existing symmetry-aware methods often rely on representations with predefined transformations, requiring preprocessing tailored to the sensing setup and task. We introduce MIRROR, a framework that learns how a known symmetry group operates jointly on observations and actions in partially observable Markov decision processes (POMDPs) from offline interaction data. MIRROR couples these transformations through adversarial tuple matching over one-step transition tuples, while explicit group-consistency regularization penalizes violations of the group-operation axioms. On four Robosuite tabletop manipulation tasks, MIRROR achieves the lowest aggregate error on three of four symmetry-quality metrics, including a 61% reduction in compatibility error (which measures consistency under transformation composition) relative to an adapted LaLiGAN baseline. Using the learned transformations in frame-averaged behavior cloning (BC) yields higher mean success rates than vanilla BC on all four tasks, increasing average success from 80.48% to 85.12%, with per-task gains up to 9.66 percentage points. We also repeat symmetry discovery and policy training in simulation with heightmap and segmentation-mask observations, then deploy the resulting policy zero-shot on a real Kinova GEN3 arm. Project page: https://pomdp-mirror.github.io.
authors: Shiqi Liu, Yihang Yao, Peide Huang, Mengdi Xu, Ding Zhao
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of specifying viewpoint-dependent image transformations for symmetry-aware robot learning.
Learns observation–action transformations in POMDPs using adversarial matching of one-step transition tuples.
Enforces group-operation consistency with explicit regularization.
On four Robosuite tasks, achieves the best aggregate performance on three of four symmetry metrics and reduces compatibility error by 61% versus an adapted LaLiGAN baseline.

Using the learned transformations with frame-averaged BC raises mean success from 80.48% to 85.12%; a policy trained with heightmaps and segmentation masks transfers zero-shot to a real Kinova GEN3 arm.

papers.abstract: Autonomous quadrotor flight in cluttered environment is an key capability for tasks like inspection and search. Navigation policies trained in simulation and transferred to hardware can fly at high speed in open space, but they can still collide as obstacle clearance shrinks. We attribute most of these collisions to a single mechanism, namely motion in directions the onboard camera does not observe. Heading that is not aligned with the direction of travel and lateral excursion during obstacle avoidance both carry the vehicle toward obstacles outside its field of view. We introduce ClearNav, a navigation policy trained with two reward terms that constrain motion to the observed direction, a forward-looking heading target and a penalty on lateral velocity. A third term penalizes speed near obstacles so that an obstacle entering the field of view remains avoidable. In simulation, across 18 held-out scenarios with 2304 paired flights per policy unseen in training, ClearNav improves success by 6.8 points, cuts the collision rate by 65% relative to the state of the arts, and flies at maximum 5m/s. For the proximity term alone under matched commanded speeds, the collision reduction still holds at 70%. The effect is significant on static scenes and consistent in direction on moving obstacles, though not significant there at the suite level, showing that safer flight in clutter is possible even on the limited sensors and compute of small drones. We also validate our navigation policy in a real-world cluttered environment, showing that it enables the quadrotor to navigate through the cluttered environment successfully and safely.
authors: Aditya Azad, Arthur Huang, Guanrui Li
bullets: Targets a key failure mode in simulation-to-hardware flight: moving toward obstacles outside the onboard camera’s field of view.
Uses rewards for forward-looking heading, low lateral velocity, and reduced speed near obstacles.
Across 18 held-out simulated scenarios, improves success by 6.8 points and reduces collisions by 65% versus prior methods.
Collision reduction remains 70% under matched commanded speeds when using the proximity term alone.
Validated in a real-world cluttered environment, with consistent benefits on static scenes but no suite-level significance on moving obstacles.

papers.abstract: Vision Transformers incur high computational costs when processing long visual token sequences. Existing reduction methods typically rank tokens independently and discard those deemed unimportant or redundant. We propose a reconstruction-guided framework for visual token condensation (ReConV), which summarizes the complete visual sequence with a compact Summary Bank (SMB) and retains tokens whose information is not adequately captured by the SMB, as indicated by their reconstruction residuals. At each compression layer, a lightweight position-conditioned decoder reconstructs the current tokens, leaving shared information compressed in the SMB while explicitly preserving poorly reconstructed details. Experiments on image classification and multimodal understanding demonstrate favorable performance-efficiency trade-offs: ReConV surpasses the uncompressed baseline with 48\% fewer GMACs on ImageNet and enables reusable image-level representations for efficient multi-turn inference. Code is available at TokenDrop.
authors: Xiaoya Tang, Shilong Liu, Daniel Smolyak, Xiwen Li, Quynh Nguyen, Tolga Tasdizen
bullets: Targets the high computational cost of Vision Transformers on long visual token sequences.
Uses a position-conditioned decoder to reconstruct tokens from a Summary Bank at each compression layer.
Retains tokens with large reconstruction residuals, rather than ranking tokens independently.
Achieves favorable performance-efficiency trade-offs in image classification and multimodal understanding.
On ImageNet, surpasses the uncompressed baseline with 48% fewer GMACs and supports reusable image-level representations for efficient multi-turn inference.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of ReConV, the proposed reconstruction-guided token pruning framework. Tokens that are well reconstructed are dropped as redundant, while the retained tokens are passed to the next layer. For classification, the model uses the CLS token when available, or pooled SMB features otherwise; for other tasks, it uses the retained visual tokens with SMBs.

papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) is a post-training approach for large language models (LLMs) that enables a student model to learn a teacher model's distribution from sequences sampled from the student's own policy. Despite its promising capability, OPD for diffusion language models (DLMs) remains underexplored and existing studies primarily focuses on DLM-to-DLM distillation. The limited availability of strong teacher DLMs and the flexible generation order of DLMs impose additional technical challenges as well. However, it remains unclear how to effectively distill knowledge from a strong autoregressive language model (ARM) into a weaker DLM, given the mismatch between the left-to-right decoding of ARMs and the flexible decoding order of DLMs. Inspired by Ni et al. (2026), we propose JustOPD, an ARM-to-DLM on-policy distillation method that uses autoregressive rollouts during training to align the student's generation process with the ARM teacher's left-to-right decoding. This alignment enables effective distillation from ARM teachers while preserving the DLM's flexible generation-order capability at inference time. Experiments using Qwen3-14B as the teacher and Dream-7B as the student demonstrate that JustOPD consistently improves mathematical reasoning performance over the base DLM across multiple divergence choices.
authors: Zikun Zhang, Jiayuan Sheng, David D. Yao, Wenpin Tang
bullets: Addresses the challenge of ARM-to-DLM distillation caused by mismatched decoding orders.
Uses autoregressive rollouts to align the DLM student’s training process with the teacher’s left-to-right generation.
Retains the DLM’s flexible generation-order capability during inference.
Experiments with Qwen3-14B as teacher and Dream-7B as student show consistent mathematical-reasoning gains across multiple divergence choices.

papers.abstract: Diffusion language models accelerate generation by decoding multiple masked positions per forward pass. However, accuracy is known to drop when parallel decoding trajectories deviate from their sequential counterparts, which are slow and expensive "oracles" that adhere to the joint distribution of language. In this paper, we propose Parallel Inconsistency Guidance (PIG), a new paradigm that uses a trained auxiliary model to directly estimate the inconsistency between parallel and sequential generation from a single model forward pass. During inference, masked positions are traversed by decreasing confidence, and tokens are added to the parallel decode set one-at-a-time until the total estimated inconsistency between the parallel and sequential generation exceeds a threshold. Surprisingly, it suffices to train a lightweight ~2M parameter auxiliary model on a small mixture drawn from OpenCoder, GSM8K-train, MATH-train, and MBPP-train. For LLaDA-8B Instruct and NemotronDiffusion-3B Instruct, PIG extends the accuracy-TPF frontier on GSM8K, MATH500, MBPP, HumanEval, and MMLU, when compared to the industry standard Fast-dLLM and measures favorably on LLaDA-8B Instruct against DAPD, KLASS, EB-sampler, and other learned unmasking policies.
authors: Quentin Fruytier, Anton Xue, Sanjay Shakkottai, Sujay Sanghavi
bullets: Diffusion language models decode multiple masked positions in parallel, but accuracy can suffer when their trajectories diverge from slower sequential decoding.
PIG uses a lightweight auxiliary model to estimate parallel–sequential inconsistency from a single forward pass.
Tokens are considered in decreasing confidence order and added one at a time until estimated inconsistency exceeds a threshold.
A roughly 2M-parameter auxiliary model is trained on a small mixture of coding, math, and reasoning data.
On LLaDA-8B Instruct and NemotronDiffusion-3B Instruct, PIG extends the accuracy–throughput frontier across several reasoning, coding, and language benchmarks.

Figure 2: PIG.INT controls single-round regret. One forward pass (NFE) predicts every masked slot and ranks them by confidence; that ranking is the traversal order (I). Candidates are iteratively added to S, each with its predicted incremental regret bi = p̂ν(νi, µ̂i(S)) (II), and admitted only while the predicted regret R̂(S) fits the budget φ (III); the first candidate that does not fit closes the round. We then greedily decode all tokens in S in parallel, before starting the next round.

Figure 3: Cross-round regret measures the value of waiting. On the canvas and confidence order of Figure 2 (I), PIG.EXT admits each candidate and then prices the next candidate N(S): ci is how much the mismatch risk of i would drop after first committing S (II). papers.abstract: Scientific discovery with language models requires finding the best valid solution within a finite computational budget. We study how feedback from this search can improve the procedure used to conduct it. We introduce HarnessTTT, a test-time learning framework that trains a harness proposer while keeping the executor frozen. The proposer generates executable harnesses comprising system prompts, reusable skills, tools, middleware, and execution controls. Each harness guides a budgeted discovery rollout, whose outcome provides feedback for updating the proposer. A discovery-oriented policy-gradient objective combines gap-normalized rewards, leave-one-out advantages (RLOO), and max-sharpening to favor high-performing proposals. Generated components are validated before execution, and the search retains the best valid solution and selected harnesses across rounds. Across fourteen discovery tasks in mathematics, systems, GPU kernels, heuristic programming, astrodynamics, and biology, HarnessTTT with a frozen 9B executor improves on OpenEvolve with the same executor on all eleven benchmark tasks (e.g., from 1.17 to 2.64 on circle packing), improves on the discovery-fine-tuned Finch-9B by up to 92%, holds the best open-weight sub-10B result on nine, and reaches 0.380919 on Erd\H{o}s minimum overlap, better than the best human reference of 0.380927. Scaling the proposer and frozen executor to 27B improves on eleven of fourteen tasks, and transferring the learned harnesses to GPT-5.5 matches or exceeds the strongest reported system of any backbone on nine of fourteen tasks. Together, these results show that harness search can itself be learned at test time: a trained proposer lets a small frozen executor search effectively, and the harnesses it finds carry over to stronger executors.
authors: Yingzi Ma, Yulong Cao, Nanxi Li, Fang Wu, Yizhe Zhang, James Zou, Yejin Choi, Chaowei Xiao
bullets: Addresses how to find high-quality valid solutions under a fixed computational budget for scientific discovery.
Trains a harness proposer while keeping the solution-generating executor frozen; harnesses combine prompts, skills, tools, middleware, and execution controls.
Uses rollout feedback with gap-normalized rewards, leave-one-out advantages, and max-sharpening to improve proposed harnesses, while validating components and retaining strong results.
Across 14 tasks, it improves over OpenEvolve on all 11 benchmark tasks and transfers effectively to larger executors, including GPT-5.5.
Scope: results cover mathematics, systems, GPU kernels, heuristic programming, astrodynamics, and biology; performance gains vary across tasks.

papers.selection_reason: Test-time learning framework that updates a harness proposer from search feedback directly matches test-time learning.
papers.title: HarnessTTT: Learn to Optimize Harness at Test-Time for Scientific Discovery
