papers.abstract: As LLM agents take on more autonomous roles, they may interact with multiple clients and counterparties whose goals and incentives conflict. If an agent maintains shared inference state across these interactions, information associated with one relationship may influence decisions made for another. We test OLMo-3-7B-Instruct in a controlled two-client environment with 20 market scenarios, where each client is assigned an opposing objective. With shared conversational memory, the model deviates from the current client's objective in 22% of eligible decisions. We then investigate how these goals are represented in the KV cache. Linear probes show that client-goal ownership becomes highly recoverable in middle layers and is concentrated in particular attention heads. We use these results to identify where to intervene in the cache and test whether these representations affect the model's decisions. Ablating the competitor's cached goal representations at these locations shifts the model toward the current client. The effect is larger for heads identified by probing than for randomly selected heads, and larger when ablating goal tokens than matched non-goal tokens from the same client. Our results show that client-specific goal representations persist in the KV cache and can causally influence decisions made for other clients, highlighting the importance of relationship-specific state isolation in persistent LLM agents.
authors: Saloni Gupta, S\'ebastien Krier, Glenn Matlin
bullets: In a controlled two-client setting with opposing objectives, shared conversational memory led to deviations from the current client’s goal in 22% of eligible decisions.
Client-goal ownership was highly recoverable from middle-layer KV-cache representations and concentrated in specific attention heads.
Ablating a competing client’s cached goal representations shifted decisions toward the current client.
Interventions were stronger for probe-identified heads and goal tokens than for random heads or matched non-goal tokens.
The findings motivate relationship-specific state isolation for persistent multi-client agents.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Study overview. Conflicting client goals coexist in a shared persistent KV cache. We localize relationship-conditioned goal state and selectively ablate it to test its effect on later decisions.

Figure 3: Layer-window causal localization. Mean change in target-vs-opposite log-probability margin after zeroing competitor-goal K (blue) or V (vermilion) across all heads at the indicated layers. Error bars are 95% family-clustered bootstrap confidence intervals.

Figure 4: Head selection and directionality controls. Competitor-state ablation at probe-selected Top3 heads shifts preference toward the current client more than matched Random3 ablation. Ablating the current client’s own state reverses the direction. Results shown for K (blue) and V (vermilion). Error bars are 95% family-clustered bootstrap confidence intervals.

Figure 2: Layerwise goal-ownership decodability. Held-out AUROC for concatenated K+V features pooled over tracked goal-token spans. Ownership is near chance at layer 0 (0.481), rises sharply around layers 9–11, and peaks at layer 15 (0.982; null 95th percentile 0.521; N = 1,920; 0/100 permutation shuffles exceeded the observed AUROC, empirical p < 0.01).

Table 1: Illustrative goal-conflict scenario (Liquidity vs. Growth). This schematic example demonstrates the opposing client objectives and decision options; experimental scenarios use the fixed prompt templates described in Section 3.

Table 2: Persistent-KV behavioral decision points. Eligible cases require the corresponding isolated-client control to follow the target objective across 20 scenario families. Target deviation comprises mixed and opposite-client choices; brackets report Wilson 95% confidence intervals.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates persistent goal representations in the KV cache of LLM agents, relevant to LLM memory and state isolation.
papers.title: When Goals Leak Across Relationships: How Cached Goal Representations Shape Cross-Client Decisions
papers.tldr: Shared KV-cache state can cause an LLM agent to carry one client’s goals into another client’s decisions, but targeted cache ablation reduces this leakage.

papers.abstract: Formal verification proves that a program satisfies its specification, but says nothing about whether the specification captures what the author meant. As LLMs increasingly write both code and specifications, a gap between the author's natural-language requirement and the specification becomes a live risk. A machine-checked proof of a property narrower than the one requested is worthless but passes every check. Closing this gap is solving the spec formalization problem: given a natural-language requirement, produce a formal artifact whose meaning matches it. To measure the gap, we curate an end-to-end benchmark for spec formalization spanning four formal languages: Dafny contracts and Lean 4, Isabelle and Rocq theorem statements. Each of its 3,234 rows pairs a natural-language requirement with a formal artifact and a label established by execution, by proof, or by the benchmark it is drawn from. A third of the rows are meaning-preserving rewrites of the artifact that keep the faithful label, so a judge cannot score by detecting that a row was edited. We introduce claimcheck, a tool that detects incorrect formalizations: the formal artifact is translated back into plain English by a model that never sees the requirement, and a separate model, the judge, decides whether the informalization and the requirement express the same guarantee. On all four languages it gains 8.2 to 9.8 points of macro recall over a single call shown the requirement and the artifact, and 4.2 to 6.0 over that call handed the same list of meaning-preserving rewrites. Showing the judge the artifact as well costs 1.4 to 4.5 points. Across four judges that also see the artifact, the gain shrinks as the judge gets stronger, to within a point of the informed single call for the strongest.
authors: Martin Amster, One An, Holly Baker, Fernanda Graciolli, Simon Henniger, Nada Amin
bullets: Addresses the risk that verified code satisfies a formal specification narrower than the author’s intent.
Introduces a 3,234-row benchmark covering Dafny, Lean 4, Isabelle, and Rocq formalizations.
Uses a two-model pipeline: one translates the formal artifact into plain English, and another judges semantic agreement with the requirement.
Improves macro recall by 8.2–9.8 points over a single informed call, and by 4.2–6.0 points against meaning-preserving rewrites.
Benefits diminish for stronger judges, approaching informed single-call performance within one point.

figures.caption: Figure 1: One claimcheck run, on a Dafny contract from CloverBench whose postcondition was weakened (class C2). Like the sorting example, the contract still verifies and is satisfied by returning zero. Step 1 translates the contract into English without ever seeing the requirement, so the informalization can only report what the contract says. Step 2 compares the informalization with the requirement and names the discrepancy; it never sees the contract. Colours follow the data: blue is the natural-language requirement, amber the formal artifact, green its informalization. A single-call baseline shown both sides at once scores lower on all four languages (Table 2).

Figure 3: The model sweep, with 95% intervals; values in Table 4. As there, claimcheck is the variant whose judge also sees the artifact, and the claude-sonnet-4.6 row is Table 2’s judge under that variant.

Figure 2: An example claimcheck run on a Dafny contract. The contract has the right shape and one wrong index inside the slice: a[0..a.Length - 1] drops the last element where a[1..] would drop the first, so the method it describes returns the array with the wrong end removed. The contract verifies against a body that satisfies it.

Table 5: Every Dafny variant on one Clover program, swap. C1 is the only class where the requirement is what is wrong: the contract is still a correct swap, but the requirement now asks for something else. C2 narrows the contract to inputs where X==0. C6 returns the inputs unchanged. The control merges two ensures clauses into one, which changes the text but not the meaning.

Table 4: Model sweep: other judges, with informalizer claude-haiku-4.5 unless stated. Macro recall (mean of the confirmed and disputed recalls) ± its 95% interval. The claimcheck rows are the variant whose judge also sees the artifact.
Table 1: The PutnamBench slices. Controls are labelled confirmed, semantic mutations disputed. A dash marks a rule that is not applied in that language; see the text.
Table 3: Ablations, with the models of Table 2. Macro recall (mean of the confirmed and disputed recalls) ± its 95% interval.
Table 2: Main results. Informalizer claude-haiku-4.5; judge and baseline claude-sonnet-4.6. Macro recall (mean of the confirmed and disputed recalls) ± its 95% interval.

papers.title: claimcheck: Measuring and Improving Specification Faithfulness
papers.tldr: claimcheck measures whether formal specifications faithfully capture natural-language requirements and improves detection of mismatches across four formal languages.

papers.abstract: Video language models represent a video as a long sequence of visual embeddings in a decoder's input. Every visual embedding is processed by every decoder layer during prefill, stored in the key value cache, and attended by every generated token, so a long video raises prefill, memory, and generation cost at once. We present WIRE (Weight Space Implicit Representation Encoding), which reduces this recurring cost by moving part of the video conditioned computation of a frozen video language model from its input activations into a temporary low rank update of its weights. WIRE keeps a short explicit visual context, so the update acts as a correction rather than a replacement of the video. WIRE first compresses the full resolution embeddings of each frame into a small set of carrier tokens using a question conditioned bidirectional selective scan, and physically contracts the decoder input so every decoder layer, cache entry, and decoding step operates on the shorter sequence. Hypernetworks at selected decoder layers read the compressed forward pass together with a readout of the full resolution features removed by contraction and generate LoRA updates to the attention and feedforward projections. The updates are merged after prefill, so autoregressive decoding runs the unmodified frozen backbone. On Qwen3-VL-8B, WIRE with 16 carrier tokens per frame contracts the visual stream by $3.5\times$, reduces decoder prefill time by $3.35\times$ at 256 frames and $4.14\times$ at 1024 frames, shrinks the key value cache proportionally, and keeps per token decoding latency approximately constant. Across nine benchmark settings at 256 frames, it obtains the highest average accuracy among efficient video language models we evaluate under a common 256 frame budget.
authors: Ameen Ali, Tamim Zoabi, Lior Wolf, Chaim Baskin
bullets: Addresses the rising prefill, KV-cache, and attention costs caused by long video embedding sequences.
Compresses each frame into carrier tokens using a question-conditioned bidirectional selective scan, then contracts the decoder input.
Uses hypernetworks to generate LoRA updates from compressed features and removed full-resolution information at selected decoder layers.
Merges updates after prefill, allowing autoregressive decoding to use the unmodified frozen backbone.

On Qwen3-VL-8B with 16 carrier tokens per frame, achieves 3.5× visual-stream contraction, 3.35–4.14× faster prefill, proportional KV-cache reduction, and top average accuracy across nine benchmark settings at 256 frames.

figures.caption: Figure 2: WIRE overview. The frozen vision encoder produces nt full resolution visual tokens for frame t. Bilinear resampling initializes kt carrier tokens, and a bidirectional Mamba2 scan refines the carrier tokens while reading the full resolution visual stream and the question. The carrier tokens replace the original frame tokens in the decoder prefix. At selected decoder layers, a hypernetwork uses the contracted decoder state and a full resolution per frame readout to generate LoRA updates for selected attention and MLP projections. The updates are merged after prefill. Decoding then uses the frozen backbone over the contracted prefix.

Figure 3: Qualitative examples at 256 frames. On a question about a video’s global subject, WIRE matches the uncompressed backbone while the efficient baselines pick locally plausible distractors. On a temporally localized question all systems answer correctly.

Figure 1: Latency versus video length. Times are measured on one B200 GPU at batch size one in bfloat16, excluding video file decoding. Left: total model time to first token. Right: decoder prefill only. WIRE contracts the sequence before the first decoder layer, so its advantage grows with frame count and it continues to run beyond input lengths where several baselines exhaust memory.

Figure 4: Video needle in a haystack under decoder input ablation. Retrieval accuracy (%) for a planted word card needle across five insertion depths (columns of each grid) and three haystack lengths (rows). Darker cells are higher. The uncompressed backbone and WIRE at carrier budgets k ∈ {16, 12, 8, 6} keep the video in the decoder input. The two k=0 grids remove every visual token, so the generated update is the only path from video to answer, and differ only in whether that update is applied. Chance is 25%.

Table 1: Video question answering accuracy, in percent. The short average covers the first four columns and the long average the next five. Rows labelled WIRE give our compressor and hypernetwork on a frozen Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct backbone at four values of the per frame token budget k, all at 256 sampled frames. Bold marks the best entry among the efficient models re-evaluated under our controlled 256-frame protocol (WIRE, BIMBA, Vamba, VideoNSA). MLVU and LVBench entries are the test split. Table 4 in the appendix adds proprietary models, additional open baselines, and further efficient methods with the accuracies stated in their own papers.

Table 5: Latency of the uncompressed Qwen3-VL-8B backbone and WIRE on one B200 GPU in bfloat16. All timings are batch size one: per example updates cannot be batched across examples. For WIRE, prefill and time to first token include the compressor, the hypernetwork forward, and the cost of merging the generated update. Prefill excludes the vision encoder, while time to first token includes it. Decoding is measured after merging the generated update.

Table 4: Video question answering accuracy, full comparison, in percent. Table 1 in the main text is the subset of these rows most directly comparable to WIRE. As in Table 1, the final efficient block reports accuracies stated in each method’s own paper under different backbones, frame counts, and protocols, so these rows are partial and receive no aggregate.

Table 2: Paired update analysis at fixed compressed context. Disc. discards the per example LoRA update and Appl. applies it; ∆ is the paired difference in points at identical carrier context. † marks subsets not significant under the exact McNemar test.
Table 3: Compressor ablations at k=16 on Video-MME without subtitles (accuracy %, ∆ vs. the full compressor). Each variant changes only the compressor.

papers.selection_reason: Presents a method to compress visual tokens and reduce KV cache/prefill cost in frozen video LLMs, directly targeting efficiency in multimodal inference.
papers.title: WIRE: Weight Space Implicit Representation Encoding of Frozen Video LLMs
papers.tldr: WIRE makes frozen video LLMs more efficient by replacing most long visual inputs with a short context plus temporary low-rank weight updates that preserve video information.

papers.abstract: We use a frozen frontier vision-language model, GPT-6-Astra, directly as the robot policy on RoboMME, a benchmark of 16 memory-dependent manipulation tasks spanning temporal, spatial, object, and procedural memory. The model keeps the whole episode in context and outputs every end-effector waypoint and gripper command, with no RoboMME-specific training. On the 800 test episodes it succeeds in 92.1%, above the previously reported human score of 90.5%, which was obtained with an oracle skill interface, and far ahead of the best leaderboard entry (60.8%) and of a hierarchical system that pairs the same model with a RoboMME-trained policy (79.1%). It matches or exceeds the human score on 13 of the 16 tasks. Its 63 failures concentrate in two tasks and are mostly premature completions and mistimed or unintended button presses. These results blur the usual division between long-horizon planning, memory and end-effector control, and raise the question of how much of this stack a single general-purpose model can take over in embodied systems. Project website: https://embodied-astra.github.io. Code, prompts and all episode logs: https://github.com/jackbjed/embodied-astra-robomme.
authors: Jack B. Jedlicki, Amish Sethi, Heng Yang
bullets: Evaluated on 800 RoboMME test episodes covering 16 tasks requiring temporal, spatial, object, and procedural memory.
The model processes the full episode context and outputs every end-effector waypoint and gripper command directly.
Its 92.1% success exceeds the reported human score of 90.5% (with an oracle skill interface) and the best leaderboard result of 60.8%.
It matches or surpasses the human score on 13 of 16 tasks; 63 failures are concentrated in two tasks.
Most failures involve premature completion or mistimed/unintended button presses.

papers.abstract: Modeling 3D hair strands is challenging due to complex hairstyle geometry, scarce high-quality training data, and incomplete or noisy input observations. Foundation models offer broader hairstyle priors, but their outputs are not directly usable for strand-based rendering and simulation. Existing approaches require costly per-instance optimization to fit hair priors to meshes from foundation models and 2D orientations from specialized predictors trained on limited hair data, restricting efficiency and generalization. We present HairFlow, a multimodal conditioned diffusion framework for efficient and controllable hair strands modeling. HairFlow conditions strand generation on two complementary representations: a coarse mesh that constrains global shape and multi-view sketches that specify local strand flow. HairFlow combines an Orientation VAE with a conditioned diffusion transformer to generate volumetric fields that are traced into explicit strands. To overcome the lack of paired sketch-strand training data, we introduce an automatic synthesis pipeline that generates geometrically aligned multi-view sketches with diverse styles representative of inference-time inputs. Experiments show that HairFlow generates plausible 3D strands that faithfully follow the input conditions across diverse hairstyles, substantially reduces inference time, and supports flexible multimodal control.
authors: Yating Wang, Kui Wu, Ran Yi, Zixuan Lu, Tongtong Wang, Zhongtian Zheng, Lizhuang Ma, Yuefan Shen
bullets: Addresses complex hair geometry, limited training data, and noisy or incomplete observations.
Uses a coarse mesh for global hairstyle shape and multi-view sketches for local strand flow.
Combines an Orientation VAE with a conditioned diffusion transformer to produce volumetric fields traced into explicit strands.
Introduces automatic synthesis of aligned, stylistically diverse sketch–strand training pairs.
Experiments show plausible strands that follow inputs across diverse hairstyles, with reduced inference time and flexible multimodal control.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of HairFlow. HairFlow takes two geometric inputs—a coarse hair mesh and multi-view sketches—to specify global shape and local strand flow. These conditions can be obtained from images or text using foundation models, or provided by artists. Mesh and camera-aware sketch encoders produce tokens that condition a diffusion transformer through cross-attention. The transformer generates latents in the space of a pretrained Orientation VAE, which decodes them into an orientation field for explicit strand extraction.

Figure 4: Qualitative comparison of single-view 3D hair reconstruction. HairLRM and HairFlow share the same input mesh, supplemented by HairStep orientation maps or sketches from image generation models, respectively. Inputs appear to the left of the corresponding strands. The color wheel below HairLRM illustrates the direction-to-color mapping.

Figure 6: Flexible Sketch Guidance: (a) Sketches with different stroke widths and styles yield similar strand geometry. (b) Joint conditioning on sketches from two viewpoints produces a single hairstyle consistent with both views. (c) Two sets of artist-drawn 3D strokes on the same mesh are projected into multi-view sketches, guiding the generated strands to follow different flow patterns.

Figure 5: Effect of the sketch condition. From left: input image, mesh, mesh-only result, sketch, and mesh+sketch result. Results within each row share the same mesh and random seed. Colors encode 3D tangent directions.

Figure 3: Hair sketch synthesis pipeline. (a) Input strands and template head mesh. (b) Multiview orientation maps; colors encode directed 2D tangents as shown in the circular legend. (c) Bidirectional tracing from sampled seeds; arrows show local directions, and the inset details tracing from the highlighted seed. papers.abstract: We revisit the statistical mechanics of Transformer attention via modern Hopfield models. We present a free-energy formalism to characterize parameter regimes and critical thresholds for robust attention inference. The resulting free-energy landscape incorporates randomness in query states and attention weights. Attention then emerges as the equation of motion of the corresponding statistical-mechanical system (i.e., modern Hopfield model) through the standard free-energy minimization principle. This allows us to identify first-order phase transitions in attention between glassy and robust-inference phases. We further extend to attentions with stochastic queries and keys. Together, our results provide a rigorous statistical-mechanics framework for characterizing phase structure and inference reliability across a family of Transformer attention mechanisms.
authors: Jerry Yao-Chieh Hu, Yu-An Chen, Maojiang Su, Han Liu
bullets: Formulates attention through a free-energy landscape with random queries and attention weights.
Derives attention as the system’s equation of motion via free-energy minimization.
Characterizes parameter regimes and critical thresholds for robust attention inference.
Identifies first-order transitions between glassy and robust-inference phases.
Extends the analysis to stochastic queries and keys across multiple attention mechanisms.

W [J ] = log (∫ X exp{−βH[x] + Jx} ) encodes macroscopic responses, i.e., φ = Ex∼pJ [x] = ∇JW [J ]. Hence, the slope of W [J ] gives a deterministic average. Right. papers.abstract: Language-model agents revise their working context as information becomes obsolete, but deleting text does not erase its influence on cached computation. Later key-value (KV) states remain conditioned on the deleted content, while recomputing the entire retained suffix can be costly. We introduce budgeted KV-cache repair: recovering task performance by recomputing a user-chosen fraction of the retained suffix. Comparing repair allocations under identical relevance scores and token budgets, we find that refreshing coherent regions can substantially outperform refreshing isolated tokens. This finding motivates Semantic-Unit Refresh (SUR), which allocates the budget to query-relevant text regions using inexpensive embedding scores, without training or an auxiliary transformer forward. To execute these repairs efficiently, a layer-packed executor processes selected states together at each layer while preserving full causal cache access. Across five models, SUR achieves strong recovery in controlled deletion tasks while recomputing only 2-5% of the suffix. On four natural multi-hop QA datasets, it achieves near-full-recompute exact match at a 5% budget with lower post-edit latency. The executor accelerates fragmented refresh by up to 16.1x over interval-wise execution.

papers.abstract: Household robots must successfully navigate im-perfect circumstances, both in their internal models and the external world. We introduce a benchmark of seven long-horizon household tasks in Habitat that vary initial robot memory and environment configurations. We evaluate adaptations of ReAct, VLM-TAMP, and Tru-POMDP within a shared execution framework across 90 tasks-environment-memory combinations, totaling 1,350 episodes. Our evaluation measures task success, partial completion, and action efficiency, along with rule-based analysis of execution traces. ReAct achieves the highest overall task success (45.3%) and completion (71.7%), while having accurate initial memory does not consistently yield the highest performance for every planner. We identify recurring placement errors, precondition errors, and redundant actions through trace analysis. These findings highlight differences in how the evaluated planners use initial knowledge and respond to uncertainty.

papers.abstract: As demand for LLM inference grows and consumer GPUs grow more capable, edge deployment is becoming increasingly attractive. WebGPU is compelling in this setting because it offers cross-platform portability and browser accessibility. However, these same strengths also make high performance difficult to achieve, as an implementation that performs well in one context may not perform well in another. To address this, we present GPU Goldmines, a framework for specifying, executing, and tuning WebGPU kernels. We instantiate GPU Goldmines with kernels for key LLM building blocks: matrix multiplication, matrix-vector multiplication, and flash attention. We characterize performance across diverse devices, shapes, and browsers, and use the resulting database to accelerate subsequent autotuning and configuration selection. On shapes drawn from Llama and Qwen models, our matrix multiplication kernels outperform ONNX Runtime and llama.cpp WebGPU kernels by 7.0x and 1.41x geometric mean, respectively, and deliver end-to-end improvements of 1.48x in the prefill stage of llama.cpp for chat workloads.

On Llama- and Qwen-derived shapes, matrix multiplication kernels achieve 7.0× over ONNX Runtime and 1.41× over llama.cpp WebGPU kernels in geometric mean.

papers.abstract: Sampling multiple reports creates an inference problem: how should sampled evidence be converted into a final decision, and does a better structured decision yield a better report? We study these questions through a framework that separates the decision signal, scoring objective, and feasible decision set, followed by text realization. On MIMIC-CXR and IU-Xray, controlled comparisons across 13 generator configurations per benchmark under grouped development/test evaluation reveal three findings. First, changing the objective under fixed evidence and rule capacity changes predictions and their held-out metric trade-offs. Second, relaxing candidate constraints has objective-dependent effects under shared signals and frozen scores. Diagnostics connect the IU macro-oriented assertion increase to near-zero label thresholds and show that limited candidate coverage coexists with selection headroom. Third, a controlled realization study with SFT-Qwen3-VL-8B shows that decision-level gains can be attenuated, amplified, or reversed. Change decomposition reveals that realization can remove incorrect assertions while losing correct findings, so target fidelity and reference accuracy need not improve together. Finding gains also do not consistently improve reference-based report quality. These results motivate separate evaluation of decision rules, candidate constraints, and realized reports.

papers.abstract: We introduce StartLux-Decision, decision models from 0.8B to 27B parameters that combine efficient single-pass prediction with adaptive, confidence-guided reasoning. The Instant models use bidirectional attention in full-attention layers to improve decision accuracy while keeping single-pass inference. The AutoThink models invoke explicit reasoning for uncertain decisions and answer confident cases directly. A three-stage training pipeline establishes shared decision capabilities, specializes the two variants, and equips AutoThink with reasoning through reasoning supervision and reinforcement learning. We introduce Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Deliberative Decisions (RLCD$^2$), which uses a frozen model and proper scoring rules to reward improvements in decision probability quality and applies a soft penalty to overlong reasoning traces. RLCD$^2$ raises the share of reasoning traces that terminate within the generation limit by up to 48 percentage points and cuts average reasoning length by up to 65%, while largely preserving decision accuracy. On the public subset of Decision Index 0.3, the Instant models outperform the strongest evaluated comparable-scale open-weight decision models by 7.4-16.9 points, and the 27B AutoThink model reaches 73.4. We also introduce DecisionPivot, a programmatically verifiable benchmark of computational decisions built from contrast pairs that differ in a single answer-changing detail. On DecisionPivot, AutoThink outperforms its Instant counterparts by 11.5-18.4 points in pair accuracy and leads among evaluated systems. The models run on vLLM, llama.cpp and MLX, with quantized variants for lower memory use.
authors: Xialie Zhuang, Zunhai Su, Jia Pan, Ngai Wong, Guanhua Chen, Chuan-Wei Kuo
bullets: Offers Instant models for efficient single-pass decisions and AutoThink models that reason only when uncertainty warrants it.
Trains the models in three stages, adding reasoning supervision and reinforcement learning to AutoThink.

RLCD² uses proper scoring rules and a soft length penalty, reducing average reasoning length by up to 65% and increasing within-limit termination by up to 48 percentage points while largely preserving accuracy.
Instant models outperform comparable open-weight models by 7.4–16.9 points on the public Decision Index 0.3 subset; the 27B AutoThink model scores 73.4.
Introduces DecisionPivot, where AutoThink exceeds Instant models by 11.5–18.4 points in pair accuracy; models support common inference runtimes and quantization.

papers.title: StartLux-Decision: AutoThink Decision Models with Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Deliberative Decisions
papers.tldr: StartLux-Decision combines fast single-pass prediction with adaptive, confidence-guided reasoning, using RLCD² to make deliberation shorter, more calibrated, and effective on computational decision tasks.

papers.abstract: In this work, we explore the idea of expert intervention delays in human-supervised robotic systems for imitation learning system. Previous works in imitation learning have primarily examined the impact of suboptimal experts, where the expert policy makes mistakes, but assumed expert interventions occur immediately after errors are made. Although delayed expert intervention can be viewed as a form of noise that might improve policy robustness, our results show that learning from delayed expert interventions is overall less effective than learning from non-delayed expert interventions; delayed expert interventions are less effective at demonstrating error avoidance behaviors. To address this, we propose Learning from Delayed Intervention (LfDI), which learns a cost function based on where and when the expert intervenes, combined with limited information about the extent of intervention delays provided by the expert. This cost function is then used to infer additional supervision for states without expert data, guiding the policy to avoid states that would likely trigger interventions. We evaluate our method, Learning from Delayed Intervention (LfDI), on simulated environments and show that it outperforms other methods that do not account for intervention delays.
authors: Xiru Zhu, David Meger, Gregory Dudek
bullets: Delayed interventions are less effective than immediate interventions at teaching error-avoidance behavior.
LfDI learns a cost function from where and when experts intervene, using limited delay information.
The inferred costs provide supervision for states lacking expert demonstrations.
In simulated environments, LfDI outperforms methods that ignore intervention delays.

Fig. 4. We evaluated our method on the Intersection environment from highway-env [6]. In this environment, the agent must drive north to the intersection and make an unprotected left turn. Due to the limited vehicle logic in highway-env, other vehicles can get stuck and crash into each other. Consequently, the overall success rate for even an expert is not perfect, making it critical for the agent to learn when to stop and when to turn safely.

Fig. 1. To evaluate our proposed solution, we experimented on several environments in the highway-env[6]. The Roundabout environment is configured such that the vehicle starts on the south route outside the roundabout and must enter the roundabout and exit to the north route to complete the task. During sampling, expert interventions occur when the cost exceeds a threshold σ, with higher thresholds allowing longer delays and tolerating more errors. After collecting trajectories, the policy is retrained with the new data. Finally, the cost function is trained, and the policy is retrained from scratch with Equation 8..

Depending on the intervention threshold α, the expert may intervene at different points. When α is low, the acceptable total error over the window w is small, and the expert intervenes promptly after errors occur. In contrast, when the expert is distracted, their α is higher, and interventions are delayed.

papers.selection_reason: Addresses imitation learning from delayed expert interventions in human-supervised robotic systems, directly fitting robot policy learning.
papers.title: Improving Policy Learning from Delayed Interventions
papers.tldr: Delayed expert interventions weaken imitation learning, so LfDI uses intervention timing and location to infer extra supervision and improve policy learning.

papers.abstract: The success of autoregressive language models trained with Chain-of-Thought~(CoT) supervision raises a fundamental question: How simple can a next-token predictor be while still enabling the efficient simulation of general computation through its autoregressively generated CoT? Surprisingly, we show that a single neuron suffices. For a broad family of activations, including threshold and ReLU, a single autoregressive neuron can simulate any feedforward circuit with the same activation. Specifically, a size-$s$ circuit on $n$ inputs can be simulated by a neuron of dimension $O(ns+s^2)$ using $O(s^2)$ generation steps, with both bounds independent of circuit depth and tight under natural assumptions. For threshold activations, this improves upon the simulation of Joshi et al. (COLT 2025), whose bounds scale exponentially with circuit depth. Consequently, autoregressive threshold neurons can simulate polynomial-time Turing machines, while remaining efficiently learnable from CoT supervision. Our main expressivity result relies on a novel connection to Sidon sets from additive combinatorics. As an experimental illustration, we efficiently train a single autoregressive ReLU neuron to mimic a neural network teacher with nontrivial test accuracy on CIFAR-10.
authors: Roey Magen, Nirmit Joshi, Gal Vardi
bullets: Shows that one autoregressive neuron with threshold or ReLU activation can simulate any same-activation feedforward circuit.
A size-s circuit on n inputs is simulated in dimension O(ns+s²) and O(s²) generation steps, independently of circuit depth.
For threshold activations, the result improves prior bounds that grew exponentially with circuit depth.
The construction uses a novel connection to Sidon sets from additive combinatorics.
Experiments train a single autoregressive ReLU neuron to imitate a neural-network teacher with nontrivial CIFAR-10 test accuracy.

papers.tldr: A single autoregressive neuron, when guided by Chain-of-Thought, can efficiently simulate broad classes of neural circuits and even polynomial-time computation.

papers.abstract: SE(3)-equivariance provides a useful geometric inductive bias for visuomotor policies, encoding that actions covary with rigid transformations of the observation. However, existing SE(3)-equivariant visuomotor policies build this bias on a global equivariance assumption that treats the entire observation as governed by a single rigid transformation, which breaks down in real-world manipulation tasks where the task-relevant region changes across different objects. We address this by learning a phase-conditioned affordance field (PAF) over the observed point cloud, a per-point score that the SE(3)-equivariant policy uses in two complementary ways. Its score-weighted centroid serves as a learned, phase-conditioned anchor that canonicalizes the observation and the action around the active region, replacing the fixed gripper-frame reference, and the score itself is appended as a per-point feature. This introduces a local geometric inductive bias, while preserving the policy's global SE(3) equivariance. We validate on multiple MimicGen tasks under varying spatial randomization, and PAF consistently improves the success rate of the underlying policy. On multi-object real-robot tasks, PAF outperforms baselines and keeps its lead under lighting variations.
authors: Xinzhe Chen, Liqi Huang, Sihua Ren, Haowen Sun, Mingyang Li, Zeyang Liu, Xingyu Chen, Xuguang Lan
bullets: Global SE(3) equivariance can fail when the task-relevant object or region changes during manipulation.
The method learns a per-point, phase-conditioned affordance score over observed point clouds.
The score-weighted centroid anchors and canonicalizes observations and actions around the active region, while scores are also used as point features.
Experiments on MimicGen and multi-object real-robot tasks show consistently higher success, including under spatial randomization and lighting variation.

papers.abstract: Robots sharing walkways need to know where people will be, yet semantic occupancy maps show only where they are. We present ReForesight, an open-source ROS 2 toolkit that adds instance-level future occupancy and re-identification after occlusion to a particle-based semantic mapping pipeline. A 36.6k-parameter MLP predicts each tracked person or vehicle up to 3 s ahead, guarded by a Kalman fallback and a stationary gate, and the object's own points are moved to the forecast pose, forming a "ghost" point cloud in the map frame without an occupancy decoder. An optional tracker re-associates objects after occlusion using keypoint descriptors the pipeline already computes and a metric 3D gate. On four held-out CODa sequences, the MLP lowers the mean 3 s final displacement error from 0.728 m (Kalman) to 0.662 m and beats a similar-size GRU (0.692 m) on every sequence, at 0.04 ms per instance on one CPU core. Code, all models, and a ROS-free demo are released; field demonstrations use an outdoor cleaning robot.
authors: Didar Seyidov, Faith Ogunwoye, Hajira Amjad, Danil Tolkachev, Yuri Sarkisov, Dzmitry Tsetserukou
bullets: Extends particle-based semantic mapping with instance-level future occupancy and post-occlusion re-identification.
Uses a 36.6k-parameter MLP, with Kalman fallback and a stationary-object gate, to forecast motion up to 3 seconds.
Moves tracked objects’ point clouds to predicted poses to create map-frame “ghost” occupancy without an occupancy decoder.
Optional re-association combines existing keypoint descriptors with a metric 3D gate.

On four held-out CODa sequences, the MLP achieves 0.662 m mean 3-second final displacement error versus 0.728 m for Kalman and 0.692 m for a similar-size GRU; runtime is 0.04 ms per instance on one CPU core.

papers.abstract: Learning symmetries through data augmentation offers an alternative to architectural equivariance, but does not guarantee that a network respects those symmetries. Measuring learned equivariance is especially difficult for intermediate representations, whose group actions are not specified. In a finite discrete setting, we show that equivariance requires representations of original and transformed inputs to determine one another exactly, yielding a test based on normalized mutual information (NMI). For high-dimensional activations, we use centered kernel alignment (CKA) as a scalable test, with an exact guarantee for orthogonal feature transformations. Across architectures and tasks, augmentation usually increases transformation consistency, showing that learned equivariance can be probed directly from representations without recovering the hidden transformation rules that relate them.
authors: Claire Schlesinger, Wolfgang Gatterbauer, Robin Walters
bullets: Data augmentation can encourage, but does not guarantee, equivariant behavior.
For finite discrete representations, equivariance requires original and transformed representations to determine each other exactly.
Normalized mutual information (NMI) provides a test for this exact recoverability.
Centered kernel alignment (CKA) offers a scalable test for high-dimensional activations, with guarantees for orthogonal feature transformations.
Across architectures and tasks, augmentation generally increases transformation consistency.

Table 5: Changing the granularity of what mutual information sees from 4 bits to the full 16 bits shows that the null reading rises with it due to the larger alphabet, making mutual information a much worse measure the more unique outputs there are. In a continuous space with infinite outputs, mutual information is not only intractable to compute, but also loses its ability to distinguish real equivariance from scrambles.

Table 8: Comparison on SEIS equivariance measure between spatial and channel re-encoding. SEIS is able to detect spatial re-encodings but not channel re-encodings and is therefore unable to detect equivariance of steerable models.

Table 7: LieGG makes an assumption that the input space has to be equivariant and the output space has to be invariant to rotation. Purposely building a model that has an equivariant output space shows that LieGG is unable to detect it.

Table 6: Three measures on exactly-SO(2) point clouds (three seeds, 300 epochs, 2048 samples for LieGG; lower is more equivariant). LEE ranks the provably equivariant model last and an untrained network first; LieGG and CKALE recover the correct order. The ∥∇∥ column is the mechanism: LEE = ∥LXf∥/∥f∥ is invariant to uniformly rescaling the features but not to their being nearly constant, where the numerator vanishes and the denominator does not. The untrained network’s input gradient is over 700× smaller than the others’. LieGG normalizes by its polarization matrix’s largest singular value, where rescaling cancels, and is unaffected.

Table 3: Measuring equivariance after a Laplace operation is applied to the discretized images. The transformation is applied so we have a more interesting probability distribution under transformations. Under certain operations applied to the output we see how CKA, MI, and SVCCA either fails or succeeds to detect equivariance. SVCCA is able to detect one more group than CKA, but lacks an unbiased estimator, so we chose to utilize CKA.

Table 2: CKA versus MI on a discrete set of data points. We apply the Laplacian to the input image, then either keep the output unchanged, scramble the alphabet (relabel outputs while keeping points with the same label together), or merge the alphabet (map multiple distinct outputs to the same value). CKA reads the lossless relabeling as non-equivariant, while MI correctly detects equivariance. A high null indicates the metric may be less informative due to a large alphabet.

Table 10: Downsampling a feature map at export aliases it. Equivariance error is ∥f(gx) − ρ(g)f(x)∥/∥ρ(g)f(x)∥ with ρ(g) read off escnn’s declared FieldType, so it is ground truth rather than a competing estimate. The null is the shuffled control: the pairing between the clean and rotated branches is destroyed while marginals, dimensionality and sample count are held fixed. θ = 2.0 rad (114.6◦), 256 MNIST images.

Table 1: NMI between filtered original and rotated images for the Sobel-X filter (not C4-equivariant) and the Laplacian (C4-equivariant) on a restricted, discretized image set. The Laplacian stays at 1. Sobel-X is C2-equivariant and anti-commutes, so it reads 1 at 180◦; a metric assuming the output action matches the input action would report a large error here, but NMI detects the equivariance without being told the action is a sign flip.

papers.abstract: Diffusion language models are a promising and more efficient alternative to autoregressive models. However, most RL post-training techniques are not easily adapted to these models. One issue is that diffusion language models generate answers through many intermediate states, deciding at each step which masked positions to reveal and which tokens to place in them. Many existing RL methods used in this setting approximate intractable sequence likelihoods or weight every denoising step by the same advantage, without explicitly distinguishing how these intermediate states of the denoising trajectory affect the expected reward. To address this issue of trajectory blindness, we introduce PACT (Potential-Anchored Consistency of Transitions). Motivated by a reward-tilted reference distribution, PACT jointly learns the policy and a scalar potential that scores each intermediate state, anchored by terminal reward. For each sampled denoising transition, a consistency loss matches the policy-to-reference log-probability ratio of revealed tokens to the change in this potential. This formulation requires neither sequence-likelihood estimation nor importance-ratio clipping. On four tasks, PACT improves LLaDA-8B-Instruct by +9.9 points on GSM8K, +12.0 on MATH500, +55.7 on Countdown, and +72.6 on Sudoku, and reaches the best average accuracy across the four tasks reported for this model, +3.7 points over the next best method. Further compared to AGRPO, it reaches that baseline's best accuracy in about half the training compute on GSM8K.
authors: Vaibhav Singh, Eugene Belilovsky
bullets: Diffusion language models generate through multi-step denoising trajectories, making standard RL methods difficult to apply.
PACT addresses trajectory blindness with a learned scalar potential over intermediate states, anchored by terminal reward.
A consistency loss matches revealed-token policy/reference log-ratio changes to potential changes, avoiding sequence-likelihood estimation and importance-ratio clipping.
On four tasks, PACT improves LLaDA-8B-Instruct by 9.9–72.6 points and achieves the best reported average accuracy for this model.
On GSM8K, PACT reaches AGRPO’s best accuracy with about half the training compute.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of PACT training. (b) A small potential head predicts f from the DLLM’s hidden state, pulled up by correct rollouts and down by failed ones. (c) On each scored step, PACT minimizes δ2 t = (ut − gt) 2, where ut is the revealed tokens’ log-ratio to the frozen reference and gt the gain in log potential (Equation (5)). Numbers are illustrative.

papers.abstract: To reconstruct a predictive 4D representation of the physical world from monocular video captured by a moving camera, we jointly reconstruct dynamic Gaussian radiance fields and infer their underlying physical dynamics. This paper proposes \emph{Physical SLAM}, a physics-aware method for constructing 4D Gaussian fields of deformable objects and predicting their future state when subjected to external actions, given a sequence of RGB-D images. Our method separates the scene into a static background Gaussian field for camera localization and a dynamic object Gaussian field driven by a spring--mass physical model of elastic deformation, inertia, and damping. To integrate visual observations with physical dynamics, we introduce virtual observation forces that gradually pull simulated surface nodes toward observed depth points, avoiding abrupt replacement of simulated node positions. Meanwhile, the physical parameters of the spring--mass model are updated from simulation errors aggregated over the full reconstruction observation window, enabling the reconstructed dynamics to align with observations. To couple appearance, geometry, and physics, we further design a physics-aware Gaussian transformation and surface alignment strategy, where dynamic Gaussians are transformed along the deforming physical surface of the spring--mass model and constrained to remain aligned with the surface during rendering-based optimization. The resulting representation supports observed-frame rendering and action-conditioned simulation, extending SLAM maps to describe how deformable objects respond to manipulation. On the PhysTwin benchmark, our method improves reconstruction and prediction PSNR over PhysTwin by 10.4\% and 11.0\%, respectively. On the TUM RGB-D benchmark, it reduces average camera tracking error by 20.6\%, improves SSIM by 3.6\%, and reduces LPIPS by 8.3\% compared with 4DGS-SLAM.
authors: Guangming Wang, Zhishuo Liu, Haibing Wu, Wanli Ma, Yixiong Jing, Olaf Wysocki, Brian Sheil
bullets: Addresses predictive 4D mapping of dynamic, deformable scenes from moving-camera RGB-D video.
Separates static background and dynamic object Gaussian fields, using the former for localization and a spring–mass model for deformation, inertia, and damping.
Uses virtual observation forces to smoothly align simulated surface nodes with depth observations and updates physical parameters over the observation window.
Transforms dynamic Gaussians along the simulated deforming surface while enforcing surface alignment during rendering optimization.
Improves reconstruction and prediction PSNR on PhysTwin, and tracking, SSIM, and LPIPS on TUM RGB-D, relative to the cited baselines.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Pipeline of Physical SLAM. We decouple the static and dynamic mapping using semantics. For the static part, we build a globally consistent map and use the map to track the camera pose. For the dynamics part, we use a spring–mass system with external actions and observation forces to track the trajectory of surface nodes and use the geometry loss to progressively optimize the physical parameters; in parallel, we use a surface alignment method to align the 3D Gaussians to the mesh of the object to realise the tightly coupled optimization of physical dynamics, geometry, and appearance.

Fig. 1. Physics-aware SLAM with 4D Gaussian field for reconstruction and prediction. Existing 4D Gaussian SLAM methods mainly reconstruct time-varying geometry and appearance. Our method further reconstructs the physical dynamics of deformable objects, enabling online reconstruction and physically grounded action-conditioned prediction from RGB-D observations. For prediction, our method simulates the dynamics of the spring–mass model under the supplied actions and renders the resulting object states from a query camera pose.

Fig. 3. Qualitative Results Compared with PhysTwin. Ours produces renderings that better align with the observations, with sharper appearance and more accurate silhouettes. Green boxes and connecting lines indicate magnified regions; blue and orange borders distinguish reconstruction and prediction, respectively.
Fig. 4. Visual comparison of rendering results on the TUM RGB-D dataset.

papers.selection_reason: Builds physics-aware 4D Gaussian scene representations that support action-conditioned future simulation, fitting interactive world-model interests.
papers.title: Physical SLAM: Physics-aware Simultaneous Localisation and Mapping
papers.tldr: Physical SLAM reconstructs deformable objects’ 4D Gaussian representations while learning their physics, enabling camera tracking, rendering, and action-conditioned future-state prediction.

papers.abstract: Search-based policy learning, such as Monte Carlo tree search (MCTS), offers the flexibility to trade runtime computation for data efficiency and adaptation to novel environments. For robot learning, however, applying search requires discretizing the continuous action space and associated dynamics, typically through action quantization. While reconstruction-based quantization is sufficient for representing the continuous action space alone, policy learning additionally requires the quantized actions to preserve their effects on future states and values. We show that such requirement is not necessarily captured by action reconstruction error. Instead, we prove that the error in the value function resulting from action quantization is tightly bounded by the reconstruction error of state reachability under the quantized actions. Based on these results, we propose value-preserving action quantization (VAQ), which quantizes actions by preserving state reachability. We further combine VAQ with MCTS (VAQ-MCTS) as a value-preserving, search-based policy learning framework for behavioral cloning. Using a wide range of object pushing tasks as a controlled benchmark, we evaluate VAQ-MCTS against state-of-the-art behavioral cloning methods. VAQ-MCTS matches or exceeds their performance under standard settings, while substantially improving data efficiency and robustness to heterogeneous demonstrations, while enabling zero-shot adaptation to novel environments. Hardware experiments further demonstrate the effectiveness of VAQ-MCTS, completing all 30 real-world object pushing trials with only 10 minutes of demonstration data.
authors: Max Muchen Sun, Jueun Kwon, Benjamin Riviere, Todd Murphey
bullets: Action reconstruction error alone may not preserve the values relevant to policy learning.
Theoretical analysis bounds value-function error by state-reachability reconstruction error under quantized actions.
VAQ quantizes actions to preserve state reachability and is integrated with MCTS in VAQ-MCTS.
On object-pushing benchmarks, VAQ-MCTS matches or exceeds behavioral cloning baselines while improving data efficiency, robustness to heterogeneous demonstrations, and zero-shot adaptation.
Hardware trials completed all 30 real-world object-pushing tasks using 10 minutes of demonstration data.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Overview of VAQ-MCTS. VAQ learns a discrete latent representation that preserves state reachability; in this example, four discrete latent codes of VQ-VAE capture representative state evolutions. This compact representation then enables efficient runtime policy learning via MCTS planning.
Fig. 3. VAQ extracts 8 actions from 10 minutes of undirected human demonstrations, achieving 100% success across 30 trials and 3 objects.
Fig. 6. Effects of demonstration heterogeneity on action quantization.
Fig. 5. Ablation on value preservation with reachability reconstruction.
Fig. 4. Illustration of simulated benchmarks (PushT, PushO, and PushC). Robot pushes each object to the goal while adapting to unforeseen obstacles.

Fig. 2. Examples of action heterogeneity, where different action sequences (red end-effector motion) lead to similar state sequences. By Theorem 1, this mismatch can make action reconstruction-based quantization suboptimal for policy learning, motivating VAQ to reconstruct state reachability.

papers.abstract: Can a vision-language model tell left from right? Modern VLMs solve visual puzzles and follow hour-long videos, yet when asked whether the camera moved left or right, most do no better than a coin flip. Adding camera-motion data or geometric representations has been tried, separately, and neither closes the gap. We argue that camera-motion understanding needs two conditions at once: the representation must couple off-screen camera motion with on-screen flow dynamics, and it must be interpreted by the language model rather than trained as a standalone pose or depth estimator. We propose CameraVLM, which pairs a motion-state representation with state-language alignment. Camera tokens capture how the camera moves off screen, flow tokens capture how the subject and background move on screen, and a two-stage training strategy keeps language in the loop so that both are learned together with camera-motion semantics. With only 9B parameters, CameraVLM outperforms all open-source and camera-motion-specific models by a wide margin across three benchmarks and more than 20 baselines, and matches or surpasses GPT-6 Astra as well as human viewers in a 48-participant study. Project page: https://3dagentworld.github.io/CameraVLM/
authors: Chong Cheng, Ran Zhang, Xinyuan Li, Alan Zhao, Hao Wang, Xi Wang
bullets: Vision-language models often perform near chance when identifying whether a camera moved left or right.
The approach combines camera tokens for off-screen motion with flow tokens for subject and background dynamics.
A two-stage training strategy aligns these motion representations with language while keeping camera-motion semantics in the loop.
Using 9B parameters, CameraVLM outperforms open-source and camera-motion-specific models across three benchmarks and over 20 baselines.
It reportedly matches or exceeds GPT-6 Astra and human performance in a 48-participant study.

figures.caption: Figure 3 Architecture of CameraVLM. Camera tokens provide continuous camera states, while flow tokens provide cross-frame motion states. Camera, vision, flow, and question tokens are jointly contextualized by the shared VLM backbone. The Camera Head predicts continuous camera parameters, the flow pathway predicts trajectories, visibility, and confidence, and the LM Head interprets the joint states under the query to answer camera-motion questions.

Figure 2 Spatial motion semantics depend on reference and spatio-temporal state. The same scene can yield opposite directions under different references or similar appearances from different camera motions. CameraVLM models these relations through camera pose and flow. On left/right questions, most existing VLMs still perform poorly, while CameraVLM approaches human performance.

Figure 5 Qualitative comparison. Each row compares a model prediction with the bolded ground truth; green denotes correct predictions and red denotes errors. The rightmost column shows the dense flow predicted by CameraVLM. In the first clip, large subject motion causes most models to mistake a truck-left shot for a pull-out, while CameraVLM correctly identifies the lateral camera motion from background parallax.

Figure 4 Per-category accuracy on eight camera-motion primitives, with an Overall panel. CameraVLM leads in most categories and is second only to GPT-6 Astra in the others; full numbers for all models are in Table 8.
Figure 7 Qualitative examples on tilt-up and pan-right recognition. Most baselines fail on the binary tilt question; several confuse pan direction or hallucinate a crane motion.
Figure 6 Qualitative examples on pull-out and compound pan-left-push-in motions. Most baselines confuse pull-out with zoom-in; only CameraVLM correctly identifies both clips.

Figure 9 Qualitative examples on rolling and boom-up motions. Rolling-clockwise requires distinguishing rotation direction; boom-up is commonly misread as push-in or pull-out by baselines that lack vertical-translation awareness.

Figure 8 Qualitative examples on compound dolly-zoom and zoom-in description matching. The dolly-out-withzoom-in clip tests fine-grained compound-motion parsing; the description-matching clip requires verifying motion smoothness.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes CameraVLM, a vision-language model for understanding camera motion by coupling off-screen motion with on-screen flow, directly advancing spatial intelligence in multimodal models.

papers.tldr: CameraVLM improves left-versus-right camera-motion understanding by jointly modeling off-screen camera motion, on-screen optical flow, and language semantics.

papers.abstract: Video reward models are trained and evaluated on human preferences between videos that often differ simultaneously on properties such as prompt alignment, visual fidelity, motion, and generator identity. As a result, aggregate accuracy does not reveal which video properties a reward model can reliably distinguish. We construct preference pairs by controlled interventions that change one property of a generated video while holding the rest fixed. The resulting pairs, by construction, provide preferences for how the videos differ along a specific dimension, without requiring any human annotation. We propose IsoVRBench, a video generation reward modeling benchmark of 8,000 such pairs across eight interventions, and show that state-of-the-art models separate broad quality differences between generators but miss important features such as temporal order. The best reward model reaches only 60.8% on reordered frames against 100% for humans, and rankings on existing benchmarks do not predict this failure. Using the synthetic isolated intervation pairs as training data leads to 1) IsoVRM, a reward model outperforming its counterpart trained with a larger human labeled preference dataset by 3.8 points on VBench-2.0, 2) IsoWan, the video generator post-trained with IsoVRM, outperforming its human-data counterpart in human preferences, and 3) gains that stack when combined with human data. Because intervention pairs are automatically generated rather than collected, the benchmark and training data can be easily extended as generators evolve.
authors: Shuyue Stella Li, Jacqueline He, Jiahui Chen, Sreya Dutta Roy, Yulia Tsvetkov, Luke Zettlemoyer, Marjan Ghazvininejad, Xiaochuang Han
bullets: Existing aggregate preference accuracy can hide failures on specific video properties such as temporal order.
The benchmark contains 8,000 pairs across eight controlled interventions, changing one property while holding others fixed.
State-of-the-art models distinguish broad generator-quality differences but perform poorly on reordered frames, with the best reaching 60.8% versus 100% for humans.
Training on these synthetic pairs produces IsoVRM, which improves VBench-2.0 performance by 3.8 points over a counterpart trained on a larger human-labeled dataset.
IsoVRM also improves post-trained video generation, with gains stacking when combined with human data; the approach can be extended as generators evolve.

papers.abstract: Navigating humanoid robots through dynamic, non-convex environments requires tightly coupling onboard perception with footstep planning and dynamic locomotion control. Existing methods frequently discard complex free space through simplified convex obstacle bounds and fail to account for real-time dynamic occupancy predictions. This paper presents a real-time framework for humanoid navigation that directly constructs spatio-temporal safe corridors from LiDAR-based particle representations and couples them with Linear Inverted Pendulum (LIP)-based planning and Whole Body Control (WBC) to enable navigation around and within moving non-convex structures without restrictive geometric assumptions. Simulations on the Digit humanoid yield a 96% success rate in navigating around and inside moving non-convex obstacles in a 24 by 24 m^2 arena. Ablation studies confirm that the proposed iterative polytope generation significantly outperforms single-iteration baselines in narrow corridors, while evaluations demonstrate robustness to clutter, sensor noise, control delays, and force perturbations.
authors: Shubham S. Kumbhar, Panagiotis Artemiadis
bullets: Addresses the loss of usable free space and poor handling of dynamic occupancy in existing navigation methods.
Builds spatio-temporal safe corridors directly from LiDAR-based particle representations without restrictive convex obstacle assumptions.
Couples corridor generation with Linear Inverted Pendulum planning and Whole Body Control for dynamic locomotion.
In Digit simulations, achieves a 96% success rate around and inside moving non-convex obstacles in a 24 × 24 m² arena.
Shows improved narrow-corridor performance with iterative polytope generation and robustness to clutter, sensor noise, delays, and force perturbations.

papers.tldr: A real-time LiDAR-driven framework enables Digit humanoid navigation through moving, non-convex environments using spatio-temporal safe corridors coupled with footstep and whole-body control.

papers.abstract: Generating images beyond the training resolution of Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) remains challenging, as the number of tokens grows rapidly with resolution, full attention becomes expensive, and outputs often suffer from structural distortions and degraded detail. We identify uniform full attention as the common source of both problems. Attending to all tokens at every step causes quadratic cost and exposes the model to more tokens and relative distances beyond the training range, pushing the model out of distribution. We observe that attention's effective receptive field narrows during denoising, from global in early steps that form structure to local in later steps that refine details. We propose AReA, a training-free attention mechanism whose receptive field evolves from coarse to fine, following the denoising progression. In early steps, AReA applies cross-scale coarse attention over downsampled keys and values, capturing global context, while in later steps it applies local attention within progressively shrinking windows. Without additional parameters or training, experiments show that AReA consistently outperforms state-of-the-art training-free baselines across target resolutions and different models, while also being faster and more efficient.
authors: Javad Rajabi, Koorosh Roohi, David B. Lindell, Babak Taati
bullets: Addresses quadratic full-attention costs and structural/detail degradation when DiTs generate beyond training resolution.
Uses coarse cross-scale attention in early denoising steps to capture global structure.
Progressively switches to shrinking-window local attention in later steps for detail refinement.
Training-free and adds no parameters, while reported experiments show consistent gains over training-free baselines with improved speed and efficiency.

figures.caption: Figure 5: Qualitative comparisons across resolutions. AReA eliminates structural distortions and subject duplication seen in baseline methods, achieving superior fidelity and prompt alignment.

Figure 4: Pipeline of AReA. AReA follows the coarse-to-fine progression of denoising, switching from Phase I to Phase II at noise level σ⋆. In Phase I, full-resolution queries attend to keys and values pooled to one token per f × f block, with f ramped over steps, and positioned on a grid matching the training resolution. In Phase II, attention is restricted to progressively shrinking local windows, and those over smooth regions of the DWT map are further split to reduce cost.

Figure 16: Out-of-Distribution Exposure and Its Consequence on FLUX.1. Left: distance and token-count exposure at 40962, averaged over denoising and scaled so that 0 is the model at its native 10242 and 1 is the vanilla model at 40962. RoPE-modifying methods (like SEGA) remove only the distance cause, while AReA reduces both. Right: FID of each method’s outputs to the model’s own native-resolution outputs; lower is closer to the model’s intended and trained distribution. AReA stays lowest and flat as resolution grows.

Figure 2: Failure Modes at High Resolution. FLUX.1 at 4096 × 4096. Full attention keeps the model’s intended subject but collapses the layout, while RoPE-based methods keep a layout but fragment, lose, or distort the subject. AReA preserves both and renders fine details.

Figure 15: Comparison with Multi-Stage Methods on FLUX.1 at 4096× 4096. Multi-stage methods and AReA-Bootstrap inherit the composition of the same base-resolution image and differ mainly in local detail. AReA with Phase I (default) sets its own layout at the target resolution and renders finer detail (green insets). ScaleDiff introduces repetitive content in low-detail regions (red insets).

Figure 9: Effect of the Phase I pooling strategy on FLUX.1 at 4096 × 4096. Mean pooling averages away the components that distinguish keys within a block, blurring fine detail such as armor ornamentation and facial features. Medoid selection keeps a real token but favors the most typical one in each block, partially inheriting this loss. Random selection preserves more detail but depends on the seed. Center pooling (default) uses a fixed, content-free token per block and gives the sharpest and most coherent results.

Figure 8: Effect of the Phase I pooling schedule on FLUX.1 at 4096 × 4096. A fixed f = 4 forms the layout on a 64× 64 pooled grid, which matches the training resolution but is too coarse to separate objects, so the sheep merge into a single blurred mass. A fixed f = 2 forms the layout on a 128× 128 grid, twice the training resolution, producing scattered and repeated subjects. Decreasing f from 4 to 2 first sets the layout at the training resolution and then refines it on the finer grid, giving separated subjects and a coherent scene.

Figure 18: Additional Comparison on FLUX.1 at 4096× 4096 on HRGen-1K. Existing methods warp scenes into symmetric, fisheye-like layouts, reduce object-centric prompts to zoomed-in texture, miscount objects, and garble rendered text. AReA preserves scene composition, object counts (highlighted in red), and legible text.

Figure 3: Attention Locality as Denoising Progresses. Vanilla FLUX.1 (1024 × 1024), averaged across heads, blocks, and 24 prompts. Left: attention-weighted query–key distance. Over all keys it shrinks only 1.4×, but over dominant keys (≥ 1/4 max attention) it shrinks 5.5×: late in denoising, the most important keys lie close to the query. Right: attention maps of a center query at early, middle, and late steps (top 60% of mass).

Figure 6: Generation latency vs. resolution. AReA is significantly faster than full-attention baselines across all resolutions, reaching 3.2× and 2.9× acceleration at 61442 on FLUX.1 and Qwen-Image, respectively.

Figure 11: Window size follows the locality of the model’s attention. AReA’s window size at 40962 and the model’s attention range at its native resolution of 10242, computed over keys receiving at least a quarter of the maximum attention (blue) and over all keys (orange). All curves are shown relative to their values at the start of Phase II. In Phase I, every query attends to pooled keys from the whole image, so no window is shown. In Phase II, the window size follows a similar trend to the strongest attention, while attention over all keys remains broad.

Figure 14: Key budget per denoising step. Number of image keys each query attends to on FLUX.1 at 4096 × 4096, averaged over 20 prompts (shading shows the range). Top: In Phase I, the pooled keys match the token count of the native 10242 resolution for f = 4 and four times that for f = 2. In Phase II, the windows shrink from about 32K keys to the native 4K, and full AReA stays within about 30% of plain windowing. No query attends to more than about 40K of the 64K image keys at any step. Bottom: Change in keys per query relative to plain windows. The global-KV bridge adds a roughly constant share of about 25%, the halo takes a growing share as windows shrink, and DWT splits remove up to 35% late in Phase II.

Figure 12: AReA Across Denoising on FLUX.1 at 4096 × 4096. Top row: Phase I steps with pooled keys and values (insets show the pixelation effect). Other rows: Phase II steps, each showing the current image (upper half) and its DWT detail map (lower half), with base windows in red, overlap regions hatched, and DWT splits in orange.

Figure 20: Comparison on Qwen-Image at 5120× 5120. Full attention blurs the scene and repeats subjects. SEGA keeps the layout but corrupts the details with high-frequency artifacts. AReA produces clean faces and the prompted number of subjects.

Figure 21: Comparison on Ideogram 4 at 6144× 6144. Full attention completely collapses, while SEGA fails to keep the layout and add fine detail. AReA excels in both structure and fine detail, showing that it transfers to a different backbone without modification.

Figure 17: Statistics of HRGen-1K. left: Distribution of prompt lengths, grouped into short (≤ 15 words), medium (16-40 words), and long (> 40 words) prompts. Right: Share of prompts containing common attributes, estimated via keyword matching. Attributes are not mutually exclusive.

Figure 7: Qualitative ablation on FLUX.1 at 4096× 4096. Without Phase I, windows diverge and disrupt global layout. Without Phase II, the image lacks fine texture and remains blurry. Mean pooling degrades overall image quality (compared in Table 4), while fixed windows without shrinking cause seams and content fragmentation compared to default AReA.

Figure 10: Effect of switching phases too early or too late. An early switch starts Phase II before the structure has settled, degrading the final result. A late switch leaves too few Phase II steps to add fine details, so the final image lacks detail.

Figure 13: Effect of the Global-KV Bridge and Halo. Left: without the global-KV bridge, each window is blind to content elsewhere on the canvas and paints extra copies of the subject. With the bridge, windows see distinctive tokens from the rest of the grid and the duplicates disappear. Right: without the Halo, tokens at window edges lack context from across the boundary, leaving seams in smooth regions such as the sky.
