papers.selection_reason: Introduces AReA, a training-free attention mechanism that adapts receptive fields from coarse to fine, directly improving efficiency in high-resolution Diffusion Transformers.
papers.title: AReA: Adaptive Receptive-Field Attention for Efficient High-Resolution Diffusion Transformers
papers.tldr: AReA enables more efficient high-resolution Diffusion Transformers by adapting attention from global to local as denoising progresses.

papers.abstract: What information does a reinforcement learning policy omit? At each state, a standard policy stores one probability per action. It has no place to record how actions relate to each other, such as which pairs go together and which conflict. We ask when this missing structure matters, and we give exact answers. We store the policy at each state as a density matrix, a positive semidefinite, unit-trace matrix borrowed from quantum information theory. We use it here as a purely classical data structure, computed on ordinary classical hardware. The diagonal holds the usual action probabilities. The off-diagonal entries, called coherences, are new parameters. This gives density-matrix reinforcement learning (DMRL). Coherences change outcomes in two settings. First, suppose a policy is regularized toward a coherent reference policy using matrix relative entropy. The optimum then has coherences that no diagonal reference policy produces, and its action probabilities can depend on the reference policy's coherences. This is relevant to fine-tuning of large language models (LLMs) with a Kullback--Leibler penalty. Second, suppose the agent chooses a unit-vector action and the reward is a quadratic function of that vector. This could arise when an LLM judge scores a weighted consolidation of reasoning paths, or when coupled robotic sensors each respond to a mix of actions. Then some coherent policies earn strictly more expected reward than every classical policy with the same action probabilities, and we give the margin in closed form. In a two-action example, both policies assign probability $0.5$ to each action, yet the classical one earns expected reward $0$ while the coherent one earns $1$, the maximum. Outside these two settings, DMRL matches or transfers the classical results. This is a theory paper. All results are proved, and we report no empirical evaluation.
authors: Chiuman Ho
bullets: Standard policies record action probabilities but not relationships such as action compatibility or conflict.
DMRL represents each state policy as a positive semidefinite, unit-trace density matrix; its diagonal gives probabilities and off-diagonal terms encode coherences.
With matrix-relative-entropy regularization, coherent reference policies can induce optimal coherences and alter action probabilities, including in LLM fine-tuning with a KL penalty.
For unit-vector actions with quadratic rewards, coherent policies can outperform every classical policy sharing the same action probabilities; a two-action example reaches reward 1 versus 0.
The paper is theoretical: it proves the results and reports no empirical evaluation.

figures.caption: Table 1: Operator concepts and their classical analogues. Setting the off-diagonal entries of ρ (and of ρ′ and O, where relevant) to zero recovers the right-hand column. The diagonal is unchanged by this operation. The coherences have no classical counterpart because they vanish.

Table 2: Two action models. The standard basis vectors ei are unit vectors, and choosing x = ±ei earns x⊤Ox = Oii, the reward of action ai. So an agent that chooses only ±e1, . . . ,±ek is exactly the left column. This restriction is the classical baseline used throughout this subsection.

papers.selection_reason: Novel RL policy representation with coherent action structure; transferable to robot learning and LLM fine-tuning settings.
papers.title: Density-Matrix Reinforcement Learning
papers.tldr: Density-Matrix Reinforcement Learning augments action probabilities with coherence terms, enabling provable benefits in regularized policies and quadratic-reward settings while recovering classical RL otherwise.

papers.abstract: Cutting a piece of food looks effortless in human hands. For a robot, however, every cut is a high-contact interaction with a deformable, elasto-plastic object whose behavior changes with pose, contact mode, and cutting stage. Collecting real-world data is expensive and wasteful: each trial typically contaminates or damages the food, so obtaining scalable real world data for dexterous cutting is expensive and difficult. Simulation is an appealing alternative, but a large sim-to-real gap exists in both physics and perception. This gap is especially severe for topology-changing interactions like cutting, where small errors in contact, friction, or material and elasticity responses quickly compound. We propose \textsc{DexNinja}, a real2sim2real framework that turns a handful of real demonstrations into a dense and realistic training distribution. \textsc{DexNinja} (i) reconstructs object instances from real captures, (ii) randomizes physically meaningful parameters under category-level constraints, and (iii) produces augmented dexterous manipulation episodes using a custom differentiable simulator that couples robot dynamics, tactile contact, and deformable cutting. We evaluate \textsc{DexNinja} on a dexterous food-slicing task and show that (1) with tens of real demonstrations and hundreds of augmented simulator data, the success rate could reach more than 60\%. (2) the augmented data consistently improves success rates when only using real data with more than 20\% via sim-to-real, and (3) the resulting policies generalize to out-of-distribution objects with varying shapes and sizes.
authors: Haozhe Lou, Runyi Yang, Wanqi Zhong, Caiyun Liu, Yicheng Liu, Wenhao Liu, Wenlong Ma, Jiawei Xia, Kanzhi Wu, Danda Pani Paudel, Luc Van Gool, Hang Zhao, Yiming Li
bullets: Dexterous cutting is difficult because it involves high-contact interactions with deformable objects and changing contact dynamics.

The framework reconstructs objects from real captures, randomizes physically meaningful parameters, and generates episodes in a differentiable simulator coupling robot, tactile, and deformable-cutting dynamics.
Using tens of real demonstrations plus hundreds of simulated episodes, the evaluated policy achieved over 60% success on food slicing.
Simulation augmentation improved success by more than 20% compared with using real data alone.
Policies generalized to unseen objects with different shapes and sizes.

papers.abstract: Large language models can answer the same question in different styles, but users' preferred styles are hidden and vary across users and questions. We study inference-time personalization through online selection from a fixed set of prompts, each representing a persona. Users arrive sequentially, each asks a short sequence of questions, and the system displays two responses per question and observes one pairwise choice. We formulate this interaction as a variant of the contextual dueling bandit problem in which the learner starts without preference data, adapts within each session, and exploits information shared across users. The objective is to minimize cumulative strong regret, summing the utility gaps of both displayed responses relative to the user's best response among the available options. We make two contributions. First, we introduce the problem and release a reproducible preference benchmark and dataset built around a tutoring case study, containing educational questions, LLM-generated answers in six teaching styles, and pairwise judgments from LLM-simulated students with hidden preference profiles. We fit Bradley-Terry models to these judgments to obtain reference utilities for regret evaluation. Second, we propose a baseline that learns a mixture prior over users from completed sessions and adapts to each new user within the session. On students and topics never used in development, it removes 44-48% of random pairs' excess regret and achieves over half the performance of a per-user linear oracle fitted in hindsight. We release code, prompts, and the benchmark.
authors: Romain Puech, Georgy Salakhutdinov, Dimitris Bertsimas
bullets: Models personalization as contextual dueling bandits over a fixed set of persona prompts, using pairwise choices between two displayed responses.
Introduces a tutoring-focused benchmark with six teaching styles, educational questions, simulated students, hidden preference profiles, and Bradley–Terry reference utilities.
Proposes learning a mixture prior from completed users and updating preferences online for each new user.
On held-out students and topics, the method removes 44–48% of random-pair excess regret and exceeds half the performance of a hindsight per-user linear oracle.
Releases the benchmark, prompts, and code; evaluation relies on LLM-simulated student preferences.

On each question, the policy picks two of the K = 6 personas, using earlier users’ sessions and the current user’s choices so far, and the user chooses between the two generated answers. Strong regret, computed from hidden utilities, sums the gaps of both displayed answers to the user’s best answer.
Figure 2: Excess regret per user as users arrive on the three evaluation rosters (b = 24): each user’s excess regret averaged over seeds and smoothed over neighboring arrivals, with 95% bands.

papers.abstract: Multi-Head Latent Attention (MLA) compresses the KV cache into a latent representation, reducing inference memory and bandwidth. Existing MHA2MLA/TransMLA methods do not support QKNorm and require costly recovery on modern LLMs, especially MoE. We present MLAfication, a QKNorm-compatible, parameter-efficient extension of MHA2MLA. It combines calibrated KNorm, parameter-efficient distillation, contribution-aware Partial-RoPE, and activation-aware joint KV initialization. Across MHA and GQA models, including QKNorm- and MoE-equipped variants, MLAfication preserves performance under substantial KV-cache compression, surpasses the current SOTA on commonsense and long-context benchmarks, and extends MLA conversion to modern architectures. On Qwen3-30B-A3B, MLAfication delivers up to $5.35\times$ the serving throughput of BF16 GQA and, combined with 4-bit KV quantization, reduces the KV-cache footprint by $94.73\%$. Our code is available at https://github.com/JT-Ushio/MLAfication.
authors: Zile Wang, Zhide Xie, Tao Ji
bullets: Addresses the limited compatibility and costly recovery of existing MHA-to-MLA methods, especially for QKNorm and MoE models.
Introduces calibrated KNorm, parameter-efficient distillation, contribution-aware Partial-RoPE, and activation-aware joint KV initialization.
Preserves model performance across MHA and GQA models under substantial KV-cache compression.
Surpasses prior state of the art on commonsense and long-context benchmarks.
On Qwen3-30B-A3B, achieves up to 5.35× BF16 GQA serving throughput and reduces KV-cache footprint by 94.73% with 4-bit KV quantization.

papers.abstract: Multi-player interactive world models aim to simulate shared environments from multiple players' perspectives, but achieving robust generation while scaling to more players remains challenging. Existing approaches that rely on fully-connected communication (e.g., Solaris) incur quadratic attention costs as the number of players grows, while centralized approaches (e.g., $\gamma$-World) suffer from interference between unrelated events in a shared global representation. To address these challenges, we present Multics, a multi-player video generation framework with hierarchical communication that structures information exchange across player, group, and global levels. This hierarchy introduces group tokens into self-attention as intermediate group-level representations that aggregate locally relevant player information. These tokens connect to global tokens for cross-group communication, while the hierarchical topology limits direct mixing between unrelated local events. Group-token parameters are shared across group slots, allowing the same communication module to accommodate varying numbers of players without introducing new group-specific parameters. We further propose budget-constrained dynamic grouping based on recent camera trajectories, which adaptively groups relevant players while limiting unnecessary communication. Experiments demonstrate that Multics achieves state-of-the-art performance in 4- and 6-player settings, with improved cross-player consistency, player-specific action and camera controllability, and interference robustness. Moreover, Multics generalizes from 4-player training to 6-, 8-, and 10-player inference without retraining, while reducing self-attention computation compared with fully-connected communication.
authors: Kaiyi Huang, Wangbo Yu, Yukun Huang, Jiwen Yu, Kunhao Liu, Donglin Yang, Wenbo Hu, Ying Shan, Xihui Liu
bullets: Addresses quadratic communication costs and interference from unrelated events as player count grows.
Uses player-, group-, and global-level communication, with shared group tokens linking local information to global context.
Dynamically groups relevant players from recent camera trajectories under a communication budget.
Achieves state-of-the-art results in 4- and 6-player settings with stronger consistency, controllability, and interference robustness.
Generalizes from 4-player training to 6-, 8-, and 10-player inference without retraining while reducing self-attention computation.

papers.abstract: Linear-time sequence models typically store long-context information in a recurrent state. A fixed-size state limits how much information can be stored, while hybrid architectures that add full attention for better recall incur quadratic sequence cost. Alternatively, sparse attention with continued pretraining (CPT) can extend the effective context length. Generalization beyond the trained length remains challenging, however, and CPT can be costly. We introduce FreeSolo, a native sparse attention mechanism with a short-range sliding window branch and a long-range branch that selects keypoint cells for direct token attention. Its linear-time variant, FS-L, learns to prune the prefix before query-dependent selection through short CPT. FS-B searches balanced trees with $O(N\log^2 N)$ algorithmic cost including radix-sort construction. FreeSolo demonstrates better zero-shot length extrapolation than the baselines without long-context fine-tuning.
authors: Zekun Shi, Alastair James Arthur Price
bullets: Addresses the limited memory of fixed-size recurrent states and the quadratic cost of full attention.
Combines a short-range sliding-window branch with a long-range branch that selects keypoint cells for direct token attention.

papers.abstract: Soft tokens have so far been used to replace discrete chain-of-thought in latent reasoning methods. These approaches typically require multi-stage training and, in some cases, auxiliary modules, yet they still underperform supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on triples. In this paper, we ask whether soft tokens can be used to improve SFT itself, instead of as an avenue for latent reasoning. We introduce Soft Teacher Forcing (Soft-TF), a simple training algorithm that combines teacher-forced embeddings with soft tokens through random convex combinations. The soft tokens are computed in a single parallel forward pass over the ground-truth sequence. Soft-TF adds no parameters, no external model and no curriculum, and leaves inference unchanged. Experiments show that Soft-TF improves over SFT on GSM8K, MATH, MathQA and AQuA, by +2.1 to +4.1 points on GSM8K across seven Gemma, Llama and Mistral models.
authors: Mohammad Fahes, Cordelia Schmid, Anurag Arnab
bullets: Targets the underperformance and complexity of prior soft-token latent-reasoning methods.
Combines teacher-forced embeddings and soft tokens using random convex combinations.
Computes soft tokens in one parallel forward pass over the ground-truth sequence.
Requires no additional parameters, external model, or curriculum; inference remains unchanged.
Improves SFT across GSM8K, MATH, MathQA, and AQuA, including +2.1 to +4.1 GSM8K points across seven models.

We call this framework Soft Teacher Forcing (Soft-TF).

papers.abstract: Decision models such as Jev score candidate answers or actions. A small decision head trained label-free can recover about 99% of a frozen language model's multiple-choice accuracy while using only two-thirds of its transformer layers. It learns the full model's answer probabilities with KL divergence, without correct-answer labels for training. One backbone pass reads the question and all options together; the head returns probabilities for every option. We call this model FunDM (Fun Decision Model). Using 24 of Qwen3-8B's 36 layers and skipping the LM head, its +1T variant reaches 75.0% mean accuracy over eight benchmarks, versus 75.7% for the full model. On MMLU-Pro, both heads achieve 1.56 to 1.57 times batched vLLM throughput with about one-third lower peak GPU allocator memory. Both heads score higher than released Contrastive Language Models (CLM), fine-tuned CLM, and CLM-shaped heads trained from scratch on the eight multiple-choice benchmarks and coding-agent selection. Separately trained agent heads learn judge probabilities without pass/fail labels and select passing runs for 74.4 to 74.6 of 100 held-out tasks on average, versus 74 for the full-model judge and 52.0 for a CLM-shaped action-trained head. Code is available at: https://github.com/Ujjawal-K-Panchal/FunDM

On MMLU-Pro, it provides 1.56–1.57× batched throughput and about one-third lower peak GPU allocator memory.
Label-free agent heads select passing runs on 74.4–74.6 of 100 held-out tasks, outperforming a CLM-shaped action-trained head.

papers.abstract: Achieving complex, long-horizon robot behavior remains challenging because successful execution depends on skills grounded in a robot's physical affordances. Existing training-task distributions are often handcrafted or sampled from large language models (LLMs), relying on semantic plausibility rather than embodiment-specific feasibility. This mismatch can produce curricula that are too difficult, redundant, or blind to non-obvious but learnable behaviors. We propose Generative Flow on Symbolic Abstractions (FOSA), a framework for discovering embodiment-specific capabilities by learning a grounded task generator. FOSA parameterizes an abstract policy as a Generative Flow Network that constructs symbolic task skeletons. Each skeleton is compiled into a simulation environment, where low-level policy-learning performance provides the reward signal for the abstract policy. Across heterogeneous robot platforms, FOSA discovers diverse and executable tasks near the robot's empirical capability frontier. After distilling the discovered task policies into a single language-conditioned policy, FOSA improves performance on unseen complex and long-horizon tasks. The code and demonstration videos are available at https://www.youwei-yu.com/fosa.
authors: Youwei Yu, Lantao Liu
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between semantically plausible task curricula and tasks that are feasible for a robot’s physical embodiment.
Builds symbolic task skeletons with a Generative Flow Network and compiles them into simulation environments.
Uses low-level policy-learning performance as the reward for discovering tasks near each robot’s empirical capability frontier.
Works across heterogeneous robot platforms and finds diverse, executable behaviors.
Distilling the discovered policies into one language-conditioned policy improves performance on unseen complex, long-horizon tasks.

papers.abstract: Teleoperation is widely used to collect high-quality demonstrations for robot learning. Dexterous manipulation, however, requires coordinated control of motion and contact forces. Operators can specify motion, but struggle to reproduce the subtle force adjustments of human manipulation without feeling the robot's contacts. We introduce Force-Modulated Dexterity (FOMO-Dex), a unified compliance formulation for contact-rich manipulation. FOMO-Dex expresses nominal actions in coordinates defined by task geometry and contact structure. It applies force-driven motion corrections along selected directions while leaving the remaining command components unchanged. Across card picking, paper cutting, screwdriving, and nut-and-bolt assembly, FOMO-Dex reduces excessive contact forces compared with stiff control. A user study shows that operators collect more successful demonstration data per hour after brief practice. For policy learning, imitating the corrected actions improves card-picking success over imitating raw operator commands. Policies trained on FOMO-Dex demonstrations also achieve more rotation in nut-and-bolt manipulation and screwdriving than those trained on demonstrations collected with the stiff controller. Videos are shown on https://yingyuan0414.github.io/fomo-dex/ .
authors: Ying Yuan, David Held, Jitendra Malik, Haozhi Qi
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of reproducing subtle force adjustments during teleoperated dexterous manipulation.
Represents actions using task geometry and contact structure, then applies force-driven corrections only along selected directions.
Reduces excessive contact forces across card picking, paper cutting, screwdriving, and nut-and-bolt assembly compared with stiff control.
Helps operators collect more successful demonstrations per hour after brief practice.
Learning from corrected demonstrations improves card-picking success and rotational performance in nut-and-bolt manipulation and screwdriving.

figures.caption: Figure 2: System overview. A teleoperator or learned policy provides nominal arm and finger commands. FOMO-Dex uses feedback from the wrist force-torque sensor and the hand’s tactile and joint-torque sensors to adjust selected motion components before sending the commands to the robot.

Figure 3: Overview of the FOMO-Dex controller and its task-specific realizations. Task geometry and contact structure define interaction directions, along which force measurements are converted into unilateral or bilateral force errors. Direction-wise admittance then produces arm or hand motion corrections, enabling unilateral load relief, translational tool compliance, and multi-contact force regulation within the same formulation.

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) have emerged as a promising alternative for embodied intelligence by jointly predicting future world states and robot actions. However, their heavy visual encoding and iterative generative inference incur substantial latency, limiting their applicability to high-frequency closed-loop control. Existing training-free acceleration methods typically optimize a single stage, yielding limited speedups or degraded control under aggressive reuse. In this work, we systematically profile the inference overhead of WAMs and observe abundant redundancy across Transformer computation, diffusion denoising, and consecutive policy queries. However, the safe removal of such redundancy depends strongly on its impact on action prediction and control sensitivity. Based on these observations, we introduce \textbf{MARS}, a training-free and plug-and-play framework for multi-level WAM acceleration. MARS selectively removes low-impact attention computation, adaptively accelerates diffusion inference according to motion granularity, and speculatively reuses predicted future visual representations across consecutive queries with online verification. Together, these complementary mechanisms provide remarkable acceleration while limiting approximation error. Extensive experiments across LIBERO, LIBERO-PRO, and RoboCasa show that MARS achieves up to $4.00\times$, $3.94\times$, and $2.10\times$ end-to-end speedups, respectively, while maintaining task success rate close to the original policy. Moreover, MARS generalizes across different model backbones and across simulation and real-robot experiments, substantially improving the efficiency--performance trade-off of WAM inference. Our code is available at https://github.com/PKU-VaLuE-Lab/MARS.
authors: Zengyuan Zuo, Yongchang Zhang, Guangyu Zhao, Tianze Zhang, Biao Wu, Meng Fang, Yiwu Zhong
bullets: WAMs are slowed by heavy visual encoding, iterative diffusion inference, and repeated policy queries, limiting high-frequency control.
MARS is training-free and plug-and-play, targeting redundancy in Transformer attention, diffusion denoising, and consecutive queries.
It removes low-impact attention computation, adapts diffusion effort to motion granularity, and reuses future visual features with online verification.
Experiments on LIBERO, LIBERO-PRO, and RoboCasa report up to 4.00×, 3.94×, and 2.10× speedups, respectively.
The approach transfers across model backbones and simulation-to-real-robot settings, though its scope is demonstrated on the evaluated WAM tasks and systems.

figures.caption: Figure 1: WAM inference and acceleration overview. (a) The overall pipeline of a World Action Model. (b) Efficiency-performance comparison in LIBERO-PRO (Zhou et al., 2025), where our method substantially reduces latency and FLOPs with a better efficiency–performance trade-off.

Figure 3: The framework of MARS. MARS is a training-free and plug-and-play framework that accelerates WAM inference at three complementary levels. At the Transformer level, it skips lowimpact cross-attention branches and prunes low-importance self-attention heads. At the diffusion level, it uses the provisional action to estimate the motion granularity type and selects one-step generation or the multi-step solver with residual reuse. At the cross-query level, it reuses the predicted future visual tokens when they are sufficiently consistent with the observed visual changes.
Figure 5: Qualitative examples where our method improves task completion. Representative comparisons in LIBERO and LIBERO-PRO where Ours (Acc.) succeeds while the original Cosmos Policy fails.

We find that cross-attention branches at early-to-middle layers exhibit low scores (e.g., blocks 2–11) and only few attention heads show high scores (e.g., yellow entries). (b) Analysis 2: Relative L1 differences between denoising steps and the first denoising step. The denoising input varies substantially across steps, whereas the denoising output and DiT residual remain relatively stable. (c) Analysis 3: Comparison of observed and predicted images. The prediction closely matches the observation with minor variations.

papers.abstract: Dynamic spatial audio reasoning requires a model to associate changing acoustic observations with the correct source and recover its spatial state at a queried time or interval, a challenge intensified by overlapping speech and source motion. To study this problem, we introduce Sonic-Bench, comprising 2.8K first-order Ambisonics clips and 28.8K target-specific question-answer pairs across 480 simulated indoor scenes. The benchmark covers localization, distance estimation, and motion reasoning in single- and dual-source settings. We further propose SonicWorld, which integrates physical, learned acoustic, and semantic features into persistent source states through learned transitions and recurrent updates, and projects them into an Omni LLM for spatial reasoning. Compared with Spatial-Omni on the Sonic-Bench test split, SonicWorld improves direction accuracy from 31.98% to 34.69% and reduces azimuth error from 57.22{\deg} to 48.01{\deg}. In zero-shot transfer to Spatial LibriSpeech, SonicWorld retains strong localization performance, achieving 73.98% direction accuracy and 19.29{\deg} azimuth error, compared with 27.14% and 70.74{\deg} for Spatial-Omni.
authors: Chenlong Wei, Hanling Wang, Mingjin Lou, Yufan Shi, Yandong Sun, Sheldon Yu, Xiaohui Zhu, Xiaobo Jin, Yiwei Wang

Covers source localization, distance estimation, and motion reasoning in single- and dual-source settings.
Combines physical, learned acoustic, and semantic features with learned transitions and recurrent updates, then feeds source states into an Omni LLM.
On Sonic-Bench, improves direction accuracy and azimuth error over Spatial-Omni.
Transfers zero-shot to Spatial LibriSpeech while retaining strong localization performance.

papers.abstract: Tool-augmented language models ground their responses in external tool outputs, improving reliability beyond parametric knowledge alone. However, even when the correct tool is called and returns accurate information, models may still contradict such outputs, omit critical details, or generate unsupported claims. Existing hallucination benchmarks for tool-augmented dialogue primarily focus on the tool-calling stage, evaluating whether the correct tool and arguments are selected, while overlooking errors that arise during post-tool response generation. To address this gap, we introduce ToolHACE, a span-level benchmark for hallucination detection in tool-augmented LLM responses, covering five fine-grained hallucination categories. Through extensive experiments with modern hallucination detectors, we show that post-tool-call hallucinations are widespread and remain challenging to detect. Our results further demonstrate that effective detection requires training on specialized tool-augmented corpora, while transfer from tool-agnostic hallucination datasets performs poorly in this setting. These findings highlight the need for dedicated benchmarks and models for reliable hallucination detection in tool-augmented language systems.
authors: Nikolay Ivanov, Sergey Pletenev, Elisei Rykov, Anatolii Frolov, Bogdan Monogov, Alexander Potekhin, Maria Marina, Daniil Moskovskiy, Viktor Moskvoretskii, Alexander Panchenko, Ilseyar Alimova
bullets: Targets post-tool response errors such as contradictions, omissions, and unsupported claims.
Covers five fine-grained hallucination categories at the span level.
Experiments find post-tool hallucinations are widespread and challenging for current detectors.
Detectors trained on specialized tool-augmented data outperform transfer from tool-agnostic hallucination datasets.
Scope: focuses on hallucination detection after tool calls, not tool selection or argument accuracy.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Dataset generation pipeline. ToolACE dialogues are split into single-hop and multi-hop traces. Hallucinations are collected through LLM-based synthetic edits, programmatic JSON perturbations, and naturally occurring (wild) generations from small LLMs. The resulting examples are filtered by multiple judges and subsequently refined through quality-control, split isolation, and normalization.

Figure 3: Examples of Route B Hallucination Insertion in ToolHACE. Type 1a (Answer Mismatch): individual leaf values in the tool response are replaced with random values from other samples—each field is corrupted independently. Type 1b (Answer Mismatch): all values within a JSON subtree are replaced together, preserving sibling branches. Type 2 (Overgeneration): fields are deleted from the tool response, causing the model to fabricate values it can no longer ground. Type 3 (Missing Tool): the model appends a factually unsupported sentence referencing context absent from the tool response.

Figure 1: Main types of generation errors in toolaugmented LLM responses. A model can produce a correct answer, contradict the tool output, add unsupported information, omit a tool-provided fact, or introduce an unrelated tool/action request.

papers.title: ToolHACE: A Dataset for Detecting Hallucinations in Tool-Based LLM Responses
papers.tldr: ToolHACE is a span-level benchmark showing that hallucinations after correct tool use are common, difficult to detect, and require tool-specific training.

papers.abstract: Full-duplex spoken language models (FD-SLMs) support simultaneous listening and speaking, but often lag behind half-duplex spoken language models (HD-SLMs) in general capabilities. We propose Dialogue-to-Duplex (D2), a framework that converts pretrained HD-SLMs into high-capability FD-SLMs at fine temporal granularity. D2 adapts the original audio encoder to streaming through decoder-free representation distillation and learns full-duplex interaction through supervised fine-tuning. We systematically study the effects of chunk size on full-duplex interaction, general capabilities, and inference computation. We apply D2 to two distinct HD-SLM architectures, Qwen3-Omni and LLaMA-Omni 2. At a 12.5Hz update rate, Qwen3-Omni-D2 achieves 99.2% turn-taking success with 521-ms latency, 99.5% interruption success, and a state-of-the-art VoiceBench score of 70.1.
authors: Cheng-Kuang Chang, Alexander H. Liu, Brian Kingsbury, Hilde Kuehne, Rogerio Feris, Samuel Thomas, James Glass, Kai-Wei Chang
bullets: Addresses the capability gap between full-duplex and half-duplex spoken language models.
Uses decoder-free representation distillation to make the audio encoder streamable, followed by supervised fine-tuning for duplex interaction.
Studies how chunk size affects interaction quality, general capabilities, and inference computation.
Applied to Qwen3-Omni and LLaMA-Omni 2; Qwen3-Omni-D2 reaches 99.2% turn-taking success, 521 ms latency, and 99.5% interruption success at 12.5 Hz.
Qwen3-Omni-D2 achieves a VoiceBench score of 70.1, reported as state of the art.

papers.selection_reason: Converts half-duplex spoken language models into full-duplex multimodal LLMs, fitting multimodal LLM extension.
papers.title: D2: High-Capability Full-Duplex Spoken Language Models from Half-Duplex Backbones
papers.tldr: D2 converts half-duplex spoken language models into capable, low-latency full-duplex models that can listen and speak simultaneously.

papers.abstract: Frontier large language models (LLMs) now reason about space well enough to program robots, yet the world models behind robot policies are implicit, held in network weights or predicted video, and cannot be inspected or corrected directly. We present D-World, an explicit world-language-action model built on the Sense, Plan and Act decomposition. A perception agent writes the scene as an executable digital twin using generated vision and geometry code. A planning agent searches for actions in simulation and, after each executed action chunk, revises the twin's object states and named physical parameters against what the robot measured. A parameter revision is accepted only if replaying the latest chunk does not increase any measured residual beyond its tolerance, and every chunk is checked in the updated twin before it runs. Structural mismatches return to perception for reconstruction. We call this measurement-grounded cycle of correction and revision recursive self-improvement (RSI), in which the LLM stays frozen while the world it acts in improves. We model the choice of actions that both advance the task and expose model error as a dual control problem and show that the cost of incorporating evidence into the twin sets the threshold at which probing pays, so cheap local revision counteracts the turn-off of cautious controllers. Each episode runs a real-to-sim-to-real loop, and its recorded twins can be refitted and re-rendered offline into higher-fidelity environments for post-training. Because perception and planning communicate only through the twin and language, either can be replaced by a learned model, and since inference dominates the loop, the loop speeds up with faster models. On a dual-arm robot, towel and toaster tasks show local revisions, such as one reducing the bread's rendered-depth residual from 22.4 to 1.5 mm, that let execution continue without reconstruction.
authors: Xuan Wen, Baichao Wang
bullets: Addresses the opacity and lack of direct correction in implicit robot world models.
Uses a Sense–Plan–Act architecture where perception builds an executable scene twin and planning searches for actions in simulation.
Revises object states and physical parameters after each action chunk, accepting updates only when replayed measurements remain within residual tolerances.
Frames information-seeking actions as dual control, balancing task progress with exposing and correcting model errors.
Demonstrates real-to-sim-to-real operation on dual-arm towel and toaster tasks, including local corrections that avoid full scene reconstruction.

figures.caption: Figure 1: D-World, an explicit world-language-action model. Implicit models (left) keep the world in network weights or predicted video. D-World (right) writes it as an executable twin. SENSE constructs the twin, PLAN proposes trajectories and twin revisions, and a gate checks each action chunk before execution. Measurements of the real robot drive state correction and replay-checked parameter revision (RSI), and the dashed path requests reconstruction. In a bread-grasp episode, the twin shows both grippers open, ACTION shows the robot holding a lifted bread slice, and the measurement pair compares this post-lift observation with the reconstructed twin. In the language channel, PLAN asks and SENSE answers.

Figure 2: Replay-checked revision after a failed lift. In a failed bread grasp, the real bread remains in its rack while the twin lifts it with the gripper. Reducing the modeled thickness reproduces the slip during replay and reduces both the depth and the closure residual. Friction, to which this chunk is insensitive, is left unchanged. The revision passes the non-regression check and is accepted, and the next chunk attempts another grasp without reconstruction. Here j is the latest executed round and t the revision round. An earlier thickness proposal had increased the residual on the preceding chunk and was rejected.

Figure 3: Towel handling. (a) The top row shows camera images and the initial twin rendered from the same cameras, and the bottom row selected interaction and reconstruction stages, numbered by chunk. Dashed outlines mark the grasp mismatch between the twin and the robot, after which reconstruction changes the towel representation to match its observed configuration. (b) Where the time goes in the same episode. SENSE is blue, lighter while it answers a question, PLAN is orange, and the robot’s chunks are green with the numbers of (a). The bottom lanes magnify the three chunks between the two reconstructions. Model inference fills almost the entire hour, whereas the robot moves for seconds per chunk.

Figure 4: From episodes to high-fidelity worlds. (a) Each episode records observations, twins, controls and revisions. (b) Versioned libraries collect agent-written skills, such as perception and motion primitives, and scene bodies from completed episodes, whose parameters RSI has validated against the robot’s measurements. (c) Offline, recorded chunks are replayed jointly to refit parameters, and the refitted twin is rendered again with the same geometry, here in MuJoCo and in Blender. Skills and assets can be reused in later episodes, and refitted twins can serve post-training.

papers.selection_reason: Explicit world-language-action model with digital-twin self-improvement for robot manipulation and planning.
papers.title: D-World: An Explicit World-Language-Action Model with Recursive Self-Improvement under Dual Control
papers.tldr: D-World enables robots to improve an explicit, inspectable digital twin through measurement-grounded planning and execution, without updating the underlying LLM.

papers.abstract: Existing embodied navigation tasks commonly assume that traversability and object states remain fixed during an episode. Yet reaching a goal may require opening a door to access a room and then opening a container to reveal a hidden target. We formulate interactive navigation beyond reachability, unifying channel-induced changes in spatial connectivity, container-induced changes in target visibility, and their sequential dependencies. We introduce MultINav-Bench, a 3K-episode ObjectGoal benchmark in MolmoSpaces spanning channel, container, and mixed tasks, with interaction-necessity annotations covering required and unnecessary episodes. Its data generation pipeline automates task construction across multiple task types. The evaluation protocol separately measures navigation success, interaction effectiveness, and cost. We further propose MultINav-Agent, a three-stage agentic framework built on a persistent, state-conditioned interaction graph. Semantic interactive perception grounds entities and interaction states; a vision-language model selects task-relevant actions based on expected changes in connectivity and target observability; and post-interaction verification updates the graph to guide subsequent navigation, exploration, or interaction. Experiments on MultINav-Bench show that MultINav-Agent consistently outperforms adapted baselines across channel, container, and mixed tasks.
authors: Delun Li, Xueyao Wei, Rui Chen, Yifei Wang, Junzhi Yu, Wenjie Song, Xingyu Chen
bullets: Models navigation where interactions change spatial connectivity, target visibility, or both sequentially.
Introduces MultINav-Bench, a 3K-episode ObjectGoal benchmark covering channel, container, and mixed tasks with interaction-necessity annotations.
Evaluates navigation success, interaction effectiveness, and interaction cost separately.
Proposes MultINav-Agent with interactive perception, expected-change action selection, and post-interaction graph verification.
Reports consistent improvements over adapted baselines across all task types.

papers.abstract: Unified multimodal models (UMMs) provide an interface for interleaved text-image generation, where generated visual states can directly inform subsequent reasoning and synthesis. However, existing systems are still primarily demonstrated on short trajectories or simplified visual content. We develop a large UMM natively trained on interleaved multimodal data, with strong capabilities in image synthesis, text rendering, complex composition, and multimodal planning, and study how to extend these native capabilities to substantially longer autoregressive trajectories. The main challenge is that generated images continuously accumulate in context: irrelevant or imperfect visual states interfere with future synthesis, while previously established characters and scenes must still be recovered after long intervals. We introduce a visual-memory framework that maintains persistent visual references, selectively retrieves scene-relevant historical states while preserving the complete semantic history, and uses few-step self-rollout to adapt the model to imperfect generated histories. We further introduce LongMIG-Bench for evaluating long-horizon text-to-multi-image and image-to-multi-image generation. Our model achieves high-fidelity long-horizon interleaved generation with strong character and scene consistency, demonstrating how visual memory can scale native interleaved generation to substantially longer trajectories.
authors: Ziqiao Peng, Yutao Cui, Wang Lin, Zhong-Yu Li, Qingwen Gu, Tianhui Song, Chengyou Jia, Guozhen Zhang, Xuerui Qiu, Qixun Wang, Miles Yang, Zhao Zhong, Yonglong Tian, Hongyan Liu, Jun He

papers.abstract: Knowledge-based Visual Question Answering (VQA) requires reasoning that extends beyond visible image content, demanding external commonsense and factual knowledge. While recent work leverages Large Language Models (LLMs) as knowledge sources, the question of how deeply such guidance should be integrated into a vision language architecture remains underexplored. In this work, we generate structured reasoning guidance, visual focus concepts, distractor elements and external knowledge using Llama~3.3~70B and systematically compare two integration strategies within a unified frozen ViT + FLAN-T5 framework on the OK-VQA benchmark: decision level late fusion and attention-matrix injection. Contrary to the prevailing assumption that deeper integration is superior, we find that shallow late fusion achieves the strongest results (39.4% exact match, +10.0 over the no guidance baseline), outperforming deep attention modification (31.8%) under data scarce fine-tuning. We further contribute an LLM based augmentation pipeline that expands training data more than tenfold via question paraphrasing. Our findings indicate that integration depth must be matched to the data regime.
authors: Aneerban Saha, Vijay Kumar, Sameer Madhav D., Priyam Srivastava, Dhruv Bansal
bullets: Studies how deeply LLM-generated knowledge should be integrated into vision-language models for knowledge-based VQA.
Uses Llama 3.3 70B to generate reasoning guidance, visual focus concepts, distractors, and external knowledge.
Compares late decision-level fusion with attention-matrix injection in a frozen ViT + FLAN-T5 framework on OK-VQA.
Late fusion achieves 39.4% exact match, 10.0 points above the no-guidance baseline, versus 31.8% for deep attention modification.
Introduces an LLM-based question-paraphrasing pipeline that expands training data more than tenfold; results suggest integration depth should match the data regime.

papers.title: Rethinking LLM-Guided Visual Question Answering: Does Deeper Knowledge Integration Really Help?
papers.tldr: For knowledge-based VQA under data-scarce fine-tuning, shallow LLM guidance via late fusion outperforms deeper attention-based integration.

papers.abstract: Clinical decisions depend on anticipating how a patient's condition will evolve as treatment is adjusted and new evidence becomes available. Existing medical world models capture patient-state evolution, but often define the evolving state around a particular modality or task, limiting reuse as inputs or prediction targets change. These models also retain history through observation sequences or recurrent or latent summaries rather than exposing preceding patient states and clinical actions as an ordered transition context. This distinction matters because similar current measurements may follow different recent changes, treatment exposures, and observed responses. To tackle these limitations, we propose PatientWM, a clinical world-model framework built around a unified patient state and sequential latent history. Availability-aware encoders integrate observations available at each decision time into the patient state, while typed decoders produce task-specific clinical readouts without defining the state around any single target. PatientWM further conditions each next-state prediction on the current state and supplied action together with a bounded, ordered history of preceding latent patient states and clinical actions, preserving recent treatment and response context. Experiments across MIMIC-III, MIMIC-IV, and three external clinical datasets show superior performance in clinical prediction, multi-step forecasting, and action-planning evaluation. Transfer experiments further demonstrate the generalizability of PatientWM's patient state. Together, these results establish its ability to forecast clinical evolution and support planning.
authors: Ziwen Kan, Jie Peng, Bo Yan, Davis Hobley, Zheng Zhang, Yu Tian, Tianlong Chen, Song Wang
bullets: Addresses the limited reuse of modality- or task-specific clinical world models.
Builds unified patient states from observations available at each decision time.

Predicts next states from the current state, clinical action, and bounded history of prior states and actions.
Shows strong performance across clinical prediction, multi-step forecasting, action planning, and transfer evaluations.

papers.abstract: Neural operator splitting composes a library of neural operators, one per physical mechanism, into zero-shot simulators of new equations. Existing approaches, however, require these mechanisms and their labels to be specified in advance. We ask whether a pretrained library can instead be adapted and grown from unlabeled trajectories in which multiple mechanisms act simultaneously. We introduce SPLICE, a framework that discovers operators without mechanism labels on mixture data. The contributions of the candidate operators to each trajectory are inferred by solving a convex optimization problem. A calibrated test then assigns each discovered operator the mechanism it implements. Failure cases are also detectable, when the library lacks the required physics or when mechanisms are insufficiently separable. Across one and two dimensional systems, the discovered operators recover mechanisms from unlabeled mixtures and compose into zero-shot simulators of unseen equations; a frozen library can also grow an operator for physics absent from pretraining, without labels and without forgetting. On Navier-Stokes, the discovered operators compose about as accurately as their supervised counterparts.
authors: Lucas Thil, Jesse Read, Guillaume Doquet, Rim Kaddah
bullets: Removes the need to predefine mechanisms and labels when adapting neural operator libraries.
Infers each candidate operator’s contribution using convex optimization, then assigns mechanisms with a calibrated test.
Detects failures when required physics is missing or mechanisms cannot be sufficiently separated.
Recovers mechanisms from unlabeled mixtures and composes them into zero-shot simulators of unseen equations.
Can add previously unseen physics without labels or forgetting; on Navier–Stokes, performance is about as accurate as supervised counterparts.

figures.caption: Figure 2: The shared architecture and where each stage acts. (a) Every library entry is one learned time-stepper, in which an encoder maps a context window to a code θ, a hypernetwork turns θ into the weights of a vector field fθ , and RK4 advances one step, so one region of code space is one operator. (b) Build trains the library on labeled pure-mechanism trajectories. (c) Adapt and Grow alternate a convex assignment (w-step) with operator refinement (ϕ-step) on unlabeled mixtures, and reseed an operator from the worst-reconstructed window. (d) Compose beam-searches Strang compositions of library operators. (e) Identify grades each discovered operator against reference solvers on a fixed probe set. Blue nodes are data; grey nodes are learned modules.

Figure 1: The SPLICE pipeline. Build trains one operator per labeled effect and composes them, following Serrano et al. (2026); Adapt, Grow, and Identify are ours. Adapt learns operators from unlabeled trajectories, and Grow adds an operator when the data reveal dynamics the library cannot express. Identify tests each learned operator against reference solvers used only for evaluation, never for training. At test time, a beam search selects which operators of the library to compose for each unseen equation.

Figure 3: Zero-shot composition with a label-free library.Left: exact solution (top), rollout composed from discovered operators (middle) and their difference (bottom), at four times of a 60-step rollout on a coupled flow never seen in training (1282). Reading each column from top to bottom, the positions and shapes of the vortices match throughout, and the error grows mainly in intensity. The true flow fades because viscosity and drag dissipate its energy; the composed rollout does not, because the beam selects only advection operators and each operator normalizes the amplitude of its input window, so this dissipation is not represented (Appendix C.3). Right: similarity between mechanism actions, for exact (top) and discovered (bottom) operators. Euler is nearly orthogonal to the overlapping smoothing mechanisms, hence identifiable (§5.6).

Figure 5: Rollouts on three held-out 1D mixtures (§5.3): ground truth; oracle operators; discovered library LSSL; absolute error (shared scale). Top: advection+diffusion, cleanly reproduced (0.094). Middle: a traveling advection+nonlinear case, where the discovered library reproduces the transport (0.076). Bottom: an advection+dispersion case at the dispersion-limited boundary (0.147): the discovered rollout cannot travel because the residual transport there is dispersion-driven and dispersion is the rarest mechanism in the discovered pool (Appendix C.3).

papers.abstract: Generative policies such as diffusion models provide expressive data-driven priors for robot behavior, yet the situations a robot faces at execution time rarely match its training data and impose constraints and objectives the policy never learned. Existing inference-time guidance methods either rely on gradients that can push samples away from the learned prior, or on sampling procedures that can be inefficient, collapse modes, or average them into out-of-distribution predictions. We introduce MOSAIC, a mode- and support-aware framework for gradient-free inference-time control of robotic diffusion models. MOSAIC treats the initial noise and all stochastic reverse-step perturbations as a joint input to the pretrained denoising process and adapts a distribution over this input using importance weights computed from fully denoised outputs. Physical feasibility and consistency with the learned support are balanced using adaptive penalties, while mode-wise importance-weighted updates preserve modes and avoid destructive averaging. The same formulation can jointly steer multiple independently trained diffusion models through shared coupling costs, enabling coordinated behavior without requiring a joint model. We evaluate MOSAIC on navigation, dexterous grasping, motion planning with unseen geometry, and collaborative box manipulation with independently trained robot priors. Across these settings, MOSAIC adapts and composes frozen diffusion priors under new deployment constraints without retraining.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models show strong potential for end-to-end autonomous driving by leveraging world knowledge and understanding to excel in long-tail scenarios. However, current VLAs have two limitations: 1) Degeneration into vision-action (VA) models. For low latency, regression/flow-based methods directly generate actions but underuse VLM understanding, causing unsafe, unexplainable actions. 2) Autoregressive high latency. Autoregressive methods sequentially generate chain-of-thought (CoT) and action tokens, fully leveraging VLM understanding, but high latency hinders deployment. To enable low-latency deployment while using CoT to assist action generation, we propose AUGUstus, an Autonomous-driving VLA model with Unified Generation and Understanding. We unify diffusion-based action generation and autoregressive CoT understanding in one model, where understanding only serves generation. Joint CoT supervision preserves VLM spatial understanding in shared representation for safer, more accurate trajectories. AUGUstus-mode orders action generation before CoT, so CoT supervises reliable actions during training while inference needs only action output, enabling low latency. AUGUstus-GRPO, a unified GRPO algorithm, jointly optimizes action and CoT, improving action performance. Experiments show AUGUstus achieves 94.6 PDMS on NAVSIMv1 and 90.7 EPDMS on NAVSIMv2, SOTA planning without scorer module. On nuScenes, it achieves average L2 error 0.27 m and average collision rate 0.05%, best among compared methods. To validate AUGUstus practicality, we train on in-house data with 512 NVIDIA H800 GPUs for ~2 days, evaluate on an internal 1,000 km dataset, and preliminarily deploy on a real vehicle, achieving 12 Hz operation. papers.abstract: Offline reinforcement learning aims to learn effective policies from fixed datasets without environment interaction. Although generative models such as diffusion and flow matching enhance policy expressiveness, they typically start from uninformative Gaussian noise and generate actions through multi-step iteration, leading to high computational costs and failing to effectively leverage suboptimal trajectories in datasets. We propose MeanFlow2Better (MF2B), which reformulates offline RL as generative decision chunk optimization from current performance status to better performance status in a high-level latent decision space. MF2B maps trajectory chunks to high-level latent decision representations through an encoder, placing generation starting points within a structured decision space sculpted by behavioral data. The model learns a shared conditional mean velocity field in this space, constructing two flow mappings: from Gaussian-Induced Decision Sources toward positive behavioral decision regions, and from suboptimal decisions toward high-value decision regions. Both flow mappings complete decision refinement through one-step ODE integration over the unit time interval $\Delta t=1$, requiring neither multi-step iterative sampling nor backpropagation through time. Furthermore, we propose hierarchical chunk-level advantage to guide the flow direction toward high-return regions, where the high-level decisions cover multiple low-level actions, leading to sequence length compression from $T$ to $K \approx T/H$ and significantly lower computational overhead. On the D4RL Gym-MuJoCo benchmark, MF2B achieves an average score of 90.91, matching or surpassing strong baselines.

papers.abstract: Visual in-context learning (ICL) enables vision-language models (VLMs) to adapt at test time via demonstration examples, but its effectiveness depends critically on the examples selected. Recent counterfactual selection methods improve ICL by constructing demonstrations that expose how individual attribute changes affect the answer. However, they require multi-stage pipelines involving attribute extraction, caption engineering, and composed image matching. We propose a simpler alternative grounded in a key observation: a model's own prediction errors are natural counterfactual demonstrations that directly encode its failure modes. Our method, SMILE (Self-Mined Visual In-Context Learning from Errors), builds a model-specific pool of hard negatives offline by recording the target VLM's own mistakes. At test time, the prediction serves as a direction signal that surfaces, in the semantic embedding space, the past mistakes most likely to recur for the current query. This prediction-conditioned identification provides a unified mechanism for both closed-set classification and open-ended visual question answering without task-specific design. Across four benchmarks and four VLMs, SMILE delivers an average task-score gain of +3.09 points over the SOTA baseline at 5x lower latency. Project page: https://tree-shu-zhao.github.io/SMILE/
authors: Shu Zhao, Tan Yu
bullets: Visual ICL depends heavily on selecting effective demonstrations, while prior counterfactual methods require complex multi-stage pipelines.

The same mechanism supports both closed-set classification and open-ended visual question answering without task-specific design.
Across four benchmarks and four VLMs, SMILE gains an average of 3.09 task-score points over the SOTA baseline with 5× lower latency.

papers.abstract: Studying event memory requires defining events and their relationships within remembered experience. Autobiographical narratives provide evidence of this organization, but their analytical units must first be established. This study introduces a large language model framework for constructing event representations from narratives and modeling their structure and dynamics with excerpt-level traceability. Explicit boundary rules and a feature schema informed by hippocampal models of episodic memory and navigation guide event construction. In a proof-of-concept application to interviews from five participants, the framework constructed 256 event-states. Multiple correspondence analysis embedded these states in feature-based spaces, with analyses focused on a selected 4-D geometry and 10-D and 13-D reference geometries. Consecutive event-states were significantly closer than expected under randomized narrative order. In the selected 4-D ten-basin solution, similarity between basin-state feature profiles corresponded with similarity between one-step routing profiles; context, mechanism, and theme differentiated full-system pathway engagement. A successor representation modeled expected basin-state occupancy across successive steps. Correlations between basin-centroid distances and complete successor-profile distances were positive across all five basin solutions, with exploratory tests supporting correspondence in at least two solutions across all three geometries. These findings connect feature-based event representations with observed narrative transitions and modeled multistep organization. The framework translates hippocampal principles into source-linked event boundaries and state representations, providing an analytical basis for testing neural accounts of event segmentation and predictive organization during naturalistic recall.

papers.abstract: Physical AI is commonly formulated around an explicitly specified task: given a goal or instruction, a system perceives, reasons, and acts. In many real-world settings, however, important tasks emerge from continuously changing world states before a person explicitly formulates them. We study this complementary problem as Proactive Physical AI, where an AI system continuously observes the physical world, identifies situations that warrant intervention, and initiates appropriate actions at the right time. We develop ProAgent, an end-to-end system built around two components: a Jev-style proactive timing model (dubbed StreamingJev) that determines whether and when intervention is needed, and a Response Model that generates responses for people or invokes available device capabilities for physical execution. To support learning at scale, we develop an automated data pipeline that converts videos into supervision for proactive timing. Experiments demonstrate strong proactive performance under both explicit objectives and standing roles, combining more accurate intervention timing with fewer false triggers than the source-backbone baseline. Real-robot evaluations further demonstrate ProAgent's ability to identify emerging needs and translate them into appropriate physical actions.
authors: Zhenhua Yang, Jiafeng Liang, Xingyu Zhou, Yi Jiang, Xiayu Cao, Zui Chen, Luqi Wang, Haiyang Sun, Yufei Xiang, Chang Li, Rongchuan Mu, Bowen Chi, Zihe Tong, Mingyu Li, Huijie Ma, Yiqiao Yang, Baoqi Ren, Zhiming Ma, Zhihao Zhu, Jiahao Ji, Zhuoyao Wang, Qianyu Wang, Xiangyu Liu, Wang Zixiang, Shunliang Zhang, Ming Liu, Xiaocheng Feng, Duyu Tang, Bing Qin

papers.abstract: How do language models reconcile conflicting contextual evidence within a prompt? We study this question using lexical redefinition, where an explicit instruction specifies how a word should be interpreted and a subsequent sentence provides additional evidence through its usage. Across 870 word pairs, we find that lexical redefinitions are not applied as fixed rules. Instead, the behaviour depends systematically on the relationship between the explicit instruction and the intervening sentence: the contextualised usage can preserve, weaken, or completely reverse the instruction. These results suggest that the interpretation of an explicit instruction remains sensitive to subsequent contextual evidence. Lexical redefinition therefore provides a controlled behavioural paradigm for studying how language models integrate multiple sources of information within a prompt.
authors: Roksana Goworek, Haim Dubossarsky
bullets: Studies how models reconcile conflicting evidence within prompts.
Uses lexical redefinition: an instruction assigns a word’s meaning, followed by a sentence using the word.
Evaluates 870 word pairs across different relationships between the instruction and intervening sentence.
Finds that redefinitions are not applied as fixed rules; subsequent context systematically changes their effect.
Proposes lexical redefinition as a controlled paradigm for studying prompt-level information integration.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in multimodal foundation models, exemplified by GPT-6 Astra, raise the prospect of general-purpose embodied reasoning and planning. Using Internet videos for embodied pretraining calls for reliable physical-scale annotations. Yet visual geometry foundation models often recover scene structure and camera motion without reliable metric scale. We show that uncertain size priors of familiar objects can jointly constrain a reconstruction's shared scale. Building on this insight, we present UniMetric, a universal and training-free metric scale recovery framework for geometry foundation models, without additional sensors or task-specific metric supervision. Specifically, Metric Prior Acquisition elicits object height intervals from a vision-language model. Semantic-Geometric Alignment measures reconstructed object heights along the estimated support-surface normal in each frame and converts the priors into scale intervals. Global Scale Recovery reconciles these intervals through a convex objective, yielding a jointly feasible scale when they overlap and a unique compromise otherwise. The estimated sequence-level scale is applied uniformly to reconstructed points and camera translations. Controlled experiments with real VLM priors show that combining observations improves scale accuracy with exact relative object heights. To evaluate metric accuracy on GFM reconstructions without ground-truth scale alignment, we introduce MetricBench, covering twelve embodied, driving, and roadside subsets with sensor-derived ground truth. Across nine geometry foundation models, UniMetric reduces mean depth Abs Rel, reconstruction Chamfer distance, and trajectory error by 54.2%, 83.8%, and 65.6%, respectively, improving every model on all three tasks at the suite level. We release the UniMetric code and MetricBench data.
authors: Lei Yang, Yuner Zhang, Ziyang Liu, Ziying Song, Kai WU, Yiyang Gao, Jiangtao Su, Yiming Li

Introduces MetricBench, a sensor-grounded benchmark spanning 12 embodied, driving, and roadside subsets.

Across nine geometry foundation models, reduces mean depth Abs Rel, Chamfer distance, and trajectory error by 54.2%, 83.8%, and 65.6%, respectively. In scope: requires familiar objects with usable size priors and overlapping or reconcilable scale constraints.

papers.abstract: Large audio-language models (LALMs) are fast becoming a general interface to sound, yet how far their broad pretraining carries into specialized domains remains largely open. Vessel monitoring, maritime safety, and ocean sensing all depend on recognizing underwater signals, but to our knowledge LALMs have not been systematically evaluated on them. Annotated recordings are costly to collect, and a faithful synthetic alternative has to bring together many interacting factors: the structure of detection pulses, communication waveforms, and ship-radiated noise, and the sound-speed profile, geometry, and multipath propagation through which each reaches the receiver. We address this by proposing \textbf{UA-Bench}, to our knowledge the first large-scale benchmark for evaluating LALMs on underwater acoustic signal recognition. It comprises 375,051 audio records that couple parameterized sources with modeled propagation, so that every record can be traced to the conditions that produced it. The records span these three signal families, and each carries a three-level label hierarchy (13 leaf classes), a templated multi-turn dialogue, and source and channel metadata. We evaluate on a balanced 2,600-record subset with a gated coarse-to-fine protocol that locates each error at source routing, fine-grained classification, or output format, and add a paired silent-audio control to test whether the waveform is actually used. Nine open LALMs, evaluated without task-specific adaptation, reach only 2.0\%--13.1\% leaf accuracy, against a random reference of 7.7\%. The waveform helps source routing far more than leaf recognition (for one model, +29.5 versus +2.3 points over silence), and just four models gain reliably at the leaf level, by at most 4.7 points. UA-Bench thus gives a reference point for these models, and its released training partition supports follow-up adaptation work.
authors: Zhe Sun, Liang An, Jiayu Yao, Ronglai Qian, Jianing Cai, Ziwei Huang, Qing Fan, Zhiyuan Yang, Yujun Cai, Hongli Cao, Yiwei Wang, Xiaoyan Wang

papers.abstract: Recent work has investigated Omni-modal Large Language Models (OLLMs), models which can take multiple modalities and their combinations as input, as a way forward to have systems really capable of interacting with their environment. Uncertainty quantification (UQ) for OLLMs, however, remains an open problem: existing methods largely target at most two modalities at a time, require access to model internals, or re-invocation of the evaluated model. We propose a model-agnostic UQ framework that scores a Chain-of-Thought response entirely through external omni-modal embeddings, measuring the grounding of the reasoning in the multimodal input and its internal coherence. Our contribution is the family of signals and an empirical characterisation of when it is reliable, rather than any single estimator: we find the geometric scores to be largely redundant with one another (mean within-split rank correlation 0.91-0.94) but strongly complementary to answer-dispersion baselines, and their reliability to depend on the generator and the modality. The resulting confidence estimates require no access to logits, hidden states or gradients of the evaluated model and no additional inference from it; they do require segmenting the reasoning trace with an auxiliary model and, for the aggregated score, a labelled calibration set that we show can be as small as 25 examples (although we also show that such a set buys little over fixing one signal a priori). On UNO-Bench, with both a closed and an open model, our scores yield small gains over self-consistency (systematic with the closed generator, mixed with the open one) and are competitive with self-verbalisation and internal-state baselines, especially in open-ended, omni-modal questions where previous state-of-the-art baselines struggle.

bullets: Targets uncertainty quantification for inputs combining multiple modalities, beyond methods limited to two modalities.

On UNO-Bench, results provide small, systematic gains over self-consistency for a closed model and mixed gains for an open model, while remaining competitive with other baselines.
Requires an auxiliary model to segment reasoning traces; aggregated scoring may use a small labelled calibration set, though its benefit is limited.

papers.abstract: End-to-end driving requires rich spatiotemporal representations to support scene understanding and trajectory planning under strict latency constraints. However, most systems initialize their visual encoders from generic image pretraining and densely process all patch tokens for each camera view and input frame, limiting both representation quality and inference efficiency. To address these challenges, we present ConDenseDrive, a knowledge-dense and token-sparse visual encoder for end-to-end autonomous driving. Our three-stage framework first makes the encoder knowledge-dense by distilling complementary visual, semantic, and geometric knowledge from three vision foundation models. It then adapts the distilled encoder to multi-frame end-to-end driving and integrates spatiotemporal context into register tokens for planning. Finally, it makes the encoder token-sparse by applying register-guided token compression, reducing redundant patch computation and yielding a 2.0$\times$ speedup while improving planning performance. ConDenseDrive achieves 94.5 PDMS on NAVSIM v1 and 90.8 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2, and reaches 37.4 HD-Score in zero-shot evaluation on HUGSIM. Extensive experiments and qualitative analyses demonstrate that visual encoder design provides an effective route to reliable and efficient end-to-end driving.

papers.abstract: Multi-modal fusion for 3D object detection assumes that cameras and LiDAR are broadly complementary. In practice, how much each modality is trusted at a given location is decided by learned weights that are neither characterized nor auditable. We label every ground-truth object by which modalities detected it, then mine the resulting 0.4M-object database across nuScenes, KITTI, and Waymo. Because the patterns shift with distance from the ego vehicle, we read the mined model through Spatially Stratified Feature Attribution (SSFA), which conditions Shapley attribution on distance zones and exposes structure that global attribution averages away. Three assumptions built into the current fusion design do not hold. The modality-preference boundary tracks the object itself: a traffic cone is nearly six times as likely as a truck to be seen by the camera alone (16.8% vs. 2.9%), regardless of range. Camera-only detections peak at 10-30 m, inside the band usually ceded to LiDAR, and fall away on either side. The drivers of failure are not additive either: the distance - density interaction alone outweighs the entire main effect of viewing direction. We further find that modality dominance is directionally non-stationary, with objects behind the vehicle being markedly more LiDAR-dominant than those in front. We compile the mined structure into a Modality Reliability Map and inject it into four pretrained fusion detectors through a lightweight attention layer. This improves performance by up to 1.3 mean Average Precision (mAP) while fine-tuning under 4% of their parameters in 2-3 GPU-hours. Our work lifts reliability out of the weights and treats it as a quantity that can be examined before deployment. That is what a safety measure for multi-modal perception must rest on.
authors: Hongsen Cao, Mona Jaber, Shanxin Yuan, Ahmed Sayed
bullets: Mines modality detections for 0.4M objects across nuScenes, KITTI, and Waymo to characterize when cameras and LiDAR disagree.
Introduces Spatially Stratified Feature Attribution to reveal distance-dependent structure hidden by global attribution.
Finds that modality preference depends on object type and location: cameras favor some objects and peak at 10–30 m, while rear-facing objects are more LiDAR-dominant.
Shows failure drivers are interactive rather than purely additive, with distance–density effects outweighing viewing-direction main effects.
Injecting a Modality Reliability Map into four pretrained fusion detectors improves performance by up to 1.3 mAP while fine-tuning under 4% of parameters.

papers.abstract: The rapid spread of face forgeries on the Web challenges the credibility of visual content. In practical Web environments, manipulated media originate from evolving generation pipelines and undergo diverse processing during dissemination, making reliable authenticity assessment under unseen manipulations and visual changes a critical challenge. We observe that a standard LoRA-adapted CLIP detector exhibits uneven patch-level decision dependence, concen trating a disproportionate share of class-specific relevance on a small fraction of visual patches. To improve robustness to variations in such highly dependent evidence, we propose EviStress, a two-stage framework for generalizable face forgery detection with textual explanations. In the first stage, Evidence-Targeted Patch Perturbation (ETPP) estimates patch dependence from global, relational, and semantic cues and assigns positively correlated perturbation probabilities, explicitly stress-testing highly dependent visual evidence during training. We further introduce Discriminative Variation Preservation (DVP), which constrains the residual between clean and perturbed representations to retain authenticity discriminative information. In the second stage, Intrinsic Evidence Instruction Tuning (IEIT) transfers the adapted CLIP encoder into LLaVA as its vision tower and performs parameter-efficient multimodal instruction tuning, enabling authenticity prediction and textual explanation directly from the learned forgery-sensitive representation without an external detector. Experiments demonstrate improved cross-dataset and cross-method generalization and corruption robustness, with the multimodal model providing authenticity predictions and human-readable explanations.
authors: Jiuyao Jing, Xuanyu Yi, Yu Zheng, Chunlei Peng
bullets: Targets the brittleness of CLIP-based detectors that rely disproportionately on a small number of image patches.

Applies Discriminative Variation Preservation to retain authenticity-related information in perturbed representations.
Transfers the adapted CLIP encoder into LLaVA with parameter-efficient instruction tuning for prediction and explanation.
Reports improved cross-dataset, cross-method generalization and corruption robustness, with human-readable authenticity explanations.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training with generative reward models (GenRM) has become a central recipe for improving large language models (LLMs), and it is also increasingly resource-intensive: policy rollout, GenRM-based reward evaluation, and policy training all compete for GPU resources. However, existing colocated and disaggregated systems rely on static resource allocation for these roles. Such allocation cannot adapt as each role's workload changes during RL and therefore leaves a role's resources underutilized. We present PivotRL, an RL post-training system that dynamically shifts resources among different roles according to their runtime demands. PivotRL introduces a resource-shiftable runtime built on a Global Parameter Storage, together with a unified mechanism that efficiently shifts role-specific context. A shift-aware scheduler enables sequence migration upon a shift, while a planner considers the aggregate throughput benefit and the shift overhead to determine when and how to shift. We evaluate PivotRL on a 128-GPU cluster using four model groups spanning dense and mixture-of-experts models. PivotRL enables resource shifting within seconds and improves end-to-end throughput by 1.81-2.05 times over colocated deployment and 1.50-1.95 times over disaggregated deployment, while preserving RL convergence.
authors: Yanfeng Zhao, Haoyang Li, Sheng Lin, Yuming Zhou, Jiawei Jiang, Bin Cui, Fangcheng Fu
