papers.abstract:
This paper presents GpFlash, a Gaussian process library that is focused on fast training and posterior evaluations, minimal memory usage, and scalability to high-dimensional problems. GpFlash was compared to the popular GP libraries scikit-learn, GPy, GPflow, GPyTorch, and SMT on a MacBook Pro and the supercomputer Trillium. GpFlash was found to use less memory and to be faster for training and posterior evaluations relative to the other GP libraries for all cases considered. For example, when using $
x = 10^4$ training points in a 10-dimensional space GpFlash required 9.6 to 35 times less memory and was 2.6 to 54 times faster than the other GP libraries for the evaluation of the marginal log likelihood and its gradient. The memory reduction was achieved by only using one matrix of size $
x 	imes 
x$ to store different symmetric matrices in its lower and upper triangular entries. The computational speedup was the result of designing algorithms to access memory efficiently, using BLAS and LAPACK methods extensively, and factoring kernel equations so that expensive exponential calculations could be reused. GpFlash was more than 440 times faster than all of the other GP libraries considered when evaluating the posterior mean together with its gradient for the case with $10^4$ training points and 10 dimensions. GpFlash is available at https://github.com/marchildon/gpflash.
authors: Andre Marchildon
bullets: Targets fast training, posterior evaluation, low memory use, and scalability in high-dimensional settings.
Uses one n×n matrix to store multiple symmetric matrices in separate triangular regions, reducing memory requirements.
Improves speed through memory-efficient algorithms, extensive BLAS/LAPACK use, and reuse of expensive kernel calculations.
Outperformed scikit-learn, GPy, GPflow, GPyTorch, and SMT in all reported comparisons on a MacBook Pro and Trillium.
For 10⁴ points in 10 dimensions, it used 9.6–35× less memory and achieved up to 54× faster likelihood-gradient evaluation; posterior mean plus gradient evaluation was over 440× faster.

papers.abstract: In-context learning (ICL) applies large language models to new tasks by prepending a few labeled demonstrations to a query. Prior work has studied how demonstration ordering affects ICL, but the interaction between label arrangement patterns and model biases has not been systematically examined. We define label collapse as the failure mode in which the model generates query-independent labels, and show that it is architecturally universal at the tested 8-9B scale: five models spanning autoregressive (Llama-3, Qwen3.5) and discrete diffusion (LLaDA, iLLaDA, LLaDA-Instruct) families all exhibit label collapse even under the class-balanced alternating arrangement, with some label word pairs collapsing in virtually every tested condition and others flipping their collapse direction with arrangement. Critically, accuracy alone cannot detect this collapse: models can achieve near-chance accuracy while generating query-independent labels, a score indistinguishable from balanced performance, so the failure can persist undetected in deployment. We measure separation, the log-odds of the two label words at the query position (the quantity that label-bias calibration operates on), as a complementary diagnostic that exposes collapse hidden beneath surface accuracy, together with a measurement protocol that guards label extraction against tokenizer and formatting artifacts. For autoregressive models, collapse persists where the majority-label-bias account does not apply, and arrangement patterns can reverse the collapse direction; for diffusion models, we present a systematic evaluation of ICL failure modes, complementing contemporaneous studies of dLLM context comprehension and demonstration-order sensitivity, and identify open questions about how iterative denoising interacts with label biases.
authors: Ziye Guo, Ye Yuan
bullets: The study examines how label arrangement patterns interact with model biases in in-context learning.
Five 8–9B autoregressive and discrete diffusion models exhibit label collapse, including under balanced alternating demonstrations.
Some label pairs collapse consistently, while others reverse collapse direction depending on arrangement.
Near-chance accuracy can hide query-independent predictions, so accuracy is not a sufficient diagnostic.
Separation—query-position log-odds between label words—combined with artifact-aware label extraction reveals the collapse.

papers.abstract: Syntactic language models (SLMs) that generate sentences along with their syntactic tree structures have shown promise in both syntactic generalization and downstream tasks. Prior studies, however, have mostly evaluated smaller models trained on less pretraining data and tested on narrower task suites. In addition, the design space of tree linearization and attention masks remains underexplored. We conduct a large-scale empirical study of 12 controlled configurations---one terminal baseline and 11 SLM variants spanning different linearizations and masks---at scales up to 1B parameters and 100B training tokens, evaluated across 11 downstream tasks and two syntactic benchmarks. The experimental results show that SLMs with standard causal attention match or exceed structural-mask variants across downstream and syntactic benchmarks. They require no architectural modifications and remain compatible with FlashAttention. We also observe that when scaling up to the 1B-parameter scale, the top-performing SLM variant no longer shows a clear advantage over a compute-matched non-structural baseline, suggesting that SLMs may become less competitive with scale. Our code is available at https://github.com/qlwpc/TG-Interpolation.
authors: Pengcheng Wang, Zhexuan Zhang, Chao Lou, Kewei Tu
bullets: Evaluates 12 controlled configurations, including one terminal baseline and 11 SLM variants.

At the 1B-parameter scale, the best SLM shows no clear advantage over a compute-matched non-structural baseline.
The study covers different tree linearizations and attention masks, addressing an underexplored design space.

papers.abstract: Model providers can support image protection, but open-weight deployment introduces practical constraints. We propose four requirements: protection effectiveness, clean fidelity, compatibility, and tamper resistance. We incorporate long-horizon attack simulations to strengthen resistance to protection removal. Experiments with a single protection tool show improved resistance to re-alignment at a cost to clean fidelity, motivating further research toward practical model-side protection.
authors: Jihye Kang, Jiwon Park, Namhyuk Ahn
bullets: Open-weight deployment creates constraints beyond user-side image defenses.
Protection should balance effectiveness, clean fidelity, compatibility, and tamper resistance.
Long-horizon attack simulations are used to improve resistance to protection removal and re-alignment.
Experiments with one protection tool show stronger re-alignment resistance but reduced clean fidelity.
Further research is needed for practical model-side protection.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Maintaining image protection after open-weight release. A re-alignment attack removes the protective behavior of an aligned model (top), whereas tamper-resistance training helps preserve protection under the same attack (bottom). Each row shows edits of the same protected image as the attack progresses, with the corresponding clean-image edit on the right. t: attack epochs.

Figure 4: The image the artist publishes, the trigger it carries, and the target that trigger activates, on two images. (a) the original artwork; (b) the protected version the artist publishes, carrying the trigger at ϵ = 2/255; (c) the difference between (a) and (b), amplified forty times so that it is visible at all; (d) the target the protective alignment is trained to produce from (b). Columns (a) and (b) are indistinguishable by design: over the 100 evaluation images the mean distortion between them is 45.1 dB PSNR, 0.990 SSIM and 0.010 LPIPS. The target in (d) is never published. It is what the deployed model produces in place of an edit, and each target renders the identifier of the image it is assigned to, which is why the two differ.

Figure 6: The re-alignment attack on three images. Each pair is one protective alignment: the upper row of the pair received no tamper-resistance training (w/o TR) and the lower row did (w/ TR). Columns are attack epochs t ∈ {0, 1, 3, 5, 10, 20} under one seed, and the last column is an edit of an unprotected image under the same model. Without the training the protection is gone after a single epoch in all three cases, and the edit becomes indistinguishable from the clean-image edit beside it. With it the edit is still far from that clean-image edit at t = 20, although the pattern is no longer crisp. The last column is what a user who never asked for protection gets from the same model, while our clean-fidelity metric quantifies changes in reconstructions rather than edits.

Figure 5: Every model we trained, placed in the plane of the two costs a provider pays. The horizontal axis is the protection surviving twenty epochs of attack, and the vertical axis is clean fidelity against the original autoencoder, so a point up and to the right is better on both. Filled points are the four that nothing else beats on both axes at once. Inside the shaded band the protection has fallen to the level of a model that was never aligned, and one ablation lies below the axis at 9.2 dB.

Figure 3: Protection under the re-alignment attack. Protection LPIPS is measured at each attack epoch. The shaded region marks scores at or below the unaligned reference of 0.225, where protection is considered removed.

Figure 2: Directional agreement with the realignment attack. Cosine similarity is measured between encoder parameter displacements; both simulations use the re-alignment objective. Long-horizon simulation better tracks the direction of later attack updates.

Table 2: Every constant used to produce the models of Table 1. The first block specifies protective alignment of the original autoencoder; the second specifies tamper-resistance training starting from the aligned checkpoint. The simulated attacks used in tamper-resistance training are drawn from a pool of thirty-six configurations, one per epoch in the listed order, so a twenty-epoch run sees encoder-scope attacks first and decoder-tail attacks after.

Table 5: What each group of the tamper-resistance objective contributes. All models are trained for twenty epochs and evaluated under the same attack; ablations remove the epoch-long refresh or a loss component from Equation 2. Protection is measured by LPIPS between the edit of a protected image and the edit of its clean counterpart, reported before the attack and after twenty epochs of it. Fidelity is measured by the PSNR of an unprotected reconstruction against the original autoencoder’s, measured before the attack. Removal denotes the first attack epoch at which protection LPIPS falls to or below the unaligned reference of 0.225; > 20 indicates that the threshold was not reached within the first 20 attack epochs. The last two ablations illustrate that a delayed removal epoch can coincide with substantial loss of clean fidelity.

Table 4: Additional protection and clean-fidelity metrics for the models in Table 1. Protection is reported in LPIPS and SSIM between the edit of a protected image and the edit of its clean counterpart, so larger LPIPS and smaller SSIM both mean stronger protection. The fidelity column reports pre-attack LPIPS between an unprotected reconstruction and the original autoencoder’s, where smaller means less collateral damage to users who never asked for protection.

Table 1: Protection effectiveness, clean fidelity, and tamper resistance. Protection is measured by LPIPS before attack and after 20 epochs of encoder re-alignment. Fidelity is pre-attack reconstruction PSNR relative to the original autoencoder. Removal denotes the first attack epoch at which protection LPIPS falls to or below the unaligned reference of 0.225; > 20 means the threshold was not reached.

Table 3: How well each way of guessing the attacker’s position actually predicts it. Tamper-resistance training evaluates its objective at some approximation of where the attacker will be, and the two candidates are K differentiable inner steps from the current weights, or the offset reached by running the attack for one full epoch. Each row reports the cosine between that approximation’s parameter displacement and the displacement a real re-alignment attack has reached after t epochs, together with the ratio of their lengths at t=10. A cosine near zero means the approximation points somewhere else; a small norm ratio means it points the right way but has barely moved. The two blocks differ only in which objective the approximation descends; the ground truth is the same re-alignment attack in both.

Table 6: The trade-off along one run of tamper-resistance training, sampled every five epochs. The first row is the aligned checkpoint the run starts from, so reading down the table shows what each further five epochs of training buys and costs. Protection LPIPS, clean-fidelity PSNR, and removal epochs follow the definitions in Table 5. Protection is reported before attack and after one and twenty attack epochs, and clean fidelity is measured before attack.

papers.abstract: Progressive depth growth builds large networks by starting with shallow models and inserting layers during training. Recent advances in large language models have renewed interest in this longstanding approach, demonstrating benefits for training efficiency and reasoning alongside changes in internal computations. However, how growing affects representation quality and computational patterns in self-supervised vision transformers remains unclear. In this work, we systematically investigate progressive depth growth in two popular self-supervised families, namely masked autoencoders (MAE) and DINOv3, and analyze how growing affects downstream performance, intermediate representations, and internal computations. Across global and dense tasks, we show that growing improves downstream performance while reducing training FLOPs by 13.9--24.8%, with ImageNet linear-probe accuracy gains of up to 3.36 percentage points. Growing also improves downstream performance at intermediate layers and reshapes internal computational patterns, introducing recurring alternations between global and localized attention in MAE and earlier local-to-global attention progression in self-distilled DINOv3. Together, these findings establish progressive depth growth as an effective and efficient pretraining strategy for improving downstream performance across global and dense visual tasks with less computation, and advance our understanding of how growing shapes visual computation.
authors: Amir Mohammad Karimi Mamaghan, Ferdinand Kapl, Andrea Dittadi, Karl Henrik Johansson, Kaitlin Maile, Johannes von Oswald, Stefan Bauer
bullets: Studies progressive depth growth in masked autoencoders (MAE) and self-distilled DINOv3.
Reports 13.9–24.8% lower training FLOPs and up to 3.36 percentage-point higher ImageNet linear-probe accuracy.
Improves performance across global and dense vision tasks, including at intermediate layers.
Finds that growth reshapes computation: MAE develops alternating global/local attention, while DINOv3 reaches global attention earlier.
Scope: focuses on progressive depth growth’s effects on self-supervised vision-transformer representations and internal computation.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Extended MAE training. Downstream performance of MAE trained with Stacking and its fixed-depth baseline. Stacking outperforms the baseline on all three tasks even after extended training.

Figure 4: Spatial attention patterns across depth. Attention distance, spatial entropy, and query– key NMI for MAE (top) and DINOv3 (bottom). Alternating shaded bands mark groups of four layers. MAE Stacking exhibits a recurring four-layer pattern: distance and entropy peak near group starts and NMI peaks near third layers. DINOv3 growing shifts the phase of localized, query-dependent attention and the subsequent broadening of attention toward earlier layers.

papers.abstract: Vision foundation models (VFMs) provide transferable visual representations, but their inference cost limits deployment in many settings. Fine-tuning specializes a VFM without shrinking it; distillation shrinks it, but through expensive teacher-guided training. Structured pruning offers a more direct route by extracting a compact subnetwork from the VFM. However, as compression gets aggressive, existing methods fail because they treat subnetwork selection and recovery as separate axes. Across layers, capacity must follow task sensitivity rather than spread uniformly. Within a layer, a removal cannot be judged by importance alone; its impact also depends on how well the lost contribution can be recovered from what remains. Selection and recovery must therefore be decided jointly. We introduce Carve VFM, which resolves this interdependence. Given a VFM, a calibration set, and a parameter budget, it (i) searches for task-specific capacity allocations across layers; (ii) guides the search via an adaptive recovery-aware fitness criterion; and (iii) reconstructs removed behavior through iterative closed-form low-rank corrections merged into the surviving weights. The result is a dense encoder produced in minutes on a single GPU without backbone retraining. Across twelve benchmarks and four models from DINOv3 and MetaCLIP-2, Carve VFM achieves the highest reported mean accuracy in seven of eight backbone-budget configurations among the evaluated dense structured-pruning methods. Further fine-tuning surpasses the strongest evaluated edge model (88.1% vs. 85.8%), and carved models cut compute and memory while delivering 1.3-2.0x higher GPU throughput than the uncompressed one. These results show that the compact model you need is inside the VFM; it only has to be carved out.
authors: Lotfi Abdelkrim Mecharbat, Abdelrahman Elsayed, Ibrahim Almakky, Martin Tak\'a\v{c}, Mohammad Yaqub
bullets: Addresses the high inference cost of VFMs while avoiding expensive teacher-guided distillation.

Uses iterative closed-form low-rank corrections to reconstruct removed behavior in the surviving weights.
Produces dense encoders in minutes on a single GPU and reduces compute and memory use.
Across 12 benchmarks and 4 models, it reports the best mean accuracy in 7 of 8 evaluated backbone-budget settings; throughput improves 1.3–2.0× over uncompressed models.

papers.abstract: Chest X-ray (CXR) interpretation often requires integrating visual findings with task-specific evidence rather than relying on direct visual recognition alone. While tool-augmented medical agents can supply such evidence via external modules, they often lack explicit mechanisms for learning when auxiliary evidence is needed and for preventing inapplicable quantitative evidence from entering diagnostic reasoning. To address this, we propose X-Ragent, a post-training framework for tool-augmented reinforcement learning that decouples learned auxiliary-evidence seeking from validity-gated quantitative measurement acquisition for evidence-grounded CXR reasoning. We construct Rad-CoT, a 7.7K-sample corpus combining causally ordered tool-augmented trajectories with report-style diagnostic reasoning, and use it to initialize Qwen3-VL-8B via agentic supervised fine-tuning (SFT). We then optimize the policy with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) using an accuracy-gated reward that applies process-level terms for measurement consistency and auxiliary-tool cost only to correct trajectories, preventing plausible process behavior from compensating for an incorrect diagnosis. Across three CXR benchmarks, X-Ragent achieves the strongest results, including an 8.6-point improvement on the fully held-out ChestAgentBench. By seeking evidence selectively and admitting only valid measurements, X-Ragent supports more faithful and evidence-grounded CXR reasoning.
authors: Yi Wang, Zhenlong Yuan, Yuchan Guo, Maolei Huang, Zijian Song, Dapeng Zhang, Rongbin Tan, Jiyuan Wang, Zhiyuan Wang, Fangfang Lin, Shuhan Song, Huawei Cao

Optimizes with GRPO using accuracy-gated process rewards for measurement consistency and tool cost.
Achieves the strongest results across three CXR benchmarks, including an 8.6-point gain on held-out ChestAgentBench.

(iii) GRPO optimizes the policy with accuracy and format supervision, while tool-use cost and radiographic evidence consistency are gated by answer correctness. (iv) At inference, the policy selectively routes auxiliary tools, while an independent validity gate decides whether quantitative measurements are exposed; both are integrated in the second turn.

papers.abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) enables transformers to solve complex reasoning tasks by generating intermediate reasoning steps. Despite strong empirical success, the mechanisms by which such reasoning abilities emerge during training remain poorly understood, particularly from a theoretical perspective. In this work, we study this question in a stylized yet fully analyzable setting: in-context $\mathrm{K}$-nearest-neighbor ($\mathrm{K}$-NN) prediction with a one-layer transformer. Earlier work has demonstrated that one-layer transformers can be trained to perform $1$-NN without CoT (Li et al., 2024a) by having the softmax attention attend to the nearest neighbor in context. However, this result on $1$-NN cannot be extended to $\mathrm{K}$-NN for $K>1$, as softmax attention is much less naturally suited to attending to the 2nd through $K$-th nearest neighbors. We first give a rigorous negative result showing that this limitation already appears on a well-separated class of binary classification tasks for odd $K>1$. We then give an explicit construction of a one-layer transformer, and show that it can solve $\mathrm{K}$-NN via CoT reasoning. We further prove that, under a stylized training setup, gradient descent can recover this construction, thereby showing that transformers can acquire the capability to solve $\mathrm{K}$-NN through training. In addition, we show that the resulting trained model applies to a broader test class than that assumed in the training analysis. Our results shed light on how CoT expands the ability of transformers to learn and solve tasks that are otherwise hard to solve.
authors: Lyumin Wu, Yuan Cao
bullets: Studies how CoT capabilities can emerge in transformers through a provably analyzable in-context K-NN task.
Proves a negative result: direct softmax attention fails on a well-separated binary classification class for odd K>1.
Constructs a one-layer transformer that solves K-NN by generating intermediate reasoning steps.
Shows that gradient descent can recover this CoT-based construction under a stylized training setup.
Demonstrates that the trained model generalizes to a broader test class than the one used in the training analysis.

papers.abstract: Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) is widely used in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards for language-model reasoning. While \emph{value evolution along trajectory} characterizes relative token-level credit, yet standard critics often fail to track it under sparse terminal rewards. To model this evolution, we analyze the relation between successive prefix values and show that they admit a Bayesian decomposition with additive updates in log-odds space. We use this additive structure to construct Tracking-Value PPO (\method), a cumulative value parameterization that sums position-wise scalar outputs into value logits. These outputs are learned through terminal-outcome supervision on the reconstructed values. \method improves aggregate mathematical reasoning scores over PPO by 7.0 and 8.4 points on Qwen3-4B-Base and Qwen3-8B-Base, respectively, while improving out-of-distribution generalization. Gains extend to Qwen3-4B, Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B, Qwen3.5-9B and to countdown, and scientific coding tasks. Further analysis shows more accurate tracking of value evolution and more reliable advantage estimates. Our code is publicly available in https://github.com/LINs-lab/TPPO.
authors: Futing Wang, Chenxi Li, Jianhao Yan, Yun Luo, Zhi Wang, Yizhuo Li, Runzhe Zhan, Yu Cheng, Tao Lin
bullets: Addresses inaccurate token-level credit assignment under sparse terminal rewards.
Derives a Bayesian decomposition showing that successive prefix values can be updated additively in log-odds space.
Parameterizes values as cumulative sums of position-wise scalar outputs, trained with terminal-outcome supervision.
Improves aggregate mathematical reasoning scores by 7.0 and 8.4 points on Qwen3-4B-Base and Qwen3-8B-Base, respectively.
Also improves out-of-distribution generalization, advantage estimates, and performance across additional models and countdown and scientific coding tasks.

papers.abstract: Interacting with unfamiliar objects requires understanding how their parts connect and move. We introduce ViewStruct, a framework for jointly predicting connectivity and articulation in objects and scenes. Given an RGB image with aligned part segmentation and depth, optionally supplemented by images or video, ViewStruct predicts rigid-body groupings, attachments, and joint parameters. Its view-grounded representation links predictions to observed regions and expresses joint geometry in a gravity-aligned, view-relative frame, without requiring category-specific canonical orientations. A pretrained vision--language model is adapted to predict structure in seconds, without requiring observed articulation motion or per-instance optimisation. Experiments demonstrate improved structural prediction over evaluated baselines and transfer to unseen categories, asset sources, and real-world human-interaction videos, despite task-specific training exclusively on synthetic data. Simulated manipulation experiments further demonstrate the utility of predicted joints for generating robot motion trajectories.
authors: Wenjing Bian, Ranran Huang, Andreas Geiger
bullets: Predicts rigid-body groupings, attachments, and joint parameters from RGB, aligned segmentation, and depth, with optional additional images or video.
Represents joint geometry in gravity-aligned, view-relative coordinates without requiring category-specific canonical orientations.
Adapts a pretrained vision–language model for inference in seconds, without observed articulation motion or per-instance optimisation.
Outperforms evaluated baselines and transfers to unseen categories, asset sources, and real-world human-interaction videos.
Predicted joints support simulated robot manipulation trajectory generation; training is task-specific and exclusively synthetic.

papers.abstract: Adaptive optimization methods have received considerable attention in recent years due to their strong empirical performance. However, they generally require maintaining a preconditioning matrix, which incurs prohibitive computational overhead in large-scale applications. To address these limitations, we investigate the acceleration of preconditioned optimization methods through frequent directions (FD), a widely used matrix sketching technique. We first propose FTSL by integrating FD with adaptive subgradient methods under the primal-dual framework and adding back the cumulative information discarded by FD. FTSL obtains a tighter regret bound than existing state-of-the-art results. We then apply a doubling trick that further reduces the time complexity of FTSL, while maintaining the same regret guarantee. We also consider optimization over matrix-valued decision variables and exploit their structural properties to construct sketched preconditioners. We develop FTSL-Shampoo by adapting FD to Shampoo and give a novel analysis under the primal-dual framework. To further mitigate its computational complexity, we design one-sided variants of FTSL-Shampoo under both mirror descent and primal-dual frameworks. Our algorithms not only reduce the computational cost of FTSL-Shampoo, but also achieve tighter regret bounds. We extend our methods to offline stochastic convex optimization and exploit smoothness to achieve faster convergence rates. Finally, we introduce practical variants of our algorithms and empirically demonstrate their efficiency and effectiveness across a broad range of tasks.
authors: Sifan Yang, Yuanyu Wan, Yibo Wang, Lijun Zhang
bullets: Addresses the high computational cost of maintaining full preconditioning matrices in adaptive optimization.
Introduces FTSL, which combines Frequent Directions with adaptive subgradient methods and restores information discarded by sketching.
A doubling trick reduces FTSL’s time complexity without changing its regret guarantee.
Extends the approach to matrix-valued optimization through FTSL-Shampoo and more efficient one-sided variants.
Also develops stochastic convex-optimization extensions and reports empirical efficiency across diverse tasks.

papers.abstract: Parallel token proposals in language-model decoding need a joint law, not merely accurate token marginals. We construct a family of coordinate-Bethe-ansatz laws from the periodic XXZ chain and compare each with its maximum-entropy pairwise projection at identical one- and two-site moments. In the eight-site, three-excitation sector, symmetry makes their entire probability-law difference one-dimensional, determined by a contiguous three-site moment. Along the Bethe branch, this gap varies with anisotropy, changes sign, and vanishes exactly at $\Delta=(3+\sqrt{3})/2$, where the eigenstate law becomes exactly pairwise. A nonlinear readout transfers a nonzero gap into the first two token positions while preserving their separate marginals. At $\Delta=1.5$ the deterministic binary token laws differ by 0.02654573 in total variation. Exact speculative verification then gives a strict accepted-prefix advantage for a constructed target and a neighborhood within targets sharing its first-token marginal. This is a mathematical existence result. It does not establish a language-model gain or wall-clock speedup.
authors: Abraham Chachamovits
bullets: Parallel decoding requires a joint token law, not just accurate marginals.
Coordinate-Bethe-ansatz laws from the periodic XXZ chain are compared with maximum-entropy pairwise projections having identical one- and two-site moments.
For an eight-site, three-excitation sector, the law difference is one-dimensional and controlled by a contiguous three-site moment; it changes with anisotropy and vanishes at a specific value of Δ.
A nonlinear readout transfers this higher-order gap to the first two token positions while preserving their individual marginals.
At Δ=1.5, the constructed binary laws differ by 0.02654573 in total variation and yield a strict accepted-prefix advantage for a constructed target and nearby targets.
papers.selection_reason: Constructs joint laws for parallel token proposals in language-model decoding; relevant to language foundation model decoding, though theoretical.
papers.title: A Bethe-Ansatz Source of Early Token Correlations: A marginal-preserving construction for parallel proposals
papers.tldr: A Bethe-ansatz construction shows that parallel token proposals can share one- and two-token marginals yet differ in higher-order dependencies that affect speculative decoding.

papers.abstract: Relational learning typically predicts from a database state, but decision making asks a different question: how will that state change under an action? In operational systems, the answer depends on system-specific dynamics that may not be visible in the database itself. We view each such system as a relational "world" and ask whether a model can infer how it behaves from observed executions. We introduce TabWM (Tabular World Model) and WorldRel, a generator of executable relational worlds for pretraining. Given executions from an unseen world, TabWM uses them as context to predict the sparse structured edits caused by a new action without parameter updates. Across 512 held-out worlds, complete-edit F1 rises from 0.016 with no observed executions to 0.685 with 64, where a correct edit must match its operation, relational location, and value. Because these predictions are explicit relational edits, they can be applied recursively to imagine candidate futures and compare actions before they are taken. Broader search over these predicted futures improves the realized return of selected action sequences. Together, these results suggest that relational dynamics can be learned in context, broadening relational learning from modeling system state to modeling how that state changes under action.
authors: Zheyu Zhang, Gjergji Kasneci
bullets: Motivation: Relational models usually predict states, but decision making requires predicting state changes under actions whose dynamics may be system-specific.
Method: TabWM uses executions from an unseen world as context, without parameter updates, to predict sparse structured edits for new actions.
WorldRel is introduced as a generator of executable relational worlds for pretraining.
Across 512 held-out worlds, complete-edit F1 increases from 0.016 with no executions to 0.685 with 64 observed executions.
Predicted edits can be recursively composed to imagine futures; broader search over them improves the realized return of selected action sequences.

papers.abstract: Attention sinks are usually studied after they have formed. We ask whether a measurable hidden-state change appears beforehand and whether changing that geometry alters what happens later. To remove network depth as a shortcut, we compare prompts in the same model and at the same layer. When sink timing varies across prompts, simple spectral summaries of the hidden states add information beyond current attention, with the clearest prompt-specific signal in a short window about two to three layers before sink formation. The predictive strength varies across cohorts, so we treat the spectrum as a readout of a pre-sink state change rather than a universal warning statistic. The signal is broader than one measured extreme activation. We then modify only the singular values of the post-layer hidden states after current attention has already been computed. These interventions change later sink behavior in Qwen2.5, GLM-Z1, and GPT-OSS relative to norm-matched random spectral perturbations. In Qwen2.5, the immediate suppressive effect is accompanied by a reduction in next-layer query--key preference for position~0, and the learned spectral directions remain stable when estimated from substantially less training data. Together, the results show that attention sinks are preceded by a short spectral reorganization of hidden states, and directly perturbing this geometry can causally alter subsequent sink formation.
authors: Fan Yang, Yue Song
bullets: Spectral summaries provide prompt-specific information about sink timing beyond current attention, especially two to three layers beforehand.
The predictive signal varies across prompt cohorts, so it is a pre-sink state-change indicator rather than a universal warning statistic.
The effect reflects broader spectral structure, not just a single extreme activation.
Post-attention singular-value interventions alter later sink behavior across Qwen2.5, GLM-Z1, and GPT-OSS, compared with norm-matched random perturbations.
In Qwen2.5, suppression reduces the next-layer query–key preference for position 0; learned spectral directions are stable with substantially less training data.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of the observational and causal analyses. (A) We compare prompts in the same model and at the same layer before either has formed a sink, and ask whether their hidden-state spectra already differ before their later sink timing diverges. (B) After the source-layer attention has been computed, we modify only the singular values of the post-layer hidden state while keeping the token mean and singular subspaces fixed; current attention is therefore unchanged, and we measure how later sink behavior responds. (C) In Qwen2.5, the immediate effect of the spectral edit is associated with a change in the next layer’s relative QK preference for position 0 and a corresponding change in position-0 attention. (D) Tracking the perturbation across layers shows that its norm can survive while its full hidden-state direction rotates and its targeted spectral component may either persist or weaken, helping explain why the downstream effect depends on where the edit is introduced.

Figure 2: The spectral increment is concentrated in a short pre-sink window. (A) In the primary pooled matched-depth analysis, adding spectral features to current attention improves prediction over several short horizons but not at six layers. (B) The pattern remains after removing model–layer spectral means using training-fold statistics. (C) When ranking is evaluated entirely within matched model–layer cells, the clearest prompt-specific gains occur at Within 2 and Within 3, while the Within 4 estimate is near zero. Points show ∆AP and horizontal bars show prompt-bootstrap 95% confidence intervals; the vertical dashed line marks ∆AP= 0.

Figure 7: Qwen3.6 hybrid-attention boundary. Accepted sink-state fractions are shown only at the 16 full-attention checkpoints. The recurrent peak–collapse–reappearance pattern persists across context length and query-window choices, whereas the location and prevalence of the first threshold crossing vary substantially. This behavior supports treating Qwen3.6 as a recurrent, architecture-gated sink regime rather than an ordinary persistent-onset process.

Figure 4: Broader activation-state controls contain more of the predictive information carried by the spectrum. (A) Compact hidden-state amplitude and concentration controls leave a substantial positive spectral increment, whereas broader activation-state descriptions reduce the remaining increment toward zero. (B) In the nested pooled-GLM Exact 1 analysis, local computational families— including query–key preference, value magnitude, attention–value statistics, and branch scales—also leave a positive spectral increment, while conditioning on the distributed activation state leaves little additional spectral value. Points show the remaining ∆AP after adding spectral features, horizontal bars show prompt-bootstrap 95% confidence intervals, and the vertical dashed line marks ∆AP= 0. These comparisons measure predictive redundancy, not causal mediation.

Figure 5: Qwen3 sink timing varies across prompts while the stringent extreme-activation event remains depth-locked. (A) Median maximum-to-median hidden-activation ratio, with interquartile bands, for prompts whose sinks form at block 3 versus block 7. Under the 104 criterion, both groups exhibit the same abrupt extreme-activation event at block 6, after the early-onset group has already formed a sink and one block before the dominant late-onset group does. (B) Sweeping the extreme-activation criterion shows that this shared event depth is not specific to the single 104 threshold. Across stringent thresholds from 2×103 to 2×104, both onset groups first cross at block 6 even though their sink onsets remain at blocks 3 and 7. The figure therefore shows a timing mismatch: the stringent extreme-event depth does not encode the prompt-specific difference in sink onset.

Figure 8: Route-to-spectrum regression with nonlinear depth control. Jacobian route variables explain spectral-α shifts under prompt-grouped out-of-fold evaluation, but most of this explanatory power is shared with flexible model-specific nonlinear depth. Adding route variables to the polynomial-depth baseline yields only a marginal improvement (R2 OOF : 0.846 → 0.850; ∆R2 = 0.004).

papers.selection_reason: Studies hidden-state geometry preceding attention-sink formation in LLMs; fits LLM architecture/behavior.
papers.title: Before Attention Sinks Form: Hidden-State Geometry Reveals and Modulates Their Formation
papers.tldr: A short-lived reorganization in hidden-state spectra precedes attention-sink formation, and modifying this geometry can change later sink behavior.

papers.abstract: Video-to-robot pipelines for quadrupedal imitation insert a learned lifting stage, either a monocular depth model or a per-clip 3D reconstruction, to recover the one axis a side-view camera cannot see. We present CopyQuad, which omits that stage and pins the missing axis to the robot's own stance width instead. The setting is side-view footage of sagittally dominated motion, where limb motion is almost entirely in the image plane. A frozen 2D keypoint detector and a fixed analytic retargeting then turn a single uncalibrated clip into a robot reference whose foot targets are reachable by construction, so no per-clip trajectory optimization is needed. One phase-indexed reward structure, whose only per-behavior freedom is three scalars from a shared sweep, learns a dog walk, a horse walk, a horse trot and two non-periodic gestures, all deployed zero-shot on hardware. We then measure what omitting the axis costs. In a training-free rigidity test, a video depth model varies the distance between the animal's hips by $40$ to $107\%$ of its own mean and a single-image metric model by $22$ to $58\%$, though that distance cannot move. Motion capture puts the true lateral paw travel of a dog walk at $4.5$ cm peak to peak, a mean deviation near $1.4$ cm against the $3.5$ cm of lateral foot error our policies already leave, so the discarded axis sits below the pipeline's resolution. Depth repaired to feasibility never beats the constant, and the unrepaired estimates put the robot on the ground.
authors: Mohamad H. Danesh, Raina Hu, Mengxue Xu, Hsiu-Chin Lin
bullets: Targets sagittally dominated motion, where limb movement is mostly visible in the image plane.
Uses frozen 2D keypoints and fixed analytic retargeting to produce reachable foot targets without per-clip optimization.
A shared phase-indexed reward structure learns four gaits and two non-periodic gestures, all deployed zero-shot on hardware.
Measurements show true lateral paw motion is smaller than existing policy foot error, while depth-based alternatives are unstable or infeasible.
Scope is limited to motions where the discarded lateral axis is small relative to the pipeline’s resolution.

papers.abstract: Multimodal reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards commonly assigns one sequence advantage to an entire response. This outcome-level signal distinguishes overall response quality but leaves changes in visual-evidence use across generated tokens implicit. We introduce VAttnPO (Visual Attention-Guided Policy Optimization), which uses answer-conditioned visual attention to refine token-level credit while preserving the verifier-derived trajectory-mean advantage. A frozen old policy constructs a visual reference by teacher forcing the known correct answer and produces a visual distribution for each rollout token. VAttnPO measures their agreement in visual-attention space using Jensen--Shannon divergence, rather than reading guidance from teacher output-token distributions or introducing an attention-matching objective. Trajectory centering, relative-position weighting, and credit balancing turn this agreement into a zero-mean, position-aware correction to the GRPO sequence advantage. Token intervention, visual-index permutation, and trajectory analysis provide diagnostic evidence linking this signal to model behavior, visual correspondence, and generation position. On Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct, VAttnPO raises six-task image AVE from 70.97 with GRPO to 73.50 and scores higher on every reported structured, video, and MME metric. Gains over GRPO also hold on Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct and InternVL3-8B-Instruct.
authors: Lihao Zheng, Zhenwei Shao, Zhou Yu, Yan Yang, Haoyi Sun, Qian Wang, Ning Mao, Pan Zhou
bullets: Problem: Sequence-level advantages do not reveal how visual evidence contributes across individual generated tokens.
Method: A frozen old policy compares rollout-token visual attention with attention from teacher-forced correct answers using Jensen–Shannon divergence.
The resulting signal is trajectory-centered, position-aware, and balanced before correcting the GRPO sequence advantage.
Diagnostics examine token interventions, visual-index permutations, and generation-position effects.
On Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct, image AVE improves from 70.97 with GRPO to 73.50; gains also hold across other reported models and metrics.

papers.abstract: Visual contrastive decoding corrects answers using the prediction difference between the original image and a reference condition, yet the same contrast also turns supported abstentions into incorrect answers. We find that abstentions are lost at two stages: contrastive decoding with candidate filtering can exclude the abstention token before any comparison takes place, and the reference branch's response to the abstention instruction is removed when the reference prediction is subtracted. We therefore propose instruction-preserving decoding, which keeps the effect of the abstention instruction on the original-image prediction intact while leaving the contrast strength freely adjustable. Using a perturbed image and an image-free prediction as references, we obtain IP-VCD and IP-M3ID. On decision utility (DU), which credits both correct answers and supported abstentions, both methods outperform all compared non-IP baselines on every one of nine models on VizWiz, and IP-VCD also leads on eight of nine models on Food-101. Candidate measurements and paired per-question comparisons show that computing the instruction effect and the visual contrast term separately lets contrastive decoding support both correct answers and supported abstentions.
authors: Haonan Zhang, Ting Jin, Wenzhong Tang, Shuai Wang
bullets: Visual contrastive decoding can wrongly eliminate supported abstentions during candidate filtering or reference subtraction.
The proposed method preserves the abstention instruction’s effect on the original-image prediction while keeping contrast strength adjustable.
Two variants use perturbed-image and image-free references: IP-VCD and IP-M3ID.
Both outperform non-instruction-preserving baselines on decision utility across nine models on VizWiz; IP-VCD leads on eight of nine models on Food-101.
Separate measurement of instruction effects and visual contrast supports both correct answers and supported abstentions.

papers.abstract: Accurate modelling of soft tactile sensors remains difficult because finite element methods (FEM) are computa- tionally expensive, while real-time simulators often lack fidelity for hyperelastic deformation. Large physical datasets are also impractical to collect because repeated testing can damage fragile sensors. We present a data-efficient framework that combines limited real-world validation, high-fidelity FEM, and graph neural networks (GNNs) for accurate real-time prediction of two-dimensional tactile deformation in a planar soft tactile structure. The key idea is to decouple validation from training: 82 camera-tracked contact configurations are used only to tune and validate an ANSYS FEM model, which then generates 768 synthetic contact scenarios for GNN training. We evaluate both forward prediction from marker deformation to contact localisation and inverse inference from contact configuration to marker deformation. The validated FEM achieves sub-0.5 mm error in more than 90% of validation cases, while the learned GNN surrogate reaches a mean absolute error of 0.32 mm with millisecond-scale inference, compared with minute-scale FEM simulation. Models trained entirely on synthetic FEM data retain sub-millimetre accuracy on real measurements from the 2D tactile structure, demonstrating strong sim-to-real transfer within the tested planar setting. We further integrate the learned model into a real-time visualisation pipeline, enabling rapid deformation prediction for virtual prototyping and simulator-based design exploration without extensive physical testing.
authors: Silvia Terrile, Kaichen Shi, Taejun Kwon, Jiseok Lee, Nathan Lepora, Yeejin Lee, Saekwang Nam, Efi Psomopoulou
bullets: Addresses the high computational cost of FEM and the difficulty of collecting large physical datasets for fragile tactile sensors.
Uses 82 camera-tracked real contact configurations to validate FEM, then generates 768 synthetic scenarios for GNN training.
Supports both forward contact localisation from marker deformation and inverse deformation prediction from contact configuration.
Validated FEM has sub-0.5 mm error in over 90% of cases; the GNN achieves 0.32 mm mean absolute error with millisecond-scale inference versus minute-scale FEM simulation.
Demonstrates sub-millimetre sim-to-real performance and integration into a real-time visualisation pipeline for planar tactile structures.

papers.abstract: Cross-task generalization remains difficult for world action models (WAMs), even when their predicted futures depict plausible manipulation. This gap can be attributed directly: we make this gap directly testable by decoupling a WAM into a world model and an inverse-dynamics model (IDM), then holding the IDM fixed while replacing the source of future images. We introduce Align Once, Evaluate Everywhere (AoE), a camera-space inverse-dynamics model pretrained on large-scale robot data, which provides this recovery interface for different future sources across tasks and environments. Through it, we find that actions recovered from recorded futures of unseen tasks execute almost as well as replayed demonstrations, whereas futures predicted by world models collapse across benchmarks. The failures are not generic: they concentrate on the gripper and interaction geometry while generation capacity is spent on task-irrelevant background. This diagnosis suggests that supervision should target exactly these regions. We therefore introduce the vision-to-action (VITA) loss, which passes generated futures through the frozen AoE and penalizes discrepancies in the recovered actions, redirecting generation toward action-relevant detail. Across two world models and three manipulation benchmarks, this simple change raises the execution success of generated futures from near zero to 47.0%. The same loss also transfers to WAMs and yields consistent gains in native control.
authors: Chen Zhao, Zipeng Ye, Yihan Lin, Yuchen Xie, Jing Zhang
bullets: AoE decouples world models from inverse-dynamics models by holding the IDM fixed while swapping future-image sources.
Actions recovered from recorded futures of unseen tasks nearly match replayed demonstrations, but actions from predicted futures fail across benchmarks.
World-model errors concentrate on gripper and interaction geometry, while generation focuses on task-irrelevant backgrounds.
The VITA loss uses frozen AoE-recovered actions to emphasize action-relevant visual details.
Across two world models and three manipulation benchmarks, VITA raises generated-future execution success from near zero to 47.0% and improves native control.

papers.abstract: State space models provide efficient linear-complexity processing for long sequences, but their performance frequently degrades as context length grows. We propose SuPER-Mamba, a training-free framework that uses Surprisal as a model-intrinsic signal for long-range state routing in pretrained Mamba models. SuPER-Mamba computes position-wise Surprisal from next-token predictions, aggregates neighboring responses through Local Pooling, and uses the resulting scores to prioritize Global-Channel updates without query-dependent scoring or additional training. We evaluate SuPER-Mamba on three state-space models across the LongBench-E benchmark. The results show that SuPER-Mamba improves the average score from 8.06 to 15.69, corresponding to a 94.7% relative gain over the Base Models and a 13.1% improvement over the state-of-the-art prior baseline. Ablation and length-wise analyses further support the effectiveness of the proposed routing framework.
authors: Zhetong Zhang, Gayan K Kulatilleke
bullets: Addresses performance degradation in state space models as context length increases.
Computes position-wise surprisal from next-token predictions and smooths it with Local Pooling.
Uses surprisal scores to prioritize Global-Channel state updates without query-dependent scoring or additional training.
Evaluated across three state-space models on LongBench-E, improving the average score from 8.06 to 15.69.
Ablation and length-wise analyses support the effectiveness of the routing framework.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of the SuPER-Mamba framework. Phase 1 performs offline Context Scoring. (a) Surprisal Calculation computes position-wise Raw Surprisal Scores from the next-token prediction probabilities of the pretrained Mamba. (b) Local Pooling aggregates neighboring predictive responses using category-specific Mean or Max Pooling to obtain Pooled Surprisal Scores. Phase 2 uses these scores for long-range state routing. The historical Top-K Content positions selected by the Pooled Surprisal Scores are combined with the most recent R = 32 Content positions to form the final routing set. For long-range state updates, Instruction and Query positions do not participate in Content Selection and retain their original state updates, while among Content positions, only the selected positions update the predefined Global Channels. All Content positions continue to participate in the original recurrent computation, so the complete input is neither removed nor truncated.

Each configuration is evaluated on 50 samples from each of the 13 datasets. (a) analyzes the routing budget K with k = 18 and Mean Pooling fixed, testing K ∈ {256, 512, 768, 1024, 1536, 2048, 3072}. (b) analyzes the Local Pooling kernel k with K = 1024 and Mean Pooling fixed, testing k ∈ {3, 5, 7, 9, 12, 15, 18, 21}. Boxes summarize the result distributions across all tested settings for each category, gray diamonds indicate the common reference configuration with K = 1024, k = 18, and Mean Pooling, and red circles indicate the best observed setting for each category in the corresponding parameter analysis.

Figure 1: Motivation of SuPER-Mamba. A pretrained Mamba produces position-wise Surprisal from nexttoken prediction probabilities while processing the input context. Relatively predictable local content typically produces lower and more stable Surprisal responses, whereas less predictable local changes may produce larger responses. SuPER-Mamba treats these responses as model-intrinsic predictive feedback and further investigates the relationship between such local predictive feedback and signals for long-range state allocation.

papers.abstract: Recent Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models increasingly use natural-language instructions to condition autonomous driving behavior. Yet existing closed-loop benchmarks primarily measure route completion, safety, and rule compliance, leaving a fundamental question unresolved: does language actually determine which feasible behavior the vehicle executes? A trajectory may be safe and successful while still violating or even ignoring the passenger's instruction. To address this, we introduce \ltd, a benchmark designed to directly test this capability. Its key evaluation unit, the paired counterfactual unit (PCU), holds the initial driving scene fixed while changing only the instruction. This design enables us to distinguish isolated instruction success from counterfactual paired success across four instruction-following scopes. To test whether this distinction persists across evaluation regimes, we instantiate Language2Drive in complementary closed-loop CARLA simulation, reconstructed real-world scenes, and open-loop driving benchmarks, including our released CARLA-Language2Drive simulator with purpose-built maps. Evaluating representative driving VLAs across these settings reveals a striking mismatch between strong driving competence and weak language control: 93.2% of successful rollouts do not have a successful counterpart under the alternative feasible instruction. This failure is dominated by one-sided completion, where a model repeatedly executes one preferred behavior but fails when the same scene requires the counterfactual alternative. These results expose two fundamental limitations of current evaluation: isolated success and driving scores, which are widely used by conventional driving benchmarks, can substantially overstate language-following capability, while current driving VLAs themselves lack reliable instruction following under matched counterfactual tests.
authors: Zihan You, Zehua Fan, Wenqi Lyu, Aoqi Wang, Ni Wang, Yifei Yang, Linge Zhao, Huan Li, Sining Ang, Yuguang Yang, Jueyu Chen, Xiangyu Li, Qianshan Wei, Jieyuan Pei, Yuxin Wang, Zhiwen Chen, Jiaqi Li, Wenxuan Song, Yanyuan Qiao, Benjin Zhu, Haoang Li, Yan Wang
bullets: Introduces paired counterfactual units (PCUs), which keep the scene fixed while varying only the instruction.
Separates isolated instruction success from paired counterfactual success across four instruction-following scopes.
Evaluates VLAs in closed-loop CARLA, reconstructed real-world scenes, and open-loop driving benchmarks.
Finds that 93.2% of successful rollouts lack a successful counterpart under an alternative feasible instruction.
Failures are mainly one-sided completion: models repeatedly choose a preferred behavior instead of following the requested alternative.

papers.abstract: Memory-based long-video generation aims to combine user control with long-range visual consistency. We organize this process into three functional components: a planner, an adapter, and a generator. Representative multi-shot systems couple memory to generator-specific interfaces or use predefined agent workflows, rather than independently training a memory policy for cross-shot objectives. We introduce REEL, a general-purpose visual-memory planner. Through a unified tool interface, REEL learns to retrieve references, create missing visual evidence, and update persistent memory. Backend-specific adapters translate its evidence plans into supported conditioning inputs, allowing the same policy to guide different black-box video generators. To train REEL, we construct two high-quality datasets, REEL-SFT-4k and REEL-RL-1k, covering diverse interaction patterns and prompt types. Training proceeds in three stages: supervised fine-tuning, single-shot Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), and multi-shot GRPO. Multi-shot GRPO carries policy-generated memory across consecutive shots, so later outcomes guide earlier reference selection and memory updates. REEL-Bench tests identity preservation and intended state changes under text-only requests and timed reference-image uploads. On JoyAI-Echo~1.5 and MiniMax-H3, REEL improves cross-shot consistency on ST-Bench by 15.1\% and 20.7\%, and Core-100 on our proposed REEL-Bench by 2.41 and 8.32 points, respectively, over the no-memory baseline.
authors: Hang Xu, Guohui Zhang, Xiaoxiao Ma, Hu Yu, Jie Huang, Jiayin Xiao, Lin Song, Haoyang Huang, Nan Duan, Feng Zhao

Uses a planner–adapter–generator design: the planner manages memory, while adapters translate plans for different black-box video generators.
Trains with supervised fine-tuning followed by single-shot and multi-shot GRPO, enabling later shots to inform earlier memory decisions.
Evaluated on identity preservation and intended state changes with text requests and timed reference-image uploads.
Improves cross-shot consistency over no-memory baselines on JoyAI-Echo 1.5 and MiniMax-H3, including 15.1% and 20.7% gains on ST-Bench.

papers.title: REEL: Learning to Retrieve, Evaluate, and Evolve Visual Memory for Any Long-Horizon Multi-Shot Video Generation

papers.abstract: Visual token compression has emerged as a critical technique for reducing the inference cost of Vision-Language Models. Existing methods select tokens based on text relevance, visual diversity, or a fixed combination of both---treating the relevance-diversity balance as a universal constant independent of the input. We conduct a systematic analysis to challenge this assumption. At the dataset level, grid-searching the optimal relevance-diversity weight per benchmark reveals substantial cross-task variation. More critically, we further maximize per-sample answer likelihood to recover sample-level oracle weights, finding that their distributions not only differ markedly across benchmarks but also exhibit high within-benchmark variance. Based on these observations, we propose SAVER, a framework for Sample-Aware relevance-diversity balanced Visual tokEn Reduction. We first derive a Geometric Intent Prior (GIP) from the spatial concentration of text-relevant tokens to infer a sample-specific relevance-diversity weight, and then apply this weight to jointly select tokens via a Weighted Text Centroid (WTC) for relevance scoring and a Visual Marginal Coverage Gain (VMCG) for diversity. SAVER requires no additional training and achieves sample-aware balancing entirely at inference time. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SAVER consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines across diverse benchmarks, retaining 96.5% of full-model performance on LLaVA-1.5-7B with only 11.1% of the original visual tokens, and further generalizing to LLaVA-NeXT and Mini-Gemini.
authors: Yihang Huang, Peisong Wen, Chenhao Zhou, Difu Feng, Qianqian Xu
bullets: Fixed relevance–diversity weights vary substantially across tasks and even among samples within the same benchmark.
SAVER infers a sample-specific weight from the spatial concentration of text-relevant tokens using a Geometric Intent Prior.
It combines Weighted Text Centroid relevance scoring with Visual Marginal Coverage Gain diversity selection.
The training-free method retains 96.5% of full-model performance on LLaVA-1.5-7B while using 11.1% of the original visual tokens.
It also generalizes to LLaVA-NeXT and Mini-Gemini.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) implemented with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) has driven substantial progress in training reasoning language models. However, verifiable outcome rewards provide an imperfect measure of reasoning quality: a correct final answer may not be supported by the reasoning trace, whereas an incorrect rollout may contain a nearly correct reasoning trajectory. We present empirical evidence for this mismatch and hypothesize that the resulting reward noise contributes to instability in reinforcement learning for both reasoning accuracy and token efficiency. To address this credit assignment challenge, this paper proposes double-rollout reinforcement learning. For each sampled rollout, we truncate its reasoning trace, sample multiple continuations from the truncated prefix, and replace the original reward with the mean continuation reward, yielding a more robust estimate of reasoning quality. This double-rollout algorithm incurs only a moderate increase in compute cost and yet reaches substantially higher accuracies across math and coding tasks and across Qwen and Nemotron models than baseline algorithms with fewer RL steps. For example, using only DAPO data it trains Nemotron-3-Nano-30B-A3B to reach 95.4% on AIME 2026, versus 91.5% by GRPO and substantially above state of the art for this model size, within 30 RL steps. When combined with length-based rewards, the same algorithm further improves the accuracy-efficiency Pareto frontier over existing efficiency optimizations. These findings suggest that the double-rollout reward estimation is an effective and cost-efficient way to improve both the accuracy and token efficiency of reasoning RL.
authors: Haifeng Qian, David Mosallanezhad, Christian Munley, Adithya Renduchintala, Oleksii Kuchaiev
bullets: Verifiable final-answer rewards can misrepresent reasoning quality, creating noisy credit assignment and unstable RL.
For each rollout, the method truncates the reasoning trace and samples multiple continuations from the prefix.
It replaces the original outcome reward with the mean continuation reward as a more robust quality estimate.
The approach adds moderate compute cost and improves math and coding performance across Qwen and Nemotron models.
Combined with length-based rewards, it further improves the accuracy–efficiency trade-off.

papers.tldr: Double-rollout reinforcement learning improves reasoning accuracy and token efficiency by estimating reward from multiple continuations of truncated reasoning traces.

papers.abstract: Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) is commonly used to enhance the capabilities of large language models (LLMs) in solving complex multi-turn tasks. During rollout, agentic RL exhibits a workload pattern distinct from that of traditional RL: multi-turn interactions repeatedly introduce prefill requests, causing prefill and decode workloads to coexist throughout rollout. This workload makes prefill-decode (PD) disaggregation, a design widely used for online LLM serving, promising for speeding up agentic RL rollout. This paper shows that PD disaggregation can improve rollout efficiency by (a) mitigating interference among data-parallel attention modules, (b) enabling stage-specific parallelism, and (c) reducing end-to-end trajectory completion time. However, a fixed prefill-decode allocation may fail to sustain these benefits as workload composition varies across tasks and over time. We therefore present Prorsa, an agentic RL framework for prediction-guided prefill-decode resource allocation. Prorsa observes the lifecycle of every trajectory to forecast short-horizon prefill and decode demand. These forecasts then guide worker allocation decisions and trigger role switching of rollout engines, aligning prefill and decode capacity with anticipated workload demand. Across synchronous and asynchronous agentic RL settings, Prorsa achieves end-to-end rollout speedups of 1.11x-4.05x over prefill-decode colocation.
authors: Chiheng Lou, Xiangwei Deng, Bangjun Xiao, Xiaodong Ji, Yikai Zhao, Xin Jin, Hailin Zhang
bullets: Agentic RL’s multi-turn rollouts repeatedly mix prefill and decode requests, creating interference and changing workload demands.
Prefill-decode disaggregation improves efficiency through reduced attention-module interference, stage-specific parallelism, and shorter trajectory completion times.
Prorsa forecasts near-term prefill and decode demand from each trajectory’s lifecycle.
It reallocates workers and switches rollout-engine roles to match anticipated workload composition.
Across synchronous and asynchronous settings, Prorsa achieves 1.11×–4.05× rollout speedups over colocated prefill and decode.

papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) representation learning is challenged by noisy signals, inter-subject variability, and heterogeneous electrode montages in different datasets and recording settings. Recent self-supervised EEG pretraining methods improve transferability by converting heterogeneous recordings into unified token or sequence representations, but channel-aware designs may still encode montage- or dataset-specific regularities. We propose HyBRA, a self-supervised framework based on hyperbolic global-local brain-region aggregation. HyBRA maps heterogeneous channel observations into a fixed regional token space by combining electrode coordinates, region priors, and feature-dependent hyperbolic distances. A channel-evidence injection branch preserves fine-grained discriminative cues during aggregation. The resulting tokens are processed by a Region-Time Transformer and pretrained with masked reconstruction of latent features and region-level signals. HyBRA outperforms the compared methods in average balanced accuracy on six benchmark datasets. Under a controlled six-fold evaluation on OpenBMI-MI, HyBRA matches CSBrain in balanced accuracy, improves AUROC by 1.84 percentage points and AUPRC by 5.23 percentage points, and uses 96.8\% fewer parameters. Matched comparisons on TUAB and TUEV show higher balanced accuracy for hyperbolic matching than for Euclidean distance or cosine similarity.
authors: Xin Liu, Feng Lu, Wei Li
bullets: Maps variable EEG channels into fixed regional tokens using electrode coordinates, region priors, and feature-dependent hyperbolic distances.
Preserves fine-grained channel information through a channel-evidence injection branch.
Uses a Region-Time Transformer with masked reconstruction of latent features and region-level signals for pretraining.
Outperforms compared methods in average balanced accuracy across six benchmark datasets.
On OpenBMI-MI, matches CSBrain in balanced accuracy, improves AUROC by 1.84 and AUPRC by 5.23 percentage points, while using 96.8% fewer parameters.

papers.abstract: Generating accurate 3D molecules requires jointly determining a variable number of atoms, their identities, and geometry across spatial scales: global shape emerges coarsely, whereas chemical bonds demand fine local precision. Existing atom-based diffusion and flow models operate largely at a single scale, while dense spatial fields become costly at high resolution. We introduce OctMole, a multiscale octree flow framework for 3D molecular generation. A hierarchical occupancy flow progressively resolves sparse molecular support from coarse to fine, and a joint atom flow assigns atom types and continuous in-cell offsets to occupied leaves. This decomposition combines efficient global structure with subcell geometric precision, while cell corruption improves robustness to generated support. On QM9 and GEOM-DRUG, OctMole achieves strong chemical, distributional, and geometric quality, with particularly clear gains over Uni-3DAR on GEOM-DRUG and substantial efficiency gains over dense 3D generation. As an additional capability, intermediate occupancy states and selected regions provide spatial conditioning without task-specific retraining, supporting multiscale shape conditioning, regional editing, linker generation, and shape interpolation. Code and pretrained checkpoints are available at https://github.com/octree-nn/octmole and https://huggingface.co/Disembo/octmole, respectively.
authors: Yu-Tong Jin, Yi-Yang Tian, Qiwei Ye, Peng-Shuai Wang
bullets: Models sparse molecular structure from coarse global shape to fine local geometry.
Uses a hierarchical occupancy flow plus a joint atom flow for atom identities and in-cell offsets.
Cell corruption improves robustness to generated molecular support.
Shows strong chemical, distributional, and geometric quality on QM9 and GEOM-DRUG, with efficiency gains over dense 3D generation.
Enables spatial conditioning for shape control, regional editing, linker generation, and shape interpolation without task-specific retraining.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces OctMole, a multiscale octree flow framework for 3D molecular generation. The hierarchical spatial flow approach is a transferable technique for 3D generation tasks.
papers.title: OctMole: Multiscale 3D Molecular Generation with Hierarchical Spatial Flows

papers.abstract: Physics-informed generative models augment a data-fitting objective with residual penalties that encourage physical constraints to hold in generated samples. However, improving constraint satisfaction need not improve fidelity to the data distribution. We study this conflict in residual-regularized diffusion models and identify two possible consequences. First, the same prediction error can incur different residual costs near different feasible states, preferring states with lower residual sensitivity (avoidance). Second, this preference can extend to feasible states outside the data support, where the residual also vanishes (leakage). Motivated by this analysis, we propose a data-anchored penalty that weights prediction errors by the residual Jacobian at the clean training sample and normalizes the resulting magnitude. This removes the incentive to relocate to less sensitive states without changing the model architecture or sampling procedure. Experiments on a controlled synthetic system, three PDE systems, and molecular transition-state generation with flow matching demonstrate the benefits of anchoring. Code is available at https://github.com/TanjaBien/anchored_diffusion.
authors: Tanja Bien, Samir Darouich, Llu\'is Pastor-P\'erez, Vinh Tong, Loay Mualem, Mathias Niepert
bullets: Physics constraints may improve residual satisfaction while reducing fidelity to the data distribution.
Residual sensitivity varies across feasible states, creating incentives for avoidance and leakage.
The proposed penalty weights prediction errors using the residual Jacobian at clean training samples and normalizes the magnitude.
Experiments cover a synthetic system, three PDEs, and molecular transition-state generation with flow matching.
The method improves anchoring without architectural or sampling-procedure changes.

figures.caption: Figure 4: Trade-offs between distributional fidelity and physical accuracy on Burgers (left), Darcy (middle), and advection (right). Each point shows the MMD and mean absolute residual |R| for one reported setting. Both axes are logarithmic, and lower left is better. Stars denote DM, orange squares PIDM, and blue circles the anchored objective. Dashed lines connect nondominated settings within each regularized method. A setting is nondominated if no other tested weight of the same method reduces one metric without increasing the other. The line segments serve as visual guides. Rings and labels mark the lowest-MMD setting for each regularized method, breaking MMD ties by lower residual. The labeled c values are the coefficients used in each method’s objective.

Bottom, their angular density compared with the data distribution (dashed) and the residual sensitivity σ(θ) (grey). The first column uses the flat residual as a control. Right, median radial residual |∥x∥ − 1| and distance to the data plane ∥x3:D∥ as functions of the penalty weight.

Figure 11: Burgers samples by sensitivity σ. Top, per-sample residual of DM, the anchored objective (c = 10−2) and PIDM (c = 10−1, left). Bottom, density of σ for the data and each model. PIDM generates only samples far less sensitive than the data, while the anchored samples are closer to the data than those of DM and have a lower residual in every sensitivity range.

Figure 2: Comparison of the standard and data-anchored objectives for the displacement illustrated in Figure 1. Curves show the change in expected loss relative to the predictions at x0, with the perturbation distribution held fixed. The dashed curve shows the added denoising cost. (a) The standard residual penalty can decrease enough to outweigh this cost, favoring predictions centered at y. (b) Anchoring the residual Jacobian at x0 removes this saving, so displacement can only increase the expected combined loss, whose minimum remains at x0.

Figure 1: Illustration of avoidance. The training solution x0 and an alternative solution y both satisfy R = 0, but the same zero-mean perturbation δ produces a smaller expected residual penalty near the less sensitive solution y. Shifting predictions from x0+ δ to y+ δ therefore reduces the residual penalty while adding an expected denoising cost of ∥y − x0∥2. The combined objective prefers this shift when the weighted residual reduction exceeds the added denoising cost. If the favored solution lies outside the data support, this preference results in leakage.

papers.selection_reason: Addresses distributional bias in physics-informed generative models. The proposed 'data-anchored penalty' is a transferable technical contribution for learning physical dynamics.
papers.title: Characterizing and Mitigating Distributional Bias in Physics-Informed Generative Models
papers.tldr: Residual penalties can make physics-informed generative models avoid data-supported states or leak into unsupported feasible states; a data-anchored penalty mitigates both without changing architecture or sampling.

papers.abstract: Relevance prediction between user queries and items is a fundamental component of e-commerce search systems. Traditionally, high-quality relevance labels are obtained through human judgment, which is reliable but expensive, slow, and difficult to scale. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) enable automated relevance judgment at scale, achieving performance comparable to human annotators. However, such systems often rely on large commercial LLMs with complex prompts, resulting in high inference costs and limited throughput. In this work, we propose a framework that bridges this gap by distilling a high-performing LLM-based relevance judgment system into efficient multimodal student models. We first curate a small, high-quality human-annotated dataset to serve as ground truth. Using this dataset, we develop a reliable LLM-as-a-judge pipeline through careful prompt engineering and iterative refinement. This pipeline is then used to generate large-scale relevance labels, which serve as training data for compact multimodal models. Our distilled models achieve performance close to the teacher system while significantly improving latency, cost, and scalability. This approach enables practical deployment of high-quality relevance prediction systems in production environments.
authors: Tomasz Gniazdowski, Mohammadreza Momenifar, Nadia Vase, Shahram Khadivi, Wiktor Walentynowicz, Nicola Ueffing, Jan Pawlowski, Piotr Szymanski, Abraham Bagherjeiran
bullets: Addresses the cost, latency, and scalability limits of LLM-based relevance labeling.
Builds a reliable teacher pipeline from a small, high-quality human-annotated dataset and iterative prompt refinement.
Uses the teacher to generate large-scale relevance labels for training compact multimodal student models.
Students perform close to the teacher while improving inference efficiency and deployment practicality.
