papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) have achieved high success rates on familiar manipulation tasks, yet it remains unclear whether such scores reflect genuine zero-shot generalization and perturbation robustness. Existing evaluation frameworks provide limited capability-level diagnosis and combinatorial perturbation coverage, often without connecting diagnosis to targeted model refinement. We introduce VLA-GAUGE, a diagnostic framework that unifies both evaluations under a shared executable task representation. It combines (1) paired in-distribution and out-of-distribution tasks across six capability suites, (2) single-factor sensitivity analysis with combinatorial perturbation screening and evaluation, and (3) diagnosis-driven refinement through targeted data augmentation and model fine-tuning. We evaluate 12 VLAs spanning different model sizes and action-modeling paradigms under a unified protocol. We find that (1) The mean Zero-Shot Score on VLA-GAUGE is only 22.3%, with SimpleVLA-RL scoring 8.0% and ranking second to last among the evaluated models. (2) Under three representative combinatorial perturbation configurations, the mean R-Score is 9.3. (3) Diagnosis-driven fine-tuning improves $\pi_{0.5}$'s zero-shot generalization and robustness under a selected perturbation combination on held-out scenarios by 72.4 and 31.8 scoring points, respectively; the latter exceeds the 10.9-point gain from LIBERO-Plus single-factor fine-tuning despite fewer successful training trajectories. These results show that high reported success rates on familiar manipulation tasks do not guarantee strong zero-shot generalization to unseen tasks or robustness to combinatorial perturbations, while diagnostic evaluation provides actionable signals for targeted model improvement.

Diagnosis-driven fine-tuning improves held-out zero-shot generalization and robustness for π₀.₅ by 72.4 and 31.8 scoring points, respectively.
Scope: findings focus on manipulation-task VLAs and the evaluated task suites and perturbation configurations.

papers.abstract: World models capture environment dynamics and support counterfactual reasoning for planning. In image-goal navigation, where the target often lies beyond the current field of view, the agent must not only model environmental dynamics but also maintain a persistent spatial memory of the scene. Existing approaches either introduce spatial context by fine-tuning pretrained models on the target task, which underexploits their spatial priors, or rely on external 3D reconstruction, which is computationally expensive for real-world deployment. In this paper, we propose the Geometry Grounded World Action Model (G$^2$WAM) for image-goal navigation. G$^2$WAM encodes spatial cues through a learned scene-coordinate localization module that anchors the current, goal, and history frames in a common reference frame, yielding a stable and consistent spatial context that enables efficient navigation without explicit 3D reconstruction. Following the world-action-model paradigm, G$^2$WAM jointly predicts future states and actions, eliminating the need for costly cross-entropy method (CEM) style planning. In addition, G$^2$WAM operates entirely in latent space, avoiding the computational burden of pixel-level reconstruction and substantially reducing inference cost. Across four trajectory prediction benchmarks, G$^2$WAM reduces average ATE and RPE by 40.1% and 35.2%, respectively. In closed-loop navigation experiments, it improves the success rate from 54.0% to 63.0% and the success weighted by path length (SPL) from 36.4% to 59.2%, while maintaining high efficiency.

Reduces average ATE and RPE by 40.1% and 35.2% across four trajectory prediction benchmarks.
Improves closed-loop success rate from 54.0% to 63.0% and SPL from 36.4% to 59.2%, while maintaining efficiency.

papers.abstract: An ordered visual code lets a short prefix stand in for an image, and the training loss decides what that prefix contains. Under pixel reconstruction the first bits go to the directions of highest variance, and we prove that a caption can then be independent of the entire first half of a code that is rate-optimal for pixels at every length. In the rate-distortion sense a caption is therefore not the low-rate code of its image, unless the code is built to make it one. We study that construction and what it costs. We cast captioning and text-to-image generation as successive refinement under a distortion measure that changes along the code, from caption log-loss in the early stages to pixel distortion in the last, so that each stage is compared with its own optimum. Putting words first then costs nothing among the caption stages exactly when the captions form a summarization chain, and it costs the pixels at most the caption uncertainty left in a pixel-optimal reconstruction, which is large for short prefixes and small at full length. We build RUNG, an ordered code whose prefixes are supervised by a summarization ladder of captions and whose full length reconstructs the image; generation extends the code past the prompt and captioning truncates it. With data and capacity held fixed, ordering by language instead of reconstruction raises prefix-caption information 2.9 times and GenEval from 0.76 to 0.83, at a measured cost of 2.8 dB PSNR at a quarter of the code and 0.1 dB at full length. RUNG-XL (3.4B) reaches 0.88 GenEval and 87.6 DPG-Bench in 32 network evaluations and 0.91 GenEval when errors are redrawn at the rung where they appear; its coarse and fine captions agree 94.1% of the time, and it edits images without inversion.
authors: Ruilin Gong, Hao Gong
bullets: Pixel-optimal codes prioritize high-variance visual information, so short prefixes may contain little caption-relevant content.
The paper formulates captioning and image generation as successive refinement with caption loss early and pixel distortion late.
RUNG supervises code prefixes with a hierarchy of captions, then uses the full code for image reconstruction.
With fixed data and capacity, language-first ordering raises prefix-caption information 2.9× and GenEval from 0.76 to 0.83.
The approach costs 2.8 dB PSNR at one-quarter code length but only 0.1 dB at full length; RUNG also supports editing without inversion.

papers.abstract: Basic probabilistic models form the basis of modern deep learning largely by defining the final activation layer of a network and allowing the networks outputs to be interpreted through a probabilistic lens. By increasing the complexity of these final activation layers to include features such as spatial regularisation, allow for these models to improve in performance without requiring significantly more data. The challenge however is to ensure that these more complex probabilistic graphical models adapt well to being used in tandem with deep learning, that is, ensuring they converge and have meaningful derivatives. The goal of this paper is to show two algorithms with provable convergence properties to allow this type of regularisation for image and signal classification models. Through both rigorous mathematical analysis and in silico experiments, we can show the differing performance between these solution types.
authors: John S. H. Baxter
bullets: Motivates richer probabilistic output layers to add spatial regularization without substantially increasing data requirements.
Addresses the challenge of obtaining meaningful derivatives and convergence when pairing graphical models with deep networks.
Introduces two solution approaches for pairwise conditional random fields with convergence guarantees.
Evaluates the approaches through mathematical analysis and in silico experiments, showing differences in their performance.

papers.abstract: Feature caching has become a mainstream training-free strategy for accelerating video diffusion models by reusing intermediate outputs across denoising steps. However, existing adaptive methods rely on heuristic difference measures misaligned with actual generation quality, employ a single global threshold that ignores heterogeneous phase dynamics, and never validate their budget estimates against true approximation error, allowing systematic bias to propagate uncorrected. We propose \textbf{AlignCache}, a closed-loop caching framework that directly aligns scheduling decisions with their true influence on the final generated video through three tightly coupled components: (1) phase-adaptive budget routing that partitions the denoising trajectory into structurally distinct phases, each governed by an independent threshold and a staleness-aware guard; (2) closed-loop threshold calibration that exploits counterfactual error measurement at the classifier-free guided output level to adjust decision boundaries online via an EMA feedback loop; and (3) momentum-augmented draft synthesis combining direction-magnitude gated residual extrapolation with anchor-guided unconditional correction. By transforming scheduling from a static risk accumulator into a feedback-driven, self-correcting controller, AlignCache consistently achieves superior acceleration-quality trade-offs across state-of-the-art video generation models. Our code is available at https://github.com/jiangjyjy/AlignCache.
authors: Jiyue Jiang, Zhiyu Huo, Yuhan Chen, Yanruisheng Shao, Gong Zhang, Lei Deng
bullets: Targets heuristic caching decisions, global thresholds, and uncorrected approximation error in existing methods.
Routes caching budgets across denoising phases with independent thresholds and staleness-aware safeguards.
Calibrates thresholds online using counterfactual classifier-free-guided error measurements and EMA feedback.
Uses momentum-based draft synthesis with gated residual extrapolation and unconditional correction.
Reports consistently better acceleration–quality trade-offs across state-of-the-art video generation models; specific gains are not given.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of AlignCache. (a) Pipeline of phase-adaptive budget routing. The system decides whether to skip or perform exact computation based on the cumulative risk budget Bt, age cap Apt , and dynamic threshold θp,t. The process computes exact outputs and counterfactual skip drafts, then derives the skip distortion. The calibration ratio is updated from observed distortion and combined with the dynamic threshold. The resulting scale factor and phase partition θp determine θp,t in part (a). (c) Process of momentum-augmented draft synthesis. The current residual is predicted from the two most recent exact anchors a(t) and a−(t), applying momentum correction when direction and magnitude align, or a first-order estimate otherwise. The final drafts (ĉt, ût) feed into part (b).

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) is reshaping how large language models (LLMs) acquire reasoning capabilities, yet the optimizers used remain largely inherited from teacher-forcing training. This raises a fundamental question: does RLVR induce a distinct optimization geometry that calls for a different optimizer? We investigate this question through the spectral structure of LLM gradients and find that gradient energy progressively concentrates into a shrinking effective subspace, which is characteristic of RLVR, as it is absent under supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and is largely removed when the verifiable reward is replaced by a random one. Moreover, the rank required to capture a fixed fraction of gradient energy steadily decreases over training, revealing that the effective dimensionality of useful updates itself evolves with training. These findings motivate a new optimization principle: rather than prescribing the update rank externally, an optimizer should adapt its rank to the evolving spectral structure of the gradient. We introduce Ares (Adaptive Rank-Effective Spectral Optimization), which estimates the effective update rank from the gradient's spectral energy distribution, tracks its evolution, and confines the gradient signal driving each update to the resulting low-rank subspace. Across LLMs of different scales, Ares improves accuracy over widely used optimizers and generalizes across RLVR algorithms and tasks. Results suggest that effective optimization may require optimizers to be designed around the geometry and dynamics of the training process. We release the code and data at https://github.com/RUCAIBox/Ares.
authors: Zhipeng Chen, Wayne Xin Zhao, Ji-Rong Wen
bullets: RLVR gradients progressively concentrate energy in a shrinking effective subspace, unlike gradients from supervised fine-tuning or random-reward training.
The rank needed to capture a fixed share of gradient energy decreases during training, indicating that useful update dimensionality evolves over time.
Ares estimates gradient spectral energy, tracks effective rank, and restricts each update to the resulting adaptive low-rank subspace.
Across LLM scales, RLVR algorithms, and tasks, Ares improves accuracy over commonly used optimizers.
The findings suggest RLVR may benefit from optimizers designed for its specific gradient geometry and dynamics.

We distinguish three properties: whether the method restricts the update to a low-rank subspace, how the rank/update subspace is determined, and whether that determination is spectral-driven, i.e., inferred from the gradient’s spectral energy distribution during training. Ares infers the dimensionality of the update subspace from the evolving gradient spectrum.

papers.title: Spectral-Driven Adaptive-Rank Optimizer for Large Language Model Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards
papers.tldr: RLVR creates an evolving low-dimensional gradient structure, motivating Ares, an optimizer that adapts update rank to this spectral geometry and improves accuracy across models, algorithms, and tasks.

papers.abstract: Safe robot navigation in unknown, dynamic environments requires more than geometric collision checking: a robot still far from an obstacle may be unable to avoid it because of its speed, orientation, or the obstacle's motion. Hamilton--Jacobi (HJ) reachability analysis captures this in a value function whose sign separates states that admit a safe continuation from those where collision is unavoidable, but computing it online for every newly observed environment is too expensive. This dissertation trains neural implicit representations offline on reachability solutions to give optimization-based controllers this information in real time. Since the value function never exceeds the constraint, it equals a directly computed constraint, such as a signed distance, minus a nonnegative dynamics correction. Learning only this correction keeps represented obstacles outside the predicted safe set despite approximation errors. The first two of five methods use the learned function as a terminal constraint in model predictive control, for static local environments and predicted obstacle motion. The next two use it as a barrier candidate in control barrier function safety filters, for static environments and, through pairwise barriers in relative coordinates, for a varying number of moving obstacles. Simulations and hardware experiments on ground and aerial robots show better collision avoidance than geometric and hand-designed baselines, especially for short horizons and moving obstacles. The fifth method replaces the grid-based offline solver, which limits the first four to low-dimensional models. For control-affine dynamics with polytopic inputs, the HJ Hamiltonian is maximized at a vertex, so a parallelizable tree search over vertex inputs can generate training labels. With a loss from the HJ variational inequality, these labels yield barrier candidates for systems with up to 13 states.
authors: Bojan Deraji\'c
bullets: HJ reachability identifies states where collision is unavoidable, but online computation is too expensive for newly observed environments.
Neural implicit models learn the nonnegative dynamics correction to signed-distance constraints, preserving conservative safety under approximation error.
The learned representations support model predictive control and control-barrier-function filters for static environments and moving obstacles.
Simulations and hardware experiments on ground and aerial robots show improved collision avoidance, particularly with short planning horizons and moving obstacles.
A tree-search labeling method avoids grid-based solvers and extends barrier-candidate generation to control-affine systems with up to 13 states.

figures.caption: Figure 2.3: Offline–online pipeline shared by the methods of this dissertation. Offline, a solver computes HJ value functions Vw for a set of training conditioning inputs, and these solutions supervise the learned safety model. Chapters 3 to 6 obtain them from a grid-based solver, while Chapter 7 replaces this block by vertex-restricted search combined with a physics-informed loss. Online, the current conditioning input w selects the scalar field V̂ ( · | w) whose value and gradient the optimization-based controller evaluates. The compact main network takes the robot state x as input and is conditioned on w, either through parameters generated by the optional hypernetwork (dashed) once per update, as in Chapters 3 to 5, or directly when the hypernetwork is omitted. The main network is evaluated and differentiated at every query.

Figure 1.3: Typical mobile robot navigation architecture. Perception converts sensor data into maps, state estimates, and obstacle information. A global planner provides a route toward the task goal, a local planner converts this route and the latest observations into executable local motion, and a feedback controller tracks the resulting reference. An optional safety filter (dashed) supervises the nominal command and modifies it when it violates the specified safety condition.

Figure 3.7: Success rates in the Monte Carlo simulation study for the two robot models (columns) and the two environments (rows), with 100 runs per configuration. The models are trained on warehouse data only and evaluated in both environments. The performance of the distance-based baselines degrades considerably as the prediction horizon becomes shorter, while the NTC-MPC method maintains higher success rates across all horizon lengths. The RWMSE-trained model also consistently matches or outperforms its MSEtrained counterpart.

Figure 4.2: RNTC-MPC architecture. Tracked obstacle positions and velocities are extrapolated over the MPC horizon and converted into a predicted SDF sequence. The stage-matched SDFs define the collision-avoidance constraints, while selected snapshots near the terminal stage form the conditioning input of the hypernetwork. The hypernetwork runs once per planning cycle and generates the main-network parameters. Inside the nonlinear program, the terminal constraint is the predicted terminal SDF minus the nonnegative main-network output, as in Equation (4.6). The solver evaluates this assembled function and its derivatives repeatedly.

Figure 7.1: Finite-horizon trajectories for the inverted pendulum, generated by (a) model predictive path integral (MPPI) sampling over the full control set and (b) the proposed vertex-restricted beam search. Both methods start from the same 160 random initial states, drawn as circles and colored by the worst constraint value mink c(xk) reached along the trajectory, so that red marks a constraint violation. The subsequent states are drawn as small arrows that point in the direction of motion. The black lines mark the constraint boundary and the purple dashed lines the boundary of the numerically computed maximal safe set. The vertex-restricted search keeps the pendulum inside the constraint set from almost every initial state in the numerically computed safe set, while the full-control sampler fails from many of them.

Figure 3.2: Architecture of the NTC-MPC local planner. From the current sensor data, an SDF is computed and used both as the geometric stage constraint of the MPC problem and as the conditioning input wk of the hypernetwork. The hypernetwork, a convolutional backbone with a fully connected head, outputs the parameters of the compact main network, which represents the estimated value function V̂Ψ( · | wk). The nonlinear program (NLP) solver queries the main network for the value and gradient of the terminal constraint at every optimizer iteration, while the hypernetwork is evaluated only once per planning cycle.

Figure 5.3: Architecture of the ORN-CBF safety filter. The discretized SDF wj computed from the observation oj is used twice, as the conditioning input of the hypernetwork, which generates the parameters Θ of the main network representing the nonnegative residual r̂Ψ, and as the input of the interpolant representing the observed constraint function c( · | oj). Barrier value and gradient are assembled by subtraction as in Equation (5.9), and the Lie derivatives Lf0ĥΨ and LgĥΨ parameterize the CBF-QP Equation (5.13) together with ĥΨ. The softplus output of the main network is not drawn as a separate stage. The hypernetwork runs once per observation update, and the main network and the interpolant are queried at control rate.

Figure 1.5: Organization of the dissertation. After the introduction and the preliminaries, Parts I and II group the technical chapters by controller interface, and within each part the development progresses from static to dynamic environments. Part III varies a third design choice, the origin of the reachability supervision. The concluding chapter compares the methods of the three parts.

Figure 3.10: Representative hardware experiment with the Dubins car model and horizon N = 10 (1 s). The upper row shows the overlaid robot motion for the three planners, where both baselines collide with the obstacle (red) while NTC-MPC avoids it (green). The plots show the time evolution of the predicted terminal value V̂Ψ(xN |k | wk) and of the observed obstacle distance c(xk | ok), with the zero level marked by the dotted line. In this configuration, the obstacle distance of the baselines remains positive until shortly before the collision, while NTC-MPC begins to avoid the obstacle when its terminal value approaches zero, several seconds earlier.

Figure 4.10: Motion efficiency in simulation over the scenarios completed by all planners. (a) Travel times from start to goal, which are similar across methods. (b) Mean travel time against success rate, with one marker per method and horizon. Higher success and shorter travel time are preferable, so the lower right region is favorable. RNTC-MPC achieves the highest success rate at every tested horizon with a mean travel time close to the lowest.

Figure 4.11: (a) Per-run mean and (b) per-run maximum lateral deviation from the reference path in the simulation study, shown over the horizon length for the scenarios completed by all planners. VO-MPC deviates most at the three shorter horizons, which reflects its evasive velocity constraints, while RNTC-MPC remains comparable to the geometric baselines. The deviations of all methods are larger at long horizons than at short ones, since a longer look-ahead triggers earlier and wider avoidance.

Figure 1.4: Qualitative positioning of the reviewed method families and this dissertation. The horizontal axis indicates adaptation to new local observations, and the vertical axis indicates the extent to which safety reasoning accounts for robot dynamics and actuation limits. Placements represent typical formulations, and the learning-based safety filters include both learned barrier functions and learned reachability values. This dissertation studies reachability-informed safety constraints across static and dynamic environments and across MPC and safety-filter interfaces.

Figure 6.6: Ground-robot simulation study over 100 randomized pedestrian-crowd scenarios per density. (a) Success rates of the four MPC-based planners and of the CN-CBF safety filter. The advantage of CN-CBF increases with the crowd density. (b) Path lengths and (c) times to goal of the scenarios completed by all methods. Boxes span the interquartile range, lines mark the median, and whiskers extend to 1.5 times the interquartile range. The higher success rates of CN-CBF are not obtained through detours or overly conservative motion.

Figure 6.8: Quadrotor simulation study over 100 randomized scenarios per density, comparing the CN-CBF filter against the collision-cone CBF (C3BF) and the higher-order CBF (HO-CBF), all combined with the same LQR nominal controller. (a) Success rates. (b) Path lengths and (c) times to goal of the scenarios completed by all methods, with boxes as in Figure 6.6. CN-CBF maintains the highest success rates at every density while matching the baselines in path length and motion time.

Figure B.1: Two-dimensional slices of the learned barriers V̂Θ for the 15 evaluated systems under vertex-restricted supervision (first seed), in the order of Table 7.1, with red shading marking the states predicted to be unsafe. The black line is the constraint boundary, the green line the boundary of the predicted safe set, the orange dash-dotted line the boundary of the set that the rollouts of Section 7.5.2 validate as safe within the slice, and the purple dashed line the boundary of the numerically computed maximal safe set where a numerical solution is available.

Figure 8.1: The five methods organized by the design choices that separate them. The columns of the grid give the controller interface, its rows give the environment class for which the reachability targets are computed, and each box names the learned representation and its conditioning input. The band below the grid holds the third design choice, the source of the supervision, which VertexCBF generates from the vertex structure of the input set instead of taking it from a grid-based solver.

Figure 1.1: Mobile robot navigation in an unknown warehouse environment shared with other agents and perceived through local onboard sensing. The space outside the perception field is unknown, and the robot must react to new observations while maintaining safety margins under its dynamics and actuation limits.

Figure 3.5: Effect of the training objective for the Dubins car model, evaluated on the validation set. (a) Safe-set IoU over training epochs for models trained with RWMSE and MSE under identical settings and initialization. (b), (c) Confusion matrices of the safe/unsafe classification for RWMSE and MSE, with entries in percent of all grid states. RWMSE yields a consistently higher IoU and fewer misclassifications on both sides of the boundary.

Figure 3.3: Training procedure for the NTC model. Each SDF conditioning input w from the dataset is processed by the hypernetwork into the main-network parameters Θ(w), and all states of a state-space grid are propagated through the main network to predict the value function over the grid. HJ reachability analysis, using the same SDF as the constraint function c( · | w), provides the numerical target values V∞( · | w). The loss L compares predicted and target value functions, and its gradient updates the hypernetwork parameters Ψ. The main-network parameters are outputs of the hypernetwork rather than free variables. The figure shows a single training pair, so the batch and grid indices of Equation (3.7) are omitted.

Figure 4.5: Residual parameterization versus direct value regression at equal model capacity, evaluated on the validation set for three main-network sizes (2790, 4519, and 6670 parameters). (a) Safe-set intersection over union (IoU) over training epochs, with the residual models in green and the direct-regression models in orange, and the line pattern indicating the network size. The residual models start higher, converge roughly five times faster, and end higher. (b) Final IoU after 100 epochs. The residual models reach a higher IoU at every size, and the smallest residual model outperforms the largest direct-regression model.

Figure 6.7: Example scene from the ground-robot simulation study. (a) The Gazebo environment with the robot navigating among pedestrians controlled by the social-force model. (b) The corresponding local perception, with detected pedestrians, their estimated velocities, and the planned motion of the robot. (c) Positional slice of the composite barrier ĥcn in the robot frame, with the robot at the origin heading to the right (dart), evaluated over hypothetical robot positions at the current heading, with red shading marking the unsafe positions and arrows showing the pedestrian velocities. The pairwise zero level sets (gray) surround the collision disk of each pedestrian (black) and are elongated along the direction in which that pedestrian moves relative to the robot, while the composite zero level set (green) traces a smooth outline around their union without touching the collision disks.

Figure 6.4: Block diagram of the CN-CBF safety filter. The robot state and the current obstacle-state estimates feed three parallel blocks. The batched CN-CBF evaluation of Figure 6.3 returns the composite barrier value and its gradients, the robot dynamics model supplies f0(x) and g(x), and the backward-difference estimator in Equation (6.16) supplies the obstacle state derivatives. Together they parameterize the CBF-QP Equation (6.18), which minimally modifies the nominal command unom.

Figure 6.9: Composite barrier value ĥcn (green) and distance mini crel(zi) to the nearest pedestrian (dashed) over time during a successful collision-avoidance run of the CN-CBF filter on the physical delivery robot. The barrier value anticipates the encounter well before the distance becomes small and briefly becomes negative under model mismatch and measurement noise. The physical buffer contained in Rmin prevents a collision during this interval.

Figure 1.2: Unsafe states for a mobile robot avoiding a static obstacle and a dynamic obstacle crossing its path. The shaded regions are still collision-free, but neither full braking nor maximal steering to either side prevents collision. For the static obstacle, the region grows roughly with the braking distance. For the moving obstacle, it is additionally shaped by the relative motion. A controller that monitors only current distance (dashed trajectories) may enter this region, but a dynamics-aware controller (solid trajectory) evades while recovery remains possible.

Figure 3.1: Effect of the terminal constraint on an MPC local planner that approaches a static obstacle, shown at two consecutive planning steps. Each red-shaded region is a slice of the backward reachable tube (BRT) of the observed obstacle, that is, of the set X \ S⋆(ok) of states from which collision can no longer be avoided under the actuation limits. The slice depends on the heading, so a solid outline belongs to the current state and a dashed outline to the terminal state. In the lower row the dotted body marks the position at step k. Left: the terminal constraint is distance based, so every state predicted at step k keeps a nonnegative distance to the obstacle and the planner continues straight ahead. At step k + 1 the robot has entered the BRT, and every admissible input sequence collides at some later instant. Right: the reachability-based terminal constraint xN |k ∈ S⋆(ok) makes the planner steer away already at step k, so the robot remains outside the BRT one step later.

Figure 5.10: Representative quadrotor scenario. (a) Executed motion under the LQR nominal controller with the ORN-CBF safety filter among the ten cylindrical obstacles (gray), colored by time. The filter steers the quadrotor around the obstacles with which the goal-directed LQR would otherwise collide. (b) Evolution of the barrier value ĥΨ(x(t) | wj), which decreases toward zero during the avoidance maneuvers and remains positive throughout the run.

Figure 4.12: Executed trajectories over all 100 simulation runs for each planner at N = 10, corresponding to a 1 s prediction horizon, plotted as lateral deviation d against the distance along the reference path. Green denotes successful runs and red denotes collisions. SDFMPC remains close to the reference but collides frequently, VO-MPC deviates widely from the reference, and the planners with learned terminal constraints achieve moderate deviations with fewer failures.

Figure 4.3: RNTC training procedure. Each obstacle trajectory is split at a reference instant. Selected snapshots before that instant form the conditioning input w of Equation (4.5), which the hypernetwork converts into the main-network parameters Θ(w). The generated main network produces a nonnegative residual on the state-space grid. The subsequent trajectory segment defines the time-varying failure set used to compute the numerical HJ target V ( · | w) at the reference instant. Subtracting the predicted residual from the reference-instant SDF yields the value-function estimate used in the training loss. The figure shows a single training pair, so the batch and grid indices of Equation (4.10) are omitted. Signal names match Figure 3.3.
Figure 7.8: View from the onboard computer of the delivery robot during a trial, showing the front camera image, a positional slice of the learned barrier, and the output of the perception module.

Figure 4.1: Effect of the terminal constraint on an MPC local planner among moving obstacles, shown at two consecutive planning steps. The robot tracks the reference path to the right at constant speed and with a limited turning rate, while an obstacle crosses that path from the front left. Each red region collects the states from which a collision can no longer be avoided under the actuation limits. It extends along the obstacle velocity relative to the robot, so it is not aligned with the drawn velocity arrow, and the region at the terminal instant is the region at the current instant displaced and rotated according to the obstacle motion over the horizon. In the lower row the dotted outlines mark the positions at step k. Left: constraints formed from the current observation refer only to the unsafe region at the current instant, X \ S0|k, so the planner continues straight ahead at step k. At step k + 1 its state lies inside that region, where continued straight motion and both extreme steering maneuvers end in the predicted obstacle. Right: the terminal constraint xN |k ∈ SN |k of RNTC-MPC refers to the predicted geometry and is already active at step k, so the planner turns away and its plan remains feasible one step later.

Figure 7.7: Hardware experiment with the delivery robot. (a) The recorded robot motion and the tracked pedestrians in the workspace, drawn as circles colored by time. Opaque circles mark the two encounters in which a pedestrian crosses the path of the robot. (b) The composite barrier value ĥcn over the run, with the zero level marked by the dotted line. While no pedestrian is tracked, the barrier is undefined and its value is drawn at 3 m. (c), (d) The nominal and the filtered acceleration and turning-rate commands. The filter deviates from the nominal command only while a pedestrian is on an intercepting course, and the barrier value becomes slightly negative for a short period while the pedestrians pass the robot.

Figure 4.15: Onboard view during a hardware trial. Top left: boundary of the predicted terminal safe set relative to the predicted pedestrian motion. Bottom left: front-camera view. Right: detected pedestrian and predicted trajectory used to construct the SDF sequence.

Figure 4.8: Gazebo simulation environment. Six cylindrical obstacles with randomly initialized positions and velocity vectors (arrows) move at constant speed within a corridor and reverse direction at its edges. The robot must navigate from the start position to the goal position ahead of it, using only local observations.

Figure 4.14: Executed trajectories of the four planners in one representative hardware scenario with a single crossing pedestrian, with one run per planner under the same experimental setting, plotted as lateral deviation d against the distance along the reference path, with the dots along each trajectory colored by time. SDF-MPC fails to react and collides after about 2.5 m (red cross). VO-MPC evades with a detour of up to 0.8 m and DCBF-MPC with up to 0.16 m, while RNTC-MPC resolves the encounter with a deviation of only a few centimeters by adjusting its timing along the path.

Figure 3.9: The ten static obstacle configurations used in the hardware experiments, viewed from the external camera. The robot starts below the lower edge and must reach a waypoint near the upper edge of the scenario image.

Figure 6.10: Barrier values and distance to the nearest obstacle over time in the quadrotor hardware experiments with five moving obstacle drones, for (a) the CN-CBF filter, (b) the C3BF filter [162], and (c) the HO-CBF filter [61], all around the same LQR nominal controller. For the two baselines, which impose one constraint per obstacle, the five pairwise barrier values h1, . . . , h5 are shown individually, and each HO-CBF barrier is the distance to the corresponding obstacle by definition. Only the CN-CBF filter keeps the distance positive throughout, while both baselines collide (red circles).

Figure 7.2: Learned barriers V̂Θ for the inverted pendulum under the three supervision settings, (a) no data (ND), (b) full-control data (FCD), and (c) vertex-restricted control data (VRCD), shown in the (θ, ω) plane with red shading marking the states predicted to be unsafe. The black lines mark the constraint boundary, the purple dashed lines the boundary of the numerically computed maximal safe set, and the green lines the boundary of the predicted safe set. The physics-informed loss alone (ND) collapses to a trivial constant solution with an empty predicted safe set. Full-control supervision (FCD) produces a barrier that is safe but strongly conservative. Vertex-restricted supervision (VRCD) approximately recovers the maximal safe set while keeping its predicted safe set inside the constraint set.

Figure 7.6: Sensitivity to the weight λ of the physics-informed term on the inverted pendulum. (a) Validation metrics. (b) Mean squared error against the numerically computed value function. Curves are means over three seeds and the bands are one standard deviation. In the shaded region the predicted safe set is empty for λ = 0.7, where ηeff is zero and ρFS is undefined, and every state predicted safe is unsafe for λ ≥ 0.9.

Figure 4.9: Monte Carlo simulation results over 100 randomized scenarios. (a) Success rate against the prediction-horizon length. RNTC-MPC achieves the highest rate at every tested horizon and consistently exceeds direct-regression NTC-MPC. (b) Per-run mean NLP solve times over the scenarios completed by all planners, which remain considerably below the 50 ms control-update period. Boxes span the interquartile range, lines mark the median, and whiskers extend to 1.5 times the interquartile range.
Figure 5.6: Ground-robot simulation study. Left: scene from the Gazebo warehouse environment. Right: the corresponding local observation from which the ORN-CBF barrier is generated.
Figure 5.8: Quadrotor simulation study. Left: scene from the Gazebo forest-like environment. Right: the corresponding local observation.

Figure 5.11: Ground-robot hardware experiments. Left: the differential-drive robot among the static obstacles. Right: visualization of the local observation from which the barrier is generated onboard.

Figure 5.5: A learned ORN-CBF for the Dubins car on a validation observation. (a) The observed SDF c( · | o) with the obstacle outlines c = 0 (black) and the robot position at heading θ = π/2 (dart, moving upward). (b) The numerical HJ target V∞( · | o) at the same heading with its zero level set (dashed). Red shading marks the unsafe states, which extend beyond the obstacle outlines in the directions in which the robot approaches the obstacles head-on, and the orange square marks the central 16 × 16 positional patch on which the residual network is trained. (c) The learned barrier ĥΨ( · | w) on this patch whose zero level set (green) closely follows the HJ boundary. The asymmetry of the unsafe region reflects the turning limitation of the constant-speed vehicle.

Figure 5.2: The critical moment of an observation update. Geometry that the current observation does not contain is drawn faded and with dashed boundaries. (a) At tj, a previously unobserved obstacle lies beyond the boundary of the sensing window of half-width ρ. Neither the failure set F (grey) nor its BRT B∞(F) (red) is part of the observation oj. (b) Between two updates the robot travels at most vmax∆to, and the window is recentered at the new robot position. The new observation thus gains a band of that depth beyond its previous boundary (dashed) and now contains most of the obstacle. Under the boundary-appearance assumption, previously unseen obstacles can appear only inside this band, and hence at least ρ− vmax∆to away from the robot. Continued safety requires the state to lie outside B∞(F) at the instant at which the barrier is replaced.

Figure 3.6: Gazebo simulation environments. Left: warehouse environment, from which all training observations are collected. Right: house environment, used exclusively for evaluation to assess generalization under a distribution shift in obstacle geometry.

Figure 3.8: NLP solve times of the three planners for (a) the Dubins car and (b) the dynamic unicycle as functions of the horizon length, pooled over both environments. Each box spans the interquartile range of the per-run mean solve times of the successful runs, the line marks the median, and the whiskers extend to 1.5 times the interquartile range. The neural terminal constraint adds an approximately horizon-independent offset over SDF-MPC, while the stage-wise DCBF-MPC constraints scale faster with the horizon. All values remain considerably below the 100 ms planning period.

Figure 3.4: Learned safe set for a sample observation from the validation dataset (Dubins car). (a) Local occupancy grid o. (b) The corresponding SDF c( · | o), whose zero level set (black) outlines the obstacles. (c) Slice of the learned value function V̂Ψ( · | w) at heading θ = π/2, that is, for a robot at the marked position (dart) moving upward. Red shading marks the states predicted to be unsafe. The predicted safe-set boundary V̂Ψ = 0 (green) closely follows the numerical HJ boundary V∞ = 0 (dashed). The unsafe region extends beyond the obstacle outlines, most visibly below the obstacles, which the robot approaches head-on at this heading.

Figure 4.4: Pointwise optimum ŷ∗ of the CME loss Equation (4.12) as a function of the target y for different weights λ. For λ = 1 the loss reduces to MSE and the optimum is the identity (dashed). As λ decreases, predictions near the zero level set are displaced away from zero, while the sign, the zero crossing, and the behavior for large |y| are preserved.

Figure 5.9: Outcomes of the quadrotor simulation study over 200 randomized scenarios per configuration, split into successes, timeouts, and collisions. (a) In the training domain, the learned filters succeed in more than 90% of the runs, compared with 58.5% for the hand-tuned ECBF. (b) In the out-of-domain environment with unseen obstacle radii, the success rates of the learned filters decrease by at most two percentage points, while that of the ECBF decreases to 45.0%.

Figure 6.5: Positional slice of the learned pairwise barrier ĥΘ for the ground robot, at relative heading θrel = π (obstacle moving head-on toward the robot) and obstacle speed vo = 1.2 m s−1, in the robot body frame. The robot is located at the origin and heads along prel x . The collision set (black circle, zero level of crel) is the disk of relative obstacle positions within Rmin of the robot. The numerically computed unsafe region (red shading, zero level of V∞ dashed) extends several meters ahead of the robot, because an oncoming obstacle in this region can force a collision on a robot that cannot stop and that turns at a limited rate. The zero level set of the learned barrier (green) closely matches the numerical HJ boundary and, by construction, never enters the collision set.

Figure 7.5: Slices of the learned barrier V̂Θ for the six-degree-of-freedom underwater vehicle in the (py, pz) plane, one for each step size of Table 7.3, with red shading marking the states predicted to be unsafe. The black line is the constraint boundary and the green line is the boundary of the predicted safe set. The predicted safe set becomes visibly smaller at the largest step size.

Figure 6.2: Smooth composition of two pairwise barriers along a one-dimensional slice of the state space, for example a straight path from one obstacle to the other. (a) The two pairwise barrier values (blue and orange) form the nonsmooth pointwise minimum (dashed), whose kink at x̄ marks the change of the active obstacle. The composite barrier ĥcn = µβ (green) runs below that minimum, with a gap that is largest at the kink, where it attains the bound lnm/β of Equation (6.12). The composite safe interval (green) is slightly smaller than the one given by the exact minimum (gray). (b) The softmax weights Equation (6.13) along the same slice transfer the gradient continuously from one obstacle to the other instead of switching at x̄, and a larger β narrows this transition.

Figure 5.7: Success rates of the ground-robot simulation study over the MPC predictionhorizon length, with 100 randomized runs per configuration. The safety filters ORN-CBF and ON-CBF are combined with the plain SDF-MPC planner. Both outperform every MPCbased planner for N ≤ 20, including the reachability-informed NTC-MPC of Chapter 3, which reaches a similar rate at N = 30. ORN-CBF achieves the highest rates overall.

Figure 5.12: Barrier values of the ORN-CBF and ON-CBF filters in one representative obstacle configuration of the ground-robot hardware experiments, with one run per filter under the same experimental setting and the zero level marked by the dotted line. Briefly negative values are followed by recovery, and no collision occurs. The physical inflation margin separates the represented failure boundary from physical contact.

Figure 5.4: Closed-loop arrangement of the ORN-CBF safety filter for a robot that operates on local observations. A nominal controller of arbitrary design issues the command unom. From the current observation oj, ORN-CBF generates the barrier candidate ĥΨ( · | wj) once per observation update, as detailed in Figure 5.3. The CBF-QP Equation (5.13) then evaluates this barrier at the measured state x at control rate, modifies the command minimally if needed, and forwards the filtered control u⋆ to the robot. The dashed arrows indicate that the nominal controller may use the same two signals, on which the filter places no requirement.

Figure 6.3: Structure of the CN-CBF barrier evaluation. The current obstacle states are stacked into a batch, combined with the robot state x into the batch of relative states zi = σ(x, qi), and propagated in parallel through the shared residual network r̂Θ and the closed-form pairwise constraint crel. Their difference yields the pairwise barrier values of Equation (6.8), which the smooth aggregation µβ reduces to the composite value in Equation (6.11). One reverse-mode differentiation pass through this graph returns all gradients in Equation (6.15).

Figure 4.7: Effect of the training objective on the safe-set IoU, evaluated on the validation set over training epochs for the same residual model trained with the CME loss (λ = 0.1) and with plain MSE under identical settings. CME converges faster, reaching the final MSE level after about 20 epochs, and ends at a higher IoU (≈ 0.975 versus ≈ 0.967).

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models are often pretrained via imitation learning, making reinforcement learning (RL) post-training important when deployment moves beyond demonstration coverage. Existing refinement paradigms expose a reliability--efficiency tension: model-free refinement avoids simulator bias but is interaction-intensive, whereas model-based refinement can exploit unreliable imagination even as its simulator adapts. We propose Model-Evolving Reinforcement Learning (MERL), a trust-calibrated framework that couples policy optimization with an online-updated simulator comprising a world model and a reward proxy head. Across stages, simulator reliability controls the imagined-data ratio and rollout horizon; within rollouts, chunk-level trust controls replay selection and optimization weight. For recursive imagination without exact grounded continuations, a residual predictor estimates trust without querying future ground truth. On perturbed LIBERO-PRO tasks, MERL reaches 79.7% average success, improves high-threshold learning speed by 10.9% over the matched model-free control, and outperforms same-protocol external baselines across three training seeds. Fixed-data adaptation from 50 demonstrations per task achieves 80.0% average success on two physical-robot tasks.
authors: Wenzhan Li, Yiran Qin, Heng Zhou, Huirui Wang, Yulan Guo, Ruimao Zhang
bullets: Addresses the efficiency–reliability trade-off between interaction-heavy model-free refinement and potentially biased model-based refinement.
Couples policy optimization with an online-updated world model and reward proxy, using simulator reliability to adjust imagined-data ratios and rollout horizons.
Uses chunk-level trust for replay selection and optimization weighting, with a residual predictor for recursive imagination without future ground-truth queries.
On perturbed LIBERO-PRO tasks, achieves 79.7% average success and 10.9% faster high-threshold learning than matched model-free control.
With 50 demonstrations per task, reaches 80.0% average success on two physical-robot tasks.

papers.abstract: In parallel decoding, diffusion language models commit several tokens per forward pass, so co-committed tokens cannot see each other, breaking multi-token format units that parsers need. On ECHO, an open-weight one-step chest X-ray (CXR) report generator, 32.7-36.7% of evaluation reports lack a parseable Impression heading and score as empty. We propose intent-triggered anchoring, a training-free decoding rule that completes a format unit once the model commits its first token, inserting only units with a unique, content-free completion; fallbacks write the unit when the model stops or loops without starting it. On three CXR evaluation sets, the rule raises readable rates from 63.3-67.3% to 100.0% with no regressions and a 95th-percentile latency ratio of 0.68-1.28 against official decoding. Broken headings state findings absent from the reference; adding the heading at the end leaves them in 15.5-31.0% of reports, our rule in at most 0.6%. For math answer markers, the rule raises accuracy in the most parallel setting of five diffusion language models by 5.8-20.8 points on GSM8K and 5.1-17.1 on GSM-Symbolic, held out from tuning. With lenient answer extraction, gains are 3.3-12.5 and 2.7-6.3 points; the rule adds 1.4-8.6 points over a stop-only fallback for four of the five models.
authors: Junhyeok Lee, Kyu Sung Choi
bullets: Parallel decoding can commit tokens simultaneously, preventing tokens within required format units—such as headings or answer markers—from attending to one another.
The training-free rule completes a format unit after its first token when the completion is unique and content-free, with stop-or-loop fallbacks.
Across three CXR evaluation sets, readable reports increase from 63.3–67.3% to 100.0%, with no regressions and latency ratios of 0.68–1.28 at the 95th percentile.
For math answer markers, accuracy improves by 5.8–20.8 points on GSM8K and 5.1–17.1 points on GSM-Symbolic in the most parallel setting.
The approach reduces broken headings that state unsupported findings to at most 0.6% of reports; scope is limited to format units with unique, content-free completions.

papers.abstract: Improving an agent through successive revisions requires balancing exploration and evaluation under a limited budget. A narrow search can miss useful sequences of edits, while fully evaluating every intermediate version can exhaust the budget before those sequences yield a verified improvement. We introduce Speculative Recursive Self-Improvement (SpecRSI), which drafts executable successor agents before their predecessors are fully evaluated, while requiring complete verification before adoption. Verification-Aware Tree Search (VATS) allocates the budget between further edits and outstanding checks using the predicted verified return of a continuation. Group Verification Optimization (GVO) learns the improver from completed searches while keeping the real evaluator fixed. In the main scientific comparison, terminal gains exceed Janus by 33.3%--40.0%. Additional evaluations show that SpecRSI outperforms Janus in all 50 scientific backbone--task pairs and exceeds MetaRSI-v1 by 1.85%--2.38% in macro-average system score across twenty backbones. Coding-validation success reaches 69.4% versus HGM's 64.3% at a 20.8% lower target-cost index.
authors: Xin Xu, Ke Cheng, Hao Wang, Yangru Huang, Yanghao Xiao, Zhichao Chen, Zhisheng Zhong, Xun Liu, Yi Li, Qian Li, Haibin Lv, Jun Zhang, Jie Jiang, Zhouchen Lin

Uses Group Verification Optimization to train the improver while keeping the evaluator fixed.
Terminal gains exceed Janus by 33.3%–40.0%; SpecRSI wins across all 50 scientific backbone–task pairs.
Coding-validation success is 69.4% versus HGM’s 64.3% at a 20.8% lower target-cost index.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) can substantially improve the reasoning capabilities of large language models, but an effective training run requires considerable resources. Reusing the computation acquired through RL across models would extend the value of that training. We propose GrowRL, an RL method that organizes learned updates into compact computational pathways through structural growth. GrowRL freezes the pretrained backbone and adds an independent causal attention branch and a feed-forward network branch at each Transformer layer. Zero-initialized output projections preserve the pretrained policy at initialization, and RL updates only the added pathways. The learned pathways remain explicit after training, allowing transfer to structurally compatible target models and subsequent adaptation with the target backbone frozen. The architecture also supports sequential transfer of additional pathways. By keeping the learned attention and feed-forward computation separate from the pretrained weights, GrowRL provides an explicit structure for preserving and reusing the outcome of an RL run. Experiments across five backbones show competitive mathematical reasoning and out-of-distribution performance with a small number of trainable parameters. Learned pathways provide immediate gains across all three transfer directions, with performance after only 10 target-side updates already close to that after 100 updates in every case. These results support computational pathways as parameter-efficient and reusable units of reinforcement learning adaptation.
authors: Haolin Tian, Yikang Li, Tonghan Wang

papers.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models scale model capacity efficiently by activating only a small subset of experts for each input, while still requiring all parameters to be stored in memory, resulting in substantial memory overhead. Expert merging techniques have recently emerged as a promising compression paradigm that reduces this overhead by consolidating multiple experts into a smaller set. However, existing approaches have two key limitations: (i) direct convex interpolation in parameter space is not generally guaranteed to yield meaningful interpolation of expert functions; and (ii) estimating expert similarity or merging coefficients often relies on calibration data, introducing dependence on the calibration distribution. To address these limitations, we propose Spectrum-Aware Latent Expert Merging (SLEM), a calibration-free expert merging framework that occurs in a structured latent representation of expert weights using a VAE. SLEM groups experts within and across layers based on latent similarities and derives merging coefficients from expert weight spectra. It then performs geometry-aware latent interpolation and decodes the resulting representations into merged expert weights. Compared with existing expert merging methods, SLEM achieves comparable or better performance on general knowledge benchmarks and higher average performance on generation benchmarks involving mathematical reasoning and code generation.
authors: Dohyeon Kim, Bedionita Soro, Bruno Andreis, Sung Ju Hwang
bullets: MoE models reduce computation but retain all expert parameters, creating substantial memory overhead.
Existing merging methods may produce poor function interpolation and depend on calibration data.
SLEM uses a VAE-based latent representation, grouping experts by latent similarity within and across layers.
It derives merge coefficients from expert weight spectra and applies geometry-aware latent interpolation.
The method achieves comparable or better general-knowledge performance and higher average performance on math-reasoning and code-generation benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Deep reinforcement learning has shown strong potential for vision-based autonomous driving, but policies trained in simulation often suffer severe performance degradation when deployed in the real world. Existing sim-to-real methods commonly address this gap through image-transfer-based domain adaptation or policy-agnostic domain randomisation. However, the former requires laborious acquisition of target-domain data and is often limited to the deployment domain, whereas the latter introduces unguided perturbations that may not reflect the underlying sim-to-real discrepancy, leading to suboptimal transfer performance. To overcome these limitations, we propose XFD, an explainable artificial intelligence (XAI)-guided Fourier domain generalisation framework for pure-simulation sim-to-real reinforcement learning. The proposed framework extracts explainability attribution maps from simulated observations, and converts these attributions into policy-conditioned Fourier-domain interventions. By perturbing appearance-sensitive spectral components while preserving task-defining spatial structures, XFD constructs robustness-enhancing visual domains entirely within simulation. Subsequently, the proposed robust policy optimisation guides the policy towards attending to task-critical features while suppressing sensitivity to irrelevant visual information. Extensive experiments in simulation and zero-shot real-world deployment demonstrate that XFD consistently improves traveled distance and reward over standard policy and randomly domain-randomised baseline, especially on unseen maps with cluttered backgrounds. Attribution-based analysis further proves that the proposed policy preserves more consistent task-relevant visual evidence across simulation and real-world observations.
authors: Wei Yao, Chuyao Wang, Ziwei Wang, Nabil Aouf
bullets: Addresses severe sim-to-real degradation in vision-based autonomous-driving reinforcement learning.
Uses simulated-observation attribution maps to identify and perturb appearance-sensitive Fourier components while preserving task-relevant structure.
Optimises policies to focus on task-critical features and reduce reliance on irrelevant visual cues.
Simulation and zero-shot real-world experiments show improved travel distance and reward, particularly on unseen cluttered maps.
Attribution analysis indicates more consistent task-relevant visual evidence across simulation and reality.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models answer questions about images they were never shown, a failure called mirage. Such an answer can be correct without being justified by the evidence, and the difference matters wherever a model's output is checked by someone who did not see its input. We locate the failure in the training objective: cross-entropy separates a model that reads the image from one that ignores it by only the conditional mutual information between answer and image, and no training example rewards declining. We formalise support completion, TIDE, which also shows each training question with a blank image, a same-domain wrong image and an out-of-domain image, with targets that decline, and prove that under TIDE every image-blind predictor is suboptimal by at least 1.04 nats per example, that the optimum declines exactly on the counterfactual kinds while keeping its behaviour on valid images, and that for any finite model the error of its answer-or-decline decision, declining on valid input plus answering on invalid input, is bounded below by how well its representation separates valid from invalid evidence. On Qwen2.5-VL-7B under a frozen held-out protocol with two judges, the three-condition predecessor of TIDE reduced the invalid-evidence mirage rate from 0.759 to 0.097 and the blank-image rate from 0.700 to 0.003 at a false-abstention cost of 0.126; label-free grounding raised the rate to 0.859, a likelihood-advantage contrast moved it only to 0.718 because its empty-image term carries no gradient, and grounding applied after support completion re-opened the mirage. The four-condition protocol on three base models, with seeds and component ablations, is in progress and not reported here.
authors: Alfaj Uddin Ahmed, Md. Shaown Miah, Md Arid Hasan, Syed Ishtiaque Ahmed, Sayeed Shafayet Chowdhury
bullets: Mirage occurs when models answer questions about unseen or irrelevant images, even if the answer happens to be correct.
The proposed support-completion objective presents valid, blank, same-domain wrong, and out-of-domain image conditions, with decline targets for invalid evidence.
Theory shows image-blind predictors are suboptimal under TIDE and links decision errors to how well representations separate valid from invalid evidence.
On Qwen2.5-VL-7B, a three-condition predecessor reduced invalid-evidence mirages from 0.759 to 0.097 and blank-image responses from 0.700 to 0.003, with a false-abstention cost of 0.126.
The full four-condition evaluation across three base models is still in progress; reported results use a predecessor protocol and two judges.

papers.selection_reason: Addresses a core failure mode of vision-language models via a new training objective, directly relevant to multimodal LLMs.
papers.title: Teaching Vision-Language Models to Decline: Support Completion Against Mirage
papers.tldr: TIDE trains vision-language models to decline when an image does not support an answer, substantially reducing unsupported image-question responses while preserving valid-image behavior.

papers.abstract: Vision-based tactile sensors enable fine-grained perception for dexterous robotic manipulation, but current marker-based designs tightly couple surface texture and contact force signals within a single observation. Existing data-driven decoupling methods rely on serial mask-based inpainting, which suffers from mask-sizing dilemmas caused by physical indentation effects, error retention, and lack of real paired data for supervision. To address these challenges, we propose DeTac, a novel dual-branch generative framework that concurrently extracts clean shading and marker images from a single mixed tactile image. DeTac leverages full-image synthesis to naturally bypass mask dependency and introduces a cross-branch synergistic optimization that enables mutual supervision, effectively preventing error retention. Furthermore, we construct a strictly aligned, real-world paired tactile dataset using custom hardware to provide high-quality supervision. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DeTac achieves state-of-the-art decoupling accuracy, significantly facilitating downstream surface reconstruction and force estimation tasks while exhibiting cross-sensor generalization.
authors: Zhirui Zhang, Yunkai Tang, Jiahang Li, Fan Fei, Jinnuo Zhang, Kairan Ding, Jieji Ren, Yandong Guo, Boxin Shi
bullets: Addresses signal entanglement in marker-based vision-based tactile sensors and limitations of mask-based inpainting.
Uses full-image synthesis to concurrently generate clean shading and marker images without mask-size dependence.
Applies cross-branch synergistic optimization to reduce error retention through mutual supervision.
Introduces a strictly aligned real-world paired tactile dataset for supervised training.
Reports state-of-the-art decoupling accuracy, improved surface reconstruction and force estimation, and cross-sensor generalization.

figures.caption: Figure 1: (a) Markerless sensors capture shading images to reconstruct surface but lack spatial references for force estimation. (b) Marker-based sensors enable force sensing via embedded markers, but introduce coupled signals and indentation artifacts. (c) Serial pipelines suffer from mask-size dilemmas, error retention, and lack of real paired training data. (d) DeTac uses a dual-branch framework with cross-branch optimization, trained on a self-collected aligned paired real dataset.

Figure 2: Overall pipeline of DeTac. (a) DeTac takes as input a mixed tactile image and consists of two parallel branches (Sec. 3.1): a conditional diffusion-based shading restoration branch and a lightweight marker extraction branch. (b) The cross-branch synergistic optimization (Sec. 3.2) exploits marker-aware spatial structures for mutual supervision using surrounding indentation loss for shading restoration and change-marker consistency loss for marker extraction.

Figure 3: Hardware design and data acquisition setup. (a) Exploded view of the MC-Tac [52] sensor equipped with an outer shell featuring 20 cylindrical alignment pins arranged in a ring for repeatable positioning. (b) The data acquisition system features a collection pad with a 5 × 5 array of interchangeable texture units, each surrounded by 20 holes that mate with the sensor’s alignment pins. Rotating the sensor and fully inserting the pins into different indexed holes under consistent force enable repeatable sampling of 20 contact poses per object before and after marker fabrication.

papers.title: DeTac: Dual-branch Decoupling of Texture and Force Signals in Vision-Based Tactile Sensors

papers.abstract: Preference alignment enables language models to better reflect human values, but the preference data contains sensitive information, especially when derived from surveys about political beliefs, social norms, religion, gender attitudes, and cultural values. This paper studies privacy-preserving alignment on questionnaire-derived data from the World Values Survey, where supervision takes the form of ordinal labels rather than standard pairwise rankings. Existing efforts mainly focus on general privacy protections upon model training, while data-specific methods for survey data remain unexplored. We first show the vulnerability of aligned models, then formulate the task as rating prediction and introduce label differential privacy. Building on this formulation, we construct a differential private pipeline utilizing three privacy mechanisms: randomized response, exponential mechanism, and DP-SGD. Experiments show that simple label-level mechanisms outperform gradient-level methods, and proper aggregation function for preprocessing also make large contribution. The new fine-grained private comparison motivates explorations toward language model alignment with formal privacy guarantees.
authors: Xiuyuan Qi, Yi Wang, Wenjie Wang
bullets: Survey-based preference data can reveal sensitive political, religious, social, gender, and cultural beliefs.
The study formulates alignment as rating prediction rather than pairwise preference comparison.
It evaluates randomized response, the exponential mechanism, and DP-SGD for privacy protection.
Label-level mechanisms outperform gradient-level protection in the reported experiments.
Preprocessing and label aggregation choices substantially affect privacy-preserving alignment.

papers.abstract: Humans expand their locomotion capability by wearing appropriate footwear, such as hiking boots for mountains or skates for ice. Footwear changes the ground-contact interface and enables traversal of otherwise difficult terrain. In contrast, locomotion controllers are typically trained for a fixed morphology, and their performance can degrade when shoes alter foot geometry, mass, and friction. We propose SHOES, a sample-efficient framework for adapting locomotion policies to footwear-induced morphology changes. SHOES freezes a simulation-trained nominal policy and fine-tunes only lightweight, identity-initialized modulation modules on the robot, preserving the initial behavior while enabling efficient hardware adaptation. We also introduce SafeBox, a workspace-aware waypoint sampler that constrains online adaptation within a user-defined workspace. The simulation results with a shoe-equipped Unitree Go2 show that SHOES substantially recovers locomotion performance after footwear-induced morphology changes using limited additional adaptation. Under the same adaptation budget, SHOES outperforms FiLM-only, Linear Adapter-only, and residual-RL baselines. Real-world experiments on a Unitree Go2 fitted with human shoes further evaluate the effectiveness of SHOES for hardware deployment.
authors: Kota Tsuruhara, Tsung-Yuan Chen, Kento Kawaharazuka
bullets: Addresses performance degradation caused by changes in foot geometry, mass, and friction from added footwear.
Freezes a simulation-trained nominal policy and fine-tunes identity-initialized modulation modules for sample-efficient adaptation.
Introduces SafeBox, a workspace-aware waypoint sampler that keeps online adaptation within user-defined limits.
Simulation on a shoe-equipped Unitree Go2 substantially recovers locomotion performance and outperforms several adapter and residual-RL baselines under the same adaptation budget.
Real-world experiments with human shoes further assess deployment on a Unitree Go2.

papers.abstract: 3D scene graph generation requires understanding both object semantics and metric spatial relations. However, existing open-vocabulary methods often struggle with spatial predicates because language similarity reflects semantic co-occurrence rather than explicit geometry. We propose GHOST, a Geometry-constrained Hybrid diffusion framework for Open-vocabulary 3D Scene graph generaTion. GHOST jointly models continuous node geometry and discrete edge predicates, following a geometry-to-constraint-to-predicate denoising process to ensure geometrically consistent relation prediction. It introduces language-grounded constraint induction, which maps predicate embeddings to differentiable geometric constraints that guide both layout refinement and predicate reweighting. A Geometry-Topology Collaborative Denoiser further couples node and edge reasoning through noise-adaptive interaction and orientation-aware modeling. Experiments on 3DSSG demonstrate state-of-the-art performance in both closed-set and open-vocabulary settings, including over 17-point gains over RelationField on spatial predicates.
authors: Changqun Feng, Wangxiandi Yin, Xin Hu, Ruiting Dai, Feiyang Yang, Jielei Wang, Tao He
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between language similarity and explicit 3D spatial geometry in open-vocabulary relation prediction.
Uses a geometry-to-constraint-to-predicate denoising process to jointly model continuous node geometry and discrete edge predicates.
Induces differentiable geometric constraints from predicate embeddings to refine layouts and reweight relation predictions.
Employs a Geometry-Topology Collaborative Denoiser with noise-adaptive interaction and orientation-aware modeling.
Achieves state-of-the-art results on 3DSSG, including over 17-point gains over RelationField on spatial predicates.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of GHOST. GHOST jointly denoises object geometry and relation predicates through a hybrid reverse diffusion process. At each step, the Geometry-Topology Collaborative Denoiser (GTCD) first refines object geometry, then applies language-grounded constraint guidance to enforce geometric consistency, and finally decodes predicate tokens conditioned on the corrected layout. This denoise→ project→ decode ordering ensures that the recovered scene graph is both spatially coherent and open-vocabulary capable.

Figure 1: VLM-based open-vocabulary 3DSGG methods perform about 30 points worse on spatial predicates than on nonspatial ones (a), because they rely on language co-occurrence priors rather than true 3D layout, e.g., a model may predict “pillow on sofa” simply because the relation is common, while ignoring the actual scene layout (b). GHOST replaces such priors with explicit geometric constraints, substantially narrowing this gap (c).
Figure 5: Geometric Oracle Experiments. Even a perfect geometric oracle applied post-hoc yields only modest spatial gains over the one-shot baseline.

Figure 4: Qualitative OV scene graph predictions on 3DSSG [43]. Top: comparison between RelationField and GHOST. Bottom: a GHOST failure case caused by an object recognition error from the upstream detector. Green = correct; red = error.

papers.tldr: GHOST improves open-vocabulary 3D scene graph generation by coupling language-grounded geometric constraints with diffusion-based joint reasoning over objects and spatial relations.

papers.abstract: Fine-tuning large language models at scale is increasingly limited by the memory cost of backpropagation. Zeroth-Order (ZO) optimizers reduce this burden by relying only on forward function evaluations, but they still exhibit a substantial performance gap to first-order (FO) optimizers such as Adam. We argue that this gap does not arise solely from the absence of explicit gradients: FO fine-tuning also benefits from informative low-rank optimization geometry, large-scale signal aggregation, and well-conditioned update directions. Motivated by this, we introduce StructZO, a structured Zeroth-Order optimization framework for memory-efficient LLM fine-tuning. StructZO performs large-query ZO estimation within an activation-induced informative subspace and applies spectral control to the resulting reduced-space update before mapping it back to the original parameters. This lets ZO aggregate useful directional signals in a compact, geometry-aware space while avoiding the activation and optimizer-state memory costs of backpropagation. We show theoretically that, when the induced subspace captures concentrated optimization-relevant directions, StructZO reduces the effective ZO estimation dimension from $mn$ to $mr$, with the remaining projection error governed by the spectral tail of the activation Gram matrix. Empirically, across OPT-series and Llama3.1-8B on diverse downstreamtasks, StructZO improves over the strongest existing ZO baselines by up to $8.7%$ relative on average and up to $26.9%$ relative on individual tasks, while remaining within $1.5%$ of FO-Adam on average. These results suggest that structured and spectrally controlled ZO updates can substantially narrow the gap between ZO and FO optimization.
authors: Xuanlin Yang, Jia Li, Zhouchen Lin
bullets: Targets the high memory cost of backpropagation and optimizer states in large-language-model fine-tuning.
Uses large-query zeroth-order estimation within an activation-induced informative subspace, then spectrally controls and maps updates back to the full parameter space.

Theoretical analysis reduces the effective estimation dimension from $mn$ to $mr$ when optimization-relevant directions are concentrated; projection error depends on the activation Gram matrix’s spectral tail.

papers.abstract: The growing use of language models for forecasting motivates a broader evaluation of their world-model capabilities. Such evaluation must go beyond predictive accuracy to assess hidden-state inference and intervention prediction. Real-world forecasting benchmarks offer limited access to hidden-state ground truth and controlled experiments. We introduce CivWorldBench, a benchmark built on a multi-agent strategy game engine with recorded internal states, controlled observations, and paired intervention rollouts. Its 1,900 decision points from 475 worlds support three task levels: association forecasting, belief inference, and intervention prediction. Reference predictors support attributable evaluation of capability gaps, with an expert harness and empirical ceiling estimates contextualizing scores. Stored trajectories make intermediate predictions verifiable, while agent-play experiments test whether world-model capabilities support decision-making. The main panel comprises eleven frontier language models. Composite benchmark scores correlate with real-world forecasting leaderboards on matched model panels, more closely than with a general-capability index, supporting its use as a proxy for real-world forecasting capability. Strong association forecasts do not consistently extend to belief inference or intervention prediction, and effect magnitudes remain poorly calibrated despite informative direction predictions. Process verification reveals errors missed by final-answer evaluation, and structured reasoning improves intervention prediction for the strongest model in the process study. Agent-play experiments identify useful assisted plans and motivate evaluating decision-relevant capabilities beyond association forecasting. These findings identify hidden-state inference, intermediate-state prediction, and effect calibration as priorities for world-model training.
authors: Ang Li, Haofei Yu, Zhengwei Tao, Liang Chen, Kuan Li, Miaomiao Li, Chenran Cai, Bin Liang, Jiaxuan You, Kam-Fai Wong
bullets: Benchmark uses a strategy-game engine with recorded states, controlled observations, and paired intervention rollouts across 1,900 decision points from 475 worlds.
It evaluates association forecasting, belief inference, and intervention prediction, with reference predictors, expert harnesses, and estimated performance ceilings.
Scores correlate with real-world forecasting leaderboards, while strong association forecasting does not reliably transfer to hidden-state or intervention tasks.
Models often predict intervention directions correctly but poorly calibrate effect magnitudes; process verification uncovers errors missed by final answers.
Agent-play studies find useful assisted plans and highlight the need to evaluate decision-relevant world-model capabilities.
