papers.abstract: Diffusion models, particularly Diffusion Transformers, achieve strong image and video generation quality but remain expensive at inference time due to repeated denoiser evaluations. Feature caching offers a deployment-friendly acceleration strategy by reusing or predicting intermediate representations without retraining the generator or modifying the sampler. However, existing cache-then-forecast methods often rely on Taylor-style finite-difference extrapolation, which can become unstable over longer cache intervals, and typically predict local module outputs whose errors may accumulate through subsequent denoiser blocks. We propose \textbf{BeziCast}, a training-free diffusion acceleration framework that forecasts output-proximal denoising representations using low-order B'ezier trajectories. BeziCast estimates B'ezier control points via Tikhonov-stabilized fitting, providing a smooth, capacity-controlled temporal parameterization that avoids explicit high-order derivative estimation and decouples trajectory capacity from cache-query density. To moderate aggressive extrapolation, we further derive equivalent forecasting weights and introduce a convex-hull-inspired guardrail that detects high-risk predictions and softly pulls them toward a conservative simplex-projected estimate. Extensive evaluations across advanced image and video diffusion models demonstrate the effectiveness of BeziCast. In particular, BeziCast accelerates FLUX.1 by up to (4.79\times) and HunyuanVideo by up to (4.11\times), while preserving substantially better generation quality than competing acceleration baselines.
authors: Lei Zhu, Mujie Lin, Ruochong Zheng, Guangyi Wang, Hao Li, Peng Jin, Chang Liu, Jie Chen
bullets: Targets the high inference cost of repeated denoiser evaluations in image and video diffusion models.
Uses low-order Bézier trajectories with Tikhonov-stabilized fitting to avoid unstable high-order derivative extrapolation.
Forecasts output-proximal representations, reducing error accumulation across subsequent denoiser blocks.
Applies a convex-hull-inspired guardrail that softly shifts risky forecasts toward conservative simplex-projected estimates.
Reported speedups reach 4.79× for FLUX.1 and 4.11× for HunyuanVideo, with better quality preservation than competing baselines.

papers.abstract: Visual artifacts such as charts, technical diagrams, webpages, and document pages underpin scientific, commercial, and engineering workflows. Editing these artifacts requires direct modification, dependency-aware updates, preservation of unaffected content, and compliance with domain constraints. We define this capability as Visual Artifact Operation (VAO). Prior benchmarks test parts of this problem, including cascading updates in charts. We study direct edits, dependent updates, and preservation across visual domains and pixel, code, and agent paradigms under one image-only protocol. We introduce Visual Artifact Operation Bench (VAO-Bench), comprising 1,573 manually screened tasks across nine artifact categories and three difficulty levels. VAO-Bench uses executable artifacts and deterministic rendering to trace reference transformations and annotate direct edits, dependent updates, and preservation constraints. All systems receive the same source image and instruction; we evaluate pixel-space editors, code-generating multimodal systems, and tool-using agents on direct-edit accuracy, dependency-aware update, content preservation, domain validity, and visual quality. Experiments show that executable-code systems better support dependent updates, while pixel-space editors offer faster execution and strong visual quality. Explicitly stating dependencies improves both paradigms, identifying implicit-update inference as a central bottleneck. VAO-Bench provides a reproducible foundation for dependable visual artifact editing across generation paradigms.
authors: Shun Guo, Shuizhou Shi, Boao Wang, Wei Xiong, Siyu Sun, Jiangtong Li, Jie Li
bullets: Defines Visual Artifact Operation as direct editing, dependency-aware updates, preservation of unaffected content, and domain-valid outputs.

Code-based systems handle dependent updates better, while pixel editors execute faster and produce strong visual quality.
Explicit dependency instructions improve both paradigms; inferring implicit updates remains a key bottleneck.

papers.abstract: Recent world action models draw on video generation priors to jointly predict future observations and robot actions. Adapting these priors to control requires determining how future predictions should guide policy learning. RAP-WAM combines predictive Rehearsal and Action Perturbations (RAP) with future-supervised queries and Coupled Action Projection for policy learning. Predictive rehearsal trains on model-generated inputs while retaining recorded targets, and accumulates recurring errors into a spatial prior. We perturb actions and measure changes in video predictions. Action-response-based spatiotemporal credit assignment combines these responses, prediction error, and the rehearsal prior to allocate visual supervision; spatially aggregating the responses determines supervision intensity across future action steps. No separate scoring network or deployment-time probe is required. The base learns from a video-pretrained backbone without intermediate pretraining on external embodied data. We evaluate the fixed base and its agent-refined, task-conditioned system. On 42 RoboDojo tasks, their average success rates are 12.85% and 15.62%, with Scores of 17.86 and 20.59. Across 15 real-robot tasks, the complete system achieves 89.00% task-macro-average success, exceeding the strongest of five baselines by 37.67 percentage points. Across 315 fixed-output simulation windows, 45.21% of response-top20 positions fall outside error-top20, revealing information beyond prediction error.
authors: Yuanpeng He, Ceyao Zhang, Fangjing Li, Kefei Zhu, Lijian Li, Yueheng Li, Tianjia He, Wenpin Jiao, Zhi Jin, Yaodong Yang, Yuanpei Chen
bullets: Addresses how future video predictions should guide policy learning in world-action models.
Uses predictive rehearsal, action-response perturbations, future-supervised queries, and Coupled Action Projection.
Allocates visual supervision using prediction error, action responses, and a spatial rehearsal prior without a separate scoring network or deployment-time probe.
On 42 RoboDojo tasks, average success was 12.85% for the fixed base and 15.62% after agent refinement.
On 15 real-robot tasks, the complete system achieved 89.00% task-macro-average success, 37.67 percentage points above the strongest of five baselines.

papers.abstract: Current image-text evaluation often relies on a global score, which gives limited insight into which semantic details are supported by the image. Explainable metrics provide rationales, but the visual evidence supporting those rationales can still be difficult to verify. We introduce VisExMEM, a reference-free evaluator that decomposes captions into atomic claims, localizes visual evidence, verifies each claim, and averages claim-level support into a global score. Explanations use the same evidence and decisions. We train Qwen3.5-based 4B and 9B models on 100K samples with multi-task SFT, counterfactual refinement, and evidence-aware GDPO. Across eight benchmarks, VisExMEM-9B achieves the highest descriptive composite among open-source evaluators in our comparison, exceeding VQAScore by 11.7 points while remaining competitive with GPT-5.6 Sol. We also introduce AGITA-Bench, containing 600 human-annotated image-text pairs and 8.7K atomic claims for global and claim-level evaluation. For untuned Qwen3.5 and GPT-5.6 Sol controls, decomposed prompting raises the same composite by 3.6-5.1 points relative to holistic prompting. Human evaluation shows that VisExMEM explanations outperform prior explainable metrics and approach GPT-5.6 Sol.
authors: Subhadeep Roy, Christoph Leiter, Steffen Eger
bullets: Addresses the limited interpretability and verifiability of global image-text evaluation scores.

Across eight benchmarks, VisExMEM-9B reports the highest descriptive composite among compared open-source evaluators and remains competitive with GPT-5.6 Sol.

papers.abstract: Industrial recommendation rankers keep scaling in width and depth to billions of parameters, but this increasingly incurs costs in parameter growth, distributed communication overhead, and training inefficiency. We introduce \underline{C}hain \underline{D}imension \underline{S}caling (CDS), a scaling strategy orthogonal to width and depth. CDS repeatedly applies a single feature-interaction block with parameters shared across iterations, so the number of iterations (the chain length) becomes a new scaling dimension that adds no parameters. A lightweight intra-chain residual connection stabilizes optimization and improves quality. CDS enables two regimes. In the \emph{compression regime}, shallow blocks with a longer chain match deeper baselines with fewer parameters and faster training; in the \emph{quality-scaling regime}, increasing chain length under a fixed parameter budget yields consistent offline and online gains, suggesting the chain dimension adds modeling capacity beyond parameter reuse. We evaluate CDS in a large-scale multi-task short-video ranking system in production. In the compression regime, CDS stays within $0.03\%$ of baseline offline quality while reducing trainable parameters by 26.6\% and improving training throughput by 6.4\%, with neutral-to-positive online participation. In the quality-scaling regime, quality improves monotonically with chain length. Wall-clock analysis shows the efficiency gain comes mainly not from reduced FLOPs but from lower cross-device synchronization overhead and reduced optimizer update cost. These results position parameter-shared iterative computation as a practical, communication-efficient scaling axis for industrial ranking systems.
authors: Zhimeng Jiang, Yuening Li, Ruixiao Sun, Yuanzhen Lin, Kun Jin, Chuan He, Liang Liu
bullets: Addresses the parameter growth, distributed synchronization, and training inefficiency of width/depth scaling.
Shares block parameters across a configurable chain length, with an intra-chain residual connection for stable optimization.

papers.abstract: Deploying robots in human-shared environments requires deciding not only how to navigate, but also when dedicated social signals are worth emitting. Classic observation-based inference can be misleading in such settings: confounding factors may bias the estimated relationship between a signal and the task outcome, leading to incorrect decisions. Causal inference provides a framework for disentangling these relationships by modelling the mechanisms linking observations, actions, and outcomes, and by estimating interventional effects after accounting for confounding paths. We study a human-robot interaction scenario in a corridor and use a causal model to estimate whether a social navigation signal causally improves transit success. We represent the interaction as a causal DAG involving robot action, pedestrian occupancy, available space, task outcome, and a controlled confounder (static obstacles). We compare the interventional estimate with the observational estimate obtained by conditioning only on the robot action, which does not explicitly model interventions. Our results show that accounting for confounding variables can reverse the conclusions drawn from naive observational analysis: the observational estimate wrongly suggests that the social signal is detrimental, whereas the causal estimate shows that it is beneficial. This discrepancy highlights how failing to account for confounding can lead to incorrect conclusions and demonstrates the importance of causal models for context-aware signalling decisions in social robot navigation.
authors: Francesco Baldo, Luca Castri, Gloria Beraldo, Nicola Bellotto
bullets: Studies when social signals are worth emitting in human-shared corridor navigation.

Highlights causal modeling as important for context-aware signalling decisions.

papers.abstract: Repetitive structures can give an incorrect pose candidate more inlier support than an accurate one, causing visual localization to select it. History-Guided Pose Reselection (HPR) uses coarse position forecasts from up to five past localization outputs to distinguish well-separated current-query candidates. The best-fitting forecast proposes an alternative; HPR accepts it only if every well-fitting forecast is much closer to it than to the localizer's pose. HPR needs no odometry and returns the selected candidate unchanged, using prediction for selection rather than pose refinement. With one development-set threshold, HPR improves recall within 5 meters and 10 degrees in all 12 main configurations of Hierarchical Localization (HLoc), MASt3R-based pose generation, and JIST-based retrieval, losing successes on fewer than 0.4 percent of queries. On NAVER Gangnam B1, HPR corrects 97 HLoc failures and loses six successes; gains persist within 0.25 meters and 2 degrees on all three HLoc test sets. Median HPR runtime on HLoc candidates is below one millisecond, excluding pose generation. Recovery weakens under less frequent localization.
authors: Jaehyun Kim, Wonseok Kang, Tae-Wan Kim

papers.abstract: Robot learning has undergone significant advancements in the domain of compliant control and robotic assembly. The development of novel methodologies has transcended the capacity to address discrete tasks, such as grasping or inserting, and has evolved to encompass the comprehensive construction of entire assemblies. Conventional benchmarks, which are predominantly focused on single tasks, are no longer adequate to address the complexity and interconnected nature of modern manufacturing processes. Consequently, the necessity for benchmarks to encompass a broader spectrum of assembly and subassembly steps is becoming apparent. In light of these developments, we propose LABIT, an industrial robotic assembly benchmark for long-horizon manipulation. This benchmark encompasses DIN-norm assembly tasks, including screwing, placing, inserting, and snapping, under both high and low tolerance conditions. The successive nature of these assembly steps implies that prior errors can influence subsequent manipulation. Consequently, this benchmark is particularly relevant for assessing the robustness of intelligent robotic systems. The proposed benchmarking protocols and novel performance metric, based on a taxonomy of assembly complexity in conjunction with the comprehensive list of parts and their corresponding CAD models, serve as essential tools for research and development in the field. To provide a baseline, we evaluate the benchmark using traditional force-position control and report reliability and score metrics per primitive, subtask, assembly category, and subassembly. Accompanying data is available at https://irp-hka.github.io/robotic-assembly-benchmark/.
authors: Constantin Schempp, Christian Friedrich, Luca Kofler, Laura Suhm

papers.abstract: Although users may express different personalization needs across tasks, these task-specific behaviors can reflect shared underlying preference mechanisms. Existing LLM personalization methods often focus on surface-level interactions or undifferentiated histories, overlooking the shared mechanisms underlying these behaviors. We introduce PersonaFactors, a framework that distills reusable and interpretable personalization factors from heterogeneous user interactions. We construct a library of thirteen PersonaFactors by extracting evidence-grounded rationales and clustering recurring patterns across tasks, and develop a dynamic factor-guided generation framework that selects factors relevant to each user's history and current request. Across four personalization benchmarks and four backbone models, Dynamic PersonaFactor achieves the best score on every reported metric. Representation analyses further show that PersonaFactors and user history induce partially overlapping low-dimensional representations, and that their joint use yields complementary shifts. Taken together, these findings suggest that factor-based and history-based personalization can mutually reinforce each other.

papers.abstract: Large language models are increasingly deployed in morally and legally sensitive contexts, yet little is known about how they internally represent distinctions between moral reasoning styles. We ask whether a model's differential response to rule-framed and consequence-framed moral questions reflects distinct internal structure or merely surface lexical sensitivity. We construct a 2$\times$2 factorial dataset crossing reasoning style (rule-based vs. consequence-based framing) with judgment polarity (permissive vs. prohibitive), drawn from three established moral reasoning benchmarks and evaluated on a cleanroom test set of novel phrasings that includes conflict pairs where the two framings predict opposite labels. Using linear probing and activation steering, we identify two orthogonal directions in the residual stream: Dir-A tracks reasoning style and Dir-B tracks judgment polarity, each near-blind to the other factor (cross-correlation $|r| < 0.04$). This double dissociation replicates across three instruction-tuned models from different developers at comparable proportional depth, and it is not knife-edged in layer: the directions are recoverable and causally effective throughout an extended band of the network. Dir-A can causally change judgments, and in conflicting scenarios, it selectively corrects errors in rule-based judgments without changing consequence-based judgments, suggesting that it does not simply make the model more likely to accept everything. Generalization beyond the training templates is partial: the direction transfers across benchmark sources, but its advantage over lexical baselines on novel phrasings is modest. We therefore frame the result as moral reasoning style sensitivity, a geometrically dissociable and causally effective structure, rather than internalized normative reasoning.
authors: Eugenie Shi
bullets: A 2×2 dataset separates rule- versus consequence-based framing from permissive versus prohibitive judgments, including conflicting cases.

Steering the style direction changes judgments and selectively improves rule-based responses in conflicts without broadly increasing permissiveness.
Transfer across benchmarks occurs, but gains over lexical baselines on novel phrasings are modest; the findings do not establish internalized normative reasoning.

papers.abstract: Looped Language Models (LoopLMs) improve parameter efficiency by recursively reusing shared Transformer modules, yet their repeated computation over evolving recurrent states poses new challenges for low-bit deployment. Existing post-training quantization (PTQ) methods, largely designed for feed-forward Transformers, fail to account for cross-loop activation dynamics, heterogeneous loop sensitivity, and recursive error propagation, leading to substantial performance degradation at low precision. To address these challenges, we propose LoopQuant, a loop-aware PTQ framework for accurate and efficient low-bit quantization of LoopLMs. LoopQuant is built on three core components: 1) Cross-Loop Distribution Canonicalization (CLDC) learns a shared quantization-friendly representation across recurrent states while preserving parameter sharing; 2) Interaction-Aware Loop-wise Precision Allocation (ILPA) allocates activation precision under a fixed bit budget by modeling task-level loop sensitivity and cross-loop interactions; and 3) Loop-Conditioned Task Calibration (LCTC) further aligns quantized inference with the low-bit recursive trajectory through lightweight task-space calibration. Extensive experiments across LoopLM architectures demonstrate that LoopQuant consistently outperforms existing low-bit PTQ methods. On Ouro-2.6B, LoopQuant under W4A4 surpasses all W4A8 baselines in performance, while reducing model memory by 65.3% with only 3.4% additional storage overhead over naive INT4 and achieving a 1.7 times decoding speedup over BF16. These results demonstrate a strong balance among accuracy, compression, and inference efficiency, providing a practical and deployment-friendly solution for low-bit LoopLM inference. The code is available at [https://github.com/Kishon-zzx/LoopQuant].
authors: Zhixiong Zhao, Zukang Xu, Xing Hu, Lifeng Liu, Guangyu Sun, Dawei Yang
bullets: Addresses activation shifts, heterogeneous loop sensitivity, and recursive error propagation that undermine standard PTQ methods.
Uses Cross-Loop Distribution Canonicalization to learn a shared quantization-friendly representation while preserving parameter sharing.
Allocates activation precision through interaction-aware, loop-wise sensitivity modeling under a fixed bit budget.
Applies lightweight loop-conditioned task calibration to align quantized inference with low-bit recursive trajectories.
On Ouro-2.6B, W4A4 surpasses W4A8 baselines, cuts memory by 65.3%, and achieves 1.7× BF16 decoding speed with 3.4% storage overhead over naive INT4.

papers.abstract: Video world models must generate physically plausible futures, not just realistic frames. Existing approaches typically use semantic, physical, or predictive information to guide the visual generation stream, leaving a fundamental question: where inside the generator should predictions of scene evolution live? Standard video tokens jointly encode appearance and dynamics, but provide no distinct state for learning and reading predictive dynamics. We answer this question with the Physical Registry: temporally grounded registry slots inside a video DiT that are initialized from an observation-conditioned forecast, co-evolve with video tokens, and receive future-representation supervision, making predictive dynamics an explicit, readable state of the generator. In a controlled comparison of predictive-state interfaces on Physics-IQ Verified, Physical Registry improves vanilla fine-tuning by 9.9/8.7 points on I2V/V2V, the largest gain among the interfaces we compare. Across all Cosmos and WAN backbones, Physical Registry improves Physics-IQ Verified scores. With only 0.45% additional parameters, it enables Cosmos 3 Nano 16B to surpass the published I2V score of Cosmos 3 Super 64B (43.56 vs. 42.7). On WorldModelBench, it also improves physical adherence and the total score for all four evaluated backbones. Because the registry becomes candidate-specific while remaining readable, the Physical Registry Selector (PRS) ranks emerging futures by how far their intermediate registry readouts depart from the shared forecast before full denoising is complete. Across four backbones, this selection improves I2V scores by 5.6-15.9% without completed-video external scoring. Together, these results support a broader principle: dynamics prediction should live as an explicit model state that co-evolves with the video representation. papers.abstract: Speech-driven visual grounding in remote sensing (RSVG) removes the typing bottleneck of text-based interaction and is intended to preserve prosodic intent, enabling hands-free target acquisition in time-critical missions. The direct-audio paradigm, mapping raw speech straight to a bounding box and bypassing automatic speech recognition (ASR), was recently adopted by RSTalker, but what such grounders actually learn about language remains unmeasured. SemEcho grafts a frozen Whisper speech pathway onto a VLTVG grounding host so that speech and text share one decoder, making the paired text, free by construction since speech corpora in this task are synthesized from DIOR-RSVG expressions, a training-time teacher and a fair, same-host text upper bound. On this instrument we dissect three semantic injection channels (feature-mimicry distillation, word-level CTC supervision, and two-stage ASR pretraining) with linear semantic probes, and release Audio-DIOR-R (80,973 training clips; 10 timbres x K=3; Qwen3-TTS synthesis with online sox noise lambda in [0, 0.4]) and Audio-DIOR-Comp, a re-split holding out 17 attribute-category combinations under a 2x2 acoustic-semantic protocol. Our anatomy yields four findings. (i) Whether direct alignment beats a domain-trained ASR cascade is decided by recognizer quality: against a weak in-domain cascade (CTC 0.53) direct wins by 9.0 Acc@0.5 points with transcription errors concentrated on spatial-relation words, but a strong in-domain cascade (CTC 0.029) reaches the text upper bound (80.8 vs. 81.0) and beats even the strongest direct model by 8.8 points; the anti-ASR premise holds only against weak recognizers.
authors: Zhongyu Pang
bullets: Speech-driven remote-sensing grounding aims to enable hands-free target acquisition while preserving prosodic intent.
SemEcho combines a frozen Whisper speech pathway with a VLTVG grounding host, using paired text as training-time semantic supervision and an upper bound.
It evaluates feature-mimicry distillation, word-level CTC supervision, and two-stage ASR pretraining with linear semantic probes.
The study introduces Audio-DIOR-R and Audio-DIOR-Comp for acoustic and compositional evaluation.
Against a weak in-domain ASR cascade, direct grounding gains 9.0 Acc@0.5 points; a strong cascade nearly matches the text upper bound and exceeds the strongest direct model by 8.8 points.

papers.abstract: Agentic video reasoning systems gather and assess video evidence across stages, selecting relevant spans as visual evidence for answering questions. New candidates and observations prompt reassessment of the current span, but revisions can correct localization errors or discard useful evidence already present in the adopted span. Systems therefore need to connect evidence organization across stages with temporal state control, allowing accumulated information to jointly inform revision assessment while explicit adoption decisions govern how assessment outcomes affect downstream visual evidence. We introduce VideoSlate, a stateful commit-control framework built around shared evidence. A typed evidence blackboard links candidate spans, provenance, construction, and verifier observations, enabling an incumbent-relative certifier to assess revision support from the candidate, current span, and related proposals. Based on certification, the controller authorizes a revision or retains the current span, separating evidence accumulation from state updates and recording each decision and its evidence on the blackboard. Extensive evaluations across video grounding and grounded question-answering benchmarks show that VideoSlate can improve temporal localization through selective revision.
authors: Shuo Zheng, Yuanjie Dang, Peng Chen, Jianjun Xiang, Ronghua Liang, Mohammed Bennamoun, Qiuhong Ke
bullets: Addresses the risk that iterative evidence gathering either retains localization errors or discards useful existing evidence.
Uses a typed evidence blackboard to track candidate spans, provenance, construction, verifier observations, and related proposals.
An incumbent-relative certifier evaluates whether a proposed revision is supported by accumulated evidence.
A controller explicitly commits to revising the span or retaining it, while recording each decision and its evidence.
Evaluations on video grounding and grounded question-answering benchmarks show improved temporal localization through selective revision.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Two outcomes of selective temporal revision. Blue and orange outlines mark the incumbent and challenger; coral reference spans and IoU values are evaluation-only overlays. Bottom: deferral preserves the incumbent and avoids a harmful expansion.

Figure 2: VideoSlate’s selective temporal state revision. Ground & Propose obtains raw spans and their verifier support before constructing additional candidates. Record & Certify links candidates to their sources and scores replacement using stored source features. Decide & Commit selects the strongest challenger, using separate interval observations to resolve score ties when available. Only acceptance changes the committed span; both retention actions preserve it with distinct traces. The blackboard records proposals, evidence, and decisions throughout the step. Score bars are schematic.

Figure 1: (a) A challenger selected by VideoMind’s verifier can overwrite a stronger incumbent; deferral preserves it. (b) Selective commits retain beneficial revisions while suppressing harmful writes. (c) The certifier jointly assesses relative support, source support, and proposal context from the evidence blackboard. The controller uses the best candidate’s replacement score to authorize replacement or retain the current result.

papers.abstract: Generalist robot manipulation can benefit from pretrained vision-language models (VLMs) for semantic reasoning and video generation models (VGMs) for world modeling. However, existing unified models that directly fuse them through shared attention at multiple layers can make it harder to draw on their specialized capabilities. We introduce PINT, a unified model that coordinates semantic reasoning, world modeling, and action generation through a shared chunk-level Predictive Intent while preserving expert-specific pathways. PINT inserts learnable Intent Tokens into the VLM sequence to form this representation, conditioning both the VGM and an Action Expert (AE). It replaces only the VGM's prompt conditioning and retains the VGM at inference, where the AE reads its representations through one-way attention. Rather than prescribing what Predictive Intent should encode, PINT learns it jointly from the native prediction objectives of the VLM, VGM, and AE, which provide complementary views of the same upcoming task execution. Training uses two stages: Stage 1 freezes the VGM so that future video prediction shapes Predictive Intent with task-relevant future dynamics, while Stage 2 fixes the learned Intent and adapts the VGM and AE. Without embodied pretraining, PINT achieves strong in-distribution (ID) performance and substantially improves out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization, reaching 15.5% on RoboTwin 2.0-Hard compared with 1.8% for Fast-WAM and 3.2% for StarVLA, and 79.5% on LIBERO-Plus compared with 51.5% and 75.0%, respectively. Across five real-world bimanual tasks, PINT reaches 68% ID and 24% OOD success, compared with 35%/9% for pretrained Motus and 67%/35% for pretrained $\pi_{0.5}$.
authors: Xinyu Guo, Chao Jing, Li Yi, Xingyu Chen, Zhengxing Wu
bullets: Addresses the challenge that tightly fusing VLMs and VGMs can weaken their specialized capabilities.
Uses learnable Intent Tokens from the VLM to condition a video generation model and an Action Expert through one-way information flow.
Learns Predictive Intent jointly from VLM, VGM, and action-prediction objectives, using a two-stage training strategy.
Reports strong in-distribution performance and improved out-of-distribution generalization, including 15.5% on RoboTwin 2.0-Hard and 79.5% on LIBERO-Plus.
In real-world bimanual tasks, achieves 68% in-distribution and 24% out-of-distribution success without embodied pretraining.

figures.caption: Figure 2. PINT architecture and attention design. papers.abstract: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) trains a large language model using supervision from a teacher instantiated from the same model as the student. The teacher is conditioned on privileged information (PI), such as verified solutions. The student, which does not observe PI, learns from the teacher's next-token distributions along its own sampled responses. However, PI can bias supervision toward shortcut reasoning with limited verification or reconsideration, accompanied by a sharp drop in the entropy of the output distribution. To address this challenge, we introduce self-distillation with verbal regularization (VRSD), which uses system prompts to regulate how the teacher uses PI, thereby encouraging rethinking and exploration to counteract premature commitment. Theoretically, we model prompting as attenuating the influence of PI on the teacher distribution and derive conditions for entropy preservation. Across three models and four tasks, VRSD improves Pass@1 over OPSD in 11 of 12 model-task settings, by 3.9 percentage points on average, while generally maintaining higher token entropy.
authors: Jiazheng Li, Yawei Li, Junru Lu, Zhenyi Shen, Di Yin, Lin Gui, Xing Sun, David R\"ugamer, Xinpeng Wang, Yulan He
bullets: OPSD trains a student from a same-model teacher conditioned on privileged information, such as verified solutions.
Privileged information can encourage shortcut reasoning, premature commitment, and sharply reduced output entropy.
VRSD uses system prompts to make the teacher rethink and explore rather than over-rely on privileged information.
A theoretical analysis models prompting as reducing privileged-information influence and derives conditions for preserving entropy.
Across three models and four tasks, VRSD improves Pass@1 over OPSD in 11 of 12 settings by 3.9 percentage points on average, while generally maintaining higher token entropy.

figures.caption: Figure 1: VRSD counteracts OPSD’s shortcut bias with a teacher-only prompt. Left: student pt (blue), self-teacher qt (red), and prompted teacher qdt (green) under different conditioning. Middle: The log-probability shifts ut induced by PI c can favor immediate commitment to the supplied answer (“42”) and suppress reconsideration (“Wait”, “However”), concentrating qt and lowering its entropy H(qt). Numerical values are illustrative. Right: The system prompt d encourages verification and reconsideration. By attenuating ut, the prompt can restore probability to reconsideration in the teacher qdt while retaining support for the answer. Under our affine model, Theorem 4.1 and Corollary 4.2 show that attenuation preserves the teacher’s entropy under mild conditions.

Figure 6: Pass@1 (%) on Qwen3-4B of the control whose teacher gets only the system prompts (aspect prompts, no privileged information c), next to the untrained model, OPSD (c only) and VRSD (c and system prompt).

Figure 2: Estimated PMI attenuation induced by the teacher prompt d. Points show γ̂, obtained by averaging per-prefix estimates within each problem and then across problems; error bars show 95% bootstrap confidence intervals (CIs). Dashed lines mark no attenuation. The CIs lie below this baseline, indicating that the system prompts attenuate PI-induced log-probability shifts on average.

Figure 4: Pass@1 of Qwen3-4B under different teacher prompt designs. Each dk bar shows training with only the k-th teacher prompt from the VRSD (multi) prompt set, used for all rollouts. Each of these prompts encourages a different approach to the problem, such as focusing on selected aspects. “Concat.” concatenates all K prompts into one. VRSD (single) uses a composite prompt d, whereas VRSD (multi) assigns different prompts dk to different rollouts. The multi-prompt variant achieves higher Pass@1 than both the individual prompts and their concatenation across all four tasks.
Figure 3: Average token entropy H(p) of the distilled students. VRSD generally yields higher entropy than OPSD; the detailed values and their ratios to OPSD are listed in Table 7 in Appendix E.

Figure 5: Sampled-token PMI on the initial Qwen3-4B policy, following the visualization of Shen et al. (2026a). Hexagonal bins group observations by pt(yt) and qt(yt); color shows the mean ut(yt), clipped to [−2, 2]. The dashed diagonal indicates unchanged probability.

Figure 7: Illustrative teacher continuations on a half-written chemistry problem (gold answer C) completed by untrained Qwen3-4B with solution c (OPSD teacher) and with c plus the elimination prompt d1 (verbatim, reasoning tags removed). While both reach the correct answer, the prompted teacher explicitly evaluates and rules out alternative options.

Each ratio is relative to OPSD: the method’s value divided by the OPSD value for the same model and task. < denotes a ratio below 0.1. VRSD generally yields higher student entropy than OPSD.

Table 1: Task performance (%) across three models and four tasks. P@1, M@16, and W@16 denote Pass@1, Maj@16, and Worst@16, respectively. “Untrained” denotes the model before task-specific training. “Average” denotes the mean performance across all four tasks. Blue rows highlight VRSD; bold and underlined values denote the best and second-best results, respectively.

Entries report the mean increase across three models, in percentage points. The count (n/3) indicates how many models show an increase. Compared with OPSD, VRSD students more frequently exhibit the patterns encouraged by teacher prompts.

Prefix share gives the percentage of all evaluated prefixes with |ut(yt)| > 1. Cov denotes mean Covqt(ut, log qt). Cov > 0 gives the percentage of prefixes with positive covariance within each group.
Table 10: Pattern rules. A rule fires when the stated condition holds.

RG↑ (reasoning gain) is the Pass@1 difference between retaining the full reasoning and removing it, in percentage points. MR↓ (misleading-reasoning rate) is the percentage of all evaluated answers that are correct without reasoning but incorrect when the full reasoning is retained. Compared with OPSD, VRSD achieves higher mean RG and lower mean MR, providing evidence of more faithful reasoning.

Each ratio is relative to the OPSD teacher for the same task. > denotes a ratio above 100: on SQL the OPSD teacher reproduces the query in c almost verbatim (H(q)=0.0001). The prompts raise the teacher’s entropy on every task; the two Python prompts that ask for a minimal program (d1, d2) are the exception.

Table 4: Estimated PMI attenuation before task-specific training. The mean coefficient γ̂ is obtained by averaging the per-prefix estimates in Eq. (11) within each problem and then across problems, with 95% bootstrap CIs over problems.

Table 9: Prompt sets for the teacher on Qwen3-4B (%), full numbers for Figure 4. dk alone: every rollout is trained toward the teacher prompted with that one aspect prompt. Concatenation: d1, . . . , dK joined into a single prompt. Chemistry only has K=3.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces Verbal Regularization for Self-Distillation (VRSD) to prevent shortcut reasoning in LLMs by regulating the use of privileged information. Relevant to LLM training and self-distillation.
papers.title: Self-Distillation with Verbal Regularization
papers.tldr: Verbal regularization improves on-policy self-distillation by prompting teachers to use privileged information less rigidly, promoting exploration and better task performance.

papers.abstract: Recent years have witnessed rapid progress in joint audio--visual generation. However, audio--visual synchronization remains a challenge, as generated speech and sound often temporally misalign with visual events. A key bottleneck is the lack of human-annotated data, reliable evaluation benchmarks, and synchronization-aware evaluation models for generated audio--visual outputs. To address these limitations, we conduct a comprehensive study spanning data, benchmarking, and reward modeling. We first introduce SyncReward-Data-80K, a dataset containing 80K professional synchronization ratings for clips from eight audio--visual generators. A taxonomy-guided construction pipeline covers four sound-event families: Speech, Onset, Instrument, and Ambient. We further construct \textbf{SyncReward-Bench}, a held-out benchmark of 1K clips, each independently rated by multiple professionals. Using this benchmark, we systematically evaluate specialized synchronization metrics and omni-modal models, revealing their substantial misalignment with human judgments. Finally, we develop SyncReward, a reward model that combines semantic--temporal contrastive pretraining on real clips with human supervision on generated clips. As an evaluation metric, SyncReward achieves the strongest agreement with human ratings among the evaluated methods. As a reward, it improves synchronization through inference-time best-of-$N$ selection and reinforcement learning based post-training. We will release the data, benchmark, model, and code at https://github.com/WeChatCV/SyncReward.
authors: Kaisi Guan, Ying Ba, Wenjing Wang, Xihua Wang, Chen Li, Jing Lyu, Ruihau Song
bullets: Addresses the lack of human-aligned data and reliable synchronization evaluation for audio–visual generation.
Releases SyncReward-Data-80K with professional ratings spanning Speech, Onset, Instrument, and Ambient sound events.
Introduces SyncReward-Bench, a 1K-clip held-out benchmark with multiple independent professional ratings.
Finds that existing synchronization metrics and omni-modal models often misalign with human judgments.

Combines semantic–temporal contrastive pretraining with human supervision; it achieves the strongest agreement with human ratings among evaluated methods and improves synchronization via best-of-N selection and reinforcement-learning post-training.

figures.caption: Figure 5: Qualitative effects of SyncReward-guided DiffusionNFT post-training. Each example compares outputs before (top) and after (bottom) post-training using three video frames and the corresponding log-mel spectrogram. Dashed lines mark frame timestamps t1–t3, and displayed scores are SyncReward predictions. Left: Post-training improves visible lip articulation during speech. Right: Vocal correspondence improves, but the instrument specified by the prompt is absent, illustrating a trade-off between synchronization and prompt fidelity.

Figure 2: Sound-event taxonomy and human-rated examples. Examples span four sound-event families, 16 classes, and eight audio–visual generators. Headers report dataset-level rating counts for each family and class. Each card presents three sampled video frames, an event description, the generator name, and a human synchronization score. Scores indicate unsynchronized (0), partially synchronized (1), and fully synchronized (2) clips. Examples are selected to illustrate category coverage and different synchronization levels, rather than the dataset’s score distribution.

Figure 4: Clip representations and human synchronization ratings. Each panel shows a separate PCA projection fitted on validation features, with a class-balanced subset of held-out test clips colored by human synchronization ratings. Curves show class-wise PC1 densities; ellipses indicate one-standard-deviation covariance contours, and connected markers denote class means in rating order. Axis labels report explained variance, and coordinates are not shared across models.

Figure 3: Two-stage training of SyncReward. Stage 1 trains the audio and video encoders through contrastive learning with aligned segment pairs, within-clip temporal negatives, and cross-clip semantic negatives from the same batch. Stage 2 freezes both encoders and trains a cross-modal Transformer and score head using human synchronization ratings, combining regression and pairwise ranking losses. The model outputs a clip-level synchronization score in [0, 2]. Flame and snowflake icons indicate trainable and frozen modules, respectively.

Table 1: SyncReward as a metric. We report Spearman’s rank correlation (ρ × 100) and pairwise ranking accuracy (Pair Acc., %) for four on-screen sound categories: Speech, Onset, Instrument, and Ambient. Clips are grouped by the sound category used to construct their prompts. All comparisons are rank-based and require no score calibration. papers.abstract: Rotary Positional Embedding (RoPE) is widely used to encode relative positions in Transformers. In multi-view settings, however, patch coordinates are defined independently in each image: the same 3D point can therefore have different coordinates across views, making them insufficient for establishing cross-view correspondences. We introduce WorldRoPE, a probabilistic world-centric RoPE for multi-view attention. At each layer, WorldRoPE back-projects each patch token into a set of volumetric Gaussian primitives in a shared world frame. These primitives represent multiple plausible 3D supports for a token, jointly capturing alternative depth hypotheses, depth uncertainty, and the finite spatial extent of its patch frustum. When a key token's support is projected into a query view, it induces a distribution over where that key may appear in the query image. WorldRoPE integrates the rotary operator over this distribution in closed form, combining rotations at the projected primitive centers according to their mixture weights with covariance-dependent attenuation. This makes attention less sensitive to uncertain key locations in the query view, without rasterizing or warping token features. The formulation reduces to deterministic RoPE when the support collapses to a point. Across layers, the predicted geometry guides cross-view attention, while the updated features refine the geometry used at the next layer. Experiments on novel view synthesis, depth estimation, and 3D geometry reconstruction demonstrate the effectiveness of WorldRoPE for multi-view Transformers.
authors: Mijeong Kim, Kyujin Lim, Bohyung Han
bullets: Per-image patch coordinates cannot reliably establish correspondences for the same 3D point across views.
Each token is back-projected into volumetric Gaussian primitives capturing alternative depths, uncertainty, and patch-frustum extent.
The method integrates RoPE over the induced projected-location distribution using mixture weights and covariance-based attenuation.
It guides cross-view attention with predicted geometry while allowing updated features to refine geometry across layers.
Experiments show effectiveness for novel view synthesis, depth estimation, and 3D geometry reconstruction.

papers.abstract: Feed-forward transformer models have driven remarkable progress in 3D vision,yet their quadratic complexity renders them impractical for long video sequences. Streaming 3D reconstruction addresses this bottleneck by processing frames sequen?tially with constant memory. However, existing recurrent architectures inevitably suffer from progressive degradation over long sequences, as they fail to account for the intrinsic reliability of observations and the accumulated confidence of the historical state, leading to severe error accumulation. To address these issues, we introduce BAT3R, a training-free Bayesian adaptation framework comprising two synergistic modules: State Innovation Gating (SIG) and Bayesian-guided Adaptive State Updating (BASU). SIG acts as a distributional regularizer that anchors state evolution to its geometric initialization, effectively arresting representational drift during long-term inference. Building on this, BASU reformulates state update as a recursive Bayesian inference process within a Kalman filtering framework. By jointly modeling the temporal reliability of observations via information-theoretic gain and spatial relevance via cross-attention maps, BASU achieves an asymmetric spatio-temporal state fusion: well-consolidated historical regions are protected from redundant updates, while genuinely novel scene content is aggressively incor?porated. Extensive experiments on standard benchmarks (7-Scenes, TUM, ScanNet, KITTI, etc.) demonstrate that BAT3R consistently outperforms state-of-the-art online 3D reconstruction methods, with the most significant gains observed on long sequences and complex scenes.
authors: Lijian Li, Yuanpeng He, Yudian Zheng, Chung-ju Huang, Linyu Li, Dongming Jin, Wenpin Jiao, Zhi Jin, Chi-Man Pun
bullets: Streaming reconstruction uses constant memory but recurrent methods accumulate errors over long videos.

Experiments across standard benchmarks show consistent gains over existing online 3D reconstruction methods, especially on long and complex sequences.

By balancing observation reliability with historical confidence, the framework achieves robust, uncertainty-aware 3D scene reconstruction.

papers.abstract: Bubbly flows involve strongly coupled bubble motion, deformation, and hydrodynamic interactions, making high-fidelity simulation computationally expensive. We propose a neural surrogate that jointly predicts bubble trajectories and interface deformation in a compact, shared representation, replacing costly mesh-resolved simulation with fast generative inference. Because two-phase flow dynamics is nonlinear and chaotic, we treat forecasting as a conditional generative problem rather than deterministic regression, predicting entire future windows in a single pass. We train and evaluate the surrogate on BubbleSH, a Front-Tracking dataset of rising deformable bubble swarms, assessing performance using trajectory, shape, and distributional metrics over kinematic, morphological, and interaction-based properties. The surrogate reproduces key flow statistics while running several orders of magnitude faster than the underlying DNS solver.
authors: Kiet Bennema ten Brinke, Rachna Ramesh, Douwe Orij, Ivo Roghair, Vlado Menkovski
bullets: Targets the costly simulation of coupled bubble trajectories, deformation, and hydrodynamic interactions.
Represents bubble state compactly with shared spherical-harmonic features.
Uses coupled flow matching to generate entire future windows probabilistically, accounting for nonlinear and chaotic dynamics.
Evaluated on the BubbleSH front-tracking dataset with trajectory, shape, and distributional metrics.
Matches key flow statistics and runs several orders of magnitude faster than the underlying DNS solver.

papers.abstract: Multimodal model predictive control (MM-MPC) avoids local minima among moving obstacles by solving one optimal control problem (OCP) per combination of avoidance sides, so its computational cost grows exponentially with the number of decision-critical obstacles. We propose SideNet-MPC, which replaces this enumeration with a mode decision learned by imitating MM-MPC as an expert. A graph neural network is trained to predict the expert's minimum-cost mode, one avoidance side per obstacle. Its edges encode, for each obstacle pair, the gap predicted for the moment the vehicle first reaches either obstacle, so a neighbor that blocks a preferred passage can reverse the proposed side. The expert's selection rule compares its minimum-cost mode with the previously executed mode; SideNet-MPC keeps this rule and substitutes the network proposal for the minimum-cost mode. Hence at most two OCPs are solved per control period, and every applied input still comes from an OCP with control barrier function constraints rather than from the network. In $100$ seed-matched closed-loop Monte Carlo runs of mixed traffic, SideNet-MPC reaches $93\%$ of the expert's success rate and needs \SI{18.6}{ms} per control period on a single thread, 48\% less than the expert's \SI{35.5}{ms} on sixteen parallel threads. In a controlled gap sweep, its proposed side reverses in the same gap interval as the expert's, whereas proposers without pairwise edges, trained on the same data, never reverse and all deadlock at the blocked gates of a deterministic scene.
authors: Changyu Lee, Byung-Kwan Lee, Kanghoon Yoon
bullets: MM-MPC avoids local minima by enumerating avoidance-side combinations, but this cost grows exponentially with decision-critical obstacles.
A graph neural network predicts one avoidance side per obstacle, using pairwise gap information to account for blocked passages.
The controller preserves the expert’s mode-selection rule and solves at most two optimal control problems per control period.
In 100 seed-matched mixed-traffic runs, it achieved 93% of the expert’s success rate and reduced reported control time from 35.5 ms to 18.6 ms.
Pairwise graph edges enabled side reversals in the same gap interval as the expert; models without them deadlocked in the tested deterministic scene.

papers.abstract: Training-free language-based video anomaly detection (VAD) uses frozen vision--language models (VLMs) and large language models (LLMs) to localize abnormal events without task-specific model-weight optimization. Existing approaches increasingly exploit broader temporal and semantic context, yet generic context does not necessarily foreground abnormal events or specify how video-level semantics should modify local anomaly scores. We introduce a training-free semantic feedback framework that uses VAD-guided active observation for video anomaly understanding (VAU) and returns the resulting anomaly-focused description to refine temporal detection. Starting from an upstream anomaly-score curve, we adapt reasoning-based iterative frame selection: high-score regions seed the observations, and anomaly scores together with VLM relevance assessments guide subsequent temporal exploration. A frozen video-language model generates a single open-ended anomaly description from the selected frames. The description is returned through two complementary feedback levels: video-level feedback determines whether the score distribution should be suppressed, preserved, or sharpened, with selective visual rechecking, while local feedback retrieves event-related windows and promotes scores only after target-local visual verification. All model weights remain frozen, and feedback is applied once without regenerating the description. On the HIVAU video-summary evaluations of UCF-Crime and XD-Violence, VAD-guided observation improves GPT-rated reasonability, detail, and consistency over the matched CLIP-guided variant. For VAD, semantic feedback improves the re-evaluated upstream detector from 84.36% to 86.25% AUC on UCF-Crime and from 68.07% to 72.58% AP on XD-Violence, where the final AUC is 91.74%.
authors: Hangil Park, Seungheon Kim, Tae-Kyun Kim

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can reduce hallucination by abstaining from questions they would likely get wrong. Abstention can be implemented outside the model (selective answering) using a confidence threshold that controls the answer rate (coverage), or learned inside it (abstention training), which can perform better but fixes coverage once trained. To compare the two, we match their coverage and decompose risk (error rate) into answering ability and distinguishing ability, i.e., how well the model answers and how accurately it abstains, respectively. The decomposition shows that abstention training performs better mainly by answering better: with strong confidence estimators, the two have nearly equal distinguishing ability. This motivates Train for Accuracy, then Post-hoc Select (TAPS), a modular approach that keeps coverage controllable, needs only standard post-training and an off-the-shelf confidence estimator, and benefits from advances in either component. Across three LLMs and three factual QA benchmarks, TAPS with a probing-based confidence estimator attains 1.5--9.4 percentage points lower mean risk than three representative abstention training methods at matched coverage. Within TAPS, accuracy training often weakens the model's own confidence signals, yet refitting the estimator largely preserves distinguishing ability. Together, these results establish TAPS as a strong yet controllable baseline and raise the bar for future abstention training: sacrificing control over coverage should yield gains beyond what can be achieved by optimizing answering and abstaining separately.
authors: Junwei Zhang, Yifei Wang, Wanli Yang, Hexiang Tan, Rui Tang, Xin Chen, Jingang Wang, Du Su, Fei Sun
bullets: Abstention reduces hallucinations by skipping questions the model is likely to answer incorrectly, but learned abstention fixes coverage after training.

Across three LLMs and three factual QA benchmarks, TAPS reduces mean risk by 1.5–9.4 percentage points versus three abstention-training methods.
Accuracy training can weaken the model’s native confidence signals, but refitting the estimator largely preserves abstention quality.

papers.abstract: Articulated object manipulation tasks such as opening doors, tightening bolts, and pulling drawers impose kinematic constraints on a robot end-effector's motion that neural policies may fail to satisfy. Unlike hybrid force-position control that strictly separates force and position control into orthogonal subspaces, impedance control modulates a mechanical impedance system in the form of a virtual inertia, damping, and stiffness. However, selecting task-appropriate impedance gains remains challenging for robot policies. In this paper, we address this problem for the case of manipulating articulated objects. Our constraint-decomposed impedance control method uses the sampling diversity of a generative policy to estimate the feasible motion directions in twist space. The key idea is to infer the feasible and constrained subspaces of twists from an ensemble of trajectories generated by the policy from the same observation. Principal component analysis (PCA) of the end-effector twists determines the feasible twist subspace, which is then used to form 6x6 impedance gain matrices. For many common articulated objects, the feasible twist subspace is independent of the object configuration, so the subspace and resulting gains are estimated once and held fixed during manipulation, minimizing computational overhead. For less common cases where this independence does not hold, we instead estimate a configuration-independent twist subspace of higher dimension that contains the local feasible subspaces, allowing the same fixed-gain strategy to be used. Experiments across simulated and real-world single- and multi-DoF objects show that the proposed method consistently reduces constraint-violating contact loads relative to isotropic impedance control while maintaining task execution.
authors: Kyungseo Park, Byeongdo Lim, Jungbin Lim, Minseok Choi, Frank C. Park
bullets: Targets manipulation tasks such as doors, bolts, and drawers, where end-effector motion must satisfy kinematic constraints.
Uses PCA over multiple policy-generated trajectories from the same observation to separate feasible and constrained twist directions.
Constructs 6×6 impedance gain matrices from the estimated feasible twist subspace.
For configuration-dependent constraints, uses a higher-dimensional, configuration-independent subspace to retain fixed gains and low computational overhead.
Simulated and real-world experiments on single- and multi-DoF objects reduce constraint-violating contact loads versus isotropic impedance while preserving task execution.

papers.abstract: Test-time agentic computation can improve multimodal large language models (MLLMs) through planning, tool use, iterative perception, and reflection, but indiscriminate computation may duplicate resolved work, introduce noisy evidence, and perturb correct predictions. We propose that such computation should be residual: allocate additional computation only to requirements unresolved by the base model and, after a localized failure, recompute only the affected states. We instantiate this formulation in ReTAC, a training-free multiagent framework for video spatial reasoning. ReTAC organizes supplementary computation around unresolved requirements. It plans ordered steps to acquire missing spatial evidence and combines the observations with compatible native evidence for reasoning. In addition, it uses stage-aligned verification to localize failures to planning, perception, or reasoning. Dependency-based recovery recomputes only affected states while reusing unaffected ones. Extensive experiments show that ReTAC achieves the highest overall score among the compared methods across three mainstream MLLMs and two widely adopted benchmarks. Further analyses show that gains from additional computation depend not only on how much is used, but also on where it is allocated and which valid intermediate states are preserved.

bullets: Addresses redundant, noisy, or disruptive computation in MLLMs during video spatial reasoning.

Applies stage-aligned verification to identify whether failures arise from planning, perception, or reasoning.
Uses dependency-based recovery to recompute affected states while preserving valid intermediate results.
Achieves the highest overall score among compared methods across three MLLMs and two benchmarks, according to the abstract.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have advanced robotic manipulation by connecting visual perception and language instructions to action generation. However, many manipulation tasks depend on auditory cues that cannot be reliably inferred from visual observations and may need to be elicited through physical interaction. To address this gap, we present ListenVLA, an audio-conditioned VLA policy built on GR00T N1.7 for sound-guided manipulation. ListenVLA combines semantic audio embeddings with waveform-derived acoustic cues over a causal audio history and conditions continuous action generation through audio tokens and feature modulation. Moreover, we introduce an audio-action binding objective that uses context-matched demonstrations to link auditory differences to demonstrated action differences. The objective supervises short-horizon differences between flow-velocity predictions under different audio conditions, with shared pure-noise action inputs and fixed non-audio observations, alongside full-chunk action supervision. Furthermore, we develop LIBERO-Audio, an eight-task benchmark covering sound-based target selection, responses to auditory events, and physical interactions that reveal acoustic evidence. Experiments on LIBERO-Audio and three real-world manipulation tasks show excellent performance. Ablation studies support the contributions of binding supervision and audio modulation, while audio swap tests show that sound influences action predictions. Our code and videos are available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/listenvla-F18D

Presents LIBERO-Audio, an eight-task benchmark spanning sound-based selection, auditory-event responses, and interactions that reveal acoustic evidence.
Reports strong results on LIBERO-Audio and three real-world tasks; ablations and audio-swap tests support the roles of binding supervision and audio modulation.

papers.abstract: Despite rapid progress, generalist robot policies remain brittle during execution. Reliable deployment therefore requires runtime monitoring that provides timely warnings of failure. Existing monitors commonly estimate risk from current observations or policy signals without explicitly predicting the future consequences of proposed actions. To anticipate such risks before action execution, we introduce ReAP, a future-aware runtime monitoring framework that combines visual failure recognition with action-conditioned failure prediction. Specifically, ReAP first trains a visual detector on successful and failed rollouts to learn a failure-relevant representation space and estimate current risk. An action-conditioned predictor then forecasts the resulting future representation in this space to estimate future failure risk. At runtime, the detector and predictor provide complementary signals for current-state failure recognition and future-aware risk assessment. Experiments across diverse robot policies in simulation and the real world demonstrate that ReAP effectively balances failure-detection accuracy and warning timeliness.
authors: Jingyuan Liu, Yunpeng Qing, Changxu Wei, Zhi Hou
bullets: Addresses the brittleness of generalist robot policies and the need for timely deployment warnings.
Learns a failure-relevant visual representation from successful and failed rollouts to estimate current risk.
Predicts the future representation resulting from a proposed action, enabling future-aware risk assessment.
Combines current-state detection with action-conditioned prediction to balance detection accuracy and warning timeliness.
Evaluated across diverse robot policies in simulation and the real world.

papers.abstract: Contact-rich insertion requires robots to combine visual alignment with tactile adjustment. However, existing visuotactile chunk-based policies collapse tactile feedback into a single generation-time fusion pathway, leaving persistent contact states, abrupt contact events, and future contact consequences implicitly modeled in a single representation. We present PACE (Phase-Aware Contact-Event Conditioning), a temporal-role tactile conditioning framework for chunk-based insertion policies. PACE organizes a shared tactile stream into three temporal roles: persistent contact states condition action-chunk generation, abrupt contact events correct the generated chunk, and contact-consequence prediction shapes action representations during training. This design preserves chunk-level action continuity while assigning distinct pathways to different temporal roles of contact feedback. Across five real-robot insertion tasks, PACE achieves an average success rate of 90.7%, outperforming vision-only and generation-time tactile-fusion baselines by over 44 percentage points; on the ManipulationNet benchmark, PACE maintains 88.7% success across six geometry-clearance configurations, including an industrial-grade 0.1-mm clearance. Ablations confirm the complementary contributions of the three temporal roles, mechanistic analyses show that PACE separates normal insertion progress from contact events requiring immediate correction, and cross-signal and cross-architecture experiments indicate that this temporal-role principle extends across different physical feedback signals and policy backbones. Videos and materials are available at https://pace-insertion.github.io/.
authors: Zhiyuan Chen, Shixiong Xu, Shuai Chen, Yangwei You
bullets: Targets the challenge of combining visual alignment with persistent and abrupt tactile contact during insertion.
Uses persistent contact states to condition action-chunk generation and abrupt contact events to correct generated chunks.
Trains contact-consequence prediction to shape action representations while preserving chunk-level action continuity.
Achieves 90.7% average success across five real-robot tasks and 88.7% across six ManipulationNet configurations, including 0.1-mm clearance.
Ablations and cross-architecture/signal studies support the complementary and transferable nature of the three temporal roles.

papers.abstract: Video-based interactive world models aim to enable real-time, user-controllable environments. Yet most existing systems are trained and rolled out at a fixed temporal rate, limiting both runtime-rate adaptation and physical-horizon coverage -- a limitation we term temporal-rate coupling. Specifically, when runtime generation throughput differs from the learned temporal rate, the generated world evolves unintentionally more slowly or quickly. Moreover, using a single temporal rate imposes an inherent trade-off between temporal granularity and physical horizon: higher rates capture finer motion but cover a shorter duration under a fixed context window. To address both limitations, we introduce Rate-Adaptive Rollout (RAR), a framework that enables interactive world models to roll out at controllable temporal rates. At its core, Stride-RoPE aligns latent frames sampled at different rates on a shared physical-time coordinate, enabling consistent multi-rate rollout, unseen-rate generalization, and online rate switching without discarding history. Meanwhile, RAR uses multi-stride video sampling to enable joint learning of fine-grained dynamics and long-horizon evolution. Across action- and camera-controlled environments, RAR achieves temporally consistent multi-rate rollout and online rate switching while preserving high-rate generation quality and extending physical horizons under matched training budgets. RAR also transfers to pretrained world models while preserving perceptual quality.
authors: Yaoyang Liu, Dongyu Yan, Yihua Du, Shengju Qian, Zeke Xie, Xin Wang, Ying-Cong Chen, Long Chen
bullets: Addresses temporal-rate coupling: fixed training and rollout rates can cause unintended slowdowns or speedups and limit horizon coverage.
Uses Stride-RoPE to align latent frames across sampling rates on a shared physical-time coordinate.
Supports unseen-rate generalization and online rate switching without discarding prior history.
Multi-stride video sampling jointly learns fine-grained dynamics and long-horizon evolution.
Demonstrates consistent multi-rate rollout, preserved high-rate quality, longer horizons, and transfer to pretrained models across action- and camera-controlled environments.

papers.abstract: Self-attention assigns two functions to one mechanism-where to read and how to mix-at the price of O(L^2) training, an O(T) decode state, and position signals bound to the training length. Existing attention-free alternatives all optimize the single function of generation. We propose FON (Fusion-Organ Network), which differentiates one weight stack into a drafting organ (multi-tap learnable delays + content-adaptive recursion; causal, O(S) training, O(1) decode state, no sequence-level quadratic attention) and a revision organ that re-processes the written prefix through multi-scale ripple kernels injected via weak gates, never generating. At 30M parameters, iso-parameter and iso-token budget, FON reaches perplexity 131.03 on WikiText-103, beating Transformer (197.73) and Mamba2 (152.53); the advantage persists under all depth-aligned baselines and at the 70M tier (-20.8%). At 8x length extrapolation FON degrades by ~8-9% without positional-encoding engineering, between ALiBi and RoPE. The revision channel provides a structural pathway for in-domain infilling that causal architectures lack in principle (+19% over on-demand coupling), at a perplexity cost indistinguishable within measurement precision. We report all costs and boundaries: impaired long-range retrieval, synthetic-task disadvantages, weaker out-of-domain code infilling than a same-recipe Transformer, and a 6.5-12.3x wall-clock gap.
authors: Helong Hu (Zhanjiang Campus, Guangdong Ocean University, Zhanjiang, Guangdong, China), Hongdan Pan (Maoming Administrative Service Center, Maoming, Guangdong, China), Shuiqing Hu (China Pacific Insurance)
bullets: Drafting uses learnable delays and content-adaptive recursion with O(S) training and O(1) decode state; revision reprocesses prefixes via gated multi-scale ripple kernels.
At 30M parameters, FON achieves 131.03 perplexity on WikiText-103 versus 197.73 for Transformer and 152.53 for Mamba2; gains persist at 70M parameters.
At 8× length extrapolation, perplexity degrades by about 8–9% without positional-encoding engineering.
Revision enables in-domain infilling, improving performance by 19% over on-demand coupling at no measurable perplexity cost.
Limitations include impaired long-range retrieval, weaker synthetic-task and out-of-domain code-infilling performance, and a 6.5–12.3× wall-clock gap.

papers.abstract: Video anomaly understanding (VAU) aims to generate language-level interpretations of anomalous events in long videos, requiring visual evidence that supports explanation beyond anomaly detection alone. Existing VAU pipelines commonly rely on anomaly-centric or predefined temporal sampling strategies, which efficiently emphasize suspicious moments but overlook contextual cues, object interactions, and temporally distributed evidence needed for reasoning. Motivated by recent progress in learnable temporal selection for long-video question answering, we revisit VAU temporal sampling as a downstream-aligned evidence selection problem. We introduce the semantic-conditioned Temporal Sampling Q-Former that learns to select temporal visual evidence through the VAU generation objective. Since generic VAU prompts provide weak video-specific guidance, we condition the sampler on CLIP-embedded object tags automatically extracted from the input video. These tags are used only for temporal evidence selection and are not appended to the LLM generation prompt, separating sampler conditioning from prompt augmentation. The proposed sampler operates in visual-token space, computes soft temporal selection weights from frame-level representations, and merges duplicated selections before response generation. Experiments on HIVAU-70K show that our model achieves the best performance among the compared fine-tuned models, while ablations demonstrate that learnable temporal sampling improves over fixed anomaly-focused sampling and that CLIP-embedded object-tag conditioning further improves over generic-prompt conditioning. Our results suggest that temporal sampling in VAU should be aligned with explanation-oriented evidence utility rather than anomaly saliency alone.
authors: Hangil Park, Seungheon Kim, Tae-Kyun Kim
bullets: Targets video anomaly understanding, where explanations require contextual cues, object interactions, and evidence spread across long videos.
Introduces a Temporal Sampling Q-Former that learns soft temporal evidence selection from the VAU generation objective.
Conditions selection on automatically extracted CLIP-embedded object tags without adding them to the LLM prompt.
Operates in visual-token space and merges duplicate selections before response generation.
On HIVAU-70K, it performs best among compared fine-tuned models; ablations show gains over fixed anomaly-focused and generic-prompt sampling.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of the proposed temporal evidence selection framework. The video is encoded by a frozen visual encoder, and the temporal Q-Former selects visual evidence from uniformly sampled candidate frames. Object-centric tags are encoded by a frozen CLIP text encoder and mapped to the temporal Q-Former hidden space by a trainable semantic projection layer. The resulting object-tag embedding sequence Zc is used only to condition the temporal sampler. The selected evidence tokens are projected and then consumed by the LLM with the original prompt q.

Figure 3: Qualitative comparison of temporal evidence selection on HIVAU-70K. We compare ATS, CAES, and the object-tag-conditioned Temporal Q-Former. The proposed sampler retrieves explanation-supporting evidence missed by fixed anomaly-focused samplers, including brief causal moments and temporally distributed contextual cues needed for anomaly reasoning.

Figure 1: Conceptual illustration of the evidence mismatch in video anomaly understanding. Anomaly-centric selection captures salient anomaly peaks, but its non-peak selections are not necessarily useful for explaining why the event is anomalous. Explanation-supporting selection retrieves anomaly evidence together with explanation-helpful non-peak cues, such as scene context, object roles, and surrounding reactions, leading to a more complete natural-language explanation.
Figure 5: Full sampled-frame sequences visualization for Fig. 3.

Figure 4: Task-wise sampling analysis on HIVAU-70K. Each cell reports the corpus-level metric difference over ATS for a given granularity/task pair; positive values indicate improvement over ATS. Uniform sampling and ATS share the same checkpoint and differ only in the inference-time sampling rule. The Temporal Q-Former comparison uses a separately trained end-to-end variant, so it should be interpreted as the effect of replacing the fixed sampler with a learned evidence selector.

papers.abstract: Training neural networks in reduced precision can yield significant efficiency gains, yet all existing methods that scale to standard computer vision benchmarks retain floating-point in at least one stage, typically the weight update or optimizer state. We present a training algorithm that scales to modern deep neural networks, in which every tensor (weights, gradients, and activations) is stored as INT8, and every operation (forward pass, backward pass, weight update, optimizer update) is performed in integer arithmetic. Specifically, tensors are stored as signed integer mantissas paired with explicit power-of-two exponents, on which integer-only operations are performed using five custom composable building blocks (products, sums, divide-by-constant, nonlinear functions, and weight updates). This allows complete implementation of trainable integer layers, including convolutions, batch and layer normalization, softmax, and GELU. A per-group velocity mechanism with independent exponent tracking preserves gradient precision across neurons and channels with diverse magnitudes. As every tensor fits in INT8, training memory is roughly 4x smaller than the FP32 baseline. We validate our training algorithm on CNNs (ResNet-18/34/50/101, MobileNetV2) and Vision Transformers (ViT-Ti / B), demonstrating for the first time that training neural networks with INT8 tensors and integer arithmetic can achieve competitive accuracy on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100 and ImageNet at a reduced memory budget.
authors: Hazem Hesham Yousef Shalby, Fabrizio Pittorino, Manuel Roveri
bullets: Addresses the floating-point weight updates or optimizer states retained by prior reduced-precision training methods.
Represents INT8 mantissas with explicit power-of-two exponents and uses five composable integer building blocks for core training operations.
Supports integer implementations of convolutions, normalization, softmax, GELU, and optimizer updates.
Uses per-group velocity and independent exponent tracking to preserve gradient precision across differently scaled channels and neurons.
Evaluated on CNNs and Vision Transformers across CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet, achieving competitive accuracy with roughly 4× lower training memory than FP32.

papers.abstract: Garment manipulation requires inferring both garment identity and complete configuration from partial, self-occluded observations. This creates a chicken-and-egg problem: completing a partial observation requires a garment-specific deformation prior, while identifying the garment requires a configuration that explains the observation. We introduce ClothAtlas, which jointly identifies garments and estimates their complete configurations from partial point clouds and a library of canonical meshes. A shared graph-conditioned flow-matching model samples configurations for each candidate mesh and ranks candidates by observation fit. The model accommodates different mesh shapes, vertex counts, and connectivities, allowing new garments to be added from canonical meshes alone without retraining. On held-out DexGarmentLab garments, ClothAtlas ranks the correct mesh first among 221 candidates for all 22 test garments from a single flat observation. From a single self-occluded observation, it identifies 15/22 garments, compared with 8/22 for a deterministic graph estimator. Persistent vertex identities support grasp-target localization on real garments, reducing mean error from 15.4 to 6.4 cm overall and from 17.0 to 8.3 cm on occluded targets compared with dense descriptor matching. Project page: https://clothatlas.github.io/
authors: Jens Lundell, Alberta Longhini, Lei Shu, Hemal Arora, Evan Robert, Carlota Par\'es-Morlans, Marcel B\"usching, M{\aa}rten Bj\"orkman, Jeannette Bohg
