papers.abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has been becoming a promising 3D reconstruction technique because of its advantage of high-fidelity rendering effect with high efficiency. However, it still suffers from coarse density control and semantically blind loss functions when reconstructing the fine-grained structures in complex urban scenes. Thus, this study proposes SG-GS, a semantic-guided 3DGS method for fine-grained structure reconstruction. It takes the semantic segmentation deduced by the Segment Anything Model (SAM) as a constraint and systematically integrates it into both Gaussian density control and loss function design. On the one hand, a semantic-constrained adaptive density control mechanism is constructed, which dynamically allocates gradient thresholds to different semantic regions of the scene and introduces an additional boundary-enhanced densification strategy, so that new Gaussians are directed to structurally critical regions. On the other hand, a multi-feature guided loss function is designed, and fine-grained supervision signals are gradually introduced through a phased progressive training strategy, alleviating the artifacts caused by the lack of semantic constraints in the basic loss. Experiments on three datasets show that the proposed method consistently improves reconstruction accuracy. Compared with the original 3DGS, the PSNR increases by approximately 2.7% to 5.2%, while artifacts on linear structures and boundary blurring are effectively mitigated. The method can serve the fine-grained 3D reconstruction of urban scenes.

papers.abstract: Quantization has emerged as one of the primary techniques for reducing the memory footprint of large language models during inference. A prominent example is Quantized Johnson$-$Lindenstrauss (QJL), which compresses KV caches using 1-bit asymmetric quantization while approximately preserving the inner products required by the attention mechanism. Recent theoretical and practical work aims at replacing the dense Gaussian projections used by the aforementioned transforms with more structured embeddings $-$ such as compositions of randomized Hadamard transforms $-$ while retaining the same embedding dimension. In this paper, we introduce two constructions based on a composition of randomized Hadamard transforms, albeit with a Gaussian rather than Rademacher diagonal in the second stage. The first adds Gaussian dithering to smooth the quantizer, while the second inserts a random permutation to regularize the covariance structure of the resulting Gaussian measurements. We prove embedding-dimension and running-time guarantees analogous to those of Fast JL in the non-quantized setting. The first construction achieves $m=O(\varepsilon^{-2}\log^2(d/\delta))$, while the second achieves $m=O(\varepsilon^{-2}\log(d/\delta))$ under a restriction on $m$. Both constructions can be applied in $O(d\log d)$ time.
authors: Angelos Korakitis, Vasileios Nakos
bullets: Targets efficient KV-cache compression for attention via approximate inner-product preservation.
Replaces dense Gaussian projections with compositions of randomized Hadamard transforms and Gaussian diagonals.
Gaussian dithering smooths quantization in the first construction; a random permutation regularizes measurement covariance in the second.
Both methods run in O(d log d) time.
Embedding dimensions are O(ε⁻² log²(d/δ)) for the first and O(ε⁻² log(d/δ)) for the second, with a restriction on m for the latter.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces structured quantized Johnson-Lindenstrauss transforms for KV cache compression, fitting memory-efficient inference.
papers.title: Fast Quantized Johnson$-$Lindenstrauss Transforms
papers.tldr: Two fast structured constructions make 1-bit Quantized Johnson–Lindenstrauss transforms computable in near-linear time while preserving theoretical embedding guarantees.

papers.abstract: Frontier LLM agents perform complex interactive tasks, but their inference costs motivate transferring their experience to smaller open-source agents. Distillation and latent communication typically require target-model training or access to source-model internals. We study how textual frontier-model trajectories can provide reusable local controls for a frozen agent. Inspired by protocol reverse engineering, we introduce $\textit{Agentic Latents}$, comprising anchored states and dynamic profiles of feedback--response cycles elicited by replay in the target model. Our training-free framework, $\textbf{REVEAL}$ ($\textbf{REV}$erse $\textbf{E}$ngineering $\textbf{A}$gentic $\textbf{L}$atents), uses these profiles and trajectory outcomes to match and select local events from successful and failed rollouts of the same task and source model. Their response-transition contrasts yield a target-specific steering direction, applied before each response. Within-benchmark evaluations on Terminal-Bench 2.1 and Humanity's Last Exam with tools report higher accuracy than unmodified agents across three targets. Representation analyses and behavioral case studies support reusing frontier-model experience as local activation control.
authors: Yuetian Du, Meng Wang, Yucheng Wang, Zhangzhe Chen, Wei Wang, Boyu Yang, Weiqi Zhai, Bing Zhao, Ming Kong, Zhan Zhou, Jie Liu, Qiang Zhu
bullets: Addresses the cost of transferring frontier-agent experience when target training or source-model internals are unavailable.
Constructs agentic latents from replayed feedback–response cycles, including anchored states and dynamic profiles.
Matches local events across successful and failed trajectories to derive response-transition steering directions.
Applies the resulting control before each target-agent response.
Within-benchmark evaluations on Terminal-Bench 2.1 and Humanity’s Last Exam with tools report higher accuracy across three target agents; analyses support local activation control as the mechanism.

papers.abstract: Flow Matching (FM) has recently emerged as a principled and efficient generative modeling framework for reinforcement learning (RL), enabling expressive, multimodal policy parameterizations via deterministic probability transport. Compared to diffusion-based policies that rely on stochastic denoising chains, FM uses sampling based on ordinary differential equations (ODEs), with learned velocity fields, which can substantially reduce inference latency and simplify the incorporation of RL objectives. As research in flow-based RL rapidly accelerates across offline continuous control, online fine-tuning, and foundation model alignment, the literature has become highly fragmented. In this survey, we provide a comprehensive taxonomy of flow-matching approaches in reinforcement learning. We organize the literature along two axes: the target distribution being modeled (e.g., action policies, value critics, transition dynamics) and the mechanism of RL signal integration (e.g., energy-weighted regression, flow-based policy gradients, and group relative policy optimization). Furthermore, we survey emerging frontiers such as discrete and non-Euclidean action spaces, provide a systematic comparative analysis against Gaussian and diffusion baselines, and outline critical open problems. Ultimately, this survey serves as a foundational roadmap for the next generation of generative reinforcement learning and alignment.
authors: Nabuat Zaman Nahim, Fairoz Nower Khan, Peizhong Ju
bullets: Flow matching enables expressive, multimodal RL policies through deterministic probability transport and ODE-based sampling.
The survey covers offline continuous control, online fine-tuning, and foundation-model alignment.
It classifies methods by modeled target distributions, including policies, value critics, and transition dynamics.
It also categorizes how RL signals are integrated, such as energy-weighted regression, flow-based policy gradients, and group relative policy optimization.
Emerging topics include discrete and non-Euclidean action spaces, alongside comparisons with Gaussian and diffusion-based approaches.

figures.caption: Figure 3: A Taxonomy of Flow Matching in Reinforcement Learning. We categorize methods by

Figure 2: How flow matching is integrated with reinforcement learning. A common flow-policy backbone defines an expressive action generator through a learned velocity field and ODE sampler. In offline RL, the reinforcement signal typically enters at training time, most often by reweighting the flow-matching objective using value or energy estimates. In online RL, the signal enters through policy optimization using environment interaction, typically via stochasticized flows, pathwise gradients through the ODE, or group-based updates such as GRPO. Across both settings, additional stabilizers such as KL regularization, Wasserstein anchoring, clipping, and support constraints are often used.

Figure 1: Flow Matching in a nutshell. Top: flow matching learns approximately straight probability transport from a simple base distribution to the target data distribution. Bottom left: training is simulationfree: one samples (x0, x1, t), constructs an interpolation point xt, and regresses the learned velocity field vθ(xt, t) toward the target conditional velocity ut. For the common linear optimal-transport path, the target velocity is simply x1−x0. Bottom right: after training, new samples are generated by integrating the learned ODE from base noise to the target distribution.

papers.abstract: Feed-forward reconstruction recovers camera poses and dense geometry from image sets whose views are assumed to come from a single scene. In practice, uncurated image collections often contain views from disjoint scenes, and reconstructing these views jointly can corrupt camera poses and geometry. Existing pipelines typically resolve view associations in separate stages before final reconstruction, leaving view graph initialization and reconstruction inference only loosely coupled. We introduce Graph3R, which unifies view graph initialization with feed-forward reconstruction through a shared geometric representation. A lightweight verification head predicts pairwise covisibility from the multi-view features of $\pi^3$ to construct a view graph. This graph classifies the input views into scene groups. For each group, we mask the shared features before decoding camera poses and dense geometry. Reusing the multi-view features allows Graph3R to reconstruct disjoint scenes separately with a single backbone pass. Across three benchmarks, Graph3R improves average maximum recall at 100% precision by upto 8.99 percentage points over the baseline, while improving reconstruction quality on mixed-scene inputs. Regarding the multi-session mapping task, Graph3R improves cross-session localization and achieves competitive pose estimation accuracy, while delivering a runtime speedup of approximately $35.9\times$ over the baseline when reconstructing the query group. By integrating learned view association with geometric inference, our approach takes a step toward end-to-end reconstruction from uncurated image collections.
authors: Jingwen Yu, Hengli Wang, Jianhao Jiao, Zhonghang Liu, Ping Tan, Hong Zhang
bullets: Addresses pose and geometry corruption when uncurated image collections mix disjoint scenes.
Uses a lightweight covisibility-verification head over multi-view features to build a view graph and group images by scene.
Masks shared features per group, then decodes poses and dense geometry while reusing a single backbone pass.
Improves average maximum recall at 100% precision by up to 8.99 percentage points across three benchmarks and improves mixed-scene reconstruction quality.
For multi-session mapping, improves cross-session localization, maintains competitive pose accuracy, and reports an approximately 35.9× query-group reconstruction speedup over the baseline.

papers.abstract: Test-time-training (TTT) layers update fast-weight memory while processing an input sequence. A gradient-based update, however, does not by itself establish how the memory revises an existing association. We study the structure and empirical role of prediction-derived updates in released TTT implementations. For dot-product objectives, we characterize the absence of a prediction-error residual and establish conditions under which inner-loop ascent and descent are equivalent after reparameterization. For the LayerNorm-based squared-error objective used by TTT-Linear and TTT-MLP, we derive the inner gradient and identify a prediction-derived component that cancels at the released initialization in the zero-epsilon limit. We then measure the full normalized prediction's contribution on three trained checkpoints. Removing this contribution while retaining the LayerNorm Jacobian gives a mean gradient norm ratio of 0.25 to 0.32 across the models. On 100,303 tokens from War and Peace, the same intervention with local per-token norm matching raises perplexity by 2.8-2.9% on TTT-Linear-760M and 1.3B, whereas freezing all fast-weight updates raises it by factors of 4.2-4.5. Separate synthetic tests illustrate the dependence of plain delta-rule overwriting on step size. The results distinguish a prediction-derived update from its behavioral value and show why implementation analysis and live interventions are both needed to assess test-time memory.
authors: Yuhe Hu, Wen Jia Hu
bullets: Analyzes prediction-derived updates in released test-time-training (TTT) implementations.
For dot-product objectives, finds no explicit prediction-error residual and shows ascent/descent equivalence under reparameterization in certain conditions.
For LayerNorm-based TTT-Linear and TTT-MLP objectives, derives the inner gradient and identifies a component that cancels at initialization in the zero-epsilon limit.
Removing the component reduces gradient norms to 0.25–0.32 of the original and modestly increases perplexity, while freezing all fast-weight updates causes much larger degradation.
Synthetic tests show that plain delta-rule overwriting depends on step size.

papers.abstract: Mamba-based super-resolution models are efficient alternatives to Transformer-based restoration backbones, but their low-bit post-training quantization remains challenging because selective scan, Mamba's input-dependent state-space operator, induces different activation ranges across spatial tokens. Thus, a single layer-wise clipping range poorly matches all tokens. We propose Token-Group Quantization, a hardware-friendly activation PTQ framework that statically approximates a hardware-unfriendly post-scan grouping oracle, where tokens with similar preferred clipping ranges are assigned to the same group. To avoid runtime post-scan grouping in static low-bit inference, a lightweight predictor infers the groups from pre-scan features available before the quantized scan path. During calibration, we form pseudo-labels by clustering post-scan activation descriptors that capture similar rounding--clipping behavior. At inference, the frozen predictor maps pre-scan features to groups and selects entries from offline-calibrated group-wise clipping-bound tables, without runtime statistics collection, dynamic clipping updates, or post-scan group assignment. To address low-bit restoration degradation, we further introduce a Frequency-Preserving Refinement (FPR) objective for clipping-bound calibration. FPR aligns Fourier amplitude and phase between full-precision teacher and quantized student outputs to preserve high-frequency structures. Across PTQ protocols, bit-widths, backbones, and tasks, our method consistently outperforms prior Mamba and SR PTQ baselines, transfers to Transformer SR and Vision Mamba classification, composes with rotation-based quantization, and achieves 2.23x speedup on Jetson Orin Nano over FP16. Code is available here.
authors: Jinwoo Chung, Jangho Kim
bullets: Mamba’s selective scan creates token-dependent activation ranges, making one layer-wise clipping range ineffective.
A lightweight pre-scan predictor assigns tokens to groups using offline-calibrated, group-wise clipping bounds—without runtime statistics or post-scan grouping.
Pseudo-labels come from clustering post-scan activation descriptors with similar clipping and rounding behavior.
Frequency-Preserving Refinement aligns teacher and quantized outputs in Fourier amplitude and phase to retain high-frequency details.
The method reportedly improves over prior PTQ baselines across settings, transfers beyond Mamba SR, and reaches 2.23× FP16 speed on Jetson Orin Nano.

papers.abstract: Current ASR models perform well on general benchmarks but still struggle with acoustically ambiguous words. Visual context can aid recognition in screen-based scenarios, yet existing benchmarks provide limited insight into the benefits of different types of visual evidence. To address this gap, we introduce ScreenASR-Bench , a tiered benchmark with three progressively challenging levels: Explicit Textual Evidence (ETE), based on direct on-screen text; Explicit Visual Evidence (EVE), using visible content rather than on-screen text; and Implicit Semantic Evidence (ISE), requiring scene-level inference. Extensive experiments on ASR models, Large Audio-Language Models (LALMs) and Omni models show that incorporating visual context substantially improves recall over the audio-only setting across all three model families. The gains are largest for ETE and smallest for ISE, indicating that models leverage direct visual evidence more effectively than indirect semantic cues. To facilitate future research on visually grounded speech recognition, we publicly release ScreenASR-Bench.
authors: Mingwei Fu, Zheshu Song, Zhikai Zhou, Shen Huang, Shidong Shang, Mengxiao Zhu
bullets: Targets acoustically ambiguous words in screen-based ASR scenarios.
Introduces three tiers: Explicit Textual Evidence, Explicit Visual Evidence, and Implicit Semantic Evidence.
Tests ASR, Large Audio-Language, and Omni models with visual context.
Visual input improves recall across all model families, with the largest gains for direct on-screen text and the smallest for scene-level inference.
The benchmark is publicly released to support research on visually grounded speech recognition.

papers.abstract: Head-mounted body and bimanual motion capture supports self-avatars, teleoperation, and embodied demonstrations. However, a single egocentric camera is vulnerable to a limited field of view, scale ambiguity, and hand-object occlusion. We present EgoWholeView, a wearable capture system of six synchronized wide-angle RGB cameras with a role-specialized pipeline. The outward views localize the rig in a world frame, while an overlapping downward pair independently predicts SMPL-X body and MANO hand parameters. Both predictors are adapted to egocentric fisheye data. To combine the two, reliability cues measured from the predictions themselves weight the fusion of body and hand joint rotations, while shape is aggregated across views and frames. The pair's baseline fixes metric scale, and triangulation recovers root translation. Relative to monocular prediction, fusion reduces PA-MPJPE by 3.7% for the body and 11.2% for the hands, and temporal refinement lowers angular-acceleration magnitude by 32.2% and 31.0%, respectively. On our six-camera recording, the pipeline produces body and hand states in a shared world frame using benchmark-fitted gates without retuning, and temporal refinement lowers hand acceleration magnitude by 41.08%. Using only RGB cameras and no third-person view, EgoWholeView offers a low-cost, portable route to egocentric interaction data.
authors: Yaoqing Hu, Xuguo He, Daohan Cui, Yukun Shi, Kai Chen
bullets: Addresses egocentric capture challenges including limited field of view, scale ambiguity, and hand–object occlusion.
Uses outward cameras for world-frame localization and a downward overlapping pair for SMPL-X body and MANO hand estimation.
Fuses body and hand rotations using prediction-derived reliability cues, aggregates shape across views and time, and recovers translation through calibrated stereo triangulation.
Compared with monocular prediction, fusion reduces PA-MPJPE by 3.7% for the body and 11.2% for the hands.
Temporal refinement reduces angular-acceleration magnitude by 32.2% for the body and 31.0% for the hands, with 41.08% hand reduction on the authors’ recording.

papers.abstract: Deep-search agents are commonly trained by distilling tool-use trajectories from stronger teacher models. However, structurally complex questions may remain relatively easy for teachers familiar with key entities in the underlying entity graph, resulting in lower search demand and weaker supervision. We refer to this teacher-specific variation in question difficulty as teacher-relative difficulty and investigate entity familiarity as an early predictor. We first introduce Evidence-Verified Entity Familiarity (EVF), which estimates familiarity by verifying a teacher-generated factual brief against online evidence. Across multiple teachers, EVF is significantly correlated with teacher-relative difficulty with AUCs of 0.60--0.70. However, its high cost makes it impractical for constructing entity graphs at scale. To address this limitation, we propose Self-Reported Entity Familiarity (SEF), a lightweight gating signal that directly asks a teacher whether it is familiar with an entity before admitting that entity into the graph. Across multiple teachers, trajectories from SEF-gated synthesis exhibit greater observed search demand and yield higher downstream student accuracy than those from ungated synthesis. Because familiarity is teacher specific, we further study cross-teacher reuse. We screen graphs collected for other teachers using Kimi-K3's SEF judgments and use the retained graphs to produce 5,411 additional trajectories. Combined with 2,200 trajectories from newly constructed, SEF-gated graphs, these data improve Qwen3.8-27B's accuracy from 44.10% to 66.41% on a BrowseComp subset, and achieving state-of-the-art performance among models of comparable size on BrowseComp, SEAL-0, HLE-text, and xbench. Overall, SEF provides a low-cost way to synthesize more informative supervision for deep-search distillation.
authors: Yifei Liu, Zhixiang Liang, Wentao Tan, Yicheng Wang, Jiaqi Wang, Nan Duan, Qiong Cao
bullets: Teacher familiarity can make complex questions easier for the teacher, reducing search demand and weakening training signals.
Evidence-Verified Entity Familiarity (EVF) predicts teacher-relative difficulty, but its online verification cost limits scalability.
SEF cheaply asks teachers about entity familiarity before including entities in search graphs.
SEF-gated trajectories show greater observed search demand and improve downstream student accuracy.
Combining newly collected and cross-teacher-reused data raises Qwen3.8-27B accuracy on a BrowseComp subset from 44.10% to 66.41%.

papers.abstract: World-action models should preserve the intended manipulation across equivalent descriptions of a spatial goal. We evaluate this consistency in 864 rollouts from three models across four RoboLab scenes, holding initial states and task goals fixed. Describing relations through the reference object rather than the object-to-move lowers the rate of reaching a stable placement by 12.2 percentage points on average. The effect of instruction rephrasing varies across spatial relations, so aggregate scores can hide sensitivity to wording. Standalone tests of the policies' language understanding identify relation reversals and show that adding images can disrupt otherwise correct text-only interpretations. Rollout analysis also distinguishes spatial placement from instruction following: moving the wrong object can satisfy the requested relation, and rates of stable placement fall from 43.2% at any time to 21.8% at episode end. These findings motivate a more thorough evaluation of world-action models' steerability, language understanding, and grounding. Evaluations should test consistency across equivalent instructions, verify that the intended object moved, and check whether the requested arrangement persists to the end of the rollout.
authors: Ali-Adeeb Abbas, Esmaeil Seraj, Behrad Toghi, Taskin Padir
bullets: Evaluates instruction consistency across 864 rollouts, three models, and four RoboLab scenes with fixed initial states and goals.

Rollout analysis separates spatial placement from instruction following: the wrong object may be moved, and end-of-episode stability is lower than transient success.
Findings call for evaluations that test equivalent instructions, verify object identity, and assess whether arrangements persist to episode end.

papers.abstract: LLM agents increasingly control robots using VLA policies, perception models, and procedural knowledge. These modules are difficult to reuse because their interfaces, embodiment assumptions, and conditions of use differ, and their benefits on physical tasks remain unclear. We package them as embodied skills that extend agent skills with explicit embodiment assumptions and conditions of use, building 250 action, perception, and experience skills from 1,052 resources. On this basis we introduce EmbodiedSkillBench, which runs an agent in a closed observation-action loop and records success, actions, tokens, and wall-clock time. It supports three modes: native control, skill-only execution, and Agent-Directed Reuse (ADR), a mode we propose in which the agent keeps its native controls and decides for each skill whether to invoke, modify, or ignore it. Across four agents on 100 perturbed LIBERO-Pro tasks, we find that skills help an agent only as far as they exceed what it can already do. Skill-only execution lifts GPT-5.6-Sol from 11% to 63% and Kimi-K3 and Claude-Opus-5 by about 20 points, while cutting their token usage by 58% to 85%. Yet all four agents then end up between 61% and 64%, and GPT-6-Astra falls from 92% under native control to 61%. This suggests that as agents grow stronger, the role of embodied skills shifts from supplying missing capability to reducing cost: GPT-6-Astra already solves most tasks through native control, so restricting it to skills removes more than it adds. Under ADR, which lets it keep native control and call skills selectively, GPT-6-Astra recovers to 85%, within 7 points of native control, while using 14.1% fewer tokens and 11.9% less time. With Jev as a skill choosing motion directions and gripper actions, it reaches 81% with 50% fewer tokens and 57% less time. The code is available at https://github.com/HanZhi306/EmbodiedSkill-Bench.
authors: Zhi Han, Zihan Guo, Chenxi Zeng, Zicai Cui, Yue Xin, Ming Zhou, Dongzhan Zhou, Weinan Zhang, Yang Li
bullets: Benchmarks embodied skills—action, perception, and experience modules—with explicit embodiment assumptions and usage conditions.

ADR lets the strongest agent retain native control while selectively using skills, recovering 85% success with 14.1% fewer tokens and 11.9% less time.
The benchmark includes 250 skills built from 1,052 resources and measures success, actions, token usage, and wall-clock time.

papers.abstract: Morphogenesis is driven by the interplay of genetic regulation and tissue mechanics. In vivo video data is limited, particularly under genetic mutations and environmental perturbations, making generalization beyond the most representative conditions in the dataset challenging. However, at tissue scales, the dynamics of Drosophila can be described as a continuum flow, motivating the usage of representations learned across other physical systems as priors for developmental dynamics. We investigate finetuning Walrus, a Continuum Dynamics Foundation Model pretrained across a broad set of simulated continuous systems, on tissue velocity fields from only 12 wild-type Drosophila blastoderm videos. We evaluate autoregressive prediction both in-distribution and zero-shot under unseen temperature and genetic perturbations. Zero-shot refers to evaluation on perturbation conditions never seen during wild-type finetuning, without any additional training. In-distribution, a Fourier Neural Operator model trained from scratch achieves best performance on VRMSE. However, Walrus (CRPS) is the strongest model under the most severe distribution shift of unseen samples of mutated embryos and temperature conditions. Interestingly, predictions capture the shape of the mean surface tissue velocity trajectory and its separation between 17{\deg}C and 27{\deg}C, including the timing of the peak at Germ Band Extension onset, a biologically meaningful milestone of embryo development. Our results provide preliminary support that representations learned from different dynamical systems can transfer to experimental morphogenesis in developmental regimes, provided they admit a continuum description. More broadly, our results motivate further study of physics foundation models as a new complementary tool for the simulation of morphogenesis in low-data regimes.
authors: Louisa Cornelis, Haewon Jeong, Irina Espejo, Payel Mukhopadhyay
bullets: Uses only 12 wild-type blastoderm videos to fine-tune Walrus on tissue velocity fields.
Evaluates autoregressive prediction both in-distribution and zero-shot on unseen temperature and genetic perturbations.
A Fourier Neural Operator trained from scratch performs best in-distribution on VRMSE.
Walrus achieves the strongest CRPS performance under the most severe shifts involving mutated embryos and temperature conditions.
Predictions recover biologically meaningful temperature-dependent trajectories, including peak timing at Germ Band Extension onset.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of the Walrus finetuning workflow and zero-shot experiments. The finetuned model is evaluated on zero-shot prediction on unseen deviations of wild-type development (right): first on temperatures 17 and 27 ◦C (top) and second on three genotype variations (differing in dorsal contraction (DC), ventral furrow (VF), and germ band extension (GBE) modules) (bottom).

Figure 4: Root-mean-square (RMS) surface velocity trajectories across thermal regimes. papers.abstract: Text-to-image models have made remarkable progress in visual fidelity and instruction following, yet complex compositional generation remains challenging. Existing agentic approaches address this limitation through iterative generation and editing, adapting their actions based on interaction history. However, they typically fix the continuation state (i.e., the image from which refinement proceeds) to the latest image. Since iterative editing is not necessarily monotonic, the agent may continue refining from the latest image even when it has already degraded. In this work, we introduce GenRevisit, an agentic framework that extends action selection to joint continuation-state and action selection. The agent can not only use interaction history to adjust editing instructions but also select an image candidate to edit, jointly deciding where to continue from and how to refine. We train GenRevisit with SFT followed by agentic reinforcement learning. To address the coarse credit assignment of final outcome reward in GRPO, which assigns the same trajectory-level advantage to all actions, we further propose Normalized Action Credit Assignment (NACA) to redistribute positive advantage according to each action's contribution to reducing the remaining objective. On GenEval2, GenRevisit achieves GM scores of 84.3 and 74.4 with Qwen-Image-2512 and Z-Image-Turbo, surpassing the strongest baselines using the same generators by 12.7 and 10.9 points respectively. GenRevisit achieves state-of-the-art performance on GenEval, GenEval++, and GenEval2 among baselines.
authors: Zixu Wang, Xiaoran Zhao, Yahui Liu, Feng-ao Wang, Junhao Xiao, You Shu, Bing Liu, Yiting Liu, Songlei Jian, Zhiliang Tian, Dongsheng Li
bullets: Addresses degradation caused by always refining the latest image in iterative editing.
Jointly selects a continuation image from interaction history and the next editing action.
Uses supervised fine-tuning followed by agentic reinforcement learning.
Introduces Normalized Action Credit Assignment (NACA) to assign credit based on each action’s contribution.
Achieves state-of-the-art results among baselines on GenEval, GenEval++, and GenEval2; on GenEval2, it improves GM scores by 12.7 and 10.9 points with two generators.

papers.abstract: Time series (TS) anomaly detection (AD) lacks a universal detector, with the best choice determined by the series rather than by the algorithm. Existing methods therefore either select one detector for each series or average a pool of them. However, both assume that no label ever arrives, while a deployed monitor does receive them, since an operator confirms the alarms it raises. In this paper, we propose ONESHOT, which uses a single confirmed anomaly to weight the pool rather than to choose one detector from it. Specifically, we score each detector on the confirmed anomaly, and those scores become the weights of a soft mixture over the whole pool. We show that a single confirmed anomaly is enough to come close to the best detector for the series. Across 152 univariate and 73 multivariate series, ONESHOT outperforms the strongest single detector, averaging the whole pool, and even picking the best detector on the confirmed event. Code is available at: https://github.com/seunghan96/one_shot.
authors: Seunghan Lee, Jun Seo, Jaehoon Lee, Junhyeok Kang, Sangjun Han, Sungdong Yoo, Minjae Kim, Tae Yoon Lim, Dongwan Kang, Hwanil Choi, Soonyoung Lee, Wonbin Ahn

Code is publicly available on GitHub.

papers.abstract: Spatial transcriptomics jointly captures molecular state, tissue morphology, and spatial organization, yet spatial-domain methods are typically compared only at late training checkpoints, obscuring differences in convergence efficiency. We introduce MP-MNCA, a morphology-prior masked neighbor cross-attention framework that preserves the full 3,000 dimensional highly-variable-gene representation while selectively routing molecular information across spatial neighbors, with histological similarity incorporated as a continuous attention prior under a self-supervised masked neighbor-contrastive objective. Across 12 heterogeneous human dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) sections, MP-MNCA is evaluated against established spatial-domain baselines using both convergence trajectories and epoch-wise spatial-domain visualizations. Our results show that MP-MNCA (i) reaches coherent spatial-domain structure in substantially fewer training epochs, as reflected quantitatively by convergence curves and qualitatively by progressive spatial grids, and (ii) maintains strong clustering quality, achieving a mean peak refined ARI of 0.546 versus 0.549 for the strongest baseline (STAIG), while attaining the highest mean refined NMI of 0.657 versus 0.640. Moreover, MP-MNCA outperforms STAIG on 7 of 12 sections in ARI and 11 of 12 in NMI, demonstrating faster convergence without sacrificing spatial-domain quality.
authors: Sidharthan Sivacoumar Chitra, Sanjeev Manivannan
bullets: Addresses the limited comparison of spatial-domain methods during training by evaluating convergence trajectories and epoch-wise spatial visualizations.

Uses histological similarity as a continuous attention prior within a self-supervised masked neighbor-contrastive objective.
Across 12 human DLPFC sections, it reaches coherent spatial structure in fewer epochs than established baselines.
Its mean peak refined ARI is 0.546 versus 0.549 for STAIG, while mean refined NMI is higher at 0.657 versus 0.640; it outperforms STAIG on 7/12 sections in ARI and 11/12 in NMI.

(C) Two independently masked molecular views are optimized with a self-supervised neighbor-contrastive loss without pseudo-labels or layer supervision. (D) Inference uses unmasked expression followed by PCA-assisted tied-GMM clustering and spatial refinement.

papers.title: MP-MNCA: Morphology-Prior Masked Neighbor Cross-Attention for Efficient Spatial Domain Identification

papers.abstract: Autoencoders are the core component of latent video generative models, compressing high-dimensional videos into compact latent spaces for downstream generation. However, existing video autoencoders are primarily optimized for pixel-level reconstruction, providing limited supervision for learning structured latent representations. We argue that videos should not be treated merely as signals to be reconstructed, but rather as 2D projections of dynamic 3D worlds that exhibit explicit and well-structured geometric properties. Building on this insight, we propose \textbf{V}ideo \textbf{G}eometry \textbf{G}rounded \textbf{A}utoencoder (\textbf{VGGA}), a geometry-aware video autoencoder that explicitly incorporates geometric constraints into the reconstruction process. Specifically, VGGA grounds the learned representations along three complementary geometric dimensions: \emph{Structural Depth}, \emph{Motion Correspondence}, and \emph{Projective Warping}. These objectives are unified within a Video Geometry Decoder, which employs a shared spatio-temporal upsampling trunk to jointly optimize geometric learning and RGB reconstruction. Through these geometry-grounded objectives, VGGA encourages the latent representations to capture the underlying 3D structure and motion of dynamic scenes. VGGA consistently improves video generation across both geometry-centric and human-motion domains, reducing gFVD by 28.1\% on RealEstate10K and 37.7\% on Taichi-HD. Notably, these substantial generation improvements are achieved while maintaining comparable reconstruction quality, demonstrating that geometry-grounded representation learning yields a more effective latent space for video generation.
authors: Chaofan Gan, Yian Zhao, Shijie Li, Tieyuan Chen, Zicheng Zhao, Mehrtash Harandi, Weiyao Lin
bullets: Motivation: Pixel-reconstruction objectives provide limited supervision for learning structured video latents.
Method: Incorporates Structural Depth, Motion Correspondence, and Projective Warping constraints through a shared Video Geometry Decoder.
Core idea: Treats videos as 2D projections of dynamic 3D worlds, encouraging latents to capture scene structure and motion.
Results: Reduces gFVD by 28.1% on RealEstate10K and 37.7% on Taichi-HD across geometry-centric and human-motion domains.
Scope: Gains are reported while maintaining comparable reconstruction quality.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of VGGA. Our VGGA introduces a Video Geometry Decoder to ground compressed video latents in dynamic 3D geometry. A shared Spatio-Temporal Upsampling Trunk (ST UP Trunk) lifts the latent to a frame-aligned decoded representation, on which RGB reconstruction jointly acts with three geometry grounding tasks, including structural depth, motion correspondence, and projective warping.

papers.abstract: Latte art is a complex task requiring dexterity and precision, making it a challenging and commercially relevant task. A one-shot learning system is employed in which a single barista demonstration is segmented into five functionally distinct phases, each encoded as an independent Cartesian Dynamic Movement Primitive (CDMP) with its own parameters. Against a single-CDMP baseline, per-phase encoding reduces transition endpoint error by 3.2-4.5 times and art-stroke shape error by 2.7 times, reproducing jug tilt to below 1 degree RMS in the pouring phases. The learnt pour scales from a 280mL to a 400mL cup through a single spatial offset and a scaled recipe, with no re-demonstration. The phase-based CDMP approach generalises beyond latte art to any demonstration task whose phases have distinct spatial or temporal requirements whilst demonstrating the ability to adapt reproductions to suit different task requirements.

papers.abstract: Open-vocabulary 3D Gaussian segmentation typically binds semantic features to the per-Gaussian state via per-scene gradient training (1-4 h) or the more recent closed-form distillation. Both commit each primitive to a single feature; therefore, boundary Gaussians spanning multiple 2D instances are forced into a hard decision that degrades retrieval accuracy and yields unstable mask boundaries at render time. We present DIGS, a training-free framework with two stages, class-agnostic mapping and multi-modal encoding, that decouples instance discovery from linguistic naming. At the Gaussian level, our distribution-informed representation maintains an explicit top-$M$ label distribution per primitive, updated by a tempered Dirichlet rule; preservation of multi-peaked label distributions at boundary primitives allows a late-argmax renderer to recover clean instance boundaries. A bidirectional state machine aggregates these distributions into a persistent class-agnostic instance ontology. The instance-level encoding stage then fuses the CLIP visual embedding of each instance's isolated 3D footprint with the CLIP-text embedding of an LLM-generated attribute description, disambiguating visually similar instances. On a single A100, DIGS completes mapping and instance encoding on LERF-OVS in 1.0-3.2 min per scene, depending on whether LLM fusion is enabled, and serves native 3D queries in 5.4 ms. It reaches 71.95% mean mIoU on LERF-OVS, outperforming both the training-free SFS and training-based LaGa baselines. DIGS also achieves the highest mean mIoU on LERF-Mask and 3D-OVS and surpasses Gaga and ObjectGS on Replica under their respective evaluation protocols. Code is available at https://github.com/ZephyrZos/DIGS.
authors: Zhifan Zeng, Wenbo Xiao, Arcot Sowmya, Changming Sun

papers.abstract: Situated 3D Question Answering requires models to interpret a 3D scene relative to an agent's pose. Existing methods commonly convey that pose through a natural-language situation description, which may be unavailable or costly to obtain in real-world deployments. While some methods additionally incorporate numerical pose, we find that randomly shuffling the agent pose causes little performance degradation, indicating limited functional dependence on the numerical pose. To address this gap, we introduce EgoAlign, a simple 3D language model that represents a scene in an agent-centric coordinate frame, together with a dedicated egocentric alignment stage comprising four complementary tasks: object category recognition, egocentric direction prediction, metric distance estimation, and spatial relation prediction. This stage teaches the model to consistently interpret scene geometry relative to the agent's pose before task-specific fine-tuning. EgoAlign achieves the strongest performance on SQA3D, Real-3DQA, and MSQA among compared methods while remaining highly efficient. More importantly, removing textual situation descriptions yields comparable or better downstream performance, whereas shuffling EgoAlign's numerical pose causes substantial degradation. These results show that EgoAlign establishes agent-centric spatial context directly from numerical pose without requiring textual situation descriptions.

bullets: Addresses the cost and unavailability of natural-language situation descriptions in real-world 3D deployments.

Removing textual situation descriptions preserves or improves performance, while shuffling numerical pose substantially degrades it.
Demonstrates that numerical pose can directly establish the agent-centric context needed for situated 3D understanding.

papers.abstract: Recent multimodal large language models (MLLMs) achieve strong results on video question answering, yet often fail to recover the temporal structure that makes a video coherent. They may merge neighboring events, miss single-event progression, or infer implausible relations across events. We study structured temporal understanding as the ability to recover event structure from visual evidence, including event boundaries, single-event progression, and multi-event relations. We argue that this gap arises from a mismatch between current post-training objectives and temporal reasoning, where caption-style supervision allows models to rely on language shortcuts rather than visual temporal grounding. To address this, we propose EventLens, a vision-centric reinforcement learning framework that learns video understanding through event-structure recovery. Instead of reconstructing captions, EventLens trains models to recover temporal structure under controlled perturbations, such as altered temporal granularity, reversed progression, and shuffled event order. We instantiate this framework with a three-level temporal ontology and derive three verifiable task families: event segmentation, progression discrimination, and multi-event relation reasoning. These tasks admit deterministic rewards, enabling task-specialized GRPO training without human preference labels or learned reward models. We further introduce multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MT-OPD) to consolidate specialized policies into a unified model. Experiments on Qwen3-VL backbones show consistent improvements on temporal grounding and event-sensitive reasoning benchmarks, while preserving general video-QA performance. Learning curves further demonstrate that EventLens achieves comparable downstream transfer with significantly reduced training cost compared to direct mixed RL optimization.
authors: Guowen Zhang, Boshen Xu, Zihao Yue, Ziheng Wang, Xiaokun Liu, Xin Tao, Wenyu Qin, Pengfei Wan, Qin Jin
bullets: Targets temporal-structure failures such as merged events, missed progression, and implausible cross-event relations.
Uses vision-centric reinforcement learning with controlled temporal perturbations, including altered granularity, reversed progression, and shuffled event order.
Trains three task families: event segmentation, progression discrimination, and multi-event relation reasoning, with deterministic rewards and task-specialized GRPO.
Uses multi-teacher on-policy distillation to combine specialized policies into one unified model.
Reports improved temporal grounding and event-sensitive reasoning while preserving general video-QA performance and reducing training cost versus direct mixed RL.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of EventLens. EventLens adopts a two-stage training pipeline for event-structure reinforcement learning. In Stage II, MT-OPD routes each student trajectory to the corresponding teacher and distills dense token-level teacher logits into one deployable student. The teacher is selected by recovery family, so each student trajectory is supervised by the teacher trained with the matching verifier.

papers.abstract: This manuscript presents DeepThink, a knowledge-addressable framework for recurrent language modeling. A Knowledge Bank stores typed Knowledge Units, a Knowledge Activator selects units from the current execution state, Knowledge Assembly produces an executable configuration, and a Shared Thinking Operator updates that state. An output stage then organizes generation. This organization exposes knowledge capacity, activation width, and recurrent depth as separate design variables, supporting both complete parameter packages and fine-grained expert or low-rank modules. We formalize the interfaces and their execution semantics, including state-dependent selection, parameter-space assembly, and thinking followed by generation. For compatible templates and complete runtime-state configurations, we establish an exact Fixed-Schedule Realization of an existing fixed-depth model. Exact shared-base reparameterization and pretrained output-tail reuse provide complementary initialization constructions. Together, these results define a route from pretrained models to dynamically selected and assembled recurrent computation. A synthesis of conditional computation, recurrent models, modular parameters, and knowledge interfaces positions DeepThink within the research landscape and identifies the design questions arising from their integration.
authors: Weiguo Chen
bullets: Separates knowledge capacity, activation width, and recurrent depth as independent design variables.
Uses a Knowledge Bank, state-dependent Knowledge Activator, Knowledge Assembly, Shared Thinking Operator, and output stage.
Supports complete parameter packages as well as fine-grained expert and low-rank modules.
Proves exact realization of compatible fixed-depth models under fixed schedules and gives reparameterization and output-tail reuse initialization schemes.
Frames open design questions at the intersection of conditional computation, recurrence, modular parameters, and knowledge interfaces.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) can answer many geometric and physical reasoning questions correctly, yet still behave inconsistently in interaction, for example, abandoning a correct answer when confronted with a confident but incorrect user assertion. Standard single-turn accuracy cannot distinguish such capitulations from beneficial corrections because it scores each response in isolation. We introduce GRIP, a controlled benchmark with 34 procedurally generated reasoning domains, 100,000 images, and 600,000 questions spanning geometric, spatial, visual, and physical reasoning. Each scene is generated by deterministic code, and every answer is derived directly from the underlying scene state, providing exact ground truth without human annotation. On GRIP, we propose Dual-Loop Evaluation. A closed loop probes each image with a five-step compositional question ladder to localize where reasoning fails. An open loop then re-elicits the model's answer under controlled challenges, including peer-model responses and unsupported user assertions. Because ground truth is known exactly, answer changes can be signed as corrections (wrong-to-right) or capitulations (right-to-wrong), separating two failure modes: rule absence and rule fragility. The dataset is available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/bilaljawaid980/GRIP-Benchmark, with further details at https://bilaljawaid980.github.io/grip-benchmark/.
authors: Bilal Jawaid, Hamza Hanif, Muhammad Maaz Uddin, Anas Zafar, Inad Alqurashi, Aizan Zafar, Osama Farooqui, Sheheryar Khan, Ferhat Sadak, Shaina Raza, Rizwan Qureshi
bullets: Introduces a procedurally generated benchmark covering 34 geometric, spatial, visual, and physical reasoning domains.
Uses 100,000 images and 600,000 questions with exact ground truth derived from deterministic scene states.
Applies Dual-Loop Evaluation: compositional question ladders diagnose reasoning failures, while controlled challenges test answer stability.
Separates rule absence from rule fragility by labeling answer changes as corrections or capitulations.
Provides the benchmark publicly; the abstract does not report model-specific performance results or limitations.

figures.caption: Figure 2: The GRIP evaluation pipeline. Scenes and answers are produced together by a single seeded generator, so no annotation step exists. The harness issues one request per item and stores every response verbatim before any parsing, enabling scoring to be re-run without re-querying any model. Scoring is a three-stage offline pass: a deterministic typed comparator; a semantic validator applied only to items the comparator rejected; and a human audit of the validator’s decisions. Because stage 2 only processes rejected items, it can promote an item from incorrect to correct but never demote it.

papers.abstract: We propose the task of Interactive 4D Volumetric Liquid Forecasting: predicting the spatiotemporal evolution of a future dense 3D liquid velocity field conditioned on how a solid object moves through it. This task provides an upstream physical forecasting primitive for systems that need to reason about motion-conditioned liquid response, including robotic liquid manipulation, digital twins, and rigid-fluid video generation. Existing works have made efforts in predicting flow around static or prescribed solid geometries and synthesizing visually plausible fluid motion. Yet these approaches provide limited coverage for interactive liquid dynamics, as they are not capable of forecasting how a moving solid induces a future full-domain liquid response. In this forecasting scenario, the hydrodynamic effect is condensed near an evolving liquid-solid interface, but the prediction target is a global spatiotemporal rollout. To address this challenge, we propose a two-level recurrent forecasting framework, TIDE/TIDES: TIDE isolates localized interface-driven forecasting, while TIDES adds transport-aware coupling and explicit stabilization to reduce accumulated rollout error. Across adapted neighboring baselines, controlled component ablations, motion/size OOD tests, and long-horizon evaluation, TIDES achieves the best forecasting performance and the ablations identify localized interaction, transport coupling, and stabilization as the key contributors. Together, our task formulation, benchmark, and TIDE/TIDES study establish a controlled foundation for moving-solid-conditioned dense liquid forecasting. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/jongwonryu/TIDE-TIDES.
authors: Jongwon Ryu, Sunjae Yoon, Junyeong Kim
bullets: Targets global, spatiotemporal liquid-flow rollouts conditioned on solid-object motion, addressing a gap in interactive fluid forecasting.
TIDE models localized, interface-driven effects, while TIDES adds transport-aware coupling and explicit stabilization for rollout robustness.
Experiments include baseline comparisons, component ablations, motion/size out-of-distribution tests, and long-horizon evaluation.
TIDES achieves the best reported forecasting performance, with localized interaction, transport coupling, and stabilization identified as key contributors.
The task, benchmark, and code provide a foundation for robotics, digital twins, and rigid-fluid video generation.

papers.abstract: Interactive world models must capture how multiple participants jointly change a shared environment while observing different parts of it. Competitive games make this challenge concrete: players cooperate and compete, while fog of war, team vision and camera placement determine what each can see. Modeling these interactions requires data that connect individual observations and actions to shared state and events. We introduce the Esports World Model Dataset (EWM), a collection of human gameplay spanning StarCraft II, Dota 2 and Counter-Strike 2, with 3,053 games and maps and approximately 4,880 player-view hours, including estimated hours for the ongoing CS2 extension. It includes 4,628 completed StarCraft II views, all ten perspectives for 303 Dota 2 matches, and up to ten views per round in CS2. Across these views, replay-clock alignment connects rendered video with game-native actions, structured state and events from the same match. The three games expose complementary observation conditions: private fog of war, shared team vision and first-person viewpoints. In StarCraft II, player-specific entity records further distinguish live observations from remembered snapshots and link co-observed entities across opposing views. Together with temporal alignment, these records allow researchers to distinguish legitimate information differences from disagreement about shared state. By connecting human decisions, shared dynamics and player-specific information, EWM supports research toward jointly controlled multiplayer world models and interactive environments populated by teammates and opponents learned from human play.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in 3D reconstruction enable the extraction of temporally consistent 3D motion from RGB observations; however, current Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models still predominantly rely on 2D image-text priors. Therefore, they do not accurately represent the fundamental dynamics of the 3D world associated with physical actions. This over-reliance on static 2D visual cues limits the capacity of VLA models in achieving robust robot manipulation. To address these limitations, we introduce FlowVLA, a reconstruction-guided, pluggable 3D flow learning framework aimed at empowering VLA models with an inherent understanding of action-relevant dynamics. Instead of requiring explicit 3D sensor inputs or altering the inference-time architecture, our method is designed to utilize temporally aligned 3D flow only during training. This allows the model to learn the dynamic evolution of the physical scene while preserving the computational efficiency of conventional 2D VLA backbones. To bridge scene-level dynamics with robotic manipulation, we propose a modular 3D flow learning framework with dual-level flow supervision. Specifically, point-level flow guides the model to forecast the future displacements of task-critical 3D points, while TCP-level flow aggregates these motions to align with the robot's TCP trajectories. This dual-level flow supervision encourages the model to focus on semantically meaningful dynamic regions, effectively coupling scene-level motion with precise control signals. Extensive evaluations across simulation and real-world experiments demonstrate that FlowVLA consistently improves manipulation performance, zero-shot robustness, and optimizes data efficiency. FlowVLA adds only lightweight auxiliary heads during training and discards them at inference. Therefore, FlowVLA introduces no additional 3D sensor inputs, architectural modifications, or inference-time computation.

papers.abstract: Although post-training significantly enhances model performance, the use of massive undisclosed data raises concerns about benchmark contamination and copyright infringement. This drives growing interest in training data detection for post-trained models. Existing evaluations for training data detection often leverage benchmarks constructed post hoc, which can introduce distribution shifts. Alternatively, controlled evaluations rely on small-scale training setups that diverge from realistic post-training settings. As a result, their reported performance may not faithfully reflect the effectiveness of detection methods in real-world scenarios. To this end, we introduce \textsc{\method}, a reliable benchmark designed to evaluate detection methods in realistic, large-scale post-training settings. Built on a multi-stage pipeline, \method\space encompasses stage-specific models throughout the post-training lifecycle, spanning SFT, DPO, and RL. To perform a reliable evaluation, we construct model-specific evaluation sets across four diverse tasks, featuring distribution-matched members and non-members with verifiable membership labels. Our results reveal that even the best-performing method achieves an average AUC of only 0.529 on our benchmark, which approaches random-guessing level (0.5). Furthermore, our analysis suggests that evaluation protocols can significantly affect measured detection performance. These findings highlight the significant potential for developing effective, practical, and robust detection methods under realistic scenarios.
authors: Hengxiang Zhang, Junxian Liu, Hongxin Wei
bullets: Existing evaluations may misrepresent detection performance because of post hoc distribution shifts or small-scale training setups.

papers.abstract: Dynamic sparse training (DST) aims to reduce training costs while maintaining accuracy. Existing DST methods mask out parameters but keep matrix dimensions unchanged. Training speedups therefore depend on specialized support, such as sparse kernels. We introduce BARTER, a structured DST framework that reduces training cost using standard dense kernels by keeping training tensors physically compact while dynamically reallocating capacity across layers. Unlike existing works that require computing gradients for all parameters, BARTER instead uses statistics collected only from active units during ordinary backpropagation to prune and clone attention heads and feed-forward channels under separate fixed global budgets. At each topology update, it resizes the affected parameter tensors and remaps their optimizer states, so subsequent training steps operate directly on the compact model. Training and fine-tuning experiments with Transformer-based vision models on two image classification benchmarks at densities from $0.1$ to $0.7$ show competitive Top-1 accuracy relative to full-tensor DST baselines. On an NVIDIA L40, BARTER achieves speedups of up to $6.29\times$ in measured training segments and reduces peak allocated GPU memory by up to $81.3\%$ relative to these implementations. An iPhone 13 Pro Max training benchmark additionally shows a $2.78\times$ speedup over the full-tensor DST baseline.
authors: Yueyuan Sui, Payal Mohapatra, Qi Zhu, Stephen Xia
bullets: Targets the overhead of conventional DST methods that mask parameters but retain full matrix dimensions.
Uses active-unit statistics from ordinary backpropagation to prune and clone attention heads and feed-forward channels under separate global budgets.
Resizes affected tensors and remaps optimizer states after topology updates, so later steps run on the compact model.
Across Transformer vision models and image-classification benchmarks, it maintains competitive Top-1 accuracy at densities of 0.1–0.7.
Reports up to 6.29× training speedup and 81.3% lower peak allocated GPU memory on an NVIDIA L40; an iPhone benchmark reaches 2.78× speedup.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of our approach, BARTER. Budgeted initialization produces a compact model with fewer attention heads and FFN channels while retaining all Transformer layers. During training, statistics from active units guide capacity reallocation across layers. For each unit type, the method selects the eligible receiving layer with the highest growth priority, prunes eligible units with the lowest pruning scores outside that layer, and adds the same number of units by cloning parents with the highest growth scores within it. These updates preserve the global head and FFN budgets separately. Each clone copies its parent’s input parameters, while the parent’s output weights are split between the parent and clone. The affected parameter tensors and optimizer states are resized accordingly, and training continues on the compact model with standard dense kernels.

papers.selection_reason: Structured dynamic sparse training that physically compacts model tensors to reduce training compute and memory, relevant to efficient AI.
papers.title: BARTER: Compact Dynamic Sparse Training with Standard Dense Kernels
papers.tldr: BARTER makes dynamic sparse training faster and more memory-efficient by physically compacting Transformer tensors while dynamically reallocating sparse capacity using standard dense kernels.

papers.abstract: We present Unravel, a training-free framework that turns a single image into an interactive 3D scene, where every object is an independent and movable asset. Existing generators either produce one entangled geometry in which no object can be moved, or predict all objects in one feed-forward pass, where a wrong guess cannot be detected or repaired. Unravel instead takes a different approach: it first takes the scene apart, and then puts it back together. Starting from the input image, an agentic harness that iteratively peels the image layer by layer, and adopts point cloud as major modality for spatial relationship recovery. Specifically, a vision-language model plans which objects are fully visible, an image editor removes them and restores the occluded regions. Every edit is verified before being incorporated into the reconstruction. This process gradually turns occluded parts of the scene into direct observation, allowing objects to be reconstructed when they are best exposed rather than hallucinated from the original image alone. The scene is then rebuilt in reverse removal order, so that the supporting objects are naturally placed before the objects they support. Since a single-view image only reveals part of an object, we treat the observed points as a lower bound on its size: an asset may grow to cover its points, but can not shrink away from them. Finally, we physically settle the reconstructed scene to remove floating objects and interpenetrations, followed by an agentic audit that corrects remaining placement errors. Extensive experiments on diverse indoor scenes show that Unravel recovers more objects, places them more faithfully, and produces scenes that are more physically-plausible than existing methods.
authors: Hui Shan, Keyang Luo, Binjia Zhou, Ming Li, Kai Li, Xin Wang, Zhenyang Li, Zesong Yang, Weikai Chen, Runze Zhang, Xin Wang, Yanwei Fu, Zhen Chen, Xiangru Huang
bullets: Targets the limitations of entangled scene generators and one-shot object prediction, where objects cannot be moved or errors are difficult to fix.
Uses a training-free agentic process: a vision-language model selects visible objects, an image editor removes them and restores occlusions, and each edit is verified.
Represents spatial relationships with point clouds and reconstructs objects in reverse removal order to preserve support relationships.
Treats visible points as a minimum object extent, then physically settles the scene and audits placements to reduce floating and intersecting objects.
Experiments on diverse indoor scenes report more complete object recovery, more faithful placement, and greater physical plausibility than existing methods.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of Unravel. (a) Agentic layer-wise deconstruction. An agentic loop plans, edits, and verifies removals until the room is empty. Independent 3D assets are extracted before removal. Per-round reconstructions are aligned and fused into an instance-labeled point cloud. (b) Support-aware scene recomposition. Assets return to the environment shell in reverse removal order. One-sided extent constraints guide registration to their point clusters. Physical settling and a final audit refine placement.

Figure 4: Layer-wise deconstruction and point cloud fusion. The upper block shows planner outputs, removal targets, and edited images across six rounds. Red boxes mark targets, and green boxes mark protected objects. The lower block shows aligned per-round reconstructions and cumulative fused point clouds, starting with the original-image reconstruction. Fusion retains removed-object geometry and adds surfaces reconstructed from edited images.

Figure 2: Single-image interactive scene reconstruction. One-shot generators such as MIDI (Huang et al., 2025) and SAM 3D (Chen et al., 2026) recover independent assets, but under occlusion they misplace objects and distort the geometry of hidden parts (red highlights). Unravel recovers occluded objects with faithful geometry and placement (green highlights).

Figure 5: Qualitative comparison of single-image scene reconstruction. Each input is followed by two views of each reconstructed scene. The two Astra variants separate direct scene generation from placement with shared assets. GPT-6 Astra (Ultra) + TRELLIS2 receives the same generated meshes and corresponding 2D instance masks used by Unravel. Red boxes highlight placement discrepancies in the agentic results.

Figure 8: Complete deconstruction traces on four scenes. For each scene we show the input image, three views rendered from the reconstructed scene, the edited image of every round, and the assets extracted in each round. Red boxes mark the removal targets of each round, and duplicate assets are omitted for space.

Figure 9: Deconstruction traces on four more scenes. For each scene we show the input image, three views rendered from the reconstructed scene, and the edited image of every round. Red boxes mark the removal targets of each round.
Figure 10: Additional reconstructions on eight further scenes. For each scene we show the input image and three views rendered from the reconstructed scene.
Figure 11: Reconstructions from real photographs. Each row shows an input image on the left and three views of the reconstructed scene on the right.

Figure 6: Generated assets with and without deconstruction. Each column shows one object. The top row is generated from the mask in the input view, and the bottom row from the mask captured at the best-observed moment. Incomplete masks lead to broken geometry, spurious parts, and hallucinated contents, while Unravel keeps the assets faithful.

Figure 7: Comparison with Seeing Through Clutter. The input image is on the left, followed by two views of Seeing Through Clutter in the middle and two views of Unravel on the right. Seeing Through Clutter is shown as colored geometry and Unravel as a textured scene.

Table 1: Ablation on five scenes. Area ratio and UCR summarize coverage for objects removed after the first round, using Unravel’s masks and point clusters as references. UCR (under-coverage rate) denotes the percentage with coverage below 70%. VLM and Human report mean fidelity scores (1 to 10) over all 160 objects. Point counts are scene averages.

papers.selection_reason: Presents a framework for recovering interactive 3D scenes from a single image using point clouds and VLMs. This falls squarely under 3D perception and scene reconstruction.
papers.title: Unravel: Recovering an Interactive 3D Scene from a Single Image
papers.tldr: Unravel reconstructs a single image into an editable, physically plausible 3D scene by iteratively separating, repairing, and reassembling objects.

papers.abstract: Serving stacks for large language models manage context through four recurring mechanisms: incremental edits to a growing context, branching and snapshotting for tree search, identification of reusable prefixes for KV-cache reuse, and encoding of repeated segments. Each mechanism is served today by a different specialist structure. We show that all four reduce to a single persistent weight-balanced rope whose every node carries a polynomial hash of its subtree over a Mersenne prime, so that the structure supports logarithmic edits and logarithmic verified content-identity queries at the same time. We validate each mechanism with pre-registered, replicated experiments, then compare against a deployed specialist per mechanism: the Ropey editing library, a faithful PagedAttention copy-on-write block table, and the vendored SGLang radix matcher. On workloads that interleave edits with identity queries, Hashrope is net-superior to Ropey by a factor that grows without bound (369.7x at one million characters). Against the radix matcher on a live vLLM stack serving Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct-1M on four A100 GPUs, Hashrope identifies a one-million-token shared prefix exactly and 1.20x faster, at a context length the dense engine cannot even prefill.
authors: Muntaser Syed (Florida Institute of Technology), Ameerah Alsulami (Florida Institute of Technology), Marius Silaghi (Florida Institute of Technology)
bullets: Targets incremental editing, branching/snapshotting, KV-cache prefix reuse, and repeated-segment encoding.
Stores a polynomial subtree hash over a Mersenne prime in every rope node to support content-identity checks.
Uses persistent structure sharing for logarithmic updates and queries across evolving contexts.
Validated through pre-registered, replicated experiments against Ropey, a PagedAttention copy-on-write table, and SGLang’s radix matcher.
Reported 369.7× advantage over Ropey at one million characters and 1.20× faster exact detection of a one-million-token shared prefix than the radix matcher in a live vLLM setup.

papers.selection_reason: Persistent data structure for LLM context and KV-cache management; directly relevant to efficient serving and long-context handling.
papers.title: Hashrope: A Persistent Data Structure for Mechanisms of LLM Context Management
papers.tldr: Hashrope unifies four LLM context-management mechanisms in one persistent, hash-augmented weight-balanced rope with logarithmic edits and verified identity queries.

papers.abstract: SLAM (Simultaneous Localization and Mapping) is a core technology in autonomous systems that enables them to estimate their own position and build a map of unknown environments simultaneously. SLAM systems in dynamic environments are of great practical importance. However, existing dynamic SLAM approaches still have several limitations like over-removal and high computational costs. To address these limitations, we propose a real-time RGB Dynamic SLAM framework that precisely removes moving objects at the pixel level without relying on predefined labels or segmentation models. Our system combines pixel motion predicted by ego-motion using DUSt3R with point tracking from All-Tracker, removing only actually moving pixels by analyzing discrepancies between the two motion sources. Unlike object-level masking methods, our approach eliminates only currently moving regions, allowing temporarily static parts to be utilized for tracking. Operating at approximately 10 FPS, the system achieves real-time performance on standard 30 FPS video streams by subsampling every 3 frames. Relying solely on RGB inputs, this significantly improves upon state-of-the-art dense dynamic SLAM approaches (0.5-3 FPS), presenting a highly practical solution.
authors: Yewon Kim, Paul Hongsuck Seo, Sang Chul Ahn
bullets: Addresses over-removal and high computational cost in existing dynamic SLAM systems.
Compares ego-motion-based pixel motion from DUSt3R with All-Tracker point tracking to identify moving pixels without labels or segmentation models.
Uses pixel-wise rather than object-level masking, retaining temporarily static regions for tracking.
Runs at approximately 10 FPS on subsampled 30 FPS video, using RGB input alone.
The reported scope is dense dynamic SLAM, with performance positioned against methods running at 0.5–3 FPS.

papers.abstract: Learned world models for autonomous driving operate in unconstrained latent spaces, yet the physical systems they represent are governed by strict non-holonomic constraints: ground vehicles cannot realize instantaneous pure lateral motion. We study long-horizon latent rollout modeling for autonomous driving and ask whether rollout quality can be improved by assigning a motion-aware geometry to latent transitions, rather than by redesigning the predictor architecture. Starting from an unconstrained latent rollout baseline, we introduce Directional Pullback Regularization (DPR), a training time method that defines a kinematics-aware anisotropic Riemannian metric in decoded state space and pulls it back through the decoder Jacobian to the latent manifold. The resulting latent-space metric assigns higher cost to latent directions that decode to lateral vehicle motion, while preserving the original encoder-dynamics-decoder backbone. This yields a clean three-way comparison among an Unconstrained Latent Rollout model (ULR), an Euclidean Pullback Regularization ablation (EPR), and the full directional method (DPR). We evaluate all models on open-loop ego-motion rollout over a common 10-second test horizon, using training rollout lengths of 1, 3, 5, and 10 steps. Across all four training regimes, DPR achieves lower 10-second final displacement error than both ULR and EPR. The strongest relative accuracy gain appears for models trained with 3-step rollout supervision, where DPR reduces the 10-second final displacement error by approximately 44 percent relative to ULR. The strongest overall control-relevant tradeoff is obtained for longer rollout-trained models, especially at 10 steps, where DPR simultaneously improves displacement error, lateral motion consistency, and forward motion preservation relative to both ULR and EPR.
authors: Shatadal Mishra, Ahmadreza Moradipari, Nejib Ammar
bullets: Addresses non-holonomic motion constraints in unconstrained latent rollouts without changing the predictor architecture.
Pulls a kinematics-aware anisotropic metric from decoded state space back onto the latent manifold.
Compared with unconstrained and Euclidean pullback baselines across 1-, 3-, 5-, and 10-step training rollouts.
DPR achieves lower 10-second final displacement error in every training regime; the largest relative gain is about 44% after 3-step training.
With longer rollout supervision, especially 10 steps, DPR also improves lateral-motion consistency and forward-motion preservation.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Method overview of the proposed directional pullback regularization (DPR) framework. The upper row shows the baseline open-loop rollout pipeline: the motion history, current state, and road curvature are assembled into the observation ot, encoded into the latent state zt, propagated by the latent dynamics model to produce ∆zt, decoded back to state space, converted to the predicted increment ∆̂xt, and integrated to obtain the next rollout state. The lower row shows the regularization path. The latent update and decoder Jacobian define the decoded tangent ut = Jψ(zt)∆zt/∆t, which is evaluated under the kinematics-aware Riemannian metric Mβ(x̂t). Pulling this metric back through the decoder Jacobian yields the latent-space metric Gβ(zt), and the resulting metric loss is combined with the prediction loss to form the total training objective. The dashed arrow indicates the backpropagated training signal through which the pullback regularizer shapes latent transitions.

Fig. 3. Key 10-second results across training rollout lengths for the unconstrained baseline (ULR), the Euclidean pullback ablation (EPR), and the proposed directional pullback model (DPR). The panels show final displacement error, ground-truth-frame lateral error, and the fraction of rollout steps with forward velocity above 0.5m/s. DPR is the only variant that consistently improves 10-second final displacement error across all training rollout lengths, and in the longer-rollout regimes it also maintains or improves the forward-valid fraction while reducing lateral-motion error.

Fig. 2. Average displacement error over the evaluation horizon for the three compared models: the unconstrained baseline (ULR), the Euclidean pullback ablation (EPR), and the proposed directional pullback model (DPR). Each subplot corresponds to a different training rollout length U ∈ {1, 3, 5, 10}, and DPR is shown with the validation-selected directional weight β∗ for that training regime. Across all training rollout lengths, DPR reduces longhorizon displacement error relative to both ULR and EPR, with the strongest gains appearing for longer self-fed rollout training.
