papers.abstract: Omni-modal large language models (Omni-LLMs) extend LLMs to process heterogeneous modalities (e.g., vision, audio, and IMU signals) alongside language, enabling a broader range of multimodal tasks. Yet we find that these models often fail to express information from non-textual modalities even when they perceive it correctly. We term this disconnect knows-but-cannot-say. To investigate this phenomenon, we introduce Token-level Modality Alignment (TMA), which measures the alignment between individual modality representations and response representations. Our analysis shows that non-textual representations are less aligned with response tokens and receive less attention than textual representations, suggesting a potential explanation for uneven modality preferences. Motivated by these findings, we propose OmniCatalyst, a simple perceive $\rightarrow$ infer strategy that complements the original modality inputs with self-generated text, making non-textual knowledge more accessible. Across seven Omni-LLMs, OmniCatalyst consistently improves performance (+7.29%) and yields more balanced modality preferences, with further gains from diverse training strategies. Further analysis demonstrates that the knowledge extraction phases increase TMA, suggesting that improved alignment makes non-textual information more accessible during response generation. In summary, our findings uncover how Omni-LLMs can better express modality knowledge through language. Our code is available at https://github.com/naver-ai/OmniLLM.
authors: Na Min An, Taekyung Kim, Jaemyung Yu, Hyunjung Shim, Dongyoon Han
bullets: Identifies a “knows-but-cannot-say” gap between multimodal perception and language responses.
Introduces Token-level Modality Alignment (TMA) to measure alignment between modality representations and response tokens.
Finds that non-textual modalities receive less response-token alignment and attention than text.
OmniCatalyst uses a perceive → infer strategy to supplement original inputs with generated textual knowledge.
Across seven Omni-LLMs, it consistently improves performance by 7.29% and balances modality preferences; gains are linked to increased TMA.

figures.caption: Figure 3: TMA distributions and accessibility to the generation pathway. (a) Within samples, input modality (e.g., video and audio) tokens with higher TMA tend to receive higher attention weights from generated-token queries relatively, but exhibit low absolute TMA values. In contrast, text tokens yield higher attention weights and TMA values than non-text tokens, regardless of insertion position. (b) Across samples, text representations systematically exhibit higher TMA and attention than non-textual representations, revealing their greater accessibility to language-centric generation. Note that TMA measures not the amount of information, but its alignment with generation.

Figure 7: Probe of how Omni-LLM attention changes. The knowledge-extraction step in OMNI-CATALYST enables the model to “hear” better, which in turn affects the refined answering stage, showing more balanced “seeing” and “hearing.” Our TMA filter, applied on top of the raw attention weights on the original modalities, shows clearer visualizations of where the generated response aligns (compare (a) and (b)).
Figure 8: TMA and attention distribution for each modality. The knowledge extraction step of OMNI-CATALYST selectively shifts TMA and attention for the weaker modality (here, audio).

Figure 4: TMA reveals a gap between what Omni-LLMs know and what they can express. (a) Knowledge performance remains high regardless of the TMA of masked tokens, whereas answering performance is substantially lower and further degrades when higher-TMA tokens are masked. (b) Increasing the number of input modalities increases both the mean and variance of TMA, indicating more heterogeneous accessibility to response generation.
Figure 2: Comparison of modality alignment metrics. Unlike prior metrics, our TMA captures the token-level alignment distribution per sample.
Figure 5: Modality extension. OMNI-CATALYST is applicable to various modalities.
Figure 6: OMNI-CATALYST adaptability. Applying OMNICATALYST during both training and inference further improves Omni-LLM performance.

Figure 1: The “knows but cannot say” problem in Omni-LLMs. (a) Omni-LLM often embeds sufficient modality knowledge, yet it produces an incorrect answer when directly responding (left). By complementing the relatively weak modality, audio recovers the correct answer (right). (b) This phenomenon becomes more pronounced as the number of modalities increases.
Figure 9: Performance and preference relation. Reasoning performance correlates positively with modality preference balance.

Table 1: Comparison across different training-free methods. OMNI-CATALYST consistently outperforms corresponding baselines without an external reasoning model (ThinkOmni) and without an adaptive agentic framework (CoM).
Table 2: Comparison against SelfCoT. OMNI-CATALYST generally improves performance over the baselines across different audio types.

papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses multimodal LLMs (Omni-LLMs) and the issue of modality alignment (knows-but-cannot-say). Proposes TMA and OmniCatalyst, which are relevant to multimodal reasoning and instruction following.
papers.title: Omni-Modal LLMs Know More Than They Say
papers.tldr: Omni-LLMs may correctly perceive non-text inputs but fail to verbalize them; OmniCatalyst improves access to this knowledge by converting modality inputs into self-generated text.

papers.abstract: Puzzles offer a natural testbed for Large Language Models (LLMs) reasoning because they pose verifiable goals under partial information and require multi-step decisions to reach a solution. However, existing puzzle benchmarks typically focus on narrow environments with rigid mechanics and tightly constrained solution targets. To bridge this gap, we introduce the Active Probing Benchmark (APB), which generalizes puzzle-solving by casting concept identification as an interactive reasoning task that integrates specialized knowledge assessment into the puzzle setting. Specifically, APB evaluates whether models can acquire information via multi-turn active probing and inference to pinpoint 960 target concepts of specialized difficulty across eight diverse academic domains. Our evaluation reveals a counter-intuitive phenomenon: most open-source reasoning models significantly underperform their standard instruction counterparts. This finding suggests that in interactive settings, these models struggle to leverage procedural reasoning to reliably access and apply specialized domain knowledge. Beyond these empirical insights, APB provides a scalable pipeline for generating benchmarks that probe knowledge reasoning under interaction across diverse settings.
authors: Xin Cheng, Junming Yang, Ning Xu
bullets: Reframes puzzle solving as interactive concept identification under partial information and verifiable goals.
Evaluates multi-turn probing and inference over 960 specialized concepts across eight academic domains.
Finds that most open-source reasoning models underperform their standard instruction-tuned counterparts in this setting.
Suggests reasoning models struggle to use procedural reasoning to access and apply specialized knowledge interactively.
Provides a scalable pipeline for generating interactive knowledge-reasoning benchmarks.

(Middle) Multi turn active probing: the model under test iteratively asks multiple-choice queries Qt, receives feedback At from a knowledge oracle, and updates its hypotheses to reduce the candidate space until the target is identified or a turn budget is exhausted. (Right) Performance comparison: average success rates show that several open source “Thinking” models underperform their “No-Thinking” counterparts. Full results are reported in Table 2.

papers.abstract: Deploying LLM agents in non-stationary environments requires continually revising their instructions as the task drifts, yet rewriting after every reported mistake can turn noisy feedback into persistent errors. This raises an often-overlooked scheduling question in prompt adaptation: when should feedback trigger a lasting instruction update, and at what editor-call cost? Taking inspiration from proportional-integral-derivative (PID) control, we introduce a family of lightweight gates that react to the current error, accumulate evidence over time, and roll back deterioration after an edit. We benchmark these gates against both simple baselines and advanced prompt optimizers (TextGrad and GEPA), over a diverse suite of drifting tasks, LLM parameter sizes, feedback-noise levels, and random seeds. PID-gated continual prompt adaptation yields a more favorable Pareto trade-off between task performance (high accuracy, low error) and editor-call budget than the baselines considered, pointing to control-theoretic scheduling as a simple, general tool for robust prompt adaptation under unreliable feedback.
authors: Zhentao Xu
bullets: Addresses when feedback should trigger lasting prompt updates in drifting, non-stationary tasks.
Uses lightweight proportional, integral, and derivative signals to respond to current errors, accumulate evidence, and roll back harmful edits.
Benchmarks against simple baselines, TextGrad, and GEPA across drifting tasks, model sizes, noise levels, and random seeds.
Reports a more favorable performance–editor-call Pareto trade-off than the considered baselines.
Scope: focuses on scheduling prompt edits under unreliable feedback, not on eliminating feedback noise itself.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Cost–quality tradeoff across all three feedback-noise levels on Qwen3-14B (mean over 5 seeds). Marker face shade encodes noise: hollow η = 0, half-filled η = 0.1, solid η = 0.2. Lines connect the three noise points for each method. Points near the top-left (bottom-left for MAE/RMSE) indicate a better cost–quality trade-off. PID gates sit on a better frontier than TextGrad and GEPA at every noise level.

Figure 2: Cost-quality snapshot at η = 0.1 on Qwen3-14B (one marker per method, mean over 5 seeds). Higher accuracy and lower MAE/RMSE are better; fewer calls are cheaper. Points near the top-left (or bottom-left, for MAE/RMSE) indicate a better cost-quality trade-off.

Figure 1: The regulated textual feedback loop. Signals enter from outside: target yt from the left, input xt from above. The Sensor flips the label with probability η (labels are either categorical, as in Parity, or bucketed categorical, as in Guess number / moving target). The comparator produces the observed error et (binary for Parity, bucketed distance for numeric tasks); when the controller fires, editor g rewrites the prompt θ.
Table 3: Recurring symbols.

papers.tldr: PID-inspired gates make continual prompt adaptation more robust to noisy feedback while reducing unnecessary editor calls.

papers.abstract: An agent can retain successful trajectories without learning which part of an experience should repair a new discrepancy. We formulate passive imitation (PI) as an architectural loop that localizes a violated contract, extracts a local goal, proposes an effect-matched skill, tests a small patch, and retains evidence after full-task verification. We instantiate this loop as a deterministic symbolic controller and analyze its finite repair-query complexity under explicit identifiability and noninterference assumptions. Across ten simulated tool worlds, PI solves all 600 cold held-out composition tasks with three allowed small trials, compared with 6.17% for a whole-trajectory control, while an equally expressive compositional repair control matches PI. On an unseen tool revision, PI achieves 70.0% success versus 24.0% without small trials and 79.0% with self-trial enumeration; an exploratory 24-task adaptation stream subsequently raises first-submission success to 100%, supporting a limited correction-and-retention mechanism rather than a unique incentive advantage or general intelligence. The CPU-only implementation, integrity checks, and reproducible results are available at https://github.com/FriendOfYishan/PI.
authors: Kai Hu, Hua Huang
bullets: Frames imitation as a loop that localizes violated contracts, extracts local goals, proposes effect-matched skills, tests small patches, and retains evidence after full-task verification.
Implements the approach as a deterministic symbolic controller and analyzes finite repair-query complexity under identifiability and noninterference assumptions.
Solved all 600 cold held-out composition tasks with three small trials, while whole-trajectory control solved 6.17%; an equally expressive compositional repair control matched it.
On an unseen tool revision, success was 70.0% with small trials, versus 24.0% without them and 79.0% with self-trial enumeration.
Results support a limited correction-and-retention mechanism, not a unique incentive advantage or general intelligence.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Left: final success on previously unseen revision C after A/B acquisition, with persistent state frozen. The no-trial controller does not use K. Right: first-submission success after separate C acquisition tasks in the exploratory follow-up. Lines show means over ten worlds; PI and compositional repair overlap. Repeated evaluations use the same frozen final C tasks. Learning C changes the interpretation from unseen-revision transfer to retention within a learned revision.

Figure 1. The implemented passive-imitation loop. Structured feedback and public lineage identify the local scope; symbolic effect recognition supplies candidate skills. A local trial pass permits a tentative patch. Full-task acceptance contributes evidence for later proactive reuse. Candidate sources may include other executions or the controller’s own trials.

papers.selection_reason: Localized repair, test-time skill patching, and evidence retention fit adaptation and memory interests.
papers.title: Imitation Holds a Key to Evolution: Localized Repair and Verified Skill Acquisition for Adaptive Agents
papers.tldr: Passive imitation enables adaptive agents to repair localized failures and retain verified skills, achieving strong performance in simulated tool-composition tasks under stated assumptions.

papers.abstract: 3D instance segmentation requires representations that are both geometrically structured and semantically discriminative. Pure 3D encoders model spatial structure well but often lack strong appearance semantics, while directly lifting 2D priors into 3D by concatenation injects rich semantics without ensuring that they align well with the underlying 3D structure. In this paper, we address this problem by formulating 2D-to-3D semantic transfer as a \textbf{masked semantic reconstruction} task. Specifically, we mask a subset of background lifted 2D priors and train the 3D encoder to recover the missing semantic priors, providing explicit supervision for distilling rich 2D semantics into the 3D backbone. We further propose \textbf{geometry-modulated semantic injection}, which uses raw 3D geometry to modulate lifted 2D priors before sparse encoding, so that geometry explicitly controls semantic injection and alleviates the distribution gap between 2D semantic features and 3D geometric features. Experiments on two baseline frameworks demonstrate that the proposed method achieves state-of-the-art results in both full-data and few-shot settings on ScanNetV2 and ScanNet200. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/yharoldsu0627/Geometry_Guided_Semantic_Reconstruction
authors: Yuanhao Su, Shaofeng Zhang
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between geometrically strong 3D encoders and semantically rich but potentially misaligned lifted 2D features.
Masks background 2D semantic priors and trains the 3D encoder to reconstruct them, explicitly distilling 2D semantics.
Uses raw 3D geometry to modulate semantic features before sparse encoding, improving geometry–semantic alignment.
Achieves state-of-the-art results across two baseline frameworks in full-data and few-shot settings on ScanNetV2 and ScanNet200.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of the proposed framework. Multi-view DINO-X features are lifted to 3D points and processed by a sparse 3D encoder. During training, a subset of background superpoints is masked in the lifted 2D stream and reconstructed from geometry-modulated encoder features. The aggregated superpoint features are finally decoded into instance masks.

Figure 4: Qualitative comparison on the ScanNetV2 validation set. Our method yields cleaner instance boundaries and more complete instance separation in the highlighted regions, especially under occlusion and around thin or ambiguous structures.

Figure 1: Comparison of three paradigms for 3D instance segmentation with 2D priors. (a) Pure 3D encoding preserves geometry but lacks rich semantics. (b) Direct concatenation injects lifted 2D priors, yet the transfer remains passive. (c) Our method combines geometrymodulated semantic injection and masked semantic reconstruction to enforce explicit semantic transfer.

Figure 3: Efficiency of superpoint-level representation. Superpoint-level 2D priors reduce loading time from 263.3 ms to 0.4 ms and memory from 475.5 MB to 0.8 MB per scene, a 600× reduction compared to point-level priors.
Figure 6: Sensitivity analysis on ScanNetV2. Left: reconstruction weight λrec with r = 0.1. Right: masking ratio r with λrec = 1.0.
Figure 5: Efficiency comparison on ScanNetV2. Reconstruction adds no inference cost; modulation increases parameters and FLOPs, leading to modest latency increase.

Best and second-best are marked in bold and underline.

papers.abstract: Differentiable simulation enables efficient policy optimization through analytic gradients, yet safety is commonly incorporated as a weighted penalty, requiring manual tuning of the trade-off between task performance and constraint satisfaction. We instead formulate obstacle avoidance as an explicit constraint and train quadrotor policies using primal--dual gradient descent--ascent through a differentiable simulator. We introduce two key components to enable effective constrained training. First, we propose a bounded clearance-based constraint function that provides informative gradients around the safety boundary while preventing large violations from destabilizing primal--dual optimization. Second, we introduce log-mean-exp (LME) aggregation to smoothly emphasize critical per-step safety violations across a trajectory and training batch within a single constraint governed by one dual variable. Together, these components enable the desired safety level to be specified directly while balancing constraint satisfaction and task completion. We theoretically prove that the proposed optimization with differentiable simulation converges to feasible policy under mild assumptions. Experiments demonstrate improved safety--performance trade-offs over fixed-penalty and existing policy-learning baselines, as well as generalization to denser out-of-distribution environments. Finally, the learned policy transfers zero-shot to Gazebo/PX4 and a physical quadrotor without additional fine-tuning.
authors: Yan Rui Tan, Praveen Krishnapur, Zeyu Feng, Han Bao, Yew-Soon Ong, Fan Shi
bullets: Models obstacle avoidance as an explicit constraint rather than a weighted penalty.
Uses a bounded clearance constraint for stable, informative safety gradients.
Applies log-mean-exp aggregation to focus one dual constraint on critical trajectory and batch violations.
Experiments show improved safety–performance trade-offs, denser-environment generalization, and zero-shot transfer to Gazebo/PX4 and a physical quadrotor.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: A. Comparison of our proposed bounded constraint cost with a conventional unbounded signed-distance-based cost proposed in [4]. B. Our permutation-invariant policy architecture for mapping vehicle states and variable obstacle configurations to control actions.

Fig. 4: A. Representative trajectories of the baseline policies and our proposed method. B. Representative OOD trajectories comparing our method with B2N(BPTT). B2N fails near obstacle-adjacent goals (green/red) and in the narrow passage (blue), while ours succeeds in all cases. C. Consistent trajectories across differentiable simulation, Gazebo, and real-world deployment demonstrate zero-shot sim-to-real transfer. D. Real-world quadrotor trajectory over a 12-leg continuous circuit, with waypoints distributed on a 3 m-radius circle centered on the obstacle configuration.

Fig. 5: A. λ evolution with our proposed bounded constraint cost. B. λ evolution with the unbounded constraint cost used by B2N [4] with β2 parameter sweep. C. Analysis of constraint aggregation. LME closely matches the exact maximum in separating colliding from collision-free trajectories and remains consistent across rollout horizons, unlike cumulative aggregation.

Fig. 1: Zero-shot deployment of our primal–dual policy on a physical quadrotor. Due to practical limitations in reproducing the exact obstacle geometry, the physical obstacles serve as proxies for the virtual cylindrical obstacles perceived by the policy. The inset shows the corresponding trajectory in the policy’s perceived environment.
Fig. 3: Training convergence of B2N (BPTT) and B2N (PPO), with B2N (BPTT) converging to a better-performing policy.

papers.abstract: Hour-long videos, streaming feeds, and movie-length content are pushing vision-language models (VLMs) past their breaking point -- the standard recipe of encoding each frame into visual tokens yields sequences that grow linearly with video length, causing prohibitive memory consumption and inference latency. Existing approaches, such as token reduction and keyframe selection, shorten the token sequence but leave the O(n) scaling intact, failing to resolve the fundamental bottleneck. We propose FramePack-U, a strikingly simple, training-free frame packing framework that compresses arbitrarily long videos into a fixed size visual representation at constant memory cost. FramePack-U requires no fine-tuning or architectural modification -- it plugs directly into off-the-shelf VLMs at inference time. Inspired by FramePack from the generation literature, we propose a content-aware compression strategy for visual understanding under a fixed token budget. Specifically, FramePack-U (1) scores each frame by its semantic similarity to the text prompt and ranks frames in a diversity-driven manner, and (2) packs the selected frames at varying resolutions into a fixed-length context window. This concentrates the memory budget on frames that are both instruction-relevant and visually diverse. While FramePack-U can in theory pack arbitrarily many frames into the fixed budget, we identify an empirical instantiation that generalizes robustly across settings. Extensive experiments on LongVideoBench, MLVU, and Video-MME show that FramePack-U consistently outperforms full-resolution baselines and prior token reduction and keyframe selection methods across diverse model families, parameter scales, and frame budgets. Notably, on Qwen3.5-35B-A3B with a 128-frame budget, FramePack-U yields gains of +12.9\%, +10.6\%, and +9.7\% over the official model on the three benchmarks, respectively.
authors: Shuo Gao, Chenhao Zheng, Zhongzheng Ren
bullets: Addresses the linear memory and latency growth caused by encoding every video frame as visual tokens.
Uses a training-free, inference-only strategy that ranks frames by prompt relevance and diversity, then packs them at varying resolutions.
Works with off-the-shelf VLMs without fine-tuning or architectural changes.
Experiments on LongVideoBench, MLVU, and Video-MME report consistent improvements over full-resolution, token-reduction, and keyframe-selection baselines.
On Qwen3.5-35B-A3B with a 128-frame budget, gains are 12.9%, 10.6%, and 9.7% on the three benchmarks, respectively.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of FramePack-U. Given a long video and a text query, FramePack-U selects query-relevant and visually diverse frames, then packs them with heterogeneous resolutions under a fixed memory budget. Higher-priority frames are kept at higher resolution, while lower-priority frames are progressively compressed. The packed frames are fed into the VLM for answer generation.

Figure 5: Memory overhead of FramePack-U on Qwen3.5-9B. We evaluate the preprocess, VLM inference and overall memory overhead of both vanilla models and FramePack-U on LongVideoBench. Results of different video duration tiers are reported. More results can be found at Table 5.

Figure 6: Latency evaluation of FramePack-U on Qwen3.5-9B. We evaluate the preprocess, VLM inference and overall latency of both vanilla models and FramePack-U on LongVideoBench. Results of different video duration groups are reported. More results can be found at Table 6.

Figure 3: Qualitative comparison. Relevance-only sampling selects frames based only on queryframe similarity and often produces redundant frames, while uniform sampling preserves temporal coverage but may miss question-relevant evidence. Our strategy combines prompt relevance and visual diversity, allowing it to select frames that better cover the video while retaining key evidence for answering the question. Red boxes highlight frames that contain important visual evidence.

Figure 4: t-SNE visualization. We compare the feature distributions of frames selected by FramePack-U (n = 848, scheme d1f16d2f320d4f512) against Uniform Sampling (n = 128, full resolution) across three distinct queries. Circles mark representative frames identified by each strategy, whose corresponding visual frames are displayed in the callout thumbnails. Points are colored according to their downsampling tiers (d = 1, 2, 4).

Figure 2: Illustration of packing schemes under the same memory budget. Using a 4-frame memory budget as an example, red, yellow, and blue denote frames with downsampling factors d = 1, 2, 4, respectively. Different resolution combinations can use the same memory while packing different numbers of frames.

Table 1: Main results on Qwen3.6-27B (left) and Qwen3.5-35B-A3B (right) across different memory budgets. Subscripts indicate the gap to Vanilla at the same budget; bold and underline denote the best and second-best results among open-weight models, respectively. We find that: (1) FramePack-U outperforms all baselines substantially, (2) our top results are competitive with, and often surpasses, those of much larger proprietary VLMs.

Table 5: Memory overhead (GiB) across different model sizes. We evaluate the memory overhead of three inference stages on different video duration tiers of LongVideoBench. Preprocess stage represents the introduced CLIP-based frame ranking process. VLM Inference stage denotes the inference process of the off-the-shelf VLM. Overall results reflect the peak memory used during the end-to-end process.

Table 6: Inference latency (s) across different model sizes. We evaluate the memory overhead of three inference stages on different video duration tiers of LongVideoBench. Preprocess stage represents the introduced CLIP-based frame ranking process. VLM Inference stage denotes the inference process of the off-the-shelf VLM. Overall results reflect the total latency during the end-toend process. Noticeably, we restrict the vanilla Qwen3.6-27B model to sample a maximum of 224 frames for the memory constraint, leading to a significantly lower I/O latency.
Table 11: Performance comparison with similar token compression or key frame selection methods. ∆ denotes the performance gap with the vanilla model. Bold indicates the best result in each column.

Table 4: Ablation on prompt relevance and frame diversity using Qwen3.6-27B. − Relevance removes prompt relevance and uses a prompt-agnostic diversity-based ordering, while − Diversity ranks frames only by query-frame similarity. FramePack-U combines prompt relevance and visual diversity. Values in parentheses denote the difference between each ablated variant and FramePack-U. See Appendix B for ablations on 128- and 256-frame budgets.

Table 9: Additional ablation study on model size. We report the performance gain of FramePack-U over the vanilla baseline across different Qwen-series base models and memory budgets. Larger models generally obtain larger gains, suggesting that stronger VLMs can better exploit the packed multi-resolution visual evidence.

Table 10: Fine-grained results on LongVideoBench and Video-MME. For LongVideoBench, we report the overall accuracy and the results on the 15s / 60s / 600s / 3600s subsets. For Video-MME, we report the overall accuracy and the short / medium / long subsets. Only the default diversity-aware packing strategy of FramePack-U is reported, with the vanilla baseline included as reference. ∆ denotes the difference between FramePack-U and Vanilla under the same setting. Bold indicates the best result in each column or sub-column.

We report results under 128-, 256-, and 512-frame memory budgets, where each budget denotes the cost equivalent to processing the corresponding number of full-resolution frames. papers.title: Elephant in the Fridge: Constant-Memory Frame Packing for Long Video Understanding
papers.tldr: FramePack-U enables VLMs to understand arbitrarily long videos with constant memory by packing prompt-relevant, diverse frames into a fixed-size visual representation.

papers.abstract: Test-Time Reinforcement Learning (TTRL) enables large language models to adapt directly on unlabeled test problems by constructing pseudo-labels from multiple sampled responses. However, existing TTRL methods typically apply the same expensive sampling and optimization procedure to all test problems, despite substantial differences in their training utility. In this paper, we study whether such problems can be identified before costly test-time training, without access to ground-truth answers. We uncover a stable relationship between internal response representations and problem-level empirical accuracy. Specifically, we define COS as the cosine similarity between a model's response representation and a correctness-related direction constructed from an independent question-answering dataset. COS consistently correlates with problem solvability across different models, datasets, and experimental settings, and we further provide a theoretical analysis explaining this relationship. Building on this finding, we propose SelectTTRL, a representation-guided data selection method that ranks test problems using COS and applies TTRL only to a selected percentile interval. SelectTTRL leaves the standard TTRL pipeline unchanged for the selected problems, while avoiding unnecessary multi-response sampling and reinforcement learning updates on the remaining ones. Experiments across multiple reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that SelectTTRL substantially reduces test-time computation while maintaining or improving the performance of standard TTRL. Code is available at https://github.com/heyiliyi/SelectTTRL-public.
authors: Yi Li, Linan Yue, Weibo Gao
bullets: TTRL can waste costly sampling and optimization on problems with limited training utility.
A cosine similarity score (COS) between response representations and a correctness-related direction estimates problem solvability without ground-truth answers.
COS is reported to correlate consistently with problem-level empirical accuracy across models, datasets, and settings.
SelectTTRL ranks problems by COS and applies standard TTRL only within a selected percentile interval.
Experiments on multiple reasoning benchmarks show substantially lower test-time computation with maintained or improved TTRL performance.

papers.abstract: Generalist visual-navigation policies tell a robot which direction to go but not how far. A separate lifting step is needed at deployment to convert their unitless trajectory into a metric path that a controller can track; existing scalar lifters apply uniform scaling that misses per-waypoint corrections, while in-policy approaches that inject monocular depth into the policy inherit the prediction errors of the depth model near obstacles and at close range. We present PathLift, a per-waypoint depth-conditioned adapter that lifts a pre-trained visual-navigation policy by consuming an explicit, sensor-grade depth source (RGB-D, stereo, or projected LiDAR) and fitting per-waypoint magnitude and lateral residuals to a canonicalized prior. PathLift consistently improves closed-loop navigation across diverse visual-navigation policies in simulation and on a real wheeled robot under both stereo and LiDAR depth. By turning the policy's unitless intent into a depth-feasible metric path in a single feed-forward pass, the adapter lifts real-world success without test-time optimization.
authors: Gwanjun Shin, Hyeongseok Suh, Hongmo Jung, Jongwoo Lim
bullets: Addresses the need to determine how far a robot should travel, not just which direction.
Uses a depth-conditioned adapter that predicts per-waypoint magnitude and lateral residuals relative to a canonicalized prior.
Supports RGB-D, stereo, and projected LiDAR depth while avoiding monocular-depth errors near obstacles and at close range.
Improves closed-loop navigation across diverse policies in simulation and on a real wheeled robot with stereo and LiDAR.
Runs in a single feed-forward pass without test-time optimization.

papers.abstract: Detailed video captioning has become an essential semantic interface for multi-modal understanding and generation. While existing methods mainly target short videos, extending them to long videos remains challenging, primarily due to limited context windows of current video understanding models. A naive solution is to adopt segment-wise captioning followed by concatenation, yet this paradigm often suffers from inconsistent subject references and fragmented long-range narratives. To mitigate these issues, we introduce PIGEONS, an incremental long-video captioning model built upon a Persistent Identity Gallery and an Evolving Overarching Narrative Summary. Before caption generation, PIGEONS scans the entire video to construct an identity gallery that captures key subjects along with their visual references, thereby providing a stable referential anchor. The model then performs clip-by-clip captioning conditioned on the persistent gallery and an evolving overarching narrative summary, which compactly maintains and updates essential long-range contextual information after each captioning step. To enable these capabilities, we develop a three-stage training strategy that integrates supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning. Extensive experiments demonstrate that PIGEONS markedly improves long-video captioning performance, achieving superior accuracy, completeness, and subject referential consistency over existing methods, while maintaining competitive performance on short-video captioning.
authors: Xinlong Chen, Weihong Lin, Yuanxing Zhang, Xinyu Liu, Yue Ding, Bozhou Li, Bohan Zeng, Yang Shi, Qiang Liu, Pengfei Wan, Liang Wang, Tieniu Tan
bullets: Addresses fragmented narratives and inconsistent subject references caused by segment-wise captioning and limited context windows.
Builds a Persistent Identity Gallery from the full video to maintain stable visual references for key subjects.
Generates captions clip by clip while updating an Evolving Overarching Narrative Summary for long-range context.
Uses a three-stage training strategy combining supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning.
Experiments report improved long-video captioning accuracy, completeness, and referential consistency, with competitive short-video performance.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable success across a wide range of language tasks. At their core, autoregressive LLMs are conditional probability models that learn to approximate the next-token distribution given the preceding context. Despite this probabilistic nature, the stochastic dynamics of autoregressive decoding have rarely been investigated from a rigorous probabilistic perspective. In this work, we define the per-step prediction error as the difference between the sampled token indicator and the model's conditional predictive distribution, and prove that the cumulative error process is a martingale with respect to the decoding filtration, implying that its conditional first-order moment is identically zero. Beyond this first-order property, we derive a closed-form expression for the second-order behavior of the martingale sequence: its predictable quadratic variation reduces to $\sum_t\left(1-p(y_t\mid y_{<t})\right)$, computable from realized token probabilities alone. This identity establishes a direct theoretical connection between sequence fluctuations and predictive uncertainty during autoregressive decoding. White-box experiments on Llama-3.x and Qwen2.5 families (1B to 72B parameters) verify that the empirically measured second-order moments closely match the theoretical predictions derived from our martingale analysis. These results provide a probabilistic framework for analyzing autoregressive LLM decoding, reveal intrinsic probabilistic fingerprints of different language models, and establish a rigorous mathematical foundation for LLM-generated text detection and uncertainty quantification.
authors: Xiahui Zhu, Zhenyi Qi, Wanwei Liu, Haoang Chi, Yang Tan, Xinyu Sun, Ji Wang
bullets: Defines per-step prediction error as the sampled-token indicator minus the model’s conditional token distribution.
Proves that cumulative prediction error is a martingale with zero conditional first-order moment.
Derives predictable quadratic variation as \(\sum_t(1-p(y_t\mid y_{<t}))\), computable from realized token probabilities.
Experiments on Llama-3.x and Qwen2.5 models from 1B to 72B parameters closely match the theoretical second-order predictions.
Provides a framework for studying model-specific probabilistic fingerprints, text detection, and uncertainty quantification.

figures.caption: Figure 1: A stochastic process perspective of autoregressive generation. Existing analyses focus on local token-level uncertainty, while the evolution of prediction errors across the entire generation sequence remains unclear. Our perspective models autoregressive decoding as a stochastic process, where cumulative prediction errors form a martingale and exhibit predictable second-order dynamics without requiring full prediction distributions.

Figure 4: Verification of the second-order martingale identity on Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct. The empirical second-order moment closely matches the theoretical prediction throughout the generation sequence.

Figure 3: Empirical verification of the first-order martingale property on Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct. The sampled vocabulary dimensions exhibit random fluctuations, while their averaged cumulative error remains around the theoretical expectation E[Mt] = 0.
Figure 2: The case where Ey≤t [∥Mt∥22] isn’t maximized when ∑t i=1 Var(wi) is maximized.

papers.selection_reason: Provides a martingale-based probabilistic analysis of autoregressive LLM decoding, relevant to LLM uncertainty quantification and generated-text detection.
papers.title: Autoregressive Decoding as a Martingale: Characterizing the Stochastic Dynamics of LLM Generation
papers.tldr: Autoregressive LLM decoding can be modeled as a martingale whose predictable fluctuations are determined by the probabilities assigned to the generated tokens.

papers.abstract: Neuromorphic sensing and computing promise low latency and high energy efficiency for robotics, yet most event-based visual place recognition (VPR) pipelines reintroduce dense, frame-like computation downstream of an inherently sparse sensor, forfeiting the sensor's latency advantage. In this paper, we address the problem of resolving an event-based VPR query in tens of microseconds on a commodity CPU. We train a two-layer spiking neural network (SNN) with additive spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP), which drives the learned weight matrix towards a strongly bimodal distribution, amenable to aggressive magnitude pruning. At inference, our pipeline exploits this sparsity by reading only the pruned weights corresponding to the query's active pixels. As surviving weights share a near-uniform magnitude, each neuron's score reduces to an integer count of matching synapses instead of a weighted sum, lowering per-query latency. This computation is small enough to remain resident in a CPU's fast on-chip cache. On three event-based VPR benchmarks, our sparse SNN exceeds the recall of LENS, an existing event-based SNN, while reducing per-query latency by 5.5-6.2x to tens of microseconds. It matches the recall of a dense variant of our network and of the sum-of-absolute-differences (SAD) baseline, while reading 10x fewer weights than the dense variant. We further characterise how recall and latency scale with the number of active pixels and reference places. These results suggest that the sparsity of both event-based input and learned weights can already be exploited for low-latency inference on conventional processors.
authors: Somayeh Hussaini, Tobias Fischer, Michael Milford
bullets: Targets the compute bottleneck caused by dense, frame-like processing in event-based VPR pipelines.
Uses additive STDP to produce bimodal weights that support aggressive magnitude pruning.
Exploits sparse active pixels and near-uniform surviving weights, replacing weighted sums with integer synapse-match counts.
Across three event-based VPR benchmarks, achieves 5.5–6.2× lower query latency than LENS while improving recall.
Reads 10× fewer weights than the dense variant and studies scaling with active pixels and reference places.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Method overview. Preprocessing: event windows are accumulated into frames, downsampled, and reduced to their top-𝐾 active pixels. Training: additive STDP with winner-take-all mechanism assigns one neuron per reference place and makes the weights bimodal. A threshold between the modes prunes the weight matrix and leaves ③ a binary weight matrix. Sparse inference: a query’s ① 𝐾 active pixels select ② only 𝐾 rows of the weight matrix. With each weight stored as ④ one uint8, ⑤ a single 256-bit SIMD instruction sums 32 weights using ⑥ integer additions. The argmax gives the prediction ⑦ in tens of microseconds on one CPU core.

Fig. 4: [Top] Breakdown of the measured 6.73× kernel speedup of our sparse SNN over the dense SNN on QCR-Event (𝑁in = 1024, 𝑁out = 1600, 𝑘 = 100) into the factors of Table I. [Bottom] Share of total per-query latency attributed to each pipeline stage, for the same setting. The stages are preprocessing, per-call overhead, thread fork/join, weight accumulation, and readout (argmax). Preprocessing takes similar absolute time in both backends, so its larger share for sparse (85% vs 41%) reflects the sparse network’s lower cost. Thread fork/join appears only for the dense backend, which parallelises across 8 cores. Sparse runs single-threaded. Accumulation dominates the dense’s network cost (44%), whereas the sparse’s integer-add accumulation is comparatively small (9%).

Fig. 2: R@1 and latency performance comparisons across all methods and datasets. [top] Top-1 R@1: our sparse SNN exceeds LENS’s R@1 and matches dense SNN’s and SAD’s R@1 across all datasets. [bottom] Average per query latency, divided into preprocessing (light gray) and network time (solid colour). Labels give each method’s total (black) and network-only (solid color) speedup over LENS. LENS’s network stage dominates its latency, whereas our sparse SNN and SAD reduce network time to single digits. Dense SNN has a higher network latency than our sparse SNN but it is still substantially lower than LENS’s.

Fig. 6: Scalability experiment on how increasing the number of active pixels per frame impacts the R@1 and the per-query latency of our sparse SNN, dense SNN, SAD and LENS. R@1 increases with active pixel count and plateaus at 100–200 pixels (9.8–19.5% of the image). We chose 100 for balanced accuracy and sparsity. Beyond this, SAD and LENS stay stable, but our dense and sparse models degrade at high pixel counts as denser inputs become harder to discriminate, impacting sparse more as it collapses all active weights to a single value. Latency-wise, sparse tracks SAD up to ∼200 pixels before rising with pixel count, while dense stays flat throughout due to always processing the full frame regardless of sparsity.

Fig. 3: Learned weights across varying number of active pixels. Solid lines show the median line of the inactive pixel and surviving weights, with shaded bands of the same colour spanning the 25–75th (darker) and 5–95th (lighter) percentiles. The dashed line is the pruning threshold 𝜂 (Equation (6)). From 5 to 200 px, surviving weights are saturated at 𝑊max and clearly separated from the inactive weights. With few active pixels, the inactive weights remain close to their uniform initialisation,𝑈 (0, 0.5𝑊max ) . From 400 px, the active pixels need more than each neuron’s fixed weight budget. Then, normalisation drives the inactive weights to zero, while the surviving weights fall below 𝑊max and become more variable (median 0.36 𝑊max at 1024 px).

Fig. 5: Scalability of per-query latency with the number of reference places for our sparse SNN, dense SNN, SAD and LENS. Our sparse SNN scales similar to SAD throughout, flat and lowest below ∼ 103 places, and increasing roughly linearly while remaining the fastest. Dense SNN’s latency increases moderately until ∼ 103 places and grows the fastest beyond that. LENS stays flat at 130 − 140𝜇𝑠 while its fixed GPU overhead dominates its negligible per query compute, then increases linearly once that compute becomes significant.

TABLE I: Per-query inference cost of the dense and sparse backends on QCR-Event (𝑁in = 1024, 𝑁out = 1600, 𝐾 = 100). The top panel gives the work each backend must perform, in arithmetic, memory traffic and issued AVX2 instructions (256-bit registers hold 8 float32 or 32 uint8 lanes), which were verified with hardware performance counters. Every ratio is the dense value divided by the sparse value. The bottom panel is a breakdown of the measured 6.73× kernel speedup compared to dense SNN into its contributing factors.

papers.selection_reason: Sparse SNN inference for event-based visual place recognition reduces latency; efficiency contribution.
papers.title: Removing the Compute Bottleneck for Event-based Visual Place Recognition with Spiking Neural Networks
papers.tldr: A pruned two-layer spiking neural network enables event-based visual place recognition in tens of microseconds on a commodity CPU by reducing inference to sparse integer matching.

papers.abstract: Not every moment in a video is equally useful for recognizing an action. A few decisive moments often carry the evidence: the instant an object moves, the peak of a dive, or one object placed on another. Existing video datasets rarely provide large-scale, action-conditioned labels for which short segments carry that evidence. This work asks whether vision-language models can identify meaningful moments at scale and whether those labels improve action recognition.We introduce Meaningful Moments (MM), a corpus of about 4.58 million VLM-generated per-segment importance scores for nearly 500,000 class-labeled videos spanning Something-Something v2 (SSv2), Kinetics-400 (K400), and Diving-48 across 622 action classes. We freeze the action classifier and vary only temporal sampling. An alpha-parameterized comparison of importance-led selection against an importance-inverted control separates gains from the VLM signal from gains caused by variable-density sampling alone. Across all three datasets, VLM-derived importance is informative: at the hard-cut endpoint, keeping VLM-important segments outperforms keeping VLM-designated filler. Usefulness depends on class structure. On Diving-48, importance-led fast-forwarding preserves full-video recognition while the inverted control collapses by roughly 30 percentage points. On K400, hard-cut selection beats uniform sampling by 1.45 percentage points, rising to 2.05 under threshold selection. On SSv2, the labels carry signal but do not recover full-video performance. Direct scoring matches greedy removal within its noise floor at roughly 25 times fewer oracle calls, and a four-VLM cross-oracle study shows consistent downstream trends. We release the importance labels and evaluation protocol under CC-BY-4.0; SSv2 class strings remain under CC-BY-NC-4.0.
authors: Cameron Keith, SouYoung Jin
bullets: Introduces about 4.58 million per-segment importance scores for nearly 500,000 videos across SSv2, Kinetics-400, and Diving-48, covering 622 action classes.
Uses frozen action classifiers and controlled temporal sampling, including importance-inverted selection, to distinguish VLM signal from variable-density sampling effects.
VLM-important segments preserve full-video performance on Diving-48, improve Kinetics-400 accuracy over uniform sampling, and provide signal but not full recovery on SSv2.
Direct scoring achieves results comparable to greedy removal with roughly 25× fewer oracle calls; trends are consistent across four VLMs.
Releases the labels and evaluation protocol under CC-BY-4.0, with SSv2 class strings separately licensed under CC-BY-NC-4.0.

papers.title: Meaningful Moments: A Corpus of VLM-Derived Temporal Importance Labels for Video Action Recognition
papers.tldr: Meaningful Moments is a large corpus of VLM-generated temporal importance labels showing that selecting action-critical video segments can improve or preserve recognition, depending on the dataset.

papers.abstract: For context-based question answering, using one large model for both evidence extraction and answer reasoning requires substantial memory and computation. Existing approaches trade accuracy for efficiency within a single model only. We propose a multi-model approach for efficient inference: our method, PAIR, employs two differently sized models for evidence extraction and answer reasoning, respectively. A smaller Reader model processes and retains the full context, while a larger Reasoner model sees only the question and generated sequence without directly attending to the context. These capabilities are fused at the logit level: at each token, both Reader and Reasoner produce a prediction, and their logits are combined into one, behaving as a single next-token-prediction model. Fine-tuning further boosts their performance. On HotpotQA, PAIR with a 32B Reasoner retains 96% of that same 32B model's full-context accuracy while using roughly one quarter of its KV memory. At 45.7K-token contexts, PAIR achieves up to 3.2$\times$ higher end-to-end throughput than the full-context 32B model on the same GPU. PAIR also improves the accuracy-memory and accuracy-throughput trade-offs over evaluated token-reduction baselines. Its accuracy-preserving behavior generalizes across Qwen2.5, OLMo-3, and Gemma-3 model families.
authors: Sejun Park, Haocheng Xia, Yongjoo Park
bullets: Addresses the memory and computation costs of using one large model for both evidence extraction and answer reasoning.
The Reader processes the full context, while the Reasoner receives only the question and generated sequence.
Combines Reader and Reasoner logits at each token to form a single next-token prediction; fine-tuning improves performance.

papers.abstract: Spiking Transformers achieve energy efficiency by discarding softmax normalization in favor of thresholded, binary attention. However, this removal breaks the thermodynamic framework used to analyze attention networks, as the normalized measure and partition function cease to exist. We restore this theoretical foundation by proving that softmax-free spiking attention operates exactly as the zero-temperature limit of a product of independent two-level systems. This correspondence places spiking attention strictly in the frozen ordered phase of the thermodynamic phase diagram for all inputs. Consequently, the entropic cost of organizing attention collapses, replaced by a Landauer-type physical floor governed by action-potential generation. Furthermore, this ordered-phase pinning mathematically explains the optimization difficulty caused by vanishing surrogate gradients. We validate this theory with forward-relaxation experiments, placing both standard and neuromorphic attention mechanisms on a unified thermodynamic axis.
authors: Roberto C. Sotero, Pouya Taghipour, Jose M. Sanchez-Bornot

Connects ordered-phase pinning to vanishing surrogate gradients and difficult optimization.
Forward-relaxation experiments place standard and neuromorphic attention mechanisms on a unified thermodynamic axis.

papers.abstract: We study pretraining when compute is abundant but unique training data are finite, requiring repeated training on the same data. We first revisit infinite-compute pretraining (Kim et al. 2026) and show that its frontier depends critically on choices previously fixed or studied only in isolation. In particular, optimizing batch size together with epoch counts reveals a U-shaped relationship between validation loss and batch size, favoring smaller batches than typical pretraining, likely because small-batch gradient noise provides implicit regularization. We further find that training recipes, previously optimized under a single-pass assumption, can be tuned, e.g., repacking documents into new sequences every epoch, weight tying, and positive embedding weight decay. We then relax the infinite-compute assumption. In particular, smaller-than-typical batch sizes can require prohibitively long sequential training, motivating to treat GPUs and time as separate resources. Tighter deadlines favor larger batches, and latency-oriented parallelism can trade additional GPUs for shorter training. Nevertheless, even under a fixed time budget, a smaller batch with fewer GPUs can achieve lower validation loss than a larger batch with more GPUs, challenging the common practice of increasing data parallelism to maximize GPU utilization under a deadline. Together, our results identify underexplored factors in repeated-data training and provide concrete guidance on how training recipes and resource allocation should change from single-pass pretraining.
authors: Sewon Min
bullets: Validation loss follows a U-shaped curve with batch size, with smaller-than-typical batches often performing best due in part to implicit gradient-noise regularization.
Repeated-data training benefits from recipe changes such as reshuffling document packing each epoch, weight tying, and positive embedding weight decay.
When time is limited, larger batches can reduce sequential training time, while extra GPUs can trade cost for lower latency.
Even under a fixed deadline, a smaller batch using fewer GPUs may outperform a larger batch using more GPUs, challenging GPU-utilization-focused scaling.
The study focuses on finite-data, repeated-training regimes rather than standard single-pass pretraining.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action models for embodied navigation typically rely on RGB observations, limiting their applicability in lights-out industrial environments where visible illumination may be unavailable. We study illumination-independent navigation using spatial audio for target localization and depth for obstacle-aware geometry. To support this setting, we introduce DarkNav-Bench, a benchmark with 24 industrial scenes and four progressively challenging acoustic conditions. We further propose ADAPT, an audio-depth action-planning framework equipped with spatial-audio perception and optimized for closed-loop navigation through reinforcement learning (RL). Our key RL contribution, transition-aware reward shaping (TARS), defines a pose-aware shortest-action potential over a position-heading graph. Unlike conventional geodesic-progress rewards, TARS accounts for both feasible movements and in-place rotations, providing action-consistent feedback for policy optimization. Experiments show that ADAPT consistently outperforms training-based navigation baselines and zero-shot multimodal models on both seen and unseen scenes. On unseen environments, it achieves 90.6% success under Clean conditions and retains 60.0% success under the most challenging Localized Noise setting. These results demonstrate the potential of spatial audio and depth as complementary modalities for reliable RGB-free navigation in lights-out industrial environments.
authors: Wenjun Huang, Shenghao Fu, Yian Jin, Yang Ni, Yifan Li, Lichi Li, Xingjian Diao, Pengfei Zhang, Yutong Song, Hanning Chen, Jiarui Cui, Tianyu Yang, Shilong Li, Yu Kong, Mohsen Imani

papers.abstract: Predictive coding networks (PCNs) promise properties not offered by backpropagation-trained networks: learning from purely local information, a single network that both discriminates and generates, and flexible inference by energy minimization. However, their iterative inference is expensive, making hardware acceleration desirable, and a useful, efficient accelerator needs both depth and aggressive quantization. Canonical state-based PC delivers neither: its inference signal decays exponentially with depth, so deep models fail to train, and low precision makes it worse. We show that pairing two recent methods carries the full PCN property set into the deep, 4-bit regime: bidirectional PC (bPC), which unifies discrimination and generation, and the error-based reparameterization (ePC), which optimizes prediction errors rather than states during inference. Error optimization delivers the output signal to every layer in a single backward pass, removing the signal decay; one additional element, global-norm clipping of the error gradients, stabilizes the error dynamics at depth. The resulting ePC+bPC model trains stably up to at least eight layers and retains its full-precision accuracy and clean class-conditional generation under W4A4E4 quantization-aware training, across FP4 and three posit formats. On six-layer networks, where state-based bPC collapses to chance, ePC+bPC classifies more than 50 accuracy points above it after one epoch of training, with class-conditional generations 5-9x better in RMSE. 4-bit quantization is nearly free: full-precision and 4-bit accuracies differ by at most ~5 points, and by under two in the best-performing formats. We characterize the two failure modes the method overcomes, bounded signal decay in state-based PC and error divergence in unregularized error optimization, and discuss implications for a 4-bit-native PCN accelerator.
authors: Garrett Kinman, Zeljko Zilic
bullets: Canonical state-based predictive coding suffers from signal decay with depth, worsened by low-precision quantization.

On six-layer networks, it substantially outperforms state-based bPC after one epoch and produces better class-conditional generations.
Quantization causes little accuracy loss, though the study focuses on the tested architectures and formats.

papers.abstract: Recent trackers built on foundation models such as the Segment Anything Model (SAM) achieve strong performance by propagating object masks through memory. However, this strength is also a key source of failure: under occlusion, reappearance, or distractors, an incorrect prediction can enter the tracking loop and be propagated over time, resulting in persistent identity drift. Existing approaches seek to prevent such failures through improved memory and temporal modeling, but once a failure occurs, the tracker has no explicit mechanism to recognize or correct it. We address this gap with Dual-Agent, a failure-aware tracking framework that complements propagation with explicit verification and recovery. We address this gap with Dual-Agent, a failure-aware tracking framework that complements propagation with explicit verification and recovery. A vision-language verification agent first reasons over spatio-temporal context to determine whether the tracker is still following the target. When a failure is detected, a correction agent uses temporal context to recover the target before tracking continues. The correction agent is trained on real SAM3 failures, augmented with targeted identity-switch and distractor perturbations that expose it to challenging ambiguities during recovery. On LVOS-v2 and SecVOS, Dual-Agent improves SAM3 by 1.2 and 2.7 $J\&F$, respectively. Importantly, the proposed framework transfers without retraining to SAM2.1, SeC, and Cutie, as well as to long-term video object tracking benchmarks including LaSOT-ext, TNL2K, and VOT-LT2022. Our results show that explicitly reasoning about when tracking fails and how to recover provides a complementary path to robust tracking beyond improving propagation alone. Project page: valaybundele.github.io/Dual-Agent.
authors: Valay Bundele, Susmit Agrawal, Mehran Hosseinzadeh, The Nam Nguyen, Hendrik P. A. Lensch
bullets: Targets persistent identity drift caused by incorrect masks being propagated through tracker memory under occlusion, reappearance, or distractors.
Uses a verification agent to reason over spatio-temporal context and identify whether tracking has failed.
Uses a correction agent trained on real SAM3 failures plus identity-switch and distractor perturbations to recover the target.
Improves SAM3 by 1.2 J&F on LVOS-v2 and 2.7 J&F on SecVOS.
Transfers without retraining to multiple trackers and long-term video tracking benchmarks, according to the abstract.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive (AR) video generation enables long-horizon synthesis but requires repeated forward passes through large diffusion transformers. Training-free caching reduces this cost by reusing intermediate computation, yet existing controllers often couple two decisions: when to synchronize the cache exactly and how much computation to repair between synchronizations. We introduce Frequency-Step Cache (FSC), which separates these roles. FSC schedules exact full-computation anchors on a dense-to-sparse trajectory, while a lightweight latent-space risk based on frequency-resolved drift and token age controls inter-anchor repair through whole-step replay, selective token recomputation, or full repair. On SkyReels-V2, whole-step reuse provides most of the acceleration, while selective token computation is most effective as fidelity repair. A controlled ablation shows that using one reactive signal for both synchronization and repair reduces fidelity at matched latency, with the same separation advantage observed on FramePack and Matrix-Game. Across multiple autoregressive video backbones, FSC improves speed-quality trade-offs. On SkyReels-V2, FSC-Speed reaches 2.36x speedup versus MotionCache's 2.275x while improving SSIM by 0.019 and PSNR by 0.5 dB. At MotionCache-matched speed, FSC-Quality improves SSIM by 0.031 and PSNR by 1.0 dB and lowers LPIPS by 0.024. Without retuning, FSC-Quality transfers to SkyReels-V2 14B at 2.12x speedup versus 1.79x for MotionCache.
authors: Kerry Xu, Param Misra, Zachary Stenglein, Athri Karunamurthy, Fanjiang Ye, Yuke Wang
bullets: Targets the high cost of repeated diffusion-transformer passes in long-horizon autoregressive video generation.
Uses dense-to-sparse exact-computation anchors for synchronization and frequency-resolved drift plus token age to select repair intensity.
Supports whole-step reuse, selective token recomputation, or full repair; whole-step reuse drives most speedup, while selective computation mainly restores fidelity.
On SkyReels-V2, FSC-Speed achieves 2.36× speedup with +0.019 SSIM and +0.5 dB PSNR over MotionCache; FSC-Quality improves matched-speed quality, including +0.031 SSIM and +1.0 dB PSNR.
Transfers without retuning to SkyReels-V2 14B and shows benefits on FramePack and Matrix-Game.

papers.title: Frequency-Step Cache: Separating Synchronization and Repair for Efficient Autoregressive Video Diffusion
papers.tldr: Frequency-Step Cache accelerates autoregressive video diffusion by independently scheduling exact cache synchronization and adaptive latent-space repair, improving speed–quality trade-offs across multiple backbones.

papers.abstract: With ever increasing personalized large language model (LLM) services, the next question to answer is how to improve the quality of services/users' experiences, which is indicated by personalized LLM generation accuracy/quality and inference latency. Although state-of-the-art designs, e.g., parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT), retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) or Full PEFT+RAG, can help, they largely ignore the heterogeneous semantic concentrations of users' historical data and cannot fully unleash the potential of personal data for personalized LLM performance enhancement. In this paper, we propose PEFT Union RAG (PUR), a novel ``fast and accurate'' approach that exploits the semantic concentration of users' personal historical data to split workload between PEFT and RAG, aiming to improve personalized LLM performance in terms of better generation accuracy/quality and lower inference latency. Briefly, PUR partitions user's personal historical data and assigns semantic concentrated ``core'' information to PEFT for offline parametric fine-tuning, while retaining dispersed information for RAG. During the online LLM inference, PUR directly generates responses for ``core'' queries covered by the PEFT region and invokes RAG only for sporadic ``peripheral'' queries. Experimental results show that, by appropriately splitting workload between PEFT and RAG, PUR consistently achieves the best generation accuracy/quality for various users across multiple tasks, while reducing inference latency by 14.4%--46.6% compared with the best performed method.
authors: Xingke Yang, Sicong Li, Lingfeng Yao, Rui Chen, Changqing Luo, Xin Fu, Miao Pan
bullets: Targets the limitations of using PEFT or RAG alone, or combining them without considering users’ heterogeneous data semantics.
Partitions personal historical data into a concentrated “core” region for offline PEFT and a dispersed “peripheral” region for RAG.
During inference, core queries are answered directly through the fine-tuned model, while RAG handles sporadic peripheral queries.
Across multiple tasks and users, PUR reports the best generation accuracy/quality and reduces inference latency by 14.4%–46.6% versus the best-performing comparison method.

papers.abstract: Reusable skills improve multimodal agents without updating model weights, but their effectiveness depends on both the evidence presented and the procedure used to read it. We introduce ViewCraft, which jointly evolves an executable evidence interface and its reading procedure. The interface selects, transforms, and organizes observations; the reader interprets the resulting views. Failure traces guide revisions, replay and paired evaluation retain useful changes, and interface projection recovers visual edits from eligible rejected joint proposals. Across eight benchmarks, ViewCraft improves over direct execution by an average of $6.1$ points in task score, with gains on every benchmark. The advantage persists at a matched input-token budget. On all five multi-source tasks, the learned interface uses 8%-15% fewer input tokens than Initial skill. The learned skills also transfer across executors and outperform direct execution in every evaluated transfer, supporting evidence construction and reading as a coupled, reusable skill.

Learned skills transfer across executors, supporting coupled evidence construction and reading as reusable capabilities.

papers.abstract: We present Gen Through the Lens, a camera-controllable image-to-video generation framework that synthesizes videos from a given reference image while enabling realistic and physically consistent camera operations. Unlike previous models that treat camera motion as abstract conditioning or rely on a single coordinate system, our approach explicitly decomposes and fuses control signals across three coordinate spaces: the camera coordinate (modeled by intrinsic parameters), the world coordinate (represented by spatial geometry hints), and the object coordinate (described by 3D bounding boxes of target subjects). Through cross-coordinate conditioning fusion, these heterogeneous cues are unified to guide the generative process, enabling precise control of camera motion, focus, and framing while preserving temporal and spatial coherence. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method produces controllable and visually consistent results across diverse camera operations, outperforming existing approaches in both realism and editability.
authors: Shuai Li, Jinxu Xiang, Xinyuan Li, Hanlei Guo, Xiyang Tan, Alan Zhao, Xiaotong Zhao, Ran Zhang
bullets: Addresses limitations of methods using abstract camera conditioning or a single coordinate system.
Decomposes control signals into camera intrinsics, spatial geometry hints, and 3D bounding boxes for target subjects.
Fuses these heterogeneous cues to control camera motion, focus, and framing while maintaining temporal and spatial coherence.
Experiments show visually consistent, controllable results across diverse camera operations, with improved realism and editability over existing approaches.

papers.abstract: Large language model serving is increasingly limited not only by model size and GPU speed, but also by scheduling during autoregressive decoding, where continuous batching interleaves requests at token granularity as sequences arrive and finish. We study whether lightweight scheduling policies can improve latency-throughput tradeoffs without changing model architectures, kernels, or deploying learned schedulers. We implement a Python/PyTorch continuous-batching testbench with real Hugging Face execution and evaluate eight policies across 1,152 GPU-model-scheduler-workload runs using ShareGPT-derived traffic, six Qwen, Gemma, and Mistral models, and Modal L40S, A100, and H100 GPUs. Scheduler choice changes throughput, TTFT, completion latency, and tail behavior under fixed model, GPU, workload, batch size, and prefill budget. Aging shortest-prompt-first is the strongest practical baseline in many L40S and mixed-workload settings, while oracle remaining-length scheduling shows that job-size knowledge alone is insufficient because batching and hardware effects also shape performance. The custom dataset has been uploaded to Hugging Face.
authors: Ashman Mehra, Akshan Agarwal, Aryeh Carmi
bullets: Scheduling during autoregressive decoding affects throughput, time to first token, completion latency, and tail behavior.
The study evaluates eight policies across 1,152 GPU–model–scheduler–workload configurations using real Hugging Face execution.
Experiments span six Qwen, Gemma, and Mistral models, ShareGPT-derived traffic, and L40S, A100, and H100 GPUs.
Aging shortest-prompt-first performs well in many L40S and mixed-workload settings.
Oracle knowledge of remaining sequence length is insufficient by itself; batching and hardware effects also influence performance.

papers.selection_reason: Empirical study of lightweight scheduling policies for continuous-batching LLM serving, directly targeting latency-throughput efficiency.
papers.title: Lightweight Scheduling Policies for Continuously Batched LLLM Serving Across GPU Architectures
papers.tldr: Lightweight scheduling policies can substantially shape continuous-batching LLM serving performance, with aging shortest-prompt-first often providing a strong practical tradeoff across hardware and workloads.

papers.abstract: Qwen3-8B reviewing Llama-3.1-8B in math adds 33.2 points, yet Qwen3-8B alone is 6.4 points more accurate than the result. Reviewing another model's answer is usually judged by its gain over the generator. We show that this confuses verification, which adds accuracy beyond either model alone, with capability transfer, where a stronger reviewer supplies answers it could have given on its own. Measured against the stronger model alone, across 48 pairs of 12 open-weight models (3B to 72B) in math, knowledge, code and reasoning, review beats it in only 9 of 96 review directions, and does worse the larger the capability gap. The reason is that the reviewer mostly follows the generator, discarding its own correct answers. Review costs 2.6 to 2.8 times as much as the stronger model alone, while a selector using the same two calls is 2.7 to 4.2 points more accurate than review and cheaper. Studies of verification should report the stronger model alone, not only the gain over the generator. Code and per-question results: https://github.com/Kamilaabb/verification-or-capability-transfer
authors: Yirui Zhang, Yash Raj Shrestha
bullets: Across 48 model pairs and 96 review directions, review outperformed the stronger standalone model only 9 times.
Review performance declines as the capability gap between generator and reviewer grows.
Reviewers often follow the generator and discard correct answers they could have produced independently.
Review costs 2.6–2.8× as much as using the stronger model alone.
A selector using the same two calls was 2.7–4.2 points more accurate than review and cheaper.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes verification versus capability transfer in LLM pipelines, relevant to LLM evaluation and reasoning.
papers.title: Review Rarely Beats the Stronger Model: Separating Verification from Capability Transfer in LLM Pipelines
papers.tldr: LLM review often transfers a stronger model’s capability rather than adding verification, making it less accurate and more costly than simply using that stronger model.

papers.abstract: Predictive video representations do not by themselves specify how a multimodal system should handle missing sensors. We transfer frozen V-JEPA2 features to a set of heterogeneous sensors comprised by RGB video, depth video, and radar time series. A shared fusion model uses modality queries, fixed sensor slots, and explicit availability to classify breathing activity and pose from all seven non-empty sensor subsets. The contribution is a controlled evaluation of subset supervision, pooling capacity, and representation transfer on 39 OMuSense-23 subjects with five subject-group folds and three seeds. With matched downstream parameter counts, the final model reaches recording-level activity macro-F1 of $75.23%\pm0.60$ averaged across seven subsets. Supervising all subsets in each batch improves the matched query-pooling control by 1.923 percentage points (conditional 95% subject-bootstrap interval [0.647, 3.209]), while query pooling shows no clear advantage over matched mean pooling under balanced supervision. Radar probes support transfer beyond pooled wavelet pixels, 64-token inference approximately preserves mean activity performance, and the tested Consensus-JEPA loss adds no measured benefit against its exact control.
authors: Yunxiang Luo, Constantino \'Alvarez Casado, Xiaoting Wu, Nhi Nguyen, Le Nguyen, Manuel Lage Ca\~nellas, Miguel Bordallo L\'opez
bullets: Evaluates all seven non-empty sensor subsets using modality queries, fixed sensor slots, and explicit sensor availability.

Query pooling shows no clear benefit over matched mean pooling under balanced supervision.
Radar probes support representation transfer beyond pooled wavelet pixels; 64-token inference approximately preserves mean activity performance.

papers.abstract: A stored fact may stop being valid when a user changes a preference or an event replaces an earlier one. We study whether a language model can learn these changes in its parameters and answer correctly from only a question and the current time. Engram Injection stores facts in LoRA adapters and supplies the clock through FiLM conditioning on a frozen Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct model. We compare it with additive clock conditioning, prompting with the full dated history, and retrieving four dated records. We train six matched adapters across three seeds after fixing a sampler that could admit test-age examples into training. The training audit reports no such examples among 127,760 evaluated training inputs. On 62 pairs of questions asked before and after an update, at an elapsed age of seven days excluded from training, both adapter methods answer zero pairs correctly under the primary blinded assistant review with order code 1 held fixed. Full-history prompting answers 59/62 pairs correctly, and retrieval answers 62/62. Separate experiments show that adapters can store facts and that removable memory units can support local deletion. Combining fact selection with time-based version selection remains unsuccessful. These results separate learning a fact from learning when to use it.
authors: Sam Siavoshian, Omar Ramadan, Amir K. Saeed, Benjamin A. Johnson, Benjamin M. Rodriguez
bullets: Problem: Facts may become outdated, requiring models to use the current time to choose the valid version.
Method: Store facts in LoRA adapters and provide time via FiLM or additive clock conditioning on a frozen Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct model.
Evaluation: Compare adapters with full-history prompting and retrieval on 62 before/after update question pairs at an unseen seven-day age.
Result: Both adapter methods answer 0/62 pairs correctly under the primary review, while full-history prompting answers 59/62 and retrieval 62/62.
Scope: Adapters can store facts and support local deletion, but jointly selecting facts and their time-valid versions remains unsuccessful.

papers.abstract: Collision-resilient airframes allow quadrotors to survive impacts, but do not ensure autonomous post-collision recovery. Innovation gating in stock onboard estimators often rejects valid external velocity measurements after high-speed impacts, compromising recovery. We present REFLEX, a collision-recovery flight mode that runs entirely on the flight controller, requiring neither contact sensors nor a companion computer. Its proprioceptive recurrent policy stabilizes the vehicle without position, velocity, heading, or altitude estimates. The translational estimate is reinitialized while REFLEX is active, and a trust gate checks estimator consistency before returning control to the stock autopilot. The policy is trained in simulation using proximal policy optimization, with episodes initialized from post-impact states measured in 47 real collisions. In hardware experiments, REFLEX recovered 19 of 22 wall impacts at 5.03 $\pm$ 0.09 m/s, compared with 1 of 14 for the matched stock autopilot. These included 15 consecutive recoveries in a single flight. A separate exploratory flight demonstrated two additional recoveries at 6.02 and 6.05 m/s within the same flight, exceeding the previously reported velocity for autonomous wall-collision recovery by 64%.
authors: Jakob Hermeler, Luca Girardi, Gabriel Maquignaz, Stefan Leutenegger, Stefano Mintchev
bullets: Addresses estimator failures after impacts, where valid velocity measurements may be rejected.
Runs entirely on the flight controller without contact sensors or a companion computer.
Uses a PPO-trained recurrent policy, estimator reinitialization, and a consistency gate before handing control back to the stock autopilot.
Recovered 19 of 22 wall impacts at 5.03 ± 0.09 m/s, versus 1 of 14 for the matched stock autopilot.
Also demonstrated recoveries at 6.02 and 6.05 m/s in one exploratory flight.
