papers.abstract: Context-based offline meta-reinforcement learning (COMRL) has advanced almost entirely through better task representations, which separate task identity from artifacts of the behavior policy so that the latent reflects the task alone. The implicit expectation has been that a clean representation will transfer to out-of-support (parameter-extrapolation) tasks. On such a task, however, the encoder produces a latent outside the training support, where the policy has never been trained. We address this gap with Pessimistic Latent Task-aware Optimization (PLATO), which exposes the policy to off-support latents during training. PLATO assumes a mild manifold hypothesis: task latents lie on a low-dimensional manifold, and out-of-support tasks lie farther from the training centroid. It exploits this geometry by perturbing inferred latents outward from the centroid to synthesize counterfactual tasks. A learned decoder ensemble then rolls out short trajectories at each perturbed latent, and the policy is updated on the imagined transitions under a pessimism weight that down-weights steps on which the ensemble disagrees. We prove that the perturbation leaves the training support by a controllable margin and that the out-of-support generalization gap is bounded by the same perturbation reach, and we give explicit conditions, verified empirically, under which the epistemic disagreement at the perturbed latent stays bounded away from zero. On eight MuJoCo continuous-control benchmarks, PLATO consistently improves out-of-support returns over strong COMRL baselines while remaining competitive on in-distribution tasks. Our code is available at https://github.com/deephoony/plato.
authors: Chang-Hoon Jeong, Kisung Shin, Hanwool Sul, Byoung-Tak Zhang
bullets: Problem: Clean task representations may encode out-of-support latents where the policy has not been trained, limiting extrapolation to unseen tasks.
Method: Perturb inferred task latents outward from the training centroid to create counterfactual tasks under a low-dimensional manifold assumption.
A learned decoder ensemble generates short imagined trajectories, while ensemble disagreement down-weights uncertain policy updates.
Theory: The perturbation exits the training support by a controllable margin, and the out-of-support generalization gap is bounded by this reach.
Results: Across eight MuJoCo continuous-control benchmarks, PLATO improves out-of-support returns over strong COMRL baselines while remaining competitive in-distribution.

papers.abstract: In embodied manipulation, Vision Language Action (VLA) models can execute atomic skills, but long-horizon manipulation requires recombining these skills without demonstrations for every skill combination. The full instruction route treats skill chaining as long-horizon imitation. In a controlled study, full instruction training on limited skill combination sequences reaches 40.0% ordered success on covered combinations but only 7.7% on recombination, suggesting memorization of sequence templates rather than robust skill recombination. We introduce Hierarchical Subtask Execution (HSE), a diagnostic framework that exposes skill recombination through a shared modular interface over the planner, trigger, and policy, decomposing long-horizon failures into separable modes. We introduce RoboCombine, a benchmark for skill recombination without combined skill training trajectories, with metrics for ordered success and transition conversion across subtask boundaries. RoboCombine reveals that atomic competence alone does not ensure ordered execution. Failures concentrate at transitions where downstream subtasks launch from handoff states from preceding subtasks rather than canonical atomic starts. We identify this mismatch as the start state gap. To address it, we introduce Pose Robust Task Initialization (PRTI), a lightweight atomic task post-training strategy that broadens start state coverage beyond canonical starts. Under oracle timed HSE on RoboCombine, PRTI reaches 18.16% ordered success, compared with 4.21% under random perturbation and 9.47% under a robot-reset oracle, without combined skill training trajectories. These results show that combinatorial generalization requires handoff robust atomic skills that convert first stage progress into reliable downstream execution, not merely decomposition into known subtasks. Code: https://github.com/AutoLab-SAI-SJTU/RoboCombine.
authors: Xupeng Zhang, Yantai Yang, Chang Guo, Zhaokai Yin, Zhipeng Zhang
bullets: Full-instruction training appears to memorize seen sequence templates: 40.0% success on covered combinations versus 7.7% on recombinations.
HSE diagnoses failures across planning, triggering, and policy execution through a shared modular interface.
RoboCombine evaluates skill recombination without combined-skill training trajectories using ordered-success and transition-conversion metrics.
Failures cluster at subtask boundaries, revealing a start state gap between canonical starts and handoff states.
PRTI broadens atomic-task initialization and reaches 18.16% ordered success under oracle-timed HSE, outperforming the reported perturbation and reset baselines.

papers.abstract: Mixture-of-experts (MoE) models activate only a few experts per token, but when their expert weights are offloaded to host memory, host-to-device (H2D) expert transfers enter the critical path of decoding. Speculative decoding verifies several draft tokens in one forward pass, yet in an MoE model each verified token activates its own experts, so a larger draft tree transfers more experts. Because of this H2D cost, speculative decoding commits several tokens per verification cycle yet is sometimes even slower than autoregressive decoding. Based on this observation, we propose SpecFit, which chooses the verified draft subtree to maximize predicted throughput rather than acceptance length. SpecFit estimates the expected number of committed tokens from draft path probabilities and predicts cycle time from the node count and the per-layer union of the experts the subtree activates; this union is a monotone submodular coverage function, so each node pays only for the experts it adds. An exact search over ancestor-closed subtrees returns the subtree with the highest predicted throughput; run after each draft level, the same search also decides when to stop drafting, and the unmodified target verifies the result. On CNN/DailyMail summarization and a GSM8K subset with Qwen3-30B-A3B, SpecFit decodes 21.6% and 7.0% faster than EAGLE-3 with the same expert cache and 1.97x and 1.72x as fast as vanilla EAGLE-3. Code is available at https://github.com/Chlience/SpecFit.
authors: Hongliang Cao, Xiuyu Li, Siqi Wang, Ziming Wang, Jingmin Zhu, Hailong Yang
bullets: Offloaded MoE inference makes host-to-device expert transfers a decoding bottleneck, so longer drafts are not always faster.
SpecFit predicts committed tokens from draft-path probabilities and cycle time from subtree size and the experts activated across layers.
It searches ancestor-closed draft subtrees using a monotone submodular expert-coverage cost and also determines when to stop drafting.
With Qwen3-30B-A3B, it decodes 21.6% faster on CNN/DailyMail and 7.0% faster on a GSM8K subset than EAGLE-3, using the same expert cache.
Scope: results are reported for the stated summarization and math benchmarks with an offloaded MoE model.

papers.abstract: Large reasoning models generate reasoning trajectories token by token. At a given prefix, multiple next-token candidates may be plausible, yet shape subsequent reasoning and differ in their chances of leading to the correct answer. Whether these differences are reflected in internal representations remains unclear. To study this question, we define relative long-horizon candidate value to quantify within-prefix differences and construct the Reasoning Candidate-Token Value (RCTV) dataset, pairing mathematical reasoning prefixes with plausible next-token candidates and their empirical long-horizon candidate values. Using RCTV, we examine hidden states, multilayer perceptron outputs, and attention outputs at candidate positions with sparse linear probes. Experimental results provide evidence that relative long-horizon candidate value is linearly decodable from these representations at multiple layers. Candidate-value probes can also outperform probability- and embedding-based baselines. Furthermore, a controlled online intervention experiment shows that using the decoded signals to guide token selection during generation can improve the chances of eventual success. Our findings provide evidence that internal representations encode information about relative long-horizon candidate value, offering insights into how local candidate-level representations relate to long-horizon reasoning outcomes.

papers.abstract: Crowdsourced disaster imagery provides timely, ground-level observations when conventional disaster mapping is delayed or incomplete, yet its geographic value depends on where observations are produced, how they are interpreted, and whether they can be reliably located as actionable Geospatial Intelligence (GEOINT). Using more than a decade of PhotoMappers, a crowdsourced disaster-mapping initiative, this study examines the changing geography of disaster information and asks how emerging GeoAI models compare with human geographic interpretation. We combine longitudinal spatial analysis with cross-view geolocalization using street view imagery (SVI) and remote sensing imagery (RSI), and evaluate vision-language models (VLMs) reasoning through 30 indicators spanning geographic cues and reasoning evidence. The results reveal a geographically and temporally uneven archive shaped by changing disaster types, Community Lifelines, and operational priorities. Integrating VGI, SVI, and RSI with Sinkhorn re-ranking achieves 40.90% R@1, 61.10% R@5, and 69.45% R@10, while yearly R@1 varies markedly from 25.00% to 65.07%. Geographic reasoning is similarly uneven: Qwen3.6-27B achieves an overall agreement of 67% compared with 51% for InternVL3-8B, with both models showing greater difficulty with localized and place-specific evidence than broad spatial configurations. We argue that the value of GeoAI lies less in replacing volunteered geographic interpretation than in complementing it, scaling candidate retrieval while retaining human judgment for ambiguous and consequential cases. This provides a pathway toward more human-centered and responsible GeoAI for disaster mapping. All data and code are openly available at https://github.com/bobleegogogo/PhotoMappers-VLM.
authors: Hao Li, Wenping Yin, Fabian Deuser, Jia Jia, Ziqi Liu, Levente Juh\'asz, Fan Zhang, Filip Biljecki
bullets: PhotoMappers’ archive is geographically and temporally uneven, reflecting changing disaster types, Community Lifelines, and operational priorities.

Qwen3.6-27B shows higher agreement with geographic reasoning evidence than InternVL3-8B, but both struggle with localized, place-specific cues.
The study advocates human-centered GeoAI that scales candidate retrieval without replacing expert or volunteer interpretation.

papers.abstract: VLMs provide promising solutions to embodied reward design. Most current methods that train VLMs as reward regressors not only require extensive annotations but are also primarily designed for finetuning pretrained policies, and perform less well in the more challenging from-scratch RL setting. This issue stems from a fundamental mismatch: regressing precise rewards is misaligned with what VLMs naturally excel at. We posit that it is more aligned with VLMs' inherent multi-modal VQA capabilities for the models to function as success detectors, and propose VLM success reward via Exploration-Augmented Key-Observation Gating (VLMeg) to well harness VLM for embodied reward design. As the core of VLMeg, the proposed exploration-augmented key-observation gating first determines whether the current RL episode is judgment-worthy based on its similarity to a generated success trajectory. Then, the key observation with the lowest confusion from the judgment-worthy episode will be selected for VLM evaluation as episodic reward. This gating mechanism not only avoids redundant calls but also enables higher detection accuracy of VLM. Considering the sparsity of judgment-worthy episodes, the advanced exploration incentives based on the generated trajectory are introduced, enabling more efficient exploration toward judgment-worthy trajectories for more VLM reward triggers and thus gaining higher RL efficiency. Extensive experiments in MetaWorld demonstrate VLMeg achieves state-of-the-art from-scratch RL, outperforming advanced VLM-based baselines on 12 challenging reward-free tasks. Furthermore, VLMeg also enables effective RL without any ground-truth reward in 3 challenging real-world experiments. Code will be open after acceptance at https://github.com/Raina915/VLMeg.
authors: Xin Liu, Yutong Jiang, Jian Su, Ziheng Wang, Chuang Wang, Haoran Li, Dongbin Zhao
bullets: Addresses the annotation burden and poor from-scratch performance of VLM reward regressors.

Adds trajectory-based exploration incentives to reach more VLM reward-triggering episodes efficiently.
Achieves state-of-the-art from-scratch RL on 12 challenging MetaWorld reward-free tasks and works in 3 real-world experiments without ground-truth rewards.

For qualified trajectories, the observation most similar to the success-frame set is selected as the key observation. The initial frame, success reference, and selected key observation are then sent to the frozen VLM for success detection, and the resulting episodic success reward is combined with exploration incentives to improve RL efficiency.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) demonstrate strong generalization across a broad range of reasoning and generation tasks, but their large parameter counts impose substantial memory and computation costs, hindering deployment in practical resource-constrained settings. One-shot low-rank compression is a promising solution since it reduces model size and inference cost effectively. However, existing SVD-based methods primarily target multiple-choice benchmarks and often fail to preserve performance on generation tasks. Moreover, their rank allocation strategies are typically heuristic. We propose GA-SVD, a generation-aware low-rank compression framework for LLMs. First, we introduce Generation-Aware Weight Whitening (GAWW), which leverages gradients from on-policy knowledge distillation to construct whitening transformations aligned with generative behavior. Second, we develop an evolutionary global rank allocation method that searches for effective layer-wise rank allocation under a given global compression ratio. Across extensive experiments on Mistral-7B, Qwen3 series, and Llama-3.3 models, evaluated on both multiple-choice and generative benchmarks, GA-SVD consistently outperforms existing SVD-based baselines and achieves state-of-the-art (SoTA) results. We further demonstrate scalability by applying our method to models with up to 70B parameters.
authors: Shengkun Tang, Cong Zeng, Zongfang Liu, Dan Alistarh, Zhiqiang Shen
bullets: Targets the difficulty of preserving generative performance under low-rank LLM compression.

Employs evolutionary search to optimize layer-wise rank allocation for a target global compression ratio.
Evaluated on Mistral-7B, Qwen3, and Llama-3.3 across multiple-choice and generative benchmarks.
Reports consistent gains over existing SVD-based baselines and scalability to models up to 70B parameters.

Finally, Evolutionary Global Rank Allocation searches for an effective layer-wise rank configuration under a global compression budget, producing the final GA-SVD compressed LLM.

papers.abstract: Structured pruning is typically formulated as identifying which model dimensions to remove, often within the model's original representation. However, the effect of coordinate deletion fundamentally depends on the basis in which pruning is performed. This raises a more fundamental question: how should the basis be chosen specifically for coordinate deletion? We introduce WUSPruner, a transform-based framework for structured pruning of large language models. We formulate basis selection as a local linear reconstruction problem that directly minimizes the reconstruction loss induced by pruning. Inspired by the second-moment transformation in WUSH, we consider a WUS transform constructed jointly from activation and weight statistics. We show that under positive-definite second moments, WUS transform minimizes the local reconstruction loss over all invertible changes of basis. In the resulting basis, the activation and weight second moments are simultaneously diagonalized and balanced, causing the deletion error to decompose into independent spectral contributions and yielding a principled criterion for coordinate selection. Guided by this result, we develop a scalable pruning method based on blockwise WUS transformations and compact input projections. Experiments on Llama and Qwen models from 8B to 72B parameters show consistent improvements over structured pruning baselines across language modeling, knowledge, commonsense reasoning, mathematics, and code generation benchmarks, while also delivering practical reductions in inference latency and memory usage.
authors: Shengkun Tang, Dan Alistarh, Zhiqiang Shen
bullets: Structured pruning performance depends on the coordinate basis used for deletion.
The method selects a basis by minimizing local linear reconstruction loss caused by pruning.
Under positive-definite second moments, WUS jointly diagonalizes and balances activation and weight statistics, making deletion error spectrally separable.
A scalable implementation uses blockwise WUS transforms and compact input projections.
Experiments on 8B–72B Llama and Qwen models report consistent gains over pruning baselines across diverse benchmarks, with reduced latency and memory usage.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of WUSPruner. WUS constructs a basis from activation and weight second moments such that the transformed moments are balanced and diagonalized with a shared spectrum S. This makes the pruning loss decompose into independent coordinate-wise contributions, allowing transformed coordinates to be ranked by si and the least important matched dimensions to be structurally removed.

Figure 2: Sensitivity analysis of WUSPruner with respect to block size, calibration set size, and pruning ratio on Qwen3-8B and Qwen3.5-9B. Larger block sizes generally yield lower perplexity, consistent with a closer approximation to the original WUS transformation, while increasing computational overhead. WUSPruner remains stable across a wide range of calibration set sizes, and its performance degrades smoothly as the pruning ratio increases.

papers.abstract: Audio Large Language Models (Audio LLMs) are embedded in agents for smart homes, vehicles, wearables, and embodied systems, where acoustic inputs can propagate from perception into persistent state and consequential execution. This setting extends security analysis beyond model behavior to the system conditions that determine how acoustic inputs can influence agent behavior and external actions. Existing surveys examine acoustic security, LLM-based agents, and edge deployment in isolation, leaving their security interactions in deployed Audio LLM-based agents insufficiently characterized. This survey introduces an Acoustic Sensing-to-Action (S2A) system model that traces these security implications along the path from acoustic sensing to external execution, while accounting for edge-cloud runtime and lifecycle transformation. We use the model to synthesize attacks, defenses, and evaluation methods across the acoustic, agent, and edge-system literature. The synthesis shows that security gaps can emerge within components and at the transitions between stages, where protections developed for one stage do not necessarily provide end-to-end assurance in the deployed system. These findings motivate security evaluation that follows acoustic influence from sensing to action across persistent state, system boundaries, and changing deployment conditions in real-world agents.
authors: Binhong Wang, Haidong Kang, Yanfeng Zhang, Hong-Ning Dai, Guo Yu, Shangce Gao
bullets: Focuses on smart homes, vehicles, wearables, and embodied systems where audio-driven decisions can have consequential effects.

Synthesizes attacks, defenses, and evaluation methods across acoustic security, LLM-agent, and edge-system research.
Finds that vulnerabilities arise both within individual components and at transitions between stages, limiting the assurance of isolated protections.
Motivates end-to-end evaluation that tracks acoustic influence across persistent state, system boundaries, and changing deployment conditions.

papers.title: From Acoustic Sensing to Physical Actions: A Comprehensive Survey of Security Risks in Edge-Deployed Audio LLM-Based Agents
papers.tldr: A survey presents an end-to-end framework for analyzing how acoustic inputs can create security risks as they flow through edge-deployed Audio LLM agents into persistent state and physical actions.

papers.abstract: Video understanding agents rely on a harness to acquire evidence, use tools, and reason, but improving it requires substantial effort. Recent self evolution methods seek to optimize harnesses through execution feedback to reduce human intervention. However, existing methods often rely on annotated video questions and answers or focus on updating model parameters, leaving harness evolution from unlabeled videos underexplored. VideoEvoHarness jointly evolves a Questioner and a Solver harness from unlabeled videos with frozen model parameters. The Questioner constructs questions and computes reference answers directly from video memory records. Question quality assessments and Solver execution trajectories guide question generation policy revisions. The Solver supports evolving skills, strategies, hyperparameters, and tools using execution feedback. Executable strategies define workflows in code, reducing repeated interpretation of natural language instructions. Each round, candidate harnesses are compared on identical validation questions, with validated improvements retained for later use. Experiments on benchmarks and a dedicated benchmark question set, using videos disjoint from evolution videos, show higher overall accuracy than initially and transfer gains across backbones. Overall accuracy on this set also improves progressively across rounds. This supports our foundational framework for harness evolution from unlabeled videos, opening a promising direction for self evolving video agents. Code is available at https://github.com/Wei-Xin-Xu/VideoEvoHarness.
authors: Weixin Xu, Yifan Liu, Yi Wang, Mingfei Rong, Zhenyu Yang, Zhisheng Zhong, Shengsheng Qian, Changsheng Xu
bullets: Addresses the challenge of improving agent harnesses without annotated video question–answer data or parameter updates.
The Questioner generates questions and reference answers from video memory, using quality assessments and Solver trajectories to revise its question-generation policy.
The Solver evolves skills, strategies, hyperparameters, and tools; executable code-based workflows reduce repeated interpretation of natural-language instructions.
Candidate harnesses are evaluated on identical validation questions, retaining validated improvements across rounds.
Experiments report higher accuracy than the initial harness, transfer gains across backbones, and progressive improvement across evolution rounds on disjoint videos.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of the VideoEvoHarness framework. Execution feedback supports revisions to the question generation policy and the Solver’s skills, strategy code, hyperparameters, and tool operations. Validated updates enable both agents to evolve from unlabeled videos while keeping model parameters fixed.

Figure 1: Comparison of video agent evolution paradigms. (a) Agent code evolution revises agent code through review and diagnosis, and relies on previously annotated questions, answers, and evidence. (c) VideoEvoHarness derives questions, reference answers, and source intervals from video memory, and uses validated feedback to support Questioner refinement and Solver updates across skills, strategy code, hyperparameters, and tools, while the model stays frozen.

papers.abstract: Compressing the key-value (KV) cache is essential for serving long-context large language models (LLMs) under memory constraints. While current scalar quantization methods achieve significant compression, they typically face a quality-fidelity trade-off, either suffering from performance instability at 2-bit precision or necessitating 3-bit keys to maintain model quality. In this work, we demonstrate that a uniform low-bit k2v2 configuration (2-bit keys and 2-bit values) can preserve near-baseline quality by using vector quantization (VQ) based on the $E_8$ lattice for KV keys. We show that structured VQ exploits correlations across adjacent dimensions to achieve signal-to-quantization-noise ratios (SQNR) higher than those of independent scalar quantization at the same key payload rate. To ensure practical utility, we adapt a table-based asymmetric scoring algorithm that avoids explicit codebook dequantization during attention computation and preserves decode-throughput parity with scalar baselines. Across five LLM families, our $E_8$ k2v2 approach yields \textasciitilde$6\times$ KV compression, roughly 20\% smaller than scalar k3v2 (3-bit keys and 2-bit values), while retaining near-baseline long-context perplexity. In our full-suite perplexity evaluation, $E_8$ improves over scalar k3v2 in 80\% of model--dataset--context settings. These results indicate that $E_8$ lattice VQ improves quality per byte while keeping throughput at parity, suggesting that structured key quantization is a useful primitive for KV-compression stacks. Overall, our work provides a low-overhead primitive for expanding the quality-memory frontier in long-context LLM inference.
authors: Sasho Nedelkoski, Alexander Acker, Soeren Becker, Dominik Scheinert, Odej Kao
bullets: Addresses the quality instability of 2-bit KV-cache quantization and the memory cost of using 3-bit keys.
Uses E8-lattice vector quantization for keys to exploit correlations across adjacent dimensions and improve quantization efficiency.
Applies table-based asymmetric attention scoring to avoid explicit codebook dequantization.
Across five LLM families, E8 k2v2 is about 20% smaller than scalar k3v2 and improves perplexity in 80% of evaluated settings.
Provides a structured, low-overhead primitive for improving the quality–memory trade-off in long-context inference.

papers.abstract: We adapted Nemotron-3-Nano-30B-A3B for eight Indian languages without changing its backbone architecture. We expanded the vocabulary in place from 131,072 to 163,072 entries using continued byte-pair encoding and AdaptMix rebalancing, reducing tokens per word by 38.6%. We initialized new input and output rows by averaging their original constituent rows, then trained them on 90% Indic and 10% English text before updating the backbone. Continual pretraining then progressed through broad training, high-quality annealing, and long-context training over approximately 1.27 trillion tokens. The annealed checkpoint gained 12.9 points on the Indic MILU benchmark but lost 3.4 on English MMLU. We also report practical negative results. Direct token addition underperformed continued byte-pair encoding. AdamW weight decay changed rows intended to stay fixed. Perplexity on an Indic-heavy holdout did not select the learning rate that best preserved English performance.
authors: Avinash Benki, Prasanjith Pasunuti, Sutanshu Saksena Raj, Parijat Chatterjee, Nayanjit Sarkar, Daksh Maan
bullets: Expands the tokenizer in place from 131,072 to 163,072 entries using continued byte-pair encoding and AdaptMix, reducing tokens per word by 38.6%.
Initializes new input/output rows from constituent embeddings and trains with 90% Indic and 10% English text before updating the backbone.
Continual pretraining uses broad training, high-quality annealing, and long-context training over approximately 1.27 trillion tokens.
The annealed checkpoint improves Indic MILU by 12.9 points but decreases English MMLU by 3.4 points.

Negative results show direct token addition underperforms continued BPE, AdamW alters supposedly fixed rows, and Indic-heavy perplexity does not reliably select the best learning rate for English retention.

papers.abstract: Large language models are generally more capable than smaller ones, but their memory requirements can make local deployment difficult. We ask whether part of this capability gap can instead be recovered by running a smaller or more compressed model multiple times and selecting among its outputs using public or model-generated tests. Single-user local inference can leave hardware underutilized, allowing parallel candidate generation to trade additional test-time computation for accuracy at modest latency cost. Across four code-generation benchmarks, verified retry recovers substantial accuracy lost to model size or compression. A 7B Qwen model with eight parallel attempts essentially matches a 32B model on MBPP+ and exceeds it on the other three benchmarks, while using about $4\times$ less model memory, running up to $6\times$ faster, and using less energy, as measured on Nvidia GPU. We observe similar tradeoff across model sizes, compression levels and hardware choices, although exact benefit depends on the hardware profile and problem setting. These results show that model capacity can be traded for verified test-time computation when correct solutions remain reachable within a modest retry budget.
authors: Tomer Galanti, Josh Susskind, Eran Malach
bullets: Runs multiple candidate solutions in parallel and selects them using public or model-generated tests.
Across four code-generation benchmarks, retries recover substantial accuracy lost from smaller or compressed models.
A 7B Qwen model with eight attempts nearly matches a 32B model on MBPP+ and surpasses it on the other benchmarks.
The approach can reduce model memory by about 4×, run up to 6× faster, and use less energy in the reported Nvidia GPU setting.
Benefits vary with hardware and problem setting, and depend on correct solutions being reachable within a modest retry budget.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Retry trades a small amount of additional memory for higher accuracy. Each curve traces accuracy from K = 1 to K = 50 against model memory, defined as checkpoint weights plus KV cache. The dashed line marks the one-shot accuracy of native bf16 Coder-32B.

Figure 3: Retry closes much of the gap between the 7B and 32B models when the smaller model still generates correct solutions. The curves show the accuracy difference between Coder-32B bf16 and Coder-7B AWQ4 as the number of attempts increases, using public tests, model-generated tests (CodeT), and the fraction of tasks with at least one correct candidate. The gap largely disappears on HumanEval+, MBPP+, and BigCodeBench, but remains on LiveCodeBench because the 7B model fails to generate correct solutions for some tasks.

Figure 2: Parallel retry can make a smaller model both faster and more accurate. The curves show accuracy versus measured B200 wall-clock time as the number of attempts increases. The × marks Coder-32B with one attempt, and the circles mark eight attempts.

Figure 6: Parallel decoding reduces the energy cost of additional attempts. Solid curves show measured B200 energy for the native Qwen2.5-Coder models. Dotted lines show the energy that would be used if every attempt cost as much as a single attempt. Absolute energy should not be compared across panels because the benchmarks use different workloads and generation limits.

Figure 4: Retry recovers lost one-shot accuracy only when correct solutions remain reachable. Panel (a) compares one-bit Bonsai with its bf16 Qwen3.6-27B parent, and panel (b) compares Coder7B with Coder-32B. Bars show the change relative to the higher-precision or larger reference for accuracy after eight verified attempts and for the fraction of tasks solved at least once within 50 attempts. Quantization largely preserves candidate coverage, whereas reducing model size can lower it, most clearly on LiveCodeBench.

Figure 5: Verified retry has different effects across compact checkpoints. Points show retried accuracy minus one-shot reference accuracy, with 95% paired task-bootstrap intervals. Each comparison uses its common task set, so the plotted differences need not exactly match subtraction of the rounded full-population values in Table 13. Blue intervals are above zero, red intervals are below zero, and gray intervals cross zero. Granite-Code uses Granite-Code-34B as its reference rather than Qwen2.5-Coder-32B, so its effect sizes are not directly comparable with the other rows.

Figure 8: Deep retry separates failures of selection, generated tests, and candidate generation. Curves use Qwen2.5-Coder-7B candidate pools through K = 500. Solid curves show public-test selection, CodeT, and simple test-pass counting. The remaining curves show the best accuracy possible from the generated-test outcome patterns and the fraction of tasks with at least one correct candidate. BigCodeBench has the largest gap between these two upper bounds, showing that its generated tests often fail to distinguish correct from incorrect programs.
Figure 7: Quantization changes serving time as well as memory use. Each quantized checkpoint is compared with the bf16 model of the same size.

Accuracy uses public-test selection on the full benchmark sets; wall time and energy come from matched 40-prompt B200 workloads and should be compared only within a benchmark. Table 5: Accuracy and model-generated verification for the Qwen3.6-27B precision variants. All accuracy columns use the full task population for each experiment. “Usable tests” reports the fraction of tasks for which a usable generated test suite was produced.

Table 14: Most of the benefit of retry arrives at moderate budgets. For each model, “Gain” is the fraction of its improvement from K = 1 to K = 50 that has already been obtained at the displayed K. Wall time is reported relative to the same model at K = 1.
Table 19: CodeT aggregation helps most for smaller models on MBPP+. Values are the accuracy difference between CodeT and simple test-pass counting at K = 50, with paired 95% bootstrap intervals.

Table 15: Retry sharply reduces how often the selector must fall back. The left block varies the retry budget for Coder-7B; values below K = 50 are averaged over 120 candidate subsets and K = 50 is exact. The right block compares native model sizes at K = 50.

Table 17: Additional model sizes on MBPP+ at K = 50. All four accuracy measures in each row are computed from the same candidate pool. The 1.5B and 14B checkpoints belong to the native Qwen2.5-Coder scale ladder. Qwen2.5-72B is a separate general model and is included only as an additional accuracy comparison.

Accuracy is retried/reference, and ∆ is the paired accuracy difference where confidence intervals are available. Granite-Code uses Granite-Code-34B as its within-family reference.

papers.selection_reason: Studies verified retry to recover capability under memory constraints, trading test-time compute for accuracy and energy; relevant to efficient LLM deployment.
papers.title: Fewer Bits, More Tries: Recovering Capability Under Memory Constraints
papers.tldr: Verified parallel retries let smaller or compressed language models recover much of the code-generation capability of larger models under tight memory limits.

papers.abstract: Gnani-Evon-v3.3-30B-A3B is a long-context hybrid Mamba-Transformer mixture-of-experts model for reasoning, instruction following, and tool use in English and eight Indian languages. Starting from NVIDIA's Nemotron-3-Nano-30B-A3B checkpoint, it retains the 52-layer backbone and changes the vocabulary, training data, and post-training objectives. An in-place expansion from 131,072 to 163,072 tokens reduces mean Indian-language fertility by 38.6%. The new embedding rows are initialized from their upstream decompositions and warmed before the backbone is updated. Continual pretraining then adds broad English-Indic data, high-quality annealing, and direct training at a 131,072-token sequence length. The central result appears after post-training. Reinforcement learning across four verifiable task environments improves mathematics, graduate-level science, and instruction following, but degrades Indic extractive question answering because the rewards do not require an answer in the requested language. The share of Indic extraction items answered in English rises from 8.7% to 91.7%. Accuracy conditional on answering in the target script roughly doubles, which is consistent with preserved reading ability but is measured on a self-selected subset. Two unreleased studies test repairs. A scoped Indic reward restores the language convention. A 26B-A4B generative judge outperforms a 235B-parameter model on RM-Bench, and distillation restores 81% of the capabilities displaced by optimizing against it. Relative to the architecture-identical starting checkpoint, the released model gains 5.2 points on an Indic aggregate while giving up 1.7 points of English retention. The unreleased Indic-aware branch trades further, gaining 14.6 Indic points at a cost of 5.4 in English. A planned FP8 release reduces the artifact to 32GB with near-zero mean change across 32 paired benchmarks.
authors: Sutanshu Saksena Raj, Prasanjith Pasunuti, Parijat Chatterjee, Daksh Maan, Purusharth Malik, Nayanjit Sarkar, Avinash Benki
bullets: Supports reasoning, instruction following, and tool use across English and eight Indian languages with a 163,072-token vocabulary/context expansion.
Vocabulary expansion reduces mean Indian-language fertility by 38.6%; continued pretraining adds broad English–Indic data and long-context training.

Reinforcement learning improves mathematics, graduate-level science, and instruction following but causes Indic extraction answers to shift from 8.7% to 91.7% English when rewards omit language constraints.
Relative to its starting checkpoint, the released model gains 5.2 Indic-aggregate points while losing 1.7 English-retention points.
Unreleased repairs include scoped Indic rewards and a smaller generative judge that recovers capabilities through distillation; an FP8 release is planned.

papers.abstract: Rapid advances in large language models have made software engineering agents capable of tackling complex coding tasks. Within a containerized environment, a coding agent receives tool responses or execution results, and determines its later actions by those earlier results. However, most existing coding agents never look ahead: their policies do not anticipate the consequences of actions, and the terminal reward barely attributes a failure to certain earlier steps, so an ill-judged edit can corrupt the repository state irreversibly before any signal arrives. Recent code world models aim to address these challenges, but they are either trained and then frozen before reinforcement learning (RL), or reduced to an auxiliary next-token loss on the environment's outputs. We present ANTE (Anticipate, Then Execute), an agentic RL framework that verifies the policy's pre-action predictions by real execution and turns them into per-step credit for its actions and trust-or-abstain decisions. With an internal belief stated before each action, Belief-Anchored Policy Optimization (BAPO) turns the settled predictions into per-step advantages by anchoring credit on the policy's own forecasts. To turn the trained forecasts into better actions at inference, thereby facilitating effective test-time scaling, ANTE-TTO (test-time optimization) selects among candidate actions without an external scorer. ANTE raises Qwen3-32B from 25.0% to 57.2% pass@1 on SWE-bench Verified, 6.2% above a matched GRPO baseline trained without the belief state; its world model's accuracy climbs from 44% to 69% during RL, and the learned foresight capability transfers across harnesses and out-of-distribution domains. In summary, we aim to build a code world model that knows what has happened, what holds now, and what the next action will achieve.
authors: Yi Ge, Kangrui Ruan, Jifan Chen, Manish Prajapat, Christian Bock, Xiaoyang Wang, Rein Houthooft, Aritra Sengupta, Varun Kumar
bullets: Coding agents often act reactively, making early mistakes that can irreversibly damage repository state before terminal feedback arrives.

Belief-Anchored Policy Optimization (BAPO) converts verified forecasts into action advantages during reinforcement learning.
ANTE-TTO uses the learned forecasts to select among candidate actions at inference without an external scorer.
On SWE-bench Verified, ANTE improves Qwen3-32B pass@1 from 25.0% to 57.2%; its world-model accuracy rises from 44% to 69% and transfers across harnesses and out-of-distribution domains.

papers.abstract: Generating complete 3D assets from sparse, unposed images requires preserving observed geometry while completing unseen regions. Joint reconstruction and generation offers a way to address both goals: reconstruction recovers the geometry observed in the input images, while generation contributes learned shape priors. However, combining camera-relative reconstruction with canonical-space generation introduces a coordinate mismatch that makes direct geometric interaction more difficult. Moreover, conditioning each 3D location on all views without accounting for their relevance may mix useful geometric evidence with unrelated image content, hindering local detail recovery. We present UniForge3D, which jointly models reconstruction and generation in a shared anchor-guided space, resolving their coordinate mismatch. This space follows the anchor view's azimuth while keeping the object upright. The two branches exchange features bidirectionally to predict per-view point maps and a complete sparse voxel structure. We further condition point-map prediction on the generated structure to establish pixel-to-voxel correspondences and select the most informative input view for each voxel. Features from the selected views then guide detailed shape generation, helping preserve observed geometric details. Our method achieves state-of-the-art appearance and geometry results on Toys4K and GSO, generating complete 3D assets with improved fidelity. Project webpage: https://xishuxishu.github.io/uniforge3d-project/
authors: Wenjue Chen, Wenyue Chen, Heliang Zheng, Rongfei Jia, Yuan Liu, Meng Li
bullets: Addresses coordinate mismatch between camera-relative reconstruction and canonical-space generation from sparse, unposed images.
Uses a shared space aligned with the anchor view’s azimuth while keeping the object upright.
Enables bidirectional feature exchange to predict per-view point maps and a complete sparse voxel structure.
Uses generated structure to establish pixel-to-voxel correspondences and select informative views for each voxel.
Reports state-of-the-art appearance and geometry results on Toys4K and GSO, with improved asset fidelity.

papers.abstract: Sexual harassment represents a pervasive societal challenge, with a substantial proportion of incidents remaining unreported due to insufficient evidence and delayed intervention mechanisms. Smart surveillance systems capable of detecting such incidents in real-time could assist law enforcement and serve as a deterrent. However, video-based harassment detection poses significant challenges, including variations in clothing, illumina- tion, partial occlusions, low resolution, and diverse camera view- points. Despite its social importance, this problem has received limited research attention, primarily due to the scarcity of large- scale annotated video datasets. To address this gap, we extend the Sexual Harassment Video (SHV) dataset to 600 short video clips sourced from YouTube and annotated into harassment and non-harassment categories using consistent labeling guidelines. We fine-tune three state-of-the-art video transformer models, VideoMAE, ViViT, and TimeSformer, pretrained on Kinetics- 400, for binary harassment classification. Experimental results show that all three models achieve competitive classification performance, with TimeSformer attaining the highest test accu- racy of 92.27%, outperforming VideoMAE 91.71% and ViViT 91.16% on the extended SHV test set. Our analysis reveals that performance is notably influenced by dataset size, video quality, frame sampling strategy, and model architecture. This work presents a comprehensive evaluation of modern video transformers for this sensitive real-world task.
authors: Jubayer- Al- Mahmud, Md Shamimul Islam, Md Nur Hossain
bullets: Addresses real-time video-based harassment detection despite visual challenges and limited annotated data.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models are typically deployed as isolated single-agent policies. When several such agents share a workspace, they can coordinate implicitly, by observing one another, or explicitly, by exchanging messages, but it remains unclear when explicit communication becomes necessary. We introduce CoLA (Coordination via Learned Adapters), which keeps each agent's VLA backbone frozen and trains a lightweight message channel and a per-arm diffusion action head on top, with fully decentralised execution. Across three tasks that differ in how much each agent can observe, the channel matters only when information is private. On an occluded tray handover, where the box's colour marker is visible to one agent only, CoLA reaches 76.0% success versus 1.3% with messages zeroed throughout training. On two-arm and three-arm handover tasks, removing messages has no measurable effect with a shared overhead camera (90.6% vs. 88.3% at two arms; 63.5% vs. 60.0% at three), but lowers success on the two-arm task's wrist-only variant (74.8% vs. 64.3%). This architecture generalises across different VLA backbones as well. With a frozen $\pi_{0.5}$ backbone on the same occluded tray task, CoLA matches the overall success rate of a LoRA-fine-tuned baseline (37.3% vs. 34.7%) using a fraction of the trainable parameters. When CoLA places the box, it selects the correct tray 71.8% of the time, whereas the independently fine-tuned baseline, whose placing arm never sees the marker, selects it at chance level (34.7% against 33.3%).
authors: Ahaskar Kashyap, Jiawen Zong, Boyu Ma, Chuhao Zhou, Jingliang Li, Stefano V. Albrecht, Jianfei Yang
bullets: Uses a trained message channel and per-arm diffusion action heads on frozen VLA backbones with decentralised execution.
Communication is valuable mainly under partial observability, such as an occluded handover where only one agent sees the box marker.
With shared overhead-camera views, disabling messages has little effect on two- and three-arm handover performance.
On a wrist-only variant, messages improve success from 64.3% to 74.8%; on the occluded tray task, success is 76.0% with messages versus 1.3% when removed during training.
CoLA generalises across VLA backbones and matches a LoRA-fine-tuned baseline while using fewer trainable parameters.

figures.caption: Figure 1 CoLA framework overview. (a) Decentralised inference: each agent’s frozen VLA backbone (Octo-Base or π0.5) encodes its local observation. Its CoLA module compresses the backbone feature into a compact message (dm = 64), decodes the partner’s message, and concatenates the result with its own representation to form zi. This vector conditions a U-Net action head via FiLM, which predicts a coordinated action chunk (K = 10). (b) Adapter and action-head training: backbone features are cached offline and the backbones stay frozen. Only the CoLA modules are trained with a behavioural cloning loss, with gradients flowing end-to-end through the communication channel. (c) Multi-agent broadcast: each agent broadcasts its message to all other agents and receives theirs, so the same design scales to N ≥ 3 agents.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive (AR) video diffusion models enable streaming generation of long videos but suffer from significant memory overhead due to the rapidly growing KV cache. Existing KV cache quantization methods are primarily designed for LLMs and transfer poorly to video models, where activations exhibit different statistics and strong spatiotemporal redundancy. We observe that the video KV cache is largely predictable over time, with a clear asymmetry. Keys are highly predictable from their temporal history, while values depend primarily on the current key and need a short history of preceding values. Based on these observations, we propose \textbf{\method}, a training-free predictive KV cache quantization framework for AR video generation. \method predicts keys and values according to their distinct dependencies and stores only the residuals at low precision. Both predictors are lightweight, calibrated once offline by linear regression on a small set of BF16 samples, and remain fixed across prompts and generation runs. Experiments on Self-Forcing, Causal Forcing, and LongCat-Video-13B show that \method consistently achieves higher generation quality than existing KV cache quantization methods at comparable or higher compression ratios, reaching up to $6.71\times$ KV cache compression with the best overall quality--efficiency tradeoff. Our code will be released on GitHub.
authors: Jiahui Hu, Weile Mo, Peiliang Cai, Jiacheng Liu, Jinkui Ren, Xiantao Zhang, Xiaobing Tu, Linfeng Zhang
bullets: AR video diffusion models face rapidly growing KV-cache memory overhead during long-video streaming generation.
Existing LLM-oriented KV quantization methods transfer poorly because video activations have distinct statistics and strong spatiotemporal redundancy.
TempoKV predicts keys from temporal history and values from the current key plus a short value history, then stores residuals at low precision.
Predictors are calibrated once offline with linear regression on a small BF16 sample set and remain fixed across prompts and runs.
Across Self-Forcing, Causal Forcing, and LongCat-Video-13B, it reports better quality than existing methods at comparable or higher compression, with up to 6.71× compression.

figures.caption: Figure 2: TempoKV Framework. (a) Offline Calibration: a clean BF16 KV trace is collected from 8 calibration prompts, and predictors are fitted on it by linear regression. (b) Online Inference: K̃t,s is predicted from the reconstructed K history, and Ṽt,s from the aligned K̂t,s together with the reconstructed V history. Only the low-bit residual Rt,s is stored.

Figure 6: Quality preservation over long video generation. (a) Imaging Quality across increasing video lengths, where TempoKV remains close to the BF16 baseline and consistently outperforms existing quantization methods. (b–c) PSNR and SSIM comparisons further show that TempoKV better preserves quality under aggressive KV compression.

Figure 1: Magnitudes of KV caches and their prediction residuals on Self-Forcing. Top: the original KV cache magnitudes at representative layers and heads. Bottom: the corresponding residual magnitudes after applying TempoKV. Prediction reduces the dynamic range of both keys and values, suppressing outliers across latent frames and channels.

Figure 4: Qualitative comparison of long-horizon generation with Self-Forcing. While KIVI, QuaRot, and RTN exhibit progressively stronger visual degradation over time, TempoKV maintains greater temporal consistency, with results remaining close to the BF16 reference.
Figure 11: Qualitative comparison on Causal Forcing at INT2. TempoKV maintains superior temporal coherence and visual fidelity at a higher compression ratio.
Figure 10: Qualitative comparison on LongCat-Video-13B at INT4. TempoKV maintains superior temporal coherence and visual fidelity at a higher compression ratio.
Figure 7: Predictor ablation. (a–b) Reconstruction error of the K and V caches on different effective bits. (c) Per-dimension difference between the cross predictor and the temporal-only predictor.

Figure 3: Asymmetric predictability of video KV cache. (a) Temporal history predicts keys well, while values benefit substantially from the aligned key. (b) This advantage holds across all layers. (c) The gain remains stable over long generation.

papers.abstract: Enabling the reuse and composition of knowledge and capabilities distributed across foundation models is an important step toward building scalable artificial intelligence (AI) systems. However, architectural differences and incompatible representations make it difficult to transfer and integrate these capabilities through a unified cross-model interface. To address this challenge, we propose SuperAI, a cross-architecture multi-model fusion framework that integrates complementary capabilities from multiple source models into a host model through orthogonal alignment of low-dimensional task-relevant representations. Specifically, we first extract task-relevant representations from the source models and the host model using shared anchor samples, and apply principal component analysis (PCA) to construct low-dimensional functional subspaces with the same dimensionality. Next, we use orthogonal Procrustes mappings to align the source and host coordinate systems, establishing cross-model correspondences while preserving the internal geometry of each source subspace. Finally, we train a lightweight residual multilayer perceptron (MLP) with joint supervision on task outputs and source-model increments, learning input-dependent residual increments that are injected into the host model for multi-model capability fusion. Experiments on three host models across 15 capability domains show that SuperAI achieves higher average domain scores than the evaluated cross-architecture fusion methods and better preserves general capabilities as the number of source models increases. Ablation studies further support the effectiveness of orthogonal alignment, nonlinear residual mapping, and joint supervision.
authors: Jingtong Dou, Chuancheng Shi, Wenhua Wu, Wei Bao, Fei Shen, Zhiyong Wang, Tat-Seng Chua
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of combining knowledge across models with different architectures and incompatible representations.
Extracts task-relevant subspaces using shared anchor samples and PCA, then aligns them with orthogonal Procrustes mappings.
Uses a lightweight residual MLP with joint supervision to inject source-model capabilities into the host model.
Evaluated across three host models and 15 capability domains, it achieves higher average domain scores than evaluated cross-architecture fusion methods.
The method better preserves general capabilities as more source models are added; ablations support its alignment, residual mapping, and joint supervision components.

papers.abstract: Recent native 3D generators achieve high-quality asset creation by modeling structured 3D latents with flow-based transformers, but their high-resolution generation remains computationally expensive due to costly iterative sampling. In this work, we introduce a few-step distillation framework for native 3D generation, enabled by continuous self-consistency training with a custom JVP FlashAttention kernel and an analytic velocity regression objective for sparse structured 3D latents. To stabilize joint optimization, we further introduce an adaptive loss weighting strategy that automatically balances them without manual tuning. Beyond acceleration, we reveal a previously overlooked failure mode of few-step native 3D generation: sampling-induced latent distribution drift preserves geometric correctness but disrupts downstream PBR texture synthesis, causing texture artifacts on geometrically valid assets. To address this issue, we propose Channel Match, a training-free adaptive per-channel latent calibration method that restores the latent distribution without modifying either generator. We validate our approach on TRELLIS.2 at the $1024^3$ resolution setting. Our two-step model achieves $4.5\times$ faster geometry sampling while maintaining geometry quality comparable to the many-step teacher, and Channel Match further improves rendering quality by recovering the latent interface between geometry and appearance generation.
authors: Di Yang, Zhihao Li, Yanhai Xiong, Yufei Wang
bullets: Few-step sampling reduces the computational cost of high-resolution 3D generation.
The framework uses continuous self-consistency training, analytic velocity regression, and adaptive loss weighting for sparse 3D latents.
Channel Match is a training-free, per-channel latent calibration method that restores compatibility between geometry and PBR texture synthesis.
On TRELLIS.2 at 1024³ resolution, the two-step model provides 4.5× faster geometry sampling with comparable geometry quality to its many-step teacher.
Calibration improves rendering quality by mitigating texture artifacts on geometrically valid assets.

papers.abstract: Efficient neural architecture search (NAS) requires accurate performance estimation under limited evaluation budgets. Existing zero-cost proxies (ZCPs) provide fast training-free signals, but each proxy usually captures only a partial property of an architecture, leading to unstable rankings across datasets and search spaces. In contrast, GNN-based predictors can improve accuracy, but often depend on labeled architectures, graph encoders, and costly representation learning, which makes them less suitable for extreme few-shot settings. We propose FENAS, a topology-agnostic few-shot prediction framework that turns complementary initialization priors into robust ranking signals. Its core component, CAST, is a feature pipeline that combines copula alignment and synergy transformation. CAST maps heterogeneous ZCPs into a compact feature manifold, enabling lightweight meta-learners to produce reliable rankings from scarce supervision. On NAS-Bench-201, with only 0.5% labeled samples, FENAS achieves a Kendall's Tau ($\tau$) of 0.70, outperforming representative topology-based few-shot predictors in this low-label regime. In closed-domain search, FENAS evaluates the NAS-Bench-201 space in approximately 1138 seconds and achieves competitive test accuracy. By providing a fast, reliable, and structurally simple evaluation mechanism, FENAS supports the design of automated neural architectures under limited evaluation budgets.
authors: Yifeng Mao, Yuze Feng, Yutong Shen, Liyang Gao, Zhixiang He
bullets: Targets unstable architecture rankings from individual zero-cost proxies and the high labeling cost of GNN-based predictors.
CAST uses copula alignment and synergy transformation to map heterogeneous proxies into a compact, unified feature space.
A topology-agnostic meta-ensemble produces rankings from very limited labeled architectures.
With 0.5% labeled samples on NAS-Bench-201, FENAS reaches Kendall’s τ of 0.70 and evaluates the search space in approximately 1138 seconds.
The reported scope includes closed-domain NAS on NAS-Bench-201; broader generalization is not established by the abstract.

(3) Metapredictor: a lightweight meta-learner uses extremely few-shot labels to output accurate performance rankings.

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) improve robotic manipulation by jointly predicting future visual states and actions, yet most existing methods make decisions primarily from the current observation. This limits their reliability in long-horizon tasks, where visually similar states may correspond to different interaction histories and task stages. Moreover, directly incorporating historical observations can introduce stale, stage-mismatched, or error-contaminated information, leading to inaccurate world prediction and accumulated closed-loop errors. We propose RM-WAM, a reliable memory-augmented World Action Model that treats memory as a context-dependent predictive resource rather than universally useful historical context. RM-WAM represents history using complementary short-term visual state memory and latent event memory, which respectively capture recent interaction dynamics and longer-term state transitions. A counterfactual memory learning scheme varies the accessible history while keeping the current inputs and prediction targets fixed, enabling the model to learn a context-dependent utility estimate for historical memory. Based on this estimate, a utility-aware gating mechanism adaptively controls memory injection into the world-action backbone. Experiments demonstrate that RM-WAM highlights the importance of reliable and selective memory utilization in long-horizon tasks.
authors: Cui Miao, Junhao Yu, Ping Liu, Ning Yang, Xuhua Chen, He Zheng, Xiaodong Wang, Tao Zhang
bullets: Long-horizon manipulation is challenging because similar observations can reflect different histories or task stages.
Naively using history may introduce stale, mismatched, or error-contaminated information.
RM-WAM combines short-term visual-state memory with longer-term latent event memory.
Counterfactual memory learning estimates when historical context is useful, while utility-aware gating controls its injection.
Experiments demonstrate the importance of reliable, selective memory use in long-horizon tasks.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) offer a new approach to wearable-sensor-based human activity recognition. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) further introduces similar motion examples and discriminative sensor knowledge, enabling decisions grounded in observations relevant to the current query. More evidence, however, does not necessarily mean better-organized evidence. When online prompts and LLM agents primarily orchestrate inference, decisions about which activities to compare and when to invoke discriminative knowledge remain concentrated at inference time. As the activity vocabulary grows, the model must repeatedly process more candidates and associated knowledge, whereas pruning candidates too early risks excluding the true activity. We propose confusion-hierarchy evidence-aware reasoning (CHEAR), which moves part of this knowledge organization offline. CHEAR constructs and validates an activity hierarchy from recurrent cross-subject retrieval errors and builds corresponding activity-pair knowledge. At inference time, the hierarchy orders candidate comparisons; the LLM retains candidates progressively, and local discriminative knowledge is accessed only for the remaining activities. Across eight datasets, CHEAR achieves 86.79\% mean cross-subject accuracy, a 75.91\% candidate reduction rate, and 96.44\% true-activity retention. Per-sample token use is 85.15\% lower on average than in a variant without the hierarchical structure. Mean accuracy across eight cross-dataset transfer directions is 88.81\%. These results show that organizing candidates and discriminative knowledge around observed activity confusions reduces online LLM input while maintaining recognition performance.
authors: Xiangqing Lu, Tao Zhu, Mingxing Nie, Liming Chen

papers.abstract: Evaluating robot manipulation policies through repeated physical trials is costly. We study whether an action-conditioned world model can serve as a closed-loop test environment whose policy success rates track those on real robots. Beyond realistic video, the model must return the camera views and proprioceptive state needed for the policy's next action and preserve failed-action outcomes to avoid overestimating policy capability. We introduce ProWorld, a world model that jointly predicts multi-view video and robot state, then feeds both back to a frozen policy for repeated interaction. ProWorld comprises a shared transformer for joint video-state flow prediction and Shared-Time View Encoding to distinguish cameras while preserving temporal synchronization. To reduce interaction hallucinations that turn missed grasps into successful lifts, we augment training with failed interactions collected in high-fidelity simulation, reducing inflated success rates in the generated environment. ProWorld achieves the highest overall TriWorldBench score among the compared methods. Across three policies and four local manipulation tasks, it attains a Pearson correlation of 0.95 and a Spearman correlation of 0.94 between generated and real success rates. These results support joint visual-proprioceptive feedback and failure-aware training as a basis for world-model-based policy evaluation.
authors: Zijun Wang, Tianyi Yan, Haokun Lin, Panwen Hu, Bohang He, Siyu Ren, Xiaoyu Guo, Weijia Liufu, Shuoshuo Xue, Fengjiao Chen, Zipeng Ye, Xuezhi Cao, Zutao Jiang, Hanhui Li, Xiaodan Liang

Uses a shared transformer and Shared-Time View Encoding to model multiple cameras and temporal alignment.
Trains on failed interactions to reduce hallucinated recoveries that inflate simulated policy success.
Across three policies and four local manipulation tasks, generated and real success rates correlate strongly (Pearson 0.95; Spearman 0.94).

papers.abstract: LLMs increasingly support sensor-based human activity recognition (HAR) by linking motion signals with activity semantics and physical knowledge. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) grounds decisions in sensor examples and domain features, enabling training-free target-user inference with less dependence on raw numerical arrays. However, existing LLM/RAG-based HAR typically searches single-level activity spaces using static population knowledge. Consequently, they compare many unrelated candidates using the same static population evidence and overlook personalized motion patterns. We propose OntoAR-HAR, an ontology-guided agentic RAG framework combining static population and personalized knowledge. Its tree-structured activity ontology decomposes classification into local decisions among semantically related activities. The static store supplies node-constrained examples, while offline-discovered executable signal features provide numerical evidence for local distinctions. During inference, the personalized store collects selected user observations, which the LLM integrates with static knowledge and signal features while traversing the ontology to an activity label. Cross-subject and heterogeneous-sensing experiments show complementary gains from hierarchical retrieval and personalized memory across multiple LLM backbones, achieving state-of-the-art performance. By explicitly modeling hierarchical relations across activity granularities, OntoAR-HAR also addresses the long-overlooked semantic inclusion problem and avoids treating related labels as independent categories.
authors: Xiangqing Lu, Tao Zhu, Liang Yu, Shuangjian Li, Lulu Ban, Furong Duan, Mingxing Nie, Liming Chen, Yaping Wan
bullets: Addresses the limitations of flat activity search and static population knowledge in LLM/RAG-based HAR.
Uses a tree-structured ontology to make local decisions among semantically related activities.
Combines node-constrained examples, executable numerical signal features, and user-specific observations during inference.
Experiments across subjects, sensing setups, and multiple LLM backbones report complementary gains and state-of-the-art performance.
Models semantic inclusion between activity labels rather than treating related activities as independent categories.

papers.abstract: Category-level 6D pose and shape estimation requires recovering an object's pose and geometry from partial observations without an exact instance model. We present ASM-6D, which couples generative complete-geometry prediction with explicit category-level pose-shape inference through shared correspondences. Given an RGB-D image, ASM-6D generates alternative complete 3D correspondence hypotheses whose point identities are shared with a category-level Active Shape Model (ASM), including occluded points. Each hypothesis is fitted directly for rotation, translation, metric scale, and instance shape without a separate correspondence-assignment stage. We analytically eliminate translation and shape coefficients, reducing fitting to a nine-variable scaled-rotation optimization problem that enables efficient batched evaluation of multiple hypotheses in real time. ASM-6D achieves state-of-the-art performance on ROPE and HouseCat6D benchmarks. Ablations demonstrate the importance of generative correspondence prediction and active shape variation. The representation also supports shape completion, shape-dependent pose ambiguity, tracking, and robotic grasping at 6-38 Hz, depending on the inference budget.
authors: Ho Jin Choi, Minku Kim, Nadia Figueroa
bullets: Generates multiple complete 3D correspondence hypotheses, including occluded points, with identities shared by a category-level Active Shape Model.
Directly estimates rotation, translation, metric scale, and instance shape without a separate correspondence-assignment stage.
Analytically eliminates translation and shape coefficients, reducing optimization to a nine-variable scaled-rotation problem for efficient batched inference.
Reports state-of-the-art performance on ROPE and HouseCat6D, with inference rates of 6–38 Hz depending on the budget.
Also supports shape completion, shape-dependent pose ambiguity handling, tracking, and robotic grasping.

papers.abstract: Depth estimation and Gaussian reconstruction share a need for multi-scale feature processing, yet use different prediction interfaces and training objectives. Whether a decoder's internal computation can be optimized once and reused across these systems remains a structural design question. Search over primitive configurations alone leaves the organization of transformations fixed. To address this gap, we propose GeoBridge, an evolutionary framework for transferable decoder topologies. First, GeoBridge makes stage-internal topology searchable through residual, sequential, and parallel composition of configurable primitives. Shape-preserving composition retains the stage interfaces of a fixed multi-scale scaffold. Second, a functional-tree encoding supports stage-aware crossover and hierarchical mutation, while a gradient sensitivity-alignment proxy evaluates candidates without training. Multi-objective evolution balances this proxy with computation and parameter cost. Third, selected topologies are instantiated and trained in target systems with task-specific prediction interfaces. A single source search takes approximately 12 GPU hours. GeoBridgeNet-A3 achieves the best depth accuracy among four adapted decoder baselines under a common encoder and training protocol on NYU Depth V2 and KITTI. The same topology reaches 27.11 dB PSNR in Gaussian novel-view synthesis on RealEstate10K, and its refined representations support open-vocabulary segmentation on LERF. These results support decoder topology as a reusable design object across the evaluated geometric vision systems. Code and pretrained weights are available at https://github.com/EMI-Group/GeoBridge-NAS.
authors: Rui Wang, Haoyu Zhang, Ran Cheng
bullets: Addresses the limitation of searching primitive configurations while keeping decoder transformation organization fixed.
Searches residual, sequential, and parallel stage-internal compositions while preserving fixed multi-scale interfaces.
Uses functional-tree encoding, stage-aware evolutionary operators, and a training-free gradient sensitivity-alignment proxy with compute and parameter costs.

A single source search takes about 12 GPU hours; the selected GeoBridgeNet-A3 achieves the best depth accuracy among four adapted baselines and reaches 27.11 dB PSNR for Gaussian novel-view synthesis.
The topology also supports open-vocabulary segmentation on LERF, suggesting decoder topology can transfer across evaluated systems.
