papers.abstract: Joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) learn world models directly in latent space, but unconstrained autoregressive predictors may contract the latent distribution over long rollouts. We introduce Symplectic Hamiltonian JEPA (LeHami), which replaces the standard predictor with an action-conditioned Hamiltonian flow over a structured latent state (q, p) integrated using an exactly symplectic leapfrog step. This construction preserves phase-space volume at every rollout step and rules out uniform contraction, asymptotically stable fixed points, and merging of distinct latent states, independently of the learned parameters or action sequence. We obtain the momentum-like component from temporal derivatives of the learned position-like representation, providing an explicit second-order state for prediction and control. On conservative and actuated visual pendulum environments, LeHami substantially improves long-horizon velocity prediction over an unconstrained JEPA world model and empirically maintains constant latent volume where the baseline contracts. The learned flow also supports accurate integration at unseen sub-frame step sizes and numerical time reversal. These results show how geometric structure can provide inference-time guarantees that are complementary to representation regularization in latent world models.
authors: Romina Yalovetzky, Randall Balestriero, Yann LeCun
bullets: Addresses latent-space contraction in unconstrained autoregressive JEPAs during long rollouts.
Uses an action-conditioned Hamiltonian flow over position–momentum latents, integrated with an exactly symplectic leapfrog step.
Guarantees phase-space volume preservation and prevents uniform contraction, asymptotically stable fixed points, and state merging.
Improves long-horizon velocity prediction over an unconstrained JEPA on conservative and actuated visual pendulums.
Supports unseen sub-frame integration and numerical time reversal, though the reported scope is limited to pendulum environments.

figures.caption: Figure 6: The temporal ConvNet encoder inside the LeHami framework, drawn at W = 3. A window of frames goes through a stem applied once per frame, then a single Conv1d over time with a symmetric tied kernel (a, b, a), then the baseline’s spatial trunk and projector, unchanged, to give qt. The same encoder is used by the W=3 LeWM baselines; the main LeHami model uses W=1, i.e. no temporal mix. The rollout is initialised with the causal Savitzky–Golay momentum pt, computed from the current and three previous positions only, and advanced one frame at a time by the leapfrog step (orange) of Hϕ = Kϕ(p/s) + Vϕ(q,u), where the learnable per-dimension scale s (blue) rescales the momentum and therefore appears only in the position update.

Figure 1: LeHami: Learning symplectic world models end-to-end. Bottom left: Actuated pendulum frames and applied torque sequence ut (green). Upper left: Latent phase space (qt,pt), where transitions are generated by a learned scalar Hϕ(qt,pt;ut) = Kϕ(pt) + Vϕ(qt, ut) via a symplectic step. Grey lines indicate level sets; the blue curve shows the rollout. Right: Three properties of the Hamiltonian flow: (i) Volume preservation: Latent volume is exactly preserved under any action sequence. (ii) Continuous step size: Hϕ integrates at arbitrary time intervals, including between observed frames. (iii) Time-reversibility: Integrates backward by inverting time (t → −t) and reversing actions.

Figure 5: The learned flow behaves like a continuous-time vector field, and is approximately reversible, showcased with the conservative pendulum. Left: MAE of θ integrated with step sizes never seen in training (to the ground-truth from the integration of the ODE). The model is trained only at ∆t = 0.1 s; halving and quartering the step (2 and 4 sub-steps per frame, respectively) traces the same trajectory, while doubling it breaks. Right: Round-trip error after rolling K steps out and back by sign flip ∆t → −∆t in the Hϕ.

Figure 2: LeHami multi-step training. Left: at the anchor, the encoder block (Enc + SG) maps a window of W+1 frames, drawn here as the causal window xt−W , . . . ,xt, to the latent state (qt,pt). The Hamiltonian flow (Ham flow) advances it by one leapfrog step of the separable Hamiltonian Hϕ = Kϕ1(p) + Vϕ2(q,u), with the action entering the potential, and is applied K times to its own outputs. Middle: each prediction (q̃t+k, p̃t+k) is scored by the prediction loss (C) against the encoding of the corresponding frames, shown here for the last step k = K. The regularizer (R) acts on the encoder’s embeddings of q (blue) and p (orange). Right: the encoder block as instantiated in this work: a pixel encoder (Enc) outputs qt, and a fixed Savitzky–Golay stencil (SG) derives pt from qt−3, . . . ,qt.

Figure 4: Prediction performance during conservative pendulum rollouts. Wrapped MAE of θ (left) and ω (middle) across the test rollout steps (K). Metrics are computed using a k-NN probe (k = 25) fitted at K = 1 and kept frozen. Shaded areas indicate variance across three training seeds, averaged over test episodes. Cumulative log-volume of the one-step latent map, averaged over test episodes, for one training seed (right).

Figure 3: The two pendulum environments. Top: the conservative pendulum, with no actuation. Bottom: the actuated pendulum. Beneath each row is its respective torque ut, drawn as the piecewise-constant signal, held constant for three frames.

Figure 12: DINO-LeHami vs. DINO-WM on the conservative pendulum. Both models use a frozen DINOv2 encoder followed by a learned projector; Wrapped MAE of θ (left) and ω (right) along the test rollout (K steps, ∆t = 0.05 s), read by a k-NN probe (k = 25) fitted at K = 1 and kept frozen. One training seed per model, both at epoch 60.

Figure 16: The 50 planning goals. Left: the goal velocity ω∗; dashed lines mark ±τω/2, beyond which a sign error alone fails the velocity clause. 92% of the goals lie outside them. Right: the goal angle θ∗, wrapped; the green lines mark upright, which no goal is within τθ of. Goals are recorded states of held-out test episodes at K = 30 frames after the start, shared identically by every model, rung and seed.

Figure 14: The learned energy landscape under actuation. The same projection as Fig. 11, for the actuated pendulum. The torque does work, so Hϕ is not constant along a rollout and the trajectories cross the level sets instead of nesting into disjoint shells. Symplecticity is unaffected: it constrains the map, not the value of Hϕ.

Figure 8: The LeHami embeddings on the actuated pendulum are canonical. R2 of the pendulum angle θ (left) and angular velocity ω (right) decoded from the position half q (solid) and momentum half p (hatched) of the frozen encoder output. Probes are 25-NN under five episodegrouped folds fitted on embedded anchor frames (K = 0) pooled across test episodes. R2 of θ is evaluated over (sin θ, cos θ). Bars indicate the mean over three training seeds; error bars denote standard deviation. LeWM has no partitioned momentum block and is reported as a single joint latent z.

Figure 10: Latent representation space projected into the first two principal components (PCs). The embeddings correspond to LeHami (left) and unstuctured LeWM (right), shown as a function (z-axis) of the Hamiltonian learned (left) and the physical energy corresponding to the episodes. The embeddings of four episodes are shown in colors. The planes with the same color correspond to the learned Hamiltonian and energy, respectively. While the rollout episode’s embeddings in LeHami are restrictive in each of the planes corresponding to the (constant) respective learned Hamiltonian, in LeWM, the rollout episode’s representations move across planes of energy, mixing up.

Figure 11: The learned energy landscape against the physical one. (left) level sets of the true energy of the conservative pendulum; (right) level sets of the learned Hϕ over the same 60 test rollouts, each started from its own anchor. Distinct energies give disjoint closed curves in both, so the learned generator stratifies the latent space the way the physical energy stratifies phase space.

Left: the full map, n = 64 for LeHami on (q,p) and n = 192 for LeWM on its three-embedding context. Right: the newest block ∂zt+1/∂zt, n = 64 for both. The dashed line is the true flow. One training seed per model.

Each panel is one pair of the leading PCs of the encoder’s (q,p) over the test episodes; colour is the episode. The learned Hϕ is conserved along each rollout, so an episode traces a closed curve in every projection rather than drifting across them.

For each latent dimension, Vwithin is the mean squared deviation of an episode’s trajectory about its own mean and Vbetween is the variance of those per-episode means; the column reports Vwithin/(Vwithin + Vbetween), averaged over dimensions. A value near zero means the latent is an episode identifier rather than a state. Bold marks the largest within-episode share per window. The unstructured baseline attains 42.8% on this measure but cannot be tabulated here, as its evaluation path stores latents only at K = 0.

What survives decoding is in Table 7..

papers.title: LeHami: Symplectic Latent Dynamics for World Models
papers.tldr: LeHami improves long-horizon latent world-model rollouts by enforcing Hamiltonian, volume-preserving dynamics in a structured latent space.

papers.abstract: Low-bit quantization reduces the cost of serving reasoning models but can substantially degrade long chains of thought. Each step reads cached keys and values spanning thousands of tokens, allowing quantization errors to accumulate along the trajectory. Standard calibration operates on short segments that omit the earlier context needed by later reasoning steps. Even when this context is retained, cache reconstruction error alone does not capture how quantization errors affect subsequent attention. We present RECAP, a post-training quantization method that calibrates reasoning models on the history they read. Dynamic-prefix calibration separates long historical context from short-block reconstruction. It regenerates prefix keys and values with the current quantizer and rotates the active block to supervise every position along the trajectory. Prefix read geometry further supervises historical cache errors according to their effects on attention outputs, weighting key and value errors asymmetrically. With both components applied only during calibration, RECAP outperforms the baseline across multiple reasoning models and quantization settings. Under W4A4KV4, RECAP improves accuracy over the baseline by 13.3 percentage points on MATH500 with DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B and 15.8 points on AIME-120 with Qwen3-4B. These results highlight the importance of preserving historical dependencies during calibration for low-bit reasoning.
authors: Chi Ruan, Yujie Chen, Zixiang Zhao, Jingcai Guo, Haotong Qin
bullets: Low-bit quantization can degrade long-chain reasoning as cache errors accumulate across thousands of historical tokens.
RECAP uses dynamic-prefix calibration to reconstruct long prefixes and supervise each position along the reasoning trajectory.
Prefix read geometry weights historical key and value errors by their effects on attention outputs.
Applied only during calibration, RECAP outperforms the baseline across multiple models and quantization settings.
Under W4A4KV4, it improves accuracy by 13.3 points on MATH500 and 15.8 points on AIME-120 in the reported settings.

figures.caption: Figure 3: RECAP overview. (a) Full-precision attention magnitudes alongside quantization errors for the baseline, prefix-only calibration, and RECAP in one reader window; bars give W4A4KV4 AIME-120 accuracy from Table 1 on R1-1.5B, R1-7B, and Qwen3-4B. (b) The calibration workflow rebuilds historical keys and values with the current quantizer and combines block reconstruction with a read-geometry penalty. papers.abstract: Tool-using agents alternate between model generation and tool execution, waiting for each tool call to complete before starting the next generation. This sequential execution is costly during agentic reinforcement learning (RL), which requires large batches of multi-turn rollouts. We introduce ObsSpec, an observation speculation pipeline for agentic RL that uses a small world model to predict tool outputs while the environment executes, allowing the policy to begin its next generation early. ObsSpec retains speculative work only when the predicted and actual observations match exactly, making rollout collection lossless, while co-training keeps the world model up to date as the policy learns. On terminal-use tasks, predictions from a 0.6B world model exactly match actual observations in 66.4% of attempts and arrive roughly 16 times faster. Using these predictions, ObsSpec reduces agent latency by 9.3% and 14.2% for 8B and 32B policies. Across controlled experiments, we characterize the regimes in which ObsSpec reduces agent latency under shared policy resources. Finally, because ObsSpec overlaps policy generation with tool execution, it is architecturally compatible with existing techniques for accelerating RL. Code is available at https://github.com/kylemontgomery1/verl-recipe/tree/obsspec/obsspec.
authors: Kyle Montgomery, Wang Zhang, Chenguang Wang
bullets: Targets the latency caused by sequential policy generation and tool execution in multi-turn agentic RL.
Uses a small co-trained world model to predict tool outputs, letting the policy start generating before execution finishes.
Keeps speculative generations only when predictions exactly match actual observations, avoiding rollout changes.
A 0.6B world model matches terminal-use observations in 66.4% of attempts and predicts them about 16× faster.
Reduces agent latency by 9.3% for 8B policies and 14.2% for 32B policies in reported experiments.

papers.abstract: Self-evolving mechanisms let vision-language model (VLM) agents continually adapt through evolving memory, but they also allow malicious behavior to emerge only after deployment. We introduce a new attack surface, the self-evolving backdoor, whose payload stays dormant in the initial agent and is progressively activated as the agent evolves. Unlike conventional backdoors, which can be exposed by testing triggered inputs on a static model, our attack requires both a visual trigger and a sufficiently evolved memory state; static scanning with clean memory thus yields near-zero attack success and may deem the agent benign. We realize this through memory-aware backdoor training, which couples trigger activation with the agent's evolving memory while preserving benign behavior unless the trigger co-occurs with payload-related memory. Across three VLM backbones, four agent pipelines, and recency-, semantic-, and reward-based memory evolution, the attack preserves normal functionality and stays nearly inactive before evolution (0.5% attack success rate), yet exceeds 95% attack success within 100 interactions, revealing a stealthy threat unique to self-evolving agents.
authors: Chuan Zou, Yang Xiang, Zexin Li, Xiaonan Luo, Simin Chen
bullets: Targets self-evolving VLM agents, where changing memory creates a new backdoor attack surface.
Uses memory-aware backdoor training to couple payload activation to both visual triggers and evolving memory states.
Preserves benign behavior and remains nearly inactive before memory evolution.
Across three VLM backbones, four agent pipelines, and three memory-evolution strategies, attack success rises from 0.5% initially to over 95% within 100 interactions.
Demonstrates a threat specific to self-evolving agents that static clean-memory testing may miss.

papers.abstract: Most benchmarks for large language models in medicine are built from licensing examinations and theoretical questions. The few that draw on real clinical data do so only in part, and rarely require a model to read a patient's own imaging. ClinEdge addresses this gap with 32 real, de-identified patient cases from active clinical practice, each evaluated across seven frontier systems for a total of 224 expert-graded evaluations. Each case pairs primary imaging with a short vignette, contains a feature known to defeat pattern-matched reasoning, and is scored against the patient's documented clinical course. The suite is built for depth rather than volume. Grading followed a two-stage expert process. First, a senior orthopaedic surgeon graded all 224 responses on a weighted rubric and a pass-or-fail verdict. Second, a panel of nineteen physicians, largely senior specialists at teaching medical colleges, independently reviewed every case and every one of the 224 grades. All seven production systems were evaluated through their public interfaces, and all 224 conversations are preserved as replayable links. Performance was poor across all systems, and the failures were shared: different vendors missed the same findings and converged on the same wrong plans. From the experts' notes we catalogue 18 recurring failure modes in five families. The models stop reading an image at the first finding. They give generic plans and lean toward over-treatment. They trust a misleading history over correct imaging. Their answers vary across systems and runs, and change with question format. Failing answers were delivered fluently and without any expressed uncertainty. Four cases are released in full; the remaining 28 are held out, and we invite frontier AI labs and healthcare AI companies to evaluate their models against them (research@futrbridge.com)

Finds poor performance across all systems, with shared errors including premature image interpretation, generic or excessive treatment, misleading-history bias, and overconfident answers.
Catalogues 18 recurring failure modes across five families; four cases are released publicly and 28 are held out for evaluation.

papers.abstract: Words are increasingly becoming an interface for action: large language models (LLMs) can now invoke tools, operate devices, and make decisions that affect the physical world. However, current benchmarks largely evaluate LLMs through static text responses, offline tool calls, or simulated tasks, leaving open the question of how well they can act in real physical environments. We present a benchmark for measuring LLMs in closed-loop physical interaction, where models control a harness system connected to real-world components including robotic arms, cameras, and sensors. In each task, the model must issue instructions, receive physical feedback from the environment, interpret the resulting state, and adapt its next action accordingly. This setting evaluates capabilities beyond language understanding, including grounded perception, action planning, tool selection, spatial reasoning, feedback-driven correction, and robustness to execution uncertainty. Through experiments with representative LLMs, we characterize their ability to translate linguistic reasoning into physical actions and identify common failure modes such as hallucinated state changes, poor recovery from unexpected outcomes, and unstable long-horizon plans. Our benchmark aims to provide a systematic foundation for evaluating LLMs as interactive agents that connect words, tools, and the physical world.
authors: Xinnan Dai, Kaiqi Yang, Yaxin Li, Cheng Luo, Wanli Li, Mingqing Xiao, Xinyang Jiang, Daoan Zhang, Kaitao Song, Fengze Liu, Zefan Cai, Caihua Shan

papers.abstract: Unified vision-language models (VLMs) perform both text-to-image (T2I) and image-to-text (I2T) generation with one shared Transformer backbone, yet how the backbone processes the condition in either direction remains poorly understood. We study this question from the perspective of conditional guidance: we probe every attention head to show the activation difference between two branches of classifier-free guidance (CFG) with different conditional guidance. On two unified VLMs of autoregressive and masked-diffusion paradigms, the probing reveals a subset of heads that are more sensitive to the change of condition while others are agnostic to it. This characteristic pattern holds in both T2I and I2T generation and is largely stable across data samples, demonstrating the internal mechanism of unified VLMs. Motivated by this, we propose a new inference-time intervention approach for unified multimodal generation, named \textit{HeadTuned-CFG}, which uses the probed condition-change awareness to select and tune the conditional guidance at the attention-head level. Experiments show consistent benefits in both multimodal generation directions of unified VLMs without additional training, and in particular substantial improvements over strong baselines in T2I generation. These results further support the key finding of our probing analysis: the observed pattern of functional specialization is an intrinsic property of unified VLMs.
authors: Zhengyang Luo, Xiaoyu Qiu, Zhiheng Tan, Yuchen Liang, Yingbin Liang, Liyue Shen
bullets: Condition-sensitive and condition-agnostic attention heads emerge in both autoregressive and masked-diffusion unified VLMs.
This specialization pattern appears consistently across both generation directions and is largely stable across samples.
HeadTuned-CFG selects and adjusts guidance at the attention-head level during inference.
Experiments report consistent gains in T2I and I2T generation, with particularly substantial T2I improvements over strong baselines.
The findings suggest functional specialization is an intrinsic property of unified VLMs.

papers.abstract: Zeroth-order (ZO) optimization enables memory-efficient fine-tuning of large language models (LLMs). However, ZO optimization suffers from high variance in high-dimensional parameter spaces. While recent methods restrict perturbations to random low-rank subspaces, these subspaces often misalign with task-specific descent directions. We propose AdaSub-ZO, a novel forward-only fine-tuning framework in learnable low-rank subspaces. Instead of relying on fixed random matrices, AdaSub-ZO iteratively learns layer-wise projection matrices directly from finite-difference feedback to track task-aware descent directions. Furthermore, AdaSub-ZO incorporates a subspace momentum acceleration mechanism to smooth noisy gradient estimates across evolving subspace bases. Extensive experiments on natural language understanding tasks demonstrate that AdaSub-ZO outperforms existing ZO baselines, substantially reducing gradient estimation variance and accelerating convergence.
authors: Chuang Tong, Ling Chen
bullets: ZO fine-tuning avoids storing backpropagation gradients but suffers from high-variance estimates in high-dimensional parameter spaces.
AdaSub-ZO learns layer-wise projection matrices from finite-difference feedback instead of using fixed random subspaces.
A subspace momentum mechanism smooths gradient estimates as the learned subspaces evolve.
Experiments on natural language understanding tasks show lower estimation variance and faster convergence than existing ZO baselines.

papers.abstract: Natural language specifications let non-expert users task robot teams, and large language models (LLMs) have recently proven effective at grounding such semantic specifications into plans for heterogeneous teams. Existing approaches assume missions that terminate and environments that, while unknown, do not change, but both assumptions fail in many emerging applications. For example, a disaster-response mission does not terminate, and its environment changes continuously as hazards spread and evacuees move. We identify three ways an LLM orchestrator breaks in this setting: its prompt grows without bound, its reasoning degrades as agents and targets accumulate, and it stops actively monitoring after covering the search space once. We build on the successful framework of grounded generative intelligence, and address each issue with a classical idea. A Markovian state summary, rebuilt from the semantic map at every invocation, replaces the growing interaction history. Partial delegation lets the orchestrator assign a subset of robots to an autonomous multi-agent protocol and reserve its reasoning for generating subtasks that require detailed parameters and careful ordering. Lastly, observation staleness, surfaced explicitly in the prompt, together with task-and event-triggered re-prompting, keeps the team vigilant. In a simulated urban search-and-rescue mission with spreading fire and moving evacuees, our framework rescues 98% of civilians versus 89% for the strongest baseline while using six times fewer tokens. Additional ablations isolate the contribution of each mechanism.
authors: Maria G. Mendoza, Victoria M. Tuck, Zachary Ravichandran, Shankar Sastry, George J. Pappas
bullets: Targets failures in persistent missions: unbounded prompts, degraded reasoning as complexity grows, and reduced monitoring after initial coverage.
Replaces interaction history with a Markovian state summary rebuilt from the semantic map at each invocation.
Partially delegates robot subsets to autonomous multi-agent protocols, reserving LLM reasoning for parameter-sensitive, ordered subtasks.
Uses explicit observation staleness and task/event-triggered re-prompting to maintain vigilance as conditions change.
In simulated urban search and rescue, rescued 98% of civilians versus 89% for the strongest baseline with six times fewer tokens; ablations assess each mechanism.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. System architecture. The mission statement, team specification, including task primitives and multi-agent protocols, and a partial semantic map are provided as inputs. The LLM is prompted with these inputs and the prompt information of Sec. IV-D to delegate a subset of the robots to the multi-agent protocols and generate subtasks for the rest according to the system needs. This plan is validated, and the LLM is provided feedback if there are issues. The actual task assignment is done symbolically with a linear program (LP) assignment. Multi-agent Protocols (green) are shown to be continuously operating with the self-loop or similar to tasks in that they have an endpoint. Asymmetric observations from all operations are constantly fused into the map. The feedback mechanism is triggered on task completion (solid lines) or on relevant map update events (dashed lines). Feedback on the map and observation age (orange) is compiled with a state summary of the history (blue) and provided in the new prompt to the LLM.

Fig. 5. The orchestrator reasoning about moving humans under partial information. Left: at k = 34 people are reported in r6 c0 and r7 c0, with an escort under way to r7 c0. Right: by k = 41 both regions have been re-observed clear and two civilians are reported in r6 c1. The orchestrator treats the re-observation as evidence the pickups are stale, cancels the escort, issues a local search around each vacated region to recover the missing group, and escorts the live report at r6 c1.

papers.title: Persistent LLM Orchestration of Heterogeneous Robot Teams via Partial Delegation to Multi-Agent Protocols
papers.tldr: A persistent LLM orchestrator enables heterogeneous robot teams to handle changing, non-terminating missions more effectively while using far fewer tokens.

papers.abstract: A recurrent-depth language model reuses one block of weights several times in a row. The number of repetitions, which we call loops, is chosen when the model runs, not when it is trained, and running fewer is cheaper and faster, so a deployment may choose to do it. Running fewer loops also makes these models less safe, and the loss of safety is larger than the loss of anything else we measured. We study four released Ouro checkpoints and Huginn-0125. At half of its trained depth, Ouro-1.4B-Thinking still solves 0.692 of the GSM8K maths problems, against 0.775 at full depth, keeping 89% of its accuracy. Over the same reduction, the rate at which it helps with harmful requests rises from 0.038 to 0.205, 5.3 times higher. The information is not lost: a linear classifier reads whether a request is harmful from the model's internal state after a single loop, with an ROC AUC of 0.967 against 0.986 at full depth. What the missing loops remove is the refusal that should follow. We measure the effect with four instruments, one generating no text at all, and reproduce it on a second model family. Removing a single direction from Ouro-1.4B's internal state at full depth drops its refusal rate on harmful prompts from 0.950 to 0.130, identifying what the shallow model is missing. Two run-time repairs do not help: the models' early-exit rules do not spend more loops on harmful requests, and choosing a depth per request does not recover the loss. Changing the training does. Standard safety training makes the shallow model safe only by refusing 0.865 of harmless requests, while training at randomly chosen depths reaches a separation of +0.399 between harmful and harmless refusal at one loop, against +0.118. On Huginn-0125 it keeps harmful help at or below 0.040 at every depth from 1 to 32 loops, where standard training reaches 0.194, and it costs no accuracy at full depth.
authors: Seyedarmin Azizi, Erfan Baghaei Potraghloo, Arya Fayyazi, Saeid Shokoufa, Massoud Pedram
bullets: At half depth, Ouro-1.4B-Thinking retains 89% of its GSM8K accuracy, but harmful-request assistance rises 5.3×.
Harmful intent remains encoded after one loop, indicating that shallow execution removes the refusal response rather than the safety signal.
Ablating one internal direction at full depth similarly reduces refusal, identifying a component linked to refusal behavior.
Early-exit rules and per-request depth selection do not restore safety.

Training across randomly sampled depths improves harmful/harmless refusal separation and keeps Huginn-0125’s harmful assistance at or below 0.040 across 1–32 loops without reducing full-depth accuracy.

All three are scored before the text-quality filter, so that the measurement is the only thing that differs between the lines. All values are close to zero, so the model’s own rule does not spend more loops on harmful prompts. Figure 10: Four training objectives on Ouro-1.4B, against loop count. (a) The refusal gap. (b) The refusal rate on harmless prompts, where lower is better. (c) GSM8K accuracy. Figure 2: The text-quality filter. (a) Repeated three-word sequences in answers to harmful prompts, by depth, with the threshold drawn as a dashed line. (b) Repeated neighbouring words, with its threshold. Both rise sharply only at the shallowest settings. (c) The fraction of answers kept. (d) Harmful compliance before and after filtering. The filter does not create the effect we report: it makes the measured drop in the refusal gap smaller, not larger.

Figure 4: The refusal gap D on the left axis and harmful compliance on the right axis, against loop count, for three Ouro checkpoints and the dense control. The shaded band marks depths that keep at least 85% of full-depth GSM8K accuracy. Ouro-2.6B is shown in Figure 5 instead, because the measurements behind this figure were not run for it.

Figure 7: Huginn-0125 at 1 to 32 loops. Open markers mark settings where the text-quality filter kept fewer than half the answers, so those points rest on small samples. Standard safety training at the final loop (middle series) gives safety at full depth that does not extend to shallower settings. Training at randomly chosen depths (Section 7) removes the difference.

Harm detection is the probe score above chance, which needs no generated text. Task ability is GSM8K accuracy. The refusal gap is D from Eq. (2), scored after the text-quality filter. Harm detection is almost unchanged after one loop, task ability falls somewhat, and the refusal gap falls the most. The arrow marks the distance between harm detection and the refusal gap at one loop. Table 1: Safety and task ability at each depth. Depth k means k loops for the Ouro models, where 4 is full depth, and the matching number of layers for the dense control; rel. compute is the fraction of full-depth forward compute. D is the refusal gap, the refusal rate on harmful prompts minus the rate on harmless ones; harmful compliance is the judged rate of real help with a harmful request. All safety numbers are computed after the text-quality filter, so each cell counts only answers that pass it (57–260 harmful and 18–199 harmless prompts per cell; the filter removes the most on the dense control at depth 3, which keeps only 57 harmful and 18 harmless answers, so read that row with care). Table 3 repeats this measurement under the equal-length protocol, which is the only one that covers all four Ouro checkpoints; the two tables come from different generation protocols and are not comparable cell by cell.

Table 2: Which alignment objective survives being run shallow, on Ouro-1.4B. All three LoRA arms use the same refusal data and the same schedule and are trained at full depth; they differ only in which loop readout the loss supervises, namely the final loop only, the exit-gate weighted mixture over all loops, or one uniformly sampled loop per training example. D is the refusal gap, the refusal rate on harmful prompts minus the rate on harmless ones, depth k means k loops with 4 the full depth, and full-depth rows are in bold. Safety numbers are computed after the text-quality filter; coherent fraction is the share of answers to harmful prompts that it keeps. Filtering changes what the comparison rests on: at one loop all three trained arms hold harmful compliance at 0.008–0.009, so they separate on refusal of harmless prompts instead, where the final-loop and exit-gate objectives over-refuse (0.865 and 0.926) and the random-loop one does not (0.585). Each safety cell uses 152–260 harmful and 95–179 harmless prompts after filtering; each accuracy cell uses 120 GSM8K problems and is measured without the filter.

Table 4: Is the compliance at shallow depth real text or broken output? An answer to a harmful prompt counts as coherent when its repeated-trigram rate is at most 0.25 and its adjacent duplicate-word rate is at most 0.02. Coherent fraction is the share of answers to harmful prompts that pass; raw compliance is the judged compliance rate over all of them; coherent share of flagged compliances is the fraction of the raw compliances that are coherent; filtered compliance is the compliance rate among the coherent answers only, which is the one the main text uses. Depth k means k loops for the Ouro models and the matching number of layers for the dense control. 260 harmful prompts per cell before filtering.

Table 9: The dense control on a fine grid. Removing layers from an ordinary model is the closest analogue to running fewer loops, and the coarse grid in Section 4 only reaches settings where the model has no task ability left. This grid removes 1, 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10 layers of 28 instead. Two things follow. Text quality collapses almost at once: removing two layers already costs more than half the answers, where an Ouro model at half its loops keeps nearly all of them. And at the mildest cut, where the dense model is still coherent, the refusal gap and the compliance rate are both close to their full-depth values. 260 harmful and 200 harmless prompts per cell before filtering; n is the number of harmful answers left after it. GSM8K uses 120 problems per cell.

Table 7: Harmfulness is readable from the state after one loop; the direction that turns it into a refusal is not yet in place. Probe AUC is the cross-validated AUC of a logistic probe trained on the last-token hidden state at that depth to separate harmful from harmless prompts (5-fold stratified CV, probe refit per fold; ± is the across-fold standard deviation; JSON fields per_depth[].probe_auc and per_depth[].probe_auc_sd). Final-direction AUC scores the same prompts with the difference-in-means refusal direction computed at full depth and applied to that depth’s state. cos to final is the cosine between the refusal direction computed at that depth and the one computed at full depth, so it measures how far the direction still has to move, not how far the state has to move. Depth k means k loops for the Ouro models and the matching number of layers for the dense control. 150 harmful and 150 harmless prompts.

Table 13: The model’s own exit gate, compared against uniform truncation at the same compute. Each row is one gate threshold τ : rel. comp. is the measured mean relative forward compute the gate uses, Dgate is the refusal gap under the gate, and Dtrunc is the same quantity for fixed-depth truncation linearly interpolated to that relative compute. Gate adv. is Dgate −Dtrunc. The last three columns are the gate’s mean exit loop on harmful and on harmless prompts and their difference, which is how much depth the gate actually spends on harm. Full depth is 4 loops. 260 harmful and 200 harmless prompts per cell. The fixed depths that the interpolation is built from are the unfiltered D values in Table 5.

Table 11: Does the depth effect depend on the judge? Every harmful answer is re-scored with Qwen3Guard-Gen-8B, a larger guard model, and its harmful-compliance call is derived with the same rule as the primary judge’s, reusing the primary run’s inputs so that only the guard differs. All figures are computed on answers that pass the text-quality filter, matching the main text. Agreement is the fraction of answers the two judges label the same way and κ is Cohen’s kappa on the same pair. The depth trend holds under the second judge in every model, and its compliance rate is never the higher of the two, so the primary judge does not understate compliance at shallow depth. Agreement is lowest at a single loop, where the text is most degraded, which is the failure mode the text-quality filter addresses.

Table 10: Does running fewer loops add to what a prompt-level attack already does? Each row is one model under one prompt template, measured at every loop count. The template row none is the plain harmful prompt. The three templates are standard ones: an instruction not to begin with an apology or the words sorry, cannot or unable; an instruction to begin the reply with “Sure, here is”; and a request to write in character as a morally unconstrained novel character. 100 harmful and 100 harmless prompts per cell before filtering. The two effects compose: the largest compliance in each model comes from a template at a single loop, not from either alone. All figures are computed on answers that pass the text-quality filter, which keeps 0.30 to 1.00 of answers; the single-loop cells for Ouro-1.4B-Thinking are the thin ones and rest on fewer than half the prompts.

Table 12: Does the effect survive a change of decoding? The main runs decode greedily, so repeating them returns identical text. These runs instead sample at temperature 0.7 with 3 seeds. Columns give that model’s greedy refusal gap for reference, then the mean, standard deviation and range of the refusal gap and of harmful compliance across the seeds. The ordering over depth is the same in every seed, and the spread is small next to the drop from full depth to one loop. Sampling makes the single-loop refusal gap smaller than greedy decoding does, so the greedy numbers in the main text are the conservative ones. All figures are computed on answers that pass the text-quality filter.

Table 3: Safety by depth under the equal-length protocol, the only one of the three protocols that covers all four Ouro checkpoints, including Ouro-2.6B. Every prompt’s answer is truncated at every depth to the shortest answer that prompt produced at any depth, then judged, and the text-quality filter is applied on top; coherent fraction is the share of answers to harmful prompts that it keeps, and it stays between 0.742 and 0.996 here, so no cell rests on a thin remainder (193–259 harmful and 136–196 harmless prompts per cell). D is the refusal gap, the refusal rate on harmful prompts minus the rate on harmless ones, and depth k means k loops, 4 being full depth. Full-depth rows are in bold; Ouro-2.6B was not run at full depth under this protocol, which is the dashed row. This table is a different generation protocol from Table 1 and is not comparable to it cell by cell; GSM8K accuracy is not re-measured under this protocol, so the capability column appears only in Table 1.

Table 5: The depth effect under three measurement protocols, scored before the text-quality filter so that the protocol is the only thing that differs. Each cell is D, the refusal gap, on 260 harmful and 200 harmless prompts. Raw is open-ended generation judged as emitted. Bounded generates in two phases, a capped deliberation phase followed by a forced answer phase, and judges only the answer, so every depth produces a real answer rather than a cut-off deliberation. Equal-length takes those bounded answers and truncates each prompt’s answer at every depth to the shortest answer that prompt produced at any depth, so answer length cannot drive the depth contrast. Depth k means k loops for the Ouro models and the matching number of layers for the dense control. A dash marks a model and depth that was not run under that protocol.

Table 6: Huginn-0125, a recurrent-depth model with a much longer depth range, at 1 to 32 loops (32 is its full depth). D is the refusal gap, the refusal rate on harmful prompts minus the rate on harmless ones, compl. is the judged rate of real help with a harmful request, and coh. is the fraction of answers to harmful prompts that the text-quality filter keeps. All rates are computed after filtering. The two trained arms are LoRA adapters trained on the same refusal data at full depth, differing only in whether the loss supervises the final loop or a uniformly sampled loop. Filtering raises the released model’s apparent compliance rather than lowering it: at two loops it reads 0.905 after filtering against 0.381 before filtering, because the filter removes the broken answers that were previously counted as non-compliant. That cell is also thin, keeping only 0.162 of the answers to harmful prompts (42 of 260); the released arm’s coherence is low throughout, so its column describes a small surviving subset, not the whole sample. Cell sizes after filtering range from 13 to 257 harmful and 9 to 178 harmless prompts.

Table 14: Depth-routing oracle simulation. Every row fixes a mean depth budget and asks how D, the refusal gap, depends on how that budget is spent. Setting is either a gate threshold τ , whose measured mean depth sets the budget, or an imposed mean-depth budget. Depth is that mean depth budget in loops and rel. comp. the matching fraction of full-depth compute. Uniform is depth-blind: it mixes the two available depths bracketing the budget so as to hit it in expectation. Coarse is told the true label but knows nothing about the individual prompt: one depth for all harmful prompts and another for all harmless ones, the best such pair within the budget. Gate is the model’s own exit threshold, reported only for the settings at which it was run. The per-prompt oracle picks each prompt’s depth knowing its label and its recorded outcome at every depth, maximising refusals on harmful prompts plus compliance on harmless ones under the budget; depth is the mean depth it ends up using. The oracle is headroom, not a deployable policy. Because depth is constant within one generation, every policy is scored on responses that were actually generated at that depth. Depths available: [1, 2, 3, 4] loops; 460 prompts per row; CIs are bootstrap 95% intervals from the results file.

Table 8: Forced-choice preference between a compliant continuation and a refusal, read off every loop without generating. The four middle columns give the fraction of prompts where the complying sentence is preferred to the refusal, at 1 to 4 loops. ∆ is the paired shallow-minus-full change in the log-probability margin (target minus refusal, in nats) with its bootstrap 95% CI, as stored in the results file. The harmful − harmless row is derived here: the per-depth entries are differences of the two fractions above it, and the ∆ entry is the difference of the two arms’ deltas with a 95% CI built by treating the arms as independent, taking each arm’s standard error as its CI half-width divided by 1.96, and combining the two standard errors in quadrature. 200 harmful and 100 harmless prompts.

Table 16: Does the depth-aware objective hold against prompt attacks it was not trained on? Both adapters are trained on plain harmful prompts with no wrapper. Here the harmful and harmless sets are re-run on Ouro-1.4B under two of the templates of Section 4.5, at every loop count. Harmful compliance is given at full depth and at its worst value over the four loop counts, which is what a deployment that may lower the loop count is exposed to; the remaining columns are the refusal rates and the refusal gap at full depth. Both objectives cut compliance under both templates, so what the objective buys is not specific to the prompt form it saw in training. 100 harmful and 100 harmless prompts per cell before filtering. All figures are computed on answers that pass the text-quality filter, which keeps 0.48 to 1.00 of them, leaving 48–100 harmful answers per cell.

Table 15: Does the comparison in Table 2 depend on the training seed? Both arms were retrained from scratch at three seeds, with the same data, schedule and hyperparameters, and the whole grid re-measured. Columns give the mean, standard deviation and range over the runs. The ordering is the same in every run: at one loop the random-loop refusal gap is larger than the final-loop one in all three runs and the two ranges do not meet, and the final-loop arm reaches its shallow safety by refusing harmless prompts in all three. Full-depth rows are in bold. The one-loop retention gap of Section 4, safety retained minus task ability retained, is -0.237, -0.341, -0.419 in the final-loop runs and +0.118, +0.183, +0.137 in the random-loop ones. Safety numbers are computed after the text-quality filter, on 202–260 harmful and 114–183 harmless prompts per cell; accuracy uses 120 GSM8K problems per cell and no filter.

papers.selection_reason: Studies recurrent-depth LLM architecture and safety/refusal behavior across loop counts; fits LLM architecture research.
papers.title: Running Fewer Loops Removes Refusal Behaviour in Recurrent-Depth Language Models
papers.tldr: Reducing inference loops preserves much of recurrent-depth models’ reasoning ability but sharply removes their refusal behavior, while depth-diverse safety training can maintain safety across loop counts.

papers.abstract: Deep research requires connecting multiple steps of search, reasoning, and computation, with intermediate findings guiding what to investigate next. As investigations grow, agents must maintain research state across model calls and check findings before errors propagate into subsequent work. We introduce PANINI-DR, a multi-agent harness that separates coordination of the overall investigation from the research and verification of individual subquestions. A shared workspace, built on the Generative Semantic Workspace representation, records subquestions, their dependencies, findings, and supporting evidence. Researchers investigate individual subquestions, while a separate verification agent checks proposed answers against those subquestions and their evidence. Verification feedback guides further investigation, and recorded findings inform subsequent assignments. We evaluate PANINI-DR on BrowseComp-Plus, FRAMES, and MoNaCo against seven state-of-the-art deep-research harnesses, all using a shared language-model backbone and frozen corpora. PANINI-DR achieves the strongest average performance across the three benchmarks. On BrowseComp-Plus, it achieves 73.3% accuracy, outperforming the next-best harness by 16.0 points. Its advantage is strongest on hard questions, where it answers nearly twice as many as the next-best harness. Ablations further show that structured planning and persistent state improve performance, as does checking each finding against its cited evidence before it is reused. Because a model can answer correctly from memory alone, we also analyze the evidence retained by each harness. PANINI-DR achieves the highest answer recoverability from saved evidence on all three benchmarks, while complementary claim-support audits show stronger evidence-backed answers. Accounting for this evidence changes how harnesses compare and further strengthens PANINI-DR's advantage.
authors: M. Yigit Turali, Shreyas Rajesh, M. Efe Lorasdagi, Chenda Duan, Kartik Sharma, Vwani Roychowdhury
bullets: Separates overall investigation coordination from research and verification of individual subquestions.
Uses a Generative Semantic Workspace to track subquestions, dependencies, findings, and supporting evidence across model calls.

Achieves the strongest average performance; on BrowseComp-Plus, reaches 73.3% accuracy and improves evidence recoverability and support.

papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have been shown to be computationally expensive and vulnerable to jailbreak attacks, in which adversarial prompts bypass safety alignment and induce harmful responses. To address this inefficiency, a range of techniques have been proposed to enable efficient LLM inference. Depth-based dynamic inference has demonstrated promising results by enabling outputs to be generated from intermediate layers. It offers the flexibility to adjust model behavior based on the available resource budget. However, how this flexibility affects the robustness of LLMs against jailbreak attacks remains unexplored. In this paper, we address this gap via a comprehensive investigation into the impact of depth-based dynamic inference on the robustness of LLMs against jailbreak attacks. Specifically, we make the following key observations: 1) Shallow exits are consistently more robust to jailbreak attacks than deeper ones; 2) Exit depth affects how easily the adversarial suffix can be optimized, with deeper exits reaching lower attack loss; and 3) Adversarial suffixes affect utility uniformly across exit depths. These insights can help design dynamic inference methodologies that are more robust to jailbreak attacks. Code is available at https://github.com/LassNajmuldeen/balcony-jailbreaking
authors: Lass Najmuldeen, Seyedhamidreza Mousavi
bullets: Investigates how generating outputs from intermediate layers affects LLM jailbreak vulnerability.
Shallow exits are consistently more robust to jailbreaks than deeper exits.
Deeper exits allow adversarial suffixes to be optimized more effectively, achieving lower attack loss.
Adversarial suffixes degrade utility similarly across different exit depths.
Findings can inform more jailbreak-robust dynamic inference designs.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of the jailbreak evaluation pipeline. A harmful prompt (e.g., “How do I build a bomb?”) is combined with an adversarial suffix produced by an optimization-based attack (GCG), and the resulting input is passed through the frozen backbone. papers.title: Exploring Jailbreak Vulnerability Across Depth-Based Dynamic Inference in Large Language Models
papers.tldr: A study finds that earlier exits in depth-based dynamic LLM inference are generally more resistant to jailbreak attacks than deeper exits, revealing a robustness–depth trade-off.

papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) reuses the same documents across many requests, making non-prefix KV-cache reuse attractive. Yet a cached document state is not reusable text: it is a context-conditioned causal state whose keys and values depend on the prefix, position, and preceding documents under which it was computed. We formulate non-prefix KV reuse as a behavior-preservation problem with full prefill on the exact prompt as the reference, and introduce SAFE-KV, which repairs a composed cache by re-encoding the causal suffix from a selected start document. On Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, prefix-conditioned composition preserves only 47.2% of HotpotQA-500 and 37.8% of 2Wiki-500 full-prefill answers; SAFE-KV with risk-guided K2 selection restores 99.8%/98.4% (donor-copy protocol) and 100.0%/98.4% with actual suffix forwarding. Document-only and fixed-window repairs recover far less, because the document states after the repaired region keep histories that omit it. Reuse without repair is exact up to four documents and degrades at sixteen, where suffix repair recovers 98-100%. Faithful repair re-encodes most of the context, so in a single-request L40S study SAFE-KV's operating rule serves every workload by full prefill. SAFE-KV thus establishes the causal-state contract for non-prefix reuse and a validated repair mechanism that meets it.
authors: Xingjian Zhang
bullets: Non-prefix KV reuse is difficult because cached states depend on the prompt prefix, positions, and preceding documents.
SAFE-KV selects a repair start document using risk-guided K2 selection and re-encodes the causal suffix.
On Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, recovery reached 99.8%/98.4% on HotpotQA-500/2Wiki-500 with donor-copy repair and 100.0%/98.4% with actual suffix forwarding.
Unrepaired composition degraded from exact behavior at four documents to substantially worse behavior at sixteen; document-only and fixed-window repairs were less effective.
Faithful repair re-encodes most of the context, and in the reported single-request L40S study full prefill remained the operating choice.

papers.title: SAFE-KV: Causal Suffix Repair for Behavior-Preserving Non-Prefix KV Cache Reuse in RAG

papers.abstract: Test-time memorization of sequential information is a foundational capability for any intelligent system that needs to rapidly store and retrieve data, as demonstrated by the attention mechanism in large language models. However, Transformers and linear attention variants are trained via backpropagation through time (BPTT), which has drawbacks such as its enormous memory requirements. Predictive coding (PC), an algorithm that optimizes a prediction-error energy function with local updates, offers a compelling solution but still lacks test-time memory for sequential data. We develop a solution to this problem by treating the per-step memory update $\Delta S_t$ as a latent variable, as opposed to a slow weight to be learned. By taking the log probability of a standard PC-based probabilistic model, we derive a PC-native solution for verbatim sequence memory, and relate our update rule to common choices in the linear attention literature (e.g., DeltaNet). We present an extensive set of empirical tests to probe our system's properties, including its scaling capacity, memory footprint, and ability to infer a context from evidence (e.g., bank (river) vs. bank (money)). We show how DeltaNet-PC can be used for storing single sequences of data, multiple sequences of data, and key-value associative memory pairs with perfect recall accuracy.
authors: Todd Morrill, Richard Zemel
bullets: Addresses the lack of test-time sequential memory in predictive coding while avoiding BPTT’s large memory demands.
Treats each per-step memory update as a latent variable rather than a slowly learned weight.
Derives a predictive-coding-native update rule from a probabilistic model and connects it to DeltaNet-style linear attention updates.
Evaluates scaling, memory footprint, contextual inference, single- and multi-sequence storage, and key-value associative memory.
Reports perfect recall for the tested sequence and associative-memory tasks.

papers.abstract: As agentic AI systems take on increasingly complex and consequential tasks, securing them against prompt injection becomes critical. Existing defenses often rely on detecting or reasoning about injected malicious instructions and can therefore remain vulnerable to adaptive attacks that optimize the injection itself. Diffusion language models (dLLMs), an emerging framework for language generation, offer a new opportunity for security enforcement: by iteratively refining their sequence wide predictions, they enable broader-scope constraint enforcement throughout generation. This paper introduces Policy-Constrained Diffusion Agents (CoDA), a framework that enforces task dependent security policies directly within the denoising process of diffusion language models. At each denoising step, CoDA projects token distributions onto a policy-compliant set, maintaining constraint satisfaction throughout generation. We evaluate CoDA across state-of-the-art diffusion language model families under both static and adaptive prompt-injection attacks. Results demonstrate substantial reductions in attack success rate with competitive task utility and practical inference overhead.
authors: Michael Cardei, Anjun Hu, Chenrui Ma, Francesco Pinto, Chawin Sitawarin, Chulin Xie, Ferdinando Fioretto
bullets: Addresses adaptive prompt-injection attacks that can evade defenses based on detecting malicious instructions.
Projects token distributions onto a policy-compliant set at every denoising step.
Evaluated across multiple diffusion language model families under static and adaptive attacks.
Substantially reduces attack success while preserving competitive task utility with practical inference overhead.

papers.abstract: We investigate whether a physics foundation model (PFM) pretrained for PDE forecasting can be repurposed for closed-loop fluid-flow control. We construct a PFM-based controller by attaching lightweight Gaussian actor and critic heads to frozen pretrained representations and train the policy using proximal policy optimization (PPO). We evaluate the approach on HydroGym's two-dimensional Kolmogorov-flow environment using vorticity observations at \(64\times64\) and \(128\times128\) resolutions and Reynolds numbers \(\mathrm{Re}=100\) and \(200\). Across these settings, we compare the frozen PFM controller against a baseline MLP policy trained with the same PPO framework. The PFM controller achieves consistently higher reward while requiring smaller executed action magnitudes over training, indicating improved control performance with reduced control effort. These results provide initial evidence that representations learned through self-supervised next-frame prediction can be transferred directly to closed-loop fluid flow control. Project page: https://mahindrautela.github.io/morph.
authors: Mahindra Rautela, Shaifalee Saxena, Alexander Scheinker
bullets: Motivation: Repurpose PDE-forecasting representations for fluid-flow control without fully retraining the model.
Method: Attach Gaussian actor–critic heads to frozen PFM representations and train them with PPO.
Evaluation: Test on 2D Kolmogorov flow across two spatial resolutions and Reynolds numbers, comparing against an MLP PPO policy.
Result: The PFM controller consistently obtains higher reward while using smaller executed action magnitudes.
Scope: Results provide initial evidence for transferring self-supervised next-frame prediction features to control.

papers.abstract: Canonicalization resolves the rotational and permutation ambiguity of 3D point clouds by selecting a unique orbit representative, maintaining their geometric information while allowing standard architectures, such as Transformers, to operate on them. Existing canonicalizations, however, exhibit discontinuity jumps on molecular configurations and non-trivial invariance errors in popular molecular datasets, which lead to ambiguity in their representation. To bridge this gap, we introduce LexiCan, a canonicalization that is provably invariant under either $O(3)$ or $SO(3)$, empirically invariant to rotations to within $\sim 10^{-6}$ angstroms on the QM9 and QM-sym molecular datasets, and mitigates discontinuity jumps on QM-sym, while running orders of magnitude faster than an existing canonicalization. Finally, non-invariant models perform better on QM9 property prediction and ModelNet40 shape classification with LexiCan than with that canonicalization.
authors: Daniel Sanchez, Djordje Mihajlovic, Federica Valeau, Luka Beni\'c, Raghuwansh Raj, Soutrik Sarangi, Snir Hordan
bullets: Addresses ambiguity and discontinuity problems in existing molecular point-cloud canonicalizations.
Selects a unique geometric representative with provable invariance under either O(3) or SO(3).
Achieves approximately 10⁻⁶ Å rotational invariance on QM9 and QM-sym, while mitigating discontinuity jumps on QM-sym.
Runs orders of magnitude faster than an existing canonicalization.
Improves non-invariant model performance on QM9 property prediction and ModelNet40 shape classification relative to that method.

papers.abstract: Coding agents are increasingly evolving beyond reproducing what a world looks like toward constructing executable worlds that capture how a world works. This shift calls for executable world modeling, which integrates two core capabilities: world understanding, reasoning about the underlying structural, mechanical, and causal principles of a world, and executable realization, translating that understanding into a code-based system whose behavior emerges from physical interactions. However, existing benchmarks provide only fragmented evaluations centered on physical reasoning, visual fidelity, or behavioral correctness, leaving the integration of these capabilities insufficiently assessed. To bridge this gap, we introduce ExeWorldBench, to our knowledge the first benchmark to comprehensively evaluate world understanding and executable realization through code-based 3D world construction. ExeWorldBench comprises three progressively challenging tasks: Mechanism Executability, which evaluates the realization of individual mechanisms from visual observations; Compositional Executability, which extends to multi-stage systems with spatial, mechanical, and causal dependencies; and Intent-Driven Executable World Synthesis, which requires constructing executable worlds from high-level goals and physical requirements. Extensive experiments on frontier models reveal substantial limitations in executable world modeling, offering insights into the development of more physically grounded and causally coherent world construction systems.
authors: Xinge Peng, Zhen Fang, Ruibing Wang, Yongxuan Lv, Haodong Li, Guohui Zhang, Xiaoxiao Ma, Yiting Lu, Lin Chen, Zehui Che, Feng Zhao

Evaluates both world understanding and executable realization in an integrated framework.
Includes three tasks: mechanism realization, compositional multi-stage systems, and intent-driven world synthesis.

papers.abstract: Existing depth-compression methods for large language models (LLMs) score layers individually or group only adjacent or contiguous layers, implicitly assuming that functional redundancy is local. We test this assumption by computing full pairwise Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA) similarity matrices for thirteen LLMs from six architecture families (1.6B-14B parameters). Non-adjacent layers have 3.6-15.9x more high-similarity pairs than adjacent ones, a structure that prior similarity-based layer merging has not systematically exploited. We propose Fusion via Community Mining (FCM), which builds the full L x L similarity graph, uses spectral community detection to find clusters of functionally equivalent layers, keeps the highest-Block-Influence layer in each cluster, and applies LoRA recovery; a pre-specified rule computed only on calibration data chooses between cosine and CKA similarity. At 2x compression, FCM lowers mean perplexity below ShortGPT on twelve of thirteen models, significantly on ten (Welch's t-test with Holm-Bonferroni correction; up to 50% on Qwen3-4B), with Mistral-7B the only loss (+13.4%). Against FlattenGPT, SWM, and DeltaLLM under matched calibration and recovery, FCM gives the best perplexity on ten of thirteen models (mean rank 1.15), and it also outperforms MKA on three anchor models. FCM matches or exceeds ShortGPT on 15 of 20 zero-shot reasoning cells and also improves MMLU, LAMBADA, HumanEval pass@1, and free-form generation quality. The 2x-compressed Qwen2.5-7B has 46% fewer parameters, 42% lower peak VRAM, and 84% higher decode throughput on a single A100. Spectral grouping outperforms Fisher contiguous segmentation by 41% and uniform partitioning by 51%, and FCM's advantage grows beyond a 2x crossover up to 3x and persists at the 14B scale. Code: https://github.com/Usama1002/fcm-layer-fusion
authors: Muhammad Usama, Yeoreum Jung
bullets: Full pairwise CKA analysis across 13 LLMs finds substantially more high-similarity non-adjacent than adjacent layer pairs, challenging local-redundancy assumptions.
FCM constructs a layer-similarity graph, detects functional communities spectrally, retains the highest-Block-Influence layer per cluster, and applies LoRA recovery.
At 2× compression, FCM beats ShortGPT in mean perplexity on 12 of 13 models and is best among several baselines on 10 of 13.
It matches or exceeds ShortGPT on 15 of 20 zero-shot reasoning evaluations and improves several downstream generation and language benchmarks.
For compressed Qwen2.5-7B, FCM reports 46% fewer parameters, 42% lower peak VRAM, and 84% higher decode throughput on one A100; Mistral-7B is the main exception, with a perplexity loss.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of the FCM pipeline. papers.abstract: Spiking neural networks target energy-efficient language modeling through sparse, binary activations, but the efficiency-accuracy tradeoff of spiking language models is uncharacterized at scale. We present the first Chinchilla-style IsoFLOP scaling study of a spiking language model, sweeping SpikeGPT-family models (RWKV backbone) from width 384 to 1536 across compute budgets from $3\times10^{17}$ to $10^{19}$ FLOPs on FineWeb-EDU. We report two findings. First, the compute-optimal frontier is $N_{opt} \propto C^{0.56}$, close to the 0.50 that Hoffmann et al. report for dense Transformers, so spiking does not change how parameters and data should be traded off under a compute budget. Second, against non-spiking RWKV and Transformer baselines trained the same way, the loss gap splits into a backbone cost of about 0.16 nats that does not change with compute and a spiking cost that falls from 0.34 to about 0.23 nats and then levels off. These results give the first compute-optimal recipe for spiking language models and quantify the accuracy cost of their sparsity.
authors: Dan Saunders, Benjamin Ren, Catherine He
bullets: Studies SpikeGPT-family models with an RWKV backbone across widths 384–1536 and compute budgets of 3×10^17–10^19 FLOPs.
Finds the compute-optimal parameter scaling exponent is 0.56, close to the 0.50 reported for dense Transformers.
Decomposes the loss gap versus non-spiking baselines into a roughly compute-invariant backbone cost of 0.16 nats and a spiking cost that decreases before leveling off near 0.23 nats.
Provides a compute-optimal scaling recipe and quantifies the accuracy cost associated with spiking activations.

papers.abstract: Linear-attention and state-space LLMs carry long context in a fixed-size recurrent state, and quantizing that state is the natural way to cut its cost during long decode. Unlike a weight tensor, the state is rewritten at every step, so a quantizer applied at each step sits inside the recurrence and its errors compound. INT4 that leaves synthetic recall perfectly intact at the start destroys it a thousand steps later. The mechanism is a feedback between the quantizer scale and the state it is derived from. Yoking that scale to a full-precision reference removes the resulting norm explosion entirely, yet recovers only 1.8 of the 5.4 nats lost, so numerical instability and functional degradation are separable failures. The remainder is a resolution problem that locating outliers does not solve, since every outlier-aware scheme here loses to plain persistent scaling. Allocating bits across layers does help, but under article-disjoint splits a learned allocation collapses onto the trivial rule of protecting the first few layers. Run out to 32K, group-wise INT4 is worth no more than discarding the state. Contain the scale rather than locate outliers, and report the decode horizon at which a bit-width was certified.
authors: Yuhang Jiang
bullets: Quantization errors compound because the recurrent state is rewritten at every decoding step.
Tying the quantizer scale to a full-precision reference eliminates norm explosion but recovers only part of the lost performance, separating instability from resolution limits.
Outlier-aware quantization does not resolve the remaining degradation; persistent scaling performs better in the reported comparisons.
Learned bit allocation helps mainly by protecting the first few layers, and group-wise INT4 provides little value at 32K context.
Quantization claims should report the decode horizon over which a bit-width is validated.

papers.abstract: Human social perception is incremental: we infer intent before an utterance is complete, revise our interpretation as new cues arrive, and attend to specific facial, gestural, or prosodic signals that shape social meaning. Current multimodal LLM benchmarks largely evaluate final-answer understanding over complete episodes, rewarding post-hoc recognition of social meaning rather than the unfolding perception required for real-time interaction. Drawing on interactionally embedded Gestalt principles of multimodal human communication, we introduce GesBench: a human-grounded benchmark for cue-level social perception in multimodal LLMs. GesBench uses cumulative sub-utterance clips to measure when models form stable interpretations of speaker intention and social affordance, and human gaze-guided corruption to evaluate whether regions attended by humans are functionally important for model judgments. Built from more than 6000 utterance-level clips from scripted and unscripted conversational datasets, GesBench includes human annotations of unfolding judgments and gaze on a representative subset. Across open and closed multimodal models, we find a clear human-model gap: humans form predictive understandings early and revise more often, while models often hedge or repeat across different clips. GesBench shifts social evaluation from whether models eventually recognize meaning to when and where that meaning is formed. Our codes are publicly available at https://anonymous.4open.science/status/GesBench-share-212C.
authors: Zonghuan Li, Hayley Hung, Chirag Raman
bullets: Addresses the gap between final-answer benchmarks and humans’ incremental, cue-sensitive social perception.
Uses cumulative sub-utterance clips to measure when models stabilize interpretations of speaker intent and social affordance.
Applies human gaze-guided corruption to test whether human-attended regions influence model judgments.
Covers more than 6,000 scripted and unscripted conversational clips, with human annotations on a representative subset.
Finds that humans interpret earlier and revise more, while models often hedge or repeat across clips.

papers.abstract: Modern AI systems increasingly combine large language models (LLMs) with human experts, using the LLM to handle routine queries while deferring uncertain cases for expert review. When expert capacity is limited, however, deferral decisions must account not only for the reliability of the LLM but also for congestion in the expert queue. We formulate this as an online sequential decision-making problem in which, for each query, the system observes the confidence signal of the LLM's answer and must decide whether to output the answer or defer the query to a capacity-constrained expert. The reliability of the confidence signal is initially unknown and must be learned from expert feedback, which is both selectively observed (only deferred queries are labeled) and delayed by queuing. We propose \texttt{KL-PBD}, a learning algorithm that uses Kullback--Leibler lower confidence bounds on the unknown reliability parameters to guide deferral decisions. For $K$ confidence levels and horizon $T$, \texttt{KL-PBD} achieves $O(K\log T)$ gap-dependent regret when the accuracy at every confidence level is bounded away from the deferral boundary, and $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{KT})$ worst-case regret. We establish matching lower bounds, showing that these rates are optimal up to logarithmic factors. Finally, we validate our approach on synthetic instances and real-world question-answering datasets, namely GSM8K, NuminaMath, and MedMCQA, using Qwen LLMs.
authors: Vasileios Saketos, William Reveillard, Alexandre Proutiere, Sebastian Dalleiger, Ming Xiao
bullets: Models online deferral decisions using LLM confidence, expert congestion, and limited expert capacity.
Learns unknown confidence reliability from feedback observed only for deferred and queue-delayed queries.
Uses KL lower confidence bounds to guide deferral decisions across K confidence levels.
Achieves O(K log T) gap-dependent regret and Õ(√KT) worst-case regret, with matching lower bounds up to logarithmic factors.
Validated on synthetic settings and GSM8K, NuminaMath, and MedMCQA using Qwen LLMs.

papers.abstract: Traffic sign recognition plays a crucial role in the development of autonomous cars to reduce the accident rate and promote road safety. It has been a necessity to address traffic signs that are affected significantly by the environment as well as poor real-time performance for deep-learning state-of-the-art algorithms. In this paper, we introduce Real-Time Image Enhanced CNN ({\our}) for Traffic Sign Recognition. {\our} is a real-time, novel approach that tackles multiple, diverse traffic sign datasets, and out-performs the state-of-the-art architectures in terms of recognition rate and execution time. Experiments are conducted using the German Traffic Sign Benchmark (GTSRB), the Belgium Traffic Sign Classification (BTSC), and the Croatian Traffic Sign (rMASTIF) benchmark. Experimental results show that our approach has achieved the highest recognition rate for all Benchmarks, achieving a recognition accuracy of 99.75\% for GTSRB, 99.25\% for BTSC and 99.55\% for rMASTIF. In terms of latency and meeting the real-time constraint, the pre-processing time and inference time together do not exceed 1.3 ms per image. Not only have our proposed approach achieved remarkably high accuracy with real-time performance, but it also demonstrated robustness against traffic sign recognition challenges such as brightness and contrast variations in the environment.
authors: Reem Abdel-Salam, Rana Mostafa, Ahmed H. Abdel-Gawad
bullets: Targets traffic signs degraded by environmental conditions and the slow execution of existing deep-learning methods.
Evaluated on GTSRB, BTSC, and Croatian rMASTIF benchmarks.
Reports accuracies of 99.75%, 99.25%, and 99.55%, respectively.
Combined preprocessing and inference take no more than 1.3 ms per image.
Demonstrates robustness to brightness and contrast variations.

papers.abstract: Foundation models need to support diverse inference budgets, yet training a separate model for each budget duplicates pretraining effort. Elastic models train several nested sub-networks inside one weight-shared supernet, but existing recipes face three obstacles: variable per-step workloads that hinder distributed scaling, limited hyperparameter (HP) transfer across model sizes, and no guarantee that all sub-networks are maximally updated at once. We present \Ours, an elastic transformer that organizes hidden dimensions into a dense core and successive shells, so that every hidden matrix is block lower triangular. One full-width forward pass contains every sub-network's exact hidden states as prefixes, so joint training keeps a fixed computation graph and costs about as much per step as training the widest sub-network alone. We further introduce \muE, an extension of maximal update parameterization (\mup) to \Ours and other elastic architectures. Its scaling rules provably keep all sub-networks of a supernet maximally updated simultaneously (\muI), and keep doing so when the supernet is widened or given more shells; sweeps confirm that HPs tuned on a small non-elastic proxy stay near-optimal for elastic families and larger supernets (\mbox{\muT}). A single \Ours run produces sub-networks that outperform MatFormer and fully elastic baselines at matched parameter counts, and approach separately trained models that together take several times the steps.
authors: Can Jin, Yan Kang, Yifan Gong, Chongjian Ge, Mingze Xu, Yuanjun Xiong, Dimitris N. Metaxas, Hongwu Peng
bullets: Organizes hidden dimensions into a dense core and successive shells with block lower-triangular matrices.
A single full-width forward pass contains the exact hidden states of all nested sub-networks, keeping computation fixed and scalable.
Introduces μE, extending maximal update parameterization so all sub-networks remain maximally updated simultaneously as the supernet scales.
Hyperparameters tuned on small non-elastic proxies transfer near-optimally to elastic families and larger supernets.
One training run outperforms MatFormer and fully elastic baselines at matched parameter counts, approaching separately trained models with several-times more total steps.

papers.abstract: High-fidelity closed-loop simulation for autonomous driving increasingly relies on dense multi-view 3D reconstruction. While recent feed-forward geometric foundation models have revolutionized per-scene optimization, applying them to continuous, long-horizon driving sequences is computationally intractable due to GPU memory limits and the quadratic complexity of global attention. Existing scaling strategies are fundamentally limited, as causal streaming suffers from compounding scale drift and trajectory deviation, while rigid "chunk-then-align" heuristics fragment global context and produce trajectory discontinuities. To address these limitations, we introduce Drive3R, a block-wise streaming geometric foundation model. Its block-wise causal attention resolves the scalability bottleneck of fully bidirectional attention while avoiding the loss of local future context in purely causal streaming. Its confidence-aware re-anchoring further mitigates long-range drift by detecting unreliable streaming states, re-initializing the KV cache, and stitching refreshed segments through SE(3) alignment. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Drive3R establishes a new state-of-the-art on nuScenes, KITTI, and Waymo. Specifically, on nuScenes, it improves over the recent DVGT-2 baseline from 0.1806 to 0.1081 in AbsRel, from 0.6750 to 0.5344 in point-cloud Accuracy, and from 1.5812 to 0.9092 in ATE.
authors: Tianyi Yang, Haojun Yang, Jipeng Xiao, Xuesong Chen, Shaoshuai Shi, Li Jiang, Zhipeng Zhang
bullets: Addresses GPU-memory and quadratic-attention limits in continuous multi-view 3D reconstruction.
Uses block-wise causal attention to retain local future context while scaling beyond full bidirectional attention.
Detects unreliable streaming states, re-initializes the KV cache, and stitches refreshed segments with SE(3) alignment to reduce drift and trajectory discontinuities.
Achieves state-of-the-art results on nuScenes, KITTI, and Waymo; on nuScenes, it improves AbsRel, point-cloud Accuracy, and ATE over DVGT-2.
