papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought prompting enables reasoning in large language models but produces explanations that are difficult to verify, expensive to generate, and not always faithful. We introduce a Structural Chain-of-Thought framework where models generate executable computational graphs instead of free-form reasoning. The final answer is obtained by deterministically executing the graph. The model is trained using graph-based reinforcement learning that rewards structural validity, answer correctness, and node overlap with reference graphs. Experiments across five benchmarks and four model families show that our method consistently improves accuracy over supervised graph training and can reduce generation length by up to 5-6x compared with standard GRPO and chain-of-thought supervised training. Our faithfulness experiments reveal that models trained with our approach tend to rely on deriving their answers from the generated graphs rather than producing post-hoc rationalizations as usually in chain-of-thought reasoning.
authors: Petr Senatorov, Karim Vafin, Elena Tutubalina, Oleg Somov
bullets: Addresses unverifiable, costly, and potentially unfaithful chain-of-thought explanations.
Generates computational graphs whose final answers are obtained by deterministic execution.
Uses graph-based reinforcement learning to reward valid structure, correct answers, and overlap with reference graphs.

Across five benchmarks and four model families, improves accuracy over supervised graph training and cuts generation length by up to 5–6× versus standard GRPO and supervised chain-of-thought training.
Faithfulness tests suggest models derive answers from their graphs rather than merely producing post-hoc rationalizations.

papers.abstract: Text-to-video (T2V) models are highly sensitive to prompt specificity, while iterative prompt optimization typically improves generation quality only through repeated video generation and vision-language model evaluation at inference time. We propose TIDE, a framework that distills this costly search process into an interpretable and reusable prompt-rewriting Skill. TIDE formulates prompt rewriting as a set of source-conditioned rule modules, each targeting a distinct semantic dimension. Once distilled, the frozen Skill activates the relevant rules and generates both positive and negative prompts in a single LLM call, followed by only one T2V generation, without test-time visual search or backbone fine-tuning. Evolved using only 100 prompts over 14 hours, TIDE achieves prompt-optimization performance comparable to computationally expensive search-based methods. Moreover, when transferred to previously unseen video-generation models, TIDE outperforms existing approaches specifically designed or trained for those models. Code is available at https://github.com/xiningin/TIDE_T2V.
authors: Chengxing Zhou, Yuliang Huang, Jingwei Song
bullets: Targets the high sensitivity of text-to-video quality to prompt specificity and the cost of test-time visual search.
Uses source-conditioned rule modules for distinct semantic dimensions, producing positive and negative prompts together.
Requires no test-time visual search or text-to-video backbone fine-tuning after distillation.
Evolved from 100 prompts over 14 hours and achieves performance comparable to costly search-based methods.
Transfers to unseen video-generation models and outperforms approaches designed or trained for those models.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Pipeline of the proposed TIDE framework. (1) Prompt Rewriting: Given a raw prompt—typically a short user query—the rewriter activates relevant Skill rules to produce an enhanced prompt. (2) Trajectory Generation: The generated video is critiqued, suggestions guide revised prompt candidates, and tournament selection chooses the next-round incumbent; this loop repeats to iteratively improve generation quality. (3) Experience Distillation: Prompt-optimization trajectories yield reusable, dimension-specific patches for the corresponding rule pools. Once full, a pool’s patches update the associated rule and synchronize it with the Skill for subsequent rewriting.

papers.abstract: Diffusion language models (DLMs) offer new opportunities for controllable text generation. However, their controllability, defined as the ability to satisfy task constraints while preserving their original capabilities, remains underexplored. DLMs' bidirectional attention allows control tokens to guide generation from arbitrary positions in the output sequence, but effective guidance depends on the compatibility between their content and placement. To this end, we propose AnchorDLM, a framework in which an anchor generator produces an anchor consisting of a short output fragment and its position for each query. The anchor is placed as control tokens at the specified position to initialize the output sequence of a frozen DLM and guide subsequent denoising. We train the anchor generator with reinforcement learning (RL) to jointly optimize anchor content and placement, using rewards computed from the DLM's generated outputs based on answer correctness and constraint satisfaction. Moreover, through the lens of discrete flow matching (DFM), we interpret anchor placement as helping to reshape the initial velocity field that guides generation. Experiments on code generation and mathematical reasoning across five DLM backbones show that AnchorDLM improves controllability and further yields gains in reasoning performance across diverse benchmarks.
authors: Feiyu Qu, Zheng Huang, Andrea Zanette
bullets: Addresses the challenge of satisfying task constraints without degrading DLM capabilities.
A learned anchor generator produces a short output fragment and its insertion position for each query.
The anchor initializes a frozen DLM, guiding subsequent bidirectional denoising.
Reinforcement learning optimizes anchor content and placement using answer correctness and constraint-satisfaction rewards.
Experiments across five DLM backbones show improvements in controllability and reasoning for code generation and mathematics.

papers.abstract: LLM multi-agent systems split work across agents that communicate through text. An agent summarizes its findings, another agent receives the text. This constrains communication to discrete tokens and costs redundant compute, limiting bandwidth and capabilities of multi-agent systems. Recent works demonstrate KV-cache transfer between LLMs but they either require the LLMs to be within the same family or cannot function across context, thus requiring the receiver to prefill text. We present SwaT (Swarm Telepathy), the first cross-family KV-cache transfer method that allows prefill-free communication in multi-family multi-agent systems. In an agent-to-agent communication setting, combining SwaT with recent advances in KV-cache compaction beats text-to-text communication in both accuracy and speed, with a mean of $40\%$ higher accuracy and a mean of $4\times$ faster wall-clock time. Experiments show SwaT achieves high performance on 17 benchmarks across 12 LLMs and 6 families. Additionally, given a sender Vision-Language Model (VLM), SwaT is able to transfer the vision capabilities to a text-only receiver LLM exceeding text-to-text communication despite SwaT being trained on text-only data. SwaT keeps both sender and receiver models frozen without fine-tuning and only requires $<50M$ tokens and $<1$ GPU-day to train.
authors: Abdulrahman Alabdulkareem, Irene Tenison, Yang Zhang, Yada Zhu, Boris Katz, Dan Gutfreund
bullets: Addresses the bandwidth, redundant-compute, and context limitations of text-only communication between agents.
Transfers KV caches across model families without requiring the receiver to prefill the communicated text.
Combined with KV-cache compaction, it reports 40% higher mean accuracy and 4× faster mean wall-clock time than text-to-text communication.
Evaluated across 17 benchmarks, 12 LLMs, and 6 model families.
Can transfer a sender VLM’s vision capabilities to a text-only receiver, while keeping both models frozen.

papers.abstract: AI coding agents operate in iterative loops: they modify code, run tools, inspect the results, and decide what to do next. We call the design of this process loop engineering, which includes context management, model selection, compaction, and termination. Existing efficiency work mainly compresses tool observations or routes selected turns to cheaper models, but the practical opportunity for these optimizations remains unclear. We analyze 600 publicly released coding-agent trajectories spanning two agent scaffolds and two language models. Median observations contain only 118-286 tokens, while the large build logs commonly used to motivate compression occur near the ninety-ninth percentile. Moreover, 98.6% of input tokens are served from a prefix cache, so flat input pricing overestimates loop cost by roughly 7x on average under near-ideal caching. We derive and empirically validate a closed-form break-even condition for model delegation. Delegation increases cost in half of the evaluated settings, near the predicted boundary. More broadly, turn count explains 84% of the variance in log trajectory cost, compared with 4% for mean observation size; the most expensive trajectories have the most turns despite having the smallest observations. These associations suggest that observation-focused methods target a secondary cost factor, and identify unnecessary turns as the larger and largely unexamined opportunity, though we do not establish that turns can be removed while holding task success fixed. We release TurnCost, a tool for re-scoring trajectory corpora under alternative caching, pricing, compression, and routing policies.
authors: Pramod Kumar, Raj Kumar Pandey
bullets: Analyzes 600 coding-agent trajectories across two scaffolds and two language models.
Median observations are small (118–286 tokens); large build logs are uncommon, appearing near the 99th percentile.
Prefix caching serves 98.6% of input tokens, making flat input pricing overestimate loop cost by about 7× on average.
Turn count explains 84% of variance in log trajectory cost, versus 4% for mean observation size.
Delegation raises cost in half of evaluated settings, and the study does not show that reducing turns preserves task success.

papers.abstract: Quantization plays a crucial role in efficiently deploying deep learning models on resource-constrained devices. Post-training quantization does not require access to the original dataset or retraining the full model. Current methods that achieve high performance close to baseline results typically require INT8 fixed-point integers. However, achieving higher model compression with lower bit-widths often leads to significant performance degradation. In this paper, we propose VLCQ, a post-training quantization method that relaxes the fixed-point encoding constraint, enabling more flexible exploration of quantization techniques through variable-length encoding. This approach achieves competitive or improved performance while reducing bit-widths, without requiring access to training data or model fine-tuning. Extensive experiments on image classification, segmentation, and object detection demonstrate that VLCQ improves model compression and accuracy compared with state-of-the-art post-training quantization approaches. For per-channel quantization, VLCQ surpasses FP32 accuracy and Piece-Wise Linear Quantization (PWLQ) on most evaluated models, achieving up to 6x compression compared with FP32 and up to 1.7x compared with PWLQ. When prioritizing compression with limited accuracy loss, VLCQ achieves up to 12.25x compression compared with FP32 with less than 4% performance degradation. For per-tensor quantization, VLCQ is competitive with Data-Free Quantization (DFQ), while providing greater flexibility to achieve lower bit rates across different tasks and models.

papers.abstract: Argument structures represent how individual arguments interact within a discourse. However, leveraging these structures to infer meaningful knowledge remains challenging, as it requires a formal representation of how argumentative influence propagates across the structure. We propose Neuro-symbolic Argumentation Reasoning System (NARS) for performing persuasiveness detection directly from online discussions. The neural component employs retrieval-augmented iterative LLM reasoning to extract bipolar argument structures, while the symbolic component applies gradual argumentation semantics to propagate argumentative influence over the structure. Using the Webis-CMV-20 corpus, we construct CMV2BAS, a dataset of long, multi-threaded ChangeMyView discussions annotated with LLM-derived bipolar argument structures and labeled with delta events (view change vs.\ no change). We investigate whether gradual argumentation semantics can effectively detect persuasiveness, whether augmenting them with argument quality and graph-based centrality improves performance, and whether symbolic reasoning remains necessary in the presence of modern LLMs. NARS achieves F1=0.57 and AUC=0.56 under its best configuration, outperforming zero-shot Qwen3.6:27B and GPT-oss:20B. We identify support-dominant discussions and long argumentative chains as key failure modes limiting attack influence propagation. Our work demonstrates the feasibility of operationalizing formal gradual argumentation semantics over noisy real-world discourse for scalable macro-level persuasion analysis, while highlighting key challenges and directions for future research in neuro-symbolic argumentation reasoning. We release both CMV2BAS dataset and the NARS framework for public use.
authors: Siddharth Bhargava, Sara Tonelli, Patricia Mart\'in-Rodilla

papers.abstract: Visual agents that interleave reasoning with tool invocation have posed a promising direction for multimodal tasks. However, learning effective tool invocation usually relies on curated question-answer pairs or expert demonstrations at scale, which are expensive to acquire. In this study, we propose Marvo, a simple-yet-effective self-evolution approach that enables learning tool invocation from unlabeled images. Marvo consists of two agents: (1) a challenger that generates question-answer pairs from unlabeled images, and (2) a solver that learns tool invocation by solving questions through reinforcement learning. To encourage effective tool invocation, a good training question should be difficult enough to warrant tool use, yet remain within the solver's capabilities. To this end, we introduce a margin reward to the challenger, defined as solver's performance difference with and without access to tools. With the margin reward, we create an adaptive curriculum that encourages the solver to learn effective tool invocation. Across benchmarks covering agentic reasoning, visual search, mathematical, and general real-world reasoning, Marvo improves average accuracy by up to 7.1\% --- demonstrating margin reward as a preferred way to scale question complexity without human supervision.
authors: Wenxi Yang, Yuzhong Zhao, Baochang Zhang, Yunfan Liu, Qixiang Ye
bullets: Addresses the costly reliance on curated question-answer pairs and expert demonstrations for training tool-using visual agents.

Scope: training relies on unlabeled images, while the approach targets adaptive question complexity without human supervision.

papers.abstract: As text-to-speech (TTS) systems continue to advance, provenance tracking and security verification of synthesized speech have become increasingly important. Audio watermarking provides active provenance by embedding imperceptible, machine-recoverable information into speech. However, existing post-hoc methods typically modify the waveform after synthesis, leaving the watermark vulnerable to compound perturbations. To address this limitation, we propose GAMW, a watermark injection framework integrated into the TTS generation process. Before waveform synthesis, GAMW embeds a content-adaptive multi-bit watermark residual into the generated representation, and its decoding objective combines focal modulation with dynamic per-bit weighting. We train and evaluate GAMW separately on two TTS backbones. With a 16-bit payload, GAMW improves decoding accuracy over the strongest baseline by 9.2 and 23.5 percentage points under individual and compound perturbations, respectively, while maintaining competitive speech quality. Reliable clean-speech decoding is also retained at higher payloads. Code is available at https://github.com/ZConJugaTe/GAMW.
authors: Yihang Zhang, Weicai Yan, Qifei Zhang, Yangyang Wu, Tao Jin

papers.abstract: Larger sample budgets benefit from higher sampling temperatures in LLMs, but what temperature tuning optimizes and why it works remain poorly understood. We seek to answer these questions: we pose decoding as pass@$k$ maximization subject to two constraints that encode critical decoding failure modes: an entropy floor preventing diversity collapse, and a cross-entropy ceiling preventing implausibility. We prove that this maximization takes the form of a single closed-form conditional sampling rule, the \emph{tilted temperature} $q^\star \propto \bigl(p e^{\eta V}\bigr)^{1/T}$. Here, the tilt comes from a verifier potential $V$ that quantifies how likely a partial generation is to eventually pass. Ordinary temperature sampling, verifier-greedy decoding, and reward-tilted policies represent special cases. We further show that, under a natural rule for scaling the diversity budget with sample size $k$, the resulting optimal temperature increases with $k$, turning empirical choice into a theorem. The optimum still needs the unknown verifier potential, which we estimate using two design approaches. In the online setting, our J-EOS algorithm jointly tracks the two constraint multipliers and learns the verifier potential from binary pass/ fail feedback alone. In the offline setting, we show that when the model is calibrated, its log-probability tracks correctness up to an affine map. Under this condition, the tilt collapses into the exponent and the optimum reduces to ordinary temperature sampling. Calibrated Temperature Decoding (CTD) then fits one scalar offline and samples with zero additional inference-time overhead relative to temperature sampling. Building on these decision rules, we design a practical decoding algorithm for code generation and evaluate it alongside CTD on benchmarks including HumanEval and MBPP, showing improvements over standard and adaptive decoding baselines.
authors: Nikolaos Papagiannis, Ananth Grama, Wojciech Szpankowski
bullets: Frames decoding as maximizing pass@$k$ under an entropy floor and cross-entropy ceiling to preserve diversity and plausibility.
Derives the closed-form rule q⋆ ∝ (p e^{ηV})^{1/T}, where V estimates a partial generation’s likelihood of eventually passing.
Proves that the optimal temperature increases with sample budget k under a natural diversity-scaling rule.
Introduces J-EOS for online learning from binary pass/fail feedback and CTD, which fits one offline scalar with no extra inference-time overhead.
Reports improvements over standard and adaptive decoding baselines on code-generation benchmarks including HumanEval and MBPP.

A node is a committed prefix (a state) wt−1; an edge is a token w ∈W , so every node has |W | children (drawn as 2 for legibility) and the tree has depth n. A leaf is a complete sequence wn carrying the terminal reward Jn+1(w n) = U(wn); every step contributes the per-step reward ρt = µE n H(qt) + λ ∑ w qt log pt. The proof is two decoupled passes. Backward (right, Lemma 1): the cost-to-go Jt(w t−1)—equivalently the potential Vt(w | wt−1) := Jt+1(w t−1w) that lives on the child—is formed from the children by a single log-sum-exp, Jt = 1 µ⋆ log ∑ w pλ ⋆ t eµ ⋆Jt+1 ; this uses only (p, U, λ⋆, µ⋆), no policy and no fixed point. The subtrees hanging off distinct children (shaded blue/green) are disjoint, so the tail conditionals decouple across them—this is exactly what lets the global max over q split into an independent per-node max (principle of optimality, Lemma 3). At each node that per-node problem is one Gibbs program (Lemma 2), solved by the tilted-temperature rule q⋆t ∝ ( pt e ηVt )1/T (dashed box). papers.abstract: Large language models can post-edit ASR by using linguistic context to compare N-best hypotheses and rewrite the transcript when needed, often improving WER without retraining the recognizer. However, prompt-only correction is brittle: it may over-edit when top-1 is correct and hallucinate when the reference is absent, and often needs very large models. We propose oracle-guided fine-tuning that turns N-best lists into supervision via three curated pools: corrections (reference in the list but not top-1) to teach selection, regularizers (top-1 correct) to discourage unnecessary rewrites, and hard negatives (reference absent) to suppress hallucination. Fine-tuning on this data provides more effective supervision than random subset fine-tuning for learning a hybrid select-or-rewrite policy, with the clearest gains from around 3B parameters on the proprietary dataset but less conclusive results on CommonVoice, a divergence suggesting that public read-speech text may overlap with LLM pretraining and mask genuine post-editing gains.
authors: Shiran Liu, Gaohui Xu, Sergio Burdisso, Thibault Ba\~neras-Roux, Shashi Kumar, Petr Motlicek
bullets: Prompt-only ASR post-editing can over-edit correct top-1 hypotheses, hallucinate when the reference is absent, and require very large models.
The method builds three supervision pools from N-best lists: corrections, regularizers, and hard negatives.
Fine-tuning learns a hybrid select-or-rewrite policy and is more effective than random subset fine-tuning.
The clearest gains appear with models around 3B parameters on a proprietary dataset, while CommonVoice results are less conclusive.
The CommonVoice divergence may reflect overlap between public read-speech text and LLM pretraining data.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Pipeline overview of the oracle-guided select-or-rewrite framework. ASR beam search produces N-best lists for training and test utterances. Training N-best lists are compared with references and curated into behavior-targeted pools for LoRA fine-tuning, while test N-best lists are given to the LLM for generative selection or rewriting and evaluated with WER.

Fig. 4. Example of LLM-based hypothesis selection using raw ASR hypotheses. The Top-1 hypothesis contains a lexical substitution, where “thanks a lot for” is misrecognized as “things are up with”. The correct phrase appears in lower-ranked N-best candidates, and the LLM selects it to produce the normalized output. This illustrates recoverable-error correction through listwise comparison of raw beam-search hypotheses.

papers.tldr: Oracle-guided fine-tuning teaches language models to select correct ASR hypotheses or rewrite them only when needed, reducing brittle corrections and hallucinations.

papers.abstract: Self-evolving agents are usually scored by endpoint Gain: held-out success after an update minus success before. That difference can credit a frozen rescore as evolution. We introduce Trace Evolution Bench (TEB), a protocol that separates that rescore from a context or weight update, together with three frozen 80/20/40 packs. An update is accepted only when validation does not fall, held-out identifiers never enter the update, and a text update is not ranked with a weight update. The primary scoreboard is coding, graded by hidden unit tests in a closed workspace. On that pack (40 held-out tasks, one family), DeepSeek v4 Pro under no_evolve never changes its policy yet moves 7.5, 5.0, and 12.5 percentage points across three seeds. Of nine text-update cells inspired by GEPA, ACE, and ExpeL, seven have positive excess above that seed's own band, and one gepa_llm seed moves down by the width of its band (-12.5, regression 0.48). GLM and MiniMax do not reproduce that seven-of-nine pattern. No method stays above its own band on every seed of all three models: GLM has two paired cells above their own bands, and MiniMax expel_llm seed 44 is a third (regression 0.30). The methods were fixed on a validation screen before held-out was read. Office, graded by rule-bounded delivery, and manufacturing table QA are separate packs: office DeepSeek does not exceed its own bands (widest 17.5 points), and manufacturing has no paired positive excess beyond its seed band.

bullets: Introduces TEB, which distinguishes frozen rescoring from context or weight updates using validation gates and held-out tasks.

DeepSeek’s no-evolve baseline changed by 7.5, 5.0, and 12.5 percentage points across seeds despite no policy update.
Seven of nine text-update cells exceeded their seed-specific baseline bands, but the pattern did not reproduce for GLM or MiniMax.
Positive excess was not consistent across all seeds and models; office and manufacturing packs showed no comparable robust improvement.

papers.abstract: Beliefs in a Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP) are posterior distributions over the hidden state given the agent's history of actions and observations. They summarize everything the history says about the state, so planning in a POMDP is planning in a Markov decision process (MDP) over beliefs. Belief MDPs have continuous state spaces even for finite POMDPs, and exact planning in them is intractable in general. Planners must therefore approximate beliefs and estimate values. Monte Carlo planners do both inside a search tree, with an approximate belief at every node and a value estimate at every leaf. Approximations usually consist of sets of sampled states, with leaf values coming from rollouts, hand-designed bounds, or learned networks. Policies and values computed from these approximations are limited by their quality, and prior methods with learned networks rely on hand-chosen summaries of the sampled states. A belief representation should be computable from the parent node's representation through the POMDP's dynamics, let the search sample from it, and be learned so that it provides the information that policies and value functions need. We present Belief Embedding Tree Search (BETS), a Monte Carlo planner that meets these requirements by representing each node's belief with a generative distribution embedding (GDE) while updating it through the POMDP dynamics. BETS trains its belief model alongside its policy and value networks through experience, with the realized hidden state of the POMDP as the belief model's training target. We evaluate BETS on six configurations of RockSample, LightDark, and PocMan against BetaZero and three planners without learned components. BETS is competitive or leading on all six, while every baseline falls far behind on at least one. Where beliefs are highest-dimensional, it outperforms them by a large margin, even without search.
authors: Christopher Solinas, Radovan Halu\v{s}ka, Martin Schmid, Michael Buro, Nathan R. Sturtevant, Michael Bowling
bullets: POMDP beliefs are continuous posterior distributions, making exact planning generally intractable.
BETS represents each search-tree node’s belief with a generative distribution embedding (GDE).
The embedding is propagated through POMDP dynamics and supports sampling for Monte Carlo search.
Belief, policy, and value models are trained jointly from experience using the realized hidden state as the belief target.
Across six RockSample, LightDark, and PocMan configurations, BETS is competitive or leading and performs especially well in high-dimensional beliefs, including without search.

papers.abstract: Repetitive, degenerate generation is a persistent failure of LLM decoding, and the standard remedies (temperature, nucleus, and top-$k$ sampling) are static heuristics. By Kac's lemma and the AEP, a stationary source takes time exponential in its entropy to repeat a block. We therefore maximize the entropy of the sampling distributions under one cross-entropy budget that keeps the output plausible under the model. Offline, the solution is temperature sampling, with the inverse temperature as the budget's Lagrange multiplier. \emph{Our contribution is the online problem}: the conditionals $p_1, p_2, \dots$ are revealed one at a time, and the sampling distribution $q_t$ must be chosen causally from $p_1, \dots, p_t$ while the budget couples the entire horizon. The optimal temperature is thus a global shadow price that must be estimated from a prefix. We propose Entropic Online Sampling (EOS), which re-solves for the temperature on each prefix. We prove it loses $O(R\log n)$ entropy against the offline optimum while overshooting the budget by $O(R\log n)$, with $R$ an instance-dependent drift parameter. A budget-tightened variant is exactly feasible at the same rate. Conversely, every exactly feasible online algorithm must lose $\Omega(R)$, so EOS is optimal up to a $\log n$ factor. When the conditionals are drawn from a finite mixture, $R=\tilde{O}(\sqrt{n})$. Experiments confirm that EOS tracks the offline temperature and beats fixed-temperature sampling in entropy.
authors: Jin Sima, Nikolaos Papagiannis, Ananth Grama, Wojciech Szpankowski
bullets: Static temperature, nucleus, and top-k sampling can cause repetitive generation and do not adapt to changing token distributions.
The method maximizes sampling entropy subject to a horizon-wide cross-entropy budget, selecting temperature causally from the observed prefix.
EOS loses only O(R log n) entropy relative to the offline optimum and overshoots the budget by the same order; a tightened variant is exactly feasible.
No exactly feasible online method can avoid an Ω(R) entropy loss, making EOS optimal up to a logarithmic factor.
Experiments show EOS tracks the offline temperature and achieves higher entropy than fixed-temperature sampling.

papers.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models combine specialized experts through an input-dependent routing mechanism, and their sparse variants underpin many modern large-scale systems. Yet the statistical cost of adaptive routing remains only partially understood. We study the estimation error of least-squares MoE estimators when both the experts and the gating network are Lipschitz in their parameters. We represent each MoE as a gate--expert pair in a Gated Hilbert Space, whose norm $\|\cdot\|_\Delta$ separates the contributions of routing and expert discrepancies. Using its empirical representation, we derive an oracle inequality with a fast rate of order $\tilde{\mathcal O}\big((Kd_{\mathrm{pr},e}+d_{\mathrm{pr},g})/n\big)$ for dense MoEs with $K$ experts. For sparse Top-$k$ and Top-$p$ routing, the selection map is discontinuous in the gating parameters. We handle this by partitioning the gating class according to the selection patterns it induces on the sample. The resulting bounds match the dense rate up to an additive routing cost governed by the Natarajan dimension of the selector. We show that such a routing-complexity condition cannot be dropped: Lipschitz continuity in the parameters alone does not suffice. For linear softmax gating, the routing cost is of the same order as the gating term. Finally, for linear experts, we establish a matching minimax lower bound of order $Kd_{\mathrm{pr},e}/n$, showing that the rates are optimal up to logarithmic factors.
authors: Sagar Ghosh, Huy Nguyen, Alessandro Rinaldo
bullets: Derives fast-rate oracle inequalities for least-squares MoE estimators with Lipschitz experts and gating networks.
Dense MoEs achieve rates of order Õ((K d_pr,e + d_pr,g)/n).
Sparse Top-k and Top-p routing incur an additional cost tied to the selector’s Natarajan dimension because routing is discontinuous.
Shows Lipschitz parameterization alone is insufficient to control sparse-routing complexity; linear softmax gating has routing cost comparable to its gating term.
For linear experts, a matching minimax lower bound establishes optimality up to logarithmic factors.

papers.abstract: Real-world Vision-Language Navigation (VLN) requires agents to act under partial observability, where map structure, semantic cues, and target locations may be incomplete or incorrectly inferred by foundation models. This paper presents a lightweight, training-free, and uncertainty-aware framework for cooperative multi-agent multi-target search in mapless environments. Instead of learning an end-to-end navigation policy, the framework separates high-level semantic reasoning from low-level execution through a scalable graph-optimization backbone. Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) serve only as hypothesis generators, proposing semantic zones, target-location cues, and possible navigable connections. These outputs are treated as uncertain priors and further refined using online observations and graph-context evidence. Cooperative navigation is then formulated as a rolling-horizon multi-agent mixed-integer linear program with a lexicographic objective that first maximizes target-directed reward and then reduces travel distance, uncertain-edge use, and repeated visits. Experiments derived from 100 Matterport3D test cases show that the proposed framework improves target coverage and search efficiency over representative baseline methods, while shared information and joint planning enable more balanced workloads across agents. By operating on an abstract graph without relying on embodiment-specific policy parameters, the framework scales across varying numbers of agents and targets, generalizes to unseen environments, and accommodates different perception modules and low-level controllers without task-specific retraining.
authors: Fan Pu, Keshu Wu, Jiwan Jiang, Shiyu Shen, Zhiwen Fan, Zhengzhong Tu, Jiachen Li, Yang Zhou
bullets: Addresses partial observability and unreliable foundation-model inferences in multi-target embodied search.
Uses MLLMs as hypothesis generators, then refines semantic zones, target cues, and connectivity with online observations and graph context.
Plans via rolling-horizon multi-agent mixed-integer linear programming with lexicographic priorities for target reward, shorter travel, fewer uncertain edges, and fewer revisits.
Experiments on 100 Matterport3D test cases report improved target coverage and search efficiency over representative baselines, with more balanced workloads.
Its abstract-graph design supports varying agent and target counts, perception modules, and low-level controllers without task-specific retraining.

papers.abstract: Contrastive learning has become the standard paradigm for multimodal representation learning, aligning semantically matched pairs while separating mismatched ones in a shared embedding space. Although various contrastive training strategies have been proposed across negative selection, batch construction, and gradient modulation, their actual effectiveness under controlled, reproducible conditions remains poorly understood. This motivates a fundamental question: Do sophisticated contrastive strategies consistently bring meaningful downstream gains in multimodal embedding learning? To address this, we systematically evaluate representative strategies under a unified benchmarking framework on MMEB. Surprisingly, direct evaluations reveal that most existing strategies offer marginal gains over a standard aligned baseline, with several even degrading overall performance. To uncover the underlying failure modes, we introduce an MLLM-as-a-Judge diagnostic framework that dissects top-1 retrieval behaviors into labeled positives, false negatives (unlabeled valid matches), and hard/easy negative errors. Our systematic analysis yields three key insights: (1) Gradient distortion: Upweighting gradients from high-similarity negatives consistently hurts downstream generalization; (2) Distribution illusion: Wider separation between positive and negative similarity distributions does not necessarily translate to better retrieval performance; and (3) Synergistic training: While false-negative mitigation or hard-batch construction yields limited gains in isolation, integrating hard-negative mining, false-negative mitigation, and hard-batch construction achieves optimal performance, delivering an average improvement of 6.0% on MMEB with Qwen2-VL-2B. Overall, our findings demystify popular contrastive strategies and provide actionable recipes for training universal multimodal embedding models.
authors: Duo Li, Haojun Pan, Zuhao Yang, Xintong Wang, Chengfu Huo, Shijian Lu, Liang Ding
bullets: Most existing negative-selection, batch-construction, and gradient-modulation methods offer marginal gains over a standard aligned baseline, and some reduce performance.
An MLLM-as-a-Judge framework diagnoses top-1 retrieval errors as labeled positives, false negatives, or hard/easy negative mistakes.
Upweighting gradients from high-similarity negatives consistently harms downstream generalization.
Greater separation between positive and negative similarity distributions does not necessarily yield better retrieval.
The strongest results come from jointly using hard-negative mining, false-negative mitigation, and hard-batch construction.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of the MLLM-as-a-Judge analysis framework. Given the same query and labeled positive, we collect top-1 predictions produced by different contrastive training strategies. The MLLM judge categorizes the prediction as a labeled positive, an alternative valid positive (i.e., false negative), a hard-negative error, or an easy-negative error. This decomposition enables a more fine-grained analysis than standard exact-match Precision@1.

Figure C.1: Overview of the MLLM-as-Judge prompt. The judge receives the query, the datasetdesignated positive, the model’s top-1 prediction, and an explicit mapping between images and their roles. It first verifies the designated positive and then categorizes the top-1 prediction as the designated positive, a false negative, a hard negative, an easy negative, or an uncertain case. Task-specific criteria guide judgments across the five MMEB task families, and a constrained JSON schema enables automatic parsing and aggregation.

Figure 2: Similarity distributions of nine training strategies on MMEB. All methods are evaluated on the same 7,200 queries, comprising 200 randomly sampled cases from each of the 36 datasets. Positive (P) denotes the similarity between a query and its designated target, while Hard Negative (HN) and Easy Negative (EN) denote the mean similarities to its Top-5 and Bottom-5 non-positive candidates, respectively. OVL(P,HN) and OVL(P,EN) measure the distribution overlap between the Positive distribution and the HN and EN distributions, respectively; lower values indicate better distributional separation.

Table 1: Overview of representative contrastive training strategies. Dependencies indicate whether a method requires external scoring or additional preprocessing. Entries under Optimization Dimensions indicate what aspects each contrastive learning method targets explicitly. Static denotes that the corresponding optimization signal is fixed before training, whereas Adaptive denotes that it evolves with the student model.

Table B.3: Ablation study of B3 using Qwen2-VL-2B on MMEB. We remove false-negative mitigation (FN), hard-negative mining (HN), or batch construction (BC) from the full B3 framework while keeping the remaining training and evaluation settings unchanged. Scores are mean Precision@1 (%) over the corresponding datasets, and Overall is the average across all 36 MMEB datasets. The best result in each column is highlighted in bold.

Table 4: MLLM-as-a-Judge analysis of top-1 predictions on MMEB. All methods are evaluated on the same 7,200 cases, with 200 cases sampled from each of the 36 datasets. Labeled Positive matches the annotated target; False Negative is a different but semantically valid answer; and Semantic Valid is their sum. Hard Negative denotes a related but incorrect prediction, while Easy Negative denotes a clearly irrelevant prediction; Semantic Error is their sum. GM, FN, HN, and BC denote gradient modulation, false-negative mitigation, hard-negative mining, and batch construction, respectively. Arrows indicate the preferred direction, and the best results are shown in bold.

Table 3: Comparison of multimodal contrastive training strategies on MMEB using Qwen2-VL2B. The evaluation metric is mean Precision@1 (%) across the corresponding datasets. IND and OOD denote the averages over in-distribution and out-of-distribution datasets, respectively. GM, FN, HN, and BC denote gradient modulation, false-negative mitigation, hard-negative mining, and batch construction, respectively. Training time denotes the training wall-clock time; one-time preprocessing costs are excluded. The best results are shown in bold.

Table 2: Training-setting alignment. We align the learning rate (LR), maximum number of visual tokens, LoRA rank, and pooling strategy for the VLM2Vec baseline on MMEB using Qwen2-VL2B-Instruct. papers.abstract: Industrial anomaly detection benchmarks have advanced rapidly, yet they remain largely static and therefore underrepresent deployment settings in which inspection systems must be extended from one industrial component to another over time. In our setting, continual industrial anomaly detection is framed as a task-incremental problem: each component defines a task, while the learning objective remains semi-supervised. The goal extends beyond conventional anomaly detection, since models should preserve their performance on all components as they are sequentially exposed to new components. This framing is especially relevant because many existing industrial pipelines either assume fully supervised defect labels or study only isolated datasets, leaving open the question of how semi-supervised anomaly detectors behave across a sequence of heterogeneous components. We address this gap by organizing the benchmark as a sequence of related component-level tasks and by defining multiple scenarios, including random, easy-to-hard, and hard-to-easy. In addition to single-dataset continual scenarios, we propose challenging scenarios spanning across multiple datasets. We further evaluate continual performance from two complementary perspectives: image-level anomaly detection and pixel-level anomaly localization. By recasting industrial anomaly detection as a continual benchmark rather than a static train/test problem, our work establishes a concrete path toward studying knowledge retention, adaptation, and generalization in evolving industrial environments.
authors: {\L}ukasz Marcjan, Dorota Wilk-Ko{\l}odziejczyk, Roberto Corizzo
bullets: Frames each industrial component as a task in a task-incremental, semi-supervised setting.
Evaluates learning sequences under random, easy-to-hard, and hard-to-easy orderings.
Includes both single-dataset and cross-dataset continual scenarios involving heterogeneous components.
Measures performance at image-level anomaly detection and pixel-level anomaly localization.
Targets knowledge retention, adaptation, and generalization in evolving industrial inspection environments.

papers.abstract: Can a volume that reproduces every external RGB view still have an incorrect density? We study this question in emission-absorption rendering with an independently parameterized, physically bounded effective source. Appearance compensates a density change by replacing the radiance that it removes from the rest of each ray. We characterize the surviving density information with a shared spatial appearance field. Our first result is an optimal density-only gain after finite-degree spherical-harmonic source refitting. A coupled tensor gauge and physical localized packets identify the sharp limiting nonlinear inverse coefficient as its reciprocal. Our second result realizes positive gain at every fixed finite degree for a residual set of isotropic spatial sources at one fixed density. At the same references, growing angular capacity hides a fixed nonzero density error while retaining physicality and any prescribed finite set of smoothness bounds. Local identifiability and the absence of a capacity-uniform recovery modulus therefore coexist. Our third result constructs an exact physical SH2 ambiguity: central density doubles and relative density $L^2$ error exceeds $14.52\%$, yet every external RGB ray is unchanged. We connect these continuum results to shared finite representations, continuous pixel measurements and density-sensitive acquisition. Complete-class certificates separate SH0, SH1 and SH2 fits at one learned density. Finite-camera results expose the distinct role of spatial capacity, and transmission measurements separate otherwise identical RGB fields. Controlled training tests and captured-smoke profiles supply mechanism evidence with explicit observation scopes. The results show why rendering accuracy alone cannot certify density: recovery also depends on appearance capacity, spatial resolution and measurement design.
authors: Jianghong Zhou
bullets: Studies density identifiability in emission–absorption volume rendering with physically bounded, independently parameterized sources.
Characterizes how finite spherical-harmonic appearance capacity limits density recovery, while increasing angular or spatial capacity can hide fixed density errors.
Constructs an exact physical SH2 ambiguity where central density doubles and relative density error exceeds 14.52% without changing any external RGB ray.
Shows that local identifiability can coexist with no capacity-uniform recovery guarantee.

Finds that transmission measurements and density-sensitive acquisition can distinguish cases that RGB rendering alone cannot; conclusions depend on appearance capacity, spatial resolution, and measurement design.

papers.abstract: Recent bidirectional encoders have been modernized with innovations from causal large language models (LLMs). However, the pretraining recipe itself remains inherited from small-scale conventions, leaving encoders underoptimized, with no single model performing competitively across both classification and retrieval tasks. In this work, we investigate how far encoder performance can be pushed by revisiting core design choices in training, revealing three key findings: (1) Encoders saturate on downstream tasks beyond a few trillion tokens, indicating that additional compute past this point does not help. (2) Across model sizes, lower masking ratios benefit classification while higher ones benefit retrieval, contradicting prior work suggesting larger ratios for larger models. (3) Distillation with pruning improves classification at low masking ratios but degrades retrieval at high ones. Guided by these findings, we present UltraBERT, a single encoder that assigns separate LM heads to low and high masking ratios within a batch and restricts the distillation objective to the low ratio. To our knowledge, UltraBERT is the first encoder to achieve state of the art on both classification and retrieval tasks, reaching 91.0 on GLUE and 47.7 on BEIR. Together, these results show how far encoder performance can be pushed and provide a principled basis for compute allocation, masking ratio design, and knowledge transfer in bidirectional models.
authors: Jungwoo Park, Taewhoo Lee, Jaewoo Kang
bullets: Encoder performance saturates after a few trillion pretraining tokens, limiting the value of additional compute.
Lower masking ratios favor classification, while higher ratios favor retrieval across model sizes.
Distillation with pruning helps classification at low masking ratios but harms retrieval at high ratios.
UltraBERT uses separate language-modeling heads for low and high masking ratios and applies distillation only to the low ratio.
It reports state-of-the-art results on both GLUE (91.0) and BEIR (47.7).

papers.abstract: Reliable individual monitoring is essential for dairy cattle welfare and early heat stress detection in Precision Livestock Farming (PLF). However, translating raw multi-camera videos into automated diagnostics remains challenging due to disconnected tracking and recognition pipelines and complex physical environments. Dense mutual occlusions and cross-camera viewpoint variations fragment identities, while environmental noise, including camera vibrations, and limited agricultural data obscure subtle heat stress cues such as rapid breathing and flank undulations. To bridge low-level visual features and high-level behavioral diagnostics, we propose CowCare, a unified framework combining viewpoint-robust tracking with spatiotemporal heat stress recognition. Its tracking module, CowTrack, maintains cross-camera identity consistency through a View-Decoupled Aggregation Network (VDA-Net). Instead of relying on static global representations, VDA-Net aggregates localized textures under heavy occlusion and uses a Viewpoint Decoupling Transformer (VDT) to suppress transient viewpoint variations. CowTrack further incorporates a causal online self-supervision mechanism for continuous adaptation to dynamic farm scenes. The resulting tracklets are subsequently processed by TSDF-Net, a fine-grained video understanding network. Its Temporal Stabilization and Aggregation Module (TSAM) suppresses high-frequency jitter, while a Diffusion Semantic Prior (DSP) uses frozen pre-trained diffusion semantics to enhance subtle behavioral signals and mitigate overfitting. Extensive evaluations on two real-world farm benchmarks demonstrate the framework's effectiveness: CowTrack achieves 83.48% HOTA and 87.72% IDF1 for global multi-object tracking on MVCow, and TSDF-Net achieves 87.72% Top-1 accuracy on HSCow. These results establish CowCare as a robust end-to-end framework for automated livestock health monitoring.

papers.abstract: Transformer architectures have achieved strong results in natural language processing and computer vision, but their deployment is limited by high computational, memory and storage costs, motivating research into model compression techniques, such as pruning, while preserving performance. Prior work has shown substantial redundancy in large language models (LLMs), and redundancy in vision transformers has also been investigated, but it remains less systematically analyzed than in LLMs. In this work, we extend similarity-based redundancy analysis to vision models by measuring cosine similarity between layer inputs and outputs to identify transformations with minimal impact. We study redundancy patterns across several transformer architectures and find that deep vision transformers such as DINOv2 and SwinV2, like language models, exhibit significant redundancy. We then evaluate how this redundancy can be exploited to improve efficiency, analyzing the trade-off between inference speed and performance degradation under different pruning strategies. Our results show that moderate pruning can yield substantial acceleration with limited impact on accuracy, and that 20% of the DINOv2 blocks can be removed without any retraining, for a 1.24x throughput gain and a 20% lower energy per image at a relative accuracy loss below 1% on ImageNet-1K. We further propose a model selection pipeline that automatically identifies the best pruned configuration for a given dataset, reducing FLOPs by 13% to 27% on average across architectures with an average accuracy change between -0.3 and +1.0 points.
authors: Alessandro Viespoli, Loris Nanni
bullets: Analyzes redundancy by measuring cosine similarity between layer inputs and outputs across multiple Vision Transformer architectures.

Moderate pruning provides favorable speed–accuracy trade-offs; 20% of DINOv2 blocks can be removed without retraining for 1.24× throughput and 20% lower energy per image, with under 1% relative accuracy loss on ImageNet-1K.
A model-selection pipeline automatically chooses pruned configurations, reducing FLOPs by 13–27% on average with accuracy changes from −0.3 to +1.0 points.

papers.abstract: Tabular foundation models adapt to new datasets through in-context learning (ICL), and, like most transformers, they tie computational depth to the number of independently parameterized layers. We ask whether the ICL stage of such a model needs a distinct set of parameters for every layer, or only depth. We introduce Tab-Loop, which replaces the 12 untied ICL blocks of TabICLv2 with 4 tied blocks applied $k$ times and changes nothing else: the encoders, decoder, synthetic prior and training recipe are shared with an untied baseline trained for the same compute. At matched pretraining compute (18.2 EFLOP) and matched inference compute (12 block applications), Tab-Loop matches the baseline with 62\% fewer parameters (10.4M vs.\ 27.6M): held-out log loss is 0.4583 vs.\ 0.4588, mean accuracy on 200 TALENT datasets is 84.10\% vs.\ 83.92\%, and Elo on 38 TabArena datasets is 1409 vs.\ 1396. A 4-block untied control with Tab-Loop's parameter count, which sees 32\% more training tables for the same compute, trails both (83.46\%; Elo 1343). Because weights are shared, depth becomes a choice made at inference. Accuracy rises with the number of loops through the trained range and holds beyond it, and continued training with deeper loops extends the useful range, reaching the baseline's stage-2 scores at 4--5$\times$ its inference compute. At this scale, the ICL stage of a tabular foundation model needs depth more than it needs distinct parameters.
authors: Tejas Vaidhya, Gaurav Sahu, Irina Rish
bullets: Replaces 12 untied ICL blocks with 4 tied blocks repeated multiple times, leaving other components and training matched to the baseline.
At matched compute, uses 10.4M versus 27.6M parameters while achieving comparable or slightly better log loss, TALENT accuracy, and TabArena Elo.
A parameter-matched 4-block untied model performs worse, suggesting recurrence—not merely parameter reduction—drives the gains.
Inference-time loop count controls effective depth; accuracy improves across the trained range and remains robust beyond it.
With further training using deeper loops, the model reaches baseline stage-2 scores at 4–5× the baseline inference compute.

papers.abstract: While asynchronous execution enables VLA models to operate in real-time environments by predicting the next chunk during execution, it inevitably introduces boundary misalignment with the committed action stream. Existing delay-aware solutions address this at the prohibitive cost of extensive retraining, architectural modifications, or fixed-prefix inpainting that inflates computation when low latency is vital. To address these problems, we propose FreeBar, a training-free real-time inference plugin that enables robust asynchronous execution with only marginal additional inference cost by casting chunk alignment in flow-based VLAs as barrier-guided action-space constraint. Specifically, FreeBar introduces a lightweight Control Barrier Function (CBF)-inspired consistency constraint between consecutive action chunks and solves the resulting correction in closed form, avoiding costly backpropagation through the VLA action head. By progressively tightening the consistency bound during generation, FreeBar aligns generated chunks with the committed execution stream while preserving early-stage generative and within-chunk future action flexibility,. Across Kinetix, RoboCasa, and diverse real-world robotic platforms with multiple VLA backbones, FreeBar improves success rates over naive asynchronous execution by 10%--15% on average, with larger gains in highly dynamic scenarios. It also preserves real-time computational efficiency, decreasing inference latency per action chunk over 45% than RTC. Additionally, as a universal plugin, FreeBar remains robust across distinct latency environments, base policies, and hyperparameter settings.
authors: Wenbo Yu, Jifan Li, Wenke Xia, Yuchen Li, Yizhuo Zhang, Pei Ren, Zhengping Che, Di hu
bullets: Addresses boundary misalignment between predicted action chunks and the committed execution stream.
Uses a lightweight Control Barrier Function-inspired constraint between consecutive chunks.
Computes corrections in closed form, avoiding backpropagation through the VLA action head.
Progressively tightens consistency during generation while preserving early and within-chunk action flexibility.
Improves success rates by 10%–15% on average and reduces per-chunk inference latency by over 45% versus RTC across simulated and real robotic settings.

papers.abstract: Embodied agents built on foundation models rely on an execution harness to organize observations, guide actions, and incorporate execution feedback into subsequent decisions. Failures can arise not only from limited model capabilities, but also from how the harness presents evidence and guides its use. These model-external mechanisms provide an adaptation target without updating model parameters, but task-specific interaction experience can be costly to collect. Task-level outcomes alone do not reveal whether relevant evidence was missing from the model input or was available but inadequately used. Moreover, these two aspects are coupled: effective action guidance may require evidence that the current context omits, while exposing that evidence alone does not ensure an appropriate response. We introduce EnactOpt, which uses limited execution feedback to jointly evolve reusable textual skills and context-construction code while keeping the underlying models and runtime fixed. It diagnoses adjacent decisions by relating action feedback to the actual model input and subsequent action. Structured episode summaries guide joint revisions through prompt-level edit operators, and candidate harnesses undergo compatibility checks and validation-based retention. Across VLABench, ALFWorld, and Embodied Agent Interface (EAI), EnactOpt improves task success by approximately 10-27 percentage points over the initial harnesses and outperforms the evaluated GEPA, TextGrad, and Trace2Skill baselines. These gains extend to task conditions not used for harness evolution or candidate selection. The results support a complementary route to embodied adaptation: turning limited execution experience into reusable behavioral improvements by jointly refining how evidence is presented and acted upon.
authors: ZhiYuan Feng, Zhuoshi Pan, Zhaolu Kang, Zhongxia Chen, Shuo Yang, Sen Ye, Heng Wang, Han Li

Improves success by approximately 10–27 percentage points across VLABench, ALFWorld, and EAI, including unseen task conditions.

papers.abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) have excelled in joint visual and language understanding, particularly in image captioning. However, LVLMs remain prone to object hallucination, describing non-existent entities in the given image. Previous remedies, including dataset-enhanced supervised training and reinforcement learning from human feedback, show promise but rely heavily on costly human involvement, limiting scalability. To address this, we propose a reinforcement learning framework to mitigate object hallucination in LVLM-based image captioning, driven entirely by natural language processing (NLP) metrics. While optimizing reinforcement learning solely on NLP metrics offers scalability, it also introduces pitfalls: reward hacking, sparse feedback, and costly training. Our framework sidesteps these by introducing an Object Consistency Score (OCS) capturing both correctness and coverage of objects, incorporating KL-regularization for denser token-level guidance, and designing a lightweight PPO variant that fine-tunes adapters atop a frozen LVLM backbone, achieving efficiency and stability. Extensive experiments on the InstructBLIP baseline demonstrate the effectiveness and generalizability of our framework, achieving a substantial hallucination reduction of up to 41\% on the COCO dataset and 29\% on the Visual Genome. Furthermore, the framework can enhance caption quality by incorporating complementary evaluation metrics such as BERTScore and METEOR. These results reveal a broader insight in multimodal learning: LVLMs can effectively self-correct hallucinations using metric feedback, motivating deeper exploration into scalable reinforcement frameworks that significantly reduce human effort.
authors: Thanh Nguyen, Hee Suk Yoon, Tung Minh Luu, Eunseop Yoon, Chang D. Yoo
bullets: Targets hallucinated objects—entities described in captions but absent from images—without human supervision.
Uses an Object Consistency Score to measure object correctness and coverage, plus KL regularization for denser guidance.
Introduces a lightweight PPO variant that fine-tunes adapters while keeping the LVLM backbone frozen.
Reports hallucination reductions of up to 41% on COCO and 29% on Visual Genome with InstructBLIP.
Can also improve caption quality using complementary metrics such as BERTScore and METEOR.

figures.caption: FIGURE 2: Detailed architecture of our framework. Specifically, the Policy Network is crafted by augmenting the shared LVLM with delicately learnable soft prompts. Meanwhile, the Value Network is formed by replacing the LLM Head with a Linear Value head. Notably, all parameters of the LVLM remain shared and frozen, with only a very small fraction (less than 0.01% LVLM weight) of trainable parameters added to the LVLM for the meticulous modeling of the policy network and value network.

FIGURE 4: Qualitative comparison between the original InstructBLIP model (Base) and the fine-tuned InstructBLIP model trained with the proposed framework (Ours) on the COCO dataset. Hallucinated objects are highlighted in red. Compared with the baseline, our method generates captions that are more grounded in the visual content and significantly reduces object hallucinations.

FIGURE 3: Simplified overview of the framework’s network components: policy network, value network, and reference network. All networks share the same frozen LVLM as its foundation. The reference network mirrors the LVLM identically, while the value and policy networks incorporate a lightweight adapter into the shared LVLM.

papers.abstract: WavePhaseNet introduced frequency-resolved semantic representations, QuantumPhaseNet introduced gauge-covariant phase connections, and ModularPhaseNet made a finite cyclic phase channel and its cycle holonomy computable in an ordinary Transformer. These constructions are complementary, yet they do not by themselves separate an observed collection of pairwise relations into a globally consistent direction, circulation around local compositions, and circulation that persists around a larger unfilled cycle. HodgePhaseNet addresses this separation by representing semantic transitions as an antisymmetric real-valued 1-cochain on a finite oriented simplicial complex. With vertex-edge incidence matrix $B_1$ and edge-face incidence matrix $B_2$, every such field has a unique orthogonal decomposition $\Omega = B_1^T\Phi + B_2\Psi + H$, where $B_1H=0$ and $B_2^TH=0$. The three component fields are unique even when their potentials are not. We give explicit projectors, a sparse implementation, integrability and gauge results, a verified numerical example, and a redesigned attention interface. The attention bias is defined on allowed ordered query-key pairs, remains consistent under arbitrary choices of edge orientation, and preserves a decoder's causal information boundary by constructing its complex from the visible prefix. Gauge invariance of the attention output is conditional on using invariant or appropriately compensated features. A simple difference of vertex embeddings has no coexact or harmonic component; a genuine relation encoder is therefore indispensable. Local circulation is not automatically contradiction, and harmonic flow is not automatically missing knowledge. These interpretations and any reduction in factual error require controlled empirical evaluation. This paper presents a mathematical and architectural proposal, not external natural-language performance results.
authors: Kiyotaka Kasubuchi, Kazuo Fukiya
bullets: Represents semantic transitions as an antisymmetric real-valued 1-cochain on an oriented simplicial complex.
Uses incidence matrices to obtain a unique orthogonal decomposition into exact, coexact, and harmonic components.
Provides explicit projectors, sparse implementation, integrability and gauge results, and a verified numerical example.
Introduces an orientation-consistent attention bias built from the decoder’s visible prefix to preserve causal information boundaries.
Presents a mathematical and architectural proposal; factual-error reductions and other language-performance benefits remain unevaluated.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Complementary roles of the earlier PhaseNet methods. Their features feed a separately learned real edge field; the Hodge layer separates that field into gradient, local coexact, and global harmonic components before returning structured features to attention.

Figure 2: One-head computation path. All decoder features and the complex are constructed from the visible prefix. Edge orientation is converted for each ordered query–key pair; the compensated gradient D is used only when its gauge assumptions hold. The learned edge bias precedes the causal mask and softmax.

Figure 3: Five-vertex example of Section 7.1. The blue triangle (1, 2, 3) is a filled face and carries the coexact field C; the orange triangle (1, 4, 5) has no face and supports a harmonic cycle H. Arrows follow the edge orientations in (24); the annotated values are component fields, not the full Ω.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a Hodge-decomposition-based attention interface for Transformers, relevant to LLM architecture research.
papers.title: HodgePhaseNet: Discrete Hodge Decomposition of Semantic Flows in Transformer Attention
papers.tldr: HodgePhaseNet decomposes Transformer semantic relations into globally consistent flow, local circulation, and larger-cycle circulation using discrete Hodge theory.

papers.abstract: With the rapid evolution of large language models (LLMs), there is an increasing demand for effective personalization techniques that can adapt model behavior to individual user preferences. Personalized LLMs must infer a user's query-dependent preferences from limited, heterogeneous, and evolving interaction histories. Existing approaches rely primarily on in-context personalization, parametric adaptation, or personalized reward modeling, but respectively incur recurring costs in context management, model optimization and deployment, or multi-candidate generation and scoring. These limitations become particularly restrictive when user observations are sparse and the preference evidence relevant to each query varies across contexts and over time. To address these challenges, we propose \modelname, a fine-grained and instance-tailored steering framework that dynamically generates sample-level interference vectors from user data and injects them into the model's forward pass for personalized adaptation. Our approach introduces: match contrast that produces user-relevant signals, fine-grained steering component that captures nuanced signals by hooking activations from attention and MLP layers, and query-conditioned aggregation module that synthesizes these signals into contextually relevant enhancements. Extensive experiments across diverse scenarios, including short-to-long text generation, and web function calling, validate the effectiveness and compatibility of \modelname. Results show that our method consistently brings significant performance gains, and show extreme superiority in fast-shifting and data-sparse environments. Additionally, \modelname rids us of training cycles and incurs light overhead of storage or inference latency. These make \modelname a strong and real-world deployable method. Implementation is available \footnote{https://anonymous.4open.science/r/FleetPilot}.
authors: Kounianhua Du, Jianxing Liu, Kangning Zhang, Wenxiang Jiao, Yuan Lu, Jiarui Jin, Jianghao Lin, Weiwen Liu, Yong Yu, Weinan Zhang
bullets: Targets personalization with sparse, heterogeneous, evolving user histories and query-dependent preferences.
Generates sample-level interference vectors and injects them into the model’s forward pass.
Combines match contrast, attention/MLP activation steering, and query-conditioned signal aggregation.
Validated across text generation and web function-calling scenarios, with reported gains especially in fast-changing and data-sparse settings.
Designed to avoid training cycles while adding limited storage and inference overhead, though specific quantitative results are not provided.

figures.caption: Fig. 2 Overview of FleetPilot. 1) Steering Vectors Preparation. During this stage, we construct contrastive prompts from user logs, where relevant context retrieved from personal corpus is concatenated with target query to form the positive sample and irrelevant context sampled from other users is concatenated with target query to form the negative sample. For each positive sample, we generate K negative samples. Each pair is then fed into the LLM in the teacher forcing mode, during which the response tokens’ activations of attention and MLP blocks are hooked. We store the difference between two sample activations of a pair to serve as the steering vector, with the text of each pair being the key for indexing convenience. 2) Instance-Tailored Personalized Adaptation and Inference. During this stage, we sample from target user’s steering vectors set to interfere model for personalized output. Concretely, we rank the similarity between query text and sample pair text to select the top-k steering vectors, which are then aggregated and injected into LLM for personalized adaptation.

Fig. 1 Personalization paradigms and the design of FleetPilot. Left: prompt-based personalization supplies retrieved history through a context window, where noisy evidence and limited model capacity constrain its use. Middle: parametric adaptation and personalized reward modeling introduce optimization or candidate-scoring stages, with challenges in sparse-data fitting, model updates, storage, and best-of-N inference. Right: inference-time steering modifies intermediate activations in a frozen LLM, motivated by the linear representation hypothesis. FleetPilot adapts this principle to personalization through three design changes: response contrast to matched contrast, whole-layer hooking to fine-grained hooking, and user-tailored to instance-tailored steering.
Fig. 3 Illustration of the heterogeneous data.
Fig. 5 Hyperparameter sensitivity analysis.
Fig. 6 Main effects analysis on Headline Generation.
Fig. 7 Main effects analysis on Abstract Writing.
Fig. 8 Main effects analysis on PersonalWAB.

papers.title: FleetPilot: Fine-Grained Steering Empowers Real-World LLM Personalization
papers.tldr: FleetPilot personalizes LLM behavior by dynamically steering internal activations using query-relevant signals from a user’s interaction history, without retraining.

papers.abstract: Sparse-view Cone-Beam Computed Tomography (CBCT) reconstruction is essential for reducing radiation dose and scan effort, but remains underconstrained due to limited projection information. Recent 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)-based CBCT reconstruction methods rely on gradient-driven densification, which becomes unstable under sparse acquisition and often leads to over-smoothed structures. We propose AD-GS, an Anatomical Density-guided 3D Gaussian Splatting framework that formulates Gaussian densification as an attenuation-aware Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampling process. By interpreting Gaussians as samples from an underlying anatomical attenuation distribution, AD-GS adaptively concentrates representation capacity in high-attenuation regions, enabling sharper structural boundaries under sparse projections. To further constrain reconstruction, we incorporate a semantic regularization based on zero-shot features from Segment Anything in Medical Images, enforcing multi-view consistency through semantic priors. Experiments on the ToothFairy3 dental CBCT dataset demonstrate that AD-GS achieves superior structural fidelity and boundary preservation compared with existing 3DGS-based approaches under sparse-view settings within the dental and maxillofacial setting. Code is available at https://github.com/yulinjiaxue/AD-GS-BMVC2026.
authors: Zonglin Li, Kexian Xie, Feiran Li, Chu Zhou, Yixing Huang, Ruiyang Chen, Zhanyu Ma, Heng Guo
bullets: Addresses instability and over-smoothing caused by gradient-based Gaussian densification under sparse projections.
Models densification as attenuation-aware MCMC sampling to focus representation capacity on high-attenuation anatomical regions.
Uses zero-shot Segment Anything in Medical Images features for semantic regularization and multi-view consistency.
On the ToothFairy3 dataset, it improves structural fidelity and boundary preservation over existing 3DGS-based methods.
Scope: sparse-view dental and maxillofacial CBCT reconstruction.

figures.caption: Figure 5: Evaluation on Downstream Task: Tooth Segmentation [19]. Side and frontal views of segmentation results obtained from different CBCT reconstructions. Geometric errors with respect to ground truth (GT), measured by SSD, are visualized using color maps. Our volume yields the most complete tooth segmentation and lowest SSD.

papers.selection_reason: 3D Gaussian Splatting for sparse-view CBCT reconstruction is a 3D reconstruction method.
papers.title: AD-GS: Anatomical Density-guided 3D Gaussian Splatting for Sparse-View Dental CBCT Reconstruction
papers.tldr: AD-GS improves sparse-view dental CBCT reconstruction by guiding 3D Gaussian allocation with anatomical attenuation and semantic consistency.

papers.abstract: Can an autonomous AI agent reverse engineer a binary as well as a skilled human analyst? Do they adopt the same strategy, and can agents scale to real-world programs? We compare human and LLM-based software reverse engineering (SRE): nine models tackle two compact static-analysis challenges previously solved by human analysts, scored with a common understanding rubric, and we record their complete interactions with IDA Pro. This lets us compare not only what humans and agents recover, but also how they investigate a binary. The best agents (GPT-5.5 Pro, Claude Opus 4.8, and Kimi K3) achieve statistically human-competitive understanding on both tasks, while weaker models remain far behind. Ablations show that the gap depends on code representation and workflow demands, not on model capability alone: open-weight models improve substantially with richer code representations, whereas frontier models show no significant change. Similar success rates hide different workflows. Humans repeatedly revisit functions and follow local program structure; strong agents jump across the binary, retrieve information broadly, and rarely return to inspected code, a behavior we call greedy fetching. This strategy is not fixed: given semantically richer code, agents fetch less without losing understanding. Because greedy fetching aggregates large amounts of code in the agent's context, we measure context-window saturation across 4,000 real-world binaries: large windows accommodate many programs, but larger applications and lower-level representations quickly exhaust them. Autonomous reverse engineering is becoming competitive, with a large speed advantage, but scaling it will require better navigation, selective retrieval, and persistent analysis state, not merely larger context windows.
authors: Samuele Doria, Stefano De Rosa, Ruoyu Wang, Zion Leonahenahe Basque, Eleonora Losiouk, Simone Aonzo
bullets: Nine LLM agents were compared with human analysts on two static-analysis challenges using a shared rubric and recorded IDA Pro interactions.
GPT-5.5 Pro, Claude Opus 4.8, and Kimi K3 achieved statistically human-competitive understanding; weaker models lagged substantially.
Performance depended on code representation and workflow demands: richer representations helped open-weight models but not frontier models.
Humans revisited functions and followed local structure, while strong agents broadly fetched information and rarely returned to prior code—a behavior termed “greedy fetching.”
Across 4,000 real-world binaries, context saturation increased with application size and lower-level representations, highlighting the need for selective retrieval and persistent analysis state.

Fig. 2. Delta matrix comparing high-performing agent traces with top human traces. Positive values are agent-skewed, and negative values are human-skewed.
Table 1. Average understanding scores and standard deviations on RPC and Secrets. Human cohorts are selected by understanding rate. Agent rows are organized by the RQ1 analysis groups.
