papers.selection_reason: Examines LLM-agent context-window saturation, greedy fetching, and need for persistent analysis state; informative for LLM memory design.
papers.title: Humans vs. Machines: A Comparison With AI Agents in Software Reverse Engineering
papers.tldr: Top AI agents can match skilled humans on compact binary reverse-engineering tasks, but their broad, context-heavy workflows limit scalability to larger programs.

papers.abstract: Activation steering has recently been used as a memory for skills: past experiences of an agent are stored as steering vectors and retrieved later. Facts and preferences about the user are assumed to need text instead. We test that assumption with a training-free activation memory beside a frozen LLM. The change an experience causes in late-layer states is stored as a shift, filed under a whitened key for the conversation's gist, and added back in a later session only when the gist matches. We argue that such a shift is a fixed average of an effect that attention, in context, recomputes for every question, so only question-independent content can survive. In a pre-registered study on Qwen3.5-2B and 9B, with judges from four model families, the memory is selective (about 98% of unrelated replies are unchanged), but facts are stored as the word to say, in the last layers only, and are almost never used (at most 15% clean use, against 96-98% in context). Leanings transfer only in a narrow strength window. Most strikingly, the reference subtracted when writing a preference decides whether its concept or its direction survives: unless the opposite is subtracted, a stored dislike is recalled as a like.
authors: Vedant Jumle
bullets: A frozen LLM stores experience effects as late-layer activation shifts keyed by a whitened conversation gist.
The method assumes stored shifts approximate effects that attention would otherwise recompute for each question.
Memory is selective: about 98% of unrelated replies remain unchanged.
Facts are rarely used correctly—up to 15% clean recall versus 96–98% when provided in context—and preferences transfer only within a narrow strength range.
The subtraction reference determines preference behavior; without subtracting the opposite, dislikes can be recalled as likes.

figures.caption: Figure 1: (a) A training-free activation memory beside a frozen LLM. In session 1 the change an experience causes in late-layer states is stored as a shift, filed under a whitened key for the conversation’s gist. In a later session the shift is added back only where the current gist matches a stored key. (b) What the stored shift carries depends on the reference subtracted when writing it. Subtracting the opposite keeps the direction; subtracting alternatives or nothing keeps the concept, so a dislike is recalled as a like. A fact is stored as the word to say. Replies are single real samples from Qwen3.5-9B (preferences α=1, fact α=2); quantitative results are in §5.

Figure 5: Dislike memories (2B: 7 items kept by the inclusion rule; 9B: 8), written with each reference and compared at the highest strength with at most 10% loops (α=1 for all). Change in judge lean against no memory: positive means the replies avoid what the user dislikes. Only the opposite reference moves replies the right way; the centroid and without references push toward the disliked thing, under every competent judge. Bars: 95% CIs.

Figure 4: Leaning memories (15 items) under the original judge. The word-list lean of non-looping replies (blue) keeps rising with strength, but the share of incoherent replies (orange) rises faster, so the judge lean of coherent recommendations (green) peaks at α≈1–2 and falls. Crosses: controls at α=2. Dashed: the experience in context.

Figure 3: Fact memories on the use prompts. As the strength grows, more replies mention the fact (blue) and more are incoherent (orange), but replies that use the fact cleanly (green, judge) stay at or below 15%. With the fact in context, 96–98% use it cleanly (dashed). Shaded: 95% CIs over items and prompts.

Figure 7: Logit lens of the stored dislike shifts at every block: mean logit of words on the liked side minus the disliked side (positive: avoids the disliked thing). The centroid and without shifts point at the disliked thing in the late layers.

Figure 2: The stored fact shift read through the output layer at every block (logit lens). The median rank of the fact’s word (e.g. Pepper) among about 248k tokens stays near 100k until the last sixth of the network, then jumps to the top.
Figure 6: Unrelated replies identical to no memory, at α=2, with the gate and with the gate forced open.

Table 2: Does each pre-registered claim hold under each judge? †Fails the sanity check below and is excluded from our conclusions. ‡Same family as the original judge; its C5 signs all agree, but its without interval touches zero.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates activation steering as persistent memory for LLMs; fits LLM memory subtopic.
papers.title: What Survives When Activation Steering Is Used as Memory
papers.tldr: Training-free activation memories are highly selective but preserve only limited, question-independent information, often distorting facts and reversing preferences.

papers.abstract: Recent video generative models have shown strong capability in synthesizing high-quality and temporally coherent videos. Yet, adapting them for controllable portrait animation remains nontrivial, as existing methods typically rely on architectural changes or extra conditioning modules, increasing complexity and reducing compatibility with pretrained models. We present CatPortrait, a simple and effective framework that enables controllable portrait animation via 3D face guidance as in-context conditioning. CatPortrait preserves the original video generation backbone and injects structured 3D facial guidance into the input space through spatial concatenation, allowing pretrained image-to-video models to animate portraits without sacrificing their pretrained priors. CatPortrait supports both video-driven and audio-driven portrait animation within a unified framework. Extensive experiments demonstrate that CatPortrait achieves competitive or superior results across both settings.
authors: Ziqi Ni, Zhou Fang, Shijian Wang, Rui Li, Yi Zhou
bullets: Addresses the complexity and compatibility issues of methods that require architectural changes or extra conditioning modules.
Uses spatial concatenation to inject structured 3D face guidance into the input space.
Supports both video-driven and audio-driven portrait animation in one framework.
Experiments show competitive or superior performance across both animation settings.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Overview of the proposed framework. During inference, the model takes a reference image IR and driving signals as inputs. A motion parameter estimator converts the driving signals into FLAME parameters (β, ψ, θ). The rendered FLAME sequence is then encoded by E and spatially concatenated with the noisy latent zt to form a conditioned latent, which, together with the identity information from IR, is fed into the video generator to synthesize the output video. During training, paired sequences are used to construct the input, and the generator is finetuned.
Fig. 2. Qualitative comparison on audio-driven talking head generation.
Fig. 3. Qualitative comparison on video-driven portrait reenactment, including selfreenactment and cross-reenactment.

Table 3. Ablation study on video-driven portrait reenactment. All variants are evaluated under the same protocol. Lower is better for FID, FVD, LMD, LPIPS, AED, and AKD. Higher is better for ID Sim. and Image Quality.
Table 2. Quantitative comparison on video-driven portrait reenactment under selfreenactment and cross-reenactment settings.
Table 1. Quantitative comparison on audio-driven talking head generation.

papers.selection_reason: Portrait animation with pretrained video generative models fits video generation and understanding.
papers.title: CatPortrait: Taming Video Generative Models for Portrait Animation via In-context Conditioning
papers.tldr: CatPortrait enables controllable portrait animation by adding 3D facial guidance as in-context input, without modifying the pretrained video-generation backbone.

papers.abstract: Personalized assistants accumulate long conversation histories, and passing the whole history to an LLM with every request is costly. We show that it is also unnecessary. On PersonaMem-v2 (180 questions), with GPT-5.6-terra and Claude Opus 5.5 as judges, a relevance-filtered context, built by sentence-level retrieval that ranks the history by similarity to the current request and stops at a fixed budget, matches full-history accuracy with only 5% of the text, cutting the judge's input about 20-fold. An LLM summary of the same length performs on par, but it needs an LLM to read the entire history, whereas retrieval needs only a small embedding model. While both sentence-level retrieval and LLM summary perform strongly, retrieval does so while placing the relevant evidence in the context for only 61% of the questions, and an oracle given only that evidence beats the full history by 15.6 points, making better context selection a promising path to surpassing the full history.
authors: Erika Hayashi, Andrew Shin
bullets: Full conversation histories are costly and often unnecessary for personalized assistants.
Retrieval ranks history sentences by similarity to the current request and selects a fixed-size relevant context.
On PersonaMem-v2, retrieval matched full-history accuracy with GPT-5.6-terra and Claude Opus 5.5 judges.
Retrieval performed comparably to an equal-length LLM summary without requiring an LLM to process the entire history.
Relevant evidence was included for only 61% of questions; an oracle using that evidence exceeded full history by 15.6 points, highlighting context selection as a key opportunity.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a relevance-filtered context method to reduce the memory footprint of personalized LLMs by matching full history with only 5% of text, relevant to LLM memory optimization.
papers.title: Do Personalized LLMs Need the Whole Conversation? Matching the Full History with Only 5% of Its Text via Relevance-Filtered Context
papers.tldr: Sentence-level retrieval can preserve full-history personalization accuracy using just 5% of conversation text, reducing judge input costs about 20-fold.

papers.abstract: Feed-forward geometric foundation models (GFMs) directly predict dense geometry and camera poses from batches of images. Emerging visual SLAM methods chain together consecutive GFM batches to form dense point cloud maps. A core challenge is how to address the ambiguous geometric scale of GFM predictions: independent predictions are locally consistent up-to-scale but not constrained by any direct physical measurements. Models trained on data with known scale improve the consistency of GFM reconstructions but again do not directly measure it. Consequently, trajectories and 3D reconstructions from GFM-enabled SLAM methods inherit this issue. Motivated by parallels with classical visual-inertial odometry, we introduce FoundationVIO which integrates inertial sensing with GFM predictions to recover metric scale reconstruction using a factor-graph based approach. We demonstrate odometry estimates competitive with classical state-of-the-art VIO methods and accurate dense reconstructions that outperform GFM-enabled SLAM methods. We also add a minimal GFM-based loop-closure mechanism to create a full Visual-Inertial SLAM system capable of creating globally accurate reconstructions and pose estimates. We evaluate our method on three datasets with well known sensor systems and demonstrate its compatibility on ubiquitous camera and IMU sensors. The method runs at approximately real-time on a consumer-grade laptop GPU. Code: https://github.com/ori-drs/FoundationVIO.
authors: Jin Rhee, Yuhao Zhang, Frank Dellaert, Maurice Fallon
bullets: Addresses the scale ambiguity inherited by feed-forward geometric foundation models and GFM-based SLAM.
Uses a factor-graph approach to integrate inertial sensing with GFM geometry and camera-pose predictions.
Achieves odometry competitive with classical state-of-the-art VIO and denser reconstructions than GFM-based SLAM methods.
Adds a minimal GFM-based loop-closure mechanism for globally accurate visual-inertial SLAM.
Evaluated on three datasets with common camera/IMU systems and runs approximately in real time on a consumer laptop GPU.

papers.selection_reason: Integrates geometric foundation model predictions with inertial sensing for metric-scale VIO/SLAM; relevant to 3D perception and foundation-model-based geometry.
papers.title: FoundationVIO: Enforcing Metric Scale in Feed-forward Visual-Inertial Odometry
papers.tldr: FoundationVIO combines geometric foundation-model predictions with IMU measurements to recover metric-scale visual-inertial odometry and dense SLAM reconstructions.

papers.abstract: Visual localization enables unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) to maintain absolute positioning in GNSS-denied environments. A common approach matches UAV images with geo-tagged orthographic maps and estimates camera pose using Perspective-n-Point (PnP) with elevations from Digital Surface Models (DSMs). However, accurate and up-to-date DSMs are often unavailable in practice. Orthographic-perspective geometry (OPG) enables DSM-free localization in scenes with varying elevations, yet existing methods typically estimate pose indirectly through intermediate matrix estimation and decomposition. To address this limitation, we propose Latent-Depth Variable Projection (LDVP), which treats the unknown scales along perspective viewing rays as latent depths. By analytically eliminating these depths and solving for the horizontal camera center in closed form given the rotation, LDVP reduces nonlinear estimation to a rotation-only problem, enabling direct recovery of metric horizontal position without assuming a planar scene. To improve localization robustness across different scene structures, we further introduce Structure-Adaptive Coupling (SAC), which uses relative scene structure inferred from monocular depth estimation to select LDVP when the matched points are not dominated by a single plane, and Planar-PnP otherwise. Our local observability analysis reveals how scene elevation variation affects the geometric constraints of OPG, providing a basis for this adaptive strategy. Extensive experiments show that LDVP consistently outperforms existing OPG-based DSM-free methods, while SAC further improves robustness across diverse scenes and substantially narrows the gap to DSM-based localization. Code will be released at https://github.com/UAV-AVL/LDVP-SAC.
authors: Yibin Ye, Xichao Teng, Shuo Chen, Xiaokai Song, Yuli Sun, Qifeng Yu, Zhang Li
bullets: Addresses the lack of accurate, up-to-date Digital Surface Models (DSMs) for UAV localization in GNSS-denied environments.

SAC uses monocular depth-derived scene structure to choose LDVP for varied-elevation scenes and Planar-PnP for predominantly planar matches.
Experiments report consistent improvement over existing DSM-free OPG methods, with SAC narrowing the gap to DSM-based localization.
Scope: performance depends on matched scene structure and the quality of inferred relative depth.

papers.abstract: Diffusion-based policies have recently emerged as a powerful paradigm for offline reinforcement learning, but their reliance on multi-step denoising introduces substantial computational overhead and requires backpropagation through time during training, limiting scalability and practical deployment. In this work, we propose \textbf{Instant Flow Q-Learning (InsQL)}, a single-step generative policy learning framework that retains the expressive capacity of diffusion models while eliminating iterative sampling and BPTT. InsQL builds on the flow-matching perspective of diffusion policies, but replaces marginal velocity parameterization with \emph{average-velocity} modeling and introduces a principled compositional mechanism, yielding a theoretically grounded objective that learns average velocity consistently across scales. This formulation provides a direct noise-to-action mapping and enables single-step action generation. InsQL further unifies compositional average-velocity modeling with behavior-regularized actor--critic optimization in a single framework, requiring only a single policy network and avoiding distillation, multi-stage procedures, and Jacobian computations during training. At inference time, actions are generated in a single forward pass and can be refined via value-guided candidate selection to improve performance. Extensive experiments on standard offline RL benchmarks and real-world robotic manipulation tasks show that InsQL matches or surpasses state-of-the-art diffusion-based methods while substantially reducing both training and inference time. Overall, these results establish compositional average-velocity modeling as an efficient and scalable alternative to multi-step generative policies for offline RL.
authors: Thanh Nguyen, Abu Hanif Muhammad Syarubany, Hwanhee Kim, Chang D. Yoo
bullets: Targets the high training and inference costs of diffusion-based offline RL policies caused by iterative denoising and backpropagation through time.
Uses average-velocity modeling with a compositional formulation to learn a direct noise-to-action mapping across scales.
Combines the generative policy with behavior-regularized actor–critic learning using one policy network, without distillation, multi-stage training, or Jacobian computations.
Generates actions in one forward pass, with optional value-guided candidate selection for refinement.
Experiments on offline RL benchmarks and robotic manipulation tasks show performance comparable to or better than diffusion-based methods while substantially reducing training and inference time.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Instant Flow Q-Learning (InsQL) overview. (a) Standard flow-matching (diffusion) policies learn an instantaneous marginal velocity field v(at, t, s) and generate actions by multi-step integration. (b) InsQL instead parameterizes the policy with an average-velocity field u(at, n, t, s) over finite intervals, enabling single-step action generation by directly mapping noise to action. (c) Velocity composition: long-interval average velocity (blue) is recursively composed from shorter-interval average velocities (green/red); in the infinitesimal limit, this recovers the marginal velocity used in FM. (d) InsQL unifies the one-step policy into a non-BPTT behavior-regularized actor–critic framework, with optional Q-guided candidate selection for test-time refinement.
Fig. 3: Evaluation tasks. (a–c) MuJoCo locomotion tasks (d) AntMaze Navigation task. (e–f) Real-world robotic manipulation tasks

papers.abstract: Lifelong learning enables artificial systems to adapt to changing environments. To achieve this, an effective artificial learner should dynamically reorganize past and new experiences, maintaining stability while enabling flexible knowledge integration. However, existing efforts primarily mitigate catastrophic forgetting, lacking the ability to adaptively update memory akin to biological systems. Here, by integrating the full memory life cycle of engram neurons into artificial learners, we propose a framework that constructs a structured memory from gradient representations, which regulates parameter updates and guides memory management. Through comprehensive evaluations on four benchmarks, our approach shows promising lifelong learning capability, maintaining stability over long task sequences and supporting flexible adaptation. Beyond the performance gains, our approach offers a computational perspective on robust and flexible lifelong learning, echoing mechanisms observed in biological memory systems.
authors: Suiyang Jiang, Bomin Wang, Hangqi Zhou, Jianfeng Feng, Xiahai Zhuang
bullets: Addresses the limited memory adaptability of methods focused mainly on catastrophic forgetting.
Models the full life cycle of biological engram neurons within an artificial learner.
Uses gradient-derived structured memory to regulate parameter updates and manage memories.
Evaluated on four benchmarks, it maintains stability across long task sequences while supporting flexible adaptation.
Provides a computational perspective on biologically inspired robust lifelong learning.
papers.selection_reason: Lifelong learning with adaptive memory management directly fits continual and online learning.
papers.title: Engram Neuron Inspired Adaptive Memorization for Lifelong Learning
papers.tldr: An engram-inspired lifelong-learning framework builds and manages structured memories from gradient representations to balance stability with flexible adaptation.

papers.abstract: GRPO-style reinforcement learning has advanced vision-language reasoning, but its sequence-level rewards provide limited credit assignment for individual reasoning tokens. On-policy distillation (OPD) addresses this issue by providing dense supervision on student-generated trajectories, yet standard OPD assigns similar importance to all teacher-preferred tokens, including template phrases and visually irrelevant continuations. We introduce Visual Counterfactual On-Policy Distillation (VC-OPD), a grounding-aware distillation method that prioritizes tokens whose correctness depends on image-specific evidence. After a teacher-supervised warm start that stabilizes response formats and reduces noisy rollouts, VC-OPD performs on-policy distillation with two teacher evaluations for each student trajectory: one under the original image and one under a counterfactual image with corrupted instance-specific evidence. The original-image teacher distribution determines the distillation target, while the original--counterfactual teacher gap estimates token-level visual dependence and softly reweights the loss. To avoid unstable response-level update scales, VC-OPD further applies mass-preserving normalization to the token weights. This design preserves the dense supervision of OPD while shifting learning capacity toward visually grounded reasoning tokens. Experiments on multimodal reasoning benchmarks show that VC-OPD improves visual reasoning performance and produces more effective token-level distillation.
authors: Jiahe Feng
bullets: Addresses weak token-level credit assignment in sequence-level GRPO rewards and uniform weighting in standard OPD.
Uses teacher distributions from the original and counterfactual images to estimate each token’s visual dependence.
Applies mass-preserving normalization to stabilize token-weighted distillation updates.
A teacher-supervised warm start stabilizes response formats and reduces noisy rollouts.
Experiments on multimodal reasoning benchmarks report improved visual reasoning and more effective token-level distillation.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of VC-OPD. The framework first warm-starts the student with filtered teachergenerated reasoning responses. During visual counterfactual on-policy distillation, student rollouts are scored by the teacher under factual and counterfactual visual inputs. The factual teacher provides the update direction, while the factual–counterfactual gap produces grounding-aware token weights that modulate the final token-level advantage.

papers.abstract: Diffusion policies are increasingly used in robotic control and manipulation, vision-language-action models, and world-model-based agents. Their ability to represent multimodal action distributions offers rich opportunities for exploration in reinforcement learning (RL). However, optimizing diffusion policies with RL can reduce the behavioral diversity and further limit their exploration capability. In RL post-training, directly fine-tuning a pretrained policy may also disrupt its acquired capabilities, while action-space residuals may lack the expressive power for multimodal exploration. Together, these issues reveal a common challenge across online and offline-to-online diffusion RL: improving task performance while retaining the behavioral diversity and capabilities needed for continued adaptation. We introduce CFG-Policy, a unified, plug-and-play framework that separates exploration and exploitation into two generative policies and combines their score or velocity fields during sampling through classifier-free guidance. For online RL, a frozen exploration branch sustains behavioral diversity while an exploitation branch learns from task rewards; for offline-to-online RL, a pretrained exploitation branch remains frozen while a trainable branch steers the composed behavior. CFG-Policy preserves the underlying RL objectives and improves performance with QSM and QVPO on 5 MuJoCo tasks and with Flow-SDE+PPO on 4 RoboTwin manipulation tasks. Project page is at https://zhy-liu.github.io/cfg-policy-page.
authors: Shutong Ding, Zhaoyang Liu, Yimiao Zhou, Jingya Wang, Jiayuan Gu, Ye Shi
bullets: Addresses reduced exploration diversity and capability loss when fine-tuning diffusion policies with RL.
Combines two policies’ score or velocity fields during sampling to control exploration–exploitation trade-offs.
Supports online RL with a frozen exploration branch and offline-to-online RL with a frozen pretrained exploitation branch.
Integrates with QSM, QVPO, and Flow-SDE+PPO across MuJoCo and RoboTwin manipulation tasks.
Provides a unified, plug-and-play framework without changing the underlying RL objectives.

papers.abstract: Pipeline parallelism has become a critical technique for training large language models. To address the throughput limitation of existing sequence-level methods that schedule subsequences unidirectionally, we propose bidirectional sequence-level interleaved pipeline parallelism (BSIPipe), which co-schedules two opposing V-shaped interleaved pipelines at the subsequence level. To bound the activation accumulation from subsequence scaling, BSIPipe introduces a basic-unit concatenation mechanism that keeps activation memory invariant to the subsequence count. To eliminate communication deadlock risk from bidirectional scheduling, BSIPipe employs a communication optimization strategy that combines topology-aware device mapping with communication-computation overlap. In addition, BSIPipe composes with tensor parallelism to overcome the memory limitation of single-dimensional parallelism, neutralizing its bidirectional memory overhead while maintaining throughput. Experiments on GPT and LLaMA3 demonstrate that BSIPipe achieves average speedups of 1.11$\times$ to 1.13$\times$ in long-sequence training over SOTA sequence-level baselines.
authors: Yuzhou Ni, Ling Chen
bullets: Addresses throughput limits of unidirectional sequence-level pipeline parallelism.

papers.abstract: Ultra-low-bit scalar quantization offers a regular arithmetic structure for efficient deployment of large language models, but preserving predictive behavior at extreme precision remains challenging: with only a few reconstruction levels, accurate weight representation must translate into consistent predictions from a small calibration set. We propose FidelityQ, a scalar quantization framework that preserves predictive fidelity at weight precisions down to 2 bits. For accurate quantization, we introduce Information-Aligned Analytic Coding (IAC), which shapes each weight row toward a centered symmetric source via randomized Hadamard mixing and fits a mirrored four-level minimum-distortion quantizer to its empirical weights. Every level set in this family decomposes exactly into two sign-valued bases with associated scales, combining source-adaptive reconstruction with lookup-free decoding compatible with scaled integer arithmetic. Our analysis further shows that residual predictive discrepancies are heavy-tailed and concentrate on tokens the teacher predicts confidently, motivating Knowledge-Intensive Calibration (KIC) for consistent quantization. KIC ranks sequences by the tail of token-wise teacher-student divergence, allocates a limited calibration budget to the highest-scoring samples, and restores predictive agreement by updating only quantization levels and scales under teacher supervision, keeping pretrained weights frozen. Experiments on the LLaMA and Qwen families demonstrate the effectiveness of FidelityQ in weight-only and joint quantization settings. On LLaMA-2-7B, FidelityQ achieves a WikiText2 perplexity of 6.62 at W2A16 and improves the prior state-of-the-art W2A4KV4 result from 8.31 to 6.96, while reducing linear-layer weight memory by 8.0x relative to FP16.
authors: Yujie Chen, Weiyan Zheng, Yiwu Yao, Tianchi Hu, Bo Wang, Jiyu Guo, Wenzhan Li, Jingcai Guo, Michele Magno, Haotong Qin
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of maintaining predictive behavior when weights use only a few quantization levels.
Introduces Information-Aligned Analytic Coding (IAC): randomized Hadamard mixing and a symmetric four-level quantizer with lookup-free sign-basis decoding.
Introduces Knowledge-Intensive Calibration (KIC), which selects high-divergence calibration sequences and updates only quantization levels and scales while freezing pretrained weights.

Experiments on LLaMA and Qwen show effectiveness for weight-only and joint quantization; on LLaMA-2-7B, it reports 6.62 WikiText2 perplexity at W2A16 and improves W2A4KV4 perplexity from 8.31 to 6.96.
Reduces linear-layer weight memory by 8× versus FP16.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of FidelityQ. The top pipeline compares a frozen full-precision teacher with the IAC-quantized model, after which KIC selects calibration data and updates only the reconstruction levels. IAC shapes the source with a randomized Hadamard transform, places four symmetric nonzero levels at minimum distortion, and decodes them exactly as two sign planes with row-wise scales. KIC ranks sequences by the tail mean of token-wise divergence, keeps the top-k complete sequences, and refines the levels using the teacher distribution and corpus targets.

(b) The same representation is smaller and faster: on LLaMA-2-7B at batch size 1, its linear-layer weights take 8.0× less memory than FP16 and decode 3.4× faster than QuIP# (Appendix D).

(b) The reduction in excess kurtosis holds across input-rotated projections. (c) With one block quantized, the fitted levels lie in a low-cross-entropy region of the model-level loss surface. papers.abstract: Multi-finger hands contact objects at different times, so a global close command can overload early-contact fingers while others are still moving. Dense tactile arrays address this problem but add hardware, calibration, bandwidth, and computation. We present an edge-native pipeline that uses only built-in joint-angle and pre-use-calibrated actuator-load feedback to recognize the grasped object and predict an independent Stop event for each finger. Four samples and their first differences form a 4-by-20 contact-evolution window. At its core is a heterogeneous dual-expert architecture, termed DualExpert, that assigns complementary tasks to a Temporal Convolutional Network (TCN) and a Finger Graph Filter Network (FGFN). The TCN models short-term contact evolution and supplies all five Stop probabilities, while the FGFN encodes finger topology and contributes only to object classification. Fixed 0.7/0.3 class-probability fusion reaches 93.78\% trajectory-level classification accuracy on 225 held-out trials, improving the standalone TCN and FGFN by 4.00 and 2.22 percentage points, respectively. The TCN Stop path attains 95.25\% F1. The dataset contains 1,500 automatically collected trajectories from five object instances. In Flash deployment, mixed accelerator execution retains 93.78\% classification accuracy and 94.84\% Stop F1 with 2.890~ms mean inference time and 9.172~ms mean sample-to-stop latency. Across 50 physical trials, the system achieves 96.00\% recognition and 98.00\% grasp success while the complete embedded board draws approximately 0.80~W.

papers.abstract: A language model that keeps learning online must not slowly erode its own base capabilities. We ask which part of a modern LLM should absorb continual updates, by measuring how each choice changes the model's internal representations. On a 48-layer mixture-of-experts model with a native pretrained N-gram memory, we train a seven-task chain under three update mechanisms with identical data and budgets: updating only the N-gram memory table, continually training one shared LoRA adapter, and training a fresh LoRA per task that is merged into the backbone. We capture fixed-context representations at every layer and task boundary. Updating only the N-gram memory changes the base model's representations of general math and code inputs by 26%/15% (relative RMS), against 64%/35% for merged and 97%/39% for shared LoRA. This drift does not grow with the number of tasks: it reaches 25% after the first task and stays there for all seven, while both LoRA variants keep accumulating. Its generic behaviour is essentially unchanged (no code problem lost, math NLL -0.01), and every change is confined to inspectable, reversible table rows. The cost appears elsewhere: N-gram memory acquires new tasks more weakly and its stored tasks interfere with one another, losing as much old-task NLL as shared LoRA. We show that this forgetting is governed by drift on the learned tasks' own inputs, measured from the checkpoint at which each was learned, not by generic drift (Spearman rho=0.85; rho=0.71 on Llama-3-8B), and we derive the exact relations behind it: with a frozen head, every pairwise logit margin changes by the projection of drift onto a head-difference direction. These results support a design principle for long-running online learning: write new knowledge only into the memory table and keep the backbone fixed; the remaining problem, interference between stored tasks, then lies inside the memory.
authors: Hao Wu
bullets: The study compares N-gram memory updates, one continually trained shared LoRA, and per-task LoRAs merged into the backbone under matched conditions.
N-gram updates cause substantially less representation drift on general math and code inputs than either LoRA strategy, with drift plateauing after the first task rather than accumulating.
Generic behavior remains essentially unchanged under memory-only updates, and changes are localized to inspectable, reversible table rows.
Memory-only learning acquires new tasks more weakly and suffers task interference, causing old-task forgetting comparable to shared LoRA.
Forgetting tracks representation drift on learned-task inputs—not generic inputs—and follows an exact frozen-head logit-margin relation.

papers.abstract: Robust motion planning and control for manipulators is the problem of guaranteeing safe execution and collision-free motion under disturbances. The Kinodynamic Motion Planning via Funnel Control (KDF) is a recently proposed planner that comes with robustness guarantees and is particularly attractive for collision-free control as it guarantees closed-loop evolution inside a funnel, i.e., a collision-free region around a nominal trajectory. Despite its attractive theoretical properties, the current approach for computing funnels is computationally demanding, which limits its expressiveness and performance. We address its current limitations by proposing a novel funnel planning and control solution. Our key tool to enable this is a neural Signed Configuration Distance Function (nSCDF) which allows us to estimate collision-free balls and gradients in a computationally efficient way. We use the nSCDF in our planner to compute a nominal trajectory, where path length and clearance are balanced. To track the trajectory with collision-avoidance guarantees, we design a funnel controller that exploits the geometric information from the nSCDF. From numerical experiments, we observe that our planner produces nominal paths $2$ times faster, while at the same time obtaining $20 \%$ shorter path length and $5$ times the clearance. Finally, we also observe improved motion performance and robustness properties when using the nSCDF for funnel control.
authors: Bernhard Wullt, Christos K. Verginis, Per Mattsson, Mikael Norrl\"of, Thomas B. Sch\"on
bullets: Targets the computational cost and limited expressiveness of Kinodynamic Motion Planning via Funnel Control (KDF).
Uses an nSCDF to efficiently estimate collision-free balls and gradients for planning and control.
Plans nominal trajectories that balance path length and obstacle clearance, then tracks them with a geometry-aware funnel controller.
Numerical experiments report paths computed 2× faster, with 20% shorter length and 5× greater clearance.
The approach also improves motion performance and robustness when the nSCDF is used for funnel control.

Fig. 3: All: A conceptual illustration of how the wrist configuration distance is computed for a 2 DOF arm, where qm is the main joint and qw is the wrist joint. The left plot is illustrated in the world space, the rest is illustrated in the configuration space. Left: The manipulator has two links (colored black). The main link is made transparent to emphasize that its collision with the obstacle is not considered. The obstacle is a disk (colored red). Its parameter vector is expressed in the base frame {0} as σ and in the wrist frame {w} as σlw. Computing the distance from the local wrist function results in a wrist movement (dashed blue arc) that moves the wrist to the obstacle boundary (transparent green). The distance or the movement does not include the main joint. Middle: Corresponding configuration space representation of the left plot. The configuration (red point); distance computed by the local wrist nSCDF (dashed blue line); the ground truth distance including the movement of the main joint (transparent red disk and green line). Right: To compute an estimate of the distance where the movement of the main joint is included, we discretize the space of the main joints (black points along the horizontal axis). For each grid point, we compute a distance, by forming the hypotenuse (red line) with the distance of the main joint (green line) and the wrist distance (blue line). This forms an estimated safe set (orange circle). From all estimates we take the smallest distance (blue circle).

Fig. 4: Illustrations in the configuration space. The SCDF, ψ, is illustrated as a colormap, with darker colors indicating lower distances. The zero-level contour, i.e., ∂Co, is represented by the solid purple curve. Left: Illustration of our medial-axis projection step. A discretized path (red points) is projected to points approximately on the medial axis (purple points), resulting in increased clearance. Middle: The projection steps result in a nonsmooth and distorted path. We solve a weighted shortest path problem by constructing a graph by using the points on the path as vertices. The edges are formed over intersecting balls (black lines). The weight function balances path length and clearance. Solving the problem results in an optimized path in the graph (red curve), which is continuously collision-free due to the intersection requirement of the resulting balls (red circles). Right: We smoothen the piece-wise linear path by solving a convex optimization problem. The key idea is to find a smooth path that is close to the original one (black curve). We do this by constructing collision-free capsules (transparent red) along the connecting line segments of the path. Each capsule is assigned a Bézier curve (colored curve within capsule). Continuity constraints are enforced with its neighboring curve. The closeness of the original path is controlled by the width of the capsules. Solving the optimization problem results in a smooth collision-free path.

papers.abstract: Multi-human cooperative object manipulation is a highly challenging topic in humanoid control. While existing methods can handle simple collaborative carrying tasks, they struggle with role-dependent, long-horizon, and sequential cooperative manipulation. To address this issue, we propose a hierarchical commander-executor framework that enables multiple agents to accomplish complex collaborative tasks in distinct ways. Specifically, a commander combines instructions and scene information for joint semantic and geometric planning. It then decomposes the task into role-specific subtasks and generates shared object-centric coordination plans, specifying execution timing, target positions, and manipulation actions for each agent. Conditioned on the commander's high-level strategy and each agent's local observations, the executor learns a low-level physics-based policy through a solo-to-cooperative curriculum to realize coordinated human-object interactions. The planned object trajectory provides a shared coordination target, while root positions and grasping instructions specify role-dependent execution cues. We evaluate our method on a variety of object manipulation tasks, demonstrating its ability to execute long-horizon tasks that combine different types of collaboration and to scale from two-agent to multi-agent cooperation. Extensive experiments further show that our approach achieves higher success rates compared to state-of-the-art methods. Code will be made publicly available at https://github.com/TJU-3DV/Co-Manipulation.
authors: Buzhen Huang, Xingchen Wu, Yuanwang Yang, Chenyi Xie, Kun Li

The method reports higher success rates than state-of-the-art methods, though specific quantitative results are not provided.

papers.abstract: We study prediction with expert advice over $T$ rounds with $K$ experts under heavy-tailed losses whose $(1+\epsilon)$-moment is bounded by $\theta>0$ for some $\epsilon\in(0,1]$. In this setting, existing algorithms designed for the case $\epsilon=1$ can be suboptimal when $\epsilon<1$, suffering an additional polynomial dependence on $K$. We characterize the minimax pseudo-regret rate as $\Theta((\theta T)^{\frac{1}{1+\epsilon}}(\log K)^{\frac{\epsilon}{1+\epsilon}})$ and establish gap-dependent lower bounds in a self-bounded environment. To attain this minimax rate without prior knowledge of either $\epsilon$ or $\theta$, we propose Adaptive Heavy-Tailed FTRL, which uses robust data-dependent scale adaptation together with truncation. We further develop Adaptive Heavy-Tailed OMD, which likewise requires neither $\epsilon$ nor $\theta$ and achieves near-optimal regret guarantees in both adversarial and self-bounded environments. Finally, when $\epsilon$ and $\theta$ are known, an FTRL algorithm with Shannon-entropy regularization achieves optimal regret guarantees in both environments.
authors: Yuki Shibukawa, Shinji Ito
bullets: Existing methods for the finite-variance case can be suboptimal when the loss-tail exponent is smaller.

Adaptive Heavy-Tailed OMD achieves near-optimal guarantees in adversarial and self-bounded environments.
With known ε and θ, Shannon-entropy FTRL attains optimal guarantees; the work also proves gap-dependent lower bounds.

papers.abstract: Humanoid Behavior Foundation Models (BFMs) can execute impressive motions, but downstream applications such as loco-manipulation demand high whole-body positional accuracy. Existing BFMs suffer from a systematic command-execution gap, where executed motions deviate from desired ones. We show that additional test-time compute can improve execution without retraining the BFM. First, we introduce Test-Time Command Optimization (TTCO), which adapts the input command to the specific BFM to produce an executed trajectory closer to the desired motion. TTCO finds such commands by sampling-based optimization through closed-loop simulations of the BFM and robot dynamics. Across three BFMs on the AMASS dataset, TTCO reduces mean global body-position error by 79-84% in simulation. Second, we analyze test-time compute scaling and derive an approximate compute-optimal strategy that can sustain performance gains as the compute budget increases. Third, TTCO can generate BFM-specific action labels from recorded robot trajectories without requiring the original teleoperation body-motion commands. Simulation and real-robot experiments show that these labels are effective for training high-level loco-manipulation policies. This method also supports reusing existing demonstrations across BFMs.

papers.abstract: Bilateral teleoperation with force feedback is becoming increasingly important, and the quality of external-torque estimation is critical to this process. However, manufacturer-provided disturbance-torque estimates on commercial robotic arms are often inaccurate, while the use of end-effector force/torque sensors adds cost and payload. We propose LETS, a physics-guided learning approach that assigns rigid-body dynamics to recursive Newton-Euler inverse dynamics and reserves learning for only the robot-specific residual. LETS uses only the robot's URDF model and joint feedback, deliberately excluding control commands and thereby decoupling external-torque estimation from control-command inputs. It trains on 12 minutes of free-motion data in under one minute, without requiring a dedicated end-effector six-axis force/torque sensor. In bilateral teleoperation, LETS achieves real-time external-torque estimation that enables stable force feedback. Its free-space error is 69% lower than the manufacturer-provided estimate, substantially reducing coupled oscillations between leader and follower; its contact error is 28% lower, yielding more accurate haptic feedback.

papers.abstract: Test-time compute (TTC), which scores multiple candidate actions at inference time, is a powerful way to improve the execution performance of vision-language-action (VLA) models, but existing methods keep the policy frozen, so the gain must be recomputed at every execution. We propose Verify, Act, Distill, a framework that consolidates the gains of TTC into the VLA itself. A fixed verifier scores candidates generated by a flow-matching VLA, the weighted aggregate is executed, and the observations and aggregated chunks from successful adaptation episodes are distilled directly into LoRA parameters with the standard flow-matching loss. This reuses supervision that TTC has already produced during execution, without additional reinforcement learning or rollouts dedicated to teacher generation. On the 40 LIBERO tasks with a SmolVLA 5k checkpoint, distilling from only 10 episodes per task raises the mean success rate of verifier-free single-candidate generation from 54.1% to 70.6%, retaining about 74% of the improvement obtained by aggregating eight candidates. Applying the same aggregation to the distilled policy further raises the success rate from 76.4% to 82.3%, with a particularly large gain on LIBERO-Long (44.0% to 57.8%), and the single-candidate policy also improves on LIBERO-plus, which contains distribution shifts. These results show that using verification as a learning signal, rather than only as an execution-time selector, both retains the improvements of TTC and re-amplifies the effect of subsequent TTC.
authors: Kaneyoshi Hiratsuka, Satoshi Yamamori, Jun Morimoto
bullets: Existing TTC improves execution by selecting among candidates but requires recomputing this selection at every execution because the policy remains frozen.

The framework uses a fixed verifier to score flow-matching VLA candidates, executes their weighted aggregate, and distills successful episodes into LoRA parameters using the standard flow-matching loss.
It requires no additional reinforcement learning or teacher-generation rollouts, reusing supervision produced during TTC.
On 40 LIBERO tasks, distilling from 10 episodes per task raises verifier-free single-candidate success from 54.1% to 70.6%, retaining about 74% of eight-candidate aggregation’s improvement.
Applying aggregation after distillation further increases success from 76.4% to 82.3%, with gains also observed on LIBERO-Long and distribution-shifted LIBERO-plus.

papers.abstract: Experience-based learning enables large language model (LLM) agents to improve over time by reusing knowledge from past executions. However, existing methods typically rely on final task outcomes as feedback for experience learning, overlooking the execution process and limiting their ability to evaluate and optimize experience based on trajectory quality. To address this limitation, we propose TQG-Exp, a trajectory-quality-guided experience-based learning framework that introduces process feedback. Specifically, we introduce Trajectory Quality Loss (TQL), which jointly considers task completion and process quality to provide a learning signal beyond final task outcomes. Based on this signal, we employ paired rollouts with and without retrieved experience to guide experience optimization. Representative trajectories are selected based on their outcomes and trajectory quality to extract task-level and task-type-level experiences. Meanwhile, differences in trajectory quality between the paired groups are used to estimate the contribution of retrieved experience and update its utility. The learned utility is then combined with semantic relevance to guide subsequent experience retrieval. Experiments on ALFWorld, WebShop, and ScienceWorld with two backbone LLMs show that TQG-Exp outperforms existing experience-based methods, improving Avg.@3 over the strongest baseline by 4.50 and 8.55 percentage points on DeepSeek-V4-Flash and Qwen3.5-Flash, respectively.
authors: Bingjie Zhang, Yibo Yang, Qiantong Liu, Benshuo Fu, Yi Chang, Dandan Guo
bullets: Existing experience-based learning often uses only task success, overlooking the quality of the execution process.

Paired rollouts with and without retrieved experience estimate how much each experience improves trajectory quality.
Experiences are selected by outcome and quality, while learned utility is combined with semantic relevance for retrieval.
Across ALFWorld, WebShop, and ScienceWorld, TQG-Exp improves Avg.@3 over the strongest baseline by 4.50 and 8.55 percentage points with two backbone LLMs.

papers.abstract: By predicting future states, latent world models provide rich self-supervision for end-to-end driving, but often inherit dense features from pretrained visual encoders as their world-state interface. This creates a mismatch: visual pretraining produces information-rich, spatially dense features, but their adaptation for motion-conditioned world modeling and planning is deferred to downstream training. The dense grid also makes future prediction more computationally expensive as visual resolution increases. We therefore argue that video pretraining should directly learn state representations suited to downstream world modeling and planning, rather than relying on downstream training to adapt inherited visual features. We propose ***MORE***, a V-JEPA framework that learns **M**otion-**O**riented **RE**gisters during video pretraining as a shared state interface for driving world models and planning. MORE injects temporally aligned ego motion into a small set of registers and uses them as the sole context for masked patch prediction, channeling dense patch-level supervision through a compact state bottleneck. A complementary blockwise register-masking objective further shapes predictive structure in the register space. During downstream training, the same register space defines the future states predicted by the world model and provides shared scene memory for trajectory generation and scoring. On NAVSIM-v2, MORE outperforms the state of the art by 1.6 in EPDMS, while achieving superior efficiency with only 1/10 the inference latency of DriveLaW. These results support learning the state interface for world modeling and planning directly during video pretraining.

papers.abstract: Cross-modal Thermal Geo-localization (TG) provides an illumination-robust positioning solution for Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) in Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS)-denied environments. However, existing thermal geo-localization methods mainly focus on near-nadir observations or depend on map-side elevation priors, limiting their applicability to continuous oblique thermal localization with only geo-referenced 2D satellite maps. To address this problem, we propose ScalLoc, a scale-aligned local-to-map localization framework for continuous oblique thermal UAV geo-localization. ScalLoc follows a reconstruction--refinement--anchoring--propagation design: it reconstructs local window geometry from thermal sequences, refines camera poses using track-based pose optimization, adaptively anchors each window to the satellite map, and propagates validated states to recover frame-level global trajectories. To support systematic evaluation, we construct Thermal-Oblique, a real thermal UAV sequence dataset containing 216 urban and rural day--night trajectories and 28,112 thermal frames with frame-level annotations. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ScalLoc reduces the mean localization error from 112.69 m to 26.97 m compared with the VGGT-only configuration, corresponding to a 76.07% reduction, and achieves the lowest frame-weighted mean position error among the compared methods. These results demonstrate the feasibility of continuous oblique thermal geo-localization using only lightweight 2D satellite maps, without requiring digital surface models or preconstructed 3D maps. Code and dataset are available at https://github.com/FloralHercules/ScalLoc.

papers.abstract: Action chunking improves temporal coherence in visuomotor imitation learning by jointly predicting sequences of future actions. However, many existing policies regenerate entire action chunks even when errors are localized, potentially replacing otherwise valid predictions. We introduce Contextual Masked Action Policy (CMAP), a visuomotor policy that refines continuous action chunks through history-conditioned local regeneration. Specifically, CMAP introduces a history-conditioned action tape that combines executed commands with masked future positions to produce coarse action predictions and per-step uncertainty scores. An uncertainty-guided span regeneration mechanism then selects a high-uncertainty contiguous span and reconstructs it using the executed history and retained future predictions as context. By jointly reconstructing neighboring actions, CMAP models local temporal dependencies while preserving all predictions outside the selected span. Extensive experiments on nine simulated and four real-world manipulation tasks demonstrate that CMAP achieves superior overall performance over several competitive baselines. Ablation studies validate the complementary contributions of its key components, while held-out trajectory analysis shows that local regeneration reduces prediction errors within selected spans.

bullets: Addresses the problem of full action-chunk regeneration replacing valid predictions when errors are localized.

Ablations and held-out trajectory analysis support the complementary components and reduced errors within regenerated spans.

papers.abstract: Data-driven weather forecasting models are commonly trained on ERA5, yet operational deployment must use timely initial states from physics-based numerical weather prediction (NWP) systems whose distributions differ substantially from ERA5. Direct initialization with these states can degrade autoregressive forecasts, motivating input adaptation that keeps the pretrained forecasting model unchanged. Here, we introduce WeatherBridge, a unified, source-conditioned adapter that maps heterogeneous operational NWP initial states to ERA5 reference states without updating the pretrained forecasting model. WeatherBridge predicts the structured residual corrections with a Swin-UNet and injects source embeddings across multiple spatial scales, allowing the model to capture shared atmospheric structure and source-specific discrepancies. Its training objective combines latitude-weighted ERA5 reconstruction with One-step Rollout Alignment (ORA), which backpropagates one-step forecast error through a frozen FuXi model to optimize the adapted states for both initial state fidelity and downstream forecast compatibility. We evaluate WeatherBridge using daily GFS, HRES, and CMA initializations from 1 January to 22 November 2025 across six variables and lead times up to 240 hours. Relative to raw source initialization of FuXi, WeatherBridge reduces the mean RMSE of FuXi over the 6- 240-hour rollout for 17 of 18 source-variable combinations, with a median reduction of 10.2% and a maximum reduction of 46.3%. The adapter trained with frozen FuXi also improves FengWu forecasts on GFS inputs without retraining either the adapter or FengWu. These results demonstrate that forecast-aware input adaptation can improve forecasts from heterogeneous operational NWP inputs and transfer across pretrained ERA5-based forecasting models.
authors: Mutian Xi, Xinyu Su, Xiaohui Zhong, Hao Li
bullets: Operational NWP states differ from ERA5, causing forecast degradation when directly fed into ERA5-trained models.
A source-conditioned Swin-UNet predicts multiscale residual corrections while keeping the forecasting model unchanged.
Its objective combines latitude-weighted ERA5 reconstruction with one-step rollout alignment through a frozen FuXi model.
Across GFS, HRES, and CMA inputs, it reduces FuXi rollout RMSE for 17 of 18 source-variable combinations, with median and maximum reductions of 10.2% and 46.3%.
The adapter also improves FengWu forecasts on GFS inputs without retraining either model, supporting cross-model transfer.

papers.abstract: Contact-rich manipulation poses a stage-dependent sensory conflict: vision and proprioception are essential for localization and approach, when force is largely uninformative and potentially distracting, whereas force becomes critical after contact, when irrelevant visual details and correlated robot states may become shortcuts. We propose DEFT-VLA (Dual-Expert Force-specialized Training for Vision-Language-Action Manipulation), which retains the task-adapted base expert for vision-dominated non-contact behavior and introduces a force-aware contact expert for critical contact stages, localizing force-conditioned adaptation to where it is needed. We further introduce a contact-localized force-attending curriculum that applies force-attending post-training only to the contact expert, progressively restoring vision and masking state tokens to suppress shortcuts. Real-robot experiments on pipette tip attachment, bimanual pipette aspiration, and whiteboard wiping show that DEFT-VLA effectively exploits force feedback to improve contact-stage performance while maintaining strong non-contact behavior and robustness to held-out grasp heights. It improves overall task success by 20-40 percentage points over the strongest baseline on each task.
authors: Zan Huang, Yibo Qiu, Kan Ding, Xuanping Zhang, Ao Tian, Ronald X Xu, Mingzhai Sun
bullets: Addresses the conflict between vision/proprioception before contact and force sensing during contact.
Uses separate experts: a base vision-dominated expert for non-contact behavior and a force-aware expert for contact stages.
Applies a contact-localized curriculum that progressively restores vision and masks state tokens to reduce shortcut learning.
Real-robot tests cover pipette tip attachment, bimanual pipette aspiration, and whiteboard wiping.
Reports 20–40 percentage-point overall success gains over the strongest baseline on each task, while retaining non-contact performance and robustness to held-out grasp heights.

During contact-expert post-training, the contact-localized curriculum gradually restores image clarity and the original state tokens to suppress visual and proprioceptive shortcuts. papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) is promising for spatial text-to-image generation, but existing work largely focuses on policy optimization, assuming accurate rewards and effective online rollouts. We observe in-domain gains with out-of-domain degradation, exposing two limitations: unreliable spatial rewards in open-world settings and rollouts lacking basic-to-complex progression. We propose a curriculum-guided RL framework. First, we introduce SpatialCritic, an agentic reward model equipped with a spatial perception harness that combines reusable verification guidance with specialized vision tools. We then construct spatial preference datasets through targeted counterfactual perturbations and perform agent-harness alignment to improve tool selection and evidence integration efficiently. Second, curriculum learning organizes shared foundational capabilities and their compositional dependencies in a capability graph for mastery-guided rollouts, periodic review, and targeted remediation. On SpaRW-Eval, SpatialCritic achieves 95.1% verification accuracy, outperforming 320B GLM-5.3-Flash with a 40x smaller 8B backbone and raising average baseline scores from 78.4 to 83.9 on SD3.5-Medium and 83.2 to 86.5 on BAGEL. Project page: https://xiaofeng-tan.github.io/projects/spatialcritic/
authors: Xiaofeng Tan, Jiaxin Lin, Haobo Yuan, Tiancheng Shen, Zihan Su, Rui Chen, Hongsong Wang, Ming-Hsuan Yang
bullets: SpatialCritic uses reusable verification guidance and specialized vision tools to assess spatial correctness in open-world images.
Counterfactual spatial preference data and agent–harness alignment improve tool selection and evidence integration.
A capability graph organizes basic-to-complex skills for mastery-guided rollouts, review, and targeted remediation.
On SpaRW-Eval, SpatialCritic reaches 95.1% verification accuracy with an 8B backbone.
Average scores improve from 78.4 to 83.9 on SD3.5-Medium and from 83.2 to 86.5 on BAGEL.

papers.abstract: Synthesizing believable 4D hand-object grasping sequences is important for character animation, extended reality, and embodied agents. Grasping requires a hand to approach, contact, and lift or manipulate an object coherently. Existing synthesis methods often model only the final static grasp or rely on additional conditions, such as language, target grasps, or object trajectories, to specify the interaction. We instead study the underconstrained problem of generating a complete grasping motion from a single initial hand-object state. Our framework decouples hand-motion generation from object-motion recovery. Given an object point cloud in the initial wrist frame and the initial parameterized hand configuration, conditional flow matching predicts a sequence-level contact map and a hand pose at each normalized sequence time. This time-indexed formulation avoids the error accumulation of autoregressive rollout while representing the complete motion. We then infer an attachment frame and recover rigid-object motion through training-free, contact-guided weighted registration. We evaluate on held-out DexYCB objects and unseen object geometries reconstructed from in-the-wild videos by Open-CHOIR. Compared with LatentHOI, our method produces smoother hand and object motion in every setting, matches or improves on its contact and penetration metrics in the wild under a shared initialization, and is about 30x faster per generated frame. In a 15-participant study, our motions were preferred in roughly two thirds of (forced-choice pairwise) comparisons. Precise contact closure on novel geometry, however, remains a key open challenge.
authors: Nga Kiu Kelly Ho, Yilin Liu, Hao Xu, Niloy J. Mitra
bullets: Addresses underconstrained grasp synthesis without language, target grasps, or object trajectories.
Predicts a time-indexed contact map and hand poses using conditional flow matching, avoiding autoregressive error accumulation.
Recovers rigid object motion via training-free, contact-guided weighted registration after estimating an attachment frame.
On held-out and in-the-wild objects, motion is smoother than LatentHOI, about 30× faster per frame, and preferred in roughly two thirds of user comparisons.
Precise contact closure on novel geometry remains an open challenge.

A geometric stage then detects the attachment frame 𝑡att and propagates the object rigidly with the hand, yielding transforms {𝑇𝑘}, through contact-guided weighted registration (Sec. 4.3).

papers.abstract: We present a learning-based framework that enables a full-scale bipedal humanoid to sprint at over 7 m/s with motion-prior-guided gait and perform aggressive cornering at high speed with a pronounced trunk lean of up to $25^\circ$. Achieving this combination is challenging: above approximately 4 m/s, periodic foot impacts induce severe, high-frequency yaw-rate oscillations intrinsic to high-speed gaits. This high-frequency temporal structure corrupts the history of proprioceptive feedback that flat-MLP policies rely on, while rendering conventional yaw-rate tracking rewards counterproductive, as they fight against the robot's natural oscillatory dynamics. Moreover, a single style prior shared across skills cannot tell which skill is commanded and inherently compromises the low-speed skill fidelity. To overcome these limitations, we adopt a causal multi-head attention (MHA) module to explicitly model the high-frequency temporal feedback. In place of the oscillatory yaw rate, we design a heading-direction reward that supervises only the low-frequency velocity direction, allowing agile turning at high speed without suppressing natural gait oscillations. We further introduce skill-conditioned multi-adversarial-motion-prior (MAMP) discriminators that condition the style reward on the commanded skill. Ablation experiments confirm that each mechanism is essential: replacing structured temporal encoding with a flat-history MLP caps the top speed; reverting to yaw-rate tracking prevents high-speed turning; and a single shared discriminator makes in-place turning collapse into a quasi-static stance. Our framework bridges the gap between raw sprinting speed and reference-motion fidelity, demonstrating stable high-speed sprinting and aggressive cornering in both simulation and real-robot deployment.
authors: Huaxing Huang, Ruidong Li, Jinchao Han, Ziyang Dong, Wenhao Cui
bullets: High-speed foot impacts create yaw-rate oscillations that disrupt flat-history policies and make direct yaw-rate tracking counterproductive.
Causal multi-head attention captures high-frequency proprioceptive dynamics in the policy.
A heading-direction reward encourages turning while preserving natural gait oscillations.
Skill-conditioned multi-adversarial motion priors maintain distinct motion styles across sprinting and turning.
Ablations and simulation-to-real deployment demonstrate stable sprinting and aggressive cornering, including trunk lean up to 25°.

(3) The heading-direction reward supervises the low-frequency velocity direction at high speed, falling back to yaw-rate tracking below vmin. papers.abstract: Robust manipulation under uncertain object dynamics and geometry remains a core challenge in real-world robotics. Policies trained under fixed assumptions often degrade when object mass, friction, scale, or shape vary. Embedding-based adaptation methods such as Rapid Motor Adaptation (RMA) address this by conditioning actions on latent representations of environment dynamics inferred from interaction history. We investigate whether this paradigm scales from single arm settings to coordinated bimanual manipulation, where higher dimensional control, coupled contacts, and shared object forces introduce additional complexity. We evaluate bimanual RMA on three contact-rich ManiSkill tasks with randomized YCB object properties. Bimanual RMA, using observation-action history and dual wrist depth images, retains privileged policy performance on bimanual picking and lifting, while an otherwise matched stationary PPO policy without latent conditioning achieves low success; all methods remain limited on long-horizon stacking. We further demonstrate direct sim-to-real transfer on a dual Franka lifting task without real-world finetuning. Together, these results suggest that latent conditioning provides useful structure for scaling robust control to coordinated bimanual systems, while longer horizon tasks require additional temporal structure.
authors: Seung-Bin Joo, Alessandro Albini, Luca Wiehe, Perla Maiolino, Daniel Olmeda Reino, Jo\~ao F. Henriques

papers.abstract: Evaluating autonomous agents requires examining whether they can translate goals into coherent action across extended interactions. In persistent environments, this requires coordinating interdependent actions under incomplete observations, accounting for delayed effects, and adapting as earlier decisions shape subsequent opportunities. We introduce ASIWorld, a survival sandbox that combines persistent world and character state with character-scoped observations and a programmable asynchronous interface to study sustained goal execution. Agents pursue interdependent production and exploration tasks through direct actions or agent-authored programs that continue running between model calls. The evaluation assesses task success, the attainment of development achievements, and survival costs, complemented by an analysis of execution behavior. In an exploratory study of nine agent configurations using a common harness, eight complete the production task and six complete both tasks. Analyses of execution trajectories and performance across difficulty levels reveal different preparation, combat, and recovery behaviors among configurations with similar task outcomes. Incomplete preparation is associated with stalled progression, while configurations that complete the tasks differ in survival costs and the fulfillment of additional achievement criteria. These findings illustrate the value of assessing sustained goal execution through both task outcomes and the behaviors and costs associated with achieving them.
authors: Jianfeng Lin, Runze Wang, Haorong Hong, Yuxuan Xie, Zeno Zeng, Zhongyuan Liu
bullets: Agents must coordinate interdependent actions under partial observations, delayed effects, and changing opportunities.

In an exploratory study, 8 of 9 configurations completed the production task and 6 completed both production and exploration tasks.
Similar task outcomes masked differences in preparation, combat, recovery, and survival costs; incomplete preparation was linked to stalled progress.

papers.abstract: End-to-end driving policies can achieve strong task performance while offering limited control over their driving style. Driving style describes how a vehicle accelerates, brakes, and maintains distance. Policies trained without explicit preference conditioning lack a direct mechanism for adjusting these behaviors at inference. We propose YOUDrive, a vision--language--action planner for continuous and composable driving-style control. Each teacher's behavior is distilled into a task vector, a learned parameter update that induces a style direction in the planner's representation. These directions can be scaled and combined at inference without retraining the backbone. Conditioned on these directions, a flow-matching decoder models a multimodal trajectory distribution and generates kinematically feasible motion alternatives. We introduce the Style Alignment Score (SAS) to describe human-referenced kinematic behavior after safety and task gating. On NAVSIM navtest, a single coefficient monotonically controls assertiveness across six teacher-derived personas, while PDMS remains above 0.90 across the tested individual and blended configurations, reaching 0.954. Further analyses reveal systematic policy-specific kinematics after controlling for scene context, whereas the evaluated discrete style labels provide limited additional explanatory power. Code, checkpoints, and the metric will be released.
authors: Guantian Zheng, Lidong Yu, Tianyu Gao, Jiaxing Chen, Jiashu Li, Chen Lv
bullets: Addresses the lack of inference-time control over acceleration, braking, and following-distance preferences in end-to-end driving policies.
Distills each teacher’s behavior into a task vector that can be scaled or combined without retraining the planner backbone.
Uses a flow-matching decoder to generate multimodal, kinematically feasible trajectory alternatives.
Introduces Style Alignment Score (SAS) for evaluating human-referenced kinematic behavior after safety and task gating.
On NAVSIM navtest, assertiveness changes monotonically across six personas while PDMS stays above 0.90, reaching 0.954; evaluated discrete style labels add limited explanatory power.

papers.abstract: Biomedical Named Entity Linking (BioNEL) is the task of mapping mentions extracted from biomedical texts to canonical entities or concepts in the standardized knowledge base. Although existing methods have achieved remarkable performance in mapping accuracy, most rely on training with domain-specific datasets, which fundamentally limits their cross-domain adaptability. To address this limitation, we propose BioNEL-RAG, a novel training-free framework that combines retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) with large language models (LLMs). Within this framework, the RAG module focuses on retrieving candidate entities, while the large language model module plays the role of selecting the most appropriate candidate for entity normalization, which is based on the analysis of the mention's context, with the aid of its remarkable text comprehension capabilities. Experimental results demonstrate that BioNEL-RAG achieves performance comparable to existing methods without requiring training on subdomain datasets, whereas these methods necessitate fine-tuning on specific subdomains such as genes, diseases, or chemical compounds.
authors: Ziyi Chen, Hui Liu, Ziyang Ling, Ronald X. Xu, Mingzhai Sun
bullets: Addresses the limited cross-domain adaptability of methods trained on subdomain-specific datasets.
Uses RAG to retrieve candidate biomedical entities from a standardized knowledge base.
Uses an LLM to select the best candidate based on the mention’s context.
Achieves performance comparable to existing methods without fine-tuning on gene, disease, or chemical subdomains.

papers.tldr: BioNEL-RAG enables biomedical entity linking without domain-specific training by combining candidate retrieval with LLM-based context-aware selection.

papers.abstract: Online continual learning (OCL) requires a learner to acquire a sequence of tasks in a single pass over the data, and catastrophic forgetting of earlier tasks remains its central challenge. Despite the many methods proposed to mitigate forgetting, the theoretical understanding of forgetting in OCL is still limited: existing analyses mostly focus on linear, overparameterized, or neural tangent kernel regimes, and it remains unclear which factors govern forgetting and how they affect it. To fill this gap, we analyze single-pass Shuffle SGD under strongly convex and general convex objectives and derive explicit upper bounds on the expected final forgetting. Further analysis of these bounds shows how the per-task data amount, task similarity, and task ordering enter them, and that their effects can differ across objective classes. Moreover, experiments with neural networks on Split-CIFAR-100 and PMNIST show that the trends suggested by our theory also appear in practice, indicating that these insights extend beyond the convex setting.
authors: Renjie Cao, Yifei Cheng, Li Shen
bullets: Studies single-pass Shuffle SGD under strongly convex and general convex objectives.
Derives explicit upper bounds on expected final forgetting.
Shows that per-task data, task similarity, and task ordering affect forgetting, with different effects across objective classes.
Neural-network experiments on Split-CIFAR-100 and PMNIST exhibit trends consistent with the theory.
The theoretical analysis is focused on convex objectives, while experiments assess whether its insights extend beyond that setting.

(c) MLP: forgetting increases with the distance between the two similar tasks and with the amount of data. All results are averaged over 5 random seeds.

papers.title: Formalizing Forgetting: Theory of Forgetting for Online Continual Learning
papers.tldr: This work develops a theory explaining how data amount, task similarity, and task order drive forgetting in online continual learning.

papers.abstract: Camera-first agents must act on the visual world as it unfolds. We argue that the central obstacle for future camera-first agents is not recognition ability - multimodal models (vision-language and live/streaming alike) generalize well through language and remain the right tool for semantic reasoning - but time. Many visual targets are ephemeral: they appear, are query-relevant, and leave within a short window. Binding memory to the same end-to-end path as reasoning means that by the time a monolithic pipeline completes, the evidence is gone. We formalize this as Ephemeral-Target Interaction (ETI) and a Perceptual Deadline Contract separating a hard memory deadline from a soft reasoning deadline, grounded in the bounded, passive nature of sensory and working memory. We propose a two-deadline architecture: an always-on, bounded, non-semantic fast path; an active remembering mechanism that commits a moment to durable memory before it is overwritten (event-driven in v1); and a deferred deliberation layer (multimodal model + tools). We instantiate the contract on real MOT17 track windows, a consistency check, and calibrate the single-path baseline from measured frontier-model latency: even a short answer takes 1.2-9.3 s, and an agentic identify-and-search longer. Answers can be late; evidence cannot be missed.
authors: Xiaofan Wu, Xi Zeng, Miaoxia Chen, Peishan Chen, Shuyan Li, Chen Wang, Jiyun Yao, Hanyong Zhong, Jiahao Zhu
bullets: The key bottleneck is timing, not visual recognition or semantic reasoning.
Ephemeral-Target Interaction (ETI) describes targets that appear and disappear before processing finishes.
A Perceptual Deadline Contract separates a hard memory deadline from a soft reasoning deadline.
The proposed architecture combines an always-on bounded fast path, active durable-memory capture, and deferred multimodal deliberation with tools.
Measured frontier-model latency suggests answers may take 1.2–9.3 seconds or longer, while evidence can disappear sooner.

Figure 3: Bounded-horizon sweep: memory recall vs passive buffer horizon H (lazy gate, period 0.5 s) vs the horizon-robust event-driven remembering.
Figure 1: Ours: always-on bounded passive store → active remembering (hard deadline) → deferred deliberation (soft deadline).
