papers.selection_reason: Proposes memory architecture and perceptual deadlines for camera-first embodied agents acting on ephemeral visual targets.
papers.title: How Should a Camera-First AI Agent Work?
papers.tldr: Camera-first agents should capture fleeting visual evidence immediately, then reason about it later, because semantic processing may outlast the moment an object is visible.

papers.abstract: Multimodal contrastive learning typically relies on manually specified scoring functions, such as cosine similarity, to quantify the similarity between representations from different modalities. Several such functions have been recently proposed to extend contrastive learning beyond two modalities. In principle, however, any function that assigns high compatibility to matched samples and low compatibility to mismatched ones could serve as a scorer. Motivated by this broader view, we instantiate the scorer with a Transformer and find that even a randomly initialized model, when kept frozen, can outperform strong handcrafted multimodal contrastive baselines, whereas optimizing the scorer jointly with the encoders is less effective. Building on this observation, we introduce the Prior-Fitted Scorer (PFS): a Transformer scorer pre-trained on synthetic multimodal data generated from structural causal model (SCM) priors before transferring it to real-world data. The SCM exposes the scorer to diverse dependency structures, including shared, pairwise, and private information, providing a structured prior over higher-order cross-modal similarity. Across four real-world datasets, frozen Transformer scorers are competitive to contrastive baselines, and prior-fitting further improves the random initialization. More broadly, our results suggest that multimodal contrastive learning need not rely on manual similarity functions: Transformers can provide strong inductive biases, while causal pretraining can further shape these biases.
authors: Tillmann Rheude, Roland Eils, Benjamin Wild
bullets: Challenges the reliance on manually specified scorers such as cosine similarity in multimodal contrastive learning.
Uses a Transformer as the compatibility scorer and finds frozen random initialization more effective than jointly optimizing the scorer with encoders.
Introduces Prior-Fitted Scorer (PFS), pretraining the scorer on synthetic multimodal data generated from structural causal model priors.
The SCM prior represents shared, pairwise, and modality-private information to shape higher-order cross-modal similarity.
Across four real-world datasets, frozen Transformer scorers are competitive with contrastive baselines, while prior-fitting improves over random initialization.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of the Prior-Fitted Scorer (PFS), illustrated on the trimodal MIMIC-Symile setting (Saporta et al., 2024). (a) We sample latent causal structures and generate synthetic multimodal tuples from an SCM prior M. (b) A Transformer scoring function sθ is pretrained on these synthetic tuples to distinguish compatible from mismatched multimodal combinations with loss L, thereby shaping its inductive bias. (c) The PFS is transferred to the real dataset and kept frozen while the modality encoders Ei are optimized through the contrastive objective. (d) After extensive tuning, the PFS is evaluated on zero-shot predicting the future chest X-ray. Overall, a PFS replaces a manually specified similarity function with a Transformer whose structure is learned from a synthetic causal prior.

Figure 2: Overview of synthetic multimodal data generation and contrastive prior-fitting. A DAG G defines causal dependencies among latent variables, while the binary assignment matrix A selects the latent subsets contributing to each modality, inducing shared, subset-specific, and modality-private information. The selected latent variables are combined through linear and nonlinear readouts to produce modality vectors. During prior-fitting, matched tuples contain modalities from the same synthetic sample, whereas negatives are formed by replacing the target modality with a sampled mismatched candidate before scoring with sθ.

Figure 3: Validation performance of well-tuned baselines, the frozen Transformer and the PFS on the UKB. a) Scaling the priorfitting with more sampled SCMs improves transfer to real-world data. b) Using the frozen PFS leads to faster convergence and higher retrieval accuracy than the baselines.

Table 2: Comparison of well-tuned models optimized with different multimodal contrastive objectives. Values represent top-1 accuracy of the retrieval task (mean ± SE). Best non-overlapping value bold.

papers.abstract: Bengali has no grammatical gender, but honorificity is obligatory: every third-person reference must choose ordinary or respectful register. English has no such signal, so the system must choose a level of deference that the source never specified. We use this property to measure how large language models (LLMs) allocate respect in English--Bengali translation. Our evaluation set contains 2{,}016 sentences across 72 occupations. Each appears in seven sentence frames under four pronoun conditions. Masculine and feminine versions differ by one word, forming counterfactual pairs. We report a single Honorific Bias Score (HBS) for each model on a 0--100 scale, covering both the gender and occupation axes. A lower score means that respect is allocated more evenly. For the occupation analysis, we compute each occupation's honorific rate across the seven no-pronoun sentence frames. The standard deviation of these 72 occupation-level rates ranges from 17.2 to 35.5 percentage points across models, showing substantial variation in how honorifics are allocated across occupations. Occupation is associated with 3.2\% to 51.5\% of the variance in register choice, compared with at most 1.2\% for gender. Gender effects are much smaller overall: only two of the nine models show significant directional gender gaps, and they favor opposite genders. HBS ranges from 19.9 to 70.1 across the nine models, showing substantial variation in how evenly the models allocate respect.
authors: Ajwad Abrar, Md Kamrul Hasan, Hasan Mahmud
bullets: Bengali requires choosing ordinary or respectful register, although English source text does not specify deference.
The benchmark contains 2,016 sentences spanning 72 occupations, seven frames, and four pronoun conditions, including one-word-difference gender counterfactuals.

Across nine models, HBS ranges from 19.9 to 70.1; occupation explains 3.2%–51.5% of register-choice variance, versus at most 1.2% for gender.
Occupation-level honorific-rate variability is substantial, while only two models show significant directional gender gaps, favoring opposite genders.

papers.abstract: Nheengatu (yrl), the Amazonian L\'ingua Geral, has 6--10 thousand speakers and is co-official in S\~ao Gabriel da Cachoeira (Brazil), yet remains poorly served by evaluated Portuguese--Nheengatu MT resources. We present the largest parallel corpus assembled for the language (14.5k Portuguese--Nheengatu pairs), anchored by the 2023 official translation of the Brazilian Federal Constitution; the first MT evaluation set built from transcribed spontaneous speech; and, to our knowledge, the first open-weight MT models dedicated to bidirectional Portuguese--Nheengatu translation. Three findings organize the paper. First, translation into Nheengatu on held-out constitutional articles plateaus on development data regardless of training length or model size, and much of the remaining error sits in conventional legal terms that the written sources do not attest consistently; a terminology success rate over a frozen lexicon shows that glossary mechanisms at training time and lexical constraints at decoding each raise term realization, the latter at a cost in repetitive output that chrF++ barely registers. Second, a corpus expansion that adds transcribed conversation raises speech chrF++ by 24--27 points while leaving written domains unchanged, a register gap that written-only benchmarks cannot see. Third, a larger NLLB model helps translation into Portuguese but not into Nheengatu on legal or speech text. For Portuguese-to-Nheengatu translation, our final systems reach 31.7--32.8 chrF++ on article-disjoint constitutional text, 64.1--64.5 on the near-domain set (62.1 after removing items with target-side content overlap), and 45.2--47.5 on speech.
authors: Fabr\'icio Carraro, Rodolfo Joel Zevallos, Rodrigo Gon\c{c}alves de Souza, Caio Henrique Faustino da Silva, John E. Ortega
bullets: Assembles a 14.5k-pair parallel corpus centered on the 2023 Portuguese translation of Brazil’s Federal Constitution, plus the first spontaneous-speech MT evaluation set.
Releases the first open-weight bidirectional Portuguese–Nheengatu MT models, with evaluations on constitutional, near-domain, and speech text.
Glossary training and constrained decoding improve realization of legal terminology, though decoding constraints increase repetitive output.
Adding transcribed conversation improves speech chrF++ by 24–27 points without improving written-domain performance, exposing a register gap.
Larger NLLB models help translation into Portuguese but not into Nheengatu; remaining errors include inconsistently attested legal terms.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Terminology realization versus chrF++ on hinted legal development data. Free beam-4 gives 30.22 chrF++ at 62.6 TSR; hard constraints with a wide beam and five hints reach 83.3 TSR at 29.37. Two settings are dominated in both dimensions at once: soft reranking (29.41/64.1) and hard constraints at beam-4 (27.43/75.8), where narrow constrained search substantially reduces reference similarity and a wider beam recovers part of the loss, as the dynamic-beam-allocation literature predicts (Post and Vilar, 2018). The decoder realizes 164 of 165 requested surface-form insertions, or 99.4%. This measures surface inclusion rather than semantic, morphological, or syntactic correctness. The wide-beam gain is hint-conditional: the argmax drops only when hints are present.

papers.abstract: The predominance of English-language Web content creates an information-access barrier for speakers of low-resource languages such as Amharic. This paper presents the design, imple-mentation, and evaluation of a bidirectional Amharic-English cross-language question answering (CLQA) system that allows a user to formulate a natural-language question in either Amharic or English and retrieve an answer from documents written in the other language. The system integrates a statistical machine translation (SMT) component for query translation, a maximum-entropy named entity recognition (NER) component for Amharic text processing, semantic-based indexing, question analysis, passage retrieval, and answer extraction. A domain-diverse Amharic-English parallel corpus was used to train the SMT component, while monolingual cor-pora supported language modeling. Documents were normalized, tokenized, stemmed, indexed, and semantically enriched before retrieval. The original evaluation used precision and recall as the principal effectiveness measures. For Amharic-to-English retrieval, the system achieved 72% precision and 79% recall; for English-to-Amharic retrieval, it achieved 65% precision and 70% recall. These findings show that a modular translation-and-retrieval architecture can provide useful cross-language access even under low-resource conditions. This revised article preserves the original experimental claims while situating them in the context of subsequent multilingual transformer and Amharic QA research.
authors: Emebet Bekele, Fekade Getahun
bullets: Addresses the information-access barrier caused by limited Amharic Web content.
Translates user questions with statistical machine translation and processes Amharic text using maximum-entropy NER.
Uses normalization, tokenization, stemming, semantic indexing, question analysis, passage retrieval, and answer extraction.
Reports 72% precision and 79% recall for Amharic-to-English retrieval, and 65% precision and 70% recall in the reverse direction.
Demonstrates useful cross-language QA under low-resource conditions; the article also contextualizes the work alongside later multilingual transformer research.

papers.abstract: Hybrid language models interleave Gated DeltaNet (GDN) layers, whose recurrent memory has a fixed size, with full-attention layers, whose key-value (KV) cache grows with the context and dominates serving memory. In this paper, we ask whether the recurrent memory already knows what the attention memory will need. We first show that which GDN heads of Qwen3.8-27B keep long memories is fixed by the weights rather than by the document. Next, we define the future utility of a KV entry by how much removing it changes the attention output over the model's own continuations, and find that the write gate, decay and write magnitude that GDN layers emit during prefill anticipate this utility before any query is seen. Because the relation is spread across many GDN heads and layers, and a linear map recovers its trend but less of its high-utility tail than a nonlinear one, we propose GateSight, which learns it with lightweight per-head multilayer perceptrons that read these signals and no attention score. Their predicted utility decides which entries each attention layer keeps, and how much each layer keeps is set by the model's native attention output gate, whose mean differs by more than an order of magnitude across layers. Finally, at serving time, GateSight scores the cache once after prefill and physically releases discarded KV entries. Experimental results on SCBench and RULER-4096 with Qwen3.8-27B and, with the same recipe, the sparse-attention model Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, up to the 262K-token limit of the models, show that with a tenth of the attention KV cache, GateSight is the most accurate of five query-agnostic methods on three of the four model-benchmark pairs and leads KVzip on all four, by 9.5 to 47.2 points. Notably, it scores a full-length context with negligible overhead relative to prefill.
authors: Junjie Li, Jiong Lou, Jie Li
bullets: GDN prefill signals—write gate, decay, and write magnitude—anticipate future KV-entry utility before attention queries are available.
Lightweight per-head nonlinear predictors estimate utility without using attention scores.
The model’s native attention output gate determines the retention budget separately for each attention layer.
After one post-prefill scoring pass, discarded KV entries are physically released for serving.

At one-tenth of the KV cache, GateSight leads KVzip across all four model-benchmark pairs and is the most accurate of five query-agnostic methods on three; scope covers Qwen3.8-27B and Qwen3.8-Flash-Next up to 262K tokens.

papers.abstract: Versatile quadruped locomotion depends on a tight coupling between what the robot perceives and what its body can execute. Yet existing visual controllers typically organize depth history using fixed temporal patterns, overlooking that the same temporal span corresponds to different spatial ranges as the robot's speed, posture, and gait phase change. Consequently, the same visual history may be insufficient in one motion state but outdated or misaligned in another. To address this limitation, we propose TempoLoco, a body-aware dynamic visual perception framework that organizes visual memory according to the robot's current locomotion state. TempoLoco learns multiple complementary temporal views from a long depth buffer, encodes them within a shared feature space, and dynamically aggregates them using proprioceptive history and multi-scale terrain evidence. This enables a single policy to align visual anticipation with the robot's current motion capabilities across complex terrains, including stairs, platforms, gaps, discrete obstacles, rough ground, and slopes. From the experiment analysis, TempoLoco achieves a 78.4% success rate, compared with 58.2% for the strongest fixed-history baseline and 62.1% for uniform multi-scale fusion. In separate capability evaluations, it completes 41/45 simulated trials across nine terrain types and 23/25 real-world trials on a Unitree B2 with a fixed arm, demonstrating robust and deployable locomotion through body-aware dynamic visual perception.
authors: Hao Zhang, Yuping Yan, Yitian Hong, Luying Feng, Tianhong Wang, Fengqi Dai, Wei Chen, Yaochu Jin
bullets: Fixed temporal visual histories can become spatially mismatched as speed, posture, and gait phase change.
TempoLoco learns multiple temporal views from a long depth buffer in a shared feature space.
Proprioceptive history and multi-scale terrain evidence dynamically select and fuse the most relevant views.
It achieves a 78.4% success rate versus 58.2% for the strongest fixed-history baseline and 62.1% for uniform multi-scale fusion.
The system completes 41/45 simulated trials and 23/25 real-world trials on a Unitree B2 across diverse terrains.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Detailed architecture of TempoLoco (actor path shown). At each 50-Hz policy step, a 37-slot depth FIFO and a five-step, 260-dimensional proprioceptive history are provided to the temporal-perception module. Four globally learned continuous strides construct complementary eight-frame histories; the displayed stride values are the initialization, and filled and hollow markers denote integer-slot and interpolated samples, respectively. A scaleshared visual encoder maps each history to a 128-dimensional feature, and a body-state-conditioned temporal gate computes online softmax fusion weights from proprioceptive history and all scale-specific visual features. The fused 128-dimensional visual representation is concatenated with proprioception to form the 388-dimensional actor input, which is processed by the four-expert locomotion MoE and the unchanged action-processing pipeline to produce 12 leg-joint targets. The actor and critic use independent temporal modules, and the critic appends 33 privileged dimensions only after temporal fusion. The lower panel shows deployment on the arm-equipped Unitree B2, with the arm fixed outside the locomotion action space.

Fig. 1. Overview of TempoLoco. Globally learned temporal strides construct complementary depth histories, which are dynamically aggregated by a body-state-conditioned gate using proprioceptive history and multi-scale terrain evidence. The resulting visual representation drives a single leg-control policy across diverse complex terrains. The strides remain fixed after training, whereas the fusion weights adapt online at every policy step. The mounted arm is fixed and excluded from the locomotion action space.

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) commonly couple video and action experts through dense, layer-wise Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) attention, exposing action prediction to irrelevant visual features while enforcing matched expert depths. This coupling hinders selective visual-feature use and introduces redundant computation. We introduce Bridge-of-Experts (BoE), instantiated as BridgeWAM, which aggregates visual, language, and proprioceptive priors through 32 Latent Bridge Queries (LBQs) into a shared, limited latent space. Joint video-action supervision lets action gradients guide the Video Expert toward representations better suited for action prediction, while the Action Expert learns to selectively retrieve task-relevant information through cross-attention. Decoupling expert depths and reusing LBQs during action denoising yield a 5.06B model with a 30-layer Video Expert and a two-layer Action Expert, achieving 98.25% success on LIBERO and 72.24% pooled success on LIBERO-Plus, demonstrating effective task execution and strong generalization with an ultralight action head. Ablations support joint representation adaptation and unified LBQ conditioning. Relative to Fast-WAM, BridgeWAM reduces single-sample inference FLOPs by 28.72% in simulation profiling and real-robot latency to 77.1 ms (a 2.47-fold speedup). Qualitative experimental results further indicate preferential attention to target objects and task destinations across perturbations.
authors: Jiaxin Fang, Ruitong Liu, Zeyu Lai, Xingyu Wang, Mingyuan Jia, Pingyue Sheng, Weikang Wan, Mengdi Xu, Yuxiang Gao
bullets: Replaces dense layer-wise video–action coupling with 32 Latent Bridge Queries that aggregate visual, language, and proprioceptive information.
Joint video–action supervision adapts visual representations for action prediction, while cross-attention retrieves task-relevant features.
Decouples expert depths and reuses bridge queries, enabling a deep 30-layer Video Expert with an ultralight two-layer Action Expert.
Achieves 98.25% success on LIBERO and 72.24% pooled success on LIBERO-Plus; reduces simulated single-sample FLOPs by 28.72% and reaches 77.1 ms real-robot latency.
Qualitative results suggest preferential attention to target objects and destinations under perturbations.

papers.abstract: Extreme low-bit weight-only quantization is an effective approach to reducing the deployment costs of large language models. Below 3 bits, scalar quantization often suffers severe accuracy loss, while vector quantization (VQ) better preserves accuracy through more expressive joint encoding. However, existing VQ methods still exhibit substantial degradation on real-world tasks, and two design challenges remain underexplored: (1) protecting sensitive weight channels within jointly encoded vectors; and (2) allocating a fixed bit budget among representation components, such as direction and radius, to suit different weight matrices. To address these challenges, we propose SAGE: Split Adaptation and Grouping by Energy for weight-only vector quantization. First, Energy-Stratified Grouping (ESG) couples channel grouping with activation-weighted fitting, grouping channels from different energy tiers within each subvector to prioritize sensitive channels. Second, Adaptive Bit Split (ABS) balances direction-codebook capacity and radius precision per matrix, selecting the split with the lowest activation-weighted reconstruction error under a fixed budget. Across benchmarks covering knowledge, mathematics, code generation, instruction following, and tool use, SAGE achieves state-of-the-art performance in the 2-bit quantization setting. On Qwen3-30B-A3B, it retains 95.3% of the BF16 model's average benchmark score. With our custom-designed CUDA kernel, SAGE delivers up to a 2.55-fold non-streaming end-to-end speedup over FP16. The code is available at https://github.com/Zincwolf/sage.
authors: Xianglong Yan, Zenan Wu, Kewei Zhang, Kaicheng Yang, Yulun Zhang
bullets: Targets severe accuracy degradation in sub-3-bit weight-only quantization, especially on real-world tasks.
Energy-Stratified Grouping mixes channels across energy tiers and uses activation-weighted fitting to protect sensitive channels.
Adaptive Bit Split assigns the fixed bit budget between direction and radius for each weight matrix based on reconstruction error.
Achieves state-of-the-art 2-bit quantization performance across knowledge, math, code, instruction-following, and tool-use benchmarks.
On Qwen3-30B-A3B, retains 95.3% of BF16 average benchmark score and reaches up to 2.55× non-streaming end-to-end speedup over FP16 with a custom CUDA kernel.

Energy-Stratified Grouping (ESG) uses calibration activations to group channels across energy tiers within subvectors and protect sensitive channels through weighted fitting. Adaptive Bit Split (ABS) compares activation-weighted reconstruction errors to select a direction-index/radius bit split per matrix, using 18 bits per eight weights. Blockwise Optimization updates radius and codebook angles to match full-precision block outputs.

papers.abstract: Set-based variational autoencoders (VecSet VAEs) represent 3D shapes as compact sets of latent tokens. Although each token originates from a query at a sampled surface location, whether these latents truly align with geometry remains unclear. We investigate this alignment and identify four issues: (i) attention-sink-like tokens that attract queries from across the shape; (ii) spatially periodic repetitions in decoder attention responses; (iii) mismatched normal information in encoder and decoder query features; and (iv) missing supervision of the intrinsic relation between signed distance fields and surface normals. To address these issues, we introduce Align-VAE with four corresponding modifications: (i) a shared bank of learnable decoder tokens provides a workspace for global computation; (ii) distance-biased cross-attention guides retrieval toward nearby predicted spatial anchors; (iii) normal-free encoder queries align the two stages' access to normal information while retaining normals in the encoder keys and values; and (iv) a screened Poisson-inspired regularizer supervises surface values and normal-direction derivatives. These changes align latent retrieval and field prediction with geometry without enlarging the per-shape code. On the ABO dataset, Align-VAE reduces Chamfer distance by 26.6% compared to the standard VecSet VAE.
authors: Huaizhi Qu, Mingxin Yang, Xintong Han, Fangneng Zhan, Chunchao Guo
bullets: Identifies four geometry-alignment issues: attention-sink tokens, periodic decoder responses, encoder–decoder normal mismatch, and missing signed-distance/normal supervision.
Introduces shared decoder tokens for global computation and distance-biased cross-attention toward nearby spatial anchors.
Uses normal-free encoder queries while retaining normals in keys and values to align information access across stages.
Adds a screened Poisson-inspired regularizer for surface values and normal-direction derivatives.
Improves reconstruction without increasing the per-shape code size; evaluated on the ABO dataset.

papers.abstract: Long-term memory benchmarks for language agents primarily evaluate whether information from earlier interactions can be retrieved and used when relevant. Persistent memory systems face an additional problem before future use is known: deciding whether a memory should remain exact, be compressed, consolidated, or deleted. Existing benchmarks capture long-range retrieval, temporal reasoning, evidence reuse, and incremental interaction, but do not directly evaluate these earlier representation decisions. We formalize memory lifecycle evaluation and introduce VitaBench, a benchmark that makes lifecycle decisions measurable through repeated memory reviews and full-horizon counterfactual evaluation. VitaBench contains a controlled Diagnostic tier that isolates future-use patterns and a Naturalistic tier that composes them into generated customer-service-style interaction streams. We characterize lifecycle decision structure with three diagnostics: lifecycle headroom, measuring the advantage of adaptive choices over the best fixed strategy; horizon reversal, measuring when short-horizon decisions change under delayed consequences; and optimal-action diversity, measuring whether different memory states favor different lifecycle operations. Across both tiers, VitaBench exhibits substantial lifecycle structure: lifecycle headroom is 1.364 in Diagnostic and 1.405 in Naturalistic, and 60.2% and 56.5% of states, respectively, change their preferred action between short and full horizons. A learned delayed lifecycle policy further improves over the best fixed strategy on VitaBench-Naturalistic, reaching 101.5 versus 83.4 joint utility. These results show that retrieving past information and deciding how it should persist are distinct evaluation problems, and that lifecycle management requires evaluation of the delayed consequences of representation decisions.
authors: Muquan Yu, Dihan Hu
bullets: Introduces memory lifecycle evaluation through repeated reviews and full-horizon counterfactuals.
Includes a controlled Diagnostic tier and a naturalistic customer-service-style interaction tier.
Measures adaptive-choice potential, horizon reversals, and diversity of optimal lifecycle actions.
Finds substantial delayed-decision structure across both tiers, with many states changing preferred actions over longer horizons.
A learned delayed lifecycle policy improves joint utility over the best fixed strategy on the Naturalistic tier.

figures.caption: Figure 1: VITABENCH evaluates memory lifecycle decisions. At each review point, a policy must choose how a memory should persist before its future use is known. VITABENCH branches from the same pre-decision memory state, applies each candidate lifecycle action, and replays the same future interaction stream for every branch. The resulting full-horizon utilities identify the preferred lifecycle action and quantify the benchmark’s lifecycle decision structure.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive world models have emerged as a powerful paradigm for sample efficient decision making, yet their open loop rollouts often exhibit increasing drift that leads to error accumulation even within a relatively small planning horizon. Hierarchical temporal abstraction is a natural candidate to mitigate such drift by reducing the effective prediction horizon; however, existing hierarchical designs can introduce added structural and conceptual complexity, sometimes making them difficult to control and limiting gains over flat baselines. To this end, we introduce MHWA (Multi-timescale Hierarchical World-Action model), which employs a strided high level context channel to reduce global context update frequency, effectively curbing the propagation of compounding drift. Crucially, via context aware routing, the gating network dynamically reconfigures a low level mixture of experts by using both global context and current observations, thereby enabling flexible high-low coordination, helping alleviate interference commonly observed in static hierarchies. Empirically, using RLiable's seed-by-game aggregation, MHWA (77M parameters) achieves an IQM human normalized score (HNS) of 0.884 across three training seeds on a 14-game Atari subset using 10% subsampled offline data, outperforming a matched JOWA-70M baseline (0.529) and achieving numerically comparable performance to JOWA-150M while using nearly half the parameters and 70.88% fewer training FLOPs per sequence.
authors: Pengcheng Pan, Guoqing Ma, Yuhan Zhang, Yang Chen, Yichen Liu, Ziheng Li, Shan Yu
bullets: Addresses error accumulation and rollout drift that limit open-loop planning in autoregressive world models.
Uses a strided high-level context channel to reduce global context update frequency and shorten the effective prediction horizon.
Dynamically routes a low-level mixture of experts using global context and current observations for flexible high-low coordination.
On a 14-game Atari subset with 10% offline data, achieves 0.884 IQM HNS across three seeds, versus 0.529 for matched JOWA-70M.
Matches JOWA-150M numerically while using 77M parameters and 70.88% fewer training FLOPs per sequence.

figures.caption: Figure 1: The architecture of MHWA. It is illustrated at a context-update timestep t = 1 +m · k. The model processes an interleaved sequence of observation (ot) and action (at) tokens. (Top) At this specific strided step, the High-Level Manager consumes the downsampled history to infer a slowly varying global context zctx, supervised by a skip-step prediction head phigho that forecasts the observation at the next coarse step ôt+k. We refer to the original, complete sequence as the dense trajectory, in contrast to the downsampled input used by the manager. (Bottom) The Low-Level Worker operates at the atomic resolution. It employs a Context-Aware Dynamic Routing mechanism where a Gating Network utilizes both the current dense input and the refreshed high-level context zctx to dynamically route computation to a sparse subset of experts (MoE). The worker’s output drives the world model heads (po, pr, pd) and the critic head (hQ).

Figure 2: Quantitative comparison of open-loop prediction within the context window (T = 5 to 8). We analyze reconstruction quality (MSE, PSNR, SSIM) of MHWA-77M against JOWA-150M and a parameter-matched JOWA-70M. While the reduced-capacity JOWA-70M degrades rapidly as rollout depth increases, MHWA remains stable and, in terms of MSE and SSIM, matches or exceeds the larger JOWA-150M. The gap between MHWA and JOWA-70M is consistent with the benefit of structural inductive bias under constrained parameters.

Figure 3: PCA visualization of expert activations in the last MoE layer. (a) Full MHWA maps Assault and Phoenix closely together, indicating they utilize similar expert combinations, which aligns with their shared vertical shooting mechanics. (b, c) This structural similarity vanishes without high-level supervision or temporal stride, indicating a failure to capture shared cross-game dynamics.

Figure 4: Long-horizon open-loop reconstruction diagnostic from t = 5 to t = 54. MHWA shows smoother long-horizon degradation than the smaller monolithic baseline and remains broadly comparable to, while being less affected by sharp fluctuations than, the 150M baseline; however, it does not eliminate eventual manifold departure.

papers.abstract: Latent diffusion models enable high-quality video generation, but video VAE encoding and decoding remain computationally expensive. Existing methods use stage-specific lightweight operators, yet either constrain spatial and temporal computation jointly or remove temporal computation altogether, without distinguishing their compression sensitivities in pretrained Conv3D. To address these limitations, we present LightVAE, a compression framework that exploits redundancy in temporal modeling and network depth. LightVAE exactly reparameterizes eligible causal Conv3D layers into an aggregate spatial response and a difference-driven temporal correction. Based on their distinct compression sensitivities, temporal low-rank compression (TLR) keeps the aggregate spatial kernel dense and applies layer-specific low-rank approximation only to the temporal correction. An algebraically equivalent folded implementation converts the arithmetic savings into practical acceleration. LightVAE further uses width-preserving block pruning to reduce depth and probe-guided feature alignment, guided by feedback from a frozen teacher suffix, to recover quality after compression. The framework also extends to video encoders. Across three video VAE backbones and two GPU platforms, LightVAE consistently accelerates decoding. For the Wan VAE family, it achieves up to $2.24\times$ and $1.11\times$ the decoding throughput of state-of-the-art efficient VAE decoders on NVIDIA H100 and RTX~5090, respectively, with higher DAVIS PSNR and lower LPIPS. On MiniMax-H3, it achieves up to $2.97\times$ the original decoding throughput while retaining 99.51\% of the original model's overall VBench-2.0 score. Our code is available at https://github.com/ModelTC/LightVAE.
authors: Shiqiao Gu, Yang Yong, Fengjun Zhong, Ruihao Gong, Chengtao Lv, Xiangyu Fan, Lei Yang, Xianglong Liu

Across three VAE backbones and two GPUs, reports up to 2.97× original decoding throughput while retaining 99.51% of MiniMax-H3’s VBench-2.0 score; Wan VAEs also show improved DAVIS PSNR and lower LPIPS.

papers.abstract: Test-Time Discovery (TTD) aims to recognize known classes and detect novel ones from a continuous unlabeled test stream after deployment. Existing TTD methods mainly rely on visual clustering or prototype comparison, and can only assign anonymous labels to discovered classes, leaving them difficult to interpret in open-world applications. In this paper, we propose SEGA, a Semantic Grounding with Attributes framework for TTD. SEGA leverages large language models to generate attribute-rich descriptions for known classes and constructs an attribute-anchored visual-semantic space during training. At test time, we introduce Relational Semantic Grounding (RSG), which grounds unknown samples with similar and dissimilar known-class anchors, prompts the LLM to generate candidate concepts, and reranks them in the learned semantic space. The selected concept is further used for confidence-guided test-time semantic stabilization. By coupling attribute-level semantic alignment with relational concept grounding, SEGA transforms anonymous test-time clusters into interpretable semantic concepts. Experiments show that SEGA improves TTD baselines with the promise of semantic grounding for open-world.
authors: Tianle Liu, Gongbo Cheng, Chenggong Ni, Minming Gu, Tao Zhou, Fuyuan Hu, Fan Lyu
bullets: Addresses the limitation that existing TTD methods discover novel classes only with anonymous labels.
Uses an LLM to generate attribute-rich descriptions for known classes and builds an attribute-anchored visual-semantic space.
At test time, Relational Semantic Grounding compares unknown samples with similar and dissimilar known-class anchors to propose and rerank candidate concepts.
Applies confidence-guided semantic stabilization to refine discovered concepts over the test stream.
Experiments show improvements over TTD baselines, though the abstract does not report specific numerical results.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Method Schema. During training, LLM-generated attribute descriptions are used to construct a semantic space and guide cross-modal alignment between images and text. During testing, we discovers unknown classes, retrieves their semantic relations to known class anchors, and queries the LLM to generate candidate category names. The candidates are then grounded and filtered by the RSG module, and the selected prediction is used to guide confidence-aware test-time updates.

Figure 1: Comparison among different discovery method. (a) Non-semantic discovery, where unknown samples are detected or clustered online but are only assigned anonymous placeholder labels. (b) Pre-known semantic discovery handles unknown sample by matching visual features to a predefined category vocabulary, but it is unrealistic and its discovery ability is limited. (c) Our method aims to more meaningful and open-ended test-time discovery where unknown classes are grounded with visual and semantic relations to known classes, and interpreted through concept generation.

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) combine action generation with future prediction, allowing predicted futures to support action evaluation and robot decision making. However, the future associated with a candidate action may contain action-induced and environment-driven changes. Directly evaluating the predicted future may not fully characterize the future change associated with the candidate action. For example, a candidate action that worsens a favorable environmental future may still yield a favorable outcome, while one that improves an unfavorable environmental future may still yield an unfavorable outcome. To analyze this issue, we formulate a Structural Causal Model (SCM) for action evaluation in WAMs. The SCM formalizes how action-induced and environment-driven changes jointly shape future evaluation, and reveals a backdoor path through which environmental evolution can also affect the future evaluation associated with a candidate action. Intervention and backdoor adjustment account for this path, providing a causal basis for characterizing the future change associated with each candidate action. Based on this analysis, we propose Causal Action-Gain World Action Model (CAG-WAM). For each candidate action, CAG-WAM predicts an action-conditioned future and an environmental future under the same current observation, and defines their evaluation difference as causal action gain (CAG) for characterizing the future change associated with the candidate action. During training, we incorporate CAG into Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to guide robot policy learning. During inference, we evaluate the initial action with CAG and, when needed, revise it using predicted future information. Experiments on multiple benchmarks support the effectiveness of CAG-WAM.
authors: Peizheng Guo, Cheng Zhang, Xingyu Zhang, Changwen Zheng, Wenwen Qiang
bullets: WAMs can misjudge actions when predicted futures mix action-induced and environment-driven changes.
An SCM uses intervention and backdoor adjustment to isolate each candidate action’s future change.
CAG-WAM compares action-conditioned and environment-only futures to compute causal action gain (CAG).
CAG guides GRPO-based policy learning and supports inference-time action revision.
Experiments across multiple benchmarks support its effectiveness.

figures.caption: Figure 2: CAG-WAM Architecture. (a) Future-Conditioned Action Model generates action chunks from the current observation and task instruction, and can additionally incorporate future feedback for action revision. (b) Paired-Future World Model predicts action-conditioned and environmental futures under different action conditions and evaluates them using the same future evaluator.

Figure 3: Training and inference framework of CAG-WAM. (a) Training: candidate actions are evaluated by comparing their action-conditioned futures with the environmental future, and the resulting causal action gain is used as the policy-optimization advantage. (b) Inference: the initial action is evaluated using the same paired-future comparison; when its causal action gain falls below the revision threshold, future feedback is used for an additional action generation before execution.

Figure 1: Motivation and causal analysis. (a) Illustrative cases where the overall future evaluation may not fully reflect the future change associated with a candidate action. (b) Structural causal model of action evaluation, including the backdoor path At ← Ot → Et+1 → Ot+1 → Yt.
Figure 4: Visualization of CAG-WAM.

papers.abstract: Large language models are increasingly deployed in applications that act on users' long-term behavior histories, from personal assistants to recommendation and advertising systems. These applications demand the user dimension of LLM intelligence: inferring a person's preferences, intent, and likely future actions from weeks to years of behavior data. Yet current models are trained on static text or synthetic data, neither of which captures how user behavior evolves over time. Real-world behavior records, already available at scale on content platforms and in personal-assistant agents, offer a natural supervisory signal. We propose user behavior as supervision and introduce Vela, a framework that converts real user behavior data into trainable tasks and trajectories. From the anonymized behavior records of 100,000 users, Vela generates 100,000 tasks across 91 real-world task templates; difficulty-based filtering and trajectory acceptance criteria retain approximately 75,000 tasks with selected training trajectories. Fine-tuning Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on these trajectories improves performance over the base model by up to 11.5 points on user-related tasks and by an average of 4 points on general benchmarks. Training on more user behavior data further improves user-related performance, and reinforcement learning after fine-tuning outperforms reinforcement learning from the base model by up to 7.7 points. These gains suggest that real-world user behavior is a scalable source of supervision for both user-centered capabilities and the broader intelligence of LLMs.
authors: Yang Xiao, Yusong Sun, Haoyi Wu, Wenyang Hui, Weiqiang Hang, Luqing Wang, Zejian Wang, Zirui Tu, Jingsheng Mao, Shaobo Hu, Yang Luo, Jiale Guo, Jin Zhang, Yudan Liu, Zhaokai Luo, Ren Huan, Yao Hu, Chengyue Jiang, Wenjie Li, Chuan Mu
bullets: Addresses the gap between static or synthetic training data and the evolving behavior needed to infer users’ preferences, intent, and future actions.
Converts anonymized behavior records from 100,000 users into 100,000 tasks across 91 templates, retaining approximately 75,000 tasks with selected trajectories.
Fine-tuning Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on Vela trajectories improves user-related task performance by up to 11.5 points and general benchmark performance by an average of 4 points.
Additional user behavior data provides further gains, while reinforcement learning after fine-tuning outperforms reinforcement learning from the base model by up to 7.7 points.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of Vela, a framework for user behavior as supervision. (1) Anonymized behavior records from 100,000 users are split into visible histories and hidden futures. (2) A set of 91 question templates spanning two families, Predictive and Rubric, is instantiated to construct 100,000 composite tasks. Predictive questions are scored against ground-truth answers derived from future behavior, while Rubric questions are scored using task-specific rubrics. (3) Tasks are filtered by difficulty, and training trajectories are generated and selected to form two training corpora: Vela-Instruct and Vela-RFT.

papers.abstract: Large language models have advanced medical reasoning, but clinically grounded reasoning in traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) remains challenging because prescription decisions require integrating domain knowledge, syndrome differentiation, treatment principles, herbal prescription composition, and dosage determination. We develop a TCM language model family comprising models with 4 billion, 8 billion, and 14 billion parameters. The artificial intelligence contribution is a staged clinical alignment framework integrating large scale continued pretraining on TCM and clinical records, complementary reasoning supervision, and prescription-centered reinforcement learning (RL). We further formulate herbal prescription generation as a structured RL problem with prescription-level feedback, enabling direct optimization of clinical decision outputs beyond knowledge reproduction and generic instruction following. The engineering application is TCM clinical decision support, particularly herbal prescription recommendation. We evaluate the models on a public benchmark containing 25,620 expert-verified items across 13 TCM knowledge and clinical reasoning tasks and on a private retrospective dataset of 4,348 spleen and stomach disease prescription cases. The 14 billion parameter reinforcement aligned model achieves a prescription generation F1 of 37.0 on the public benchmark, compared with 32.3 for DeepSeek-R1 with 671 billion total parameters, and a herb-level F1 of 52.8 on the clinical dataset with improved dosage agreement. Reinforcement post-training consistently improves prescription recommendation across all scales, while physician-source analysis shows that expert heterogeneity affects reward stability. These findings demonstrate a scalable pathway from domain grounding and reasoning supervision to clinically oriented prescription decision support.

papers.abstract: Coupling a pretrained vision-language model (VLM) with a diffusion or flow-matching action expert has become the mainstream vision-language-action (VLA) paradigm for embodied policies, yet they remain unreliable once a task demands precise manipulation, e.g., submillimeter cable insertion. We attribute this weakness to a training objective that averages flow-matching errors across contexts and flow times, allocating little supervision to the few decisive moments determining task success. Along the generative path, inference integrates a locally supervised velocity field, so equally penalized errors at different flow times can affect the executed action unequally. Consequently, precision-task performance deteriorates as physical tolerance tightens by orders of magnitude. We call this supervision imbalance across contexts and flow times Flow-Time Starvation. The remedy is to jointly align supervision allocation and representation learning with context-dependent precision demand, enabling the policy to recognize when greater precision is needed. We instantiate this precision-forcing strategy as Precision-aware Reweighting and Internalization for Skilled Manipulation (PRISM), which scores precision demand offline, strengthens flow supervision where errors are consequential and action signals are visible, and internalizes that demand in the VLM condition representation. Simulation and real-robot experiments show that PRISM preserves or improves general-task performance while raising mean end-to-end success from 38.3% to 86.7% across drive connector insertion, bimanual connector mating, and screw tightening, substantially extending the precision boundary of existing embodied policies without new sensors or observation modalities.
authors: Chenghao Yue, Peiyan Li, Hao Wang, Lei Lv, Jiahao Chen, Huaping Liu, Yu Luo, Yuanlong Zhang
bullets: Identifies “Flow-Time Starvation”: standard flow-matching objectives under-supervise decisive moments in precise tasks.
Uses offline precision-demand scores to reweight flow supervision toward consequential, observable action signals.
Internalizes precision demand in the VLM representation so the policy can recognize when finer control is needed.
Simulation and real-robot experiments cover connector insertion, bimanual mating, and screw tightening.
Raises mean end-to-end success from 38.3% to 86.7% while preserving or improving general-task performance, without new sensors or modalities.

papers.abstract: On-device inference imposes constraints on model storage and operand traffic and thus benefits from compressed operand representations, which mandate the use of encoding and decoding operators. However, na\"{\i}ve placement of codec operators can cancel the operand traffic gains sought from compression. In this work, I present an algorithm to place codec operators into a source computational graph to make it compatible with target hardware. The edges of the graph are colored so that each induced subgraph is weakly connected and has a maximal node that both postdominates all subgraph inputs and dominates all subgraph outputs; this unique node - dubbed the $\textit{absolute dominator}$ - is the natural location to observe the traffic flowing through the subgraph and learn parametric codec operators. The algorithm's time complexity is linear in the source graph's size. With respect to na\"{\i}ve local codec placement, the algorithm reduces modeled operand traffic by $24\%$-$44\%$ across four models, including $24\%$ on SigLIP and $34\%$ on SmolLM2.
authors: Matteo Spallanzani
bullets: Addresses the problem that naive local codec placement can negate compression benefits by increasing operand traffic.
Colors computational-graph edges into weakly connected subgraphs with a unique absolute dominator for codec placement.
The algorithm runs in linear time with respect to the source graph size.
Modeled operand traffic is reduced by 24%–44% across four models versus naive local placement, including 24% on SigLIP and 34% on SmolLM2.
Scope: results are based on modeled operand traffic and target hardware compatibility, as described in the abstract.

figures.caption: Figure 1: (a) Detail of a source computational graph: two upstream reshape operators (R) feed a concatenate operator (C), and the rightmost one feeds a downstream reshape operator (R). (b) The algorithm’s first step inserts input codec markers (light gray) and output codec markers (dark gray) around each operator. (c) The second step assigns each edge a semantics, partitioning the graph into weakly connected subgraphs (edges sharing a color and dash pattern); the third step then identifies each subgraph’s absolute dominator (colored node). (d) The fourth step merges the leftmost upstream reshape subgraph into the concatenate subgraph; the rightmost upstream reshape subgraph fans out to two subgraphs, and thus cannot be merged without breaking the dominance property.
Table 1: Model storage (in MiB) across the four compression policies.

Table 2: Model traffic (in MiB) across the four compression policies. Arrows report changes relative to Z, rounded to one decimal place. In the absence of hardware support for traffic optimization (e.g., fusing the accumulation and decompression of matrix-matrix multiplication outputs), less aggressive compression policies (Y, X) can increase traffic; only policy W realizes savings on every model.

Table 4: Model traffic (in MiB) across three codec placement algorithms with fixed weight compression. Arrows report changes relative to local placement, rounded to one decimal place. The local baseline places codecs at the boundaries of every operator that requires encoded operands, independently for each operator; this policy does not track cross-boundary relationships that reveal opportunities for codec parameter sharing, and thus introduces redundant decode-encode pairs. The non-local algorithms apply policy W without and with coalescence; coalescence delivers savings for U-Net, which contains several routing and data layout operators.

Table 3: Number of codec items (in M) across the four compression policies. On graphs where chains of uncompressed operators (activations, normalizations) are interleaved with isolated data layout operators (reshape, view), policies prescribing that data layout operators use compressed operands to save traffic can increase the number of codec items with respect to policies prescribing that data layout operators use uncompressed operands.

Port blocks (i.e., pairs of input- and output-port sets that must share the same semantics) are shown for each operator: ∅ indicates that all port blocks are trivial (i.e., they contain only pairs of a singleton and an empty set); [*] denotes a variadic port. Letters Z, Y, X, and W indicate the first policy that selects each operator variant.

Table 6: Model population used for evaluation. Models were traced to torch.fx.GraphModule objects using the torch.export.export function; rotary positional embedding (RoPE) and root mean square normalization (RMSNorm) subgraphs were pattern-matched and replaced with standalone operators before hardware adaptation was executed.

papers.abstract: Despite recent advances in Aerial Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN), single Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) search-and-rescue in outdoor scenarios remains challenging due to partial observability, making cross-altitude collaboration a promising direction. However, existing collaborative navigation methods rely on precise target localization and rigid goal-dispatching paradigms, ignoring high-altitude observation uncertainty and suppressing low-altitude exploration autonomy. To address these issues, we introduce BGC-Nav, a training-free cross-altitude collaboration framework that enables robust navigation via Belief-Guided Coupling (BGC). Specifically, the high-altitude UAV maintains a Global Belief Memory encoding task-conditioned priors, which the low-altitude agent incorporates into decision-making via Local Exhaustion Memory (LEM), Local Attraction Augmentation (LAA), and Directional Belief Prior (DBP) as an advisory bias rather than a rigid command. Extensive experiments on ESARBench show that BGC-Nav consistently outperforms state-of-the-art single-agent and collaborative methods. Code is available at https://github.com/uestchjw/BGC-Nav.
authors: Jiuwu Hao, Yueyang Wu, Liguo Sun, Haolin Song, Zao Zhang, Pin Lv
bullets: Addresses outdoor UAV search-and-rescue challenges caused by partial observability and uncertain high-altitude observations.

The low-altitude UAV integrates this guidance through Local Exhaustion Memory, Local Attraction Augmentation, and Directional Belief Prior.
Treats high-altitude information as an advisory bias rather than a rigid goal assignment, preserving low-altitude autonomy.
Experiments on ESARBench report consistent improvements over existing single-agent and collaborative methods.ﬁ

Fig. 2: Qualitative comparison of navigation trajectories. Unlike the dispatch-and-reach collaborative method (AeroDuo) that rigidly enforces target waypoints, BGC-Nav maintains robust target search performance by balancing global semantic guidance and exploration autonomy.

papers.abstract: Explicit point correspondence is attractive for adapting video generators: it describes how visible surfaces move, but can overwrite the appearance prior learned by a large pretrained model. We study this tension in a 5.01B-parameter text-to-video diffusion transformer. ACROSSVAM2.0 combines a confidence-weighted track-and-visibility head, zero-initialized residual feedback, and asymmetric PCGrad that removes only the auxiliary component opposing the primary flow-matching gradient on shared LoRA parameters. The design preserves the generator exactly at initialization and protects its primary update during adaptation. In a four-way ablation trained for 1,000 steps with three independent seeds, the full method lowers KLT forward-backward cycle error in all three seeds relative to a matched flow-only continuation (mean seed-level difference -0.00711, SD 0.00505), while robust sharpness remains positive in all three. An expanded 24-prompt evaluation (216 videos) yields 9.7% lower aggregate CoTracker3 cycle error than the matched control and near-matched performance on six VBench dimensions; however, the seed-level tracking effect is heterogeneous and I3D-FVD regresses from 0.1824 to 0.2022. These results support a bounded claim: conflict-aware adaptation improves correspondence consistency without broad perceptual degradation, but does not uniformly improve video quality. We release equations, pseudocode, matched outputs, source tables, and artifact provenance.
authors: Nan Wu, Yee Hung Hong
bullets: Addresses the tension between explicit surface-motion supervision and preserving a pretrained video generator’s appearance prior.

Tracking improvements are heterogeneous across seeds, and I3D-FVD regresses from 0.1824 to 0.2022; video quality is not uniformly improved.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in 3D hand-object interaction (HOI) perception have opened new opportunities for learning dexterous robotic skills from human videos. However, existing dexterous imitation learning methods often rely on costly and manually teleoperated robot demonstrations, requiring substantial human effort. Therefore, we build DEXCAST, a framework that learns dexterous robotic hand control directly from monocular RGB-D videos by leveraging joint HOI reconstructions, without requiring any teleoperation. Furthermore, how to model high-dimensional robotic hand motion and extract temporal context to inform future action generation remains a key challenge. To this end, we propose a DexHand Motion Perception Module (DMPM) to capture inter-joint coordination and temporal dependencies in compact latent representations that condition our diffusion policy. Extensive real-world experiments demonstrate that DEXCAST achieves exceptional performance across diverse dexterous manipulation tasks.

Real-world experiments show strong performance across diverse dexterous manipulation tasks.

papers.abstract: LLM-augmented data workflows often involve multiple heterogeneous models operating over substantial shared context, such as schemas, tool specifications, interaction history, and intermediate results. Although prefix caching can reduce prefilling overhead, existing approaches are largely limited to reuse within the same model because KV states are tightly coupled to model-specific architectures. We present MapFlow, a system for efficient heterogeneous LLM serving via cross-model attention map reuse. Instead of reusing KV states, MapFlow reuses attention maps, which capture token dependency patterns and are more transferable across models. To enable efficient and accurate reuse, we combine partial recomputation with lightweight linear translation across layers and heads. To make attention reuse practical for long contexts, we further introduce block-level sparse compression and a fused retrieval kernel. Experiments show that MapFlow reduces prefilling latency and improves end-to-end serving efficiency while preserving generation quality across heterogeneous model pairs and multi-turn routing workloads. These results suggest that attention maps provide an effective reusable state for heterogeneous LLM serving, especially in prefix-heavy data workflows. Our code is available: https://github.com/PKU-DAIR/MapFlow.
authors: Zhan Jin, Yuze Luo, Bin Cui, Xupeng Miao
bullets: Targets prefix-heavy workflows where multiple models share long contexts such as schemas, tools, histories, and intermediate results.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in video diffusion enable novel-view video synthesis from a single input video, supporting world modeling, embodied intelligence, and robotic simulation. However, existing methods process camera trajectories independently, lacking the cross-trajectory consistency needed for coherent, navigable 4D worlds. We introduce Demiurge, an autoregressive video rerendering pipeline built on a dynamic 4D point-cloud memory cache. It promotes cross-trajectory consistency through four components: (1) an appearance video diffusion model that synthesizes photorealistic novel-view videos conditioned on the 4D memory; (2) a memory-consistent video depth completion model that aligns known-region depths with cached geometry and completes missing regions, mitigating scale ambiguity and discontinuities during memory updates; (3) memory-aware dual-stream warping that provides high-fidelity visual guidance and occlusion cues for novel-view synthesis; and (4) geometry-aware video refinement that enhances perceptual quality. Extensive experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art performance and three key capabilities: coherent spatiotemporal lattice construction over dense multi-view trajectories; large-parallax video rerendering under challenging camera motions, including 180-degree rotations with no input-view overlap; and geometry-faithful outputs that can be directly optimized into high-quality 3D Gaussian Splatting representations with minimal artifacts. Project page: https://hanxinzhu-lab.github.io/demiurge_project_page/.

papers.abstract: Vision-and-language navigation (VLN) agents are typically evaluated by whether they reach a target and how efficiently they follow an instructed route, yet these metrics provide little information about collision behavior. Moreover, continuous VLN evaluation commonly uses a sliding regime, where an agent can slide along obstacles after a collision, potentially masking the effect of unsafe actions on navigation performance. We introduce VLN-Safe, a benchmark for analyzing collision safety under two complementary evaluation regimes: sliding, reflecting common VLN evaluation practice, and blocking, where collision-inducing actions prevent forward motion and more directly expose their consequences. Across six published agents on R2R-CE, 38.5-56.8% of successful episodes contain contact under sliding, while switching to blocking decreases success rate by 11.7-36.1 percentage points. We further analyze signals for anticipating imminent collisions and find that depth geometry and recent movement history are more informative than policy-derived signals, while safe alternatives near the policy's preferred action are rarely available. Motivated by these findings, we introduce a training-free collision guard that vetoes risky forward actions, executes an escape maneuver, and returns control to the original policy. Under blocking, the guard reduces collision steps by 62-98% and improves success rate by 6.9-29.3 percentage points across five recurrent, topological, and vision-language-action agents. Under sliding, it leaves success rate unchanged while raising the share of collision-free successes by 4.1-12.4 points. These results reveal a substantial gap between task success and collision-safe navigation and show that lightweight collision-aware intervention can improve both safety and navigation performance.

bullets: Introduces VLN-Safe, a benchmark comparing sliding evaluation with blocking evaluation that prevents motion after collisions.

Depth geometry and recent movement history better predict imminent collisions than policy-derived signals, while nearby safe alternatives are uncommon.
The training-free guard vetoes risky forward actions, performs an escape maneuver, and returns control to the original policy.

Across five agents, it reduces collision steps by 62–98% and improves blocking success by 6.9–29.3 points; under sliding, collision-free successes increase by 4.1–12.4 points without changing success rate.

papers.abstract: Sign Language Recognition (SLR) presents complex challenges due to variable signing speeds and spatial intricacies. Specifically, Indian Sign Language (ISL) requires precise modeling of its inherently bimanual nature and is bottlenecked by the scarcity of large-vocabulary benchmarks and the inability of standard models to handle irregular signing velocities. To address this, a structurally-aware hybrid framework for efficient, gloss ISL recognition is proposed. To minimize computational redundancy, an entropy-driven SVD sampler that dynamically extracts informative keyframes is used. Because this subsampling creates irregular physical time gaps, the proposed architecture employs a Continuous Dual Positional Encoding paired with a distance-aware Elastic Transformer to preserve natural signing rhythm. Spatially, a Kinematically-Conditioned Adaptive GCN explicitly models bimanual geometry using unified bone-joint features. To validate our framework, a 120-class, 9,453-video native ISL dataset is created. Augmented by Physical Node Dropout and ArcFace optimization to mitigate subject-specific memorization, our framework achieves a competitive 89.8% accuracy, establishing a strong baseline for complex sign language modeling.
authors: Pushp Garg, Himangshu Sarma, Mrinmoy Ghorai
bullets: Addresses variable signing speeds, complex spatial structure, and limited large-vocabulary ISL benchmarks.
Uses entropy-driven SVD sampling to retain informative keyframes and reduce computational redundancy.

Captures bimanual geometry through a Kinematically-Conditioned Adaptive GCN with unified bone-joint features.
Introduces a 9,453-video, 120-class native ISL dataset and reports 89.8% accuracy, with scope focused on gloss recognition.

papers.abstract: We introduce HumanPhys, a human-centric benchmark for real-world physical perception, and a training corpus emitted by the same pipeline. Each question targets a physically grounded quantity related to people, including depth, inter-person distance, gaze angle, displacement, velocity, heading-step trajectory, blink count, and contact-deformation strength. The rendered probes additionally test illumination inference from body and face cues and camera ego-motion, both with and without a person in the frame. All labels are derived programmatically from sensor calibration, source metadata, or renderer state, rather than written by annotators or produced by estimators on the benchmark frames. HumanPhys systematically probes six dimensions of human-centric physical perception: spatial state, kinematics, blink events, deformation, illumination, and camera pose. To the best of our knowledge, no existing MLLM benchmark-and-training corpus jointly supervises this set of human-centered physical quantities under direct metadata- or renderer-derived labels. The six dimensions appear only partially dissociable across the tested MLLMs. We benchmark a range of open- and closed-source MLLMs on HumanPhys and find that all six capability dimensions remain challenging for current models. We hope HumanPhys will support future research on multimodal systems that perceive and reason about people in the physical world.
authors: Yiming Zhang, Enzhi Zhou, Junan Lin, Dulan Zhou, Weiqiang Wang, Yuge Huang, Jian Liu

papers.abstract: We present CAST-ASD (Causal Attention over Speakers and Time), a causal joint model for active speaker detection (ASD). Recent ASD models improve performance by jointly processing all faces in a scene, but operate offline, with the full clip available before any frame is labelled. Low-latency causal detectors instead process each face independently. CAST-ASD combines joint face reasoning with fully causal inference. It applies scene-level attention across faces within the current frame and causal temporal attention over each face's history, enabling information sharing across speakers with zero lookahead. Its parameter count does not grow with the number of faces. On MSDWild, where most negative face-frames contain a visible competing speaker, CAST-ASD reduces competing-speaker false alarms by 32% relative to the causal per-face detector it extends, with larger gains as scene occupancy increases. It outperforms all causal baselines on both validation splits while using only one-tenth the inter-speaker parameters of a three-block fixed-roster convolution. Code and models are available at https://github.com/prathamg007/CAST-ASD.
authors: Pratham Gupta, Haotian Qi, Tushar Sandhan, Gabriel Skantze

papers.abstract: Training-free sparse attention is a practical route to efficient video diffusion transformer inference, yet existing methods typically fix the competition domain at each query row for every attention head. Prior work primarily addresses how to estimate token-level importance within this fixed domain; whether the domain itself should adapt to head heterogeneity remains under-specified. We introduce EG-Sparse, a training-free framework that routes low-entropy heads to a grouped cross-head pool while retaining per-row local selection for high-entropy heads, using only scores already materialized by the sparse pipeline. A controlled diagnostic fixes the ranking score and varies only the competition rule: grouped cross-head selection reduces low-entropy-head reconstruction error by 9.8%, whereas forcing high-entropy heads into an all-head global pool increases it by 7.9%. Across four configurations, EG-Sparse achieves higher video quality while reducing attention density and GPU denoising latency compared with strong training-free sparse-attention baselines. Mechanism ablations further show that selective domain adaptation outperforms uniform, random, and fixed domain-assignment policies. These results support competition-domain adaptation as a distinct design axis within centroid-guided training-free sparse attention.
authors: Tiantian Liu, Meng Wan, Zhiqiang Liang, Jue Wang, Ningming Nie, Yangang Wang
bullets: Existing methods use a fixed competition domain for every attention head, despite head heterogeneity.

Across four configurations, the method improved video quality while lowering attention density and GPU denoising latency versus strong training-free baselines.
Ablations favored selective domain adaptation over uniform, random, and fixed assignment policies.

This heterogeneity motivates head-adaptive competition domains.

papers.abstract: Streaming video understanding requires answering questions from the observed video, with evidence drawn from recent observations or earlier events. Historical context can improve recall but may interfere with judgments based on recent frames. Its usefulness depends on both when it is introduced and which clips are selected, while relevance alone does not guarantee sufficient evidence for an answer. We propose SPARE, a framework that combines adaptive historical retrieval with visual encoder sharing. A lightweight gate predicts whether recent observations provide sufficient evidence to answer the question. When additional evidence is predicted to be necessary, a multimodal embedding model retrieves relevant historical clips to supplement the current context. LoRA instruction tuning trains the understanding model to use recent observations and retrieved history jointly and abstain when the evidence remains insufficient. To reduce redundant visual parameters, the understanding and retrieval branches share a visual encoder while retaining separate language backbones. Four linear adapters align the shared features with the retrieval model through distillation at the visual token and final retrieval embedding levels. With visual-only inputs, SPARE achieves 77.78% on the evaluated Real-time and Backward task groups of OVO-Bench and 73.31% on StreamingBench. Compared with Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct evaluated at 2 fps, SPARE improves accuracy by 20.68 percentage points on OVO-Bench and 14.15 percentage points on StreamingBench.
authors: Senbin Xu, Zijun Zhang, Xinhua Wu, Li He, Jubo Feng, Li Qiao, Zhen Gao, Yan Zhang, Jixiang Luo, Rongrong Ji
bullets: Addresses the challenge of balancing recent observations with potentially useful—but distracting—historical context.
Uses a lightweight gate to determine whether additional evidence is needed, then retrieves relevant past clips with a multimodal embedding model.
Trains the model to jointly use current and retrieved evidence and abstain when evidence remains insufficient.
Shares a visual encoder across understanding and retrieval branches, with separate language backbones and distillation-based adapters.
With visual-only inputs, reaches 77.78% on evaluated OVO-Bench tasks and 73.31% on StreamingBench; the abstract reports gains over Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct at 2 fps.

papers.abstract: 4D Gaussian Splatting (4DGS) has emerged as a powerful dynamic scene representation, supporting real-time high quality rendering but suffers from prohibitive storage overhead. Existing methods typically attempt to solve this by treating compression as a per-scene optimization problem, limiting generalizability and applicability where low-latency compression is required. In this work, we leverage existing image and video codecs and propose a generalized post-training compression framework for 4DGS to address these issues. Specifically, we apply importance-based adaptive quantization to Gaussians according to their importance levels, effectively refining bitrate allocation while remaining fully compatible with existing codecs. To further improve compression efficiency, we utilize the statistical properties of 4DGS and propose motion- and importance-aware packing to reorganize attributes into codec-friendly 2D maps. Our approach can achieve over 40x compression rate in seconds while maintaining high quality, facilitating the practical deployment of 4DGS.
authors: Chengzhen Wu, Kelei Liu, Sicheng Li, Lu Yu, Yiyi Liao
bullets: Addresses 4DGS storage overhead and the slow, scene-specific nature of prior compression methods.
Uses importance-based adaptive quantization to allocate bitrate according to Gaussian importance.
Introduces motion- and importance-aware packing that reorganizes attributes into codec-friendly 2D maps.
Leverages existing image and video codecs for post-training compression without per-scene optimization.
Compresses 4DGS in seconds while maintaining high quality, supporting practical deployment.

Attributes are then packed to 2D maps according to their importance level and motion property, making them amendable for subsequent image and video coding. During decoding, attributes are obtained from the bitstreams and rescaled to their original value, restoring the 4DGS data for further rendering.

papers.abstract: Can autoregressive video diffusion be accelerated further when only four denoising steps remain? Existing feature caching approaches struggle in this regime, as large feature changes between denoising timesteps undermine both direct reuse and lightweight predictors. We observe that features across video chunks remain strongly correlated at matching denoising timesteps, offering a complementary source of guidance. Building on this insight, we introduce TGuide, a framework that accelerates autoregressive video diffusion through a lightweight Anchor-Transport-Correct (ATC) predictor guided by historical sampling trajectories. Our ATC combines two complementary references: the current chunk's preceding-step features preserve its spatial structure, while the previous chunk's same-timestep features provide information at the target denoising stage. By integrating these references through spatial retrieval and adaptive correction, ATC improves velocity prediction accuracy despite the large gaps between denoising steps. To mitigate error accumulation across both denoising steps and video chunks, we train the predictor on its own autoregressive rollouts, allowing it to adapt to states shaped by its own earlier predictions. An optional confidence-aware scheduler further adjusts the quality-efficiency trade-off. Experiments on Self Forcing, Causal Forcing, and HY-WorldPlay show that TGuide preserves generation quality while achieving denoising speedups of up to $1.89\times$ over the original 4-step generators. On Self Forcing, TGuide generalizes from 81-frame training videos to 333-frame generation, approximately four times the training length, while exceeding the original model's VBench score.
authors: Zhuo Chen, Bin Zou, Fanyue Wei, Lixin Duan, Angela Yao, Wen Li
bullets: Addresses feature-caching failures caused by large changes between the few remaining denoising steps.
Uses an Anchor-Transport-Correct predictor combining the current chunk’s preceding-step features with the previous chunk’s same-timestep features.
Applies spatial retrieval and adaptive correction to improve velocity prediction across large denoising gaps.
Trains on its own autoregressive rollouts to reduce error accumulation across denoising steps and video chunks.
Evaluated on Self Forcing, Causal Forcing, and HY-WorldPlay; on Self Forcing, it generates 333-frame videos from 81-frame training videos while exceeding the original model’s VBench score.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive video generators synthesize long videos through chunk-wise rollouts, yet they are typically trained to predict only the immediate future. This limited prediction horizon makes it challenging to maintain video quality over extended rollouts. To address this problem, we introduce Prospective Forcing, a multi-head prediction framework that injects long-range predictive signals into autoregressive video representations. Built on a rolling-window generator, Prospective Forcing attaches lightweight, offset-specific heads that share the same conditioning information and independently predict chunks at different future temporal offsets. By extending supervision beyond the next chunk, these heads encourage the shared history representation to retain information useful for longer-horizon prediction, supporting temporally consistent generation. At inference time, we accelerate sampling by using accepted future-chunk predictions to skip full-window backbone executions. We equip the head with learnable embeddings to generate multiple candidates for the next chunk, and a learned verifier either selects a candidate or rejects all and falls back to standard autoregressive generation.
