In zero-shot evaluation, no model identifies the gap for both polarities in over 15% of scenarios; negated definites are judged false in 84%.
Rules, chain-of-thought, and enumeration prompts have unstable effects and often reinforce the bias.

papers.abstract: Long-term memory enables LLM agents to learn from past interactions but exposes memory formation to adversarial influence. Existing studies primarily organize memory poisoning by attack channels, corruption patterns, or lifecycle stages, leaving formation interfaces insufficiently characterized. We formulate Memory Formation Poisoning as adversarial manipulation of the interfaces through which persistent agent memory is produced and committed, and introduce MemForm, a controlled diagnostic benchmark covering five interfaces: Content, Evidence, Scope, Selection, and Path Poisoning. We introduce Selection and Path Poisoning as controlled intervention categories that isolate retention and consolidation order effects, respectively. Each category pairs clean and poisoned conditions with interface-specific controls. Evaluations across six LLMs and two response formats reveal broad susceptibility at all five interfaces under the evaluated memory protocols and implementations. Crucially, authentic experiences with successful outcomes do not guarantee reliable behavior after memory formation: changes to contextual support, retention, or consolidation order can induce undesirable downstream behavior. In particular, consolidation order can alter behavior even with identical retained experiences, depending on the memory formation procedure. Additional analyses show that interface applicability depends on memory architecture and that Path Poisoning susceptibility depends on the updater. The evaluated defenses provide incomplete mitigation that varies by interface. These findings motivate protecting both what is committed to persistent memory and how memory is formed from experiences. Code and data are available at https://github.com/opanhw/memform-code.
authors: Haowen Pan, Pengyang Shao, Yunshan Ma, Yanzheng Jin, Naixin Zhai, Xiang Wang, Xun Yang

Shows that successful authentic experiences do not ensure reliable behavior when contextual support, retention, or consolidation order changes.
Finds that vulnerability depends on memory architecture and updater, while evaluated defenses provide incomplete, interface-dependent mitigation.

papers.abstract: Enterprise workflow automation typically requires retrieving a complete and accurate set of relevant information from large operational document corpora (SOPs, policy documents) given a specific scenario or request. In customer support (CS), for example, human specialists must determine the correct sequence of resolution steps for each case, a task that demands precise grounding in policy documentation. Meeting this bar in production typically requires complex document chunking, indexing, and retrieval pipelines, often layered with learned re-rankers, query rewriters, and bespoke agentic RAG infrastructure. We report a deployment case study of a simpler alternative: a portable skill consisting of a natural-language instruction, lightweight tools (a retrieval API, format-checking scripts), and a corpus enriched with an LLM-generated navigation layer, which is a structured "Wikipedia-style" index over the underlying documents. This agentic RAG approach is straightforward to implement (1-2 engineer days), portable across capable agentic harnesses (e.g., Claude Code), and performs strongly on the challenging task of CS resolution workflow generation, achieving 99.2% procedural equivalence to human-approved ground truth and 83.3% evidence sufficiency. It is also roughly an order of magnitude slower per case than our deployed production assistant (~90 s vs. ~8-9 s), so we claim no latency advantage. Our claim is scoped to that setting: a mature, well-curated corpus, a latency-tolerant workflow, and human review of every case. There, the skill did the work of a complex RAG stack, and maintenance became a matter of editing text and data rather than retraining models.
authors: Istok Bako, Bonan Min, Tiffany Shao, Claire Cheng, Yashar Mehdad
bullets: Targets accurate, complete retrieval of policy-grounded resolution steps from enterprise support documents.
Uses natural-language instructions, lightweight retrieval and validation tools, and an LLM-generated Wikipedia-style navigation layer.
Implemented in 1–2 engineer days and portable across capable agentic harnesses.
Achieved 99.2% procedural equivalence and 83.3% evidence sufficiency in the reported case study.
Scope is limited to mature corpora, latency-tolerant workflows, and human review; inference took roughly 90 seconds versus 8–9 seconds in production.

A deterministic validator admits only verbatim snippets; outputs are scored against human-approved ground truth by GUIDANCEMATCH and SNIPPETS-SUFFICIENT.

The two source measures are not directly comparable: the wiki figure counts source articles the agent fetched, whereas the production figure counts distinct sources represented in its emitted evidence, not service fetches. The production backend was the organization’s deployed search service, called at its unified-search endpoint in the configuration used by the production assistant but driven by a scripted query–retrieve–compose harness rather than by the assistant itself; it retrieved before composition and so could not re-retrieve once composition had begun. Neither the service nor its index was tuned to these cases, and its internal retrieval depth, lexical/dense weighting, query rewriting, reranking, and index freshness are not exposed and cannot be characterized from the available artifacts.

papers.tldr: A simple, portable agentic RAG skill with a navigable document index can generate customer-support resolution workflows nearly as well as human-approved procedures, but is much slower than a production assistant.

papers.abstract: Frontier AI systems are increasingly natively multimodal, jointly pretrained on multiple modalities, such as text, vision, and audio. However, the scientific understanding of the multimodal data mixtures used to pretrain these systems --- how much of each modality to mix, and at what potential interference cost to the others --- is largely absent or gatekept. In this work, we derive data mixing scaling laws for three modalities: text, vision, and audio. Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) increasingly adopt Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures, as MoEs scale efficiently and partially limit cross-modal interference. We therefore use MoEs to conduct 268 experiments ranging from 457M to 8.3B parameters, on up to 150 billion tokens. Our work leads to multiple actionable insights into multimodal data mixing for training MLLMs. First, compute optima are modality-specific: audio modality is model-heavy, favoring scaling parameters over tokens, while text and vision require balanced scaling of model size and data. Second, repeating vision or audio data beyond 2x yields negligible benefits. Finally, cross-modal interactions are highly asymmetric: vision strongly interferes with audio, whereas audio's interference with learning text and vision is negligible. Overall, we provide a principled foundation for understanding the multimodal data mixtures needed to train frontier MLLMs.
authors: Aditi Khandelwal, Ayush K. Tarun, Yixuan Xu, Imanol Schlag, Golnoosh Farnadi, Siva Reddy, Luke Zettlemoyer, Antoine Bosselut
bullets: Audio benefits more from increasing model size than from adding tokens, while text and vision favor balanced scaling.
Repeating vision or audio data beyond 2× provides negligible additional benefit.
Vision substantially interferes with audio learning, but audio has negligible interference with text and vision.
The findings offer practical guidance for selecting multimodal pretraining mixtures.

papers.selection_reason: Derives scaling laws for multimodal data mixtures in MLLMs, directly relevant to multimodal foundation model training.
papers.title: Scaling Laws for Multimodal Data Mixtures
papers.tldr: The paper derives scaling laws for mixing text, vision, and audio data in multimodal models, revealing modality-specific compute needs and asymmetric interference.

papers.abstract: A long-standing goal in robotics is to develop generalist robots that can perform tasks across a wide range of settings, flexibly specified with images and text. Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models offer a promising path toward this goal by training on large collections of robot demonstrations. However, while VLAs perform well in-distribution, they often fail under minor test-time shifts, such as changes in object positions, lighting, textures, and camera poses. To address this, we propose Quality Diversity for Diverse Environment Generation (Q-DEG), a method for improving VLA robustness by generating adversarial environments and fine-tuning the VLA on its own successful rollouts. Q-DEG uses Quality Diversity (QD) optimization to find a set of high-failure environments, while promoting diversity using policy embeddings extracted from the VLA. These environments expose vulnerabilities that can be mitigated through self-imitation fine-tuning, thereby improving the VLA's robustness. In simulation, we conduct experiments across three representative VLA models, and our results indicate that Q-DEG improves robustness to out-of-distribution (OOD) adversarial environments compared to the base VLA and VLAs fine-tuned using data collected from two red-teaming baselines. Furthermore, we demonstrate that improving VLA robustness through Q-DEG facilitates sim-to-real transfer. Our anonymous project website is at: https://qd-env.github.io/qdeg/.
authors: Shihan Zhao, Henry Chen, Ya-Chuan Hsu, Minjune Hwang, Siddharth Srikanth, Freddie Liang, Akanksha Saran, Aaquib Tabrez, Stefanos Nikolaidis, Daniel Seita
bullets: VLAs can fail under small shifts in object placement, lighting, textures, and camera pose despite strong in-distribution performance.
Q-DEG uses Quality Diversity optimization to discover high-failure environments while maintaining diversity through VLA policy embeddings.
The VLA is fine-tuned on its own successful rollouts to mitigate vulnerabilities exposed by these environments.
Experiments across three VLA models in simulation show improved robustness in OOD adversarial environments over base models and two red-teaming baselines.
Greater robustness from Q-DEG also supports sim-to-real transfer.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. papers.selection_reason: Quality-diversity adversarial environment generation and self-imitation fine-tuning to improve VLA robustness.
papers.title: Red-Teaming of Vision-Language-Action Models via Quality Diversity Environment Generation
papers.tldr: Q-DEG red-teams vision-language-action models by generating diverse adversarial environments and fine-tuning them on successful self-imitation rollouts to improve robustness and sim-to-real transfer.

papers.abstract: Computational coarse-graining aims to replace a sequence of updates with a cheaper module while preserving task performance. We present a continuation-relative evaluation framework that assesses replacements through the computation that follows them, using downstream task quality and total execution cost as joint criteria. The framework distinguishes boundary representations, summaries of skipped computation, executed operations, and downstream loss. It makes interfaces and permitted deployment information explicit, combines fine-path references with directly trained controls using the same shortened architecture, and accounts for selection overhead. An exact loss decomposition separates replacement effects at a fixed downstream action from effects of changing that action. A finite construction shows how retained information can reduce the stipulated cost of zero-error prediction under fixed information and controller restrictions. Experiments in two frozen pretrained language models show that representation fidelity and task loss can favor different fitting objectives. In a prespecified comparison on a 1.7-billion-parameter model, next-token-loss training lowers in-distribution negative log-likelihood by 0.1901 nats per scored token compared with reconstructing the skipped blocks' output, using the same optimizer and update count. This ranking reverses in all nine paired comparisons under distribution shift. In a recursive expert prototype, the jointly adapted candidate lowers task error relative to frozen-bank and router-only baselines, but trails directly trained controls, and the tested input-only selectors fail the joint quality-cost criteria. Together, the protocol and studies provide explicit criteria and diagnostics for distinguishing useful computational replacement from local approximation gains within specified interfaces and evaluation settings.
authors: Shihua Yu, Yanzhi Wang, Tianchi Chen
bullets: Defines explicit interfaces, skipped-computation summaries, downstream actions, losses, and selection overhead for coarse-graining evaluation.
Separates replacement effects from effects caused by changing the downstream action through an exact loss decomposition.

In two frozen language models, next-token-loss training improved in-distribution NLL over skipped-block-output reconstruction by 0.1901 nats per scored token, but reversed in all nine distribution-shift comparisons.

In a recursive expert prototype, jointly adapted candidates beat frozen-bank and router-only baselines but trailed directly trained controls; input-only selectors failed the joint quality-cost criteria.
Provides diagnostics for distinguishing useful computational replacement from local approximation gains within specified interfaces and deployment settings.

papers.selection_reason: Computational coarse-graining to replace expensive updates with cheaper modules, relevant to efficient AI.
papers.title: Coarse-Graining Recursive Expert Computation: Continuation-Relative Interfaces and Failure Modes
papers.tldr: A continuation-relative framework evaluates computational replacements by downstream task quality and total cost, revealing that local representation fidelity may not predict useful end-to-end performance.

papers.abstract: Generating an image with a diffusion or flow-matching model typically involves integrating a velocity field for hundreds of sequential steps. That computation suits a GPU poorly and an analog neuromorphic substrate well, where one fast, low-power physical relaxation could replace the whole sequence. Two things are needed: a generative algorithm whose computation is a relaxation, and a way to train it without backpropagation, whose global gradient transport is hard to realise in analog. Energy Matching supplies the first, sampling by gradient-descent relaxation on a time-independent potential - but obtaining the gradient that descent follows is itself a backward pass, once per integration step. We prove that a predictive coding network with a single linear injection term added to its energy relaxes to a state whose visible layer carries that gradient inherently, with an error that vanishes for small injection strengths. An Energy Matching model trained by backpropagation can therefore be loaded into this network unchanged and sampled by relaxation alone, matching the original model's FID to within 0.04 at CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-32 scale. The network can also be trained without backpropagation: Equilibrium Propagation reproduces backpropagation's parameter updates to a cosine similarity of 0.9998, and training end to end with those updates reaches an FID of 3.64 on unconditional CIFAR-10 against 3.54 for backpropagation. To our knowledge this is the first CIFAR-10 generative model trained with Equilibrium Propagation, and the first at competitive quality by any backpropagation-free rule. This quality does not require group normalisation or attention: an architecture of only convolutions and pointwise nonlinearities, both native to an analog crossbar, reaches an FID of 3.51 when trained by backpropagation.
authors: Alex Gower
bullets: Targets the cost of hundreds of sequential diffusion or flow-matching steps and the difficulty of implementing global gradient transport on analog hardware.
Uses Energy Matching with a predictive-coding network whose injected energy term makes the visible state approximate the required gradient during relaxation.
A backpropagation-trained model can be sampled by relaxation alone, matching the original model’s FID within 0.04 on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-32.
Equilibrium Propagation closely reproduces backpropagation updates (cosine similarity 0.9998) and achieves FID 3.64 on unconditional CIFAR-10 versus 3.54 for backpropagation.
The convolutional, pointwise architecture avoids group normalization and attention, supporting implementation on analog crossbars.

Figure 1: The same network, read two ways. (a) Energy Matching generates by ẋ = −∇xV , and each evaluation of ∇xV is a backward pass through the network (Jk = ∂fk/∂hk−1). (b) In the PotentialPCN the same blocks fk make predictions, but the hidden states (shaded) are not computed from them: instead they are free variables that relax by descending EPCN to stationary values h∗. Each error unit ek = fk(hk−1)−hk compares a prediction against a state, and the energy is the sum of squared errors plus a single linear term γαhN , which at h∗ N equals γV up to O(γ2). The same term fixes e∗N = γα, and the recursion e∗k = J⊤ k+1e ∗ k+1 carries it down through the same transposed Jacobians as (a), so the gradient of EPCN at the visible node is γ∇xV +O(γ2). Dividing by γ, the visible dynamics ẋ = −γ−1∇xEPCN reproduce those of (a) to O(γ): the backward pass has been performed by the relaxation.

papers.selection_reason: Backprop-free training via equilibrium propagation motivated by low-power analog neuromorphic computation, relevant to energy-efficient AI.
papers.title: PotentialEP: Backprop-Free Training of CIFAR-Scale Generative Models via Equilibrium Propagation
papers.tldr: PotentialEP enables CIFAR-scale generative modeling through physical relaxation and trains the model without backpropagation using Equilibrium Propagation, while retaining near-backpropagation quality.

papers.abstract: It is widely appreciated that robotic policies require long-term memory to perform complex tasks. However, directly conditioning policies on all past observations leaves policy learning susceptible to learning spurious shortcuts, and introduces large latency at policy deployment. As such, today's memory-augmented policies curate what to remember, either by retaining only recent frames, selected keyframes, or textual summaries, or by learning latent representations of the visual stream alone. In this work, we propose an alternative approach IMPRINT, a policy-agnostic latent memory framework that augments vision-language-action (VLA) models with multi-stream memory without explicitly constraining what the policy should remember. IMPRINT compresses different streams into a latent memory that is updated incrementally at inference, enabling low latency. To avoid shortcut learning, IMPRINT adopts a two-stage training procedure, first supervising memory to reconstruct multiple streams (observations, actions, proprioception) of past information, as well as estimate current task progress, followed by end-to-end finetuning, jointly with the policy, on action prediction. Across both simulation and real-world tasks demanding memory, IMPRINT improves average success over the base VLA by at least 26%, outperforming popular alternatives, and maintaining lowest inference latency among memory-augmented VLAs. Through careful ablations, we demonstrate the utility of incorporating diverse information streams into robotic memory, validating the advantages of foregoing history curation. Project website: https://yilin-wu98.github.io/imprint_website/.
authors: Yilin Wu, Rutav Shah, Shuaiyi Huang, Sumedh A. Sontakke, Homanga Bharadhwaj, Andrea Bajcsy, Max Simchowitz, Guanya Shi
bullets: Addresses shortcut learning and deployment latency caused by conditioning on all past observations.
Compresses observations, actions, and proprioception into incrementally updated latent memory for VLA policies.
Uses two-stage training: reconstruct past information and estimate task progress, then jointly fine-tune for action prediction.
Improves average success over the base VLA by at least 26% across simulation and real-world tasks.
Reports the lowest inference latency among evaluated memory-augmented VLAs; ablations support using diverse streams without history curation.

papers.abstract: Learning reusable skills can improve visual reasoning agents, yet applying a skill still requires the agent to implement or invoke a procedure and produce the final answer. Errors and hallucinations at these steps can prevent acquired experience from translating into reliable single-run performance. We propose VisualCoding, which combines execution-guided acquisition of reusable visual programs with direct adoption of their answers on applicable inputs. Execution-Guided Program Acquisition composes visual primitives and additional code into family-level solvers, then iteratively tests and revises them on labeled training instances. Scope-Aware Direct Execution runs a retained solver and returns its valid in-scope answer. We evaluate VisualCoding on four models across four benchmarks spanning 69 task families. VisualCoding exceeds the strongest evaluated baseline in mean accuracy by 4.45 percentage points with Gemini-3.1-Pro and by 14.78 points when reusing the frozen Pro-acquired artifacts with Flash-Lite. Ablations support execution-guided acquisition and show that direct execution outperforms textual or callable reuse of the same programs. Code is available at https://github.com/jiaq-liu/VisualCoding.
authors: Liu Jiaqi, Jin Ruinan, Li Xiaoxiao
bullets: Addresses errors and hallucinations that arise when agents must implement or invoke learned skills.
Execution-Guided Program Acquisition builds family-level solvers from visual primitives and code, then iteratively validates and revises them on labeled examples.
Scope-Aware Direct Execution returns a retained solver’s answer when the input falls within its valid scope.

Evaluated across four models, four benchmarks, and 69 task families; it improves mean accuracy over the strongest baseline by 4.45 points with Gemini-3.1-Pro and 14.78 points when transferring frozen artifacts to Flash-Lite.
Ablations support execution-guided acquisition and show direct execution is more effective than textual or callable reuse.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved strong performance in mathematical and logical reasoning, yet they still suffer from the curse of complexity and struggle as problem difficulty increases with the number of constraint interactions and the size of the search space. In contrast, satisfiability solvers such as Z3 provide scalable and verifiable reasoning through constraint solving under formal theories, but lack the flexibility to interpret natural-language problem descriptions. In this work, we propose SAT-RL, a reinforcement-learning (RL) framework that trains LLMs to interact with symbolic solvers through multi-turn tool execution. SAT-RL leverages synthetic data generation with verifiable solutions, supervised warm-up on solver-augmented traces, and solver-grounded reinforcement learning with tool-aware rewards. Experiments show that SAT-RL substantially improves symbolic reasoning with tools on both in-domain and out-of-domain logic tasks. Our code is available on https://github.com/sunjia72/SAT-RL.
authors: Jialiang Sun, Kuldeep Meel
bullets: Targets LLM difficulty with growing constraint interactions and search spaces.
Uses multi-turn tool execution to connect natural-language reasoning with solvers such as Z3.
Combines synthetic verifiable data, supervised warm-up on solver traces, and solver-grounded RL.
Reports substantial gains on both in-domain and out-of-domain logic tasks.
Scope: focuses on symbolic reasoning with external solver tools.

papers.abstract: Successor-feature-based zero-shot reinforcement learning methods pre-train a task encoder and successor-feature predictor on offline, reward-free data, then recover a policy at test time by solving a closed-form linear regression over a small labeled dataset. We identify an underexplored limitation of this approach: when the task encoder produces dense representations, the inferred reward signal becomes diffuse across the state space, reducing the contrast between goal-relevant states and the background and providing a weaker signal for the policy to follow. We address this limitation by introducing an l1 sparsity penalty that concentrates reward-predictive structure into a smaller effective subspace of the task encoder's latent space. The penalty is applied only during training and requires no architectural change or modification to the closed-form inference procedure. We instantiate this approach as Sparse-TD-JEPA, a single-line of code addition based on Temporal-Difference Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (TD-JEPA) that significantly improved its performance in zero-shot reinforcement learning. We evaluate Sparse-TD-JEPA on 65 tasks across the DeepMind Control (DMC) Suite and OGBench, covering locomotion, navigation, trajectory stitching, puzzle solving, and robotic manipulation. Sparse-TD-JEPA improves over TD-JEPA in all 13 domain-level comparisons. On DMC, it increases the average return from 661 +- 6 to 714 +- 3. On OGBench, it increases the average success rate from 38.0 +- 0.8 to 48.4 +- 2.3, with improvements of 13.4-18.0 percentage points on the evaluated antmaze navigation and stitching domains. Overall, Sparse-TD-JEPA achieves the highest mean performance among established zero-shot baselines in nine of the 13 domains. Analysis further shows that sparsity produces a sharper and more task-informative inferred reward landscape.
authors: Duaa Nakshbandi, Zhiyu An, Wan Du
bullets: Dense task representations can diffuse inferred rewards across the state space, weakening goal-state contrast.
An L1 penalty concentrates reward-predictive information in a smaller latent subspace without changing the architecture or test-time closed-form inference.
Across 65 DMC Suite and OGBench tasks, Sparse-TD-JEPA improves over TD-JEPA in all 13 domain-level comparisons.
Average return rises from 661 ± 6 to 714 ± 3 on DMC; average success rate rises from 38.0 ± 0.8% to 48.4 ± 2.3% on OGBench.
The approach achieves the highest mean performance among established zero-shot baselines in 9 of 13 domains; analysis links gains to sharper, more task-informative reward landscapes.

papers.abstract: Augmenting worker capabilities in the physical world through guidance has been a decades-long goal for AI agents. One key supporting capability is to understand what the worker is doing, seeing through the human's camera or smart glasses, and assist them in documentation. Despite advances in vision language models, their capabilities in these settings remain uncertain and are challenging to benchmark because most physical work data is proprietary, and involves too much variability to study in a principled manner. Unlike structured settings such as kitchens and warehouses that have predictable lighting, geometry, and objects, field-facing tasks such as rooftop solar installation and vehicle repair are unconstrained and high variance. Here, we model real-world physical work in Blender across eleven environments, incorporating variants in both image acceptability and documentation. The acceptability task asks whether a particular view would be suitable proof-of-work and documentation asks whether an agent can understand the task-relevant state of the environment from that view. Across 26 vision-language models, we find that top models largely solve documentation when the answer is text in frame, but are weak at reading measurements and at judging small parts and spatial relations, such as whether a tape measure leans. Acceptability is harder to pin down because human raters disagree with each other. Measured against a scorer that agrees with the raters' majority about as often as a single rater does, the best models cannot be distinguished from a single non-author rater, at a cost within the range of a human pass. In the three environments where we can trace acceptability errors, most wrong rejections come from misreading the scene rather than the requirement. On the three documentation questions for which we have real images, model rankings on rendered frames transfer to real images.
authors: Andrew Perrault (Relantic, Inc., Columbus, OH, USA), Anmol Takiar (Relantic, Inc., Columbus, OH, USA), Dominik Wienecki (Relantic, Inc., Columbus, OH, USA), Arnab Nandi (Relantic, Inc., Columbus, OH, USA)
bullets: Benchmarks documentation and view acceptability across 11 Blender environments modeling unconstrained tasks such as solar installation and vehicle repair.
Evaluates 26 vision-language models on whether views provide suitable proof-of-work and whether task-relevant state can be understood.
Models generally solve documentation when answers are visible as text, but struggle with measurements, small parts, and spatial relationships.
Acceptability judgments are difficult because human raters disagree; leading models perform similarly to an individual non-author rater.
Model rankings on rendered documentation frames transfer to real images for the three tested questions.

papers.abstract: Scientific research increasingly depends on curating experimental data from literature. Scientific data curation requires verifying exact experimental conditions (e.g., specific assays, clinical outcomes, and data availability) across long, heterogeneous files, which is a highly time-consuming process. Existing benchmarks evaluate only broad relevance on short queries, failing to capture this complexity. We introduce SciCurateBench, a benchmark of 200 expert-annotated papers from major life-science journals that challenges systems to verify conjunctive biological experimental criteria from raw, unprocessed scientific literature. We show that plain LLMs and popular reasoning, tool-using, and feedback-based agents all struggle with this task. To study what makes the task tractable, we further propose LangPoli, an integrative system in which a policy agent generates natural language action guidelines that actor agents convert into executable tools. LangPoli showed strong performance on both Paper Classification (83.16% F1 vs. 58.22% for its base LLM) and Structured Information Retrieval, and also improves re-ranking on the public benchmarks of LitSearch, BEIR, and TREC. We further explore curriculum transfer, a method that distills generalizable strategies from solved tasks to accelerate the solving of related problems. We hope this work facilitates research in truly practical scientific AI assistance. The anonymized pre-release can be found from https://anonymous.4open. science/r/scicuratebench-D885/.
authors: Minuk Ma, Kaiyun Guo, Jiarui Ding
bullets: Presents 200 expert-annotated papers from major life-science journals for evaluating experimental-data curation.
Targets verification of specific assays, clinical outcomes, and data availability across long, heterogeneous documents.
Finds that plain LLMs and existing reasoning, tool-using, and feedback-based agents struggle with the task.
LangPoli achieves 83.16% F1 on Paper Classification, compared with 58.22% for its base LLM, and improves performance on LitSearch, BEIR, and TREC re-ranking.
Explores curriculum transfer to reuse strategies from solved tasks for related curation problems.

papers.abstract: Benchmark scores tell us what an LLM can do, but not how much energy is required to deliver that capability. We directly measure this trade-off for 86 open-weight model checkpoints, evaluated on seven benchmarks and six hardware platforms ranging from a consumer GPU to an eight-GPU server. We find large differences in energy efficiency even among models with similar capability. Most configurations lie away from the score--energy Pareto frontier: they use a median of 2.6--4.8$\times$ more energy than another configuration that scores at least as well, with differences reaching 27$\times$. Reasoning can improve capability, but enabling thinking increases energy by about 3.7$\times$ on average, and the benefit depends strongly on the model family and output budget. Generated-token count is also an imperfect proxy for energy, misordering 18--24\% of model pairs. In contrast, FP8 reduces energy by roughly a quarter with little change in score, while changing hardware largely rescales energy without changing the relative ranking of models. These results show that capability alone gives an incomplete picture of efficiency. We argue that benchmark scores should be reported together with measured energy consumption under a specified serving regime and output budget.
authors: Zeyu Yang, Wes Armour
bullets: Measured 86 open-weight checkpoints across seven benchmarks, six hardware platforms, and different reasoning modes.
Models with similar scores can differ substantially in energy use; many configurations consume 2.6–4.8× more energy than an equally capable alternative, with gaps up to 27×.
Enabling reasoning improves capability in some cases but raises energy use by about 3.7× on average, depending on model family and output budget.
Generated-token count is an imperfect energy proxy, while FP8 cuts energy by roughly a quarter with little score change.
Hardware mostly rescales energy and preserves model rankings, motivating joint reporting of scores and measured energy.

papers.abstract: Retargeting human demonstrations into dynamically feasible dexterous hand trajectories requires resolving complex contact physics, yet current methods either omit physical constraints or rely on computationally expensive sampling-based optimization in simulation. Reinforcement learning has previously been used to achieve planning and control through contact dynamics; however, standard policies require object-specific training and fail to generalize across arbitrary geometries. This work reframes physics-based retargeting as a residual learning problem, where we demonstrate that zero-shot generalization across objects relies on structured state representations. Specifically, formulating the observation space to include a localized contact-error signal guiding each robot link to its target coordinate on the object surface enables a single, unified residual policy to successfully grasp novel, unseen object geometries. Rolling out this policy in simulation on a kinematic reference trajectory yields a physics-based retargeter, OATH. Operating at 0.4 seconds of compute per second of reference, OATH achieves 2.4x faster-than-real-time performance and a 60-350x reduction in computational cost compared to sampling-based methods. The system recovers 58% of held-out and 54% of unseen-object DexYCB trajectories while maintaining a sub-2 cm tracking error.
authors: Solvin Sigurdson, Prasanna Sriganesh, Juan Borbon, Joel Burdick, Dingqi Zhang, Jiuguang Wang
bullets: Addresses the challenge of producing dynamically feasible hand trajectories under complex contact physics without costly sampling-based optimization.
Uses a unified residual reinforcement-learning policy with structured observations that encode each robot link’s contact error relative to the object surface.
Generalizes zero-shot to novel object geometries, including held-out and unseen objects.
Runs at 0.4 seconds of compute per second of reference, achieving 2.4× faster-than-real-time performance and 60–350× lower computational cost than sampling-based methods.
Recovers 58% of held-out and 54% of unseen-object DexYCB trajectories with sub-2 cm tracking error.

papers.abstract: Test-time adaptation (TTA) enables time series forecasters to update after deployment as new observations become available. However, adaptation objectives that focus primarily on prediction errors at individual time steps do not fully address the needs of financial time series forecasting. In addition to pointwise return fitting, return direction and the price trajectories reconstructed from sequences of returns are also important. To better account for these properties, we introduce Direction- and Price-Aware Adaptation Loss (DPAL), which combines pointwise return fitting with directional and price-calibration terms. We apply DPAL within existing TSF-TTA frameworks without modifying the source forecaster or the adapter architecture. Across a diverse collection of financial datasets, DPAL reduces reconstructed-price mean squared error in most evaluated settings.
authors: Wuzhou Lian, Haochun Wang, Yuefan Deng
bullets: Financial TTA objectives based only on pointwise prediction errors may miss directional and price-trajectory quality.
DPAL combines pointwise return fitting with directional and price-calibration terms.
It can be applied within existing TSF-TTA frameworks without changing the forecaster or adapter architecture.
Across diverse financial datasets, DPAL reduces reconstructed-price MSE in most evaluated settings.

papers.abstract: Dexterous robot hands can receive useful motion intent from teleoperation or learned policies, but successful execution also depends on contact decisions that these commands rarely specify. We introduce DexFLEX, a contact-aware foundation controller that turns upstream fingertip-motion drafts into contact-consistent joint commands. Instead of treating a draft as a trajectory to copy, DexFLEX treats it as evidence about intent: from the current tactile-proprioceptive state, it proposes feasible short-horizon motion chunks, predicts their contact consequences, and selects the candidate that best follows the command while preserving future contact stability. At inference time, a simple Draft-Dream-Select procedure combines pure-prior proposals for recovery with draft-seeded proposals for responsiveness, then decodes the selected motion into executable joint-space targets. Across degraded-command simulation, real-world shared control, and visuomotor policy learning, the same trained controller improves robustness without retraining, increasing real-world teleoperation success from 29.2% to 78.3% and reaching 46.7% policy-learning success, 3.5 times direct joint-action prediction, and 1.56 times prior-only correction. Videos are available at dex-flex.github.io.
authors: Weikang Wan, Zeyu Lai, Jianyu Hou, Yuchen Zhou, Jiawei Fu, Henrik I Christensen, Hao Su
bullets: Addresses the missing contact decisions in teleoperation and learned motion commands.
Uses tactile-proprioceptive state to propose short-horizon motion chunks and predict their contact consequences.
Draft-Dream-Select combines command-seeded proposals with prior-based recovery, then selects stable, command-following motions.
The same trained controller improves performance across simulation, shared-control, and visuomotor policy-learning settings.
Reported success rises from 29.2% to 78.3% in real-world teleoperation; policy-learning success reaches 46.7%.

figures.caption: Figure 2: DEXFLEX pipeline. (1) A state encoder converts proprioceptive and tactile histories into a contact–proprioceptive latent zt, whose temporal history is summarized as a slow phase token gt. (2) At inference, Draft–Dream–Select proposes pure-prior and draft-seeded motion chunks, predicts their contact consequences, scores them against the upstream draft, and decodes the selected chunk into joint-space actions.

Figure 3: Robustness under command degradation. Expert commands are corrupted with additive noise, command scaling, delay, and support-finger removal. We evaluate whether each controller preserves contact stability while recovering the expert intent rather than merely damping motion.

Figure 4: Selective intervention during real-world tool use. We visualize intervention magnitude It = ∥ût − ut∥2/(∥ut∥2 + ϵ) along representative rollouts. DEXFLEX keeps intervention low during benign user motion and produces peaks near contact-critical moments such as release, impact, unstable tool contact, and regrasp.

Figure 5: Policy learning with different action interfaces. All methods use the same imagebased Flow-matching policy and 50 demos per task. Direct joint-action prediction is compared with fingertip-motion prediction executed by a prior-only DexGen controller and by DEXFLEX.

Table 2: Real-world teleoperation results. We report per-task success rate (SR, %) and average SR / CT / NHT across tasks. CT is completion time in seconds over successful trials. NHT is normalized holding time. Each method is evaluated for 20 trials per task across two operators. Averages are computed over task-level means.

Table 1: Component ablations. Metrics are averaged over the four command-degradation settings. w/o predictive score replaces the learned score with nearest-to-draft selection over the same proposal set.

papers.tldr: DexFLEX converts imperfect fingertip-motion commands into contact-consistent joint actions, substantially improving dexterous manipulation robustness.

papers.abstract: Dynamic Tensor Rematerialization (DTR) trains neural networks under a memory budget by evicting tensors and recomputing them on demand. A natural expectation is that a budget large enough to complete training stays sufficient when it is increased. Using DTR's reference simulator, simrd, to replay the public DTR training traces, we show that this expectation fails. We call the exceptions feasibility holes: memory budgets at which an eviction policy runs out of memory although both a smaller and a larger budget complete, a form of non-monotone feasibility. Under a written sweep protocol with dated amendments, a 0.01-step budget grid shows no such hole for DTR on any of six confirmatory traces, although unresolved timeouts prevent it from establishing monotonicity. Finer sampling finds holes on InceptionV4 (three regions) and U-Net (two regions), in addition to one on the ResNet-32 development trace. Every hole is reproduced by three repeats and by unmodified simrd. For one InceptionV4 pair (0.2343 versus 0.235 of peak memory) we trace the failure to individual allocations. The larger budget avoids one eviction at an operator where the smaller budget was 173,479 bytes short. The extra data it carries forward forces a later eviction of a tensor needed three operators afterwards, and rebuilding that tensor triggers a recomputation cascade that cannot fit. Keeping that one tensor resident under the same budget prevents the failure. The two simple score changes we tested do not remove holes across traces; both add failing budgets on some traces. All results are from simulation, with no allocator model; behaviour on GPU hardware is untested.
authors: Mahesh Reddy Pagadala
bullets: DTR can exhibit non-monotone feasibility: a budget may fail even when both smaller and larger budgets succeed.
Fine-grained sweeps found feasibility holes on InceptionV4, U-Net, and a ResNet-32 development trace; each hole was reproduced repeatedly and with unmodified simrd.
One InceptionV4 failure arose when extra memory prevented an eviction, causing a later eviction of a tensor needed shortly afterward and an unfittable recomputation cascade.
Two tested score changes did not eliminate holes across traces and introduced failures on some traces.
Results are simulation-only; GPU allocator behavior was not evaluated, and timeouts prevented establishing monotonicity on all confirmatory traces.

Hollow markers in the separate bottom strip are timeouts (unresolved); their vertical position carries no depth. Annotated failures are confirmed by three repeats and unmodified simrd.

Table 1: DTR failure regions supported by samples (Stages A, B and C plus confirmation runs). Brackets give the last completing and first failing sample on each side. “Confirmed” means three agreeing repeats plus agreeing unmodified simrd at the listed points, except where noted: 0.2423 has two completed, agreeing repeats and one timeout (see note a); the region remains supported by the confirmed point at 0.235.

papers.selection_reason: Studies memory-efficient training via dynamic tensor rematerialization, fitting the Efficient AI focus on reducing memory use.
papers.title: When More Memory Fails: Hidden Feasibility Holes in Dynamic Tensor Rematerialization
papers.tldr: More memory can paradoxically make Dynamic Tensor Rematerialization fail because eviction choices trigger later recomputation cascades.

papers.abstract: World-action models inherit broad visual and physical priors from video pre-training. However, standard within-video next-frame prediction allows them to rely on appearance shared between the context and future, rather than learning interactions that transfer across scenes and embodiments. We introduce WATCH, a cross-video pre-training that learns from task-paired human demonstrations collected across diverse environments. Conditioned on the video and actions of one demonstration, the model jointly predicts another demonstration's actions and future frames from its current observation. Predicting one demonstration from another encourages the model to learn task-relevant interactions that transfer across scenes and demonstrators. Our pre-training shows that these capabilities can be learned from readily scalable human-human pairs alone, without requiring matched human-robot demonstrations. Analyses before robot post-training show improved motion alignment across embodiments and better action and video prediction on unseen robots, with representations closer to those learned from robot pairs. After robot post-training, WATCH improves MimicDroid in-context success from 40.9% to 68.3% with Cosmos Policy and from 59.8% to 77.7% with Cosmos3, with the largest gains on the unseen levels. Gains persist under context-free post-training across robot embodiments. WATCH outperforms within-video pre-training and co-training baselines, supporting cross-video prediction as a scalable approach to learning transferable world-action representations.
authors: Jeongeun Park, Taekyung Kim, Dongyoon Han, Sangdoo Yun
bullets: Addresses the limitation of within-video prediction, which can rely on appearance overlap rather than transferable task interactions.
Uses cross-video pre-training on task-paired human-human demonstrations across diverse environments, without requiring human-robot pairs.
Jointly predicts the paired demonstration’s actions and future frames conditioned on the source video, actions, and target observation.
Improves motion alignment and action/video prediction on unseen robots before robot post-training.
Raises MimicDroid in-context success from 40.9% to 68.3% with Cosmos Policy and from 59.8% to 77.7% with Cosmos3; gains are largest on unseen levels and persist across embodiments.

figures.caption: Figure 1: WATCH overview. (a) Human videos of the same task are paired across collection sources and scenes. (b) Conditioned on the reference video and actions, the model predicts the target’s actions and future frames from its initial frame. The reference’s appearance does not transfer, so what it can pass on is the interaction. (c) After robot post-training, WATCH substantially improves success rates over the base model in both in-context and context-free settings.

Figure 3: Overview of WATCH. The reference video and its action trajectory, from a different demonstration of the same task, enter as clean conditioning tokens together with the query’s current frame and proprioceptive state; the query’s action chunk and future frames are the noised tokens the model denoises. Every token is tagged with its slot type and physical time, so the same sequence layout carries over to post-training with a human demonstration as the reference or with the reference slots removed. The loss is the joint velocity-matching objective of §2.1, applied to the generated tokens.

Figure 7: Alignment with a robot-trained model. Match@1 for human-trained WATCH (green) and the original video model (orange), measured against the robot-trained model on 359 EgoVerse windows (robot windows: Fig. 19). Numbers at right: mean over all layers.

Figure 12: The post-trained original video model, more frames. Attention to the current frame of the two PnPSinkToCabinet rollouts of Fig. 2a, one frame later, from the three cameras. The success (top) attends to the hand at the object, the failure (bottom) to the forearm.

Figure 20: Attention of the human-trained and the robot-trained model. Action-token attention under a same-embodiment reference, five points of its span then the query frame. (a) A Franka query, bread in basket, from the left camera for both arms. (b) A MECKA query, sort bins, over the first half of the reference, where the sorting happens.

Action-slot features of 300 RoboMIND windows, per robot, at layers 12 and 27: each model is reduced to 10 principal components, the other two are rotated onto the human-video arm’s components (two-fold cross-fit), and the three are embedded jointly with t-SNE, so every window appears three times.

Figure 4: Sensitivity to the reference demonstration. (a) Action MSE (lower is better) over 137 held-out episodes using a matched reference, a similar-motion reference from a different collection source, or a different-task reference from the same source. Brackets: Holm-corrected p-values, episode-paired Wilcoxon test. Our model is less sensitive to a change of source than of task, suggesting that our training encourages a focus on task-relevant actions. (b) Action-token attention for the same query (do dishes) with references from the same collection source (top) and a different one (bottom). Even with a reference from a different source, attention concentrates on interactions central to task execution.

Figure 2: Where a world-action model looks. Attention to the current frame, grouped by model in the order the text reads them. (a) After robot post-training of the baseline video backbone (CosmosPredict2.5), attention focuses on the hand and object in a successful rollout and on the forearm in a failed one (PnPSinkToCabinet). (b) The original video model attends broadly to edges and background on both robot frames and human demonstrations, which offer a scalable source of interaction and motion cues for robot learning. (c) On the same frames, our cross-video pre-training shifts attention toward the acting hand and manipulated object.

Figure 6: Attention visualizations under different pre-training supervision. Top four rows: side-right camera of GR1 MimicDroid rollouts of the task named on the left. Bottom three rows: three EgoVerse queries, on the query’s current frame.

Procrustes match@1 between the action-slot features of the robot-data arm and those of the human-video arm (green) or of the original video model (orange) at every DiT block, on (a) 300 RoboMIND windows and (b) 359 held-out EgoVerse windows. Each model’s features are reduced to 50 principal components and scale-normalized; one model is rotated onto the other by an orthogonal Procrustes map fitted on half the windows and applied to the other half, the halves swapping roles so that every window is placed by a map it did not contribute to. The score is the fraction of windows whose nearest neighbor among all N reference points is the window itself, so chance is 1/N : 0.0033 in (a) and 0.0028 in (b). Shaded: layers 10–27, the band of the summaries, with its mean at the right.

Figure 21: Downstream transfer under a collection budget. The human-data sweep of Figure 9 (green, blue) and the robot-pairs arm (red), under the same MimicDroid post-training. An arm’s budget is its amount of paired video times the cost of collecting a unit of that video, in units of human video; the ratio between the two is not measured here, so the band sweeps 4× to 16× and the line draws 8×. Each robot line ends at the largest robot setting we ran. Both arms start at 0 from the same model without this pre-training stage. (a) In-context, L1 to L3; (b) context-free, L1 and L2. Each panel has its own y range.

Figure 9: Scaling the pre-training data. MimicDroid success rate (%) against the portion of the paired human video used for pre-training on a fixed Cosmos Policy backbone, from no pre-training (0) to all EgoVerse pairs (100%). (a) In-context evaluation. (b) Context-free evaluation. Dashed: within-video pre-training on the 100% EgoVerse training data.

Figure 8: Pre-training supervision. Success rate (%) with post-training fixed at video + action and pre-training supervising nothing (None), the video only, the actions only, or both, on (a) MimicDroid in-context, averaged over the four tasks per level with Avg. over L1–L3, and (b) TableTop-Sim context-free.

Figure 5: Representation alignment and motion transfer across embodiments. Action-slot features from layers 10–27, with retrieval ranks and regression scores averaged over these layers, on 359 held-out EgoVerse windows (human) and 396 RoboMIND windows from three robots (robot). (a, b) Motion retrieval: share of queries whose matched window from a different collection source (a) or robot (b) falls within a normalized rank; a higher curve is better, the diagonal is chance. (c) Held-out embodiment regression: a regressor fit on two embodiments predicts nine future-motion quantities on the third; bars are the mean Spearman correlation over quantities and folds, error bars the standard error over layers.

Figure 16: Task layout across collection sources. t-SNE of layer-0 action-slot features for 95 human windows of three tasks, each recorded by two of the three sources. Color is the task, in a full and a pale shade for its two sources, and shape is the source. Under the original video model each source forms its own island within a task; under ours the two sources of a task share an island.

Action-token attention of the video backbone (upper block of each query) and ours (lower block) with a reference from the same collection source and from a different one. (a) Bagging groceries: an Aria query, the different-source reference a Scale demonstration. (b) Do dishes, the query of Fig. 4b: a Scale query, the different-source reference a MECKA demonstration.

Figure 24: Reading a 2×-speed demonstration, chunk by chunk. The same CloseLeftCabinetDoor episode (L3, camera behind the robot) under (a) Cosmos Policy without pre-training, which fails, and (b) WATCH, which succeeds. papers.selection_reason: Cross-video human-demonstration pretraining for transferable world-action models directly fits learning from human video and video world models.
papers.title: Learning Transferable World-Action Models from Task-Paired Human Videos
papers.tldr: WATCH learns transferable world-action representations by predicting one human demonstration’s actions and future frames from another, improving robot imitation across unseen environments and embodiments.

papers.abstract: We show that continuous bitstream diffusion (CoBit), originally developed for language modeling, provides a unified framework for joint and conditional multimodal generation using the same training and sampling protocol. Across image-text, speech-text and protein sequence-structure modeling, models are trained separately from scratch, but each uses a single input projection, transformer backbone, bitwise prediction head and binary score-matching objective shared across its modalities. Within each setting, a single checkpoint supports joint generation and the conditional directions included in training by changing which parts of the bitstream are observed. We first validate the approach on MNIST-Sum, a controlled image-text task pairing raw binary images with equations encoded as text, achieving near-perfect conditional accuracy and high joint consistency without learned tokenizers. We then apply the same protocol at larger scale to speech-text and protein sequence-structure modeling. Trained without text pretraining, a single speech-text model performs speech synthesis, recognition, continuation, and unconditional co-generation. Jointly generated speech and text achieve 3.5% word error rate between the generated text and automatic transcriptions of the generated speech. In protein modeling, a single CoBit checkpoint supports forward folding, inverse folding, and joint sequence-structure generation. For jointly generated proteins spanning 100-500 residues, computational refolding of CoBit's sequences yields structures that agree with the generated backbones at a mean self-consistency TM-score of 0.911. Together, these results show that CoBit provides a common generative framework for substantially different modalities and forms of cross-modal dependence, without introducing a domain-specific objective or sampling procedure.
authors: Georgios Batzolis, Georgios Kontos, Bruno Trentini, Pranam Chatterjee, Micha Livne, Mark Girolami, Luca Ambrogioni
bullets: A shared architecture uses one input projection, transformer backbone, bitwise prediction head, and binary score-matching objective for each multimodal setting.
A single checkpoint supports multiple generation directions by varying which portions of the bitstream are observed.
On MNIST-Sum, CoBit achieves near-perfect conditional accuracy and high joint consistency without learned tokenizers.
The speech-text model supports synthesis, recognition, continuation, and co-generation; generated speech and text achieve 3.5% word error rate.
For proteins, one checkpoint handles forward folding, inverse folding, and joint generation, with generated structures reaching a mean self-consistency TM-score of 0.911 after refolding.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Text-to-speech generation with CoBit-MLS. Given text and speaker tokens (extracted from a held-out example), the model is tasked with generating the speech part of the sequence. The similarity between the reference and generated waveforms is measured in terms of frame-level mel-cepstral distortion (MCD), aligned using dynamic time warping (DTW). CoBit generates the same text, but with different speech pacing and a longer pause between the two sentences. (Left) Temporal alignment of waveform frames. CoBit introduces silence between the two sentences. (Right) Pairwise MCD cost matrix and the optimal DTW path. The horizontal segment between 1.5 and 2 seconds corresponds to inter-sentence silence.

Figure 1: MNIST-Sum, a controlled image–text evaluation. (a) Four binarised MNIST digits and their equation form one flat sequence of 3,388 bits (3,136 pixel, 84 text and 168 marker bits); the zoom-ins show bits from the displayed pair. One denoiser serves both conditional directions by observing one part of the stream and denoising the other. (b) With nothing observed, the same weights co-generate an image and equation from noise; a pair is correct only when the generated equation matches the generated image. Rates use n=4,096 samples per direction; the displayed examples illustrate, but do not estimate, those rates.

Figure 6: Text-to-speech generation with CoBit-MLS. Given text and speaker tokens (extracted from a held-out example), the model is tasked with generating the speech part of the sequence. The top mel-spectrogram corresponds to the ground truth waveform, the middle one to the StableCodec reconstruction, and the bottom mel-spectrogram to the generated audio by the 633M parameter bitstream diffusion model. The tokenizer introduces visible artifacts, especially at high frequencies. CoBit generation spreads the utterance across a longer time span, without leading and trailing silence, replicating similar frequency patterns. The only exception is the gap between 1.7 and 1.9 seconds, which corresponds to the boundary between sentences.

Figure 7: Speech continuation with CoBit-MLS. Given speaker and speech tokens extracted from a 3-second audio prompt, the model is tasked with generating its own continuation. The top melspectrogram corresponds to the ground truth continuation, and the bottom mel-spectrogram to the continuation generated by the 633M parameter bitstream diffusion model. The generated spectrogram blends well with the audio prompt, introducing minimal artifacts at the prompt-continuation boundary. Speech continuation is scored not only in terms of acoustic consistency, but also for the semantic relevance and intelligibility of the generated content, shown on the right.

Figure 11: LLM-as-a-Judge score distribution for CoBit and autoregressive SLMs. CoBit-LibriTTS almost always receives the lowest possible score. A large portion of CoBit-MLS samples perform moderately better, but neither of the model can consistently achieve scores of 3 or higher.

Figure 12: Protein representation and denoising. The displayed equation describes the deterministic, unguided DDIM core. (a) Residue-aligned sequence and LFQ bits. (b) Task conditioning and successive DDIM updates with the same denoiser.

Top right: Embedding similarity of BiCodec-global FSQ components across the 1,024 BiCodec-global sequences sampled by CoBit-MLS. Both plots are averaged over sequence positions. Bottom: realized speaker diversity among the generated populations of CoBit-MLS, CoBit-LibriTTS (Steps=256, γ = 0.175) and the SmolLM-Speaker-SparkTTS autoregressive cascade (Appendix C.8), measured in terms of embeddings from the speaker verification CAM++ checkpoint.
Figure 10: Breakdown of speech-to-text WER and CER for CoBit-MLS, using the selected setting in Table 6.

Colours denote length. 100 backbones (20 per length) each receive one ProteinMPNN redesign and ESMFold refold. Intervals are 95%. Shading marks both strict criteria.

papers.abstract: We present ContinuousCloth, a continuous-time, physics-informed neural solver for deformable cloth dynamics that enforces a spring--mass ODE within a neural trajectory model. Unlike classical time-stepping simulators that return trajectories only on a discrete integration grid, ContinuousCloth supports querying at arbitrary timestamps and computing displacement, velocity, and acceleration via automatic differentiation. We evaluate ContinuousCloth along two dimensions. In a physics-only setting, ContinuousCloth achieves trajectory accuracy comparable to high-precision solvers across six diverse boundary-condition scenarios while reducing runtime by up to 17.4 times. When fused with sparse and noisy observations, the spring--mass ODE acts as a strong inductive bias for downstream tasks: interpolation and parameter estimation. That is, ContinuousCloth reduces interpolation error by 7.3 times over a data-only neural baseline in simulation and 2.4 times on real-world cloth sequences, and achieves 2.6 times lower parameter error than a differentiable-solver baseline under high-noise conditions, demonstrating consistent robustness under realistic measurement imperfections.

papers.abstract: We present CoPlanVLM, which uses a Vision Language Model (VLM) to translate a single natural-language instruction and image into coordinated paths for a team of two robots. While VLMs offer a flexible, natural-language interface for commanding robot teams, their weak spatial reasoning has greatly limited VLM-based path planning. CoPlanVLM improves the VLM's spatial reasoning and path planning abilities through three components: (1) an image overlay marking both free space and obstacles, (2) task classification that selects the most appropriate low-level planner and reasoning prompt for each instruction, and (3) task-specific chain-of-thought reasoning that prompts the VLM to identify key objects, allocate roles, and verify routes are collision-free before committing to a plan. Together, these components enable the team to complete complex coordinated maneuvers requiring both robots and divide large tasks between robots to increase efficiency. CoPlanVLM also supports detailed maneuvers involving specific routes, loops, and coverage of large areas, as well as tasks requiring directional reasoning such as north/south or left/right. We validate CoPlanVLM in both Gazebo simulation and on physical Turtlebot 4 hardware. CoPlanVLM attains an average success rate of 84.4% compared to 50.0% for the closest baseline. On trials where both methods succeed, CoPlanVLM's paths are 27% shorter on average. Project code is available at https://github.com/AICPS/CoPlanVLM.

papers.abstract: Latent world-model planning has shown promising results in goal-conditioned robotic manipulation, but remains challenging for long-horizon planning due to limited temporal guidance and inefficient action search. A distant visual goal provides little guidance for preparatory actions, while uninformed action sampling makes local optimization inefficient. We propose PILOT (Policy-Initialized Local Optimization with Temporal subgoals), which uses a video model to generate intermediate visual subgoals and a learned policy to initialize the cross-entropy method (CEM). CEM refines candidate action sequences toward each subgoal using an action-conditioned world model in a receding-horizon control loop. In our primary real-robot evaluation across four UR5e manipulation tasks, PILOT achieves 68.8% success, compared with 55.0% without policy initialization, 13.8% for policy-only execution, and 0.0% for direct final-goal planning. Simulation results show that these gains persist over longer horizons: PILOT exceeds direct execution of the same policy by 30 percentage points on long Push-T tasks and by 22 percentage points on LIBERO-10. Policy initialization also accelerates local optimization: on Push-T, CEM matches the cost reached by generic initialization after 10 iterations in only 4 iterations and reduces the final planning cost by 24.1% under the same sampling budget. These results show that combining temporal subgoals with policy-guided action search improves both long-horizon task execution and local planning efficiency. Videos are available on the webpage: https://pilot-planner.github.io/.

papers.abstract: Accurate sampling from continuous-time generative models can require many model evaluations. Low-step sampling reduces cost, but coarse updates introduce endpoint errors that can accumulate and degrade generation quality. We introduce TraceSampler, a post-training method that corrects these errors without modifying the pretrained model. Rather than optimising low-step updates directly, TraceSampler models endpoint error as a sample-specific prediction problem. A higher-step reference integration over the same interval provides the supervised target, while a compact representation makes high-dimensional error predictable from the sampling trace. This representation combines shared residual structure, trace-derived directions, and a low-rank remainder, so shallow per-step MLP heads predict sample-dependent coefficients. These coefficients drive a two-stage learned residual correction: the first stage predicts the full endpoint residual, while an intermediate backbone evaluation provides new trace information to predict the remaining residual; this evaluation is reused by the following step. TraceSampler is evaluated with Rectified Flow on CIFAR-10, SiT-XL/2 on ImageNet-256, and SD3.5 Medium for text-to-image generation. At 10 steps, it reduces trajectory MSE relative to matched-step Euler by 90.5% on CIFAR-10 and 85.6% on ImageNet-256, while achieving FID scores of 2.692 and 2.189, close to 120-step Heun references of 2.601 and 2.056 with 24$\times$ fewer backbone evaluations. On SD3.5 Medium, TraceSampler improves image quality and prompt following; at 10 steps, ImageReward rises from 0.752 to 0.906 while trajectory MSE falls by 70.7%. These gains preserve Euler's backbone-evaluation budget, add less than 0.4% inference FLOPs, and incur negligible wall-clock overhead, showing that coarse-step sampling error can be made predictable from the sampling trace and efficiently corrected.

papers.abstract: Position tracking is a well-studied problem in Euclidean navigation, yet comparatively little attention has been given to navigation on general manifolds, where motion is governed by the underlying geometry of the space. In this work, we formalize the problem of manifold navigation as a velocity-driven tracking task and propose a coordinate-chart-based learning framework in which learning models operate entirely in a Euclidean representation. Predicted trajectories are mapped to the manifold via an immersion function prior to error computation, allowing geometric consistency to be evaluated without explicitly enforcing manifold constraints during learning. Within this framework, we focus on Gated Recurrent Units (GRUs) for sequential position prediction on curved manifolds after comparisons with alternative recurrent architectures. We evaluate our GRU models, trained with pertinent custom loss functions, against both a standard MSE loss function and a naive vector-addition baseline. We evaluate our approach on both analytically (and numerically) defined manifolds, as well as a surface reconstructed from a LiDAR point cloud. Our results show that recurrent models can learn to approximate manifold-constrained dynamics from velocity sequences and consistently outperform Euclidean baselines. Our results demonstrate that certain custom loss functions significantly improve long-horizon prediction accuracy compared to conventional point-wise loss functions.

papers.abstract: Foundation models like V-JEPA are increasingly deployed across a heterogeneous edge-cloud continuum spanning smart glasses, phones, robots, and servers. Yet, they are typically trained as rigid, fixed-capacity networks bound to one device, supporting neither reconfigurable compute budgets nor collaborative execution. Existing approaches address only one axis at a time: slimmable and NAS-based methods provide width elasticity but assume single-device inference, whereas split-computing methods enable cross-device collaboration only for fixed partitions and static capacities. We introduce Elastic V-JEPA (EV-JEPA), a single model trained once and deployable everywhere along the continuum. Its width is reconfigurable, and it is natively partitionable across heterogeneous devices. At its core is Transition-Aware Triplet Training (T3). At each step we pick a narrow and a wide width, and train three paths: each width alone, plus a hybrid path that runs the early layers narrow and the rest wide. The hybrid switch point is where one device hands off to another, so the same weights learn both single-device and cross-device execution. Across various benchmarks, EV-JEPA falls within 1 accuracy point of independently trained baselines while improving over previous elastic training approaches by up to 11 accuracy points. Narrow-to-wide cross-device hybrid execution recovers to within 1.1 points of the highest-capacity standalone model and supports many-to-one, any-to-any, and variable-split configurations. Finally, we show that the elastic principle extends beyond the backbone to an elastic token compression mechanism that exposes controllable trade-offs among on-device computation, latency, and accuracy.
authors: Anxhelo Diko, Jieyu Lin, Stefano Ambrogio, Ziyun Li, Mahmoud Assran, Th\'eo Moutakanni, Barbara De Salvo, Chiao Liu

Enables native cross-device execution with flexible split points and many-to-one or any-to-any configurations.

Matches independently trained baselines within 1 accuracy point and improves prior elastic methods by up to 11 points.

We propose a single elastic network that is trained once and deployed across the entire continuum: (1) its width is reconfigurable at inference time, allowing the same parameters to serve any compute budget (Standalone Inference); and (2) its computation can be split between devices, with early layers executed on-device and remaining layers on a stronger device, communicating only compact intermediate representations (Hybrid Inference).

The ’compress module’ compresses the intermediate representation before transmission, reducing the number of tokens; the ’decompress module’ reconstructs the token grid on the target device, after which the shared elastic projection Pws→wl upscales to wl, and the remaining L− k layers execute. papers.abstract: Reconstructing accurate camera poses and floor-plan layouts from sparse, unposed, wide-baseline RGB panoramas remains a challenging open problem. Direct multi-room floor-plan prediction is especially difficult in this setting: pose, geometry, semantics, and global layout structure are tightly coupled, yet a complete floor-plan is hard to learn as a single global output. Our key insight is to keep the model's predictions strictly local. Multi-view Ordered Wall Instance Segmentation (MOIS) is designed around this concept. Each panorama column predicts only the wall it observes plus the next two adjacent walls in clockwise order. The global wall partition, room layouts, and shared coordinates emerge from deterministic aggregation of overlapping local predictions. Building on MOIS, we propose Multi-view floor-plan Feed-Forward Network (MvFFN), which jointly predicts coarse camera poses, dense global geometry, and per-wall semantic outputs. A downstream Layout Chaining (LC) post processing pipeline then assembles these predictions into multi-room floor-plans with shared global coordinates, consistent wall identities, and connected room structure. The dense MOIS predictions recover cross-view wall identity and local within-room connectivity more accurately than composed modular baselines, and the assembled layouts substantially outperform prior methods on wall and junction level accuracy. We also introduce the ZInD-CrossView dataset, which augments ZInD with globally unique wall instances and cross-view segmentation labels for this task.
authors: Yuguang Li, Yichuan Deng, Zixuan Liu, Ivaylo Boyadzhiev, Xiuyuan Wu, Xinyu Zou, Linda Shapiro, Alex Colburn
bullets: Addresses the coupled challenges of camera pose, geometry, semantics, and global structure in multi-room reconstruction.
MOIS predicts each panorama column’s observed wall and its next two clockwise adjacent walls, keeping predictions local.
MvFFN jointly estimates coarse poses, dense global geometry, and per-wall semantics.
Layout Chaining aggregates overlapping local predictions into globally coordinated, connected floor plans.
Experiments report improved wall and junction accuracy over prior methods; the work also introduces the ZInD-CrossView dataset.

Layout Chaining aggregates these local predictions into global wall identities, room-level wall sequences, and metric floor plan layouts, enabling downstream refinement.

papers.abstract: Speech large language models (LLMs) are often built using pretrained acoustic encoders as an audio interface to an LLM decoder. However, LLMs scale poorly with input sequence length, while acoustic encoders tend to produce substantially longer sequences than typical textual inputs. This motivates learning to compress encoder outputs while preserving task-oriented information. To this end, we introduce ASSET, a reinforcement learning (RL)-based framework that learns to adaptively compress encoder outputs by first partitioning them into variable-duration segments and then pooling each segment into a continuous audio token. We use group-relative policy optimization (GRPO) to train a segmenter with task performance feedback and a token-rate penalty. In automatic speech recognition (ASR) experiments, ASSET achieves performance comparable to a transcript-assisted character-boundary oracle with approximately 25% fewer audio tokens on English LibriSpeech, while improving on a phone-boundary oracle at a similar token rate on Mandarin AISHELL. Exploratory experiments on non-ASR tasks further illustrate how learned segmentation changes when the framework is adapted to tasks beyond transcription.
authors: Cihan Xiao, Yuan Tseng, Matthew Wiesner, Desh Raj, Leibny Paola Garcia Perera, Sanjeev Khudanpur, David Harwath
bullets: Addresses the sequence-length mismatch between long acoustic-encoder outputs and speech LLM inputs.
Learns variable-duration segments and pools each into a continuous audio token.
Trains the segmenter with GRPO using task-performance feedback and a token-rate penalty.
Matches a transcript-assisted character-boundary oracle with about 25% fewer tokens on English LibriSpeech.
Outperforms a phone-boundary oracle at a similar token rate on Mandarin AISHELL; non-ASR behavior is explored but not fully characterized.

(b) Task losses score sampled boundary sequences; cross-entropy updates the pooler and decoder, while GRPO updates the segmenter.
Fig. 2. 100h WER. Left: fixed strides k and Transformer/BiGRU. Right: policy/pooler detail.

papers.selection_reason: RL-based adaptive compression of speech encoder outputs into fewer audio tokens for speech LLMs; relevant to token efficiency and multimodal LLMs.
papers.title: ASSET: Adaptive Speech Segmentation via Reinforcement Learning
papers.tldr: ASSET uses reinforcement learning to adaptively segment and compress speech encoder outputs into fewer task-relevant audio tokens while preserving performance.

papers.abstract: Humans and animals do not learn vision from a fixed set of data: they move, interact, and learn from the visual consequences of their actions. Motivated by this developmental view, we study whether robots can improve visual learning by actively collecting experience through curiosity-driven interaction. We introduce DySCOVER, a self-supervised framework for active robot visual learning. A robot observes RGB frames, learns a visual autoencoder that encodes and reconstructs them, and trains a recurrent world model to predict the next visual latent state conditioned on the current state and action. The agent's policy is trained only with intrinsic rewards: reconstruction error encourages visually novel observations, while the world model's error encourages transitions whose consequences are not yet predictable. This prediction error biases the policy toward more intricate trajectories that enrich the agent's set of experiences with observations beyond those encouraged by visual novelty alone. Our experiments conducted with robotic arms as the embodied agents show that adding predictive curiosity improves the vision model over using visual curiosity alone. Across variations in initial conditions, experience capacity, embodiment, and scene content, adding predictive curiosity consistently improved visual learning. These results show that predictive curiosity can improve active visual learning beyond reconstruction-based curiosity alone.
authors: Stelios Zarifis, Panagiotis Filntisis, George Retsinas, Petros Maragos
bullets: Robots actively gather visual experience instead of learning from a fixed dataset.
A visual autoencoder reconstructs RGB observations, while a recurrent world model predicts future visual latents from states and actions.
Intrinsic rewards combine reconstruction error with prediction error to drive curiosity-based exploration.
Robot-arm experiments show predictive curiosity consistently improves visual learning over reconstruction-based curiosity alone.
The study evaluates varied initial conditions, experience capacities, embodiments, and scene contents.
