papers.abstract: Video diffusion models increasingly serve as priors for 4D generation, but the generated videos often lack geometric consistency. Recent approaches address this through post-training by designing geometric rewards, yet this can degrade texture and fine detail, requiring auxiliary appearance rewards and careful reward balancing. To address this challenge, we propose GeoFix, a unified framework that improves geometric consistency and visual quality with a single geometric reward, applicable to both training and inference-time reward alignment. Our reward measures cross-view depth consistency in static scene regions, targeting structural inconsistencies without directly constraining appearance or penalizing valid object motion. Crucially, depth agreement increases with camera field-of-view overlap even in real videos and 4D datasets, allowing a smaller camera movement to be mistaken for better geometry. We account for this effect by calibrating the reward against the overlap-dependent trend. GeoFix achieves a 39% improvement in WorldScore 3D consistency and a 4% increase in VBench Quality Score.
authors: Yeobin Hong, Hyojun Go, Dohun Lee, Jeongjae Lee, Sunghwan Hong, Federico Tombari, Zhaochong An, Jong Chul Ye, Konrad Schindler, Dominik Narnhofer
bullets: Addresses geometric inconsistency in video-diffusion-based 4D generation.
Uses one reward for both training-time and inference-time alignment, avoiding appearance-reward balancing.
Measures depth agreement in static scene regions while preserving valid object motion and appearance.
Calibrates for camera field-of-view overlap, which can otherwise make smaller camera movements appear geometrically better.
Reports a 39% improvement in WorldScore 3D consistency and a 4% increase in VBench Quality Score.

papers.abstract: Tensor parallelism ends every layer with an all-reduce that sits between two dependent matrix multiplications, so its cost cannot be hidden and grows as compute outpaces interconnect bandwidth. Sending 4-bit instead of 16-bit values would cut this cost by nearly 4x, but the all-reduce must add the values it carries, and rounding the sum injects an error at every call. Model quality depends on how these errors accumulate over layers, yet existing methods treat each call on its own. We present Echo, a 4-bit all-reduce for training and inference that controls the accumulated error. Echo moves data in 4 bits and sums in high precision, so each value is quantized at most twice per call for any number of GPUs. The summation reveals each injected error, and Echo feeds it back into later calls, so old errors cancel instead of accumulating. We prove that the accumulated error stays bounded independently of depth. On A100 GPUs, Echo is 2.09x faster than the 16-bit NCCL all-reduce on 1 GB messages. It speeds up the time to first token by up to 1.16x and the training step by up to 1.09x on an idle interconnect, and by up to 1.44x and 1.38x as background traffic grows. It keeps the average accuracy over seven benchmarks within 0.4 points of 16-bit inference on Qwen3-8B. In 10B-token pretraining, its final loss is less than 0.9% above that of 16-bit training. Echo needs no FP8 or FP4 hardware.
authors: Xingyu Xie, Xiaoyong Xie, Zhouchen Lin, Kim-Chuan Toh
bullets: Problem: 16-bit all-reduce communication limits tensor-parallel LLM training and inference, while naïve 4-bit quantization introduces repeated rounding errors.
Method: Data moves in 4 bits, sums in high precision, and each value is quantized at most twice per call; revealed errors are fed back into later calls.
Guarantee: The accumulated communication error is proven to remain bounded independently of network depth.
Results: Echo is 2.09× faster than 16-bit NCCL all-reduce on 1 GB A100 messages, with up to 1.44× faster time to first token and 1.38× faster training under background traffic.
Quality and scope: Accuracy stays within 0.4 points of 16-bit inference across seven benchmarks, and final pretraining loss is under 0.9% higher; no FP8 or FP4 hardware is required.

figures.caption: Figure 2. The quantized P2P all-reduce. (a) For P = 4, each GPU sends only its non-owned segments as 4-bit codes to their owners. Each owner dequantizes the received codes and sums them with its own unquantized segment in high precision. The reduced segment is quantized once for the all-gather, and every GPU, including the owner, dequantizes the same code to obtain identical outputs. Each element is quantized at most twice, independently of P . (b) Tiles are staggered across push, reduce, gather, and tail. Peer-visible flags signal cross-GPU readiness and CUDA events order work within a GPU, allowing quantization and transfers of different tiles to overlap.

A forward pass has N such sites, and the backward pass injects at the same sites (Sec. 5.4).

Figure 4. Worked example at P = 4. The quantizer is Eqn. (8) with b = 4 and a group equal to the two values of one segment. Bottom: the all-gather sends one quantized copy of each segment sum, so every GPU holds the same values. The last row is the error this all-reduce injects, the δk of Fig. 1. Inputs are shown to one decimal and sums to two.

papers.selection_reason: 4-bit tensor-parallel all-reduce with error compensation directly targets communication and inference/training efficiency.
papers.title: Echo: Error-Compensated 4-Bit Tensor-Parallel Communication for LLM Training and Inference

papers.abstract: Hybrid reasoning models such as the Qwen3 series switch between a THINK mode and a NO-THINK mode through a few chat-template tokens. A popular recipe trains such models with reinforcement learning in NO-THINK mode and reports improved reasoning performance. We provide evidence that much of this gain can be explained by thinking leakage: the gain comes largely from partially reactivating the reasoning abilities of the original model's THINK mode instead of learning enhanced reasoning behavior. We train Qwen3-1.7B, 4B, and 8B with GRPO in NO-THINK mode. As accuracy improves, responses become longer and more reflective, are increasingly judged by the original model to resemble its own thinking, and the model's internal activations shift toward its THINK mode. We then investigate at the level of weights, activations, and attention heads: scaling the RL update further elicits THINK-mode behavior and approaches THINK-mode accuracy but does not exceed it; in Qwen3-8B, replacing a low-dimensional THINK-related activation subspace of the RL-trained model with its original-model value removes most of the RL gain, and the reverse exchange transfers a considerable fraction of the gain to the original model; and the RL-induced shift passes through the attention heads that read the empty think block. We further identify a possible mechanism in the GRPO training signal: responses favored by the advantage-weighted update are more THINK-like, and a gradient step computed from this signal moves the model toward its THINK state. Thus, gains in NO-THINK mode can largely reflect reactivation of reasoning abilities already present in the original model.
authors: Wenxuan Zhu, Shuming Liu, Bang An, Aznaur Aliev, Bing Li, Yibo Yang, Bernard Ghanem
bullets: The study examines Qwen3 models trained with GRPO in NO-THINK mode.
Improved accuracy coincides with longer, more reflective, THINK-like responses and activations.
Stronger RL shifts the models toward THINK-mode behavior and accuracy but does not surpass the original THINK mode.
Activation-subspace and attention-head interventions transfer or remove much of the RL gain, linking it to THINK-related components.
The GRPO signal may favor THINK-like responses, causing updates toward the model’s existing THINK state.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes RL-induced thinking leakage in Qwen3 hybrid LLMs via weights, activations, and attention heads; directly relevant to LLM training and reasoning.
papers.title: The Thinking Leakage in Reinforcement Learning for LLMs
papers.tldr: Reinforcement learning gains in Qwen3’s NO-THINK mode largely come from reactivating existing THINK-mode reasoning rather than learning substantially stronger reasoning.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in multi-modal large language models have shifted toward the "thinking with images" paradigm to improve reasoning faithfulness, yet existing methods rely heavily on explicit coordinate- based grounding. We identify two fundamental limitations in this approach, i.e., a semantic gap where sparse regressions miss high-dimensional latent structures, and a resolution gap due to the granularity mismatch between patch-level tokens and pixel-level coordinates. To address these, we propose TiCO (Thinking with images without COordinates). It reformulates visual reasoning as a semantic evidence discovery process within the latent space, and evidence is injected as token-level regions without pixel coordinates. Specifically, TiCO utilizes a dedicated probe token to estimate similarity distributions and performs importance sampling over spatially connected components to generate diverse, semantically dominant evidence rollouts. Extensive experiments across multiple high-resolution and general visual reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that our TiCO consistently outperforms state-of-the-art coordinate-based methods with significantly improved inference efficiency.
authors: Meng Cao, Haoze Zhao, Yi Wang, Ian Reid, Xiaodan Liang
bullets: Coordinate-based visual reasoning suffers from semantic gaps in sparse regressions and resolution gaps between patch tokens and pixels.
TiCO reformulates reasoning as semantic evidence discovery in the model’s latent space.
A dedicated probe token estimates similarity distributions, while importance sampling over connected spatial components produces diverse evidence rollouts.
Evidence is injected as token-level regions rather than coordinate-based locations.
Experiments on high-resolution and general visual reasoning benchmarks show improved performance and inference efficiency over coordinate-based methods.

figures.caption: Figure 3 Overview of TiCO. Given an image–text query pair, the policy model first produces a semantic probe token (<GROUND>) whose embedding interacts with visual patch tokens to generate a similarity map. After thresholding the similarity distribution, spatially connected components are extracted as candidate evidence regions. These components are treated as evidence rollouts and are subsequently fed back into the policy model to generate answer rollouts.

Figure 1 Comparison between coordinate-based methods and TiCO. Traditional model Mini-o3 [19] relies on explicit coordinate regression (<box>), which is sensitive to localization errors and prone to error propagation. In contrast, our TiCO replaces coordinate prediction with latent semantic region indexing, directly attending to informative regions in the token space.

(b) Inconsistent Logic: Although the model correctly identifies the target object (a yellow bicycle) in the final observation, it produces an incorrect final answer (Option B: red) that contradicts its own internal reasoning and visual evidence.

(a) Coordinate-based methods [19, 56] localize evidence via explicit bounding-box prediction, reducing reasoning to geometric regression in image space; (b) Coordinate-free methods instead operate directly in visual token space, inducing a similarity distribution over patches and extracting semantically coherent evidence without explicit coordinates; (c) Performance–efficiency comparison on HR-Bench 8K [41]. Our TiCO achieves superior accuracy with substantially lower inference latency and fewer tokens compared to coordinate-based approaches such as Mini-o3 [19] and DeepEyes [56].

papers.abstract: Regularization-based continual learning protects each parameter in proportion to an estimate of its importance, yet these estimates come from finite samples and heuristics and are used as if they were exact. We report four studies that start from a biologically inspired mechanism and end with a statistical explanation of it. Motivated by dendritic nanotubes, we let transient lateral links diffuse importance tags between hidden units. Links between co-active units gave no significant gain, but random links with lifetimes of 25 or 200 steps raised final accuracy on 20-task Permuted MNIST by 1.5 to 2.6 points. We show that random diffusion implements linear shrinkage of importance toward the layer mean in expectation. A simulation of the link process alone predicts shrinkage weights of 0.23 and 0.52 for these lifetimes, and graph-free shrinkage at 0.25 and 0.5 reproduces both the accuracy and the dispersion of the consolidated importance, while every activity-dependent rule did worse than random links. A five-seed screen across EWC, SI, and MAS found nominal gains for SI and MAS on Permuted MNIST and losses on task-incremental Split CIFAR-100, where forgetting was small and shrinkage cost plasticity. Varying the number of importance samples then separates two mechanisms on Permuted MNIST. For EWC, the gain fell by about ten points per tenfold increase in samples, from 19.6 points with 10 samples to -0.4 with 1000, a variance effect. For MAS, a gain of about one point persisted at 1000 samples, consistent with a bias in the importance measure rather than noise. Shrinkage had no detectable effect for MAS on a domain-incremental CIFAR-100 benchmark. Finally, we show that a standard heteroscedastic empirical Bayes rule shrinks the largest Fisher-type estimates most, which may explain its poor results, and point to a log-scale alternative.
authors: Saurav K. Aryal
bullets: Activity-dependent dendritic-style links provided no significant benefit; random transient links improved 20-task Permuted MNIST accuracy by 1.5–2.6 points.
The link process is mathematically equivalent in expectation to linear shrinkage, and graph-free shrinkage reproduced both accuracy and importance dispersion.
Benefits varied across methods: SI and MAS gained on Permuted MNIST, while shrinkage hurt Split CIFAR-100, where forgetting was already small.
For EWC, gains disappeared as the number of importance samples increased, indicating variance reduction; MAS retained a smaller gain, suggesting estimator bias.
A standard heteroscedastic empirical-Bayes rule over-shrinks large Fisher-type estimates; a log-scale alternative is proposed.

papers.selection_reason: Directly studies importance-estimate shrinkage and regularization-based continual learning, fitting the continual and online learning subtopic.
papers.title: Do Artificial Neural Networks Need Dendritic Nanotubes? Two Reasons for Shrinking Importance Estimates in Continual Learning
papers.tldr: Random diffusion improves continual learning mainly by statistically shrinking noisy parameter-importance estimates toward the layer mean, with benefits depending on the importance estimator and task setting.

papers.abstract: Looped transformers reuse the same layer multiple times, allowing inference compute to be adjusted without changing the model. Recent adaptive-depth methods train the model across multiple loop depths from the beginning of training. We introduce fixed-first training, which varies model depth only during a short final phase of training. At 200M parameters, training a model of fixed-depth 2 for the first 67% of the run reduces modeled training compute by 45% while keeping mean negative log-likelihood (NLL) across inference depths within 0.5% of training across depths throughout. At 1B parameters, training initially at depth 4 reduces modeled compute by 31% to 37% and wall-clock time by 32% to 39%, while keeping final NLL within 0.8% and downstream differences within the observed seed variation. These results show that training over the full range of depths can be reserved for a short finishing phase with only small changes in performance.
authors: Andrei Piterbarg, Sean McLeish, Dhruv Pai, Benjamin Keigwin
bullets: Trains at one fixed loop depth for most of training, then varies depth only near the end.
At 200M parameters, it reduces modeled training compute by 45% while keeping mean NLL within 0.5% of full multi-depth training.
At 1B parameters, it reduces modeled compute by 31–37% and wall-clock time by 32–39%.
Final NLL remains within 0.8%, and downstream differences stay within observed seed variation.
Scope: results concern looped transformers and the tested 200M- and 1B-parameter settings.

papers.abstract: Diffusion models provide expressive trajectory priors for multi-robot motion planning (MRMP), but scaling them to large teams requires coordinating individual motions without expensive joint computation. We introduce Akule, a sparse interaction diffusion framework that augments a frozen single-robot prior with three learned modules: a reusable pairwise correction model $R_{\phi}$, a contextual selector $U_{\psi}$ that determines which corrections to evaluate, and a composer $G_{\omega}$ that combines their effects through context-dependent signed weights. This decomposition separates which interactions merit computation from how their effects should be combined into coordinated denoising updates. We train $R_{\phi}$ using matched pairwise trajectory optimizations, then learn $G_{\omega}$ and $U_{\psi}$ from physically optimized joint trajectories without requiring a prescribed ground-truth interaction graph. The resulting joint proposals are passed to a downstream search-based planner for validation and repair. Across diverse MRMP benchmarks, Akule achieves competitive planning success, complete-planner speedups of up to $25\times$, zero-shot population transfer, and successful planning with up to $256$ robots. Ablations further demonstrate that learned selection and composition reduce pre-repair conflicts and downstream repair effort relative to heuristic selection and uniform summation.
authors: Manav Vora, Gokul Puthumanaillam, Aditya Penumarti, Jane Shin, Melkior Ornik
bullets: Addresses the costly joint coordination problem in diffusion-based multi-robot motion planning.
Uses a frozen single-robot prior plus learned pairwise correction, interaction selection, and context-dependent composition modules.
Trains corrections from pairwise optimized trajectories and selection/composition from optimized joint trajectories without a predefined interaction graph.
Feeds generated joint proposals to a search-based planner for validation and repair.
Reports competitive success, up to 25× complete-planner speedups, zero-shot population transfer, and reduced conflicts and repair effort.

papers.abstract: An LLM-directed excavator can execute mechanically feasible motion whose destination or authority no longer matches the operator's approval. We propose execution-bound authorization for the approval--dispatch--execution interval. A one-use lease binds the action, generated motion, mission contract and admission tolerance; atomic dispatch rechecks current authority and measured joint drift. Periodic supervision detects revocation and requests a quintic stop with a carry-pitch endpoint, selected through sampled joint, stroke, flow and reference-acceleration checks. The framework connects exact motion identity to dispatch integrity and load-aware interruption. Evaluation combines a 672-case interface suite, four loaded digging cases in synchronous simulation, unloaded MuJoCo/Pinocchio transfers and two command-level LLM planners. The gateway admitted all 120 benign interface cases and produced zero unauthorized dispatches in the attack suite. Loaded dispatch-window tests produced zero unauthorized deposition. During simulated dump-phase revocation, maximum closed-site deposition decreased from 1.23 to 0.33\,m$^3$; loaded-slew stops used less than 75\% of nominal swing torque. These results demonstrate motion-bound authorization and quantify the retention and stopping behavior of supervised excavation skills.

papers.abstract: Pixel-space world models have recently emerged as a promising approach for GUI agents, predicting future screens prior to execution and subsequently re-perceiving them for action selection. However, this two-stage paradigm faces two key challenges in GUI environments: (L1) the high computational cost of pixel reconstruction and (L2) the need to reconstruct large and diverse appearance-level details beyond what is required for action selection. In practice, this screen-generation objective can induce an identity shortcut problem, where future-state prediction largely preserves the current state rather than capturing action-induced changes. In this work, we reformulate GUI world modeling by shifting the prediction target from full-screen reconstruction to action-induced future information in latent space. Concretely, we leverage a large multimodal model as the latent world model, whose shared representations support two dedicated heads for both action selection and predictive transition modeling. The action head directly translates these latent representations into action selection, while the transition head captures action-conditioned future information. To mitigate the identity shortcut, we further introduce an action-aware contrastive objective that encourages the transition representations to capture discriminative action-induced changes. Extensive experiments across offline and online GUI settings show that our method achieves up to 31.9% and 40.6% relative gains in success rate over pixel-space world models, respectively, while substantially reducing inference latency by up to 98.9%. Our code is available at https://github.com/sjyu001/latent2world.
authors: Seungjun Yu, Hojun Choi, Seojeong Park, Jaeyo Shin, Hyunjung Shim
bullets: Addresses the high computational cost and unnecessary visual detail of pixel-space GUI world models.
Uses a large multimodal model with shared latent representations and separate action-selection and transition-prediction heads.
Introduces an action-aware contrastive objective to avoid identity shortcuts and emphasize action-induced changes.
Reports up to 31.9% relative gains offline and 40.6% online over pixel-space world models, with up to 98.9% lower inference latency.
Evaluated in both offline and online GUI settings; the abstract does not specify task or dataset scope.

papers.abstract: Purpose : To develop and evaluate CAPTOR, a deep-learning vision-language foundation model for oncologic chest-abdomen-pelvis (CAP) CT interpretation. Materials & Methods : CAPTOR (Chest-Abdomen-Pelvis foundaTion model for Oncologic Radiology) is a contrastive vision-language model, trained using a pretraining strategy for oncologic CAP CT (in single- or multiple-series acquisitions), on a multicenter retrospective dataset from North America, Europe and Asia, predominantly from tumor lesion examinations. CAPTOR was compared with state-of-the-art CT foundation models on three downstream tasks: disease detection, survival prediction using TumorImagingBench and image retrieval. Classification and retrieval were both evaluated on held-out internal and public test sets, stratified by anatomical coverage and indication. Bootstrap resampling was used to estimate confidence intervals, and pairwise comparisons were performed using permutation tests. Results : CAPTOR was trained and tested on 25,512 and 10,794 CT-report pairs respectively. TumorImagingBench datasets comprised between 134 and 421 studies each. CAPTOR outperformed all baseline models, on the classification task, on the CAP subset (AUC 0.767, 95%CI: 0.734-0.793, vs. 0.695, 95%CI: 0.645-0.736 for the next-best, p<0.001) and oncologic subset (AUC 0.784, 95%CI: 0.759-0.805, vs. 0.734, 95%CI: 0.703-0.767 p<0.001), ranked first on three of the four oncologic prognostic benchmarks, and achieved superior retrieval performance on CAP and oncologic subsets. Conclusion : A foundation model trained on oncology-enriched CAP CT data outperformed relevant state-of-the-art models in its target clinical context, underscoring the importance of clinically aligned pretraining. We release our preprocessing, training and inference code : https://github.com/Guerbet-AI/CAPTOR and model weights : https://huggingface.co/Guerbet-AI/CAPTOR

Preprocessing, training, inference code, and model weights are publicly released.

papers.abstract: Softmax attention in Transformers suffers from quadratic complexity in sequence length, making it impractical for long-context applications. Linear attention alleviates this issue by replacing the exponential kernel with alternative functions that enable linear-time computation. Among existing linear attention approaches, recent studies have shown that polynomial kernels are particularly effective, as they exhibit sparse and spiky behavior similar to softmax attention, which emphasizes large dot products while suppressing irrelevant interactions. However, the exact computation of high-degree polynomial kernels is infeasible for high-dimensional representations. As a result, prior work relies on approximate polynomial kernels. This introduces a non-negligible approximation error. In this paper, we show that, from the perspective of polynomial kernel approximation, existing linear attention methods are still suboptimal. We propose \textbf{L}earnable \textbf{Lo}w-Rank \textbf{P}olynomial \textbf{S}ketch (LLoPS), a principled and flexible framework for approximating polynomial kernels with linear attention. Our method learns a low-rank polynomial sketch that provably achieves a strictly smaller approximation error than existing approaches. Experiment results show that LLoPS achieves the highest performance across extensive benchmarks, comparing with various linear attention baselines.
authors: Zongyue Qin, Haoran Deng, Jason Cong, Yizhou Sun
bullets: Softmax attention has quadratic sequence-length complexity, limiting long-context use.
Polynomial kernels can mimic softmax’s sparse, spiky attention patterns but are costly to compute exactly in high dimensions.
LLoPS learns a low-rank polynomial sketch to reduce approximation error in linear attention.
The framework is theoretically shown to outperform existing polynomial-kernel approximation methods in error.
Across extensive benchmarks, LLoPS achieves the best performance among the compared linear-attention baselines.

papers.abstract: ScanRefer Multiple queries require spatial disambiguation: several instances of the target class are present, and the referencer must pick one. When per-query logits were never logged, a common substitute is cross-epoch agreement. On the full ScanRefer validation set (9,508 queries; GeoClassifier with ground-truth proposals), object-level softmax is similarly miscalibrated on Unique and Multiple (ECE 0.068 vs. 0.102; the scene-bootstrap gap interval includes zero). Fixed-final agreement on the same checkpoints reports ECE 0.041 vs. 0.272 (gap +0.231). Modal-vote agreement is 0.045 vs. 0.318. Most Multiple errors are same-class wrong-instance (45.6%); geometric miss (H2) is 59.6%, and wrong-category (H1) is 16.7%. A non-monotone H1 pattern does not appear under the default fixed-final protocol, and we retract it. Logit-free thresholds rank spatially hard queries poorly. If only agreement was logged, calibrate abstention on Multiple and report wrong-instance rates with H1.
authors: Micha{\l} Zakrzewski, Mariia Shpir, Taras Rumezhak, Volodymyr Karpiv
bullets: The study evaluates 9,508 ScanRefer validation queries using a GeoClassifier with ground-truth proposals.

Most Multiple errors select the wrong instance of the correct class (45.6%); geometric misses account for 59.6% and wrong-category errors for 16.7%.
Logit-free agreement thresholds rank spatially difficult queries poorly, and the previously suggested non-monotone H1 pattern is retracted under the default protocol.
When only agreement is available, the abstract recommends calibrating abstention specifically on Multiple queries and reporting wrong-instance rates alongside H1 errors.

papers.abstract: Under a fixed context budget, which objects and relations should a 3D scene-grounded VLM see first? On ScanNet indoor referring benchmarks (Dai et al., 2017), matching the query to object category names outperforms pairwise geometry scoring at every reported K. The gaps are largest at high recall. Analytic pairwise cues beat per-object cue scoring and query-agnostic kNN graphs, including on paraphrases. MiniLM and BGE-small still score higher on those splits. We evaluate token-budgeted candidate retrieval with axis-aligned boxes, a token-ratio metric, training-free baselines, two small encoders that match q to each object's category name, and QCRR (Query-Conditioned Relation Retrieval), a deterministic pairwise-geometry scorer. Across ScanRefer gt_val plus a custom 20% scan-id split of Nr3D and Sr3D (35,504 queries; not official ReferIt3D val), additive noun matching reaches R@10 0.864 on ScanRefer against QCRR's 0.626; MiniLM and BGE-small reach 0.911 to 0.913 on ScanRefer and 0.941 to 0.947 on Nr3D. A corrected 3DGraphLLM harness (native Acc@0.25 0.67 on the full graph, n=300 ScanRefer queries) shows that context selection changes downstream accuracy under a matched object budget (Random 0.44, QCRR 0.56, MiniLM 0.67, oracle 0.70). Semantic retrieval beats hand-designed geometry on that harness. We will release the protocol, retriever implementations, and per-query outputs so new selectors can be swapped in without rewriting the analysis.
authors: Micha{\l} Zakrzewski, Mariia Shpir, Taras Rumezhak

Semantic retrieval also performs better on Nr3D and Sr3D splits, including paraphrased queries.
In a corrected 3DGraphLLM harness, downstream Acc@0.25 is 0.67 with MiniLM, versus 0.56 with QCRR and 0.44 with random selection.
The evaluation uses custom splits and a limited harness; results are scoped to the reported ScanNet-based benchmarks and budgets.

papers.abstract: We introduce ClothCode, a unified generative framework for garment state estimation and action-conditioned dynamics prediction in a shared discrete configuration space. A material-aligned tokenizer encodes garment configuration as residual vector-quantized patch tokens, while task-specific Masked Generative Transformers predict these tokens through parallel confidence-guided refinement. Across three garment templates, ClothCode reduces mean displacement error by 26.6% for state estimation and 37.0% for dynamics prediction relative to the strongest baselines. Dynamics prediction requires only 16.7 ms per window, compared with 556.2 ms for diffusion. Integrated into the same model-predictive controller, ClothCode improves real-world folding and flattening success from 56.7% to 78.9%. Further results and videos are available at: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/ClothCode-DE32
authors: Yingdong Ru, Lipeng Zhuang, Shiyu Fan, Zhuo He, Florent P. Audonnet, Gerardo Aragon Camarasa
bullets: Uses a material-aligned tokenizer with residual vector-quantized patch tokens to represent garment configurations in a shared discrete space.
Applies task-specific Masked Generative Transformers with parallel confidence-guided refinement for state estimation and dynamics prediction.
Across three garment templates, reduces mean displacement error by 26.6% for state estimation and 37.0% for dynamics prediction versus the strongest baselines.
Predicts dynamics in 16.7 ms per window, compared with 556.2 ms for diffusion.
With the same model-predictive controller, raises real-world folding and flattening success from 56.7% to 78.9%.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Overview of our discrete generative framework for model-based garment manipulation. A garment configuration is encoded as a set of discrete patch tokens shared by two Masked Generative Transformers (MGTs). (1) The discrete garment representation captures local deformation states over fixed material patches. (2) For state estimation, an MGT iteratively predicts the complete token configuration from a partial point cloud. (3) For dynamics prediction, an action-conditioned MGT predicts future garment configurations for candidate actions, allowing MPC to select the trajectory with the lowest goal cost. (4) The resulting perception–prediction loop enables closed-loop garment manipulation on a real robot.

papers.abstract: Forecasting tissue deformation from future instrument motion could support predictive planning and increasingly autonomous surgical systems. We study this problem using a scene-specific differentiable surface model fitted to an observed tool-tissue interaction window. Rather than forecasting absolute simulated positions, we introduce an \textit{observation-referenced} formulation that anchors each tissue point to its last valid observation and adds only the deformation induced by the known, preplanned future tool trajectory. This reduces sensitivity to reconstruction, initialization, and persistent simulation offsets while preserving the predicted deformation response. The physical model uses differentiable, mesh-free position-based dynamics with scene-specific rigidity, attachment, region scale, and grasp coupling. We further introduce an optional \textit{observation-referenced residual model} combining graph-spectral spatial modes with periodic harmonic dynamics for structured motion not explained by the tool input. We evaluate the framework retrospectively on 12 surgical manipulation clips from three datasets. Observation referencing provides the largest gain, with a median within-clip error ratio of $0.598$ relative to the corresponding absolute simulation forecast. The optional periodic residual further improves forecasting when the remaining motion exhibits periodic structure. These results support observation-referenced deformation prediction as a practical building block for future surgical world models, digital twins, and generative simulators that must predict how tissue evolves under instrument actions.

bullets: Addresses tissue deformation forecasting from known future instrument motion for predictive and autonomous surgery.

Anchors each tissue point to its last valid observation, reducing sensitivity to reconstruction, initialization, and persistent simulation offsets.
Optionally adds graph-spectral spatial modes and periodic harmonic dynamics to capture motion not explained by tool input.
Evaluated on 12 clips from three datasets; observation referencing achieved a median within-clip error ratio of 0.598 versus absolute simulation, while periodic residuals helped for periodic motion.

papers.abstract: Explaining a vision--language model (VLM) prediction requires tracing training-example influence to the multimodal evidence that mediates it, yet existing attribution methods largely operate only at the sample level. Recent latent-mediated influence methods provide feature-level attribution in language models, but lack the multimodal and spatial structure needed to ground influence in VLMs. We introduce MOSAIC (Multimodal Orthogonalized Sparse Autoencoders for Influence Characterization). It learns a shared sparse image--text latent space whose concepts are 1) sparse within each modality, 2) supported on contiguous image regions, 3) aligned to the phrases that describe them, and 4) approximately decorrelated. It then applies EK-FAC to decompose training-example influence through these concepts and localize their contributions to specific text phrases and image regions. We evaluate MOSAIC on Qwen and Gemma across captioning, chest X-ray understanding, and visual question answering. The learned features are more localized and coherent without degrading task behavior, and ablating influence-ranked latents changes model outputs more than ablating latents ranked by activation or frequency. We find that visual evidence can substantially reorganize training-data attribution while preserving more of the shared latent structure. MOSAIC thus connects where model behavior comes from with what multimodal evidence carries that influence.
authors: Laura Yao, Shixing Yu, Jie Peng, Promit Ghosal, Kyra Gan, Tianlong Chen

papers.abstract: Could model-free reinforcement learning algorithms actually be learning a model of the environment? In this work, we apply counterfactual interventions which hold everything about a state fixed, besides a targeted change, to explore if the value function of a Proximal Policy Optimization agent forms a world model of the Crafter environment. Despite only being trained to optimize reward, we discover that the value function learns concepts such as the rules governing when a diamond is collectible, water and food having an impact on health, heuristics regarding inventory, and more. Finally, we discuss the safety implications of our visualizations and some shortcomings of current reinforcement learning agents that will prevent us from building truly advanced machine intelligence.
authors: Shawheen Naderi, Fatemeh Akherati, Yubei Chen
bullets: Investigates whether model-free RL implicitly learns an environment model.
Uses counterfactual interventions that change one targeted state feature while holding others fixed.
Finds representations of diamond collectibility, health effects of water and food, inventory-related heuristics, and other concepts.
Discusses safety implications of interpreting value-function visualizations.
Highlights limitations of current RL agents for achieving advanced machine intelligence.

papers.abstract: Studying model training requires checkpoint trajectories, whose storage cost limits temporal resolution. Although adjacent checkpoints are numerically close, existing lossless codecs either operate on XOR bit patterns or ignore trajectory-specific conditional structure. We show that a reference weight's exponent predicts the bit length of its displacement in ordered floating-point space without side information. We introduce \textbf{ULPack}, a lossless codec which exploits this dependence by conditioning entropy models of ordered-integer residuals on the reference exponent. Across bfloat16, float16, and float32 trajectories, ULPack reduces storage by up to 27\% against ZipNN, 21\% against zstd-19, and 11.5\% against FM-Delta. Across two dense trajectories, compression improves as updates shrink and reference conditioning strengthens, while near uniform low-order bits set the remaining compression floor and earlier checkpoints add little information.
authors: Aniket Srinivasan Ashok (University of Waterloo)
bullets: Checkpoint trajectories are storage-intensive despite adjacent checkpoints being numerically close.

papers.abstract: Digital libraries increasingly host scientific publications whose figures encode primary research findings, yet making this visual content searchable, accessible, and reusable remains an open challenge. Large language and multimodal models (LLMs/LMMs) provide the possibility to automate many figure parsing tasks such as determining data trends or extracting data from plots. In this work, we consider if these models can reliably support task-oriented visual data analysis when presented with synthetic, but realistic, scientific figures that contain multiple charts. Our Visual Question Answering (VQA) process scaffolds our tasks along a four-level description model from basic conceptual answers to interpretive and analytical understanding. Additionally, we outline our process for synthetically generating our single and multi-panel (charts in which there are multiple panels present) plots and testing the data with various LMMs using quantitative analysis. In general, we find LMMs become less accurate with increasing figure complexity as the number of panels, number of plot elements, and difficulty of questions increase. Finally, because LMM accuracy is expected to change rapidly, our analysis also considers cost relative to performance as a metric to inform future user decisions. We provide the detailed question-answer pairs used in this analysis, along with the code used to generate random plots, question-answer pairs and detailed bounding-box metadata for chart elements. The code and data are available at https://github.com/ReadingTimeMachine/LLM_VQA_MultiPanel and https://huggingface.co/datasets/ReadingTimeMachine/visual\_qa\_multipanel
authors: Daniel J. Evans, J. P. Naiman, JooYoung Seo, J. Stephen Downie
bullets: Introduces a multi-panel chart VQA benchmark organized into four levels, from basic descriptions to interpretive and analytical questions.
Generates synthetic but realistic scientific plots, question–answer pairs, and bounding-box metadata for chart elements.
Evaluates multiple LMMs quantitatively while considering both accuracy and cost.
Finds performance generally worsens with more panels, plot elements, and difficult questions.
Releases the benchmark data and plot-generation code publicly.

papers.abstract: Diffusion language models (DLMs) offer parallel sampling for faster generation than autoregressive models, an increasingly important advantage as inference becomes a dominant computational workload. However, DLMs degrade quickly with fewer sampling steps, process the full sequence at every step, and require many passes over the dataset to reach good quality. We introduce Next-Concept Modeling (NCM), a two-stage, coarse-to-fine framework: a multiscale residual VQ-VAE encodes text into a hierarchy of discrete codes, and a transformer generates one level at a time, predicting all codes within a level in parallel. At matched parameter scales, NCM achieves better generative perplexity than the strongest DLM baseline on LM1B while running $21\times$ faster. On OpenWebText, NCM is competitive with the strongest DLM while running $10\times$ faster; on XSum, it matches the strongest DLM's ROUGE-L while being $31\times$ faster. On the reasoning task of Sudoku, NCM outperforms autoregressive and diffusion baselines across all difficulty levels, using fewer function evaluations. On the reasoning task of Sudoku, NCM outperforms autoregressive and diffusion baselines across all difficulty levels, using fewer function evaluations.
authors: Hermann Kumbong, Ishan S. Khare, Iddah Mlauzi, Andrew Woen, Charles Ding, E. Kelly Buchanan, Simran Arora, Azalia Mirhoseini, Christopher R\'e
bullets: Addresses diffusion language models’ slow sampling, full-sequence processing, and training inefficiency at few sampling steps.
Uses a multiscale residual VQ-VAE to encode text into hierarchical discrete codes.
A transformer predicts all codes within each hierarchy level in parallel.
Reports faster generation than diffusion baselines across LM1B, OpenWebText, and XSum while maintaining or improving quality.
Outperforms autoregressive and diffusion baselines on Sudoku reasoning across difficulty levels with fewer function evaluations.

papers.abstract: Reward design remains a major bottleneck for reinforcement learning in robotic manipulation. Handcrafted dense rewards can compensate for the limited guidance provided by sparse rewards, but require substantial task-specific reward engineering. Learning rewards from videos provides a scalable, data-driven alternative to manual reward design. However, existing video-based rewards are often computed in entangled visual spaces where task-relevant state changes are confounded with extraneous visual variation. As a result, the learned reward may respond to visual distractors instead of actual task execution. To address this limitation, we propose DiTaR (Disentangling Task-Relevant Latent Dynamics for Reward Modeling), a framework for learning dense rewards from heterogeneous videos. DiTaR learns a continuous task-relevant representation from multi-frame video latents through an asymmetric two-stage procedure that suppresses task-irrelevant visual variation. In the task-relevant latent space, we train a history- and language-conditioned rectified-flow model to capture task dynamics and derive a directional dense reward from temporal changes in dynamics compatibility. Together, these components enable reward modeling directly over task-relevant dynamics rather than generic visual variation. DiTaR substantially improves policy learning on MetaWorld-v3 and ManiSkill over video-based reward baselines, and transfers to real-world offline RL through reward relabeling. Reward analyses further show that DiTaR provides more reliable rewards.

papers.abstract: Understanding and tracking a dynamic world are fundamental to visual intelligence. Existing video benchmarks provide limited insight into whether models can maintain a coherent understanding of evolving world state. Building such a benchmark from real-world videos is challenging because the underlying world state is partially observable, making annotations hard to obtain. To close this gap, we introduce Video-Arena, a benchmark that turns competitive games into scalable, verifiable tests of how well models understand evolving world states from videos. Specifically, inspired by how humans understand dynamic events, we evaluate spatiotemporal world state understanding and tracking through three task categories: perceiving critical events, interpreting state updates, and tracking the resulting states. Our pipeline can generate videos and aligned reference labels from game records at scale. To keep evaluation affordable and reproducible, we curate a golden set of 180 tasks across 9 games and run evaluations under two protocols: native visual understanding and tool-assisted agentic analysis. The best-performing systems achieve F1 scores of and under the two protocols, respectively. The result highlights that native models struggle to perceive events reliably, while tool-assisted systems improve event recovery but still struggle to interpret state updates and track the resulting states consistently over time. Our project page is in https://videoarena-bench.github.io

papers.abstract: Classifier-free guidance (CFG) typically applies a shared scale to all latent tokens, although their velocity predictions evolve differently during sampling. We introduce Trajectory-Adaptive Classifier-Free Guidance (TrajCFG), a training-free method for flow-matching models that adapts token-wise guidance using historical changes in guided velocity direction. TrajCFG maps this feedback to bounded scales, assigning stronger guidance to larger directional changes and weaker guidance to more consistent directions. It combines adjacent-step and interval-normalized longer-span feedback, reusing standard CFG predictions without additional model evaluations. Controlled diagnostics and ablations examine the roles of directional feedback, token-wise allocation, and history-span fusion. Experiments on text-to-video, image-to-video, text-to-audio-video, text-to-image, and image-to-3D generation show improvements over base samplers across multiple backbones. For text-to-video generation, TrajCFG improves VBench Total scores by 0.30-0.75 points over the strongest evaluated baseline on each of three backbones. These results support historical directional feedback as a broadly applicable signal for fine-grained guidance allocation. The project page is available at https://jyliu-98.github.io/trajcfg-project-page/.

papers.abstract: Deformable-object manipulation requires accurate modeling of highly localized contact while maintaining simulation speeds suitable for interactive use. Uniformly fine tetrahedral meshes can resolve these interactions, but they introduce unnecessary degrees of freedom throughout the object. Coarse meshes are more efficient, yet they may under-resolve contact-induced deformation. We present a contact-adaptive mesh refinement framework that introduces spatial resolution only where it is most useful. The method uses geometric, elastic, and contact quantities already available from the deformable-body solver to score candidate edges. A fully GPU-parallel procedure then selects a conflict-free subset and updates both mesh topology and physical state directly within the simulation loop. We evaluate the approach on real deformable-object manipulation sequences. Adaptive refinement reduces simulation-to-real error, improves agreement with a fine-mesh reference, and remains substantially more efficient than uniformly fine simulation. These results show that local refinement can improve physical fidelity without incurring the cost of a globally fine discretization. The framework provides a practical basis for contact-rich simulation in interactive manipulation, sim-to-real modeling, and online physical digital twins.
authors: Gabriel Johnson, Tom Olesch, Fei Liu
bullets: Targets the trade-off between accurate contact deformation and interactive simulation speed.
Scores candidate edges using geometric, elastic, and contact information from the deformable-body solver.
Selects conflict-free refinements and updates mesh topology and physical state within the simulation loop.

Supports contact-rich simulation, sim-to-real modeling, and online physical digital twins.

papers.abstract: Image-level MRI harmonization is often evaluated with a frozen site probe, a site classifier trained on raw scans and applied unchanged to harmonized ones: a drop in its accuracy is read as removal of site effects. We audit this practice on ABIDE I (1,112 T1-weighted scans, 17 sites) with ten output sets from seven harmonization methods and controls for chance, head shape, intensity, preprocessing and target alignment. We find that this verdict depends on how the probe is trained, even among probes that classify raw scans well: across random seeds, its balanced accuracy on the same CycleGAN outputs ranges from 0.13 to 0.59 (chance: 0.06). Low frozen-probe accuracy can also arise without harmonization: a Gaussian blur, which increases the intensity distance to the target site, lowers this accuracy to chance. Moreover, where the frozen probe fails, probes trained on the harmonized scans still recover the site, even from intensity histograms alone: on HACA3 outputs, the frozen probe scores 0.25, a probe trained on those outputs 0.75, and one using only their intensity histograms 0.71. Low frozen-probe accuracy therefore does not show that site information has been removed. We recommend reporting several probes trained to convergence, probes trained on harmonized scans, and target alignment.
authors: Muhammad Muqsit Islam, Gloria Garc\'ia Cuenco, Jos\'e M. Mart\'inez, Pierrick Coup\'e
bullets: The audit examines ten harmonized output sets from seven methods on ABIDE I MRI scans, with controls for chance, image properties, preprocessing, and target alignment.
Frozen-probe balanced accuracy varies widely across random seeds on identical outputs, despite strong raw-scan classification performance.
Non-harmonizing changes such as Gaussian blur can reduce frozen-probe accuracy to chance while increasing mismatch with the target site.
Site information can remain recoverable from harmonized scans, including from intensity histograms, even when the frozen probe performs poorly.
The authors recommend multiple converged probes, probes retrained on harmonized outputs, and explicit target-alignment reporting.

papers.abstract: The rapid advancement of Large Language Models (LLMs) has driven their deployment toward general-purpose harness environments, where LLM-based agents operate in sandbox workspaces and interact directly with file systems and shells. While numerous post-training pipelines exist for tool-use agents, their counterparts for harness-based agents remain scarce and are predominantly one-shot and teacher-dependent: a stronger external model synthesizes tasks and collects trajectories, the target agent is trained once, and evaluation results are consumed by human researchers rather than fed back into the loop. Such pipelines are inherently bounded by the capability of the external model and the scope of human prior, leaving no room for self-improvement. To address these limitations, we propose ClawLoop, a framework that enables self-improving without any external teacher model and with minimal prior dependencies. ClawLoop composes three phases into a self-sustaining cycle: Task Synthesis, which generates a diverse pool of training tasks via two complementary construction routines, applies diagnosis-conditioned difficulty growth followed by both agent-free and agent-based task validation; Training, which updates the agent via SFT and/or RL; and Diagnosis and Feedback, which analyzes the agent's rollout behaviors to produce a capability analysis report that will be used as feedback for task synthesis in the next iteration. Using Qwen3.6-27B as the loop model, ClawLoop yields consistent improvements on SkillsBench, Claw-Eval-Live, and ClawGym-Bench. The iteratively refined tasks are further transferred to smaller-scale Qwen3.5-4B and 9B models with gains across all benchmarks, validating data quality independently of the loop model.
authors: Hansi Yang, Linji Hao, Hongyan Hao, An Wang, Han Wu, Qi Gu, Xunliang Cai
bullets: Addresses one-shot, teacher-dependent training pipelines for agents operating in sandbox workspaces with filesystems and shells.
Combines task synthesis, SFT and/or RL training, and diagnosis-driven feedback into an iterative loop.
Uses difficulty growth and agent-free plus agent-based validation to refine generated tasks.
With Qwen3.6-27B as the loop model, reports consistent improvements across SkillsBench, Claw-Eval-Live, and ClawGym-Bench.
Tasks refined by the loop transfer to smaller Qwen3.5-4B and 9B models, with gains across all reported benchmarks.

papers.abstract: GPT-6 Astra provides robust embodied reasoning, but frequent external queries increase inference time and token costs. We equip a frozen $\pi_{0.5}$ policy with a lightweight CALL head that learns to predict when assistance is necessary. CALL reuses features from the standard policy forward pass and operates locally without consulting external models. Astra is activated solely for critical recovery events and returns control to $\pi_{0.5}$ upon stabilization. Evaluated across 40 LIBERO tasks (200 episodes), our system achieves a 97.5% success rate, outperforming the 95.5% baseline of pure $\pi_{0.5}$. In the Object, Goal, and Spatial suites, Astra executes only 5.49% of environment steps, consuming approximately 5,027 tokens per test episode. This selective intervention preserves the fast ordinary execution of $\pi_{0.5}$ while seamlessly integrating Astra's reasoning on demand. Our project page is available at https://kykgeek.github.io/Pi05_CALL_Astra/.
authors: Jianli Sun, Chengxiang Li, Yonglin Tian
bullets: Targets the latency and token overhead caused by frequent external model queries.
CALL reuses standard π0.5 features to predict when assistance is necessary and runs locally.
Astra intervenes during critical recovery events, then returns control to π0.5 after stabilization.

papers.abstract: Large language models can translate natural-language instructions into plausible manipulation plans, but robotic execution requires physically grounded decisions that respect robot embodiment, workspace geometry, reachability, collision constraints, and grasp feasibility. This paper presents a hardware-aware large language model-vision-language model (LLM-VLM) manipulation framework for a simulated Franka Research 3 robot in NVIDIA Isaac Sim. The framework separates symbolic reasoning from metric execution: an API-hosted LLM planner receives a structured scene summary and generates only symbolic task information, including the object to manipulate, target relation, approach preference, and objects to avoid. A local Qwen3-VL 8B VLM verifier supports semantic confirmation of ambiguous objects and open-container surrogates. Both the LLM planner and the VLM verifier are prohibited from generating robot coordinates, grasp poses, keepout dimensions, gripper commands, trajectory waypoints, or success labels. Instead, these decisions are handled by deterministic grounding and execution modules that use the robot model, scene geometry, MoveIt 2 collision checking, inverse kinematics, grasp validation, release verification, and final visual assessment. Execution feedback is returned only as symbolic context for replanning. The framework is evaluated through simulated digital-twin trials involving pickup, occluded-source access, keepout reasoning, relation placement, and sequential manipulation tasks.
authors: Lonnie Tankersley, Noorbakhsh Amiri Golilarz, Soroush Korivand
bullets: Addresses the gap between plausible language-generated plans and physically feasible robot execution.
An API-hosted LLM produces symbolic task information, while a local Qwen3-VL verifier resolves ambiguous objects and container surrogates.
Deterministic modules handle scene grounding, reachability, collision checking, inverse kinematics, grasping, release verification, and visual assessment.
The system uses symbolic execution feedback for replanning without allowing the LLM or VLM to generate robot motions or coordinates.
Evaluated in NVIDIA Isaac Sim with a simulated Franka Research 3 across pickup, occlusion, keepout, relational placement, and sequential manipulation tasks.

papers.abstract: Accurate artery extraction from X-ray coronary angiography (XCA) is essential for coronary artery disease diagnosis and intervention. However, low vessel visibility, respiratory and cardiac motion, and limited annotations challenge existing methods. Moreover, most deep learning approaches produce binary vessel masks without preserving clinically relevant intra-arterial contrast information. We propose a Temporal Diffusion Bridge Model (TDBM) that formulates vessel extraction as image translation and learns from physics-informed synthetic data without manual vessel annotations. A physics-based XCA synthesis engine generates diverse, perfectly aligned pairs of contrast-enhanced and contrast-free images. Using these pairs, TDBM learns cross-domain mappings to recover high-fidelity vessel information. Temporal conditioning incorporates adjacent frames to improve consistency, while a vessel-aware contrastive loss exploits background-invariant synthetic pairs to enhance vascular discrimination. We evaluate TDBM on two XCA vessel segmentation datasets and conduct a reader study using two real-patient XCA sequence datasets. Zero-shot segmentation is further assessed on retinal imaging and fluorescence microscopy datasets. Results demonstrate that TDBM consistently outperforms existing methods and generalizes effectively across imaging modalities. Code and trained weights will be available at: https://github.com/Advanced-AI-in-Medicine-and-Physics-Lab/TDBM
authors: Jinkui Hao, Donald R. Cantrell, Ramez Abdalla, Sameer A. Ansari, Bo Zhou
bullets: Addresses poor vessel visibility, cardiac and respiratory motion, and limited annotated XCA data.
Generates aligned contrast-enhanced/contrast-free image pairs with a physics-based synthesis engine.
Uses temporal conditioning and vessel-aware contrastive learning to improve consistency and vascular discrimination.
Evaluated on XCA segmentation, real-patient sequence reader studies, and zero-shot retinal and fluorescence microscopy tasks.
Reports consistent improvements over existing methods and effective cross-modality generalization, without specifying numeric results.

papers.abstract: Sparse-view cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) is severely under-constrained by limited X-ray projections. Learned reconstruction can provide complementary anatomical information, but using it as a prior in patient-specific Gaussian reconstruction introduces two challenges. First, the discrepancy between the learned prior and current reconstruction is spatially non-uniform: some local differences contain useful missing 3D information, whereas others reflect prior bias. Second, even a volumetrically beneficial correction can conflict with the observed X-ray measurements. Since X-ray measurements are line integrals, spatially separated corrections may affect overlapping rays, with their signed projection responses reinforcing or partially canceling in the measurement residual, so their feasibility cannot always be assessed independently. In this paper, we introduce RePrior, a multi-stage progressive prior-correction framework that addresses correction actionability, measurement feasibility, and representation expressivity. Selective Correction Proposal (SCP) first identifies actionable signed local corrections from prior--reconstruction discrepancies. Measurement-Constrained Reconciliation (MCR) then jointly enforces their consistency with patient-specific X-ray measurements, while Hybrid Residual Enhancement (HRE) recovers additional correction capacity through complementary voxel- and Gaussian-domain degrees of freedom around the reconciled anchor. RePrior requires neither test-time ground truth nor case-specific network fine-tuning. RePrior gains approximately 2.6~dB in 3D PSNR over R$^2$-Gaussian across LUNA16, PANORAMA, and PENGWIN. Beyond prior-assisted reconstruction, it delivers additional gains in volumetric quality and observed-view projection fidelity, with consistent gains in held-out-view fidelity in the backbone-matched evaluation.
authors: Mengrui Yin, Tianxingjian Ding, Wufan Zhao, Ziyang Yan, Yu Tian
bullets: Addresses spatially varying prior bias and conflicts between volumetric corrections and overlapping-ray measurements.
Uses three stages: Selective Correction Proposal, Measurement-Constrained Reconciliation, and Hybrid Residual Enhancement.
Requires neither test-time ground truth nor case-specific network fine-tuning.
Reports approximately 2.6 dB higher 3D PSNR than R²-Gaussian across LUNA16, PANORAMA, and PENGWIN.
Also improves volumetric quality, observed-view projection fidelity, and—under backbone-matched evaluation—held-out-view fidelity.

papers.abstract: Existing jailbreak attacks have exposed serious safety weaknesses in multimodal large language models (MLLMs). Most prior attacks rely on specially constructed visual inputs to carry or support harmful intent. In this paper, we uncover a different vulnerability: task-relevant scene semantics alone can shift an MLLM from refusal to compliance, even when the visual input introduces no additional attack instructions and the original task intent remains unchanged. We formalize this failure as a scene-grounded visual safety vulnerability and introduce SceneSafetyBench to investigate it across eight risk categories and nine white- and black-box MLLMs. Our analysis reveals that this failure is associated with how task-relevant visual evidence influences downstream safety representations, suggesting that visual grounding alone cannot fully explain the observed safety shift. Building on this finding, we propose Scene-Grounded Attacks (SGA), which preserve the original task while constructing validated scene-grounded queries and combining their independent responses. Across nine target MLLMs, SGA achieves an average attack success rate (ASR) of 86.17%, outperforming the strongest baseline by 8.55 percentage points and achieving the highest ASR on eight models. Our results identify scene semantics as an overlooked attack surface in MLLMs and highlight a growing tension between stronger visual grounding and robust multimodal safety alignment.
authors: Tongxi Wu, Yuyang Cheng, Jiacheng Xian, Hu Huang, Zhihao Wu, Menglin Yang, Jian Zhang, Yang Gao
bullets: Identifies a scene-grounded visual safety vulnerability: task-relevant visual content can shift safety behavior without adding attack instructions or changing task intent.
Introduces SceneSafetyBench, covering eight risk categories and nine white- and black-box MLLMs.
Finds that task-relevant visual evidence affects downstream safety representations beyond what visual grounding alone explains.
Proposes Scene-Grounded Attacks (SGA), which preserve the original task and combine responses from validated scene-grounded queries.
SGA reaches an average 86.17% attack success rate, exceeding the strongest baseline by 8.55 percentage points and achieving the highest ASR on eight models.

figures.caption: Figure 4: Overview of the scene-grounded attack (SGA) pipeline. A proxy model specifies and validates the required visual evidence, while an image generator instantiates and iteratively refines the corresponding scenes. Uncovered semantic requirements are supplemented before the target model processes each validated image–question pair independently. The resulting local responses are then synthesized and evaluated against the original task.

papers.abstract: Training on broad, unfiltered data enables high-quality image generation, but can also teach models concepts that should not be generated; restricting the training data ensures safety, but reduces quality because examples containing unsafe concepts also provide useful knowledge that is not itself unsafe. Existing approaches largely address this trade-off post hoc through concept unlearning, which can lead to catastrophic forgetting as the number of concepts to remove grows. We instead ask whether unsafe concept knowledge can be compartmentalized during pretraining so that access to it can be disabled at inference. We introduce Pristine Models, a novel text-to-image generation architecture with an attention mechanism that encourages the separation of safe and unsafe knowledge into independently parameterized branches. The branch-specific parameters are learned during training, while the unsafe branch can be detached at inference. On ImageNet, Pristine Models enable safer generation while retaining much of the utility of full-data pretraining, achieving higher image quality and better text alignment than training only on safe data or applying post-hoc concept removal. We further scale our approach to CC12M, demonstrating that it remains effective in a substantially larger and more diverse open-world pretraining setting.
authors: Anirudh Sundara Rajan, Krishna Kumar Singh, Richard Zhang, Yong Jae Lee
bullets: Motivation: filtering unsafe concepts from training data can reduce useful visual knowledge, while post-hoc unlearning may cause increasing catastrophic forgetting.
Method: an attention-based architecture learns safe and unsafe knowledge in independently parameterized branches during pretraining.
At inference, the unsafe branch can be detached to restrict generation of unsafe concepts.
On ImageNet, the approach retains more utility than safe-only training or post-hoc concept removal, with higher image quality and better text alignment.
The method also remains effective when scaled to the larger, more diverse CC12M dataset.

figures.caption: Figure 8: Improved quality on safe generations. Across diverse prompts from DPG-Bench and PRISM-Bench, the Safe model often struggles with counting, compositionality, and imaginative details, while our Pristine model generates them more faithfully. The Full model is shown as a reference for the highest achievable generation quality.

Figure 14: Pristine Self-Attention. For MMDiT-style architectures, each active branch jointly updates its text and spatial tokens. Spatial updates are combined into the shared representation, while text states remain branch-specific.

Figure 6: CC12M generations. Left: on unsafe prompts, Full (Wang et al., 2026b) produces the requested concept while Safe and Pristine suppress it. Right: on safe concepts, Pristine matches Full’s generation quality. Prompts are truncated for readability; all generations use the full prompts. More examples can be found in Appendix A.1.

Across a diverse set of designated unsafe concepts, the Full model (Wang et al., 2026b) readily generates the requested concept, whereas our Pristine model successfully and consistently fails to reproduce it, instead generating semantically related but safe alternatives. The Safe model is shown for reference, trained without the corresponding unsafe data.

Figure 2: Goal. The Full Model (Wang et al., 2026b), trained on both safe and unsafe data, generates high-quality images but can reproduce restricted concepts such as SpongeBob; the Safe Model, trained only on safe data, avoids them at the cost of useful visual knowledge, here reflected in incorrect gift-wrap placement. Pristine aims to retain the useful information learned from unsafe data while isolating restricted concept-specific knowledge in a detachable branch, achieving safe generation without sacrificing quality.

Figure 12: Qualitative compartmentalization of designated unsafe concepts. Across diverse unsafe prompts, the Pristine safe branch suppresses the requested concept, while activating the unsafe branch restores it, suggesting that the unsafe branch has specialized to generating the restricted content as intended. The Full and Safe models are shown for reference.
Figure 10: On unsafe prompts (“coffeepot”, “daisy”), Pristine suppresses the requested concepts, whereas MLPSwap reproduces them more faithfully, consistent with its higher unsafe-concept leakage.

Each model is prompted with descriptions that semantically evoke an unsafe class without naming it (e.g., “a bright orange, faceted vessel” for a coffee pot, “a bright green reptile” for a snake). The Full baseline generates the concept from these implicit cues, confirming the prompts are sufficient to elicit it; the Safe baseline, trained without the unsafe data, cannot; and our Pristine, though trained on that data, also does not— falling back to a safe concept (a dog). Removal therefore generalizes beyond prompts that contain the exact class name.
Figure 4: Given a safe prompt (“gray fox”), the safe branch succeeds while the unsafe branch fails; on the unsafe prompt (“garbage truck”), the pattern reverses, which is the intended behavior.

Figure 1: An image is rarely unsafe in its entirety. A single image can entangle an unsafe concept that we wish to suppress at generation time, here a firearm, with safe, broadly useful properties like lighting, shadows, camera angle, and object interactions.

Figure 13: Given a safe prompt (“electric guitar”), our Pristine safe branch succeeds while the unsafe branch fails; on the unsafe prompt (“cauliflower”), the pattern reverses, which is the intended behavior. The Safe baseline struggles to generate the safe “electric guitar” well.
Figure 11: On safe prompts, Pristine preserves the requested dog breed, while AttentionSwap often drifts to a different breed, illustrating its weaker and more brittle safe-concept generation.

papers.abstract: Exterior Gaussian-splat twins for real-estate listings are captured to a fixed recipe: a consumer drone orbits a single property in several overlapping passes at stepped altitudes, with occasional vertical ascents, so the imagery is dense, sequential, GPS- and time-tagged, and revisits each facade from many angles. This structure is tantalizing: it suggests camera poses could be recovered by a dense pose-graph optimization (PGO) whose only unknowns are the poses, far fewer than the joint pose-and-point problem bundle adjustment (BA) solves. PGO is mature in robotics, but almost always as post-processing: it redistributes the drift of an already-decent trajectory once loop closures tie it together. Splatting captures push that regime to its limit, every frame closing loops with dozens of others, raising a clean question: does pose-only optimization reach BA accuracy? We built a system specialized to this capture structure, not a general-purpose SfM tool, to test it. It beat COLMAP on speed but never on quality; this paper is the candid post-mortem. The shortfall arises from several interacting causes, hand-set weights, greedy merging and a noisy GPS ruler, together with two limits inherent to the formulation: SE(3) edges carry no scale degree of freedom, so independently scaled sub-maps drift when merged, and a two-view edge stops short of the coupling one 3D point imposes on every frame that sees it. A viable design must add back Sim(3) constraints, absolute GPS priors, retained structure, and uncertainty-aware weighting
authors: Senthil Palanisamy, Azwad Sabik, Alan Dolhasz, Mira Slavcheva
bullets: Dense, sequential, GPS-tagged drone imagery with many loop closures motivates pose-only optimization instead of joint bundle adjustment.
The evaluated system is specialized for real-estate Gaussian-splat capture and outperforms COLMAP in speed, but not reconstruction quality.
Failure sources include hand-tuned weights, greedy merging, and noisy GPS measurements.
Intrinsic limitations include scale drift when merging submaps with SE(3) edges and weaker coupling than constraints from shared 3D points.
The abstract proposes Sim(3) constraints, absolute GPS priors, retained structure, and uncertainty-aware weighting as requirements for a viable design.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: System overview. The image stream is split into per-sequence chunks that are optimized independently as dense SE(3) pose graphs, then merged pairwise into a single graph. Every chunk-level solve is independent, which is what the design intended to parallelize across the cloud.

Fig. 4: Qualitative output of the pose-only pipeline on a self-captured house: (a) the camera poses it estimates and (b) the resulting Gaussian-splat reconstruction. The poses are close to COLMAP and the splat is recognizable; the failures analyzed below are quality and consistency gaps, not gross breakage.

Fig. 1: The pose-only intuition. Bundle adjustment (left) couples the camera poses to a large landmark cloud through observation edges. Because the landmark block C is block-diagonal and cheap to invert, BA marginalizes the landmarks via the Schur complement into a much smaller, pose-only reduced system S = B−EC−1E⊤ (right), solves it for the poses, and only then back-substitutes for the points. Since BA’s expensive core is already this pose-only system, a pose-only formulation tries to assemble S directly from inter-pose relative-pose constraints (dashed), skipping the landmark detour. Both routes target the same S; this paper asks whether the shortcut recovers bundle-adjustment-grade poses.

Fig. 5: Camera centers, PGO versus COLMAP, both aligned to the GPS metric frame (house 2, 741 images, a 148m scene with 104m of vertical ascent). Left: the two sets of centers overlaid. Right: every frame that disagrees by more than 1m is highlighted in color, the rest green. The disagreement is pervasive, 90% of frames exceed 1m (median 1.2m), and worst on the vertical-ascent frames, up to 29m. The two regimes fail differently: the near-linear ascent trajectories suffer nadir degeneracies, while the rest of the scene inherits scaling error from noisy GPS, either way enough to soften the PGO splat relative to COLMAP.

Fig. 3: Splat quality. On house 1 the pose graph places cameras close to COLMAP (0.5◦, 2m), yet the PGO reconstruction (b) is visibly softer than COLMAP’s (a), the seam blur left by scale drift across chunk merges (Sec. 5.2) that a shared point cloud would have prevented. Row (c) shows the same on a second scene (house 2): in the zoomed roof crops the PGO splat (center) smears the shingle texture, while the COLMAP splat (right) resolves individual shingles, matching ground truth (left).

Table 1: Self-captured houses. Pose deviation is relative to COLMAP. “Wall” is measured single-machine runtime; “Par” is the parallel time, the runtime the (independent) front end achieves when its steps run in parallel.

papers.selection_reason: Pose-graph camera estimation for Gaussian splatting is relevant to 3D vision reconstruction.
papers.title: When pose graphs are not enough: a failure analysis of pose-graph-based camera estimation for Gaussian splatting
papers.tldr: A specialized pose-graph optimizer is faster than COLMAP for Gaussian-splat drone captures but fails to match its reconstruction quality because pose-only constraints cannot fully resolve scale, multi-view coupling, and noisy weighting issues.

papers.abstract: Smart glasses are a promising platform for vision-language assistants, but private split inference remains expensive: protecting visual representations before transmission does not remove the cost of on-device vision encoding, wide protected tokens, or hardware-unaware execution. We present SAGE (Smart-glasses-Aware Guarded Encoding), a hardware-aware framework for efficient protected VLM inference on smart glasses. SAGE keeps raw images and unprotected visual tokens on the trusted device, reduces visual input cost, executes shape-specialized INT8 graphs, and compresses protected representations into compact 256-dimensional INT8 packets before transmission. Unlike efficiency methods optimized only for nominal model size, SAGE selects its operating point using downstream answer quality together with measured latency, memory, and thermal behavior on real Mentra Live glasses. On a matched Qwen workload, SAGE reduces glasses inference latency by 39.18%, device-sensor temperature rise by 21.91%, and protected packet size by 96.56%, while retaining 85.62% of the protected reference's relaxed utility and comparable prompted containment. Direct glasses-to-phone tests deliver all 192 packets and reduce median packet-plus-acknowledgment time from 71.3 to 10.0 ms. The compact protected interface also transfers across four additional VLM families. These results show that private wearable VLM inference must be optimized jointly across representation protection, communication, and real-device execution rather than through model compression alone.
authors: Zhimin Li, Pan Wang, Jingxian Chen, Yuantao Tang, Qian Lou, Jingtong Hu
bullets: Keeps raw images and unprotected visual tokens on the trusted glasses device while reducing visual input cost.
Uses shape-specialized INT8 execution and compresses protected representations into compact 256-dimensional INT8 packets.
On Mentra Live glasses, reduces inference latency, temperature rise, and protected packet size while retaining substantial protected-reference utility.
Direct glasses-to-phone tests reduce median packet-plus-acknowledgment time from 71.3 ms to 10.0 ms with all packets delivered.
The compact protected interface transfers across four additional VLM families.
