papers.abstract: Embodied Audio-Visual Navigation (AVN) requires an agent to locate sound targets by jointly leveraging visual and auditory cues. While prior work has achieved notable success with static sound sources, real-world scenarios often involve moving targets, giving rise to the more challenging problem of \textbf{Dynamic Audio-Visual Navigation (D-AVN)}. Existing approaches largely rely on semantic auditory features, which limits generalization to unheard sound categories and hinders fine-grained spatial reasoning. To address these challenges, we propose a novel \textbf{Two-Stage Multi-modal Learning} framework for D-AVN. In the Physical Alignment stage, the proposed \textbf{Intensity-Calibrated Geometry Encoder (ICGE)} performs physics-informed alignment of sound intensity with visual geometry to capture category-agnostic spatial correspondence. In the Scene Aggregation stage, a Transformer-based \textbf{Cross-Modal Scene Aggregator (CMSA)} dynamically integrates multi-modal features to construct a robust state representation for policy learning. Extensive experiments on Replica and Matterport3D demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art success rates, while significantly improving generalization and navigation efficiency in complex environments and under unheard sound scenarios.
authors: Jia Li, Yinfeng Yu
bullets: Addresses Dynamic Audio-Visual Navigation, where agents must find moving sound sources using visual and auditory cues.
Introduces ICGE to learn category-agnostic spatial correspondence through physics-informed sound-intensity and visual-geometry alignment.
Uses Transformer-based CMSA to dynamically combine multimodal features into a state representation for navigation policy learning.
Experiments on Replica and Matterport3D report state-of-the-art success rates with improved generalization and navigation efficiency, including unheard sounds.

papers.abstract: Multi-view perception is often treated as a safe design choice for robot manipulation: if one camera is useful, more cameras should be better. We revisit that assumption in tabletop bimanual manipulation by comparing policies trained with two large-field-of-view (FoV) wrist cameras against policies that additionally receive a head view, using controlled-variable experiments on a real bimanual platform. Across three tabletop tasks, adding a head view does not consistently improve task completion or execution quality: when the wrist cameras already observe the objects, grippers, and goal regions, wrist-only policies form a strong baseline. Restricting the wrist-camera FoV increases the potential value of a head view, but performance improves most reliably when the added view supplies concentrated, task-relevant information: region-of-interest (ROI) cropping yields more consistent head-view gains than the uncropped image, which is dominated by background and task-irrelevant regions. The data-scaling results further suggest an interaction between FoV and demonstration count: wide observations improve coverage but may require more data to stabilize, and they may reach a higher performance ceiling once enough demonstrations are available. These results suggest that camera design should be framed as a task-relevance and information-density problem rather than as a simple count of input views.
authors: Yuhui Duan, Shi Jin, Yuntian Wang, Jin Wang, Siao Liu, Wenchang Gao, Zhaxizhuoma, Yan Ding
bullets: Tests two wide-FoV wrist-camera policies against variants that also use a head view on three real tabletop bimanual tasks.
Wrist-only observations provide a strong baseline when they cover objects, grippers, and goal regions.
Restricting wrist-camera FoV increases the potential benefit of a head view.
ROI-cropped head views yield more consistent gains than uncropped views dominated by background.
FoV and demonstration count interact: wider views may need more data but can achieve a higher performance ceiling.

papers.abstract: Large language models typically support different inference budgets through separate model sizes or fixed compute configurations. In multi-turn interactions, however, compute demand can vary substantially across turns. Using a high-compute model for every turn wastes computation, while routing among independent models may require rebuilding model-specific history states after switches. We therefore ask whether a single shared model can support multiple compute budgets that can be flexibly assigned across turns. We introduce Multi-Ratio ConceptMoE, which jointly supports token-to-concept compression ratios of 2, 4, and 8 (CR2/CR4/CR8) within a shared backbone. Lightweight full-token modules reduce compression-independent cost, ratio-specific boundary routers support distinct compression levels, and cross-ratio training enables mixed-ratio processing within the same context. Across PTBench and SFTBench, the three fixed modes outperform their compute-matched MoE baselines in all 6 comparisons while remaining competitive with independently trained fixed-ratio specialists. On CodeChat and CoSQL, mixed-ratio inference improves the accuracy--compute trade-off, outperforming the Large MoE by 5.87 and 2.68 percentage points while reducing FLOPs by 41.1% and 12.3%, respectively. Under the same turn-wise budget schedule, Multi-Ratio ConceptMoE further reduces FLOPs by 78.4% and 46.9% relative to routing among independent models. These results demonstrate that a single shared model can provide multiple compute budgets for flexible compute allocation across turns.
authors: Yiyang Fu, Zihao Huang, Dongchen Han, Shukai Gong, Zhen Dong, Qiyang Min, Daquan Zhou
bullets: Addresses variable per-turn compute needs without using separate models or rebuilding history states when switching.
Uses lightweight full-token modules, ratio-specific boundary routers, and cross-ratio training in a shared backbone.

Mixed-ratio inference improves the accuracy–compute trade-off on CodeChat and CoSQL, with lower FLOPs than the Large MoE.
Under matched turn-wise budgets, it reduces FLOPs versus routing among independent models, demonstrating flexible shared-model inference.

papers.abstract: Competitive humanoid table tennis requires two distinct abilities: executing a desired return and deciding where to return the ball. We separate these two problems, with the ball landing target serving as an interface between motor control and strategy. (1) We first train a whole-body motor policy conditioned on the desired landing target, which maps the target to an executable humanoid stroke through a model-based strike planner and a learned controller. (2) We then improve the motor policy through self-play in closed-loop rallies, where the robot learns to handle incoming balls generated by another player rather than only prescribed incoming balls. At this stage, the landing targets are still sampled without considering the opponent, so the policy improves its execution without learning game strategy. (3) Finally, we freeze the entire motor stack and train a stroke-level strategic policy to choose landing targets through competitive self-play. Motor self-play improves both landing accuracy and legal-return rate during rallies. More importantly, with the entire motor stack fixed, changing only the target-selection policy leads to large differences in game outcomes: the learned strategy wins 89%, 82%, and 73% of points against center, random, and away-from-opponent baselines, respectively. The learned strategy also changes where it sends the ball according to the opponent's position and the previous target, showing that self-play learns more than simply aiming at fixed "good" locations. On hardware, the same frozen execution stack and strategic interface support complete 11-point games against a recreational human opponent, including multi-stroke rallies with both forehand and backhand returns.
authors: Fanrong Dong, Ziyi Sun, Ziqi Han, Junhan Sun, Lei Ye, Zetong Jing, Hao Zhao, Shaoxun Liu, Rongrong Wang

papers.abstract: Sampling-based model predictive control (SMPC) is increasingly practical for contact-rich manipulation because GPU-based physics simulators enable real-time evaluation of large numbers of non-differentiable contact rollouts. However, this computation budget is finite and can be spent in competing ways, including denser control exploration, representing dynamics or state uncertainty, replanning more frequently, or aligning the simulation better with the physical state. Yet, the resulting trade-offs are not well understood in real-world sim-to-real control. In this work, we address this question through a systematic study of how to allocate a fixed computation budget for SMPC in contact-rich manipulation. To enable controlled comparisons, we develop a GPU-based framework named Budget-Allocating Model Predictive Control (BAMPC), which runs on MuJoCo Warp and exposes dynamics uncertainty, state uncertainty, and temporal alignment as independent dimensions of the computation budget while using the same control stack in simulation and on a real robot. Across three contact-rich manipulation tasks, we find that the best budget allocation depends on the dominant sim-to-real error, with dynamics randomization not universally the most effective one.
authors: Magnus Dierking, Jo\~ao Carvalho, Vince Kurtz, Jan Peters, Nils Dengler, Georgia Chalvatzaki
bullets: SMPC budgets can be divided among control exploration, uncertainty representation, replanning frequency, and simulation–reality alignment.
The study introduces BAMPC, a GPU-based framework built on MuJoCo Warp for controlled budget comparisons.
BAMPC independently varies dynamics uncertainty, state uncertainty, and temporal alignment within one shared control stack.
Across three contact-rich manipulation tasks, optimal allocation varies with the primary sim-to-real error.
Dynamics randomization is not consistently the most effective use of computation.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: Overview of Budget-Allocating Model Predictive Control (BAMPC). A fixed real-time computation budget is allocated across control exploration, state uncertainty, dynamics uncertainty, and temporal alignment. Candidate controls are evaluated under multiple state and physics realizations using GPU-based MuJoCo Warp rollouts, aggregated into scalar costs, which are used by the sampling-based planner to produce the optimized spline control points. The same control stack is used in simulation and on the real robot.

Fig. 1: Under real-time constraints, SMPC frameworks have a finite simulation budget that must be allocated among competing uses, including control exploration, state uncertainty, dynamics uncertainty, and temporal alignment. The most effective allocation is task-dependent and should reflect the dominant source of sim-toreal error. BAMPC provides a common framework to expose and compare these choices across different tasks.
Fig. 3: Overview of the real-world contact-rich tasks used in our experiments.

papers.abstract: State-of-the-art perceptive humanoid locomotion is mostly built on retargeted motion capture, a generative motion prior, and a distillation stage. We report a complete system that does not require this pipeline for a humanoid to cross varied terrain. In its place, we provide a five-expert mixture routed by a terrain classifier over a sensed elevation grid, and target every foothold with a model-based planner, refined by six closed-form-gradient steps on an interpolated terrain-cost field instead of picked from a fixed grid. Driven through the same perception-to-actuation software a robot would run, inside a second, deployment-fidelity simulator, it crosses an $85$\,m five-segment waypoint course $18$ of $20$ times end-to-end ($90\%$, Wilson $95\%$ CI $70$--$97$) and succeeds $20/20$ on four of five segments scored alone, where an ablated configuration without the mixture and without refinement reaches $0\%$ on both the stair and the hurdle segment. The continuous refinement moves $72.4\%$ of foot placements across at least one grid-cell boundary, which produces real sub-grid correction. We also ran matched component studies to report what does not account for it: one expert equals five on the training distribution, four label-free routers collapse to near-uniform activation, and a self-supervised terrain embedding loses to the privileged label.
authors: Thanh Ly, Chien Le, Truong-Duy Dang, Duy M. H. Nguyen, Duy-Dung Le, Vien Anh Ngo, An T. Le

Completes an 85 m, five-segment course in 18/20 trials (90%; Wilson 95% CI: 70–97%).

papers.abstract: Frontier language models reliably refuse to explain how to cause physical harm. We ask whether this refusal survives when the same models control a robot. We introduce RoboHarm, a physical AI safety benchmark of harmful robot instructions, and test seven frontier models on it. We hold each model fixed and vary only the interface, from text to Code as Policies to vision agents that command end-effector poses or joint angles. In a MuJoCo simulation twin of a bimanual YAM arm robot, refusal falls from 73% of text requests to 18-25% once the model controls the robot, even when it is told what the objects are. On the physical robot, six models with end-effector control refused 18% of 612 trials against 19% in sim, and three with joint control refused 41% of 252 against 31%. GPT-5.6 Sol refused every text request and none of its trials on the real robot. Case studies of the robot transcripts show that models miss the hazard, name it without inferring its consequences, or act despite recognizing it, and their refusals often hinge on uncertainty about what an object is rather than on the harm of the action. Safety alignment learned in text thus fails to generalize to action, leaving current models with a poorly understood safety gap in the physical world.

papers.abstract: A longstanding goal for robot reinforcement learning (RL) is that robots learn from their own physical experience, as humans and animals do. A key obstacle to learning directly from physical experience, especially outside instrumented lab environments, is that the state of the world is usually unobservable to the learner and must be estimated from on-board sensing. Errors in that estimate corrupt both the policy input and potentially the reward signal. We study this challenge using the contact-rich task of a bipedal robot learning to score soccer goals. We estimate all key state variables on-board with an unscented Kalman filter (UKF) and no external instrumentation (e.g., motion capture or overhead cameras). Because the UKF may incorrectly estimate state when the ball is unobserved, we learn a new state representation with a recurrent state-space model (RSSM) that, critically, only corrects the RSSM's latent state when the ball is observed. Building on RLPD, we introduce RSSM-RLPD and apply it to the task of a NAO robot learning to dribble a soccer ball into a goal. We show that the robot learns to score from multiple starting positions after 30 minutes of real-world interaction, reaching 100% success against 0% for a feed-forward policy under the same training budget. We complement our physical robot experiments with a simulation study and show that RSSM-RLPD learns policies that achieve a higher success rate than behavior cloning, a feed-forward, and GRU baseline. Taken together, our results show that the addition of a learned state representation to existing on-robot learning methods enables RL from real-robot data even with a high degree of partial observability.
authors: Ryan Gao, Ashvin Anilkumar, Nicholas Corrado, William Cong, Josiah Hanna
bullets: The work addresses partial observability and onboard state-estimation errors in real-robot reinforcement learning.
A NAO robot uses an unscented Kalman filter without external instrumentation, augmented by an RSSM that updates its latent state only when the ball is observed.
The proposed RSSM-RLPD method learns to dribble and score from multiple starting positions after 30 minutes of real-world interaction.
The robot achieved 100% success, compared with 0% for a feed-forward policy under the same training budget.
Simulation results also show higher success than behavior cloning, feed-forward, and GRU baselines; the scope is demonstrated on soccer dribbling and complementary simulation experiments.

papers.abstract: Embodied Artificial Intelligence (AI) introduces cyber-physical risks because digital failures and attacks can cause physical harm. This survey organizes embodied AI safety through a four-layer reference architecture -- comprising the physical interaction, system and middleware, algorithm and decision, and cloud-edge and data layers -- and uses it to connect vulnerabilities, propagation paths, and safeguards across the system stack. It traces the evolution of safety paradigms and examines how faults and attacks cross architectural boundaries to produce physical consequences. Furthermore, the survey systematizes composite attack chains, outlines multi-layered defense strategies, and reviews representative embodied safety benchmarks. Ultimately, we advocate for unifying software alignment with rigorous hardware constraints to build trustworthy systems capable of operating safely within human-centric environments.
authors: Tuo Feng, Yue Zhang, Shiji Zhou, Zhaoxin Fan, Wenguan Wang, Xiaowei Chi, Tianyu Shen, Xiangtai Li, Xuesong Bai, Zheng Zhu, Sirui Han, Boyu Zhou, Zhaosong Wang, Shizhe Chen, Zilong Zheng, Chenjia Bai, Jiangmiao Pang, Yaodong Yang, Hao Zhao, Di Hu, Li Yi, Yan Huang, Qi Wu, Hanwang Zhang, Fei Gao, Shanghang Zhang, Hongsheng Li, Jianye Hao, Yuan Zhang, Yingjie Xia, Jian Shen, Cewu Lu, Hui Zhang, Kai Chen, Wenwu Yu, Badong Chen, Jungong Han, Yike Guo

Connects vulnerabilities, attack propagation paths, safeguards, and physical consequences across the system stack.
Systematizes composite attack chains and reviews multi-layer defense strategies and representative safety benchmarks.
Advocates combining software alignment with rigorous hardware constraints for trustworthy operation in human-centric environments.
papers.selection_reason: Survey of cross-layer safety in embodied AI.
papers.title: From bits to atoms: A survey of cross-layer safety in Embodied AI
papers.tldr: This survey presents a four-layer framework for analyzing and defending against cross-layer safety risks in Embodied AI that can turn digital failures into physical harm.

papers.abstract: Contact-rich manipulation requires a robot to be precise in free space to establish the intended contacts, and compliant once in contact to avoid excessive forces. Imitation learning has proven effective for simpler manipulation tasks, but the compliance underlying a demonstration is not directly observable and is therefore difficult to infer from demonstration data alone. We present a framework that makes compliance explicit at every stage. During data collection, the operator teleoperates the real robot while a synchronized digital twin visualizes the error between the commanded reference and the achieved pose, making the current compliance visible, and selects between two discrete compliance modes. To generalize across object poses, we combine Laplacian editing, which retargets trajectories efficiently but is not physics-consistent during contact, with simulation-based trajectory optimization, which enforces physical plausibility but offers no manual guidance. Finally, a residual reinforcement learning policy refines the interaction forces by adjusting the reference pose of the underlying admittance controller. We evaluate on three flipping and pushing tasks on a Franka FR3 based on a total of 7 demonstrations across tasks. Our method is successful on all 40 out-of-distribution trials, compared to 33/40 and 24/40 for two baselines, with our base policy alone reaching 35/40.
authors: Chunyu Jiang, Yichen Cai, Shuai Li, Wenbin Sun, Jo\~ao Carvalho, Kostas Daniilidis, Oleg Arenz, Cristiana de Farias, Jan Peters
bullets: Targets contact-rich tasks requiring precise free-space motion and safe, compliant contact.
Uses a synchronized digital twin and two discrete compliance modes to expose otherwise hidden compliance during teleoperation.
Combines Laplacian trajectory editing with simulation-based optimization to retarget demonstrations while maintaining physical plausibility.
Residual RL adjusts the admittance controller’s reference pose to refine interaction forces.
Across 40 out-of-distribution trials, the method succeeds in all trials, versus 35/40 for its base policy and 33/40 and 24/40 for two baselines.

(e) The system takes in the robot’s proprioception, stiffness of the admittance controller, external force feedback, and the object pose estimated by the digital twin to predict expected stiffness level and reference poses for implementing the task.

papers.tldr: A residual reinforcement learning framework learns contact-aware, compliant manipulation policies from just seven demonstrations by making compliance explicit and refining an admittance controller.

papers.abstract: Foundation models are expanding robot capabilities, enabling robots to handle more diverse objects, follow sophisticated instructions, and operate in complex environments. These advances bring us to a future in which robots become part of everyday household life. However, cluttered, dynamic household environments also expose robots to unfamiliar objects, tasks, and interactions, making reliable zero-shot task completion an ongoing challenge for robotics research. From a security perspective, we argue for open-world safety: household robots should preserve specified safety requirements in unseen situations, including when they cannot complete the requested task. Safety protections must account for context and interactions that persist across actions and tasks. In this position paper, we examine why existing safety methods can fail to provide this protection. Protection can fail through misinterpreted context, overlooked past interactions, or stopping and recovery strategies that become unsafe under unfamiliar conditions. We therefore propose a research agenda to specify, learn, and ground safety requirements, enforce them with reliable recovery, and evaluate the generalization of such protections. We call for household robots whose safety protections remain reliable beyond the situations, context, and history used to train and develop them, to achieve open-world safety.
authors: Yu-Lin Tsai, Muxi Lyu, Roei Herzig, Koushik Sen, Raluca Ada Popa, David Wagner
bullets: Foundation models enable robots to handle more diverse objects, instructions, and environments, but zero-shot reliability remains difficult.
Open-world safety requires preserving specified safety requirements even when a robot cannot complete a task.
Existing methods may fail by misinterpreting context, ignoring prior interactions, or using unsafe stopping and recovery strategies.
The paper proposes research on specifying, learning, grounding, and reliably enforcing safety requirements.
It also calls for evaluation focused on how well safety protections generalize beyond training and development conditions.

figures.caption: Fig. 3: A candidate architecture for the research agenda. Validity links authority, active grounding, and evidence-gated memory. Viability uses that state to preserve an enforceable response through physical execution. Evaluation varies safety-critical state and history in simulation and a physical arena, reporting harm, recovery, and task utility. The connections organize the research questions rather than prescribe a single implementation.

Fig. 2: Earlier thought experiments expose three connected failure routes: (1) missing the cord–pitcher relationship, (2) forgetting interrupted cleaning, and (3) losing load-aware recovery. The shield represents the end-to-end physical protection that must survive each change.

papers.title: Building Trustworthy Household Robots through Open-World Safety
papers.tldr: Household robots need safety protections that remain reliable in unfamiliar situations, contexts, and interaction histories—not just successful task completion in known settings.

papers.abstract: Recent progress in learned whole-body controllers for humanoid robots has enabled robust free-space motion by tracking kinematic targets such as joint or end-effector trajectories. This interface provides a useful abstraction for upstream systems, including motion capture, teleoperation, or generative models, which can specify desired motion without reasoning about forces or balance. However, this abstraction has largely been limited to robot motion, requiring task-specific controllers or retraining for object interaction. We introduce OIL, an Object Interaction Layer that extends the kinematic command interface of whole-body control to include desired object motion and contact. OIL augments a standard controller with object-centric commands and translates them into coordinated whole-body behavior while preserving locomotion and balance. This design enables a single learned policy to execute non-prehensile interactions, including pushing, pulling, two-arm pick-and-place, and locomotion-coupled transport, directly from object-level kinematic targets without task-specific retraining. In simulation, we demonstrate that object-level commands improve performance over robot-centric controllers while matching task-specific policies across variations in object properties such as mass and size. We further demonstrate zero-shot generalization to novel behavior combinations and sim-to-real transfer on the Digit humanoid robot.
authors: Pranay Dugar, Mohitvishnu S. Gadde, Rajesh Mangannavar, Aayam Kumar Shrestha, Alan Fern
bullets: Addresses the limitation of robot-centric kinematic interfaces that require task-specific controllers or retraining for object interaction.
Adds desired object motion and contact commands to a standard whole-body controller.
Supports pushing, pulling, two-arm pick-and-place, and locomotion-coupled transport from object-level targets.
In simulation, improves over robot-centric controllers and matches task-specific policies across varied object masses and sizes.
Demonstrates zero-shot behavior combinations and sim-to-real transfer on the Digit humanoid.

The Masked Humanoid Controller (MHC, green), also running at 50 Hz, combines ut and dbt with robot proprioception to produce PD targets at for all actuated joints, which are executed by a PD controller at 2 kHz. During training, the MHC weights remain frozen and only the OIL weights are optimized.

papers.abstract: Looped transformers reuse one shared block across many recurrent steps, so depth becomes a quantity that can be spent at runtime rather than a stack of distinct layers. Those extra steps help only if a write made on one recurrent step is still readable on later ones, and that depends on the linear map applied to the residual between recurrent steps. We show that whether the loop learns to track state is a geometric question about the form of this map, and we propose blockwise conformal injections: the residual splits into coordinate-aligned groups and rotates inside each one, so every group has its own timescale while the geometry stays exact within it. Our experiments show a performance increase on a demanding form of state tracking - last-token accuracy when the rest of the prefix is already correct - and on language modelling, where a signal written earlier has to be retrieved at the end of the sequence.
authors: Alexey Zemtsov, Albina Klepach, Vadim Lomshakov, Andrei Polubarov, Nikita Lyubaykin, Alexander Derevyagin, Vladislav Kurenkov, Alexander Nikulin
bullets: Looped transformers reuse one block, making runtime depth dependent on how well state persists between steps.
State tracking depends on the geometry of the residual map used between recurrent iterations.
The proposed blockwise conformal injections split residuals into coordinate-aligned groups and rotate each group independently.
This gives each group a distinct timescale while preserving exact within-group geometry.
Experiments show gains in last-token state-tracking accuracy and language modeling with delayed signal retrieval.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Each panel is the normalized Gram matrix of one write, the cosine of the angle between that write at recurrent step t and at recurrent step s. Free diagonal: the entries collapse toward one value, so the block cannot tell which recurrent step the signal came from. Conformal: the stripes depend only on how many steps apart the two appearances are, so the block can read the depth at which the signal was written. Blockwise conformal splits the state into coordinate-aligned groups. Inside a group the angles stay readable, as in the conformal panel, but the scale is now that group’s own rate, so a write occupying several groups lays several timescales on top of one another. The finer texture is that granularity: the block can still read the depth of the signal, and each group keeps it readable for a different number of steps.

Figure 1: Depiction of how a write moves across recurrent steps, once the transition operator has been applied and the result renormalized. The free diagonal stretches each coordinate by its own factor, so two writes that started apart are dragged onto one axis. A conformal transition operator is a rotation: the write travels around the circle, and the angle between two writes stays the angle they were written with. Blockwise conformal splits the state into a few groups, each turning at its own rate, so the same rotation still moves the signal, and different groups can age at different speeds.

Figure 3: Eigenvalues of the transition operator in the unit disk. Free diagonal: free radii and no phase. One shared radius is a single conformal map; one radius per group is the blockwise family; freeing every radius is a complex diagonal.

A general orthogonal factor already beats the diagonal; the most restricted writing beats it most. Cells are mean ± standard error over 10 seeds. papers.abstract: Self-driving laboratories (SDLs) aim to automate the full experimental loop, from scientific decision-making to physical execution. Ideally, AI-generated plans could be carried out directly by robotic systems, but reliable automation remains difficult in complex, open-world laboratory environments, where experiments often involve fine-grained manipulation, long-horizon procedures, and substantial variation across tasks and setups. Humans therefore remain an important execution interface between AI-generated plans and physical experiments, creating a need for clear and effective human-facing experimental guidance. Because laboratory procedures are inherently visual, spatial, and dynamic, video is particularly well suited to communicating apparatus configurations, manipulation actions, temporal dependencies, and state changes. Recent advances in video generation now make it possible to synthesize experimental demonstrations directly from an initial workspace image and a natural-language instruction. However, whether such models can reliably communicate real laboratory procedures has not been systematically studied. We introduce LabInstruct, a benchmark for situated instructional video generation in real laboratories. LabInstruct contains 204 tasks across 5 scientific disciplines, with real reference executions and structured annotations of objects, actions, contacts, and state transitions. Evaluating 8 frontier image-to-video models, we find that visually plausible generations frequently remain procedurally incorrect, revealing a substantial gap between visual realism and the reliability required for experimental instruction.
authors: Yuming Fu, Weijia Wu, Jing Chen, Jiahao Tang, Feifei Chen, Hongyu Zhu, Xin Jin, Alex Jinpeng Wang
bullets: Targets the challenge of communicating complex, fine-grained, long-horizon lab procedures in self-driving laboratories.
Introduces 204 tasks spanning 5 scientific disciplines, with real reference executions and structured annotations.
Evaluates 8 frontier image-to-video models from an initial workspace image and natural-language instruction.
Shows a substantial gap between visually realistic videos and procedurally accurate experimental guidance.

papers.abstract: The rise of large language models (LLMs) has opened a path toward generalist embodied AI, raising the question of how LLMs can act in the physical world. One straightforward approach is training the model to generate actions: collect robot-action data and video demonstration, refine LLM architecture with an action head, and train a vision-language-action (VLA) model at scale. However, we argue that coding agents have the potential to realize generalist embodied manipulation. All they need is a simple yet effective robot harness. We present RoboHarness: a robotic harness that gives LLM agents a visual-geometric control panel so that they can directly understand and invoke embodied tasks. With RoboHarness, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next outperforms state-of-the-art VLA models on BEHAVIOR Challenge 2025 tasks. The implementation will be released as open source.

bullets: Targets generalist embodied manipulation without directly training a vision-language-action model.
Provides LLM agents with a visual-geometric control panel for understanding and invoking robot tasks.

Reports better performance than state-of-the-art VLA models on BEHAVIOR Challenge 2025 tasks.
The implementation is planned for open-source release.

papers.abstract: People often learn from others' demonstrations, and inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) techniques have realized this capacity in machines. In contrast, teaching by demonstration has been less well studied computationally. Here, we develop a Bayesian model for teaching by demonstration. Stark differences arise when demonstrators are intentionally teaching (i.e. showing) a task versus simply performing (i.e. doing) a task. In two experiments, we show that human participants modify their teaching behavior consistent with the predictions of our model. Further, we show that even standard IRL algorithms benefit when learning from showing versus doing.
authors: Mark K. Ho, Michael L. Littman, James MacGlashan, Fiery Cushman, Joseph L. Austerweil
bullets: Addresses the limited computational study of teaching by demonstration.
Distinguishes intentional “showing” from simply “doing” a task.
Develops a Bayesian model of how demonstrators teach through examples.
Two experiments find human teaching behavior matches the model’s predictions.
Standard inverse reinforcement learning algorithms benefit from demonstrations intended to teach.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards improves mathematical reasoning when a final answer can be checked, but a correct answer does not certify the derivation behind it, and proof problems offer no answer to check. Replacing the check with a reasoning model as an in-loop verifier faces a fundamental obstacle: the policy must already produce occasional correct attempts for any reward to exist, which it may never do at olympiad level. We instead move verification and repair out of the training loop and into offline data generation with SPLICE, a workflow in which a second model, given only a reference solution, edits a reasoning model's traces as they are generated: it verifies progress, truncates a failed trace at its last verified step, and splices in an adaptively strengthened hint until progress resumes. The resulting dataset includes repaired examples whose sampled unaided trajectory failed, with failed continuations removed and progress repeatedly checked against the reference solution. A model finetuned on SPLICE traces outperforms the same model distilled from the reasoning model's unedited traces on AIME and, under a grading protocol validated against human grades, on olympiad proofs. The trained model's own traces show a corresponding behavioral signature: at difficult points it announces a branch in the style of the spliced hints and takes riskier steps, with predictive entropy rising there and just after, a pattern absent from the model trained on unedited traces.

papers.abstract: Post-training large language models (LLMs) on two-player zero-sum games provides a verifiable reward, and the gains have been shown to transfer to general reasoning. Existing pipelines, however, rely on a handful of hand-written games and on advantage estimators tied to them, so both the supply of games and the advantage estimate on a large corpus limit scaling. We present GameSmith, which scales both. An LLM synthesises games inside templates whose reward, observation, and hidden-information code is fixed. Each game is verified by seed-paired replay and by an independent re-implementation of its specification, then expanded into encoding, rule, and size variants, giving 26 new games in 29 families and 336 verified variants from the three SPIRAL templates. The model is distilled from the self-play of a larger teacher (Qwen3-32B) on these games and then trained by self-play reinforcement learning with CRAB, an advantage estimator that credits each decision against a shrinkage estimate of the expected return of its position and is defined on every variant. On Qwen3-4B-Base, distillation raises the 13-benchmark mean pass@1 from 45.5 to 62.5, above the three SPIRAL games at the same budget, and self-play with CRAB reaches 64.9. The ordering holds across models, and transfer grows with the number of game families.
authors: Weixian Waylon Li, Jiaxin Zhang, Han Zhou, Chengzu Li, Ke Wang, Fengxiang He, Yiwen Guo

papers.abstract: Positional embeddings encode the spatial position of each image patch in a Vision Transformer (ViT), allowing the model to distinguish different spatial arrangements of visual content. However, we know little about how the choice of embedding shapes a vision transformer's internal representation. In this work, we show that Absolute Positional Embeddings (APE) and Rotary Positional Embeddings (RoPE) encode spatial position through different internal mechanisms: APE stores position in explicit features, while RoPE builds it inside attention and rebuilds it when it is withheld. Specifically, in APE models, sparse autoencoders recover causal row- and column-specific features, whereas interventions on RoPE reveal distinct rotary components that separately encode row and column information. Additionally, causal interventions selectively disabling RoPE's row or column rotations show that decodable row and column information can be independently removed and, once rotations are restored, partly reconstructed, in part by axis-specialized attention heads. Both mechanisms are causally important for classification: permuting APE's positional features across patches reduces top-1 accuracy by 24--31 points, and ablating the rotations of RoPE's primary rebuilding head reduces it more than ablating those of any other head. Our findings show that the choice of positional encoding fundamentally changes how spatial information is organized and processed inside Vision Transformers. More broadly, our work demonstrates how mechanistic analysis can reveal how models construct, reconstruct, and maintain structured representations, providing a basis for targeted interventions in vision models.
authors: Mahmoud Mannes, Nikhil Maturi, Parva Mehta, Jiwon Jeong, Aravind Singaram Kannappan
bullets: APE represents position in explicit, patch-specific features, while RoPE encodes it through attention-based rotary components.
Sparse autoencoders identify causal row- and column-specific features in APE models; interventions reveal separate row and column rotations in RoPE.
When RoPE rotations are removed, spatial information can be partly reconstructed, with some attention heads specializing in particular axes.
Causal disruption of APE positional features lowers top-1 accuracy by 24–31 points, while ablating RoPE’s key rebuilding head causes the largest impact among heads tested.
The study shows that positional-encoding choice fundamentally shapes how spatial information is organized and processed.

papers.abstract: Self-evolving agents improve through repeated cycles of modification and evaluation. However, existing methods receive feedback on modifications only after costly evaluations, and aggregate scores may obscure distinctions between failures that require different repairs. We introduce predictive self-evolution through an editable Improvement Dynamics Model (IDM). Before evaluation, the IDM predicts task-level outcomes of a proposed modification and guides an optional revision. After evaluation, past modifications and their observed outcomes are used to improve the IDM, allowing predictive knowledge to accumulate across generations. The system can thus improve how it solves tasks, proposes modifications, and predicts their effects. Building on HyperAgents, we evaluate this approach across multilingual coding, paper review, robotics reward design, and Olympiad-level mathematical grading. Our approach outperforms HyperAgents across all four domains, with up to 46% higher average performance over generations. Gains also persist under matched token budgets that include both agent evolution and task evaluation, and extend to held-out tasks. Forecast accuracy improves as the IDM evolves, and the learned predictive knowledge transfers to improve evolution in a new domain.
authors: Zixuan Xie, Chang Xu, Yuhua Jiang, Li Zhao
bullets: Existing self-evolving agents learn from modifications only after evaluation, while aggregate feedback can hide failure-specific repair needs.
The Improvement Dynamics Model (IDM) predicts task-level effects of proposed changes and can guide revisions before evaluation.
Observed modification outcomes update the IDM, allowing predictive knowledge to accumulate across generations and transfer to new domains.
Evaluated on multilingual coding, paper review, robotics reward design, and Olympiad-level math grading using HyperAgents as a baseline.
The approach outperforms HyperAgents across all four domains, with gains of up to 46% in average performance; forecast accuracy also improves over time.

papers.abstract: Sparse attention visits few keys, yet finding them can still require scoring every key with every indexer head. We introduce DoSA (Dots Sparse Attention), a lossless method for making this computation conditional while preserving exact token selection. Its central observation is that Top-K selection requires sufficient evidence to reject a candidate, not necessarily its full score. A seed set supplies a lower bound on the winning threshold. Nonnegative head projections and joint residual bounds upper-bound positive contributions, while activation-informed aggregation bounds the magnitude subtracted by negative heads. The certificate directs full scoring toward candidates that remain eligible; exact-score filtering further reduces writeback and selection work. We establish the certificate and its exact-selection conditions, and analyze how geometry and selection margins govern its effectiveness. Our GPU implementation accelerates the complete Indexer by up to 2.74 times over SGLang and 1.69 times over LiteTopK across English, Chinese, and code workloads. End-to-end evaluation on GLM-5.2 and DeepSeek-V3.2 achieves up to 1.94 times and 1.50 times time-to-first-token speedups over the two baselines, respectively.
authors: Fanxu Meng, Taosong Fang
bullets: Sparse attention can remain expensive because every candidate may still be scored by each indexer head.
A seed set establishes a lower bound on the Top-K threshold, while bounds identify candidates that cannot be eliminated without full scoring.
The method uses nonnegative projections, residual bounds, and activation-informed bounds for negative contributions, followed by exact-score filtering.
GPU experiments report up to 2.74× faster indexing than SGLang and 1.69× faster than LiteTopK across English, Chinese, and code workloads.
End-to-end time-to-first-token improves by up to 1.94× on GLM-5.2 and 1.50× on DeepSeek-V3.2 versus the baselines.

papers.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models have emerged as an effective paradigm for scaling large language models, yet their massive parameter footprint poses severe memory challenges for deployment. Existing compression methods typically treat expert pruning and merging as disjoint operations and rely on greedy heuristics, often leading to irreversible information loss or representational pollution. In this paper, we propose PRIME, a unified optimization framework for MoE compression via adaptive PRunIng and MErging. PRIME casts the discrete prune-merge assignment step as a global Integer Linear Programming over a frequency-weighted surrogate objective, jointly selecting pruning and merging decisions while accounting for expert usage. We motivate the frequency-aware objective through an error-bound analysis under fixed representative assignments, and show that the formulation favors high-frequency experts as centroids, promoting routing stability. Extensive experiments on Qwen3-30B-A3B and Qwen3.5-122B-A10B demonstrate that PRIME achieves strong accuracy retention across knowledge, coding, math, and long-context tasks, while serving benchmarks of merged models quantify the memory and throughput benefits of expert compression in vLLM.
authors: Shanfeng Huang, Rongqian Zhang, Zhou Fang, Song Xiao, Hai Du
bullets: Addresses memory challenges from the large parameter footprint of MoE models.
Jointly optimizes prune-and-merge assignments with global Integer Linear Programming rather than separate greedy decisions.
Uses expert-usage frequency in a surrogate objective to favor frequently used experts as merge representatives and improve routing stability.
Experiments on Qwen3-30B-A3B and Qwen3.5-122B-A10B show strong accuracy retention across knowledge, coding, math, and long-context tasks.
Serving benchmarks with vLLM quantify memory and throughput benefits after compression.

papers.abstract: Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) learn world models by predicting future representations rather than reconstructing observations. Variational JEPA (VJEPA) gives this prediction probabilistic semantics and permits flexible conditional predictive families. We propose MDN-VJEPA, a multimodal probabilistic JEPA that instantiates the latent predictor as a mixture density network (MDN), representing future states with a Gaussian mixture whose components encode alternative futures, their probabilities, and within-mode uncertainty. For sequential prediction, we address two additional structural requirements: multi-modal futures should remain temporally coherent across a trajectory, and predictive beliefs should remain consistent when propagated to the same horizon through different temporal path compositions, as motivated by the Chapman--Kolmogorov equation. Together, these considerations define a three-level hierarchy of multimodal prediction, coherent multimodal trajectories, and compositionally consistent multimodal dynamics. Controlled experiments show that MDN-VJEPA closely recovers known branching predictive laws, that retaining the complete multimodal belief rather than its conditional mean can lead to materially different and substantially better planning decisions under branching futures, and that trajectory-level coupling and distributional consistency improve temporal coherence and multi-horizon agreement. These results support a simple principle: a probabilistic JEPA should preserve not only how uncertain the future is, but which distinct futures constitute that uncertainty, how they form coherent trajectories, and how those beliefs compose through time.
authors: Yongchao Huang
bullets: Addresses the limitation of representing future uncertainty only through averages in sequential world models.
Uses a mixture density network to model future latent states as Gaussian mixtures with alternative modes, probabilities, and within-mode uncertainty.
Introduces a three-level structure: multimodal predictions, coherent multimodal trajectories, and Chapman–Kolmogorov-inspired compositional consistency.
Controlled experiments recover branching predictive laws and show that retaining full multimodal beliefs can improve planning under branching futures.
Trajectory coupling and distributional consistency improve temporal coherence and agreement across prediction horizons.

figures.caption: Figure 3: MDN-VJEPA pipeline. The trainable context encoder qθ maps the observed history to the predictive state Zt, while the EMA target encoder qθ̄ produces the stop-gradient target representation ZT t+h. Conditioned on Zt and side information ξ, the MDN predictor outputs mixture weights, component means, and component covariances, which together define a Gaussian-mixture predictive law over the future representation. The direct predictive loss compares this multimodal predictive distribution with the target representation.

Figure 4: Trajectory-level mixture semantics. The current predictive context defines a distribution over a shared trajectory mode M . The context together with that same sampled or marginalized mode parameterizes all horizon-specific Gaussian predictions in the directly predicted future block. The future states are emitted in parallel rather than recursively, distinguishing Level-II trajectory coherence from the recursive transition composition introduced at Level III.

Figure 5: Level-III distributional path consistency. The same horizon-h predictive law can be reached by two computational paths: a direct prediction from Zt (upper) or recursive composition of the learned one-step MDN transition (lower). Level III regularizes the resulting distributions towards agreement. The comparison is distributional and therefore does not require component labels to align between the two paths.

Figure 24: Representative horizon-16 endpoint distributions for a pre-specified visualization seed. Left: samples from the exact simulator law. Middle: Level-II direct and recursively composed samples. Right: Level-III direct and composed samples after CK regularization. Both learned models retain the separated multimodal endpoint structure; CK changes the agreement between computational paths rather than collapsing them to a single mode.

Figure 1: An motivating branching prediction problem. A point predictor may average two valid futures into an invalid route, while a single Gaussian can represent them only through a broad unimodal belief that places probability mass between the branches. A mixture predictor can instead preserve separate alternatives and quantify both their probabilities and within-mode uncertainty. The same principle applies in latent space rather than only in observation space.

Figure 13: Secondary robustness tests. Left: increasing within-mode noise progressively blurs the two modes, making a single Gaussian increasingly adequate. Right: the Gaussian approximation is most challenged near balanced branch probabilities and improves as one branch dominates. MDN-VJEPA remains close to the known law throughout both sweeps.

papers.abstract: We present FoldBack, a self-correcting masked generative policy for long-horizon garment folding. Existing long-trajectory policies may continue after a missed or slipped grasp even when the garment has not reached the intended configuration. We structure FoldBack's recovery mechanisms around three inference-time decisions: when to refine and verify, how to roll back, and where and how to retry. FoldBack aligns refinement and grasp verification with pick-and-place events, returns the robot to a retryable pre-grasp configuration while preserving successful grasps, and selectively regenerates the failed segment and selected future actions while avoiding previous failed grasp locations. To our knowledge, FoldBack is the first editable full-trajectory policy to unify these decisions, enabling failed interactions to be detected, undone, and repaired before execution continues, without recovery demonstrations or base-policy retraining. Across 33 real garments from six categories, FoldBack achieves 75.2% final folding success and 0.837 final-mask IoU, versus 45.7% and 0.689 for the strongest prior baseline.

papers.abstract: Embodied and assistive agents must do more than recognize objects: they must reason about where an object belongs given the layout of an environment and the habits of the people who live in it. Progress on this problem has been limited, in part because no dedicated benchmark or dataset exists to define and evaluate it. Existing RGB-D scan datasets reconstruct static rooms without human activity, while human-object-interaction datasets capture motion without a navigable, fully reconstructed scene or a ground-truth notion of an object's natural destination. We introduce contextual object placement as a benchmark task: predicting an object's destination during an observed object-carrying episode. To support this task, we present Embodied Camera observations of Human Object carrying (ECHO), a large-scale synthetic dataset that pairs dense RGB-D scans of indoor scenes with recordings of an embodied human carrying everyday objects to context-appropriate destinations. ECHO is the first publicly available dataset to combine reconstructed scenes, human activity, natural language, and contextual-placement annotations. It comprises 3,805 human-annotated episodes across 159 floors of 115 HM3D scenes, involving 198 distinct objects. Each floor includes a complete RGB-D scan with human-annotated room labels and a surface list. Each episode provides synchronized RGB-D encounter clips; 6-DoF camera, human, and object trajectories; start and destination surfaces; an action caption; and a human-written context: a single sentence describing the inhabitant's routine that implies the destination without naming it. We evaluate contextual object placement using input-masked probes and an end-to-end baseline. Results show that no single input modality is sufficient, highlighting the need to jointly reason over scene structure, human activity, and contextual knowledge.
authors: Xuefei Sun
Lorin Achey
Kali Hamilton
Alberto Speranzon
Gregory Grebe
Yonatan Bisk
Christoffer Heckman
bullets: Defines contextual object placement: predicting an object’s destination during an observed carrying episode.
Provides 3,805 annotated episodes across 159 floors, 115 HM3D scenes, and 198 everyday objects.
Combines dense RGB-D scene scans, human/object/camera trajectories, destination surfaces, action captions, and routine-based context descriptions.
Evaluations with masked-input probes and an end-to-end baseline show that no single modality is sufficient.
Supports joint reasoning over scene structure, human activity, and contextual knowledge.

figures.caption: Fig. 3: ECHO end-to-end baseline. Scene-scan observations (green) are reconstructed into an object-centric map from which candidate surfaces are extracted, while the depth frames provide the walkable space and its rooms. Encounter observations (orange) recover the human trajectory and the carried object. papers.abstract: Dense visual text requires image generators to reproduce long strings across multiple regions with correct placement and legibility. As short-string rendering improves, evaluation must test sustained performance across more demanding scenes. We introduce UltraText Bench, a bilingual benchmark for prompt-only generation of dense visual text. It contains 432 prompts spanning 24 real-world scene categories and three difficulty levels, split equally between English and Chinese. Each human-reviewed prompt supplies exact strings for four to twelve text regions, paired with structured references for their content, placement, and visual attributes. We use the Q-Judger vision-language model to assess each image against the complete reference, reporting text fidelity, text clarity, spatial quality, and scene quality. Across 24 model configurations, these dimensions reveal different strengths: Z-Image-Turbo gains 3.81 clarity points over Z-Image-Base while losing 14.76 fidelity points under the reported settings. Performance also varies with workload; Qwen-Image-2512's English composite falls from 86.50 at L1 to 42.86 at L3. Ten participants took part in human evaluation of the automatic scores. papers.abstract: Existing attacks on unlearned diffusion models assume that the erased concepts are known in advance and focus on recovering them. In practice, however, model providers may not disclose which concepts have been removed, and even with access to the original base model, an adversary may still lack a clear target to attack. In this paper, we aim to answer the following critical but overlooked questions: which concepts have been erased from the model, and how many have been erased in total? To this end, we present Tracer, a framework that rapidly and accurately identifies erased concepts and estimates their number. Tracer efficiently identifies erased concepts without generating and classifying images. By combining lightweight spectral analysis of weight footprints, it enables efficient search over large candidate vocabularies. To distinguish multiple erased concepts, we introduce a footprint coverage objective that guides sequential discovery. Tracer estimates the number of erased concepts by detecting a sharp decline in candidate confidence as the selected concepts account for the erasure footprint, without requiring labeled examples for calibration. The framework requires only lightweight linear algebra and limited forward probes, with no prior knowledge of the unlearning algorithm. Experiments across text-to-image and text-to-video backbones and diverse unlearning methods demonstrate that Tracer identifies erased concepts and estimates their number in seconds, achieving 150 to 137,000 times and 133 to 20,000 times speedups over MIA and brute-force search on image and video models, respectively, with substantially higher identification accuracy.

papers.abstract: Power-law learning curves are often treated as fixed properties of a model and its data, although learning-rate and batch-size schedules can change the observed loss. We study this dependence in noisy online SGD with linear random features. Conditional on the representation, an exact Volterra equation separates two response components: a forcing term that propagates unresolved target error and a memory kernel that propagates stochastic-error injections. We prove that either component follows a power law if and only if its cumulative weighted spectral mass has the corresponding low-spectrum scaling; individual eigenvalues and target coefficients need not obey coordinatewise power laws. Under a joint schedule, intrinsic time $T_t=\sum_{s<t}η_s$ controls optimization progress, while $r_t=B_t/η_t$ controls noise injection. Their interaction yields sharp conditions under which a schedule preserves, changes, or destroys the clean power law, together with a memory ceiling on noise reduction. The power-law random-feature model realizes this mechanism in $3+3(+2)$ propagation regimes with phase-dependent compute rates. Controlled nanoGPT experiments show that (1) learning-rate and batch-size schedules with matched $B/η$ paths are nearly equivalent in intrinsic time, (2) a forcing-memory surrogate accurately predicts loss across schedules, and (3) its fitted exponents across real-world datasets identify the regime of LLMs in $3+3(+2)$ map. The source code for reproducing our experiments is available on https://github.com/yichenblue/spectra-to-schedules-in-pretraining.

papers.abstract: Embodied vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly deployed as high-level planners for robots because they generalize across diverse environments. However, this requires their safety alignment to also hold in unseen environments. Existing red-teaming assumes an adversary who optimizes the prompt, the pixels, or text in the environment, and existing benchmarks ask whether a planner recognizes or mitigates a hazard in a fixed scene. Neither asks whether a refusal the planner has already given survives an ordinary change to the environment. We ask that question by placing a single everyday object into the environment, with no pixel, gradient, or prompt under adversarial control. On $846$ tasks that a constitution-guarded planner initially refuses, we find $20.2\%$ of tasks can be flipped to compliance by one or more objects, and the number of objects differs from one task to another. In addition, the object need not be chosen for the task, i.e., items drawn from a fixed list, with no knowledge of the environment or the instruction, bypass safety about as often as items proposed for the specific task. We qualitatively contrast the tasks bypassed most and least often and find that the distinction lies in how conspicuous the hazard is in the instruction and environment. Susceptibility to safety bypass is therefore a property of the task, which we call its \emph{malleability}, and we show that it can be predicted before the target is ever queried. A composite of signals read from a small open-source VLM identifies malleable tasks $2.4\times$ as often as picking at random. Everyday objects, whether placed by an adversary or introduced by ordinary rearrangement of the environment, are thus sufficient to overturn a refusal. Because susceptibility is determined by how a task is specified, we recommend assessing malleability per task prior to deployment.

papers.abstract: Distributed inference depends on GPU collective communication that must keep pace with evolving hardware and specialized workloads. However, existing works often couple the semantics, orchestration (where and when data moves), and datapath (how data moves) of collective communication. This coupling makes it costly to adopt new hardware mechanisms and customize communication for applications. We present Purlin, a scale-up communication framework that separates these concerns. At the top of Purlin, we specify collectives as a naming of an input and output layout and a copy or reduction operation. In the middle, we introduce a shared orchestration protocol, Stage, Notify, And Consume (SNAC), which derives coordination from these specifications. Below SNAC sits a hardware-specific datapath we call Atom, which implements two key data movement primitives for collectives: copy and reduce. This separation lets us customize collectives and adopt new hardware mechanisms while reusing orchestration via SNAC. We evaluate Purlin on A100, H200, and B200 GPUs. Across seven collectives, Purlin achieves latency speedups of up to 5.14x and bandwidth improvements of up to 4.50x over baselines. Integrated into SGLang, Purlin improves offline LLM serving throughput and interactivity by 1.13x on average and up to 1.37x over baselines. For online LLM inference, Purlin improves interactivity by 1.26x on average and up to 2.85x, with the largest gain occurring under overload. For diffusion image generation, Purlin reduces end-to-end latency by up to 1.13x.
authors: Osayamen Jonathan Aimuyo
Swapnil Gandhi

bullets: Existing collective systems tightly couple what data moves, when and where it moves, and how movement is implemented, limiting customization and hardware adoption.

Evaluated on A100, H200, and B200 GPUs across seven collectives, Purlin achieves up to 5.14× lower latency and 4.50× higher bandwidth than baselines.
Integrated into SGLang, it improves LLM serving throughput and interactivity and reduces diffusion-generation latency, with gains varying by workload and load.

papers.abstract: Large language models are increasingly used to simulate response distributions in social surveys. Prior work has achieved accurate population-level simulation for individual questions. Real questionnaires, however, ask each respondent a sequence of related questions. A simulated respondent should show coherent preferences across the whole questionnaire, not merely accurate distributions for isolated items. Existing single-item methods cannot accurately reproduce how the same person answers a complete survey. We propose FullRespondent-LLM (FR-LLM), which fine-tunes two specialized LLMs: a marginal model for each item's response distribution and a respondent-level autoregressive model for dependencies across answers. Marginal-Constrained Joint Projection (MCJP) then projects the autoregressive joint distribution onto the set satisfying the item-level marginals learned by the first model. This yields complete questionnaires with realistic cross-item relationships while retaining strong item-level accuracy. On two real-world social survey datasets, FR-LLM more accurately reproduces multi-question response patterns, maintains competitive single-item accuracy, and generalizes better to unseen populations and questions. In a small commercial-survey dataset, we use simulated responses to make pricing and stocking decisions; FR-LLM achieves the highest realized profit.
authors: Ji Huang
Mengfei Li
Shuai Shao
bullets: Problem: Single-question simulators fail to capture how one respondent answers related questions across a questionnaire.
Method: Fine-tunes a marginal model for item-level distributions and an autoregressive respondent model for cross-answer dependencies.
MCJP projects the joint respondent distribution to satisfy the learned item-level marginals.
Across two real-world social survey datasets, FR-LLM better reproduces multi-question patterns while retaining competitive single-item accuracy.
It generalizes better to unseen populations and questions, and achieved the highest realized profit in a small commercial-survey application.

papers.abstract: Host-resident layer streaming enables full-parameter LLM fine-tuning beyond GPU memory, but data-parallel ranks compete for shared host resources. Replicated transfers amplify traffic, while strong scaling can expose host work as computation windows shrink. We present SlideDP, a synchronous data-parallel runtime for shared-host multi-GPU systems. It maintains one authoritative host state, decouples communication routes from state layout, and pipelines parameter delivery, gradient aggregation, and CPU updates across ranks and chunks. An analytical step-time model characterizes resource bottlenecks and pipeline exposure; runtime measurements guide communication, chunking, and activation policies under a GPU memory budget. In matched-batch sweeps, SlideDP achieves geometric-mean throughput ratios of 1.46-2.64$\times$ over SlideFormer, MegaTrain, and ZeRO-Offload. On four H100s, SlideDP approaches GPU-resident FSDP2 throughput for Qwen3-14B at a smaller batch size. With a larger batch, it processes over 1M tokens per step and exceeds FSDP2's measured peak throughput by 11.2%. Separately, it supports 256K-token sequences for the same model and fine-tunes Qwen2.5-72B on four RTX 4090 GPUs. Project page: https://github.com/RegiaYoung/SlideDP.
authors: Ruijia Yang, Shiyuan Lin, Yulong Ao, Zhiyu Li, Yingli Zhao, Xianduo Li, Yonghua Lin, Zeyi Wen
bullets: Addresses shared-host contention and redundant transfers in data-parallel host-resident LLM fine-tuning.
Uses one authoritative host state, flexible communication routes, and pipelined parameter delivery, gradient aggregation, and CPU updates.
Combines an analytical step-time model with runtime measurements to tune communication, chunking, and activation policies under GPU memory limits.
Reports 1.46–2.64× geometric-mean throughput over SlideFormer, MegaTrain, and ZeRO-Offload in matched-batch sweeps.
Supports Qwen3-14B on four H100s, including over 1M tokens per step and 256K-token sequences, and fine-tunes Qwen2.5-72B on four RTX 4090s.

papers.abstract: We introduce the Long-Short-Range Neural Network (LSR-Net), a novel neural operator architecture designed for data-driven forward evolution modeling, and extends it to the prediction of nonlinear fluid dynamics. LSR-Net learns the evolution operator of a dynamical system solely from pairs of initial and future state snapshots, which splits the learnable integral kernel into long-range (LR) and short-range (SR) components within stacked network blocks. While the SR component uses standard convolutions to capture local dynamics, the LR component employs a sum-of-exponentials (SOE) representation. This allows for the efficient computation of global interactions as a trainable Fourier multiplier, reducing computational complexity to $O(n \log n)$ where $n$ is the number of pixels in an input snapshot and requiring only a few parameters per channel. LSR-Net is evaluated on three challenging 2D benchmarks: the coupled Burgers equation, the wave equation with a spatially varying coefficient, and the nonlinear shallow water equation {(SWE)}. Results demonstrate that LSR-Net significantly outperforms the baseline short-range network (SR-Net) as well as FNO and DeepONets in predictive accuracy, achieving substantially lower relative errors by effectively capturing both local fine-scale structures and crucial global pattern interactions.
authors: Qian Hou
Sutrisno
Yuqing Li
Zecheng Gan
bullets: Learns a dynamical system’s forward evolution operator directly from initial and future state snapshots.
Splits the kernel into short-range components modeled with convolutions and long-range components represented by sum-of-exponentials.
Computes global interactions via a trainable Fourier multiplier with O(n log n) complexity and few parameters per channel.
Evaluated on coupled Burgers, variable-coefficient wave, and nonlinear shallow water equations.
Outperforms SR-Net, FNO, and DeepONets in relative predictive error by capturing both fine-scale local structure and global patterns.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Architecture of LSR-Net. Starting from the input snapshot at t = 0, the network applies M stacked LSR-Net blocks to predict the system state at time t = T . Each block combines long-range (LR) and short-range (SR) learnable integral kernels followed by nonlinear activation functions. The LR convolution is efficiently computed in Fourier space using the proposed sum-of-exponentials (SOE) kernel representation. A residual connection is introduced in each block to improve training stability.

Fig. 4. Prediction comparison for the nonlinear shallow water system. The system contains three variables: the height field h and the velocity components u and v. The four columns in each subfigure represent the initial condition, the ground truth at t = T , the predicted solution, and the absolute prediction error.

The first two rows correspond to the results produced by LSR-Net, while the last two rows correspond to SR-Net.

The wave field u is a scalar variable, while the wave speed c(x, y) varies spatially, which makes the prediction task more challenging. Each row corresponds to one neural operator model: the first row shows the results of LSR-Net and the second row shows the results of SR-Net. papers.abstract: Multimodal LLMs report strong performance on scientific reasoning benchmarks, yet most treat perception and reasoning as a single measurable process. We introduce a five-task diagnostic experiment across physics and geometry benchmarks that isolates failures to perception, reasoning, or both. Incorrect diagram interpretation degrades performance even on problems models solve correctly from text alone, and accuracy generally rises from raw images to human-authored captions. Recovery under corrected captions is high for some models, separating perception-blocked failures from genuine reasoning bottlenecks. Which reasoning error follows a perception failure depends on domain: physics failures resolve into calculation errors, geometry into conceptual misapplication. As a discussion beyond our core experiments, InternS1-mini, despite heavy scientific pretraining and thinking capabilities, falls below the weakest model from experiments on every task, with reasoning traces frequently truncating before completion.
authors: Raj Jaiswal
Sree Krishna Uppalapati
Dhruvkumar Patel
Ria Khatoniar
Tanuja Ganu
Rajiv Ratn Shah
bullets: Incorrect diagram interpretation harms performance even when models solve the same problems from text alone.
Human-authored captions generally improve accuracy over raw images.
Corrected captions reveal which failures are perception-blocked versus genuine reasoning failures.
Perception failures tend to become calculation errors in physics and conceptual misapplication in geometry.
InternS1-mini underperforms all evaluated models across tasks, often truncating its reasoning traces.↩

Figure 1: Perceptual Error Cascade across Physics (left) and Geometry (right). Each panel traces a single model failure through all three perception error types in our taxonomy: a Description Error (wrong identification of a diagram element) triggers an Explanation Error (incorrect domain reasoning built on the false premise), which produces a Value Error (a wrong quantity that invalidates the final answer). Refer section for more details (§ 3)

CQ* underperforms CQ as minimal geometry questions provide insufficient context, leading to hallucination. CQ accuracy remains consistently low across model scales, indicating that diagram misinterpretation persists regardless of model size. Representative examples in Appendix E.

Table 1: Overall Accuracy (%), Averaged Across Five Models. Per-benchmark accuracy across four diagnostic tasks, averaged over all five evaluated models (§4.3, §7). Accuracy improves as visual grounding improves.

Table 4: Perception–Reasoning Error Interaction (%). Unlike physics, InternS1-mini in geometry truncation is lower, exposing the true incorrect rate; combined with 30% truncation, total failure exceeds 95% on every task.

InternS1-mini (deeper yellow) falls below Gemma-3 27B (light yellow), the weakest standard model, on every task despite explicit scientific pretraining and extended thinking capacity.

Table 2: Comparison with Prior Work. Prior work covers at most three of the five axes; this work is the first to address all five jointly (§4.3). Partial = limited coverage; † = symbolic diagram parsing, not neural visual encoding.

papers.selection_reason: Diagnoses perception vs reasoning failures in multimodal physics and geometry reasoning, directly relevant to MLLMs and spatial intelligence.
papers.title: Lost in Perception: Isolating Perceptual and Reasoning Failures in Multimodal Physics and Geometry Reasoning
papers.tldr: A five-task diagnostic shows that multimodal physics and geometry errors often stem from diagram perception, while remaining failures reflect domain-specific reasoning bottlenecks.

papers.abstract: How many dimensions does a language model's computation actually use? The question is ill-posed until one names a functional. Task-weighted charts make it well-posed: low-dimensional coordinate systems fit against a chosen functional of the representation, under the functional's own metric, turning distillation into plain least squares. Across six models from three families, spanning 70m to 7B parameters, next-token prediction needs 70--90% of the residual stream's width to stay within 5% of intact perplexity, a width consumed by the rare tail of language, and the variance profile predicts none of it: two directions carry 90% of GPT-2's activation variance and almost none of its function. Dimension is per-functional: the model's own uncertainty reads from six coordinates where the full predictive distribution needs hundreds; and it grows with depth. The dissociation is exploitable: when only a few dimensions can be kept, charts trained under the functional's metric preserve the model's predictions better than variance-based or optimal linear compression.
authors: Alexandre Quemy
bullets: Next-token prediction requires 70–90% of residual-stream width to remain within 5% of intact perplexity across six models.
The needed dimensions are driven by the rare tail of language, not dominant activation-variance directions.
Two directions explain 90% of GPT-2’s activation variance but capture almost none of its predictive function.
Dimensionality depends on the functional: model uncertainty uses six coordinates, while the full predictive distribution needs hundreds, and dimensionality grows with depth.
Functional-metric charts preserve predictions better than variance-based or optimal linear compression when dimensions are limited.

Figure 8: The chart pipeline. papers.selection_reason: Task-weighted low-dimensional charts compress LM representations while preserving function, relevant to efficient AI and LLM analysis.
papers.title: Function Lives Where Variance Doesn't: Task-Weighted Charts of a Language Model's Computation
papers.tldr: Task-weighted charts reveal that a language model’s functional computation is often high-dimensional and poorly predicted by activation variance.

papers.abstract: Linear RNNs with input-dependent Householder-product transitions (DeltaNet/DeltaProduct-class) can provably represent hard state-tracking automata, yet trained models fail to length-generalize -- a gap recent work attributes to optimization, without a causal account. We give one, in a pre-registered, within-architecture causal ablation: the same model with one term deleted -- the additive input injection $b_t = W_b e_t$. With $b_t$, models fit length 32 and collapse out-of-distribution on parity, $S_4$, $A_5$, and non-solvable $S_5$ word problems (0.20 at position 512 on $S_5$). Without it -- input acting only through the orthogonal transitions -- the same architecture learns the exact automaton: median accuracy 1.00 at 16x the training length, at every width admitted by a representation law we state and test: the minimal number of Householder factors per token equals the maximal reflection length of the task's generators in the format-pinned representation (parity 1, $S_4$ 3, $A_5$ and $S_5$ 4); below it, nothing fits. The contrast with DeltaProduct's $S_4$/$A_5$ at $n_h{=}2$ (group-element classification, $SO(3)$ realization) shows the law is representation-relative: task format is a hidden variable in state-tracking benchmarks. Two pre-registered arms locate the mechanism. (i) Initialized at a verified-exact solution with $W_b{=}0$, Adam grows the additive path and pulls the model off the exact solution; $-b$ controls stay at 1.00. (ii) Our registered prediction that the fit routes through $b_t$ fired its kill criterion: all 49 fitting seeds retain in-domain fit under $W_b{:=}0$ -- and at law-minimal width, zeroing $W_b$ at inference restores exact generalization (parity 5/5, $S_5$ 5/5, $S_4$ 4/5, $A_5$ 4/5). The additive pathway is parasitic: it destabilizes, then conceals, a correctly learned automaton. All 202 runs pre-registered; all numbers regenerate from artifacts.
authors: Gunner Levi Howe
bullets: Adding $b_t=W_b e_t$ lets models fit short sequences but causes out-of-distribution collapse on parity and permutation-group tasks.
Removing the additive pathway yields exact automaton behavior, with median accuracy 1.00 at 16× the training length.
Generalization requires a task- and representation-dependent number of Householder factors: 1 for parity, 3 for $S_4$, and 4 for $A_5$/$S_5$.
Mechanistic ablations show Adam grows the additive path away from exact solutions, while zeroing it preserves or restores exact generalization.
The findings indicate that benchmark task format is a hidden variable and that the additive pathway can conceal a correctly learned automaton.
